A number of federations have cast doubt over whether it can proceed as planned. Two days ago, the president of Japan’s football federation, Tsuneyasu Miyamoto, said: “Based on what I’ve learnt from the news, the situation is still unsafe, so at this point, I don’t think it would be easy to hold the [Asian] Cup there.” The organisers have acknowledged postponing the tournament is an option if required. But they also signalled preparations are going ahead as planned, as the schedule for the competition was confirmed on Monday morning.

title: Why Dems’ late House reaches don’t usually pan out
body: House Democrats are pushing into redder and redder territory. History shows those last-minute moves don’t usually pan out, even in favorable cycles. Since 2018, Democrats haven’t flipped any Republican-held seat that was added to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee’s “Red to Blue” list in the September or October before Election Day, according to a POLITICO analysis. Of the 28 total candidates from 2018 to 2024 that were added in the final two months of the campaign, just three Democrats won — all in Democratic-held open seats. That’s a much lower rate than average Red to Blue performance. Out of 203 candidates added to the program in the four previous cycles, 73 flipped their seats. That’s not a shock: The DCCC tends to add the biggest reaches later as it moves through the cycle, both to make sure its best opportunities are funded first and have enough attention and to try to create a sense of momentum and map expansion for donors and the media. In fact, the DCCC used some of the seats in their latest round of additions in a recent fundraising plea sent out by Executive Director Julie Merz, who warned that without more cash the committee “could be leaving winnable races on the table.” But it illuminates how hard it is — even in the best of environments — to reach deep into red territory in order to flip House seats. And it’s especially true now, as the House battlefield has shrunk significantly since 2018 because of gerrymandering. Since the beginning of September, the DCCC has added nine Democrats to Red to Blue: independent Bill Hill in AK-AL; Will Lawrence in MI-07; Mitchell Berman in WI-01; Chris Jones in AR-02; Dwayne Romero in CO-03; Eliott Rodriguez in FL-27; Teresa Benitez-Thompson in NV-02; Blake Gendebien in NY-21; and Justin Pearson in TN-09. Democrats acknowledge these late additions are a low-percentage play. Former DCCC staffer Cole Leiter, who worked there for the 2018 and 2020 cycles, said the committee recruits and tracks reach-district candidates early in the cycle with hopes the political winds will shift their way. “That is an investment in the unpredictability of the map,” Leiter said. “Most of these seats probably won’t flip, but one or two might.” Regardless of whether or not Democrats ultimately win the seats they’ve added late this year (the DCCC added six deep-red targets to Red to Blue in early October) — the additions alone contribute to a narrative of a party on offense. And they can also be a boon for fundraising for those specific candidates as well as to entice donors with exactly which areas their dollars will go if they pony up. “Even if there's ultimately not a massive success rate in those final editions, it is not a bad thing to make sure that those campaigns have any last-minute dollars that the designation can bring,” said Meredith Kelly, a former DCCC staffer who worked the 2016 and 2018 cycles. “Just make sure that they have a surfboard in the water and have an ability to potentially take advantage of a really, really good night.” This cycle’s late-add Democrats are almost all facing cash disadvantages against their incumbent GOP opponents. Of the nine Democrats added within the past two months, only one — Benitez-Thompson, running against Republican David Flippo — has reported more cash on hand than their opponent. Five of them are facing fundraising deficits of over $1 million, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Democrats’ poor record in these seats is somewhat self-selecting — seats added to the program late in the cycle reflect the fact that Democrats weren’t initially convinced they could be flipped. Whitney Fox, who lost by 9 points to GOP Rep. Anna Paulina Luna in FL-13 in 2024 and was among the last Democrats to be added to Red to Blue when she was picked in late September, said her campaign suffered from the delay in adding her to the program, even as she acknowledged the DCCC is forced to make strategic decisions with limited resources. The late additions also limit the window that candidates can capitalize on the program’s benefits. After initially being told she wouldn’t be added and after what she said was months of making her case to the DCCC, Fox made the list just before Hurricane Milton devastated the Tampa area, which she said made it difficult to fundraise off her newly minted Red to Blue status. “I felt like it was too little, too late,” she said. The Democrat running against Luna this cycle, Leela Gray, was added to Red to Blue in late August. Fox, who is informally advising local Florida candidates this cycle, said she offered Gray advice on how to make the list early. “I was a squeaky wheel trying to talk to leadership and Democratic members of Congress, and then it got to a certain point where I was no longer the squeaky wheel,” she said she relayed to Gray. “I was going to take the spoke off the wheel and hit people over the head with it.” Still the DCCC believes this cycle will be different, history be damned. And if recent national polling showing them with a double-digit lead in the generic ballot is correct, some of these late additions might break through. “Records are meant to be broken,” DCCC spokesperson Viet Shelton said in a statement. “We’re on track to break them this year because across the battlefield, we’ve got amazing recruits and the enthusiasm to fire House Republicans for making life unaffordable is off the charts.” A version of this article first appeared in POLITICO Pro’s Morning Score. Want to receive the newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro. You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.

title: Savannah Region prepares to enforce nationwide Styrofoam ban from January 2027
body: The Savannah Regional Minister, Salisu Be-Awuribe, has reaffirmed the region’s commitment to enforcing the nationwide ban on Styrofoam products from January 1, 2027, warning that the production, importation, distribution, sale and use of the products will no longer be permitted after the deadline. He said the enforcement forms part of the government’s efforts to protect the environment, improve public health, reduce flooding and preserve the region’s tourism potential. ‎ ‎The Minister made these remarks during a Styrofoam Ban Outreach programme, where he called on residents, traders, food vendors, manufacturers and business operators to prepare for the implementation of the policy. ‎ ‎Mr Be-Awuribe said the Savannah Regional Coordinating Council, the seven Metropolitan, Municipal and District Assemblies (MMDAs), the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the Ghana Police Service and customs officers at checkpoints would be expected to ensure strict compliance. ‎ ‎He further warned that vehicles transporting prohibited Styrofoam products would not be allowed into the region after the January 2027 deadline. ‎ ‎The Minister expressed concern over the growing use and improper disposal of Styrofoam takeaway containers in communities across the region, including Damongo, Bole, Sawla, Buipe, Salaga and Daboya. According to him, the products have become a major source of litter, with discarded takeaway containers choking gutters, obstructing drains and contributing to flooding. ‎ ‎He also warned that Styrofoam waste poses a threat to domestic animals and wildlife, particularly elephants at the Mole National Park, which could mistake the discarded materials for food. ‎ ‎He added that burning Styrofoam releases harmful smoke that can affect human health and pollute the environment. ‎ ‎The regional Minister also raised concerns about the potential health risks associated with placing hot foods in certain Styrofoam containers, stressing the need for safer food-packaging alternatives. The specific health risks, however, depend on the materials used and the conditions under which they are heated. ‎ ‎The Minister maintained that the region could not achieve its tourism ambitions while communities and roads remained littered with takeaway containers. ‎ ‎“Savannah Region cannot develop tourism with litter. No tourists will come to see Mole if the road from Fufulso to Damongo or from Bole to Mole is littered with takeaway containers,” he said. Recognising the potential financial challenges the ban could pose to food vendors and traders, the Regional Minister said the EPA’s Savannah Regional Office had been directed to engage stakeholders across markets and communities to educate them on affordable alternatives. ‎ ‎He identified paper packaging, biodegradable containers, reusable bowls and traditional food-wrapping materials as possible substitutes for Styrofoam products. ‎ ‎He, however, encouraged young people in the region to take advantage of the policy by investing in the production and supply of environmentally friendly packaging materials. ‎ ‎He said government programmes, including those operated by the Ghana Enterprises Agency (GEA) and the Youth Employment Agency (YEA), could provide opportunities for young entrepreneurs interested in developing local alternatives. ‎ ‎Hon. Be-Awuribe further indicated that the government was working to reduce the cost of paper packaging by supporting local factories. ‎ ‎He urged traders and food vendors to cooperate with the authorities during the transition, emphasising that education and partnership would be prioritised over punishment. ‎ ‎As part of preparations for the enforcement deadline, the Minister announced a regional clean-up and public education campaign to run from October through December 2026. The campaign will target chop bars, restaurants, hotels, guest houses, shops, plastic retailers, schools, lorry stations and other businesses and public spaces. ‎ ‎Mr Salisu Be-Awuribe revealed that EPA would engage affected groups in local languages to ensure that residents understand the reasons for the ban, the products affected and the alternatives available. ‎ ‎The Minister cautioned that offenders could face sanctions under the applicable environmental laws, referring to fines of up to GH¢50,000 or imprisonment of up to two years, as outlined in his address. ‎ ‎”The government’s primary objective was to secure voluntary compliance rather than impose penalties on individuals and businesses. ‎ ‎“I do not want any individual, groups, institutions, or businesses to be fined. I want TOTAL compliance through partnership and understanding,” the Minister reiterated ‎ ‎He recalled that President John Dramani Mahama publicly announced the policy on World Environment Day, June 5, 2025, and subsequently declared nationwide enforcement from January 2027 on May 25, 2026. ‎ ‎He described the ban as an important step towards improving environmental cleanliness and protecting communities from the consequences of improper waste disposal. ‎ ‎Mr Be-Awuribe also highlighted the Savannah Region’s importance as Ghana’s largest region by land area, its contribution to food production in northern Ghana and its tourism assets, particularly the Mole National Park. ‎ ‎He called on traditional authorities, local government officials, civil society organisations, the media, traders and the general public to support the initiative. ‎ ‎The Minister concluded by urging residents to take collective responsibility for maintaining a clean environment, declaring that a cleaner region would contribute to better health, stronger tourism and improved economic opportunities. ‎ ‎“Clean Savannah, healthy Savannah, rich Savannah,” he said, calling on residents to work together to keep the region clean. ‎ ‎The outreach programme forms part of efforts to intensify public education ahead of the January 1, 2027 enforcement deadline, as authorities seek to prepare businesses and residents for the transition away from Styrofoam products.

title: Egypt in daily contact with Iran, US to prevent new escalation, top diplomat says
body:
CAIRO, October 26. /TASS/. Egypt negotiates with Iran and the United States as well as regional partners on a daily basis to avoid another escalation of tensions, Egyptian Minister of Foreign Affairs Badr Abdelatty said.
"Every day, we talk with the Iranians, the Americans and our regional partners to prevent a transition to a new bout of military escalation," Egypt’s top diplomat said at a joint news conference with US Secretary-General Antonio Guterres in the Arab republic’s new capital, as broadcast by the Al-Qahera Al-Ekhbariya television channel. "Military methods would not guarantee a long-lasting result of stability," Abdelatty emphasized as he called on both sides to return to the negotiating table.
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28. In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding providing for an immediate cessation of hostilities on all fronts, including in Lebanon. However, in the early morning hours of July 8, the US resumed large-scale strikes against Iran, accusing it of violating the terms of the agreements reached on the Strait of Hormuz.
On October 24, US President Donald Trump hinted that he might decide to launch new strikes against Iran if Washington and Tehran fail to reach a deal. On the next day, however, he ruled out immediate military action against the Islamic Republic for the time being.

title: Russia, Ethiopia to discuss visa facilitation for tourists, businessmen — Russian envoy
body:
MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. Russia and Ethiopia intend to explore the prospects for continuation of gradual facilitation of the visa regime for tourists and businessmen on a reciprocal basis, Russian Ambassador to Ethiopia Yevgeny Terekhin said in an interview with TASS ahead of the Russia-Africa summit.
"The question of continuation of gradual liberalization of the entry regime will be addressed depending on growth of reciprocal tourist flows and bilateral business contacts," he said.
The visa-free travel regime based on the relevant intergovernmental agreement for holders of diplomatic and service passports remains in place, the diplomat said. "Russian citizens holding standard international passports can either apply for an electronic visa or obtain a visa upon arrival in Ethiopia at the Addis Ababa airport," he added.

title: Saudi Maritime & Logistics Congress highlights maritime integration and growth opportunities in the Kingdom
body: The Saudi Maritime & Logistics Congress opened at Jeddah Superdome, bringing together government entities and industry leaders to highlight the Kingdom’s role in supply chain resilience as shifts in shipping prompt companies to reassess routes and investments. In his opening address, HE Eng Fawaz bin Zunaf Al Sahli, President of the Transport General Authority (TGA), affirmed that the Kingdom’s ambitions extend beyond ports to building an integrated transport and logistics system that reinforces its position as a trusted trade partner, noting the importance of integrating maritime and land transport. Discussions addressed Suez Canal developments, alternative shipping routes and stronger port connectivity to give cargo owners and operators greater flexibility. In this context, Mohaned El Mahgoub, Vice President at Tahaluf, said: “Bringing industry leaders together in Jeddah at this particular moment has become more important than ever. Companies are making immediate decisions about shipping routes, capacity and investments, and these decisions depend on building strong, trusted relationships across every link of the supply chain. The discussions at this year’s congress demonstrate how Saudi Arabia’s maritime and logistics capabilities are enabling companies to respond to disruption and strengthening their confidence in the routes and services they rely on. The Kingdom’s strength lies in its ability to unify these capabilities, adapt flexibly to challenges and pressures, and ensure that global trade continues to flow smoothly.” Eng Essam AlAmmari, Deputy for Maritime Transport at the Transport General Authority, said: “Developing the maritime transport sector is a fundamental pillar for enhancing supply chain resilience, improving trade connectivity and supporting the continued flow of goods across regional and international markets.” He added: “Saudi Arabia’s strategic geographic location, linking major maritime trade corridors across three continents, provides a strong foundation for expanding its role in global logistics. Our priority is to translate this advantage into greater operational efficiency, stronger international partnerships and sustainable growth in the maritime transport sector.” Participants discussed boosting transit cargo through the Kingdom to Gulf markets. Bahri, the National Shipping Company of Saudi Arabia, announced a collaboration with the University of Jeddah, while Faisal M Higgi & Associates Co Ltd unveiled its new trade name, FMH Marine Services. Technology sessions explored how automation and AI can improve vessel and truck scheduling and terminal use, while decarbonisation sessions covered biofuels, hybrid propulsion and carbon capture. Discussions also covered marinas’ role in tourism, with Oriel Blake, Marine Operations Director at Sela, highlighting specialised facilities for attracting superyachts. Rayana Al Ghamdi, Deputy General Manager at SAMACO Marine, said: “We aspire to offer more than just marina operations; we seek to support the full range of customer needs in the marine sector, from providing boats and after-sales services to marina facilities, while contributing to the sector’s growth in Saudi Arabia.” The congress continues with sessions on an integrated national logistics system and maritime competitiveness.

title: Alleged Phone-tapping: Court Rejects El-Rufai’s No-case Submission
body: The Federal High Court in Abuja on Monday dismissed a no-case submission filed by former Gov. Nasir El-Rufai of Kaduna State in his ongoing trial over alleged unlawful interception of the telephone communications of the National Security Adviser (NSA), Nuhu Ribadu. Justice Joyce Abdulmalik, in a ruling, held that the Department of State Services (DSS) had placed before the court sufficient evidence to warrant the court to call on the ex-governor to enter his defence if he so desires. The judge, therefore, ordered El-Rufai, the sole defendant in the charge, to enter his defence. The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that the the defendant had opted for a no-case submission after the DSS closed its case by calling two witnesses. El-Rufai, through his counsel, Akinyemi Aremu, had urged the court to hold that the prosecution had failed to establish a case requiring the former governor to enter a defence. In response, the DSS lawyer, Oluwole Aladedoye, SAN, adopted their counter affidavit in opposition to the no-case submission. Aladedoye argued that the defence failed to address Exhibit “B”, which the prosecution said contained El-Rufai’s alleged admission concerning the tapping of Ribadu’s phone. He submitted that since the prosecution had established a prima facie case against El-Rufai, the defendant was required by law to enter his defence.(NAN)

title: Lebanese widow can be pursued for husband's role in $2bn corruption scandal
body: A court has cleared the way for Mozambique to pursue the widow of a Lebanese tycoon for compensation for his role in a $2 billion corruption scandal. The African nation sued Iskandar Safa and his shipbuilding company Privinvest in 2023 at the High Court in London over what has come to be known as the “tuna bonds” scandal. Mozambique alleged Privinvest and Mr Safa paid more than $136 million in bribes to officials and bankers to secure favourable terms for contracts, including one designed to exploit the nation’s tuna-rich coastal waters. Mozambique agreed to guarantee the loans under contracts which were governed by English law, so the dispute has been heard at the High Court in London. Privinvest sold fishing boats, patrol vessels, and equipment to the state at vastly inflated prices after paying bribes. But Mozambique was saddled with a $2 billion debt, which brought the country's economy to its knees when the scandal came to light. Mr Safa gave evidence in the High Court proceedings when he was seriously ill with cancer. He died in January 2024, aged 68. In December 2024, a judge ordered Privinvest to pay $534 million plus interest of $40 million to Mozambique. Another judge allowed Mozambique to add Mr Safa’s widow, Clara Martinez Thedy de Safa, to the claim. This was on the basis that Mr Safa had not left a legally valid will. Under Lebanese law, the next of kin automatically assumes both the assets and debts of the deceased. Ms Safa appealed against that decision and her barrister, Robert Howe KC, told a hearing in July this year that she had no knowledge or involvement in any of her husband’s wrongdoing. Mr Howe argued that in law an English court should not accept jurisdiction over claims against a person acting as the administrator of an overseas estate. Such claims are exclusively for the courts of that country, he said. Her legal team also relied on a rule that prevents a person administering a deceased person's estate under foreign law from being sued in England and Wales. But in his ruling, Lord Justice Miles said that under Lebanese law, “there is no concept of an estate”, similar to the UK, and “the inheritance by an heir of the assets is automatic and immediate on death. The deceased’s creditors are exposed to the risk that the deceased’s assets may be mixed up with the heir’s own assets,” he said. As such, the claim against Mrs Safa was against her personally and could be heard in an English court, so her appeal was dismissed, said the judge. The actual sum that Mrs Safa inherited, or for which she is liable, has yet to be established and will be determined at future hearings. Last year, Mozambique’s former finance minister Manuel Chang was sentenced to nearly two years in jail in the US and ordered to pay back $7 million for his role in the “tuna bonds” scandal. The country was left with a fleet of 24 rusting fishing vessels, which were eventually auctioned off. According to his obituary in The Times , Mr Safa was born into a prosperous Maronite Christian family in 1955. He obtained an engineering degree from the American University of Beirut in 1978. Mr Safa fought with a Christian militia in the country’s civil war. He studied in France and also worked as an engineer in Saudi Arabia. With his brother Akram, he founded Privinvest, which specialises in warships, commercial vessels and mega yachts. His contacts in the Middle East led him to become involved in negotiating the release of French hostages held by Hezbollah.

title: Canada Receives Its First Two CF-35A Fighters at Luke Air Force Base
body: The first two Canadian CF-35s arrived at Luke Air Force Base, where they will be used for training in support of the initial phase of the RCAF’s transition from the CF-188 Hornet to the Lightning II. The Royal Canadian Air Force has received its first two CF-35A Lightning II fighters, a month after the maiden flight of the first . The aircraft arrived at Luke Air Force Base, Arizona, on Oct. 22, 2026, where they will support the initial phase of the country’s F-35 program. The RCAF announced the arrival in a post on its official X account on Oct. 23, saying the two aircraft had arrived at the U.S. Air Force base the previous day. The service also highlighted the importance of personnel and other supporting elements in building its future air and space power capabilities, beyond the acquisition of new equipment. We are developing the skilled people, integrated capabilities, and modern tools we need to meet future challenges at home and abroad. — Royal Canadian Air Force (@RCAF_ARC) October 23, 2026 These two aircraft are the first of Canada’s planned F-35A fleet, which will eventually replace the CF-188 Hornet as the backbone of the RCAF’s fighter fleet. Their arrival begins a new phase in Canada’s controversial transition to the fifth-generation fighter, although several steps remain before the first aircraft will be based in Canada. Initial Training at Luke Air Force Base The first two Canadian F-35As have arrived at Luke Air Force Base, Arizona, a major international training hub for F-35 pilots and maintenance personnel. The base hosts the 56th Fighter Wing of the U.S. Air Force and supports the training of roughly 75 percent of the world’s F-35 pilots. The F-35 training pipeline focuses heavily on sensor fusion management, network-centric warfare, electronic warfare, and low-observable tactics to master operations in contested, high-threat environments. The 9-month curriculum integrates 300 academic hours, 100 simulator sorties, and 80 live flying hours. The first Canadian F-35A Lightning II takes off for the maiden flight.l can | Source: Gherardo and Victoria Fontana The initial aircraft will support the establishment of Canada’s F-35 capability, including the training of pilots and ground personnel. Operating the aircraft in the United States allows the RCAF to take advantage of existing training infrastructure and expertise while the Department of National Defense completes the necessary infrastructure to support aircraft delivery in Canada. The first aircraft to be delivered on home soil in Canada is expected in 2028, with a planned Initial Operational Capability in 2029-2030. The government plans a Full Operational Capability in 2032-2034, with the F-35s continuing to serve beyond 2060. Canada and the F-35 Canada has been part of the F-35 program since 2002 as a Level 3 partner, however it did not immediately procure the 5th generation fighter jet. The government selected in 2022 the F-35A Lightning II for its Future Fighter Capability Project (FFCP) launched in 2017, which aims to replace the Royal Canadian Air Force’s fleet of legacy CF-188 Hornets (local designation of the F/A-18). A year later, the country finalized the agreement to acquire 88 fighter jets with an estimated investment of $19 billion. The government said this procurement represents the most significant investment in the RCAF in more than 30 years. Two CF-188 Hornet jets, 425 Tactical Fighter Squadron, fly in formation with four F-16 fighting falcon aircraft, 120th Fighter Squadron, from Buckley Air Force Base, Colorado, on September 20, 2020, over the skies of Labrador during a NORAD Arctic Air Defense Operation being hosted by 5 Wing Newfoundland, Labrador. | Source: RCAF/Master Corporal Krista Blizzard In March 2025, following the tensions between Canada and the U.S., Canada’s then Defense Minister Bill Blair told reporters that discussions were ongoing about what best serves the country’s defense needs. Blair hinted that the plan to acquire the F-35 could change, with future purchases potentially involving European suppliers. Later on, in October 2025, the government said it would get at least the 16 jets Canada already paid for. The Secretary of State for Defense Procurement Stephen Fuhr said he “doesn’t think the federal government plans to get out of its contract to buy American-made F-35 fighter jets as 16 planes are currently being manufactured.” A spokesperson later added that “Canada is contractually obligated to 16 aircraft, which are in various stages of production with the manufacturer. A decision on the full program is currently under review.” According to the publicly shared timeline , Canada expected the first F-35 to be delivered by the end of 2026. The now-delivered aircraft will stay at Luke Air Force Base in Arizona, to enable the training of Royal Canadian Air Force pilots while the Department of National Defense completes the necessary infrastructure to support aircraft delivery in Canada. The first aircraft to be delivered on home soil in Canada is expected in 2028, with a planned Initial Operational Capability in 2029-2030. The government plans a Full Operational Capability in 2032-2034, with the F-35s continuing to serve beyond 2060.

title: Nigeria needs 9% annual growth to reduce poverty – Soludo
body: Governor Chukwuma Soludo of Anambra says Nigeria needs an annual economic growth of at least nine per cent to significantly reduce poverty and create jobs. He made the assertion at the Nigerian Economic Summit 32 (NES32) with the theme “Growth that Works: Delivering Jobs, Productivity and Shared Prosperity” in Abuja on Monday. He said that Nigeria’s current growth rate of about four per cent remained inadequate to achieve rapid poverty reduction and employment generation. The governor also said that Nigeria would require an annual growth of at least 12 per cent to achieve a one-trillion-dollar economy by 2030 or 2040. He added that the country’s investment rate, estimated at 17 to 20 per cent, must rise significantly to support the required economic expansion. Soludo cautioned against being misled by large nominal spending figures, saying that consolidated public expenditure across all government levels amounted to less than one dollar per person daily. He stressed the need to channel national savings into productive investments, capable of expanding economic output, creating jobs and improving living standards. He called for stronger coordination between the federal government, states and local governments, noting that subnational authorities accounted for a substantial share of public spending. According to him, effective collaboration is essential to maximise the impact of government policies and investments across the country. Soludo cited Anambra’s free education programme, which covers kindergarten through secondary school, as an example of interventions delivering measurable social benefits. He said that the state had reduced its out-of-school children rate from 2.5 per cent to 0.25 per cent. He also cited a recent Oxford and United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) report which reportedly placed Anambra’s multidimensional poverty rate at 9.6 per cent. Soludo said that reducing food prices required structural reforms to address post-harvest losses, which he put at about 43 per cent of agricultural output. He said that improving storage, transportation and distribution systems would help to move food from farms to urban markets and reduce consumer prices. The governor, therefore, urged governments to strengthen sectoral collaboration and mobilise investments to accelerate economic growth. Soludo also called for policies that encourage exports, develop domestic value chains and promote investment in sectors where Nigeria has competitive advantages. He emphasised that stronger private-sector participation and productive investments were essential to generating sustainable jobs and ensuring that economic growth benefitted more Nigerians. title: Iraq's government struggling amid threats of rebellion, protests, rising Iran tensions - analysis
body: Iraq's government is facing a growing challenge in the country's Maysan province along its Iranian border, where local officials have threatened civil disobedience over the closure of a key border crossing. The dispute comes amid tensions between Baghdad and Tehran and renewed protests in the Iraqi capital marking the anniversary of the 2019 Tishreen movement.The developments are pushing Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi to make key decisions as he also has to deal with looming rumors of renewed war with Iran. Iran has turned Iraq into a frontline and has carried out around 1,600 attacks with drones, missiles, and local militias. Most attacks targeted US diplomatic facilities and Kurdish Iranian opposition groups. Nevertheless, Iran also wants the borders open.According to Rudaw, Zaidi ordered an investigation on Monday into Mustafa Daeer Mohammedawi, the head of Maysan's provincial council, after he threatened to block roads connecting the southeastern province with the rest of Iraq. Mohammedawi warned on Sunday that the province would resort to civil disobedience unless the Sheeb border crossing with Iran was reopened by Thursday.“If it is not opened, then the people of Maysan province will be forced to resort to civil disobedience on all roads,” Mohammedawi said, according to Rudaw. He warned that Maysan could be effectively cut off from the rest of the country.The crossing, known as Chazabeh in Iran and Sheeb in Iraq, is an important commercial route between the two countries. Baghdad closed it last Wednesday, citing the need to improve its technical and logistical infrastructure. Iraq government spokesperson Haidar al-Aboudi said the crossing lacked the necessary technical and technological preparations. Iraqi officials have also raised concerns about smuggling through the crossing. The wider story is likely related to Iranian influence on Iraq. It appears militias used an area near the crossing to target Saudi Arabia in September.Iraq-Iran border closing enables review of securityAn Iraqi border official told Reuters that the closure would enable authorities to review security arrangements and install detection equipment to prevent the smuggling of prohibited materials. Meanwhile, Abdul Amir Hassan Ali al-Taiban, an adviser to the Iraqi prime minister, claimed that drugs and currency were entering southern Iraq through crossings with Iran. Iraq referenced “uncontrolled groups,” which may be a euphemism for Iranian-backed militias.Iran's embassy in Baghdad rejected these allegations on Saturday, describing them as false and calling on Iraqi authorities to respond to statements that could damage bilateral relations. Maysan is a Shiite-majority province in southeastern Iraq. Its capital, Amarah, is an important commercial center near the Iranian border. The province's location makes cross-border trade particularly significant for the local economy.According to Rudaw, protesters gathered near the Sheeb crossing, including truck drivers whose livelihoods depend on trade with Iran. They claim they want to use the crossing for trade and regular reasons. Iraq appears to be facing pressure to keep the crossing closed.Mohammed Jassim al-Khafaji, an Iraqi lawmaker, questioned whether Zaidi had the legal authority to investigate an elected provincial council chairman. According to Rudaw, Khafaji argued that only the provincial council could remove its chairman through a majority vote.This has wider implications for the Iranian-backed militias in Iraq. The Islamic Resistance in Iraq, an umbrella organization of pro-Iran armed groups, has accused the Iraqi government of yielding to Washington's demands regarding border crossings and flights involving Iran.Iraq sees demonstrations tied to Tishreen protest movementAt the same time, Iraq is witnessing renewed demonstrations connected to the Tishreen protest movement that began in October 2019. Protesters gathered in Baghdad on October 25. It's worth recalling that in 2019 the Iranian-backed militias suppressed these protests and killed hundreds of people. The Badr Organization was one of the Iranian-backed groups accused of a role in suppressing the protests.Shafaq News also reported on the demonstrations, noting that participants waved Iraqi flags and called for political and economic reforms. The Tishreen movement represented a major popular protest movement. Beginning in Baghdad and southern Iraq, the protests were driven largely by young Shiite Iraqis frustrated with corruption, unemployment, poor services, and the influence of political factions.The demonstrators also opposed the system of sectarian political quotas known as muhasasa, which distributes political positions and resources among Iraq's major communities.According to figures cited by Rudaw from rights organizations, more than 600 protesters were killed, approximately 20,000 were injured, and around 3,000 were arrested during the movement. Badr leader Hadi al-Amiri, a senior figure in the Shiite-led Coordination Framework, recently defended the role of Iranian-backed armed groups in confronting the Tishreen movement. According to Rudaw, Amiri described the protests as “sedition” and said the Islamic Resistance in Iraq had helped preserve the political order. “The [Islamic] resistance [in Iraq] stood courageously against the Fitna [sedition] of Tishreen, maintaining the state and political order in the process,” he said at an event in late August. This shows how Iraq is divided between the militias and the ordinary people.For protesters, accountability for the violence of 2019 remains a central demand. They have been angered by Badr's appearance and its boasting of its role in killing Iraqis. Badr is the largest of the militias that are not sanctioned by the US. Most other groups, such as Kataib Hezbollah, are sanctioned as terrorist groups by Washington.Shafaq News quoted activist and journalist Muntadhar al-Zaidi, who called for accountability over the killing of protesters and criticized the concentration of political power and misuse of public wealth.According to Rudaw, the National House political party, which is associated with the Tishreen movement, called for peaceful demonstrations and reiterated demands to end corruption, reform the political system and bring weapons under state control.For Zaidi's government, the challenge is to demonstrate that state institutions can enforce the law, secure borders and respond to public demands without becoming hostage to competing political and armed factions. It remains to be seen if Iraq can free itself from Iran's influence and control.

title: Chris Brown given suspended jail sentence for London nightclub altercation
body:
Grammy-winning singer Chris Brown avoided prison time Monday after he was accused of injuring a music producer in a London nightclub in 2023 .
The 37-year-old singer was given an eight month sentence, suspended for 12 months.
Brown had faced up to three years in prison after pleading guilty to a count of affray in July for the attack on the dance floor of Tape, a private club in the swanky Mayfair neighborhood in February 2023.
Brown’s co-defendant, Omololu Akinlolu, who performs under the name Hoody Baby, also entered a guilty plea in July to a charge of affray, which is the use or threat of unlawful violence that leads someone to fear for their safety.
Akinlolu was given a four-month sentence, which will be suspended for 12 months, the judge said on Monday.
Before sentencing, Judge Tony Baumgartner told Brown, “I take account of your employment and long-established career in music. Your fame, commercial success and professional standing do not entitle you to special treatment. The law applies equally to everyone,” Variety reports .
Video footage played in court showed Brown having to be pulled away from the victim, his former friend Abraham Diaw, after striking him twice in the head with a bottle, according to The Associated Press.
“The repeated use of a glass bottle in that way, especially aimed at the head, was plainly dangerous, it carried the risk of delivering a more serious injury than was ultimately sustained,” Baumgartner said in Southwark Crown Court.
Baumgartner said Brown did not qualify for a custodial sentence because he pleaded guilty and there were several mitigating circumstances, including stable employment and charity work. The judge acknowledged Brown’s previous convictions but said he had maintained a clean record in recent years.
Shortly after sentencing, Brown shared a video to his Instagram Stories as he appeared to be in a car leaving court and gave a thumbs up to the camera.
In July, prosecutors dropped charges of assault, attempting to cause grievous bodily harm and having an offensive weapon in return for the guilty plea, according to Britain’s Crown Prosecution Service .
Brown was accused of launching an “unprovoked attack” on producer Diaw at the Tape nightclub in London in February 2023 while he was on tour.
Prosecutor Hannah Nicholls alleged that Brown struck Diaw several times with a tequila bottle and then punched and kicked him.
The attack was caught on surveillance camera in front of a club full of people, prosecutors said.
“This was a vicious and unprovoked attack by Brown and Akinlolu in a crowded nightclub where Brown used a glass bottle as a weapon to strike the victim’s head twice,” said Claire Campbell, senior crown prosecutor in CPS London South.
“This kind of violence is entirely unacceptable, and the Crown Prosecution Service will work tirelessly — with the police and partners across the criminal justice system — to pursue cases like this, and prove that no one is above the law,” Campbell added in a statement .
In July 2025, Brown entered pleas of not guilty to causing actual bodily harm and possessing an offensive weapon in a public place.
Akinlolu also pleaded not guilty to the charge of causing actual bodily harm, having previously denied attempting to inflict grievous bodily harm.
Brown was originally charged with a single count of causing grievous bodily harm after his arrest in May 2025 but prosecutors subsequently brought an indictment adding two counts: assault causing actual bodily harm and having an offensive weapon, a bottle.
The Sensational singer was released on US$6.7-million bail in May 2025, which allowed him to start his Breezy Bowl XX tour the following month.
Baumgartner said at the time that Brown could continue his tour, including several stops in the U.K., but would have to pay the bail to guarantee his appearance in court. The judge also said that Brown would be asked to forfeit the money if he breached bail conditions.
Brown’s bail conditions included surrendering his passport if he is not travelling on tour, living at a specific address known to the court, not contacting Diaw, not visiting the Tape nightclub where the incident took place and not applying for international travel documents.

title: Sybiha criticizes idea of ​​nominating Orbán for UN Secretary-General

title: Ex-Premier League star needs 50 stitches after German Shepherd attack
body: By Adegboyega Adeleye Former Premier League footballer Jermaine Pennant has revealed that he needed more than 50 stitches after a German Shepherd mauled his leg in north London, with his own dog intervening to help fight off the attacker. According to the BBC, the 43-year-old former Liverpool and Stoke City winger was walking his two dogs last week when the German Shepherd latched on to his right leg and refused to let go as he tried to protect his dog, King. Pennant said King eventually intervened and fought off the attacking dog, preventing what he described as a potentially horrific situation. “I tried to protect King but the dog got my leg, I was on the floor with the dog still attached with no sign of letting go, until King intervened as he didn’t know what was going on,” Pennant said. He told The Sun that he suffered four bite wounds and required more than 50 stitches after receiving hospital treatment. Although King sustained a small bite, Pennant said his dog was otherwise unharmed. He recalled feeling more concerned about King when he saw blood covering the animal, before realising it was not his. Pennant later shared a photograph on Instagram showing himself with his injured leg bandaged and King beside him on a sofa, describing the dog as his “hero” and thanking his partner, Mimmi Montgomery, for caring for them both. The former footballer also said he chose not to report the attack to the police. He did not provide further details about the German Shepherd or its owner. Pennant made 231 Premier League appearances during a 19-year playing career before retiring in 2018. He represented clubs including Liverpool and Stoke City and later became a football pundit for TalkSPORT. He joined Arsenal from Notts County in 1999 for £2.5 million at the age of 15, becoming the most expensive trainee in English football at the time. title: Russia Says Ukraine Has Repeatedly Struck Oleshky With Artillery, Drones Ahead of Local Ceasefire
body:
Russia's Defense Ministry on Monday accused Ukraine of repeatedly striking the Russian-controlled town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine with artillery and drones ahead of a planned local ceasefire this week, something it said had prevented the delivery of food and medicine and stopped people from leaving.
Ukraine and Russia said on Friday they had agreed to a ceasefire in Oleshky that would go into effect on Oct. 27, allowing for the delivery of aid and the evacuation of residents through humanitarian corridors.
Russia's Defense Ministry said in a statement on Monday that Ukraine had struck the town 18 times with artillery fire and carried out more than 120 drone attacks on it and the main roads around it in the week since Oct. 19.
Reuters could not independently verify that assertion, and there was no immediate response from Ukraine, which has in the past accused Russia of not letting aid in or people out of the town.
Also on Monday, the Kremlin said that the local humanitarian ceasefire agreed for Oleshky with the United States' help could set a precedent for similar ceasefires elsewhere in Ukraine.
The ceasefire comes as residents of the town, controlled by Russian forces since February 2022 and located close to the front line, have reported ​a deepening food crisis, with both sides accusing each other of blocking supplies.

title: Northern leaders must share blame for region’s backwardness – Gov Uba Sani
body: Kaduna State Governor, Uba Sani, has said political office holders in Northern Nigeria since 1999 must accept responsibility for the region’s developmental challenges, including its high number of out-of-school children. Sani made the remarks while defending President Bola Tinubu’s record in office, arguing that Northern leaders should not blame the current administration alone for problems that have persisted for decades. “I’m a northerner, and I’m telling you that anybody who held position, whether a governor, minister, senator, vice president, you should be ready to take blame,” he said. The governor cited figures on out-of-school children, stating that Nigeria had about 18 million children out of school as of 2023, with approximately 70 per cent living in Northern Nigeria. He questioned whether Tinubu, who assumed office in May 2023, should be held solely responsible for a crisis that predates his administration. Sani also disclosed that Kaduna State had about 550,000 out-of-school children when he assumed office in 2023, claiming that his administration had returned 300,000 of them to classrooms. He urged political leaders to move away from regional sentiments in their campaigns, insisting that voters should assess candidates based on their records in public office rather than their geographical origins. “The people of Northern Nigeria are very smart. You cannot come to them and tell them, ‘Vote for me because I’m a northerner.’ They will never vote for you. They can only vote for you based on your track record,” he said. The governor also highlighted federal road projects in the North-East and North-West as evidence of infrastructure development under Tinubu. According to him, more than 348 kilometres of roads had been completed in the North-East, while about 3,100 kilometres were under construction. He added that approximately 1,800 kilometres of the ongoing projects were nearing 90 per cent completion. In the North-West, Sani said more than 342 kilometres of roads had been completed, while another 1,042 kilometres were nearing 90 per cent completion. On education financing, the governor said more than 414,000 students from the North-West had benefited from the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND), with about N84 billion allocated to the region. He described the student loan scheme as an intervention for young people from low-income households who might otherwise struggle to finance their education. Sani further stressed the importance of technical and vocational education and training (TVET), saying skills development was essential to addressing unemployment and expanding opportunities for young people in Northern Nigeria. He maintained that education remained critical to the region’s development and urged political leaders to focus on policies and programmes that improve the lives of residents. title: From Survival to Scale: How fintech apps are rewiring Ghana’s MSME economy
body: With a $4.8 billion financing gap and over 90% of small businesses locked out of formal credit, a new generation of Ghanaian fintech platforms is building the digital rails that keep the economy’s backbone moving, and iSmart and Korba are showing how it’s done. Ghana’s micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) are not just a segment of the economy; they are the economy. They constitute over 90% of all registered businesses, contribute roughly 70% of Gross Domestic Product, and provide around 80% of total employment, with an estimated 1.7 million businesses employing about 8.5 million people. Yet for decades, this formidable engine has been running on a persistent and punishing constraint: access to finance. The Bank of Ghana (BoG) identifies an annual SME financing gap of approximately $4.8 billion, a chasm that has widened even as the country’s digital payment infrastructure has exploded. The paradox is striking. In June 2026 alone, mobile money platforms processed 954 million transactions valued at approximately GH¢493 billion, up more than 50% from the GH¢323 billion recorded a year earlier. Some 82% of all financial transactions in Ghana now happen digitally, supported by over 26 million active mobile money accounts. Ghana has built “extraordinary payment rails,” as BoG Second Deputy Governor Matilda Asante-Asiedu put it, but has “not yet built equally extraordinary credit rails”. Over 90% of SMEs still have zero access to formal credit. It is within this gap between the ubiquity of digital payments and the scarcity of digital credit that a quiet revolution is taking place. Ghanaian fintech companies are no longer simply moving money; they are building the operational, transactional, and trust infrastructure that allows MSMEs to professionalise, scale, and, eventually, become bankable. Two platforms in particular, iSmart and Korba, illustrate how solving unglamorous, ground-level problems is creating the conditions for broader economic participation. iSmart: Building the Full-Stack Digital Utility for the Small Enterprise Founded in Accra in 2015, iSmart International Ghana has evolved from a value-added services (VAS) provider into an ISO- and PCI-DSS-certified digital infrastructure company serving over 10,000 clients, from major banks and telecoms to small enterprises. Its proposition is not a single app but a suite of tools that meet MSMEs where they are: often on basic feature phones, often in rural areas, often without the luxury of time to learn complex software. At the heart of its MSME offering is iSmart Pay, a payment platform developed just over a year ago to help businesses receive and manage payments through three channels: mobile money, direct bank transfers, and the iSmart Pay wallet. For a market trader or a small retail shop, this eliminates the friction of maintaining separate merchant accounts for each network. For a growing enterprise, iSmart’s payment APIs and gateways provide the flexibility to integrate collections directly into their own operations. But iSmart’s deeper contribution lies in the unglamorous plumbing that keeps small businesses connected. Its USSD connectivity allows any MSME or its customers to check balances, pay bills, or access services by dialling a short code, no internet required. This “no internet, no problem” approach brings essential digital functions to millions who remain outside the smartphone economy. Meanwhile, its Customer Engagement Solutions (CESI) platform, which includes tools like Digitalk, CPaaS, and Grow, empowers telecoms, enterprises, and SMEs to manage and engage over 4.5 million subscribers across Africa, turning one-way transactions into ongoing commercial relationships. The strategic logic is clear. As research on fintech adoption among Ghanaian MSMEs has found, the perceived ease of use is the strongest driver of adoption, and the real competitive advantage emerges only when digital tools are deeply integrated into core business processes, yielding gains in cost efficiency, operational agility, and service differentiation. iSmart’s stack is designed for exactly that integration: a small business can start with bulk SMS for marketing, graduate to USSD for customer self-service, and layer on iSmart Pay for collections, all within a single, certified ecosystem. Korba: Restoring Trust and Turning Agents into Micro-Hubs If iSmart builds the broad infrastructure, Korba (operated by Halges) attacks two of the most visceral pain points facing Ghanaian businesses that accept digital payments: the fear of reversals and the struggle of mobile money agents to earn a sustainable living. Payment reversals have been a silent killer for Ghanaian merchants. A customer pays, the business releases the product, and then the customer reverses the transaction back into their wallet. Korba estimates that businesses across Ghana have lost “well over 10 million cedis” to this practice, with restaurants, delivery companies, retail shops, and online vendors bearing the brunt. KorbaPay was built to eliminate this vulnerability: when a customer pays through the platform, the funds stay with the business, and the customer cannot initiate a reversal from their end. For a small online vendor or a delivery startup operating on thin margins, this is not a feature; it is the difference between staying in business and closing shop. It restores the confidence necessary for digital commerce to function. At the same time, Korba has built a parallel solution for the army of mobile money agents and small business owners who form the last-mile distribution network of Ghana’s financial system. The Korba Agent app turns an ordinary smartphone into a point-of-sale (POS) terminal, allowing agents to offer a far wider range of services beyond basic cash-in and cash-out: airtime and data sales across all networks, utility bill payments for DStv, GOTV, StarTimes, ECG, and Ghana Water, insurance sales, and event ticketing, each earning instant commissions. For an agent whose income was previously limited to a narrow spread on mobile money transactions, this diversification can “significantly boost their income,” as the app’s own description puts it. Korba has also addressed the cost barrier. Its payment solution for businesses is priced at as low as 1.5% per transaction, with a cap for example, a fixed GHS 20 fee on transactions above GHS 3,000. This predictable, capped pricing structure is particularly important for higher-value MSME transactions, where percentage-based fees can erode already thin margins. The Wider Ecosystem and the Road Ahead iSmart and Korba are not isolated success stories. They are part of a maturing ecosystem that includes platforms like Oze, which combines digital bookkeeping with lending and has served over 10,000 SMEs and is remaking cross-border remittances; Fido, which has issued over $500 million in digital loans; and Hubtel, whose merchant payment and USSD products power tens of thousands of businesses. The Bank of Ghana is actively pushing this frontier, advancing open banking and open finance frameworks with the explicit goal of turning mobile money transaction records into usable credit histories. As Second Deputy Governor Asante-Asiedu argued, “This is not just background information. It is a credit record. We have simply not built the habit of reading it as such”. The challenges remain formidable: regulatory fragmentation, cybersecurity risks, data governance gaps, and inadequate digital infrastructure in some regions. But the direction of travel is unmistakable. The fintech applications that are transforming MSMEs in Ghana are not doing so by replicating traditional banking. They are doing it by embedding financial services into the daily workflows of small businesses through a USSD menu that works on any phone, a payment gateway that accepts whatever the customer has, an agent app that turns a kiosk into a multi-service hub, and a fraud-prevention layer that makes digital transactions safe enough to rely on. For Ghana’s 1.7 million MSMEs, the promise of fintech is not abstract. It is the ability to receive a payment without fear of reversal, to manage customer relationships without a technical team, and to build, transaction by transaction, the digital footprint that one day becomes a credit record. iSmart and Korba are proving that the most impactful innovation often looks less like a shiny new app and more like the invisible rails that allow the backbone of the economy to finally stand upright. – Kweku Hammond – Snr Sales & Marketing Consultant/ Faculty – Nova Business School Africa

title: Vučić’s Defeat Is Not Yet a Victory for Serbia’s European Future
body:
Aleksandar Vučić has lost the election, and Ukraine now has good reason to take a close look at who has won. For Serbia’s citizens, worn down by 14 years of rule under the former president’s Serbian Progressive Party, the Student List’s victory offers grounds for hope that they will finally be able to hold those who govern them to account.
For Ukrainians defending their country against Russian aggression every day, it also matters what the winners intend to do with the relationship Belgrade has built with Kyiv.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
With 98.8 percent of votes counted, the Centre for Free Elections and Democracy (CeSID), an independent Serbian election-monitoring organization, and Ipsos, the international polling company, project that the Student List will take around 140 of parliament’s 250 seats, enough to form a government on its own.
In a country where party membership has for years opened the doors of state institutions, that result matters enormously. The deaths of 16 people when the canopy of Novi Sad railway station collapsed turned a demand for accountability into a revolt against the way the country was governed. Citizens have every right to expect courts free from political pressure and close public scrutiny of how the state spends their money.
The scale of that change makes it all the more important to read carefully what the winners say about the world. The Student List brings together professors, doctors and other public figures chosen by students to represent them, yet there are no students among its candidates. Some very old political convictions sit alongside its youthful symbolism, particularly regarding Russia, Kosovo and Europe. That gives Moscow an opening to preserve its influence after the defeat of the man it has dealt with for so many years.
In these pages in August, I strongly supported Vučić’s decision to receive Volodymyr Zelensky in Belgrade. I stand by that position after his electoral defeat. Ties with a country defending itself against aggression retain their value after the politicians who built them leave office. Were we to undo every sound decision a government had made simply because its author had lost an election, Serbia’s foreign policy interests would endure no longer than an election campaign.
Vučić and Zelensky established regular contact and a working relationship that allowed them to discuss practical cooperation despite the deep differences between Belgrade and Kyiv over Moscow. After Vučić’s visits to Odesa in 2025 and Kyiv in July this year, Zelensky was officially welcomed in Belgrade on August 8. Their talks covered energy, railways, trade and Ukraine’s reconstruction. Each endorsed the other country’s European aspirations, and Serbia reaffirmed its respect for Ukraine’s territorial integrity.
Those talks have been accompanied by concrete aid. By February 2024, Serbia had allocated €3 million for Ukrainian children and €1.5 million for internally displaced people, sent 14 trucks carrying humanitarian aid and donated ambulances. It also sent equipment to help restore the electricity grid. In August this year, the Ukrainian presidency confirmed a further €2 million for the energy sector. For a country whose power stations and grid are under systematic Russian attack, such support has an immediate practical value.
There is also a military dimension, which Belgrade has spent years describing in guarded diplomatic language. As far back as June 2024, the Financial Times reported an estimate that around €800 million worth of Serbian ammunition had reached Ukraine through intermediaries since the invasion began. These were commercial exports via third countries. This year, Christopher Hill, the former US ambassador to Belgrade, described American support for the purchase of that ammunition and said those involved in Belgrade knew who the end user was.
Vučić’s policy towards Russia provided ample grounds for serious criticism, from his refusal to impose sanctions to his attendance at Putin’s parade in Moscow. His visit to Odesa ended with his refusal to sign a joint declaration calling for increased pressure on Russia. Even so, Ukrainian diplomacy managed to secure tangible benefits from that contradictory relationship. Zelensky had a duty to seek help wherever he could obtain it, including in Belgrade.
Parts of the Serbian opposition judged his visit chiefly by how much it might benefit Vučić. Srđan Milivojević, leader of the Democratic Party, which backed the Student List, argued that Vučić was using Zelensky to signal his usefulness to Berlin, expecting it in return to accept whatever election result he declared. This reduced the visit of a president whose country was under attack to a weapon in a domestic political feud, leaving Ukraine’s interests almost entirely out of the picture.
Milivojević is fully entitled to doubt Vučić’s motives. But I also expect a politician who presents his party as pro-European to recognize Ukraine’s needs. Zelensky is answerable to people who need ammunition, medicines and electricity, and every meeting that can secure such support is justified by his country’s needs. To demand that he tailor his diplomatic contacts to the mood of the Serbian opposition would reveal how little we understand the responsibilities of a president whose country is at war.
A protest letter signed by a hundred intellectuals in response to the visit displayed even more open hostility. Its signatories declared Zelensky chiefly responsible for the war, denied that Russia was the aggressor and warned that his visit threatened Serbia’s relations with Russia. That position effectively grants Moscow the right to decide whom Belgrade may receive. Appeals to Serbian dignity end, on this reasoning, in acceptance of Russian tutelage over Serbian diplomacy.
By that logic, the Ukrainian president should be held responsible both for the war Putin started and for the discomfort his visit causes Putin’s admirers. Ukrainians are expected to understand Serbia’s historical traumas, Russia’s security demands and other people’s electoral needs, while their own right to survive is subjected to endless political qualifications. It is hard to imagine greater moral arrogance than demanding that a people under bombardment spare the feelings of those who justify bombing them.
The Student List’s representatives must now show what approach to Ukraine they intend to turn into state policy. Their campaign statement of September 30 explicitly pledged that Serbia would continue to reject sanctions against Russia. University professor Radomir Saičić, a member of the Serbian Academy and one of the Student List’s most prominent figures, advocated “productive relations with Russia” during the campaign, invoking historical ties and energy needs. For Kyiv, those positions matter more than photographs of celebrations on Belgrade’s streets.
Historical ties deserve respect, and energy dependence demands serious efforts to reduce it. When used as permanent excuses for giving in to Moscow, they become instruments through which Russia maintains its advantage. The new government needs to explain what Serbia gains by making its European future dependent on the Kremlin’s mood, and how far it is prepared to limit cooperation with Ukraine for the sake of that relationship.
Invoking Kosovo makes that choice particularly difficult to defend. Ukraine has not recognized its independence, maintaining a position Belgrade regards as essential to its national interests. Russia, meanwhile, occupies Ukrainian territory and seeks to redraw borders by military force. Politicians who demand that the world respect Serbia’s territorial integrity have an added obligation to uphold the same principle for Ukraine, including Crimea and the other occupied regions.
The question for the winners is how much of the sovereignty they demand for Serbia they are prepared to recognize for Ukraine. The right to choose a government and determine a country’s future is the very basis of their electoral victory. Ukrainians are defending precisely that right against a state that denies their country’s existence. It would be a bitter outcome if politicians brought to office by citizens who had freed themselves from fear showed more sympathy for Putin’s demands than for the people he is subjecting to violence.
There is also a very practical question: who in the new majority will decide the course of those relations? Will ministers have the political backing to continue cooperating with Kyiv when the nationalist wing of their alliance objects? Will decisions on exports, humanitarian aid and diplomatic contacts serve Serbia’s interests, or the need to keep the peace among people who, until yesterday, were united by their opposition to Vučić?
The Kremlin can exploit precisely these divisions. All it needs to do is raise the political cost of every decision that helps Ukraine, present it as a betrayal of friendship with Russia and provoke disputes within the new government. Delaying contracts, halting deliveries or withdrawing from joint projects could then be presented as temporary concessions made to preserve unity. Ukrainians and Serbian citizens alike would bear the consequences, while Moscow secured the outcome it wanted.
For the pro-European members of the winning alliance, this is where they must face the responsibilities they could avoid during the campaign. They will have to state what cooperation with Ukraine they support and which decisions they regard as unacceptable. Invoking the movement’s diversity will quickly lose its force once they are voting on budgets, appointing ministers and making commitments to other countries. Every concession to Russian interests will then carry their names and be backed by their votes.
I expect Moscow to use Serbia’s relations with Ukraine to test how much influence it can exert over the new government in Belgrade. Serbia now has an opportunity to make a democratic change of government the basis for greater independence in its foreign policy, and its new representatives have a strong enough mandate to take responsibility for that choice.
Ukrainians deserve to see that independence exercised in Serbia’s dealings with them as well. Their president must be welcome in Belgrade even when his visit displeases Moscow and offers no electoral advantage to his Serbian hosts. If, after a victory won on the promise of a freer Serbia, the Ukrainian president finds his scope for cooperation with the country curtailed, Vladimir Putin will have won a share of that victory. Responsibility for that outcome will lie with those who promised their citizens a free country, then allowed a foreign regime waging a war of aggression to set the limits of its foreign policy.
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.
Dr. Orhan Dragaš is a Serbian expert on security and international relations. He is the founder and director of the International Security Institute, based in Belgrade; author of numerous expert articles, newspaper columns, as well as the books "The modern intelligence-security community, utopia or reality"; and; "Two faces of globalization – truth and deceptions."

title: Man Utd Crisis Deepens As Carrick Faces Axe
body: Winless in eight games and hovering just above the Premier League relegation zone, struggling Manchester United are facing the prospect of yet another managerial change, with Michael Carrick likely to pay the price. The former United midfielder was warmly applauded by fans as he made his way down the tunnel after his team’s chastening 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth at Old Trafford on Sunday. Moments later, a chorus of boos erupted as the players left the pitch with fans clear in their minds where the blame lies for United’s current malaise. Carrick was handed a two-year deal in May after inspiring an impressive revival following the team’s struggles under Ruben Amorim — United secured third place in the Premier League and a return to the Champions League. But a drastic decline this season is an all-too-familiar story for United supporters, who last witnessed a Premier League title triumph 13 years ago under Alex Ferguson. An emotional Carrick denied his lap of the pitch at full-time on Sunday was a goodbye as he struggles to come to terms with his team’s precipitous decline. “I definitely knew that we hadn’t cracked it and there was a lot of work to be done, but that doesn’t mean to say that it should have gone this way,” he said. Carrick, 45, is clinging on, but his position appears increasingly precarious, with former Newcastle boss Eddie Howe and ex-Germany boss Julian Nagelsmann apparently in the frame for the job. The United boss, who won multiple titles in the club’s golden era under Ferguson, was the seventh permanent appointment since the Scot retired. David Moyes was proven in the Premier League, Louis van Gaal and Jose Mourinho had stellar records, and Erik ten Hag and Amorim were seen as rising stars of coaching. Sentimental Choice Carrick is in the same category as Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, who was in charge for three years from 2018 — a sentimental choice as a former player who played a major role in the club’s glory years under Ferguson. “The Manchester United fans are singing the Michael Carrick song because I think they know what’s going to happen here. They’ve seen this before. He’s one of their own, and he’s popular,” former United captain Gary Neville told Sky Sports. “But the owners, the sporting department and the players are not popular, and they’ve badly let this football club down.” The problems at the club, as Neville points out, go far beyond the dugout. Despite fierce, ongoing protests from fans, the US-based Glazer family still hold a majority stake in the club Malcolm Glazer bought via a leveraged takeover in 2005, saddling United with huge debts. Any hopes that the arrival of British billionaire Jim Ratcliffe as a minority owner in 2024 would signal a new dawn have been dashed. Ratcliffe has overseen cost-cutting measures including widespread redundancies and ticket hikes, but the club’s debt has still soared above £1.1 billion ($1.47 billion). United, who for years bullied their rivals in the transfer market, lost out on the biggest names as they targeted a summer midfield rebuild, with Elliot Anderson, Sandro Tonali and Mateus Fernandes all choosing other clubs. United instead recruited Carlos Baleba, Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos — none of whom have made a strong impression — for combined fees of about £150 million. Significant rifts have emerged in recent weeks. Lisandro Martinez criticised director of football Jason Wilcox for not doing more to strengthen Carrick’s squad. Last week captain Bruno Fernandes publicly questioned Carrick’s tactics in a 4-1 humbling by Champions League debutants Como. Carrick is expected to take the blame, but the route back to the top for one of the world’s biggest clubs appears tougher than ever. “It can’t just be the manager again. There has got to be consequences above that. You can’t keep letting the people pick the manager who keep getting it wrong,” said Neville. “It’s years now without a Premier League title. That will be another five or 10 before you know it because there are other clubs set up for success and Manchester United aren’t.” AFP The post Man Utd Crisis Deepens As Carrick Faces Axe appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Anthropic preps for IPO in major step for AI company
body:
Anthropic, the maker of Claude, has been among the leaders in AI development.
Anthropic, the company behind the AI chatbot Claude , filed papers Monday to prepare for a potential initial public offering (IPO), taking a major step toward a listing on public markets.
The long-anticipated move comes months after Anthropic said it had "confidentially submitted a draft registration statement on Form S-1" with the Securities and Exchange Commission.
Monday's filing touts AI as "one of the most consequential technologies in human history. If managed well, it could rapidly accelerate scientific innovation, greatly increase economic growth rates, bring cures for major diseases within reach, and solve problems that have resisted generations of human effort."
At the same time, "To build AI is to harness cognition itself, and anything so powerful can be used for ill as well as good," Anthropic's filing says, noting that AI "can be misused by those who wish to do harm" and "may also behave autonomously in ways we (and our users) do not intend -- as illustrated by recent high-profile cybersecurity incidents. Losing control of sufficiently powerful AI systems could be a global security threat of the first order."
"We consider it our personal responsibility to help the world understand these risks, to prevent or mitigate them when they arise from our AI models, and to work with governments and the rest of the industry to address them at a societal level," the filing says.
Public concern over the possible risks posed by AI has grown in recent months, resulting in part from AI-related security incidents disclosed by Anthropic as well as the high-profile resignation of a researcher at the company.
In July, Anthropic said a review of more than 140,000 testing runs of its AI models had unearthed three separate self-directed cyberattacks against other organizations.
Rival companies, including OpenAI, have also revealed AI-related security incidents in recent months.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last month announced a precautionary slowdown of AI development to ensure sufficient risk prevention. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman also said last month he would dial back the pace of his company's AI development.
Anthropic earned $16.3 billion in revenue over the first six months of this year, growing nearly 14-fold from $1.2 billion in revenue in the same period a year earlier, the company's filing said.
Still, the company reported a net loss of $80.7 billion over the first six months of this year, indicating the scale of its spending over that period.
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.
