title: Russia ready to share practical AI solutions with BRICS — digital development committee
body:
NEW DELHI, October 26. /TASS/. Russia is ready to share practical artificial intelligence solutions with BRICS countries, Alexander Sidyakin, head of the State Duma Committee on Digital Development and Artificial Intelligence, said.
The lawmaker is visiting India as part of a Russian parliamentary delegation led by State Duma Speaker Vyacheslav Volodin, participating in the 12th BRICS International Parliamentary Forum.
"Russia is ready to share practical solutions in this field, and today, during the first part of our plenary session, our parliament speaker also addressed this issue," Sidyakin said at the forum’s second plenary session, titled "Innovation: The Role of Parliaments in Promoting a Human-Centered Approach to the Development of Innovation in Artificial Intelligence and Digital Technologies."
In the lawmaker’s view, the key task for the parliaments of BRICS countries is to establish the most favorable possible regulatory framework for technological cooperation among the member states. "Yes, of course, all our countries need to ensure technological sovereignty, but this does not mean withdrawing into self-isolation. It means a country’s ability to independently manage critical infrastructure in order to protect citizens’ data and choose partners without external dictates," he added.
Earlier, Volodin proposed establishing a BRICS parliamentary expert council on artificial intelligence to exchange best legislative practices.

title: Army’s Western Command to hold Mechanisation Technology Seminar in December
body:
New Delhi, Oct 26. The Indian Army’s Western Command will organise the second edition of the Mechanisation Technology Seminar (MTS 2.0) at Chandimandir Military Station on December 14-15, focusing on upgrading existing military platforms to meet the demands of future warfare.
Lieutenant General Pushpendra Singh, General Officer Commanding-in-Chief of Western Command, inaugurated the curtain raiser for the seminar at the Manekshaw Centre in New Delhi on October 26. The event was organised by Western Command in collaboration with the Society of Indian Defence Manufacturers (SIDM).
The seminar, themed ‘CHAKRA – Transforming Existing Platforms for Future Combat’, will bring together representatives of the Indian Army, defence industry and academia to explore technological innovations and ways to enhance the operational capabilities of mechanised forces.
An initiative of Western Command, MTS 2.0 seeks to improve the combat effectiveness of mechanised formations by upgrading existing military platforms with advanced technologies and transforming them into more capable, adaptable and future-ready combat systems.
The deliberations will centre on Combat Capability Enhancement, Harnessing Technology, Adaptability, Kinetics, Refurbishment and ‘Atmanirbharta’ (self-reliance). A key objective will be to translate operational shortcomings and the military’s evolving requirements into clearly defined Problem Definition Statements (PDS), which can guide the development of practical technological solutions.
The curtain raiser outlined the vision and principal areas of discussion for the December seminar, underscoring the role of technology-led modernisation, collaboration between the armed forces and the defence industry, and indigenous innovation in strengthening India’s defence capabilities.
It also provided an opportunity for military personnel, industry representatives, academics and other stakeholders to exchange views on modernising existing platforms, developing indigenous technologies and addressing emerging operational requirements.
The initiative comes amid the Indian Army’s continuing efforts to adapt its capabilities to an evolving battlefield environment, where technological advances and changing operational demands are reshaping the requirements of land warfare.
By bringing military users, industry and academia onto a common platform, MTS 2.0 aims to bridge the gap between operational needs and technological development. Its focus on upgrading existing equipment, alongside promoting indigenous solutions, is intended to improve the combat readiness, resilience and operational effectiveness of mechanised forces while advancing the broader objective of self-reliance in defence manufacturing.
The seminar is expected to provide a focused forum for identifying capability gaps and developing implementable solutions to help prepare the Army’s mechanised forces for future operational challenges.

title: Alleged wire-tapping: Court dismisses El-Rufai’s ‘no-case’ submission
body: A Federal High Court sitting in Abuja on Monday dismissed a no-case submission filed by former Kaduna State Governor, Nasir El-Rufai, in the ongoing case over the alleged unlawful interception of telephone conversations. The court, in its ruling, held that the prosecution had presented sufficient evidence to warrant calling on the defendant to enter his defence. It consequently directed the former governor to open his defence next month. Daily Trust reports that El-Rufai is standing trial on a five-count amended charge filed by the Department of State Services (DSS) over allegations that he unlawfully intercepted telephone conversations linked to Nuhu Ribadu. In February 2026, during an interview on Prime Time , an Arise Television programme, El-Rufai said “someone wiretapped” Ribadu’s phone, enabling him to listen to the National Security Adviser (NSA) instructing security operatives to arrest him. After presenting two witnesses against the former governor, the Federal Government closed its case, following which El-Rufai filed a no-case submission. Moving the application on Monday, El-Rufai’s counsel, Paul Erokoro, urged the court to discharge and acquit the former governor of the five-count amended charge. Erokoro, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN), argued that the prosecution had failed to establish a prima facie case to warrant compelling El-Rufai to enter a defence to the charges. Opposing the no-case submission, prosecution counsel, Oluwole Aladedoye, urged the court to dismiss the application and order the defendant to open his defence. Aladedoye argued that the oral and documentary evidence presented before the court was sufficient to require the defendant to answer the charges. In a brief ruling after hearing arguments from both parties, the judge, Justice Joyce Abdulmalik, ruled in favour of the prosecution and ordered El-Rufai to open his defence. She subsequently adjourned the case until November 25 for El-Rufai to open his defence.

title: Buy 1 Get 1 Free Chicken Bucket: KFC Nigeria brings back its biggest value deal Wednesday, 28th Oct
body:
KFC Nigeria is bringing back its Buy 1, Get 1 Free Chicken Bucket promotion on Wednesday, 28th October, giving customers a complete second bucket at no extra cost and as much as 50 percent in savings on one of the country’s most popular quick-service meals.
The offer applies to all three bucket sizes: 8, 12 and 21 pieces. A customer who pays the regular price for one bucket receives a second bucket of the same size free, along with an additional 4 dips, with each bucket served with 4 dips from the selection.
In a period when households are watching every naira, the structure of the offer is what sets it apart. It is not a percentage discount on a single meal but a full duplicate bucket, which makes it one of the more generous value plays in Nigeria’s fast-food market in recent memory.
The promotion follows a run that surprised many customers last month, when KFC Nigeria ran the same deal twice within weeks. The response online was immediate, with customers who took part encouraging friends and relatives to join in, while many who missed out asked when it would return.
The deal is designed for groups. Families can feed the whole household from one purchase, colleagues can pool resources for a team lunch, and friends can each contribute a share of the cost of the one paid bucket, ending up with twice the food for roughly half the spend.
On a midweek day, typical occasions include office lunches, after-school treats, family dinners, friends’ get-togethers and neighbourhood gatherings.
The promotion runs across KFC outlets in Lagos, Abuja, Port Harcourt, Enugu, Kano, Akure, Ilorin, Sagamu and Ibadan, making it one of the widest geographic spreads of any KFC Nigeria campaign this year.
Customers who prefer to order from home or the office can also access the deal on delivery through Chowdeck and Mano.
The offer is valid on Wednesday, 28th October only, and heavy demand is expected at outlets and on delivery platforms nationwide. Customers are advised to plan their visit or place their orders early, as queues and high order volumes are likely through the day. Those who missed earlier rounds have a fresh opportunity, but the window is a short one.

title: Hezbollah vows not to fight on Iran's side if war resumes — Lebanese parliament speaker
body:
BEIRUT, October 26. /TASS/. Hezbollah vows not to fight against Israel should another spiral of confrontation between Iran and the United States break out, Lebanese parliament speaker Nabih Berri said.
"This time, Hezbollah will not be drawn into the conflict on Iran's side. This position has been conveyed to President Joseph Aoun," he said, as cited by the Naharnet news portal.
Since the outbreak of the military escalation on March 2, 2026, Berri has been acting as a mediator between Hezbollah and the Lebanese government. Sources close to him told the news portal that Hezbollah’s decision to stay away from the war stems from the desperate situation the Shiite community in southern Lebanon is in following Israeli bombings. Such a step may be met negatively by the organization’s electorate, so it has to act cautiously, they explained.
According to the pan-Arabic newspaper Asharq Al Awsat, Hezbollah’s decision was agreed on with the Iranian leadership. Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Saeed Khatibzadeh, who visited Beirut on October 14-16, reportedly told Berri that Tehran would not insist on Hezbollah’s entering a conflict that is clearly unequal amid the aggressive threats from US President Donald Trump.
Iran "is capable of fighting back on its own and has made significant progress in preparing for a new attack to prevent the enemy from achieving its objectives," Khatibzadeh was quoted as saying.

title: Can AI help solve the COBOL code crisis?
body:
What do the IRS, banks, airlines, and government infrastructure around the world have in common? They’re all running on systems propped up by antique computer code that nobody dares touch, lest everything come crashing down.
OpenAI thinks it may have a solution. On October 19th, the company touted “substantial improvements” in its latest AI models’ ability to migrate aging software written in older programming languages into modern code, which it claims could help organizations with “maintaining and modernizing older systems.”
That’s a potentially massive deal. COBOL, one of the languages highlighted by OpenAI, remains stubbornly embedded in vast portions of the world’s critical infrastructure. And despite decades of efforts to banish it to history, the language has limped on, simply refusing to die.
It is hard to overstate COBOL’s ubiquity. Short for “common business-oriented language,” COBOL came into being in 1959. Nearly seven decades later, it is still everywhere. According to IBM, COBOL is the foundation for more than 40 percent of online banking systems, supports 80 percent of in-person credit card transactions, and handles 95 percent of ATM transactions. It also underpins many government systems, from Social Security to the IRS to services run by most states. One rough estimate puts the annual cost of COBOL’s inefficiencies to the US GDP at around $105 billion.
But replacing COBOL is fiendishly difficult. The same goes for other legacy programming languages, like Fortran, still in use today for everything from scientific computing and weather forecasting to atmospheric and ocean studies and codes critical to nuclear security. These systems are often too important to risk breaking, and many of the programmers who understand them have long since retired or died.
For all their impressive advances in modern software development, AI coding tools have struggled to make much headway with these legacy systems. But recent developments suggest that may be changing.
In its latest blog post, OpenAI reported promising results migrating COBOL code to more modern programming languages, including C++, Java, Kotlin, Python, and Rust, without changing what the original software does. That last bit is crucial for organizations looking to ditch code like COBOL, and OpenAI acknowledges that “a migration is considered successful only if all tests pass.”
In OpenAI’s own tests, GPT-6.1 Sol achieved 87 percent behavior preservation accuracy at low reasoning effort — how many computational steps the model spends analyzing a problem before giving an answer — climbing to 98 percent at higher reasoning. By comparison, at low reasoning effort, GPT-6 Astra scored around 86 percent, GPT-6 Sol just 21 percent, and GPT-5.6 Sol a mere 5 percent.
“These evaluation results demonstrate progress toward more accurate, affordable code migration for teams modernizing the software their businesses depend on,” OpenAI wrote.
The company also reported improvements on its models’ ability to build database software in various programming languages, including COBOL.
Anthropic also sees an opportunity in legacy systems. In February, it published a step-by-step “code modernization playbook” and pitched its coding agent, Claude Code, as a way to migrate COBOL code into modern languages like Java or Python. It offered no performance benchmarks showing how well Claude Code could perform such migrations, but declared that “the economics of COBOL modernization have shifted.” Shares in IBM, which derives part of its revenue helping companies maintain legacy systems, nosedived following Anthropic’s announcement.
Experts who spoke to The Verge agreed that AI tools have made strides in tackling legacy code in recent years. But they cautioned that advances trumpeted by OpenAI this week are a very long way from making it possible to safely replace critical legacy systems built around it.
OpenAI spokesperson Oscar Haines acknowledged in an email to The Verge that legacy code “is still far from a solved problem” and said the company is listening to feedback from developers and enterprises and exploring ways to build better tests and continue improving its models’ understanding of coding languages. Anthropic did not provide comment in time for publication.
“Rewriting code is not the same as replacing a system,” said Vadim Zaytsev, an associate professor of software evolution at the University of Twente in the Netherlands. Systems do have a lot of code — Zaytsev said the largest system he’d seen had 250 million lines of COBOL, “definitely not the world’s largest” — but that’s only part of the problem. Code may be written in multiple languages and there’s data, potentially stored in various formats, to consider, he said. There are also technical integrations with other systems and the expectations of the people and organizations to bear in mind.
All that complexity means “AI is not playing a major role at the moment in replacing or migrating legacy COBOL systems,” Zaytsev said.
OpenAI’s evaluations don’t capture this complex reality either, Arie van Deursen, a software engineering professor at Delft University of Technology in the Netherlands, told The Verge. He described the company’s blog as “superficial,” noting it offered few details about the migration task, while its language benchmark tested models on a relatively simple and well-defined task involving systems similar to those they would have encountered in training. He also stressed the huge gap between maintaining an aging system and modernizing it. “Maintaining is of course a lot easier than modernizing,” van Deursen said, calling the tasks OpenAI used to assess its models “lightyears” away from actual modernization. “The evaluations shown by OpenAI don’t address the key difficulty: Breaking up a complex legacy system into smaller units that can be replaced individually.”
The biggest challenge isn’t necessarily rewriting code. “The main challenge is indeed not understanding how the system works,” said Alastair Donaldson, a professor of programming languages at Imperial College London. Such a lack of understanding is a “very common” problem for legacy systems using languages like COBOL, he said, adding that very few people know how to program in them anymore. And while it is everywhere, Donaldson said “nobody in their right mind would use COBOL for a new development project.”
That makes robust testing crucial, Donaldson said. One approach could be to run the same workflows through the old and new systems to check they behave identically. AI could also document its code translation, ideally allowing humans familiar with the legacy language to review the work. Formal verification, which uses mathematical techniques to computationally verify that code behaves correctly, is another option, said Jacopo Mauro, a mathematics and computer science professor at the University of Southern Denmark.
Such methods are already used to verify AI-generated mathematical results, but applying them to legacy code would require a “huge amount of work,” Mauro said. Using those methods would mean code could be checked automatically, Mauro said, adding that “having this will be better than having a human check that the translation is correct.” Until then, he said, “human verification remains essential.”
And when the systems involved are as critical as those running on COBOL, experts say you need to be absolutely certain the replacement works. “In many cases even minor differences in system behaviour before and after migration are unacceptable,” Zaytsev said. While AI can definitely deliver savings and speed things up, the complexity of legacy systems means partial automation isn’t enough.
“Suppose you have a magic AI wand that handles 99 percent of your code,” Zaytsev said. “What do you do with the remaining 1 percent? That 1 percent can be a million lines of code, spread all over the place and subtly failing in more ways you can imagine within your lifetime.”

title: Iraqi PM orders investigation into provincial council threats over closed Iran border crossing
body: Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi ordered an investigation into the Maysan Provincial Council on Monday after its chairman, Mustafa Da'ir, threatened “civil disobedience” if Baghdad kept the al-Shib border crossing with Iran closed, according to Iraqi officials and media reports.Authorities closed the crossing last week as they upgraded security and detection equipment, an Iraqi official told Reuters on Wednesday.However, Kurdistan Democratic Party lawmaker Salwan Taha Akreyi told Kurdistan24 that Baghdad had shut the crossing at Washington's request to restrict transit to and from Iran and thwart Tehran's efforts to strengthen its militias in Iraq.Da'ir responded by threatening unrest and warning that he would cut the province off from the rest of the country, giving Baghdad a three-day deadline before escalating his response.Dozens of protesters also blocked roads leading to oil companies in the region to protest the closure, Asharq Al-Awsat reported.Shiite bloc rejects Zaidi's call for investigation into provincial councilThe Iraqi Shiite Islamist Badr bloc reportedly rejected the prime minister's call for an investigation, arguing that the closure was harming the region's economy and warning that prolonging the dispute risked damaging relations between Baghdad and the province, according to the independent Iraqi outlet Shafaq News.Badr also reportedly urged the government to intensify efforts to combat alleged smuggling through unofficial crossings in the Kurdistan region.The closure comes as the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz has increased Iran's reliance on land routes through neighboring Iraq and Pakistan for shipments. Tehran has strongly condemned the closure, rejecting allegations that the al-Shib crossing had been used to traffic drugs and counterfeit currency.

title: Russian ombudswoman rejects Kiev’s demand of forceful evacuation of children from Alyoshki
body:
MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova dismissed Kiev’s statements about a forced evacuation of families with children from Alyoshki as inadmissible.
"I’d like to respond to statements from the Ukrainian side which insisted, citing Ukrainian laws, that families with children be driven from Alyoshki forcefully. As a human rights commissioner, I reject the word 'forcefully.' We are talking about people who are capable of making informed decisions themselves," she argued on the Max channel. According to the Russian ombudswoman, "everything should be done voluntarily, taking into account their interests, not the interests of authorities in Kiev who have suddenly become so concerned about locals there."
If the Ukrainian side wants people to make an informed decision, it should provide them with such an opportunity, allowing them to live a peaceful life and instructing its military to stop shelling the town and laying mines on local roads every day, Lantratova maintained.
Moreover, she continued, Alyoshki in the Kherson Region is Russian territory governed exclusively by Russian law, so any reference to Ukrainian laws is unacceptable.
"[Vladimir] Zelensky stated that the Russian side ‘must’ demine everything as part of this humanitarian mission. My response is: give a direct order to your military not to shell the town and not to place mines on roads leading to it," she concluded.

title: Why the Age of AI Needs Academic Libraries More Than Ever
body: The Astana Times provides news and information from Kazakhstan and around the world. Universities are racing to embrace artificial intelligence. But who is helping students decide when its answers deserve to be trusted? Global Media and Information Literacy Week is a timely moment to recognize the academic library’s place in that task. Yet amid discussions of innovation, automation and future skills, the library is often overlooked. Many still see it as a place that buys, stores and lends books. In that view, Google reduced its importance and AI may finish the job. L-R: Diana Baidollinova, a librarian at the Teaching and Learning Support Office (TLSO); Darya Zvonareva, the head of TLSO; Aigerim Akparova, TLSO Librarian; Saqib Raza, PhD student NU; Venera Niyazbayeva, TLSO Librarian. Photo credit NU Library. The opposite is closer to the truth. AI has not made academic libraries less relevant. It has made their deeper purpose impossible to ignore. The central problem facing students today is no longer access to information. Information is everywhere. Answers appear within seconds. Generative AI can summarize articles, suggest references, produce arguments and imitate academic language with remarkable confidence. But confidence is not credibility. AI can invent citations. Search engines rank rather than judge. Predatory journals can look professional. Weak evidence travels quickly. A polished paragraph can hide a poor source, and an impressive answer can conceal almost no understanding at all. This changes the meaning of literacy. Knowing how to find information is no longer enough. Students must know how to question it. They must understand where evidence comes from, why one source deserves more trust than another, how scholarly knowledge is produced, and when an AI-generated answer should be challenged rather than accepted. This is where the modern academic library should be understood differently. A serious university library is not a warehouse of books. It is part of the university’s intellectual infrastructure. Nazarbayev University Library offers a useful example. Yes, it provides books, electronic journals, databases, study spaces and extensive digital access. It is technologically well equipped and has introduced systems that make academic resources easier to discover and use. But judging the library only by its collection would miss its most important work. NU Library supports students in literature searching, source evaluation, referencing, citation management and responsible use of information. It helps researchers navigate databases, systematic review resources, publication strategies, research visibility, bibliometrics, open access and journal selection. It also provides guidance that can help scholars identify questionable publishing practices and avoid predatory outlets. These are not administrative services. They are academic capabilities. The distinction matters because universities often speak about developing critical thinkers while underinvesting in the very institutions that teach students how knowledge should be located, tested and used. The rise of AI makes this contradiction harder to defend. A student may now produce a literature review faster than ever before. But can that student explain why the selected studies are credible? Can they distinguish a peer-reviewed source from a weak one? Can they recognize a fabricated reference? Can they identify bias in an AI-generated synthesis? Can they trace a claim back to the original evidence? If not, technological fluency has been mistaken for intellectual competence. Modern libraries are increasingly working at exactly this boundary. At Nazarbayev University, library initiatives have extended into information literacy, research support and emerging AI-related practices. Workshops and training expose students and researchers to tools for literature discovery, reference management, research evaluation and responsible academic work. Professional development initiatives also strengthen the capacity of librarians themselves to respond to changing research and teaching environments. This is the future-facing role that deserves far more attention. Academic librarians should not be treated as custodians standing at the edge of teaching and research. They are increasingly partners in both. They sit at the intersection of information, technology, scholarship and academic integrity. Few university units are better placed to teach students how to navigate a world in which information is abundant but reliability is uneven. This should also change how university leaders think about AI literacy. AI literacy cannot mean teaching students which tools to use and which prompts them to write. That is too shallow. Real AI literacy requires information literacy underneath it. Students must know how to verify, compare, attribute, question and sometimes reject what a system gives them. Without those habits, universities may produce students who are efficient users of AI but weak judges of knowledge. That is not progress. Universities should reconsider what intellectual preparedness means in an age when machines can generate answers faster than humans can verify them. That is why academic libraries matter. They are not relics of an earlier information age. They are among the institutions best positioned to help universities navigate the next one. And as AI makes information easier to produce, the universities that thrive will be those that invest just as seriously in the human capacity to question, verify and think. In an age overflowing with answers, the academic library may prove most valuable for teaching us when not to accept one. Note: The UN General Assembly commemorates the Global Media and Information Literacy Week, observed from Oct. 24-31, to raise awareness and celebrate the progress achieved towards Media and Information Literacy for all since 2021. The author is Saqib Raza, a PhD scholar in education and an MSc graduate in Educational Leadership in Higher Education from Nazarbayev University Graduate School of Education, Kazakhstan. Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the position of The Astana Times. The post Why the Age of AI Needs Academic Libraries More Than Ever appeared first on The Astana Times .

title: Ondo Assembly passes bill for establishment of state police
body: Ondo State House of Assembly has passed a bill seeking to amend the 1999 Constitution to provide for the establishment of state police services. The bill was passed following deliberations by the lawmakers at a plenary session on Monday in Akure. The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that the proposal was conveyed to the assembly in a letter from the National Assembly Clerk, Kamoru Ogunlana, which was read by the Speaker, Olamide Oladiji, on Sept. 24. The House Leader, Olatunji Oshati, who moved for the passage and its transmission to the National Assembly, said the lawmakers had considered the implications of the proposed amendment for the citizenry. Oshati said that the establishment of state police would address the numerous security challenges confronting the country. The motion was seconded by Mr Allen Oluwatoyin, All Progressives Congress (APC), member representing Ese-Odo State Constituency. Also speaking, Oladiji described the proposed establishment of state police as long overdue, saying it would enable security agencies to respond more swiftly to crime and other security concerns. He noted that state policing, being grassroots-based, would reduce crime through improved intelligence gathering and proactive security measures. “There will be greater confidence in state policing. It will strengthen intelligence gathering and provide grassroots security,” he added. The speaker, however, commended the lawmakers for their contributions to the bill and its passage. It was gathered that the bill would be transmitted to the National Assembly for further legislative consideration. (NAN) The post Ondo Assembly passes bill for establishment of state police appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Rajnath Singh to lead Indian delegation at ASEAN-Plus Defence Ministers’ Meeting in Philippines
body:
New Delhi, Oct 26. Defence Minister Rajnath Singh will lead the Indian delegation to the 13th ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations) Defence Ministers’ Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus) in Cebu, the Philippines, from October 28 to 29, where he is scheduled to address regional and international security challenges and hold bilateral talks with his counterparts from participating countries.
Singh will speak at the forum during a session on ‘Exchange of Views on Regional and International Security Issues’, according to a Ministry of Defence statement.
On the sidelines of the meeting, the Defence Minister is expected to hold bilateral discussions with his counterparts to review the progress of existing defence cooperation and explore avenues for strengthening strategic partnerships. The discussions are expected to provide an opportunity to deepen defence engagement and reinforce India's security ties with countries across the Indo-Pacific region.
The ADMM-Plus brings together the 11 member states of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and eight dialogue partners – India, the US, China, Russia, Japan, South Korea, Australia and New Zealand. The forum serves as a platform for dialogue and practical cooperation on regional security and defence issues.
The ADMM is ASEAN’s highest-level defence consultative and cooperative mechanism, while the expanded ADMM-Plus framework facilitates engagement between ASEAN members and its external partners on shared security concerns.
India became a dialogue partner of ASEAN in 1992, and the first ADMM-Plus meeting was held in Hanoi, Vietnam, on October 12, 2010. Since 2017, defence ministers from participating countries have met annually to strengthen cooperation and address evolving regional security challenges.
The Philippines is chairing the ADMM-Plus in 2026. Under the forum’s framework, India and Malaysia are jointly co-chairing the Experts’ Working Group on Counter-Terrorism for the 2024-2027 cycle, reflecting their cooperation in addressing a key transnational security threat.
India’s participation in the meeting is part of its broader engagement with Southeast Asia under the Act East policy. Through defence dialogues, joint exercises, capacity-building initiatives and institutional cooperation, New Delhi has sought to expand its strategic partnerships with ASEAN countries and contribute to peace, stability and security across the Indo-Pacific.
The Cebu meeting is expected to provide an important platform for participating countries to exchange assessments of the regional and international security environment, strengthen defence cooperation and explore practical responses to common challenges.

title: OmniBSIC Bank honoured with African Banking Excellence Award at IFAL 2026
body: OmniBSIC Bank Ghana Limited has been honoured with the African Banking Excellence Award for Growth, Innovation and Customer Value at the 12th International Forum on African-Caribbean Leadership (IFAL 2026), held in New York on the margins of the 81st United Nations General Assembly. The award recognises financial institutions across Africa that have demonstrated outstanding performance in driving growth, advancing innovation and delivering value to customers. OmniBSIC Bank’s recognition reflects its sustained transformation and growing position in Ghana’s financial services sector, supported by continued investment in technology, customer experience and strategic partnerships. The bank’s growth has been reflected in its recent financial performance. In 2025, OmniBSIC Bank more than doubled its total assets to GH¢21.58 billion, while customer deposits reached GH¢16.56 billion. Profit before tax also rose by 104 percent to GH¢641 million. Speaking on the recognition, Managing Director of OmniBSIC Bank, Daniel Asiedu, said the award was a significant affirmation of the bank’s ambition and its Ghanaian roots. “Receiving this award on the margins of the United Nations General Assembly is deeply meaningful to us. It affirms what we have always believed that a Ghanaian bank, built on local foundations and sustained by the trust of its customers, can compete and excel on the world stage. This is not merely a recognition of what we have achieved; it is a mandate for where we are going,” Mr. Asiedu said. The award comes as OmniBSIC Bank continues to implement its OmniBSIC 5.0 strategic initiative, which places technology-driven innovation, personalised service and proactive customer partnerships at the centre of its growth agenda. The bank has continued to expand its reach and deepen its engagement with individuals, small and medium-sized enterprises, corporates and institutions, while strengthening its digital banking capabilities and customer proposition. The IFAL honour adds to a strong record of local, international and pan-African recognition for OmniBSIC Bank and its leadership. The bank has been named Best Corporate Bank (Ghana) by Global Banking & Finance Review in 2023, 2024 and 2026, Fastest-Growing Corporate Bank (Ghana) in 2023, Bank of the Year at the Ghana Business Awards and Ghana Business Standard Awards in 2023 and 2024 respectively, and SME Bank of the Year at the Ghana Credit Excellence Awards in 2024. It has also been recognised twice as Most Customer-Centric Bank by CIMG and as Top Bank in Consumer Service Quality by the Ghana Customer Satisfaction Index in 2025. Daniel Asiedu receives honorary citizenship of Stonecrest In a further recognition of Ghanaian leadership and contribution to economic development, Mr. Asiedu was also conferred with Honorary Citizenship of the City of Stonecrest, Georgia, on the sidelines of IFAL 2026. The honour recognises his leadership and contribution to banking and economic development, as well as his commitment to advancing economic connections between Ghana, Africa and the global diaspora. Incorporated in 2016, Stonecrest is a municipality in DeKalb County, Georgia, with a focus on economic empowerment, inclusive development and international collaboration. Mr. Asiedu described the recognition as a personal honour and an opportunity to deepen his commitment to cross-border economic development. “I am deeply humbled by this honour from the City of Stonecrest. To be recognised by a city with such a purposeful and proud identity is an extraordinary privilege. It deepens my personal commitment to working across borders to advance economic development,” for Ghana, for Africa and for communities in the diaspora who share in our aspirations,” he said. He added: “This recognition belongs to every customer who trusts us and every staff member who makes it happen. OmniBSIC Bank is not just another bank, and moments like this remind us exactly why.” In 2026, he has been named Banking CEO of the Year (Africa) and Banking CEO of the Year (Ghana), adding to his 2023 Personality of the Year (Private Sector) honour.

title: Road to BAL: Sports Ministry ‘shocked’ over Spintex Knights stranded in Libya claims
body: The Ministry of Sports and Recreation has expressed shock over the news of Spintex Knights being stranded in Libya over an estimated $33,000 in outstanding flight costs. The Ghanaian basketball champions travelled to Libya for the first phase of the Basketball Africa League qualifiers, where they advanced into the Elite 16 stage. However, the co-founder of Spintex Knights, Dr Eric Opoku-Antwi, said the club is awaiting a response from the Ministry of Sports and Recreation on their commitment to provide support for their qualifiers’ campaign. However, the personal assistant to the Sports Minister, Wonder Mandel, says the institution is ‘surprised’ by the claims of the basketball club, as they were expected to cover their costs following a short notice to the ministry. “I was actually surprised and shocked when I started seeing these news items from yesterday morning that they were stranded at the airport,” he told CitiSports. “The CEO of Spintex Knights made the indication that they have the Libya competition covered…and they will need our help going into the Elite 16 and the bout itself next year, which the minister actually requested that they should always make sure they submit their request on time.” Spintex Knights won all three of their Group B games in the Division West preliminary to seal qualification for the Elite 16.

title: Iran becomes champion of 2026 World Wrestling Championships
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 26 (MNA) – Iran's Greco-Roman wrestling team has won the tile of the 2026 World Championships with clear at the top.
The Iranian national Greco-Roman wrestling team claimed the world championship title earler than the championships in Kazakhstan wraps up.
At the conclusion of the first four weight classes, Gholamreza Farrokhi (82 kg) won the gold medal; Payam Ahmadi (55 kg) and Ali Ahmadi-Vafa (60 kg) claimed silver medals; and Ali Oskou (77 kg) earned a bronze medal.
Despite the early win, the national Iranian Greco-Roman team has the chance to win four gold medals and one bronze medal across the six remaining weight classes.

title: Abuakwa South MP raises concerns over Ghana’s Ebola preparedness after Nigeria case
body: A Member of Parliament (MP) for Abuakwa South Constituency, Dr Kingsley Agyemang, has called on the government to strengthen the country’s public health emergency preparedness following the confirmation of an Ebola virus disease case in Nigeria. In a statement issued on Monday, October 26, 2026, the MP warned that Ghana must not become complacent, despite having no confirmed Ebola case, according to the latest official Ghanaian update cited in the statement. The MP urged the Ministry of Health and the Ghana Health Service to intensify disease surveillance, particularly at land borders, activate regional and district rapid response teams and assess the readiness of designated isolation and treatment facilities. The call follows Nigeria’s reported confirmation of an imported case of the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola on October 20, 2026. The statement said subsequent genomic analysis found the virus to be closely related to a strain identified in Kenya, although this did not establish direct transmission between the two countries. The MP said Ghana’s extensive travel links, commercial activities and population movements across West Africa made it important for the country to strengthen its defences against potential cross-border transmission. While acknowledging the Ministry of Health’s announcement of intensified surveillance and preparedness measures, including enhanced monitoring at Kotoka International Airport, the MP said the government must demonstrate operational readiness across the health system. “The lessons of previous Ebola outbreaks demonstrate that early detection, effective surveillance and rapid response remain our strongest safeguards against a public health emergency,” the statement said. Calls for funding and protection of health workers The MP also called for adequate supplies of personal protective equipment, diagnostic materials and infection prevention resources to support health facilities in responding to a possible outbreak. The statement emphasised the need to protect frontline healthcare workers through practical training, emergency simulation exercises, laboratory preparedness and clear referral protocols. It further urged the government to release funds promptly to support preparedness measures rather than wait for a confirmed case to expose weaknesses in the country’s response system. The MP said public communication must be timely, transparent and evidence-based to educate Ghanaians on Ebola symptoms, preventive measures and appropriate reporting channels without creating unnecessary panic. The statement also called for stronger collaboration with the World Health Organisation, the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention and neighbouring countries to improve information sharing and coordinate responses to potential outbreaks. MP questions government’s commitment to preparedness The MP expressed concern about what was described as insufficient publicly demonstrated progress in addressing issues raised in an earlier statement on March 27, 2026, regarding Ghana’s preparedness for public health emergencies. The MP questioned whether the government was unwilling to invest in preventive measures or had failed to prioritise the necessary resources. The statement called on the Minister for Health to account to Parliament and the public for funds allocated, released and spent on emergency preparedness, as well as provide evidence of improvements made since March. “Public health security must be measured by concrete action, not assurances alone,” the MP said. The MP urged the government to use developments in Nigeria as an opportunity to demonstrate the country’s readiness to manage a potential outbreak, warning against waiting until Ghana records its first case before identifying gaps in its emergency response system. The statement concluded that strengthening preparedness, surveillance and response capacity was essential to protecting public health and preventing a potential emergency from escalating. title: Apple updates the iPad Mini with a larger OLED display
body:
Apple announced a new iPad Mini with a larger, 8.5-inch OLED display. The company revealed the new device just days before its “Pro and tell” event on Wednesday. The iPad Mini starts at $699 for the Wi-Fi-only model, and $849 for Wi-Fi and cellular.
At 5.4mm thick, the iPad Mini is thinner and lighter than its predecessor. It also has bezels that are 24 percent slimmer. This allows the device to maintain the same small form factor with a display that’s slightly larger than the previous generation’s 8.3-inch screen. The iPad Mini offers a peak brightness of up to 1,200 nits, along with a 1-nit minimum brightness that could make it easier on the eyes in dim lighting.
The new device still doesn’t come with Apple’s ProMotion technology for smoother scrolling, as the technical specs say it supports up to 4K resolution at a 60Hz refresh rate.
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/ipadmini4.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/ipadmini5.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/ipadmini3.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/ipadmini2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
Aside from an OLED display, the new iPad Mini features an upgraded A20 Pro chip capable of running on-device AI models. This enables support for some of Apple’s new Siri AI features, including the ability to tweak the expressiveness and pace of the assistant’s voice. Although models with 128GB or 256GB of storage come with a five-core CPU with two super cores and three efficiency cores, the 512GB model offers a six-core CPU with two super cores and four efficiency cores. All models come with a 16-core Neural Engine.
Additionally, Apple says the iPad Mini comes with a new “Acoustic Display,” which it describes as including “specially designed woofers” that are “paired through the display to produce punchier bass and more volume.” It also has custom tweeters between the device’s glass and aluminum enclosure “for clearer highs.”
Some other updates include a 12MP front-facing camera that’s now on the long edge of the iPad Mini, making it easier for video calls in landscape orientation. It has an IP67 rating for protection against water and dust, in addition to Apple’s next-gen C2 cellular modem and in-house N1 networking chip. Apple promises up to 10 hours of battery life when watching videos or browsing the web on Wi-Fi.
[Image: The iPad Mini has a Super Retina XDR display. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Apple-iPad-mini-OLED-display-261026.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
This new iPad Mini follows Apple’s seventh-generation version released in 2024, which arrived three years after the sixth-generation model in 2021. That seventh-generation iPad Mini, which started at $499, was primarily a spec bump, with the A17 Pro chip, support for the Apple Pencil Pro, and an upgrade to 128GB base storage. In his review, David Pierce called it a “new low for the product” that “feels like an iPad designed by a supply chain, not by someone who actually wants you to like the product.”
The upgraded iPad Mini comes ahead of a string of other rumored product launches that could take place this week, which could include a touchscreen MacBook Pro, along with an M6-equipped MacBook Pro and iMac.
Preorders for the new iPad Mini start on Wednesday, October 28th, with availability on November 6th. The iPad Mini is available in “midnight” and “starlight” colors, along with 128GB, 256GB, and 512GB configurations. There’s a glare-reducing nano-texture display option for the 256GB and 512GB models as well.

title: Opinion| What Southern Unity SPLM candidates need to know?
body: In the ongoing SPLM Party primary elections in South Sudan, the Southern part of Unity State will be without Panyijiar County. This means Southern Unity is going to be a minority compared to northern Unity in terms of numbers. This factual concern should worry the Southern Unity SPLM candidates. At this point in time, I doubt if there will be a SPLM Party candidate from Southern Unity State who will set foot in Panyijiar to campaign, for obvious reasons that the region is not SPLM-controlled territory. Panyijiar County, which is the largest county in Unity State, is an opposition stronghold that operates on opposition politics for the good and betterment of South Sudan. Moreover, there is an adage which says “once bitten, twice shy.” The majority in Leer County are putting on SPLM caps rotationally for strategic security purposes. In other words, the residents in Leer County are donning the SPLM caps during the daytime mainly for their protection and safety. At night and in the heart, the Leer County residents are believed and perceived to be die-hard opposition supporters more than the Panyijiar group. Leer County’s rotational politics is purposeful and judicious. You will remember the Amnesty International report entitled “Leer and Mayendit: anything that was breathing was killed.” If I were a bona fide SPLM Party member, I would encourage the party leadership to offer apologies to the aggrieved members ahead of time to regain and recapture their loyalties. When D-Day approaches, Leer County will experience huge voter apathy if the sham SPLM election proceeds as planned. By definition, voter apathy means a lack of interest in an election, marred by low turnout or failure to vote. Over the years, Leer County, formerly the headquarters of Southern Unity, has had residents who are politically sensitive due to their proximity to the well-versed individuals who have mastered the arts of political maneuvering. This further begs the question: If the SPLM election was a genuine one, do you think Leer County would fail to produce a candidate for unity state governorship? In 2010, Leer County produced two candidates, namely Madam Angelina Teny and James Kuong Ninrew. If I may reiterate, there will be unprecedented voter apathy in Leer County, and there will be no votes in Panyijiar County. Moreover, the residents of Mayendit and Koch counties, which are an appendage of these disgruntled counties of Panyijiar and Leer, will still give the forthcoming SPLM election a wide berth. This means, therefore, without Leer and Panyijiar votes at their disposal, the Mayendit and Koch votes combined will be a drop in the ocean. In a nutshell, these are exactly what Southern Unity SPLM candidates need to know at this point in time. Alternatively, the Southern Unity SPLM candidates should consider negotiating for a merger with their fellow SPLM candidates from Northern Unity before it is too late. They ought to arrive at this decision after doing a SWOT analysis. I have said time and again that Southern Unity is a political desert. The three Southern Unity SPLM candidates decided to contest for the Unity State governorship on wishful thinking. They decided to run for Unity State governorship on sympathy votes. They thought that they would win the Unity State governorship, perhaps because they thought it was time for the governorship to come to the Southern Unity side. However, they need to know that power is not given, but it is taken. Unfortunately, the Southern Unity SPLM candidates do not have the numbers to take gubernatorial power from the Northern Unity side. In view of the foregoing, the few voters from Koch and Mayendit combined cannot make Gideon Gatpan Thoar, Dr. James Nhial Ruach Chinien and Gordon Lam beat the Northern Unity SPLM candidates, namely Gen. James Pui Yak, Gen. Riek Bim and Gen. Michael Chiangjeak Geay. The Taban Deng Gai factor Among the six SPLM candidates for unity state governorship, four candidates are from the former vice president Gen. Taban Deng’s camp. The fact that Taban endorsed four candidates shows a lack of a winning strategy. In the wake of his endorsement of four SPLM candidates, I asked a question: if Gen. Taban Deng could not secure the appointment of his personal aide, Gabriel Gatkuoth Tekjiek, as SPOC vice president as per the latter’s nomination by the Southern Unity Parliamentary Caucus, how will he manage to secure the election of one of his four SPLM candidates for Unity State governorship? On a lighter note, the incumbent EALA MP, Gideon Gatpan, being one of Taban’s political trainees, could have more advantage than Gen. Cheangjeak and Gen. Bim in Taban’s home turf of Guit County. But this advantage can only happen if Gen. Pui Yak from Guit County was not in the race. If by any chance Pui was absent from this race, then Gideon could earn more sympathy votes in Guit County. The Guit County voters might think that Gideon will have a soft spot for them in his future leadership. However, the entry of Gen. Pui has denied him votes from the northern unity block. Unity State needs a dirty person. In the case of Unity State, a dirty person is one who combines both a principled and flexible stance on prevailing issues. The Unity State requires a dirty person to handle the political dirt in Unity State’s bad politics. Politically, this person can go head-to-head with the incumbent if need be. Lately, I have been thinking that Pui is too good to be a Unity State governor for now. I am of the opinion that Pui is more of a philosopher than a politician. Despite Pui’s extensive academic and security background, he appears more as a diplomat who will hardly confront head-on those who are perpetuating division and a culture of impunity in the Unity State. In 2023, when I was a Unity State community leader, I learned that Pui does not admire the politics of conspiracy and clannism, which were deeply planted in the hearts and minds of our people in Unity State. In fact, if South Sudan’s national leadership were in a position to identify the capabilities of its senior professionals, Pui would be suitable to represent South Sudan at the United Nations or at the national or regional levels. More importantly, one of the unwritten political rules is that Politics is local. Therefore, I would say Gideon is good, but I don’t think he is ripe to be the Unity State governor due to the reasons expressed therein. In recent years, Unity State has witnessed and experienced numerous impunity and injustices which need to be handled not by a good and calm person, but by an outspoken and courageous person who will call a spade a spade. However, among the SPLM candidates, I don’t see anyone with the necessary attributes and leadership qualities to restore our people’s unity based on their historical commonalities. The leadership of the current governor, Dr. Joseph Monytuil, has torn our social bonds. I am sure that the day he decides to go, he will leave the Unity State no better than he found it. In Unity State, people look at themselves with fear and suspicion. At times, some people are viewed as obstacles, while other people are considered domineering or both. Interestingly, most independent and free-thinking voters from Mayom County can vote for any candidates from Southern Unity because they themselves are tired of an empty and unproductive politics of exclusion against other counties. In spite of the fact that Greater Mayom has held and occupied the governor position for about a decade and a half, Mayom County, where Governor Monytuil hails from, is not better off than the other six counties in terms of development. At times, funds and goodies meant for development are siphoned by political elites and their surrogates. Surprisingly, the first Mayom County road was constructed to connect Mayom and Warrap State. The question is: if the incumbent governor, Dr. Monytuil, was pro Mayom County and Unity State, he could have first built a modern road that connects Mayom and Rubkona and, by extension, Unity State. Technically, I think Mayom County was annexed without our consent. And this unpopular decision will require a constitutional struggle in the future. A few days ago, I opined an argument suggesting that the SPLM candidate from Mayom County cannot win unity state governorship in a free and fair primary or secondary elections. The reasons are that the bad politics of our incumbent governor and his predecessor have angered so many people in Unity State, and the people of Mayom County are no exception. Nonetheless, the two northern Unity candidates from Mayom, namely Gen. Cheangjeak and Gen. Riek Bim, have only one advantage of incumbency. Ideologically, the SPLM party is not prepared to move power away from Greater Mayom since President Kiir is still President. The latter is using the Unity State governorship position not as a tool for development but as a shield for communal and personal protection. Who is the favorite? If the Unity State governorship must remain in the hands of greater Mayom County by hook or crook, then the rest of Unity State voters must do the math. In my view, Gen. Michael Chiangjeak is the favorite candidate who will thrash Gen. Justice Riek Bim in Mayom, let alone in Unity State. He will get the political support from his former SPLM-IO members who recently joined the SPLM Party because he was their former field commander who rebelled alongside Taban Deng and Dr Riek Machar in 2013. However, the former SPLM-IO members, who had managed to read Dr. Peter Adwok Nyaba’s book entitled South Sudan: elites, ethnicity, endless war and stunted state, regarding Chiangjeak’s role when Dr. Riek Machar was being chased to the Democratic Republic of the Congo forest, will have a reason to fear and reject him in the ballot. Further, if the gubernatorial race were left to Chiangjeak and Riek Bim, most voters from Southern Unity, particularly from Panyijiar County will vote for Riek Bim. The decision by Panyijiar voters to elect Cheangjeak and Riek Bim shall be informed and influenced by two historical events. In January 2001, it was alleged that Cheangjeak was the operation commander who was commanding the then SPLM-allied rebel forces that caused the devastating fall of Nyal, Panyijiar County. In August 2024, Justice Riek Bim became the first Unity State governor to visit Panyijiar County for the first time since South Sudan gained its independence from Sudan. His historical visit was viewed positively as recognition of their mother county in Unity State and South Sudan as a whole. Those of us who have perused the international law literature will better understand what recognition means to the region and state. Historically, our first two Unity State governors, namely Gen. Taban and Dr. Monytuil, became unpopular in Panyijiar County by design or by default. When the duo was in power, they were suspected of having orchestrated a political plot against the people of Panyijiar by shutting down the Ganyliel Community Health Training Institute, commonly known as CHW. In 2010, when Gen. Taban and Dr. Monytuil were governor and national minister of health, respectively, the Ganyliel Community Health Institute was brought down immediately. It was because of these and other emotive issues of underrepresentation that Panyijiar residents are agitating for an independent administrative area similar to the Pibor and Abyei administrative areas. The political Jesus Finally, the best political strategy to garner the unity state governorship is one of two. First, the clever SPLM Candidate will pretend to be fighting Caretaker Governor Dr. Joseph Nguen Monytuil, whom the majority are opposed to. By using this deceptive tactic to confront Monytuil by discussing the critical issues affecting the state, that candidate will earn public support because the oppressed and marginalized Unity State populace will think he is a brave person who can fight injustices and insecurity alike. In one of the above paragraphs, I said Unity State residents require someone of Moulana Kalisto type, who is just considered courageous and outspoken but who is also ready to face imprisonment on behalf of the people. Perhaps this was what General Michael Chiangjeak Geay tried to do on his arrival in Bentiu a few days ago. I believe the skirmishes that happened at Rubkona airstrip were part and parcel of this deceptive strategy. Perhaps General Michael knew this was the only way to maintain unity state governorship in Greater Mayom. However, as I stated earlier, this strategy does not apply to all SPLM candidates; otherwise, someone will end up committing political suicide. For example, a candidate from Southern Unity cannot fake fighting Dr. Mayom in Bentiu unless with his expressed permission. The failure to seek his prior permission can cause someone to be treated like the self-proclaimed Ngundeng prophet Taban Kuol, who was arrested and detained incommunicado. The second strategy is to mobilize funds to feed hungry majority voters ahead of the SPLM election. At this trying moment of famine, Unity State residents needed a rare SPLM candidate who could act and perform miracles like Jesus Christ. In the bible, John 6:1-14, Jesus fed about five thousand people in Galilee. If there is a SPLM candidate who is ready to invest his money by feeding our hungry people ahead of the controversial SPLM election, he will stand a chance to win the Unity State gubernatorial race. By doing this, the candidate will be a political Jesus of our time. In conclusion, any attempt to provide food to our people at this point in time, when UN agencies such as the World Food Programme (WFP) have left, should not be treated as voter bribery, but rather as a positive move to meet people’s basic needs in compliance with basic human rights. I think the trio, namely Chiangjiek, Riek Bim and Gideon, can grab the opportunity because they both held lucrative government positions for almost a decade. The time is ripe for serious and hardcore politicians to spend their money in order to woo voters. The writer is a lawyer and criminologist by profession. title: Kumbungu NDC Youth Organiser thanks supporters after constituency elections
body: The Kumbungu Constituency Youth Organiser of the National Democratic Congress (NDC), Abubakari Mashud Wumpini, has thanked party members and supporters for their backing during the just-ended constituency elections. In a message of appreciation, Mr Wumpini expressed gratitude to traditional leaders, branch youth organisers, party executives, religious leaders, Youth Employment Agency (YEA) beneficiaries and his campaign team for their support. He said their loyalty and encouragement had strengthened his resolve to serve the constituency, particularly amid the challenges and opposition that characterised the elections. “I do not take your trust for granted, and I promise to work even harder to justify the confidence you have reposed in me,” he said. Mr Wumpini assured supporters that he would remain committed to their expectations, declaring: “I WILL NOT DISAPPOINT YOU!” He also prayed for continued unity and progress within the constituency, asking Allah to bless supporters and strengthen their bonds. The statement follows the NDC’s recent constituency elections in Kumbungu, where Mr Wumpini thanked party members for standing by him and reaffirmed his commitment to serving them with renewed determination.

title: Gazprombank is one of the largest Russian banks — Putin
body:
MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. Gazprombank is one of the largest financial institutions in Russia and is among the top three banks by the amount of assets, President Vladimir Putin said at the meeting with Gazprombank CEO Andrey Akimov.
"Gazprombank is one of the largest banks of the country, one of the largest financial institutions, among the top three by the amount of assets, the amount of disbursed loans, and the equity," the head of state said.
"The amount of assets is 17.6 trillion rubles ($218.3 bln)," Putin noted. "The equity is 1.8 trillion rubles ($22.3 bln)," Akimov said in his turn.
Gazprombank maintains an ongoing and constructive dialogue with the Central Bank, the chief executive said. "It is good to hear that," said the Russian leader.

title: Abuakwa South MP calls for strengthened border surveillance amid Ebola concerns
body: The Member of Parliament (MP) for Abuakwa South, Dr Kingsley Agyemang, has urged the government to strengthen surveillance at the country’s borders following the confirmation of an Ebola case in Nigeria. He said Ghana must intensify monitoring at major points of entry, particularly land borders, to minimise the risk of the virus spreading into the country. In a press statement issued on Monday, October 26, Dr Agyemang, who is also a member of Parliament’s Health Committee, said Ghana’s regional travel networks, commercial activities and population movements created potential pathways for disease transmission. “Early detection, effective surveillance and rapid response remain our strongest safeguards against a public health emergency,” he said. Dr Agyemang acknowledged the Ministry of Health’s announcement of intensified surveillance and preparedness measures, including enhanced monitoring at Kotoka International Airport. However, he stressed that preparedness must go beyond public announcements to demonstrate operational readiness across the health system. He called on the government, through the Ministry of Health and the Ghana Health Service, to activate regional and district rapid response teams, assess the readiness of designated isolation and treatment facilities, and ensure adequate supplies of personal protective equipment and diagnostic materials. He also urged the government to prioritise practical training for frontline healthcare workers, emergency simulation exercises, laboratory preparedness and clear referral protocols. “Adequate financial resources must be released promptly to support these interventions rather than waiting until a confirmed case exposes weaknesses in our preparedness,” he said. The MP further called for timely and evidence-based public communication to educate Ghanaians on Ebola symptoms, preventive measures and appropriate reporting channels without creating unnecessary fear. He also urged stronger collaboration with the World Health Organisation, the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention and neighbouring countries to facilitate information sharing and coordinated responses. Dr Agyemang expressed concern about what he described as insufficient publicly demonstrated progress in addressing issues he raised in an earlier statement on March 27, 2026, regarding Ghana’s public health emergency preparedness. He called on the Minister for Health to provide Parliament and the public with a clear account of funds allocated, released and utilised for emergency preparedness, alongside evidence of operational improvements achieved since March. “Public health security must be measured by concrete action, not assurances alone,” he said. Dr Agyemang noted that no Ebola case had been confirmed in Ghana as of the latest official Ghanaian update cited in his statement, but cautioned against complacency. “Ghana must not wait for its first confirmed Ebola case before discovering gaps in its public health emergency response system,” he said.
