title: U.S. Navy to Build Hypersonic Weapon Facility at NWS Yorktown for Zumwalt and Virginia Classes
body: New Naval Facilities Engineering System Command (NAVFAC) documents reveal U.S. Navy plans for a hypersonic missile storage facility at NWS Yorktown to support CPS-equipped Zumwalt and Virginia classes. NAVFAC Mid-Atlantic has published its requirements for the construction of a new facility at Naval Weapons Station Yorktown, just north of Newport News Shipbuilding and the main Naval Station Norfolk base complex. Once completed, the facility will service Conventional Prompt Strike (CPS) weapons used aboard DDG-1000 Zumwalt -class destroyers and Block V and VI Virginia -class submarines. The facility seeks to accommodate the CPS’s larger size and diameter compared to current weapons in U.S. Navy service, representing a dedicated complex on the grounds of Naval Weapons Station Yorktown to handle operational, maintenance, and storage needs. The selection of Yorktown demonstrates the Navy’s need to support CPS-carrying vessels in the Atlantic, partially owing to the eventual stationing of Virginia Payload Module (VPM) equipped submarines at Norfolk, but also alluding to a Zumwalt -class destroyer potentially transitioning its home port to the East Coast. The posted contract stipulates the facility will contain one “Containerized Large Weapons Storage (CLWS) two-bay earth-covered magazine,” alongside two mechanical buildings to sustain climate control and electricity to the main storage area, and one emergency generator facility. Each bay contains one 25-ton bridge crane (two total) designed to move along an overhead rail, likely to transport CPS rounds and sub-components about the facility prior to loading or shipping. The requirements also stress the need for reinforcement and protection. Storage and support buildings forming part of the overall facility will feature “reinforced concrete mat foundations, walls, floors, roof, and entrance and loading aprons. It will include ordnance bonding, grounding and lightning protection systems, and earth covering.” The contract explicitly states the need for magazine protection, likely in the form of a concrete roof and partial burial with earth. CPS Aboard the Zumwalts USS Zumwalt’s front AGS lifted from the bow of the ship at Ingalls Shipbuilding during CPS conversion work, May 7, 2024. Credit: Official Facebook page of USS Zumwalt. For the Zumwalt class, the fielding of CPS can only happen after each of the three vessels completes an overhaul period, where components related to the gun emplacements are stripped out and replaced by CPS housings known as the Advanced Payload Module. Efforts to convert the Zumwalts to hypersonic missile carriers came after a string of missteps for the program, which ultimately led to construction halting at three vessels instead of the intended 32, effectively rendering the now-removed Advanced Gun Systems (AGS) obsolete. Delays and rising costs have plagued ongoing conversion efforts. A Government Accountability Office report published in July 2026 found that costs for DDG-1000 modernization efforts have risen by $200 million to approximately $2 billion. Construction and refitting periods have been complicated by the need for unplanned work and specialized equipment aboard the vessels. Ultimately, as a result of these delays, the first Zumwalt back in service will complete a CPS firing in 2027, nearly two years after the initially stated date. USS Zumwalt (DDG-1000) will experience a 10-month delay in returning to service, pushing the expected return date to later in 2026. Following the lead ship, USS Lyndon B. Johnson (DDG-1002) will be the second vessel to complete her overhaul (referred to as the Mission Systems Activation period) in Q4 of FY 2028, following a 12-to-15-month delay. Finally, USS Michael Monsoor (DDG-1001) will begin conversion work early in 2027 and will not return to service until Q3 of FY 2029. CPS Aboard the Virginias The first Virginia Payload Module (VPM) destined for the future USS Arizona. The VPM can be identified through the distinctive “hump” towards the front of the compartment. General Dynamics Electric Boat image. Only Block V and VI Virginia -class submarines will utilize CPS rounds through the installation of the Virginia Payload Module, which adds four additional Vertical Launch System canisters toward the middle of the submarine. Each of the four canisters can contain either seven Tomahawk-sized munitions or three CPS rounds, allowing for 12 CPS rounds total to be carried aboard each VPM-equipped submarine. Due to the extra missile capacity, the U.S. Navy has re-designated VPM equipped submarines as Nuclear Powered Cruise Missile carrying submarines (SSGNs). The U.S. Navy currently views installation and conversion efforts aboard the Zumwalts as risk mitigation for future endeavors to mount CPS aboard Virginia -class submarines, as both mounting systems share a large amount of commonality. If successful, the Virginias will avoid the same kind of delays currently impeding the Zumwalts , and the technology related to the CPS weapon system itself will likely mature by the time the first Block V Virginia enters service. Construction work remains ongoing as the Navy prepares to induct the first of nine VPM-equipped Block Vs in 2028 (the first Block V, USS Oklahoma (SSN-802), will not feature the VPM), with the commissioning of the future USS Arizona (SSN-803) expected in 2029. Naval News recently reported on photos posted depicting the first VPM during transit to General Dynamics Electric Boat’s main facility in Groton, Connecticut prior to final assembly. In total, 19 VPM equipped submarines, split along 9 Block Vs and 10 Block VIs, will enter service. The post U.S. Navy to Build Hypersonic Weapon Facility at NWS Yorktown for Zumwalt and Virginia Classes appeared first on Naval News .

title: First Lady Melania Trump Announces Halloween at the White House 2026
body: Office of the First Lady Briefings & Statements Search Select Category All News Briefings & Statements All Presidential Actions Executive Orders Nominations & Appointments Presidential Memoranda Proclamations Fact Sheets Releases Remarks Research All Briefings & Statements Presidential Actions All Executive Orders Nominations & Appointments Presidential Memoranda Proclamations Fact Sheets Releases Remarks Research On Thursday, October 29, 2026, First Lady Melania Trump and President Donald J. Trump will open the South Lawn of the White House to trick or treaters of all ages. During this special White House tradition, thousands of children and their parents will proceed around the South Lawn to visit various trick-or-treat booths and enjoy spooky decorations featuring the harvest Moon on the South Portico of the White House. The event will take place from 3:30 PM to 7:00 PM and is open to ticketholders, including military families, law enforcement families, foster and adoptive families, and Administration officials with children. The President and First Lady will hand out commemorative candies on the South Drive for a portion of the event. Adding to the festivities and fun, the United States (U.S.) Air Force Strolling Strings will play traditional Halloween songs and modern tunes while the President and First Lady welcome children and families. Throughout the evening, the U.S. Postal Service will provide toy mail trucks and facilitate a BE BEST post card station for children. The U.S. Department of Agriculture will have a giant pumpkin photo opportunity and hand out mini pumpkins from American farmers. The U.S. Department of the Treasury will share coloring books as part of its promotion of Trump Accounts for young trick or treaters. The International Fresh Produce Association will provide apples from Michigan, and the National Confectioners Association will provide sweet treats to trick or treaters. The event will also feature participation and treats by America 250, National Aeronautics and Space Administration, National Park Service, U.S. Mint, U.S. Secret Service, and the Center of Science and Industry—which is providing a STEAM science-experiment kit for children. Please note that the U.S. Secret Service reserves the right to prohibit personal items, including but not limited to those mentioned at www.secretservice.gov/prohibiteditems . Strollers, wheelchairs, umbrellas (no metal tips), and cameras are permitted. All items needed for medical purposes will be permitted on the tour (such as wheelchairs, electric scooters, glucose tablets, and EpiPens). Please identify and explain all items needed for medical purposes to Secret Service agents upon arrival. This event will not be rescheduled if canceled due to inclement weather or any other reason. title: Russia promises “favorable conditions” to European firms a month after seizing control of Nestlé and Auchan
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Russian President Vladimir Putin claimed Russia is trying to create “favorable conditions” for European companies that stayed in the country, The Moscow Times reported . He said it on state TV weeks after his decrees put several of the largest Western businesses in Russia under Kremlin-appointed managers. Meanwhile, Russia’s own government expects investment to fall at the fastest pace in over a decade. To keep paying for its full-scale war against Ukraine, Russia has drained reserves, borrowed more, and raised taxes. Its war spending will still rise by 27% next year, as the EU moved this month to adopt its largest sanctions package against Russia’s war industry. Fresh foreign money could ease that squeeze, and the Kremlin keeps scaring it away. Putin: Europe’s companies left Russia in tears Putin made the claim in an interview with Kremlin propagandist Pavel Zarubin, which Russian state outlet Vesti published on 25 October. He claimed Russia has “many friends in Europe,” but European governments forced their businesses out: “ When some companies were leaving us under pressure from Western European governments, our friends from these countries nearly cried… Some of them, by the way, are working, and we are trying to create appropriate favorable conditions for them .” He also attacked Western sanctions, calling it stupid to ban “ everything that comes from Russia .” The decrees came first On 17 September, Putin’s decree handed the Russian assets of Nestlé, Auchan, and the former Leroy Merlin chain to a firm run by an Interior Ministry major general. US packaging maker Aptar and German wholesaler Metro followed. In mid-October, Russia seized French flooring maker Tarkett and four more foreign-owned firms. Explore further “A warning to companies that remain”: Russia takes control of Nestlé and Auchan’s assets – companies that stayed in Russia following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine The Kremlin claimed their home countries are “actively involved” in fighting Russia, and Putin cited his 2023 decree on retaliating for Western moves against Russian property. Since the full-scale war began, Russia has put 135 foreign-linked firms under such management. Asked which European companies could be next, a senior Russian official said : “ Let them be scared .” Metro reportedly asked to be taken over itself, hoping to keep more control over its fate. “We don’t steal,” Putin said three weeks earlier In early October, Putin denied that the takeovers amounted to seizures. At the Valdai Discussion Club on 1 October, he claimed : “ We take nothing from anyone, we don’t steal, and we don’t nationalize… Yes, we place some enterprises under external management .” Russia’s investment drop is the worst since 2015 Putin has demanded an urgent new “investment cycle.” Instead, his economy ministry expects investment to shrink by 5.4% this year. Russian authorities have seized assets worth 7.6 trillion rubles (about $95 billion) from their owners during the war, law firm NSP estimates. More than half of large Russian companies ended 2025 with lower profits and cut or froze investment projects. Explore further Two rubles for the army for every one on welfare, schools, and hospitals: Russia’s 2027 wartime budget Ukrainian long-range strikes add to the risk of building anything in Russia. Overnight on 26 October, drones attacked a Voronezh aircraft plant that makes parts for Russia’s military transport planes. A day earlier, drones reportedly hit a titanium plant in Perm Krai, and Storm Shadow missiles reportedly struck a battery plant in Yelets supplying Russia’s missiles and glide bombs. title: Redefining Africa’s Infrastructure: The role of technology in connecting infrastructure system
body: The asset-by-asset era is ending Infrastructure is becoming a connected system—not a collection of stand-alone assets. Roads, power, water, digital networks and logistics must increasingly work together. That shift will determine how economies scale, how reliably essential services perform and how communities thrive. PwC’s Global Infrastructure Outlook 2025-50 report anticipates that, by 2050, infrastructure will be shaped by electrification, data, automation and circular resource flows. Roads could support autonomous vehicles, dynamic pricing and wireless charging. Airports could become predictive, intermodal hubs for drones and electrified aircraft. Across sectors, intelligent systems could anticipate demand, allocate resources and lift productivity. Stop-start funding carries a long-term cost Integration demands consistency. Yet “boom-and-bust” funding cycles continue to weaken long-term planning, delivery capacity and skills—especially in capital-intensive sectors such as rail. PwC’s Rail Outlook 2050 Report points to a practical response: more consistent and predictable medium- to long-term investment planning by governments and their stakeholders. Technology is now core infrastructure There is no credible path to deeper integration without technology. PwC’s Global Data Centre Outlook 2026 – 2050 report estimates that global data-centre capital expenditure could reach US$31.6 trillion through 2050, with a plausible upside of nearly US$50 trillion if AI adoption accelerates. The opportunity extends beyond capacity. Data and AI can connect transport, energy, water and digital assets; improve real-time decisions; optimise resources; and strengthen resilience. Five moves can unlock the next wave Contract for outcomes. Make sustainability, impact, resilience and reliability central to commercial models. Innovate finance and partnerships. Public budgets cannot carry the requirement alone. Sharper risk-sharing, faster routes to bankability and stronger public-private delivery models are essential. Redesign planning and construction. Co-design, co-locate and co-optimise assets across sectors. Build with more sustainable and circular practices. Plan beyond the political cycle. Clear national and regional strategies, backed by stable regulation, can turn ambition into investable pipelines. Engage communities early—and often. Infrastructure creates value only when intended outcomes are realised by the people it serves. Every actor has a move to make Governments must create enabling regulation, transparent pipelines and credible financing frameworks. Investors must track the changing risk-return landscape and direct capital towards sectors with durable growth. Corporations must pursue cross-sector partnerships and use technology to adapt. Communities must help shape priorities and delivery. In Conclusion Africa’s infrastructure opportunity is not simply to build more. It is to connect better. Political stability, policy consistency, regulatory certainty and disciplined execution will determine whether integrated infrastructure attracts capital—and converts it into inclusive, sustained growth. Achieving this future will require leadership. Leaders must convert vision into value through clear, actionable plans. They must make difficult choices, direct scarce resources to the highest-impact projects and act with clarity and speed. They must also be prepared to adopt non-traditional models where the evidence shows they work.

title: DAC clears defence procurement proposals worth $22.28 billion; 82% to be sourced from Indian industry
body:
New Delhi, Oct 26. The Defence Acquisition Council (DAC), chaired by Defence Minister Rajnath Singh, on October 26 accorded Acceptance of Necessity (AoN) to capital acquisition proposals worth approximately ₹2.12 lakh crore ($22.28 billion) for the Indian Army, Navy and Air Force, with around 82 percent of the planned procurements to be sourced from the domestic defence industry.



The approvals cover a wide range of military equipment, including artillery systems, helicopters, air defence weapons, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), counter-drone systems, naval platforms and weather surveillance radars. The proposed acquisitions are aimed at strengthening the operational mobility, surveillance, firepower, air defence and combat capabilities of the three services.

AoN represents in-principle approval for a proposed acquisition and precedes subsequent procurement procedures, including the formulation of requirements, tendering and contract negotiations, as applicable.

For the Indian Army, the DAC approved proposals for high mobility vehicles (HMVs), a self-propelled tracked gun system, a gun-shot response system (GSRS), light multi role helicopters (LMRH), very short-range air defence systems (VSHORADS), a platform-based counter-unmanned aerial system (C-UAS), long-range unmanned aerial systems, surveillance UAVs, an integrated surveillance and strike system and a long-range Kamikaze drone system.

The proposed acquisition of HMVs is intended to improve the Army’s mobility, logistical support and ability to operate in challenging terrain. The self-propelled tracked gun system is expected to provide mechanised formations with artillery firepower and mobility suited to their operational requirements.

The GSRS will function as a force multiplier by providing real-time situational awareness, while the LMRHs are intended for use by both the Army and the Air Force. Their planned roles include reconnaissance and surveillance, combat operations, search and rescue of troops, and humanitarian assistance and disaster relief.

The proposed VSHORADS acquisition is designed to address emerging aerial threats, particularly small, next-generation targets. The platform-based C-UAS capability is intended to improve the survivability of tanks against unmanned aerial threats on the modern battlefield.

The Army’s proposed surveillance and drone systems, including long-range and kamikaze drone capabilities, are expected to enhance reconnaissance, target acquisition and strike capabilities, supporting more effective operations against emerging battlefield threats.

For the Indian Navy, the DAC granted AoN for an Active Offboard Decoy System (AODS) and other major naval platforms. The AODS is intended to strengthen the Navy’s anti-missile defence by improving the ability of ships to counter modern anti-ship missiles. By deploying decoys away from the vessel, the system is designed to divert incoming missile threats and improve the effectiveness of a ship's defensive measures.

The proposed major naval platforms, designed and constructed indigenously, are expected to incorporate modern warfare capabilities and enhance the Navy’s overall combat potential. The emphasis on domestic design and construction also aligns with the government's broader efforts to expand India’s indigenous naval shipbuilding and defence manufacturing capabilities.

For the Indian Air Force, the council approved acquisition proposals covering helicopters, air defence systems, weapons and a mobile X-band Doppler weather radar system. These procurements are intended to strengthen air defence and war-fighting capabilities while addressing operational and logistical requirements.

The proposed Special Utility Helicopters will help the IAF meet essential air transport needs. Meanwhile, the mobile X-Band Doppler weather radar system is expected to provide high-resolution, localised weather surveillance in forward areas, helping aircrews and operational commanders assess weather conditions and plan missions more effectively.

The emphasis on domestic procurement is a major feature of the latest approvals. With approximately 82 percent of the total proposed acquisitions earmarked for sourcing from Indian industry, the decisions are expected to support domestic defence manufacturers and suppliers, encourage greater indigenous production and contribute to the development of local defence technology and supply chains.

The approvals span both conventional military capabilities and emerging areas of warfare, including unmanned systems, counter-drone technology and advanced surveillance. Together, they reflect the armed forces’ efforts to adapt to changing operational requirements while strengthening their equipment base.

The ₹2.12 lakh crore ($22.28 billion) package represents the estimated value of proposals receiving in-principle approval, rather than the value of contracts already signed. The proposals will proceed through the applicable acquisition process before individual procurement contracts are concluded.

title: Crawl, Walk, Run: A Practical Path to TSN Adoption in Aerospace and Defense
body:
Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) is appearing in aerospace and defense requirements almost as if it were a box engineers can simply check: add TSN, get a deterministic network. It’s not that simple.
Current military platforms are moving toward connected architectures in which sensors, processors, mission systems, flight controls, and other subsystems share data over Ethernet. But conventional Ethernet is built around best-effort delivery: It moves data efficiently but does not guarantee that a critical message will arrive within a precise time window every time. TSN can solve this problem.
TSN adds the timing, synchronization, and traffic-management tools needed to make Ethernet more predictable, all traits that make TSN a strong candidate for the digital backbones of future aerospace and defense platforms.
The mistake would be assuming that every part of a platform should move to TSN at once. A better approach is to crawl, then walk, and then run.
Start with the problem, not the technology
The first step is deciding where deterministic networking is needed. Not every message on a military platform is time-critical. Some data can arrive a little earlier or later without affecting the mission, and standard Ethernet is perfectly suitable for that kind of traffic.
Other data is different: A control message, synchronized sensor input, or other time-sensitive information may have strict limits on latency, jitter, or delivery time. Those tasks are the places where TSN can provide real value.
This distinction is important because TSN is not simply an Ethernet switch feature – a deterministic network has to be designed as a system. The processors that create and receive the data must support the required TSN functions. The switches between them must also participate. Engineers need to understand which messages matter, where they travel, how quickly they must arrive, and how they should be handled when the network is busy.
That deeper knowledge requires network modeling and careful configuration of paths, queues, buffers, timing, and traffic priorities.
The larger the TSN footprint, the more complex the job becomes. This fact is why trying to put an entire platform onto TSN from the beginning can create unnecessary risk.
The best place to begin is with a contained problem that clearly benefits from predictable Ethernet traffic. Mission systems are a natural example: They can rely on time-sensitive data but generally present much lower burdens of proof than flight-critical avionics.
One possible application is replacing a legacy point-to-point interface. This dedicated connection is naturally predictable because the two devices communicate directly. Moving that traffic onto a shared Ethernet network introduces uncertainty. Other traffic may compete for the same network resources, changing how long a message takes to arrive.
In this case, TSN can restore predictable timing while still enabling the data to travel across a shared network. That does not mean every dedicated connection should be replaced. Consider a radar producing very large amounts of data between a sensor and its processor: If that traffic already travels efficiently over a dedicated point-to-point link, moving it onto a shared TSN backbone may offer little benefit. It could instead consume large amounts of network capacity and make the overall architecture harder to manage.
The goal should not be to find places to use TSN; instead, it should be to find problems that TSN is well-suited to solve. Small, well-defined deployments also give engineering teams practical experience with configuration, network modeling, tools, and integration before those same ideas are applied more broadly.
Walk: Build determinism across the data path
As programs and users gain experience, they can expand TSN into larger parts of the architecture. This is where end-to-end design becomes critical, as a TSN-capable switch by itself does not create a deterministic system. The processors sending and receiving data must operate within the same timing and traffic-management scheme. The network needs to understand which messages have strict requirements and which can continue to use ordinary best-effort Ethernet.
That mixed approach is one of TSN's strengths. Time-sensitive and conventional traffic can share the same network without forcing every device or message to behave the same way, and engineers can apply deterministic behavior only where needed.
As the architecture grows, interoperability becomes more important. TSN includes many capabilities and configuration options, and if vendors make different choices about how those capabilities are implemented, components may technically support TSN while still being difficult to integrate.
The IEEE 802.1DP Aerospace Profile helps address that integration problem by narrowing the range of choices around the needs of embedded aerospace networks. The goal is greater consistency across equipment and a clearer foundation for interoperability.
This strategy also fits naturally with the modular open systems approach (MOSA) and the Sensor Open Systems Architecture®, or SOSA®, Technical Standard. Open architectures make it easier to integrate and upgrade components from different suppliers. TSN can add predictable timing to the Ethernet networks connecting those modular elements.
Run: Expand without assuming everything belongs on one network
The long-term opportunity is broader use of deterministic Ethernet across the platform. Broader does not have to mean universal; after all, military platforms are systems of systems. Mission computing, sensors, weapons, platform controls, communications, propulsion, and flight-critical avionics can have very different requirements.
Some of these components may need strict isolation. Some may require redundancy, while others may need to meet demanding cybersecurity or safety-certification requirements.
When TSN moves toward flight-critical applications, the situation can get even more complicated. Safety-critical avionics require a much higher level of design assurance than most mission systems do. Engineers must be able to show that network behavior remains predictable and safe under failure conditions and changing system loads. A configurable shared network can make that task much harder.
While all of that does not mean TSN cannot eventually support those applications, it does mean that programs should build the necessary experience before taking on the hardest use cases.
A practical TSN strategy begins with a few basic questions: Which data needs deterministic delivery? What are its latency and timing requirements? Which systems need to communicate? Where can conventional Ethernet remain in place? Which legacy interfaces should be retained rather than replaced?
Only when these questions are answered should engineers decide which parts of the architecture need TSN.
Tools also make the process easier. Network-modeling software can help teams define traffic requirements and determine how switches, endpoints, paths, and queues should be configured, and directly deploy those configurations. Additionally, test environments enable engineers to experiment with TSN before introducing it onto an operational platform.
Curtiss-Wright is applying this end-to-end approach with a SOSA aligned 3U VPX demonstration system which combines TSN-enabled processing and TSN-aware networking with non-TSN processing as a single architecture. The demonstration, which will be shown at the Aerospace and Defense TSN Summit (Oct 20-23, Novi, MI), will run TSN-enabled and non-TSN data streams across the same network and show what happens as the network becomes congested, so customers can see how different Ethernet traffic types behave when the network is under load. Demonstrations like these reinforce the lesson of the crawl, walk, run approach: deploy TSN where TSN adds deterministic value, and that a phased approach to integrating TSN will ease the path to wider TSN adoption across the industry.
TSN has the potential to give aerospace and defense programs the predictable Ethernet communications they increasingly need. The fastest route to that future may be taking one step at a time before jumping in headfirst.
