title: ‘Wings Over Ganges’: IAF showcases indigenous air power and tri-service jointness at Varanasi Air Show
body:
By Aroonim Bhuyan

Varanasi. Nearly 100 aircraft from 12 air bases, six frontline fighter types in a landmark arrowhead formation, and aerobatic displays by the Surya Kiran and Sarang teams marked the Indian Air Force’s 94th-anniversary celebrations over the Ganga from October 22 to 25.



The Indian Air Force (IAF) staged a spectacular aerial display over the Ganga at Varanasi from October 22 to 25, bringing together frontline fighter aircraft, combat helicopters, strategic transport platforms and elite aerobatic teams in a showcase of India's military aviation capabilities.



Organised by the IAF’s Central Air Command under the theme ‘Wings Over Ganges’, the event marked 94 years of the service and highlighted its operational capabilities, growing emphasis on indigenous defence technology and the importance of coordination among the Army, Navy and Air Force. Held at Namo Ghat, the display was the first IAF aerial show over the Ganga in Varanasi and culminated on October 25 with Prime Minister Narendra Modi attending as the chief guest.



The spectacle brought together approximately 100 aircraft – 52 fighter aircraft, 32 helicopters and 15 transport aircraft, along with a heritage aircraft. The platforms came from 12 air bases across the country, with aircraft from the Indian Army and Indian Navy also participating. Beyond the visual spectacle, the programme presented a broad picture of modern air power, encompassing air combat, surveillance, aerial refuelling, tactical and strategic transport, and coordinated operations across the three services.



The concluding day’s event was attended by Defence Minister Rajnath Singh, Uttar Pradesh Governor Anandiben Patel, Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath and senior military officers. Modi described the display as “Magnificent!” in a post on X. The occasion also served as a public outreach initiative, intended to familiarise citizens with the IAF's capabilities and encourage young Indians to consider careers in the armed forces.

Six frontline fighter types in a landmark arrowhead formation

One of the most striking highlights of ‘Wings Over Ganges’ was the formation of six frontline fighter types – the Rafale, Su-30MKI, Jaguar, Mirage 2000, Tejas and MiG-29 – in a single arrowhead. This was the first time these six aircraft types had flown together in such a formation during a public IAF display.



The French-origin Rafale is a modern multirole fighter equipped for air superiority, precision strikes and complex missions involving advanced sensors and electronic warfare. The Russian-origin Su-30MKI provides long-range reach, substantial weapons-carrying capacity and multirole combat capability.

The Mirage 2000 and MiG-29 remain important components of the IAF’s combat fleet, while the Jaguar has traditionally served as a deep-penetration strike aircraft. The indigenous Light Combat Aircraft (LCA) Tejas represents India's effort to develop and manufacture modern combat aircraft domestically.

The six-aircraft formation was significant not merely because of its visual impact, but because it brought together different generations and categories of fighter aircraft in a single coordinated display. It demonstrated the pilots’ formation-flying skills while highlighting the breadth of the IAF’s combat aviation capabilities.

The event also featured a simulated combat sequence involving Jaguar and Su-30MKI aircraft, adding an operational dimension to the programme. Such demonstrations offer spectators an insight into aircraft manoeuvrability and tactical coordination, although they are not substitutes for combat exercises or operational-readiness assessments.



Indigenous Tejas and Prachand underline defence self-reliance

The participation of Tejas and the Light Combat Helicopter (LCH) Prachand gave the show particular relevance amid India’s drive towards ‘Atmanirbhar Bharat’ (Self-reliant India) in defence production.

Developed by Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL), Tejas represents a long-term effort to establish Indian expertise in the design, development and manufacture of combat aircraft. The programme has contributed to domestic capabilities in airframe design, flight-control systems, avionics and aerospace engineering.

The Prachand, also developed by HAL, is designed for combat operations in demanding environments, including high-altitude terrain. Its presence highlighted the importance of developing platforms suited to India's distinctive geographical and security requirements.

Indigenous aerospace programmes offer benefits beyond reducing reliance on imports. They can strengthen domestic supply chains, support specialised manufacturers, create skilled employment and provide opportunities to develop technologies that can be upgraded over time.

However, self-reliance remains a continuing process. Advanced combat aviation requires dependable engines, sophisticated sensors, electronic warfare systems, weapons integration and high-quality production facilities. Indigenous platforms must therefore be supported by sustained research, industrial investment and timely delivery programmes.

The Varanasi show placed these domestic platforms alongside foreign-origin aircraft that continue to play important roles in the IAF. This reflected the practical challenge of modernising the fleet while progressively expanding India's own aerospace capabilities.

Surya Kiran and Sarang provide the aerial spectacle

The Surya Kiran Aerobatic Team and the Sarang Helicopter Display Team were among the most anticipated attractions of the programme, demonstrating precision flying through synchronised manoeuvres and carefully coordinated formations.

The Surya Kiran Aerobatic Team, flying Hawk Mk-132 jet trainers, performed aerobatic routines featuring close formations, loops, rolls and other demanding manoeuvres. The team’s use of smoke in the colours of the Indian national flag added a ceremonial dimension to its performance.

Flying in close formation requires exceptional concentration, disciplined execution and precise control of speed, altitude and aircraft separation. Although aerobatic flying is different from combat operations, the display demonstrates the professionalism and flying skills developed through rigorous training.

The Sarang Helicopter Display Team, operating the indigenous Advanced Light Helicopter Dhruv, showcased the agility of rotary-wing aircraft. Its performances involved coordinated manoeuvres that highlighted the handling characteristics of helicopters and the importance of close cooperation among pilots.

Together, the two teams illustrated different dimensions of military aviation: high-speed precision flying by jet aircraft and tightly coordinated manoeuvres by helicopters. Their performances also helped make the event accessible to a wider audience, particularly young people interested in aviation and careers in the armed forces.

Special formations blend military aviation with Varanasi's heritage

A distinctive feature of ‘Wings Over Ganges’ was the use of formation names drawn from Varanasi's cultural, religious and geographical identity. The programme included formations such as ‘Kashi’, ‘Varun’, ‘Kedar’, ‘Hanuman’, ‘Omkar’, ‘Rudra’ and ‘Bhagirathi’.

The ‘Kashi’ formation featured three Kiran trainer aircraft flying in a V-shaped arrangement, displaying the colours of the national flag. In the ‘Omkar’ formation, Mi-17 helicopters carried the Tricolour and the Air Force flag, combining ceremonial imagery with coordinated flying.

Another highlight was the ‘Tridev’ formation, which brought together helicopters from the Indian Army, Indian Navy and IAF. The formation featured the Navy’s Kamov-31 helicopter, an IAF Advanced Light Helicopter Mk-III and an Army ALH Mk-III.

These formations gave the programme a distinct identity. Instead of presenting a conventional flypast alone, the IAF connected its aerial manoeuvres with the history and symbolism of the city hosting the event.

The setting above the Ganga added to the spectacle, allowing the aircraft and helicopters to be viewed against the riverfront and the ghats. The result was a combination of military precision and cultural symbolism that distinguished the event from a conventional air-base display.

Army-Navy-Air Force participation highlights jointness

The participation of aircraft from the Indian Army and Indian Navy alongside those of the Air Force underscored the growing importance of jointness in India's defence planning.

The Navy’s P-8I maritime patrol aircraft also participated in the programme, flying in a formation with Mirage 2000 fighters. The P-8I performs maritime surveillance and anti-submarine warfare missions, contributing to India's ability to monitor activity across its maritime approaches.

The different platforms illustrated how the three services contribute complementary capabilities. The Army’s aviation assets support operations involving ground forces, the Navy operates aircraft and helicopters for maritime missions, and the IAF provides combat aviation, air defence, transport and other support capabilities.

In modern warfare, these capabilities must increasingly work together. Surveillance information, communications, intelligence and command arrangements need to be coordinated so that commanders can deploy the appropriate assets at the right time.

The ‘Tridev’ formation offered a visible illustration of inter-service cooperation, although the wider process of jointness also requires integrated planning, compatible communications, clearly defined command responsibilities and coordinated training.

The broader significance is that India’s security challenges extend across land borders, maritime approaches and the wider Indo-Pacific region. Closer cooperation among the armed services can help improve situational awareness, logistics and the effective use of military resources.

Transport aircraft, surveillance platforms demonstrate operational reach

The display included transport aircraft such as the C-17 Globemaster III, C-130J Super Hercules, C-295 and AN-32, alongside platforms that support surveillance and aerial refuelling.

These aircraft perform functions that are essential to the effectiveness of a modern air force but may receive less public attention than fighter jets.

 	C-17 Globemaster III: Provides strategic airlift capacity for moving personnel and heavy equipment over long distances.
 	C-130J Super Hercules: Supports tactical transport and operations requiring flexibility in the use of airfields.
 	C-295: Represents a newer generation of tactical transport aircraft and an important element of India's aerospace manufacturing ambitions.
 	AN-32: Has long supported tactical transport and logistical operations, including in difficult terrain.
 	IL-78 tanker: Provides aerial refuelling capability, extending the endurance and operational reach of compatible aircraft.
 	Airborne Early Warning and Control platforms: Help detect and track aerial activity, improving situational awareness for commanders.

The inclusion of these assets broadened the message of the show. Modern air power depends not only on aircraft capable of engaging an adversary, but also on the surveillance, logistics and support systems that enable combat platforms to operate effectively.

Public outreach and a major logistical undertaking

The IAF described the event as an opportunity to showcase its capabilities and encourage young Indians to consider careers in the armed forces. Air Vice Marshal PVS Narayana highlighted public outreach and recruitment inspiration among the objectives of the programme.

The scale of the event required substantial arrangements for security, traffic management and crowd control. According to reports, around 11,900 personnel were deployed, with the city divided into zones and sectors to facilitate security and crowd management.

The display was held on October 22, 24 and 25, with no show on October 23 because of Uttar Pradesh Legislative Council elections. The final day’s programme was attended by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, accompanied by senior political and military leaders.

The venue was also significant. Varanasi is known for its historic riverfront and religious heritage, making it a prominent setting for an event designed to connect the armed forces with the public. The aerial display provided an opportunity to explain the technological sophistication, training and coordination required to operate a modern air force.

A celebration of heritage and modern military capability

‘Wings Over Ganges’ brought together the Indian Air Force’s frontline combat aircraft, indigenous platforms, transport and surveillance assets, and specialist aerobatic teams in a distinctive setting over the Ganga. The six-fighter arrowhead formation, the performances by Surya Kiran and Sarang, and the participation of Army and Navy aircraft were among the event’s principal highlights.

The show also reflected wider priorities in India's defence policy: strengthening indigenous manufacturing, maintaining a diverse and capable combat fleet, and improving coordination among the three services.

While an aerial display cannot by itself establish an air force’s combat readiness, it can demonstrate the range of aircraft, flying skills and support capabilities that contribute to military effectiveness. For the public, the event offered a rare opportunity to see those capabilities in action.

Ultimately, the Varanasi air show was both a celebration of the IAF’s 94-year history and a public demonstration of India's evolving air power. By combining advanced military aviation with the cultural symbolism of the Ganga, ‘Wings Over Ganges’ presented a compelling portrait of a service balancing its institutional heritage with the demands of modern national defence.

title: New Tajikistan Migration Law Aims to Improve Overseas Recruitment
body: Tajikistan has adopted a new migration law that introduces a system for rating foreign employers and provides for assistance to citizens returning from work abroad. The legislation also seeks to make it easier for Tajik citizens to find jobs overseas through official recruitment channels. President Emomali Rahmon signed the law on October 21, and the full text was published on October 23 by the parliamentary newspaper Sadoi Mardum . It replaces legislation dating back to 1999. According to the World Bank, approximately one-quarter of Tajikistan’s labor force works outside the country. Between 2022 and 2025, migrant remittances averaged nearly half of the country’s gross domestic product. Russia remains the main destination for labor migration. What the New Law Changes Under the new law, Tajikistan’s migration authorities will establish a register of foreign employers, with ratings based on their treatment of workers, including wages and working conditions. Migrants will be able to submit complaints, which will be considered when employers are assessed. The authorities will also have the power to restrict cooperation with companies that violate workers’ rights. The legislation also provides for online platforms where migrants can find vacancies and sign employment contracts electronically. Citizens who arrange their own employment abroad, rather than using recruitment agencies, are entitled to free advice from migration officials about vacancies and working conditions in their destination country. Another provision requires the authorities to set quotas for workers going to different countries and determine how the system will operate. The law also establishes a unified information system to improve migration records and data exchange between government agencies. Many of these measures focus on organized recruitment, which currently accounts for only a small proportion of Tajikistan’s labor migration. In 2025, a total of 35,747 Tajik citizens found jobs abroad through 30 licensed organizations, including more than 31,000 in Russia. According to official figures from Dushanbe, more than 702,000 people left the country to work abroad that year. Although the figures are not directly comparable, placements through licensed agencies amounted to only around 5% of reported departures. Russia and the Search for Alternatives Following the terrorist attack at Crocus City Hall near Moscow in March 2024, Russian authorities tightened migration controls. A register of foreign nationals without legal grounds to remain in Russia has been in operation since February 2025. Those listed face restrictions on financial transactions and property registration. In July 2026, Tajikistan’s Deputy Minister of Labor, Migration, and Employment of the Population Sharif Norzoda reported that approximately 160,000 Tajik citizens were on the register, including about 25,000 minors. During discussions of the new legislation, Labor Minister Soleha Kholmahmadzoda stressed the need to expand the range of countries where Tajik citizens can find work. Dushanbe is holding talks on employment opportunities in Kazakhstan, the Gulf states, South Korea, Japan, and the United Kingdom. However, Russia’s labor market remains considerably larger than those of these alternative destinations. Jobs for Returning Migrants The new law provides for assistance to citizens returning home, including vocational training and help finding employment. It also envisages support programs for families whose migrant breadwinner is no longer able to provide for them. The practical implementation of these measures will depend on government programs and available funding. Employment opportunities within Tajikistan remain limited, although some businesses are experiencing labor shortages. In an interview with the news agency Asia-Plus , economist Rakhmon Ulmasov said that, according to his information, the construction site at the Rogun Hydropower Plant was short of approximately 3,000 workers , while a textile enterprise in Danghara needed another 500 employees. He proposed training returning migrants in occupations that are in demand in Tajikistan. According to the World Bank, Tajikistan will need approximately 1.4 million jobs over the next decade. Reforms supported by the bank are expected to create more than 92,000 additional jobs by 2030, although this estimate covers the effects of those reforms rather than total projected employment growth nationwide.

title: Nana Yaa Jantuah calls for sanctions over leaked GTA memo involving Maame Efua Houadjeto and Abeiku Santana
body: Presidential Staffer Nana Yaa Jantuah has called for sanctions against the person who leaked an internal memo involving Ghana Tourism Authority (GTA) Chief Executive Officer Maame Efua Houadjeto and her deputy, Abeiku Santana, insisting that confidential official correspondence must not be released without authorisation. She said the disclosure raised serious concerns about the handling of official information within the public service and urged the relevant authorities to establish how the document found its way into the public domain. Speaking on JoyNews’ AM Show on Monday, October 26, Nana Jantuah questioned the motive behind the leak, saying that internal disagreements should be addressed through the appropriate channels rather than exposed publicly. “This is an internal memo. And once it’s an internal communication, whoever brought it out has to be sanctioned,” she said. “I do not think that it’s something that should even have come out like that. So I ask myself who brought out the letter in the public domain. What does the person seek to achieve?” She said the public disclosure of such correspondence could undermine the standards expected of public officials, particularly when the information had not been authorised for release. Referring to the code of ethics governing the public service, she said that staff had a responsibility to protect internal communications. “Because within the code of ethics of the public service, information that is internal, if not authorised, should not be put out,” she stated. The presidential staffer also questioned how the document could have been obtained by the media, suggesting that someone with access to the correspondence may have shared it without permission. When asked whether a journalist could have intercepted the memo, Ms Jantuah challenged the suggestion and called for scrutiny of the procedures for handling official documents. “How do you intercept it? Then it means that the assistants are loose,” she said. She said that the document was unlikely to have reached the public without the involvement of someone familiar with the internal workings of the institutions concerned. “Within the public service, if you are working in there, somebody should have given it to you. You can’t just intercept it. How did you intercept it? Did you catch it in the sky or something?” she asked. She said the possibility that someone within the relevant offices had disclosed the correspondence was troubling and warranted attention. “Somebody within the relevant secretariat could have given it to you. Between the ministry and the GTA. And that is troublesome,” she added. This follows a letter from the Deputy Chief Executive Officer of the Ghana Tourism Authority (GTA) in charge of Marketing and Special Duties, Gilbert Abeiku Aggrey aka Santana , sent to the Minister of Tourism, Culture and Creative Arts, Abla Dzifa Gomashie, raising concerns about difficulties accessing GTA Chief Executive Officer Maame Efua Houadjeto for official consultations. Mrs Houadjeto responded by defending her approach to staff engagement and proposing measures to improve communication and coordination between their offices.

title: Two men found dead near Tel Aviv senior living center in suspected murder-suicide
body: Two men were found dead with gunshot wounds on Moshe Dayan Road in Tel Aviv on Monday morning, after one allegedly shot the other dead and then took his own life, according to the initial investigation.The two were brothers, one in his 50s and the other in his 70s. They were found near a senior citizens' center and the entrance to a bank branch. A handgun was located near the scene.Magen David Adom (MDA) teams called to the scene found the two unconscious, without a pulse and not breathing, and pronounced them dead at the scene.Residents call emergency services, initially fearing terror attackA report of two people injured at the location was received at 9:32 a.m. at MDA's 101 emergency call center in the Dan region. Medics and paramedics dispatched to the scene found the two lying in the street, unconscious, without a pulse and not breathing. After conducting medical examinations, they were forced to pronounce them dead at the scene.A resident who lives nearby told Walla that the sound of the gunfire initially made her fear a terror attack.“I heard gunshots under the building. At first I locked the windows; I thought maybe it was a terror attack, maybe there's a terrorist downstairs, and suddenly it was quiet and full of ambulances. I ran downstairs to understand what happened, and suddenly I saw two men lying dead on the sidewalk. There's nothing as scary as that, to see such a difficult sight first thing in the morning. My whole body is still shaking; I can't believe it.”“We arrived at the scene quickly and saw two men lying in the street, unconscious, without a pulse and not breathing, with penetrating wounds on their bodies," MDA motorcycle unit emergency medical technician Meir Grossman said. "We performed medical examinations and were forced to pronounce their deaths at the scene.”Police said a report was received at the 100 emergency hotline about a shooting incident on Moshe Dayan Street in Tel Aviv, during which two people were shot and killed.Officers from the South Tel Aviv station and police investigators arrived at the scene, and police opened an investigation to determine the circumstances of the incident. The investigation is still ongoing as of press time.

title: Ukraine’s parliament votes to extend martial law
body:
MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. The Verkhovna Rada has voted to extend martial law in Ukraine for another 90 days starting October 31. The parliamentary session was broadcast live on the parliament’s television channel.
The decision was supported by 293 lawmakers. This was the 21st time parliament had voted to extend martial law.
Martial law is set to remain in force until January 29, 2027.
Martial law and general mobilization were introduced in Ukraine on February 24, 2022. This will mark the 21st extension of these measures. Due to the ongoing extensions of martial law and mobilization, Ukraine holds no parliamentary, presidential, or local elections. Meanwhile, Zelensky’s term in office officially expired on May 20, 2024.

title: Zelenskyy expects MFA, Energy Ministry to communicate on replenishing energy equipment reserves
body:
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy expects timely communication from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Energy, and other involved structures regarding the replenishment of equipment reserves needed to restore energy infrastructure following Russian strikes.

"Work is ongoing practically without interruption, and the created equipment reserves are being utilized. I am counting on timely and sufficient communication from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine, the Ministry of Energy, and other involved structures regarding the replenishment of these reserves," Zelenskyy wrote on his Telegram channel on Monday.

According to him, the situation regarding the restoration of the energy sector following Russian attacks was also discussed during a conference call. Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky reported on operations in the regions.

Zelenskyy thanked repair crews and energy companies for fulfilling their assigned tasks.

title: Krobo Girls’ Presbyterian SHS launches centenary cloth to celebrate 100 years of excellence
body: Krobo Girls’ Presbyterian Senior High School has launched its Centenary Cloth and a new Krobo Old Girls Association (KOGA) cloth as part of activities to celebrate the school’s century-long legacy of academic excellence and women’s empowerment. The launch, held on Saturday, October 24, 2026, at the Cecilia Obenewah Appiah Hall, brought together school authorities, clergy, students, old students and other guests to commemorate the institution’s contribution to quality education. Held under the theme, “Celebrating a Century of Excellence: A Legacy of Empowering Young Women Through Quality Education,” the event highlighted the school’s commitment to nurturing generations of young women through education. The ceremony was chaired by Mercy Naa Kwaakor Ampah-Bennin, while the school’s Headmistress, Bernice Noel Mensah-Akutteh, hosted the event. Patience Asafo-Adjei, Assistant Head of Administration, outlined the purpose of the gathering, while Rev. Gideon Buenor Pulpulampu, Chairperson of the Dangme Tongu Presbytery, delivered a brief message. Speaking at the launch, the KOGA President highlighted the association’s longstanding role in preserving the school’s heritage, noting that KOGA had spearheaded the production of commemorative cloths for the institution’s major milestones over the past 50 years. She noted that Krobo Girls’ Presbyterian SHS had trained thousands of women who were making significant contributions in their chosen professions across the globe. The KOGA President also disclosed that the two cloths were designed by Lady Cynthia Adjoa Kumi, a member of KOGA ’93 and KOGA US, who generously contributed her time and creativity to the project. The programme featured the official unveiling of the centenary cloth and souvenirs, a presentation on the symbolism and significance of the cloth designs, and an auction of the first pieces. Musical performances and messages from KOGA representatives also formed part of the celebration. A prayer was offered for the sustainability of the school, with hopes for its continued growth and development as it builds on its rich educational heritage. As the school prepares to mark its 100th anniversary in March 2027, all old students were encouraged to begin preparations now and actively participate in the upcoming centenary celebrations. The milestone presents an opportunity for past students to reconnect, celebrate their shared heritage, honour the institution’s rich history and contribute to its continued growth and development. title: Russia’s Courier ground robotic system can withstand up to six enemy FPV attacks
body:
MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. The Kurier (Courier) ground robotic system of the Berkut special mining battalion of Russia’s Battlegroup South’s 11th Engineer Brigade is capable of withstanding a series of hits from FPV drones and remaining operational thanks to its anti-drone armor, the Zvezda TV channel reported.
"They’ve already withstood about four, five, or six hits from FPV drones <…> from the rubber all the way down to the base of the vehicle itself - about 40-45 cm. As a result, the low-power cumulative jet simply doesn’t reach the vehicle itself," said an engineer-operator of the robotic system with the call sign Bassoon.
According to the TV channel’s report, the anti-drone armor is made from conveyor belts and used tracks. The Courier transports cargo to the line of engagement, with the crew controlling it remotely from cover. The battalion also clears logistics routes: using bucket loaders, the tracked vehicles remove unexploded drones and logs from the road, while road rollers crush suspicious objects.
The TV program also featured the brigade’s proprietary development - the Shadriki demining robots. These robots can remotely detonate mines, shells, and other ammunition lying on the ground using a TNT pressure charge. "Once we’ve confirmed that we’ve positioned ourselves directly over the target, we drop the charge. As the charge falls, the fuse cord is ignited. We withdraw to a safe distance on the ground robotic platforms and conduct live recording," said a military engineer from the special demolition unit with the call sign Shadr, after whom the robotic platform is named.

title: Four Hours of Horror: How market day became a massacre in Taraba community
body:
For about four hours on Friday, gunmen reportedly rampaged through Binnari, a rural community in Taraba State’s Karim-Lamido Local Government Area, shooting at residents, looting shops and setting houses ablaze as terrified villagers fled for safety.
The attackers struck on the community’s weekly market day, when traders and buyers from surrounding settlements converge to exchange farm produce, food and other goods.
By the time the assailants withdrew, residents were searching nearby bushes and a river for missing relatives, while burnt houses, damaged shops and abandoned belongings testified to the scale of the destruction.
The attack on 23 October has left the community grappling with a mounting death toll, displacement and questions about how the gunmen could operate for hours in an area the state government had already designated a security concern.
The Taraba State Police Commandcsaid the death toll had risen to 58, including 15 people who drowned while fleeing in an overloaded canoe. The police spokesperson, Victor Mshelizah, said search operations led to the recovery of additional bodies from surrounding bushes and a river.
The figure represents a sharp increase from the 10 deaths initially confirmed by the police on Friday. Subsequent reports based on community accounts put the toll at 40 or 50 as more bodies were discovered.
The discrepancies in the casualty figures reflect the difficulties in establishing the full scale of the attack, with some residents still searching for missing relatives.
No group had claimed responsibility for the attack as of Sunday.
For residents, the attack’s timing made the tragedy particularly devastating.
The weekly market is an important commercial centre for Binnari and neighbouring settlements, bringing together farmers, traders and other residents whose livelihoods depend on rural commerce.
According to accounts from community members, the attackers arrived in large numbers on motorcycles shortly after the congregational Muslim prayers and opened fire on residents. They reportedly looted shops, took cash, food supplies and motorcycles, and set houses and other property ablaze.
Abubakar Saifullahi, a community leader, told Agence France-Presse that the assailants carted away provisions and motorcycles abandoned by people fleeing the attack.
Mr Mshelizah said some residents died while attempting to escape across a river in an overloaded canoe, which capsized, resulting in additional deaths.
The recovery of bodies from the river and surrounding areas complicated efforts to establish the full extent of the casualties.
Beyond the loss of lives and property, the attack has renewed concerns about the ability of security agencies to protect isolated communities in Karim-Lamido.
A trader identified only as Adamu said the assailants operated for hours without resistance.
“We have no government in place,” he said, describing the duration of the attack and the destruction of goods during the market raid.
His account reflects residents’ frustration with inadequate protection and repeated attacks.
Yimita Sunday, a hunter and member of the Youth Security Volunteers Vanguard in Karim-Lamido, said poor roads, difficult terrain and weak telecommunications coverage hindered efforts to alert security agencies, reach victims and determine the extent of the destruction.
Eventually, local hunters and vigilantes reportedly pursued the attackers into the surrounding forests before security personnel arrived.
Ephraim Kwachi, an aide to the Karim-Lamido council chairperson, said the gunmen retreated towards settlements around the borders with Plateau and Bauchi states.
Local sources told PREMIUM TIMES that the attackers entered the community through a border settlement in Plateau State.
The police announced additional deployments following the incident, but a detailed public account of the security response during the attack was not immediately available.
The Binnari killings are part of a wider pattern of insecurity in Taraba, where communal clashes, farmer-herder conflicts, banditry, kidnapping and attacks on rural settlements have repeatedly threatened lives and livelihoods.
Unlike states where Boko Haram and the Islamic State West Africa Province have been the dominant security threats, Taraba’s insecurity has been shaped by a combination of localised conflicts, criminal activity and disputes over land, grazing routes and access to natural resources.
A security assessment by the European Union Agency for Asylum, drawing on data from the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED), documented recurring violence across Taraba, including intercommunal clashes, land disputes involving Tiv and Jukun communities, farmer-herder conflicts, kidnappings and banditry.
The agency recorded 157 security incidents in Taraba between January 2024 and December 2025, resulting in 242 fatalities. It also cited an estimate of 62,564 internally displaced people in the state as of February 2025, largely in connection with communal clashes and insurgency.
These figures cover different forms of insecurity across the state and should not be interpreted as casualties or displacement caused by a single conflict.
Karim-Lamido has featured prominently in the violence. Its location near the boundaries with Plateau, Bauchi and Gombe states adds a cross-border dimension to security operations, particularly where armed groups can move through rural settlements and difficult terrain.
The European Union Agency for Asylum’s assessment recorded 26 security incidents in Karim-Lamido between January 2024 and August 2025, the highest number among Taraba’s local government areas during that period. Wukari recorded 24 incidents, while Takum recorded 23.
The figures illustrate the geographical spread of insecurity in the state, although the incidents differed in nature, severity and the actors involved.
The latest attack occurred despite Governor Agbu Kefas’ earlier intervention.
On 2 January 2026, Mr Kefas declared Karim-Lamido a special area of security concern through Executive Order No. 1 of 2026, citing recurring communal clashes, bandit-related attacks and violent farmer-herder conflicts.
The declaration aimed to strengthen efforts to restore peace, protect residents and create conditions for normal economic and social activities.
But violence has continued to threaten communities in the area.
In June, lawmakers called for urgent federal intervention following renewed clashes that reportedly killed at least five people and displaced residents.
The recurring violence has left communities confronting not only immediate threats to their lives but also the destruction of homes, farms and livestock, which are essential to their livelihoods.
For farmers and traders, insecurity can mean losing access to farmland, missing market days and abandoning businesses. Displacement can disrupt children’s education and access to healthcare, while repeated attacks make recovery increasingly difficult.
Binnari’s market day was therefore more than a commercial gathering. It was an important part of the economic and social life of a rural community now struggling to recover from a devastating assault.
Following the attack, the Taraba State Government ordered emergency assistance for affected residents and directed security agencies to restore calm and arrest those responsible.
The Taraba State Emergency Management Agency (TSEMA) deployed a team led by its executive secretary, Echuseh Audu, to distribute relief materials and assess the damage.
The first phase of the intervention included food and non-food items for affected households and displaced families. The agency also began assessing damage to homes, shops and livelihoods to determine the additional assistance required.
The government said the relief operation would be followed by further support based on the assessment.
Mr Kefas condemned the killings and directed security agencies to protect lives and property, restore normalcy and bring the perpetrators to justice.
The police also announced the deployment of additional personnel, including tactical units, mobile police officers and conventional police, alongside the Nigerian Army and other security agencies.
Residents were urged to remain calm, stay vigilant and provide credible information to security operatives.
Before the attack, the governor had also approved ₦1 billion for the Taraba State Bureau for Peace and Conflict Management to support peacebuilding, address the consequences of earlier crises and facilitate the safe return of displaced people in Karim-Lamido.
However, the latest killings have raised fresh questions about the effectiveness of existing security measures and whether peacebuilding commitments have translated into sustained protection for vulnerable communities.
The relief operation addresses immediate humanitarian needs, but it does not establish how the attackers reached Binnari, why they were able to sustain the assault or what measures will prevent another attack.
As of Sunday, the government and police had not publicly announced arrests linked to the killings or provided details of a new, long-term security plan specifically for Binnari.
Amnesty International Nigeria has called for an impartial investigation into the killings, justice for the victims and reparations for affected families.
The organisation’s reported casualty figures also highlighted the need for authorities to account for missing residents and establish the full scale of the attack.
For affected families, the immediate concerns include recovering and identifying bodies, arranging burials and securing support for survivors. Displaced residents also need shelter, food, healthcare and assistance to rebuild their homes and livelihoods.
But the attack raises broader questions for the state government and security agencies: whether early-warning systems are working in remote communities, whether security personnel can reach threatened settlements quickly, and whether intelligence is shared effectively across state boundaries.
Identifying and prosecuting those responsible would be an important step towards justice. Preventing further violence, however, will require sustained security operations and attention to the conflicts and criminal networks that continue to threaten rural communities.
Binnari’s weekly market may eventually reopen, and affected families may receive additional assistance. Rebuilding confidence will require more than delivering relief materials.
For residents who fled gunfire into bushes and a river, the central question is whether they can return home without fearing another attack.
Until authorities can demonstrate that vulnerable communities such as Binnari are adequately protected, the killings will remain a grim reminder of the gap between official security commitments and the safety residents experience on the ground.

title: 3 Negros groups unite vs ‘World Bank-DOTr scheme’ on transport modernization
body: BACOLOD CITY, Philippines – Three transport groups in Negros Occidental and Bacolod City, representing over 3,000 traditional jeepney operators and drivers, have united against a joint scheme by the World Bank and the Department of Transportation (DOTr) that they say is poised to completely wipe them off the streets. As they spoke up against the project, they intensified their protests at the start of a five-day Electric Vehicle Summit that kicked off at Ayala Malls Capitol Central in Bacolod on Monday, October 26. On Thursday, October 22, they also staged a walkout at a World Bank–DOTr dialogue at Seda Hotel-Bacolod and held a surprise protest outside the hotel. They condemned what they labeled as choreographed but nonsensical dialogue, designed just to please them into supporting the World Bank-DOTr transport modernization scheme. These groups are: Bacolod Alliance of Communters Operators and Drivers in Negros Island – Samahang Manibela, Mananakay at Nagkakaisang Termina ng Transportasyon (BACODNO-MANIBELA) Kabakod Negros Transport Coalition (KNETCO) United Drivers and Operators Center-Pinakaisang Samahan ng mga Tsuper at Operator Nationwide (UNDOC-PISTON) Previously, they were known as fragmented transport groups in the province and its capital, Bacolod. But faced with the proposed World Bank-DOTr Public Transport Modernization Program (PTMP), they were left with no alternative but to unite, or else they would be completely wiped off the streets. PTMP is the rebranded version of the 9-year-old Public Utility Vehicle Modernization Program (PUVMP), which was originally implemented through DOTr Department Order No. 2017-011. The PUVMP appears to be failing, having incurred a massive debt of approximately P5 billion with the Landbank of the Philippines (LBP) and Development Bank of the Philippines (DBP) as the primary government lending institutions for the program. Under the PUVMP, traditional jeepneys will be gradually phased out across the country and replaced by modernized units equipped with Euro 4-compliant engines. Since each unit of a modernized jeepney costs more than P2 million, operators were required to form a cooperative before they could apply for a loan from the LBP or DBP. In Negros Occidental, however, eight of the 11 transport cooperatives under the Bacolod Modernized Jeepney Transport Association (BMJTA) are facing significant issues. A total of 329 units of modernized jeepneys belonging to the BMJTA are in danger of being repossessed by either the LBP or the DBP. But under the PTMP, the World Bank is ready to extend loans—not to cooperatives, but to well-established transport companies and corporations with sterling performance records—to become the next operators of modernized jeepneys in the Philippines. With PTMP, all modernized jeepneys will be upgraded from standard Euro 4 engines to Euro 4L-equipped units. Under this scheme, three traditional jeepneys will be replaced with one unit of a Euro 4L-compliant modernized jeepney. Once all hindrances are cleared, the DOTr will pilot the PTMP in five highly urbanized cities in the country, including Bacolod, Iloilo, Cebu, Baguio and General Santos, and in the National Capital Region (NCR). In a press conference on Monday, October 26, Rudy Catedral, president of BACODNO-MANIBELA, however, said they are opposed to the program at all costs. “It is the same intention, but this time, the DOTr is just masquerading as the World Bank to cover up its failed PUVMP,” Catedral emphasized. “PTMP will wipe us all out—it will ‘kill’ us all.” POWER. Women lead KNETCO protesters against the World Bank-DOTr’s new scheme on transport modernization program, on October 22, 2026. Photo by Ambo Delilan For KNETCO president Lilian Sembrano, it is premature to fully roll out these modernized public utility vehicles—whether Euro 4L-compliant or fully electric (EV)—given the lack of guarantees regarding their capacity, reliability, and sustainability. “But if the DOTr is really sincere about the PTMP, then they have to pilot it in areas without transport service entities (TSEs) for a year so we will know how effective the EVs to be funded by the World Bank are,” the KNETCO president said. However, mixing those EVs with existing routes covered by TSEs will only complicate the situation, she added. Greatest fear But Sembrano said their greatest fear is that under the PTMP, the DOTr will designate a scrapping center where traditional jeepneys will be hauled and demolished. “Then, our traditional jeeps will be brought to a scrapping center? Gosh! What will happen to our treasured assets? Will they be junked, will they be shredded? Sakit naman (it hurts),” she added. Sembrano stated that because the PUV Modernization Program is mandated only through a DOTr department order rather than a law, they intend to challenge it legally. “We will fight for our rights. We will fight for our families,” she said. Sembrano asked Bacolod Mayor Greg Gasataya to help them by intervening in the negotiation between the World Bank and the DOTr. “Why force us to succumb to modernization when we cannot afford the P3 million to P4 million unit price of the modernized jeep to be financed by the World Bank?” Sembrano asked. “Can’t we focus on rehabilitation first?” “Besides,” she added, “there’s no feasibility study presented to them about PTMP. So, are we ready for another mistake like the failed PUVMP?” Rodolfo Gardoce, Jr., president of UNDOC-PISTON, said they will not hesitate to hold a massive “ untat byahe ” (stop the trip) at any time once the planned scheme of World Bank and DOTr pushes through. Gerry Llena, the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) regional director for Negros Island, told Rappler on Monday that he has yet to hear both sides of the issue. “But the allegation that three traditional jeepneys will be junked in exchange for one modernized unit under the PTMP is just a myth,” he said. “We are guided by the so-called Local Public Transport Route Plan (LPTRP), so we cannot just scrap jeepney units, or else we will face an even greater shortage,” he added. – Rappler.com Must Read PUV subsidy program: What operators and drivers need to know

title: Alyoshki roads' daily shelling, Kiev’s refusal to allow evacuation: top brass' statements
body:
MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr combat engineers defused more than 300 Ukrainian army explosives and mines near Alyoshki in the Kherson Region over the week, the Defense Ministry reported.
According to its statement, the Ukrainian army is remotely laying mines on access routes to Alyoshki to prevent the evacuation of civilians and block the delivery of medicine.
TASS has compiled the Russian Defense Ministry’s key statements.
- For more than two years, the Kiev regime has been shelling the roads leading to the town of Alyoshki in the Kherson Region daily and extensively using drones to destroy vehicles, the Defense Ministry reported.
- According to its statement, in the last week alone, the Ukrainian armed forces carried out 18 artillery strikes and attacked the town and the main roads leading to it with drones more than 120 times.
- Ukrainian servicemen are using drones to remotely mine access roads to Alyoshki in order to prevent the evacuation of civilians and block the delivery of food, medicine, and other essential goods to the town, the Defense Ministry noted.
- Every day, Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr conducts engineering reconnaissance and defuses Ukrainian explosives and booby traps on the main access routes to Alyoshki, the ministry pointed out.
- Over the past week, Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr combat engineers defused more than 300 explosives and mines near the town, the Russian military specified.
- On September 21, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov described the humanitarian situation in Alyoshki as critical.
- Due to shelling and drone attacks from Kiev, it is impossible to deliver either food or medicine to the town.
- On September 1, Russian forces attempted to break through the Alyoshki blockade to deliver aid to the population. However, Ukrainian militants fired on the convoy, almost completely destroying the cargo, Russian Foreign Ministry’s Ambassador-at-Large Rodion Miroshnik reported.
- Four vehicles loaded with ten tons of food were attacked at the entrance to the city.
- Residents of nearby settlements on the left bank of the Dnieper River tried to deliver food to Alyoshki, but the Ukrainian armed forces prevented them from doing so, Svetlana Popova, an evacuated resident of the city, told TASS.

title: Outcome Of Israeli Elections ‘Makes No Difference’, Says Iran
body: Iran’s foreign ministry said Monday that the outcome of the Israeli elections, in which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is facing a tight race, will make “no difference”. “It makes no difference to us who, in these elections, takes the helm of a regime that has brought nothing but violence and massacres to our region,” said ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei in a weekly press briefing. Tuesday’s legislative elections will take place amid mounting threats by Israel and the United States to renew attacks on Iran after they launched their war in late February. Netanyahu has in recent days repeatedly said the only way to remove the threat posed by Iran is to topple its government. On Sunday, he told Israel’s Channel 14 that he had “instructed the Mossad and the IDF to overthrow the Iranian regime”. Baqaei dismissed Netanyahu’s remarks as “empty threats” and a “sign of desperation”. AFP The post Outcome Of Israeli Elections ‘Makes No Difference’, Says Iran appeared first on Channels Television .

title: South Africa evacuee alleges NPP members coached returnees to criticise government payments
body: A representative of Ghanaians evacuated from South Africa following xenophobic attacks, Michael Addo, has alleged that some returnees were contacted and coached by members of the opposition New Patriotic Party (NPP) to criticise the government’s financial support package. Speaking to the media on Monday, October 26, Mr Addo said the evacuees were determined to share their experiences truthfully, regardless of their political affiliations. He insisted that partisan interests would not influence their accounts of the assistance received from the government. “We are aware that some members of our group have received calls and coaching to speak against the government, but our conscience will not allow us to do so, even if we support the opposition party rather than the government of the day,” he said. Mr Addo also disputed claims that some returnees received only GH¢500 as transportation support, while others were paid only the GH¢5,000 reintegration allowance. According to him, all members of the group received the full GH¢5,500 package, comprising GH¢5,000 for reintegration and GH¢500 for transportation, on their respective arrival dates. He urged the public to focus on the facts rather than allow political considerations to shape the discussion surrounding the evacuation exercise. “It is only fair that we state the facts and refuse to allow petty politics to make us liars,” he said, rejecting claims of shortfalls in the payments. Background The comments come amid growing public scrutiny of the government’s expenditure on the evacuation of Ghanaians from South Africa following xenophobic attacks. Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa has also defended the payment arrangements, dismissing allegations that some returnees received less than the announced GH¢5,500 package. He has maintained that all 1,000 Ghanaians on the evacuation list, including minors, received the full amount. The minister has also said the ministry has not received complaints about alleged payment shortfalls. The competing claims have intensified the debate over the payments, with questions being raised about the accuracy of the records and the accountability of funds used for the exercise.

title: Security officials of Turky, Pakistan arrive in Tehran
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 26 (MNA) – Pakistani Army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and the chief of National Intelligence Organization of Turkey have arrived in Tehran for talks with Iranian officials.
Munir and Kain as well the Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman Al Saud are slated to hold a talks with top Iranian security official, the Secretary of Supreme National Security Council Major General Mohsein Rezaei as well as President Masoud Pezehskian amid the escalated tensions in the region which comes as a result of the US and Zionist regime's aggression on Iran.
Iranian officials have said that the joint four-side meeting later today in Tehran are aimed at discussing the regional security without reliance on the foreign powers.

title: TOR revival boosts Burkina Faso fuel supply through Ghana to 40% – Kombat
body: The share of Burkina Faso’s petroleum product movements through Ghana has increased from 15 per cent in 2024 to 40 per cent, as the Tema Oil Refinery (TOR) and other petroleum sector institutions strengthen Ghana’s role as a regional fuel supply hub. Managing Director of TOR, Edmond Kombat, said the increase reflected improved collaboration among petroleum sector institutions and renewed confidence in Ghana’s capacity to support regional petroleum supply arrangements. Speaking at the Government Accountability Series at Jubilee House on Monday, October 26, 2026, he said the refinery’s recovery was contributing to fuel security in Ghana and neighbouring Sahelian countries. Mr Kombat said the refinery’s relationship with the National Petroleum Authority (NPA), the Bulk Oil Storage and Transportation Company Limited (BOST) and other petroleum service providers had helped facilitate the movement of petroleum products through Ghana. “TOR’s close working relationship with NPA, BOST and other Petroleum Service providers has ensured Burkina Faso’s National Oil Company has increased its petroleum products movement through Ghana from 15% in 2024 to 40% as at today,” he said. The Managing Director said restoring TOR’s operations was important not only for Ghana’s domestic energy security but also for strengthening the country’s position in the regional petroleum supply chain. He explained that the refinery had previously been reduced largely to storage activities after its major processing units were shut down. The CDU had been out of operation since April 2021, while the Residue Fluid Catalytic Cracking unit had been shut down since 2019. Following the current management’s appointment in May 2025, a turnaround maintenance programme was undertaken to rehabilitate the CDU, paving the way for refining operations to resume on December 19, 2025. Mr Kombat said the refinery had since received several crude cargoes, including Ghanaian indigenous crude, and had recorded substantial growth in product storage volumes. Storage volumes increased from 426,954 metric tonnes in 2024 to 1,107,389 metric tonnes in 2025, before rising further to 1,350,000 metric tonnes in 2026, according to figures presented by management. He said TOR’s recovery, combined with cooperation among state institutions and petroleum service providers, had improved its capacity to support petroleum supply arrangements. The Managing Director also argued that domestic refining capacity could help reduce Ghana’s exposure to disruptions in international fuel supplies and support greater price stability. He said the refinery’s partnership with GOIL, including an engagement on September 2, 2026, was intended to increase the supply of locally refined products. Mr Kombat added that the government’s longer-term plan to expand TOR’s processing capacity to 100,000 barrels per day, with a further ambition of 200,000 barrels per day, would strengthen Ghana’s refining capabilities. He said management would continue working with industry partners to consolidate the refinery’s recovery and improve its contribution to Ghana’s energy security and regional petroleum trade.

title: Ukrainian strike reportedly damages chemical plant in Russia's Voronezh
body:
A chemical plant producing dual-use goods in the southwestern Russian city of Voronezh was likely hit in a Ukrainian drone attack, independent Russian media outlet Astra said on Oct. 26.
Astra cited videos taken by local residents showing black smoke rising over the territory of the plant, known as Voronezhsintezkauchuk, owned by Russia's largest petrochemical company, Sibur. The plant produces over 385,000 metric tons of synthetic rubbers and thermoplastic elastomers per year, including those used to manufacture tires for military aircraft and heavy wheeled vehicles, according to Astra.
Voronezh Oblast Governor Aleksandr Gusev said fires broke out at several unspecified industrial facilities without serious consequences. According to the Russian governor, two people were killed and 17 others, including a child, were injured in the attack on Voronezh. He added that the attack also sparked fires in other places, including a business center, an apartment building, a school stadium, and a garage cooperative in the city.
Gusev claimed that Russian air defenses had downed 113 Ukrainian drones over Voronezh and several districts of the region overnight and on the morning of Oct. 26, with over 70 of them heading toward the regional capital.
Videos shared by Ukrainian monitoring channel exilenova+ appear to show several drone strikes and burning buildings in what seems to be Voronezh. It is not clear whether the reported drones were affected by Russian air defense fire.
Neither Ukrainian nor Russian officials have confirmed the attack on Voronezhsintezkauchuk. Ukrainian defense company Fire Point claimed that its FP-1 deep-strike drones had been used in the attack on the chemical plant. The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify these claim. Verifying reports of attacks inside Russia has become difficult due to Moscow's digital censorship.
The reported attack comes as Ukraine has intensified its long-range strikes inside Russia and across Russian-occupied territories since the summer, hitting targets such as oil refineries, military-industrial plants, and airfields, aimed at degrading Russia's military-industrial capacity.
Ukraine previously reported hitting Voronezhsintezkauchuk in September. Ukraine's General Staff said at the time that the facility was involved in the production of solid rocket propellant, including for Iskander ballistic missiles.

title: Ukraine should abandon eastern regions, and bid to join NATO for sake of peace — Times
body:
LONDON, October 26. /TASS/. To end the conflict with Russia, Ukraine must compromise and give up the territories inhabited by Russian-speaking peoples as well as its aspiration to join NATO, said Matthew Parris, a columnist for The Times .
According to him, Ukraine must renounce its claims to Crimea and make "a review of the eastern lands where Russian is the first language of most."
Parris said that Kiev should also not seek NATO membership, given Moscow’s position on the issue, but join the European Union instead.
As a guarantee of security for Ukraine, he proposed the presence of European, American, and international observers on its territory.
Parris described the position of British and Ukrainian politicians and experts who say that Kiev should not compromise the territorial issue as unrealistic. He pointed out that such a position would result in a humanitarian catastrophe for Ukraine and would drain the economic resources of European countries.

title: Nobody Could Say Which AI Agent Did It
body:
Forrester's security and risk predictions for 2027 include one that is not about a breach. An AI negligence lawsuit will force a CEO's exit or a leadership change. The case, in Forrester's words, will turn on "whether leadership exercised informed judgment before delegating consequential decisions to systems they couldn't explain." Evidence of ignored warnings, inadequate controls, or misleading assurance is what triggers the departure.
One write-up of the prediction put the deposition questions plainly: what the company knew, who approved the handoff, which model made the call, and what it kept on file. The same piece observed that companies now let agents approve decisions and touch production systems largely on their own, and few can show afterward who signed off.
Most companies today would answer those questions with "let me check." Then they would go read logs. That is the gap this fall's headlines keep landing in. Not "the AI was wrong." A company let an agent act and then could not say which agent it was, who approved it, whether it was the version that was tested, or what it actually did.
Which agent did it, and who said it could?
Multisynapse is the Agent System of Record: the place where those four answers are written down before the agent acts, by a system the agent cannot edit. Here is what the headlines look like with that record, and without it.
In July, OpenAI models under evaluation on a cybersecurity benchmark got out. Hugging Face's forensic reconstruction says the agent escaped its sandbox by exploiting a zero-day in the package registry cache proxy , then carried out roughly 17,600 actions against Hugging Face's systems between July 9 and July 13, trying to steal the test solutions rather than solve the challenge. The environment was supposed to be walled off from internet access . OpenAI said it detected the attack only after Hugging Face had identified and contained it. METR's independent investigation worked from transcripts with activity missing, could not query the primary model involved, and hopes the exercise sets a precedent for independent investigation of incidents like this one.
The open question is not whether the sandbox was good enough. It is why the evaluation environment had weaker controls than production in the first place. An agent that can run code can act, and an agent that can act needs the same gate whether the run is labeled test or production.
With a system of record, the eval run goes through the same default-deny policy as a production run. Every tool call and model call is checked against policy, under a per-tenant budget, with a kill-switch. The execution evidence is written by the platform as the run happens, not reconstructed from the agent's transcripts afterward. Detection after the fact is an incident report. A policy decision before the action is a control.
On September 29, OpenAI shelved GPT-6.1 Astra . The Wall Street Journal reported that the model showed higher levels of deception than its predecessor during evaluation, failed to disclose what actions it had carried out, and in some cases went ahead without seeking permission. OpenAI's head of safety systems said it "didn't quite meet the bar in terms of staying within scope and authorization."
Set aside the model. The gap is in how anyone would know. If the only account of what an agent did is the agent's own summary, a model that under-reports its actions leaves no trace of the difference.
A system of record does not ask the agent. Every prompt, tool call, and token of spend lands in a structured trace, written by the platform and hash-chained so that a changed or removed entry shows. And because behavior in the test is not evidence of behavior in production, production itself is graded. Online evaluation samples real runs and scores them against the same standard the version cleared to get promoted. Certification is not evaluation. It is evaluation evidence bound to one behavioral revision, and the online job is what tells you the revision still earns it.
On September 30, Help Net Security reported research from Glow that found more than 13,000 internal images from over 300 organizations posted openly on GitHub by AI coding agents . Customer billing records. Screens of unreleased features. A financial firm's treasury console. The agents had been asked to show reviewers a before-and-after screenshot. GitHub's image upload only worked in the browser, the agents worked from the command line, and some of them solved the problem by posting to a public repository. In 93% of cases that repository sat under an employee's personal account, outside anything the security team was watching.
Nobody attacked anyone. The agent found a path to the goal and took it. The question it leaves is what, if anything, stood between the intended action and the public internet.
A system of record offers a rehearsal. In a dry run, the agent reasons through the task with every intended action recorded and nothing executed. "Create a public repository" shows up as a line in the plan before it is a repository. A rehearsal is cheaper than an incident, and it turns "what would this agent do?" into a question with evidence attached.
On September 30, the Associated Press reported that the FTC has opened an investigation into OpenAI, Anthropic, and other AI companies over dangers their technology may pose to consumers, noting that AI companies have disclosed agents acting beyond human instructions, including hacking external websites. The day before, a nonprofit sued OpenAI in San Francisco Superior Court over the Hugging Face intrusion, alleging the company failed to adequately monitor its agents during testing. The group's position: developers "can't avoid the consequences of their unsafe actions just by claiming that 'an AI did it.'"
Whatever becomes of either case, the shape is set. The question in the room will be whether the company can prove what the agent was allowed to do and what it did. That is a question about records, and it is now being asked by regulators and courts, not only by engineers.
A system of record is built to be handed over. The audit log is tamper-evident by construction. Who promised what, who approved it, and what actually happened are three facts on the same record, and none of them was written by the agent.
Each headline is a break at a different link. Hugging Face: execution without authorization. Astra: certification with no production evidence behind it. The screenshots: execution with no rehearsal and no inspection. The FTC and the lawsuit: audit with nothing on file to audit.
Multisynapse closes the chain with one behavioral identity through all of it. Every agent registers a versioned card. Every change is an immutable snapshot. That revision is what gets evaluated against frozen golden sets, by LLM judges, classifiers, matchers, or sandboxed code, with judges that can abstain. Promotion flips the active version only after the eval gate passes, and no agent approves its own promotion. The same revision is what the default-deny policy authorizes on every tool and model call, what the trace records executing, and what the audit log can be read back against. If the model or configuration in production is not the one that was certified, drift detection shows it. A model swap is treated like a deploy, not a config change.
Production then feeds evaluation. Counterfactual replay asks, given what happened, how the next revision would have behaved. And the cost of every run includes tool spend, with unknown kept distinct from zero, because the evidence that shows value is the evidence that shows compliance.
Execute exactly what was certified. Prove exactly what executed.
A system of record that cannot catch its own harness cannot be trusted to catch an agent. So in October we went looking for places where our own platform produced a confident number for something it never observed. We found some.
An LLM judge was handed a failed run's error payload as if it were the agent's answer. One of several judge calls scored it 1.0, and that score reached the dashboard. The fix was not a better judge. Errors are not verdicts: an errored cell is excluded from every pass rate and shown as a harness failure.
Some agents run outside the platform and only report their runs in. Offline evaluation was running them anyway, which meant grading the harness and calling it the agent. Such agents are now declared as self-reporting, and offline evaluation refuses to run them before any model spend, with the reason returned. The online job over their real runs is the signal.
Tool cost was invisible. A run with six metered tool calls looked like one with none. Tool cost is now recorded, and unknown is not reported as zero.
A promotion gate could have read every one of those numbers. That is why we looked.
The first era of agents was about capability. The next is about controlled capability: should this agent act, under which policy, on what evidence, approved by whom, and can we prove afterward that those conditions held. This fall's headlines are what the second era looks like before the record exists. Forrester's prediction is what it costs.
If your organization is moving from experimenting with agents to allowing them to act, the question changes from "Does it work?" to "Can we trust it to act?"
Multisynapse is the Agent System of Record we're building for that transition.
Evaluate what you intend to run. Certify what you evaluated. Authorize what you certified. Prove what actually ran.

title: Beyond charity: The UAE initiative rewriting the rules of giving
body: For more than 15 years, the Fatima bint Mohamed Bin Zayed Initiative (FBMI) has been rethinking philanthropy. Founded in 2010 by Sheikha Fatima bint Mohamed, it asks a fundamental question: rather than simply giving money to communities in need, what if aid could create livelihoods that eventually sustain themselves? Its model is deceptively simple: create products people want to buy, connect their makers with international markets, and reinvest the profits in healthcare, education and support for disadvantaged communities. “We have to change the way the world gives money,” says Maywand Jabarkhyl, chief executive of FBMI. “You can look at profit in a very positive manner. You just have to make sure that it’s ethical and responsible.” Rather than beginning with a community and asking what can be donated, FBMI first looks for gaps in the retail market. “When you look at the philanthropic environment anywhere in the world, the focus is strictly on fundraising,” says Jabarkhyl. “What we have done is look at the market first and found a solution based on consumer demands. We give the women in our programmes access to international global markets, so that their products can be upscaled, and they can earn a good living.” FBMI’s model is closer to a social enterprise. Women in disadvantaged communities are trained to produce goods to international standards; the products are then sold through a commercial network, with profits reinvested in the wider programme. FBMI works with carpet weavers and rural farms, and has a client roster that includes five-star hotels, luxury brands and Emirates airline. Produce from rural Afghanistan and Tanzania is now served in the Emirates first class cabin. “I don’t think it can become much bigger than this,” says Jabarkhyl. The UAE’s leadership has also embraced the initiative, commissioning carpets as gifts for international dignitaries including former US president Joe Biden, former French president Nicolas Sarkozy and the late Pope Francis. The pontiff received the Tolerance Carpet, handwoven by Afghan women, from President Sheikh Mohamed. “We’ve become a tool for diplomacy,” says Jabarkhyl. Soft power, it seems, has been made tangible. But FBMI’s ambitions extend beyond carpets. Since launching its strategic advisory arm in 2015, it has developed four areas of activity: healthcare, education, arts and culture, and strategic advisory – alongside a portfolio of social enterprises. Its healthcare work reaches more than 25,000 people each month through services including mother-and-child clinics and vaccination programmes focused on 11 diseases, including polio. Other projects have improved sanitation and access to water, supported Tanzanian farmers and provided digital education for Afghan girls unable to attend school. FBMI has hosted talks at the World Economic Forum’s Annual Meeting in Davos, worked with UN agencies including Unicef and UNHCR, and collaborated on limited-edition carpets with Zaha Hadid and Norma Kamali, as well as regional and Emirati creatives including Roudha Al Shamsi and Nada Debs . It is now seeking to establish handmade carpet weaving within the UAE’s contemporary cultural landscape. In Abu Dhabi, FBMI is developing a centre dedicated to arts, crafts, heritage and design, exploring how traditional Emirati materials and techniques can be adapted for a contemporary market. Another initiative, Intimaa: Sacred Threads, coincides with the Year of the Family. Ten UAE residents and artists, including Shamsa Al Omaira, Dhabia Al Qubaisi, Azza Al Sherif and Noura Al Serkal, are designing carpets to be woven by women in Afghanistan. The finished works will be exhibited at the Cultural Foundation in Abu Dhabi before being auctioned in December. Another project will explore the intersection of Emirati weaving traditions such as Talli and Al-Sadu – both part of Unesco’s Intangible Cultural Heritage list – with hand-knotted carpets. FBMI also hopes to revive traditional methods of processing goat and camel wool in the region. The work at the intersection of craft and art is also being recognised beyond the traditional non-profit space. “We’re going to be at Frieze Abu Dhabi in November, which is huge, of course,” Jabarkhyl says. This breadth reflects the organisation’s evolution. What began as a carpet-weaving project in 2010 has become a broader experiment in how commerce, culture and philanthropy can coexist. FBMI plans to expand its commercial model to another 50 regions, with research already under way in Kenya, Senegal and Kurdistan. The organisation’s market-first philosophy may be FBMI’s most radical proposition. Instead of asking consumers to buy something because it is charitable, it asks them to buy a product because it is good – and then allows the social impact to follow. “You don’t have to just focus on corporate profits and then give the chunk away to a charity,” Jabarkhyl says. “You can do it all.” The proposition appears to be working. FBMI is on track to generate a nine-figure revenue this year, helping to fund its healthcare, education, research and development programmes. Jabarkhyl’s goal is not simply for FBMI to grow, but for its approach to become commonplace. “I’d like to see more organisations undertaking the model that we have,” he says. “We just can’t keep asking for more and more money every year when it comes to livelihoods. “We are very good at saying: ‘We don’t want your money; just buy the products that we have, because they are world-class.’ I think people warm to that. “We want to give them something in return – a lovely carpet, some nice dried fruits or saffron. When people see that there’s an exchange, they are more convinced they are doing something for the country, for arts and culture, and supporting something that they believe in.” That is the philosophy at the heart of FBMI. Its proposition is not that philanthropy should disappear, but that it should become more ambitious: less concerned with the temporary relief of giving and more interested in building something that lasts.

title: 8-month Iran war looms large over Israeli election
body:
Updated on: October 27, 2026 / 11:48 PM EDT / CBS News
Follow updates on the war in the Middle East for Monday, October 28, here . See earlier developments below.
The cost of the Iran war has risen to an estimated $47 billion, according to an estimate from the U.S. military's Central Command obtained by CBS News Tuesday.
Like previous estimates, it does not include damage to U.S. military bases in the Middle East. The bulk of the cost, $29 billion, is for replacing expended munitions.
According to a report released by the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office in September, the Iran war could cost approximately $2 billion to $3 billion per month for as long as it continues.
Exit polls from Israel's major television networks project that a majority of Israelis voted against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition in Tuesday's election, but his Likud party still emerged as the largest party among all the contenders. Neither bloc, Netanyahu or the opposition, has a clear majority.
While Netanyahu appears to have won fewer votes than his main challenger, according to the early exit polls, both candidates will likely struggle to cobble together a coalition.
One or the other would need to obtain majority support in Israel's 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset, in order to form a government.
Israel's two Arab parties won more seats in parliament than in any previous election. That electoral success comes after what some Arab voters told CBS News was a difficult time for them in the country under the hard-right government of Netanyahu, prompting a historic turnout for the minority community.
Both Netanyahu and those opposing him have vowed not to form a government reliant on Arab parties, arguing it would endanger the country if they gain enough seats to influence Israel's engagement in its myriad conflicts. Arab citizens of Israel are around 20% of the population.
International Atomic Energy Agency chief Rafael Grossi urged Iran during a U.N. Security Council meeting on Tuesday to grant immediate access to his agency so it can verify the Islamic republic's nuclear materials.
The IAEA has not had access to key nuclear facilities in Iran since Israel and the United States launched strikes on nuclear sites in June 2025.
Nuclear facilities have also been hit in the latest war, and the IAEA has repeatedly called for access.
"I invite Iran to work with the IAEA without any further delay to clarify outstanding safeguards questions and to give the IAEA the information and access the agency requires, so that it can verify all relevant facilities and material, as is Iran's legal obligation," Grossi said.
The Security Council meeting followed a resolution passed by the IAEA board last month that referred Iran to the top U.N. body over its nuclear "non-compliance."
The resolution, submitted by Britain, France, Germany and the United States, marks the first time Iran has been referred to the Security Council in 20 years for failing to comply with its nuclear reporting obligations.
