title: Iran, Iraq trade level “on trajectory growth”: Chairman
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 26 (MNA) – An official at Iran-Iraq Joint Chamber of Commerce says that Iran’s trade relations with Iraq remain robust and nonstop in spite of temporary closure of the border between the two countries.
Head of Iran-Iraq Joint Chamber of Commerce Yahya Al-e Es’hagh made the remarks, emphasizing that there is stepped-up trade relation between the two countries which is running uninterrupted with all but one border crossing continuing to operate normally.
The chairman dismissed concerns over the temporary closure of the Chazzabeh border crossing, emphasizing that the bilateral relationship is deeply strategic and backed by strong mutual economic needs.
He noted that while localized, temporary developments may affect the immediate volume of trade, they do not undermine the fundamental pillars of cooperation between the two neighboring nations.
"The closure of a single border is not in the interest of either country," Ale-Eshaq stated, adding that active negotiations between relevant authorities in Tehran and Baghdad are already underway to restore normal operations.
He highlighted that the continued functionality of other border crossings has allowed economic actors to seamlessly redirect their activities, ensuring that commercial exchanges have not stalled.

title: AI Is Making Verification the Bottleneck for Companies
body: Somewhere in your company today, an expert rejected a perfectly plausible answer. A controller caught a revenue figure that counted deferred bookings. A security engineer blocked a release that passed every test but would have handed an AI agent write access to the production database. That override, escalation, or reversal is the most valuable data your firm produces. If you record enough of those moments and use them, alongside everything else your firm knows and measures, to train an AI model that learns from each correction, you could, in theory, eliminate the need for managers to route information and coordinate action. In doing so, execution gets turbocharged by automation. You might even be able to eliminate hierarchy altogether. That, at least, is the pitch. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella calls that feedback system the critical “learning loop” of the AI era. He also insists that enterprises need to own it rather than cede it to the frontier AI labs. Palantir’s CEO Alex Karp has likewise argued that companies and governments will need sovereign AI to preserve their independence. Jack Dorsey and Roelof Botha went further, offering a blueprint for an ambitious “company world model”: an omnipresent and continuously updated model of the entire business that could coordinate work autonomously. The vision is admittedly seductive. AI makes context extremely easy to retrieve, digest, and continuously process the moment new information arises. What once took an army of managers and multiple systems of record can theoretically be handed over to a single well-tuned AI model. The solution also draws on decades of economic thinking about why firms exist and how they organize work. In the 1930s, economist Ronald Coase argued that firms arise to reduce the costs of relying on markets: discovering prices, negotiating separate contracts, and adapting agreements as circumstances change. Firms bring activities inside their boundaries when coordinating them internally costs less than transacting through the market. In the 1970s, business historian Alfred Chandler documented how the “visible hand” of professional management outperformed market coordination in large-scale production and distribution. Their shared insight is that internal coordination can confer an economic advantage. If AI can perform that coordinating work more cheaply and reliably than layers of human managers, the economic case for those layers weakens. Dissolving the hierarchy becomes the next logical step. With AI, leaders see a chance to preserve the benefits of internal coordination while stripping out much of the friction of human-to-human management. The problem is that execution is only half of the story. The other half—and the source of some of that apparent friction—is the work of verification. Hierarchy does more than route information; it also verifies: deciding what information means, what deserves the firm’s attention, which outputs can be trusted, and which are worth generating at all. As the ability to generate text, media, and code becomes increasingly commoditized and abundant, the calculation as to which half creates the most value for companies evolves too. When execution is cheap, verification becomes more valuable, and firms turn into verification factories: institutions capable of properly steering AI-generated output and standing behind the results. This explains why AI has progressed unevenly across domains. Enterprise AI has advanced fastest where verification is relatively easy. In coding, outputs can often be tested rapidly and cheaply, helping explain why it has so quickly become a success story of AI deployment. Leaders under pressure to define an AI strategy need to recognize what its success hinges on: a coherent plan to solve the verification problem. They also need to recognize how they may be giving away their advantage in this emerging landscape by letting expertise erode and building on technology stacks they don’t own. Using the economics of verification as a framework, this piece explains what belongs in a firm’s verification loop, why leaders must retain control of it, and how doing so enables reliable autonomy without giving away the tacit knowledge and expertise that are key to long-term competitive advantage. The Verification Bottleneck Increasingly, what can be measured can be automated. Once the relevant information is codified and success can be measured, an AI model can use that feedback to hill-climb toward the desired outcome. But there is a catch: Any divergence between the context a human brings to a problem and the context available to the machine is a potential source of error. Think about the last time you wrote a prompt, only to realize midway through that you had omitted a critical dimension, constraint, or desired outcome. More often than not, the missing detail was something you understood tacitly and took for granted. This is a key reason machine intelligence can feel so “jagged:” astonishingly capable along measurable dimensions, but surprisingly clumsy everywhere else. Verification is the act of closing the gap between the weights that power an AI model and the neural paths and “weights” that power your own decision-making on the same problem. As AI makes execution increasingly cheap, the ability to properly steer and verify AI outputs better than your competitors will be the differentiator. World-class verification factories rely on two assets: unique ground truth and talent. For some firms, unique ground truth is simply a byproduct of scale and incumbency. If you process most of the world’s transactions in a domain, you observe that slice of the economy with a precision nobody can replicate. For others, it comes from extreme focus. If you have underwritten the same narrow risk for decades, you hold ground truth nobody else has seen. Neither is the prerequisite; unique measurement is. The best firms use measurement to turn market uncertainty into manageable risks, repeatable processes, and consistently better products. But ground truth alone is inert. Data only records what happened; when something falls outside the norm, it takes an expert to decide what it means and how to act on it. When domain experts set objectives and verify AI output, they draw on accumulated experience: past errors, corrections, and lessons learned. That experience is itself a form of measurement, one the AI does not have access to. Some call what remains unmeasured taste, others judgment. But these terms are vague, and their boundaries keep shifting: as model outputs improve, more of what once required human judgment is automated. A more concrete, practical distinction starts with a question: What context lives only inside a human, and what is available to the machine? Everything else follows from this distinction. Whatever isn’t yet, or cannot be, measured becomes a bottleneck to safe deployment. Unfortunately, many firms are adopting AI in ways that erode both of these critical assets, data and talent, at once. Tools that summarize documents, interactions, and context risk flattening divergent views into premature consensus, weakening the independence that makes expert talent valuable. Building on technology stacks the firm doesn’t own and letting its experts’ traces accumulate elsewhere erodes the exclusivity of its proprietary data. Together, these choices weaken the very capability that becomes more valuable as AI improves: the ability to tell whether its output is right. In a recent paper on the economics of verification, my coauthors and I mapped tasks along two dimensions: how cheap they are to automate, and how cheap they are to verify. See more HBR charts in Data & Visuals When a task is cheap to automate and cheap to verify, AI can be trusted to execute on its own without a human in the loop. We called this the “safe industrial” zone. But when automation is cheap while verification depends on human expertise, things get dangerous rather quickly. Here, we expect firms to deploy AI even when its outputs are likely to fall short. This is where a firm either defends its role as a verification factory or quietly gives it up. Catching the flaw in an output that is almost right takes experts with the independence and motivation to challenge the model, and ground truth that exists nowhere else. Right now, AI labs are doing everything they can to bring down the cost of verification across domains by aggressively purchasing specialized data and expert evaluations—even going so far as to buy the internal records of bankrupt companies. Each time they acquire richer digital traces of an economically valuable task, they turn something their models once missed into a capability they can sell. This expansion would be less threatening if firms were actively defending their position as verification factories. Most are doing the opposite: handing the labs the traces that make their tasks verifiable while letting the experts who could still catch a bad answer drift out of the loop. The sequence from there is predictable. One task at a time, the labs learn to verify what only in-house experts could verify before. The firm’s edge shrinks to whatever the labs still cannot measure. It becomes a thin wrapper around their intelligence, paying per token for capabilities it once owned while the labs capture a growing share of the actual value. Don’t Automate Away Your Expertise As firms increasingly buy inference from the same AI labs, their advantage will lie in the difference between the answers those labs provide to everyone and the conclusions they reach using proprietary data and expertise. Without that independent contribution, research suggests firms could rapidly converge toward a monoculture. Think about what managers really do. Good managers are verifiers. Yes, they route information, but in doing so they also determine what it means, what deserves others’ attention, and what meets their quality bar. In making these calls, they often retain a significant advantage even over frontier AI. Anyone with deep experience is a fast simulator of a particular slice of reality: a “world model” made of a person, fine-tuned through years of friction with a specific technology, market, customer base, or regulator. Much of the information behind that model is tacit and unrecorded, learned as much from what failed as from what worked. And in deciding what deserves attention, managers also wield real power within the organization. Now consider ceding many of those responsibilities to AI. An agent could turn sales meetings, support tickets, and internal discussions into a ranked list of product priorities, then use that list to assign work. An experienced engineer hesitates over one feature because it reminds them of a past failure, but they have not yet pinned down the connection. All they write is, “Not sure I’m fully comfortable with this.” The agent records strong customer demand and no concrete technical objection, leaving the hesitation out of its conclusions. A manager may still approve the budget, but the model has already shaped what they see and what they know to question. Handing these decisions to AI is a transfer of power, not simple automation, and it can destroy what makes a firm unique. Lose your company’s edge in what it senses and prioritizes, and everything else falls apart rather quickly. Even an AI system trained on company data is constrained by what has been measured and made available to it. It therefore risks prioritizing what the firm has already seen and codified. This can deliver measurable short-run gains by quickly routing decision-makers to existing solutions, while weakening the firm’s ability to identify and adapt to new, unstructured problems. When AI tools struggle to distinguish an emerging signal from a distraction, they can amplify what is already known at the expense of what is still taking shape, pushing the firm toward premature consensus around the wrong answer. Deployed across a firm, these tools can degrade the very expertise they draw on. Slop, but for decisions. If companies cut experts off from the friction that keeps them learning, they may not recognize the damage until the next big discontinuity, when the models are confidently wrong and no one inside the firm is still used to overruling them. Companies can deploy AI without flattening the independent thinking of their managers and experts. But doing so requires systems that preserve independent judgment, expose disagreements, and help employees test competing views against new data. Rather than compressing everything into a single company-wide memory, AI should help each employee build and continually refine their own version of it. Three design principles follow. Learning loops should test decisions against real-world outcomes and feed the insights back to both models and experts. A healthy loop starts with a clear definition of success. It records the information the AI used, the actions it took, and why experts accepted, corrected, or overrode its recommendations. The firm then tests both the AI’s recommendations and the experts’ corrections against business outcomes and new evidence from the market. Those results should guide changes to evaluation criteria, knowledge, instructions, and workflows, including what the system can approve, reject, or escalate. Proposed improvements should be tested, and the lessons incorporated into the firm’s institutional memory and shared with experts so their judgment improves too. Fine-tuning the model is one possible ingredient in this broader learning system. The loop should also flag when generation outpaces meaningful verification, a warning that the firm may be shipping output it cannot yet trust. The pattern is already visible in software: as AI adoption has accelerated, developer throughput has risen, but so have bugs and production incidents. Agents should surface relevant knowledge, not flatten it. AI agents in a firm’s communication channels should help people articulate tacit knowledge with as little friction as possible. Because agents often lack that context, they should preserve disagreements and unresolved concerns rather than compress them into premature consensus. Experts’ objections can reveal a gap between their “weights” and the firm’s telemetry, bringing previously unrecorded experience into the system. Eliciting those objections helps the firm detect new developments and identify what still needs to be measured. Preserving them also creates an invaluable record for a postmortem, when the firm must trace a failure back to the assumptions and decisions that produced it. World models should be supporting infrastructure, not decision-makers. Perhaps most importantly, an effective company “world model” should continuously spot hidden assumptions and identify where accurate data is still missing, then encourage employees to seek real-world friction to surface more robust evidence. Only through repeated contact with reality can the AI model be genuinely up to date. Sometimes, this can be as simple as connecting people who hold different pieces of relevant context so they can compare notes and make explicit what would otherwise remain uncodified. These countermeasures can help ensure that, as AI becomes embedded in every company interaction, it does not inadvertently force everyone to operate from a narrow, model-compressed version of reality. By amplifying what makes the company and its experts unique, a truly customized model can become one of the firm’s most valuable strategic assets. The goal is to keep the firm’s internal market of ideas alive: treat competing views as hypotheses, prompt individuals to test them against real-world outcomes, and feed the resulting evidence and lessons back into the firm’s institutional memories and expertise. Each turn of the loop makes the firm a better verification factory. But the ultimate design test is how AI supports consequential decisions under fundamental uncertainty. A company-wide model that decides what information matters, resolves conflicting interpretations, and allocates attention and resources risks acting like a central planner and run into Friedrich Hayek’s central critique of planned economies: the tacit knowledge it needs is dispersed among people, tied to particular circumstances, and often never written down. The model cannot reliably outperform people if it lacks critical knowledge they hold. It should help them make that knowledge explicit, test their assumptions, and learn from the results. Otherwise, it risks eroding the expertise it depends on. Owning the Weights of Production A firm can get every component of its verification factory exactly right and still fail to capture the value it generates. Capturing value requires owning the traces and feedback generated by the loop. Today, leading AI labs are courting organizations with tools that reach deep into their document repositories, communication channels, and codebases. They also tempt employees with a Faustian bargain: Let the tools record how you use your computer while you work, and in exchange we will automate your work for you. Companies may be reassured by AI labs’ “no-training” commitments for their prompts and outputs. But they also need to know who can retain and reuse the operational traces surrounding that work: which tools an agent used and in what order, how it failed, and when a human overruled it. This form of “ambient AI” captures the distinctive ways employees handle exceptions, make decisions, and prioritize information. Taken together, those traces can provide a blueprint for replicating parts of a firm’s verification engine. If providers can reuse them to build their own offerings, firms risk handing over the knowledge that gives them an edge. The stakes rise as agents become more autonomous: broader permissions and deeper context put more of the firm’s secret sauce within the provider’s reach. Companies can protect that edge in a few ways. Own the loop. Protecting your firm from suddenly finding itself competing with the AI labs’ models starts with owning the learning loop and controlling how its data is used. The fine-grained, proprietary measurements it generates capture how your experts verify outputs and correct mistakes. Letting the labs reuse those measurements helps them learn to perform that verification themselves. Start by checking exactly what your provider can retain and reuse, and what its no-training and zero-data-retention commitments do and do not cover. Embrace open-weight models. Open-weight models offer a practical way to retain greater control. They make their underlying parameters available, allowing firms to download, run, and adapt the models themselves. Firms can deploy them on their own infrastructure or through a partner whose business is providing infrastructure rather than building AI products that could compete with the firm. In either case, the arrangement should keep proprietary information, operational traces, and improvements under the firm’s control. A growing coalition is working to build a thriving AI ecosystem that gives firms an alternative to relying on the closed labs. By August, more than 120 organizations had joined the Open Secure AI Alliance to advance open models and open-source tools for AI security. Open-weight models initially attracted enterprise interest for their potential to lower costs. Their strategic appeal now extends beyond those savings to control: ensuring that the data, feedback, and improvements generated through the firm’s use of AI remain assets of the firm. Find the right partner. Owning the loop does not require building everything yourself. Working with Thinking Machines, hedge fund Bridgewater used its proprietary data to customize an open-weight model that outperforms frontier closed models on the financial tasks tested. The arrangement serves both parties. Bridgewater strengthens its own capabilities without feeding its intellectual property back into the lab’s base models. Thinking Machines can offer training infrastructure without asking customers to surrender the knowledge that gives them an edge. The partner supplies the machine intelligence infrastructure; the firm retains the learning. . . . Firms have always been verification factories, even when verification was inextricably bundled with execution. Now that AI has unbundled the two, the companies that thrive will not only build best-in-class verification systems but also keep every trace that improves them inside their boundaries. As you prepare for this shift, ask yourself: when one of your experts inevitably overrules the AI, is that correction recorded? And do you own the system that captures it? If the answer to the first is no, you do not have a verification factory yet. If the answer to the second is no, you are building someone else’s.

title: Germany is picking up new armoured vehicles
body:
The Bundeswehr has taken delivery of its first Patria 6x6 armoured personnel carriers.
The subject of Germany acquiring Finnish Patria 6x6 wheeled armoured personnel carriers as a successor to the ageing Fuchs family of vehicles has been ongoing for several years (or at least explored during that time) . The finalisation of these efforts came at the end of December following the approval of the purchase agreement by the Bundestag Budget Committee. This resulted in the conclusion of two contracts – an executive agreement and a framework agreement.
The latter concerns the purchase of up to 876 Patria 6x6 armoured vehicles in four different variants (including a self-propelled mortar with the Nemo turret). In the case of the concluded executive contract, it involves the delivery of 349 vehicles in the following versions: armoured personnel carrier (10), reconnaissance (48 with an option for a further 14), artillery reconnaissance (52 with an option for a further 398), Nemo self-propelled mortar (69 with an option for a further 61), and combat engineering (170 with an option for a further 54).
The cost of this agreement is €747 million (the price for exercising the full options is a further €212 million) . Deliveries of the first 10 carriers (in the standard ordered by Sweden) were scheduled to take place as early as January 2026, while deliveries of the engineering vehicles will begin in 2027. The engineering vehicles will be handed over from 2028, and vehicle deliveries are expected to conclude in mid-2029.
The delivery of the first five carriers took place in the first half of February, as announced by the Finnish company Patria. This occurred at the logistics base in Zeithain, Saxony. This marks the beginning of the generational replacement process of vehicles based on the Fuchs carrier, which is crucial for the German army.
“These vehicles signal the start of Germany’s transformation towards a modern, highly mobile fleet of armoured vehicles, while demonstrating the strength and efficiency of the CAVS cooperation framework,” says Jussi Järvinen, Executive Vice President at Patria.
A major milestone for the CAVS programme: Patria delivered first CAVS 6x6 armoured vehicles to Germany. 🤝 Patria has delivered the first five CAVS 6×6 armoured vehicles to the Bundeswehr, marking Germany’s transition towards a modern, highly mobile protected mobility fleet. The… pic.twitter.com/N6JPqMHeeX
Crucially, the delivery of the first 10 vehicles was to be followed by a gradual transfer of technology to Patria’s German partners, namely FFG, JWT, and KNDS, with whom relevant agreements had been previously concluded. They will be responsible for the production of the engineering and reconnaissance variants. However, full production capacity will only be utilised with subsequent orders for the needs of the Bundeswehr .
These will be significantly larger, as Germany intended to acquire over 900 vehicles of various types as part of the replacement for the Fuchs family carriers. The number of Patria 6x6s purchased now is close to the figure reported in January by the Hartpunkt service. A prelude to Germany’s acquisition of the Patria 6x6 was the Future Indirect Fire Short-Range programme, under which Berlin will acquire Nemo mortars.
Their platform will be the Finnish carrier, a larger number of which was recorded under the aforementioned framework agreement. The implementation of the programme began at the end of January, when the Bundestag approved a €50 million contract for the acquisition of three vehicles: two self-propelled mortars and a command vehicle. These will be adapted to the requirements of the Heer (German Army) and subjected to numerous tests.
The Patria 6x6 is a Finnish three-axle armoured personnel carrier designed by Patria to replace the Sisu Pasi XA-180/185/200 family of vehicles. The vehicle was developed based on the XA-200 APC using components from the heavier Patria AMV 8×8, which allowed for technical unification as well as reduced production and operating costs for the new carrier. The crew consists of two soldiers, while the troop compartment can accommodate up to eight people. The armour is designed to provide protection from Level 2 to 4 according to the STANAG 4569A standard (depending on the armour kit used). The power unit is a Scania DC09 074A diesel engine with an output of 294 kW (400 HP), which allows the 24-tonne carrier to reach a maximum speed of 100 km/h.
The carrier can be equipped with a remote-controlled weapon station or a manned turret system with a heavy machine gun, automatic grenade launcher, or automatic cannon. The Patria 6x6 can serve as a platform for many specialised versions, such as a command vehicle, self-propelled mortar, electronic warfare vehicle, or self-propelled anti-aircraft system. Currently, these vehicles serve in the armed forces of Finland, Latvia, Denmark, Ukraine, and Sweden. In the future, they will be delivered to the armed forces of Germany and potentially the United Kingdom.

title: Kazakh Cyclists Sweep UCI Asia Tour Podium for First Time
body: Kazakhstan’s cyclists have claimed all three podium positions in the final individual Asia Tour rankings for the first time. Yevgeniy Fedorov of XDS Astana Team finished the 2026 season first, followed by teammate Nicolas Vinokurov in second and Alexey Lutsenko of Switzerland’s NSN Cycling Team in third. XDS is short for Xidesheng, a Chinese bicycle manufacturer and Astana’s title sponsor, while NSN stands for Never Say Never, the sports and entertainment company that co-owns Lutsenko’s team. Fedorov earned 666.33 points , while Vinokurov finished with 576.33. Another XDS Astana Team rider, China’s Haoyu Su, placed fourth with 445.33 points. This means riders from the team occupied three of the top four positions in the rankings. The Asia Tour is a series of road races across Asia overseen by the Union Cycliste Internationale (UCI), the international governing body for competitive cycling. Its individual and national rankings also count points earned by Asian riders in UCI races elsewhere in the world. Kazakhstan’s riders have held the top position in the individual Asia Tour standings since 2018. Over nine seasons, Lutsenko has won the rankings seven times and Fedorov twice. Kazakhstan previously placed two riders in the top three on several occasions. Kazakhstan also finished the season first in the UCI Asia Tour national rankings , accumulating 2,339.99 points. Its lead over Mongolia and Japan, which finished second and third, exceeded 1,200 points. Kazakhstan has finished first in these standings every year since 2017. Iran was the last country to finish ahead of Kazakhstan, in 2016. XDS Astana Development Team, the Kazakh cycling club’s development squad, finished third in the Asia Tour team rankings , behind China’s Li Ning Star and Thailand’s Roojai Insurance Winspace. This is the best result in the development team’s history. In the UCI world team rankings , the main XDS Astana Team finished the season in sixth place, while XDS Astana Development Team ranked fourth among continental teams. For Alexey Lutsenko, this was the final season of his professional career. He discussed his retirement plans after winning the men’s road race at the Asian Games in Japan on September 23, claiming a national-record sixth Asian Games gold medal .

title: Customer Outcomes Define Service Excellence, Says Remita MD
body: The Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Remita Payment Services Limited, ’DeRemi Atanda, has called on businesses and public institutions to measure digital transformation by the outcomes customers achieve, rather than the sophistication of deployed technology. He made the call at the 2026 Service Excellence Conference held in Lagos recently, where business executives, regulators and public sector leaders discussed how technology and human interaction could improve service delivery. Speaking on the conference theme, ‘Tech-Enabled. Human-Powered,’ Atanda said organisations often invest heavily in digital platforms and automation without addressing the delays, uncertainty and difficulties customers encounter when accessing services. He urged service providers to understand customer expectations before adopting new technologies, noting that automation cannot compensate for poorly designed processes or unclear service standards. “Technology has been, and will continue to be, a means to an end, not the end itself. Customers are not looking for technology; they are looking for outcomes. Technology cannot deliver service excellence if it is optimising for the wrong expectations. The journey begins with how we understand what customers want, which ultimately comes down to less effort and greater certainty,” he said. During a panel discussion, Atanda said speed alone was insufficient to guarantee customer satisfaction, adding that a transaction could be completed quickly without meeting customer expectations. “Speed is just one attribute of service delivery. Fast service is not always pleasant, nor does it always meet customer expectations. To deliver true service excellence, you must combine speed with smart solutions and human connection. That is what builds consistency and trust,” he explained. He also stressed the importance of retaining empathy and responsiveness in digital service delivery, saying technology should not prevent customers from receiving appropriate support when problems arise. “When we speak of human connection in technology, ‘human’ does not mean manual processes. It is about the emotional component of service delivery and how people relate to your brand. As we deploy technology as an invisible layer, we must ensure that it does not remove the human touch, because technology that remembers is technology that feels human,” he added. On accountability in financial services, Atanda said businesses must take responsibility for the promises they make to customers, even when transactions depend on multiple networks and service providers. “You don’t prepare for war in the time of war; you prepare for war in the time of peace. Service providers must design for failure as seriously as they design for success. In a complex financial ecosystem, reliability is shared across multiple partners, but accountability is never shared. It is entirely yours to deliver on your promise to the customer,” he emphasised. He recommended that business leaders understand customer expectations before choosing technology, map the customer journey, incorporate empathy into service processes, prepare for service failures and assess performance using actual customer experiences rather than system uptime alone. The conference highlighted the need for organisations to evaluate digital investments based on their impact on customers.

title: Frozen Russian assets key to covering Ukraine's 2027 financing needs – National Bank governor
body:
The issue of immobilized Russian assets is being discussed in the context of the need to find confirmed sources of financing to cover the "gap" in the state budget for 2027, which Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky estimated at $32.6 billion at the Ukraine Ministerial Roundtable on October 14 during the Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank, National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) Governor Andriy Pyshnyy said.
"Currently, the IMF chief [Kristalina Georgieva] has confirmed the need for assurances from partners regarding coverage of this 'gap,' which has been verified by the IMF. The IMF is also considering, in this context, the use of immobilized assets in a way that European partners would consider acceptable to them, in order to ensure that Ukraine receives the necessary amount of financing," Pyshnyy said in an interview with Interfax-Ukraine on the sidelines of the Annual Meetings.
According to him, the IMF always discusses this issue very cautiously, recognizing that its mandate and influence are limited.
"But the IMF is involved in discussions on the format for accessing immobilized assets. For example, the Fund may recommend paying attention to a factor such as debt sustainability, so that the use of immobilized assets does not create additional interest-rate pressure for Ukraine. As for how exactly this will be structured, that will be determined by the European bureaucracy," the NBU governor explained.
He said he was optimistic about the possibility of continuing to use immobilized Russian assets to finance Ukraine and mentioned the evolution of the IMF's and the European Central Bank's positions on the issue.
"This issue requires complex, comprehensive communication on the part of the president, the government and the National Bank. You have seen how many meetings I have had here: over these past few days, I have held dozens of discussions with partners. This issue remains one of our priorities," Pyshnyy said.
As reported, in 2024, the G7 established the Extraordinary Revenue Acceleration (ERA) mechanism, providing Ukraine with $50 billion in unconditional, non-repayable financing based on discounting future cash flows from the further investment of Russian assets immobilized in Europe, primarily at Euroclear, totaling approximately EUR 200 billion. Most of the $50 billion is scheduled to be disbursed in 2025–2026, while only $1.4 billion is allocated for 2027.
In addition, after the idea of a EUR 140 billion reparations loan for the EU backed by the same proceeds from frozen Russian assets fell through in autumn 2025, the EU developed the Ukraine Support Loan (USL), a EUR 90 billion mechanism for 2026–2027 to provide military and nonmilitary support to Ukraine. This is also non-repayable assistance to Ukraine; however, the allocation of part of the funding for budget financing is tied to Kyiv's fulfillment of reform conditions.
The 2027 state budget currently provides for $52.6 billion in external financing, of which only approximately $20 billion comes from confirmed sources. In mid-October, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, taking defense spending into account, estimated Ukraine's total additional financing needs for 2027 at EUR 70 billion while in Brussels.
As part of efforts to secure these funds, according to available information, consideration is being given to launching ERA-2 and/or USL-2 mechanisms by continuing to discount future cash flows from Russian Federation assets immobilized for a longer period or investing them in higher-yielding assets.

title: Rada extends general mobilization for 90 days
body:
The Verkhovna Rada has supported President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's decree on extending the period of general mobilization in Ukraine for 90 days.

As reported by an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent, 281 people's deputies voted in favor of the relevant draft law No. 16183 as a whole during a plenary session of the Verkhovna Rada on Monday.

According to the draft law, the period of general mobilization is extended for 90 days starting from October 31, 2026.

title: Mbappe steals Yamal’s Ballon d’Or spotlight with El Clasico double
body: Seven Ballon d’Or nominees started Sunday’s Clasico at Camp Nou. Real Madrid’s Kylian Mbappe stood out from the pack, scoring both his side’s goals in a shock 2-1 win at the home of their greatest rival. Barcelona had won all nine league games to begin the season, averaging more than four goals per game, and would have gone nine points clear of Madrid had they won. But Madrid coach Jose Mourinho does not follow convention , nor did his team. They frustrated Barcelona throughout, took the lead before the break and got the winner three minutes from time following some magical skill from Jude Bellingham and then Mbappe . Madrid’s players were joined by half of their bench as they celebrated right in front of the most vocal Barca fans, which did not go down well. Raphinha had equalised for Barca after 61 minutes in front of the 62,000-strong crowd as the stadium continues its redevelopment towards a 105,000-seat capacity. El Clasico justified its status as the biggest game in world football, an intense battle between two giants powered by some of the best players. England’s Premier League may be the pre-eminent league, but Barcelona and Madrid are huge attractions; Barcelona, in particular, produces sublime footballing talents. Both clubs will be represented at the Ballon d’Or Awards at London’s Palladium Theatre on Monday. Madrid didn’t attend the previous two ceremonies after learning that Vinicius Jnr wouldn’t win an award. For Barcelona , Pau Cubarsi, Rodri and Lamine Yamal are among the 30 nominees. For Madrid, Bellingham, Marc Cucurella, Mbappe and Vinicius are in the running. Yamal and Cubarsi are both only 19 years old. Both grew up in Catalonia, north of Barcelona, as did Cucurella. Much is made of the concentration of top managers from Spain’s smallest province, Gipuzkoa, but there's a small area of Catalonia north of Barcelona with towns and villages that have produced an inordinate amount of footballing talent. Como boss Cesc Fabregas is also from here, as is Xavi Espart, yet another 19-year-old who started as right back for Barcelona in the Clasico. Fabregas, Espart, Cucurella and Yamal come from the coastal strip, Cubarsi from the inland village of Bescano and four generations of carpenters. Pau is better at passing a football than planing a plank of wood. He was originally a youth player with nearby Girona before moving to Barca. In one tournament game for Girona against Manchester United when he was 10 years old, United’s coaches said it was like playing against a one-man team, Cubarsi being that man. Nine of Spain’s World Cup squad were Catalans. Unlike Cubarsi, who won the award for the World Cup’s best young player, Yamal didn’t have a great World Cup, but he remains the hottest player in world football. When The National asked Barca fans outside Camp Nou who should win the Ballon d’Or, most chose him. The Barcelona winger is the favourite to win, along with England and Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane and then Mbappe . But Spain won the World Cup by conceding only one goal. Their defence was key. Cucurella, who grew up just a 15-minute drive from Yamal, had the better of his rival on Sunday, who was reduced to skewing a shot wide before half-time and again in the 78th minute. It was not Yamal’s night, despite Barca having 62 per cent possession and 12 shots to Madrid’s five. Yet it was Madrid who created the better chances. Cucurella was a young professional with Barca and a regular with the B team, but he never played a first-team game. Home fans sang songs about him, casting him as the pantomime villain, and howled at his heavy challenges on Yamal. But they were silenced when he released Yan Diomande, who crossed for Mbappe to capitalise on a Gerard Martin error and put Madrid ahead. La Liga had seemed predictable before the Clasico and some Madrid fans had even written their team off. With only three points separating the top three, it’s now a real title race. “The world that loves football will have stopped to watch this and they won’t have gone disappointed; this was two teams that played to win,” said the victorious Mourinho , back at Madrid following 13 years. Madrid’s win was a surprise, but a deserved one. Will there be another one in London for the Ballon d’Or ? It has been framed as a race between Yamal and Kane, but Mbappe’s two goals in the biggest game in the world on the eve of the awards make him the man of the moment.

title: 80% poultry import dependence highlights need to grow local production – Netherlands Ambassador
body: The Netherlands Ambassador to Ghana, H.E. Hans Akerboom, has expressed concern over Ghana’s dependence on imported poultry, saying the country imports about 80% of its poultry supply despite strong domestic demand. He said the situation presented a significant opportunity for Ghana to strengthen local production, create jobs and improve the livelihoods of poultry farmers and businesses. Speaking at a round-table discussion on the poultry industry in Accra on Monday, October 26, 2026, aimed at strengthening stakeholder collaboration in Ghana’s poultry sector, H.E. Akerboom said Ghana imported poultry worth approximately €18 million from the Netherlands alone in 2024. He noted that the country also imports poultry from other countries, including Belgium, the United States and Brazil, further highlighting the country’s reliance on foreign supplies. The Ambassador said the figures were worrying but also demonstrated the potential for Ghana to develop a stronger and more competitive domestic poultry industry. “This is not simply about reducing imports. It is about creating the right conditions for Ghanaian farmers to grow their businesses, supply the market day by day and benefit from the demand that already exists,” he said. He said chicken remained a popular source of protein for many Ghanaian households, creating a ready market for local farmers and businesses. However, he stressed that meeting this demand would require stronger partnership between the government, private sector, financial institutions and knowledge institutions. Ghana-Netherlands partnership H.E. Akerboom said the Netherlands was ready to support Ghana’s efforts to expand domestic poultry production through the exchange of technical knowledge, innovation and investment. He cited a visit by a Ghanaian delegation to the Netherlands earlier this year, during which officials explored opportunities to draw on Dutch expertise and investment to support the development of Ghana’s poultry industry. According to him, the Netherlands’ poultry sector has grown through sustained investment in knowledge, innovation and collaboration, lessons he said could be adapted to Ghana’s needs. He said the proposed interventions aligned with the government’s Feed Ghana programme and the 24-hour economy initiative, which could provide opportunities to strengthen agricultural production and create sustainable businesses. The Ambassador announced that he would sign an addendum to the Memorandum of Understanding governing the Ghana-Netherlands Food and Agriculture Working Group, with a specific focus on the poultry sector. He said the agreement would provide a framework for advancing cooperation and translating the shared ambition of both countries into practical outcomes. As an initial step, H.E. Akerboom said a webinar would be organised in 2027 to present the key outcomes of the round-table discussion and facilitate connections between stakeholders to encourage further collaboration. He expressed optimism that the partnership would help create opportunities for Ghanaian farmers, businesses and the wider food sector. The round-table discussion forms part of broader efforts to identify practical solutions to the challenges facing Ghana’s poultry industry and improve its capacity to meet domestic demand.

title: Russia Says Ukraine Peace Talks Won’t Slow War, Open to Local Truces
body:
Russia will not slow its offensive against Ukraine despite plans to resume US-brokered peace talks, but Moscow is open to localized humanitarian ceasefires, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Monday, Oct. 26.
Asked whether Russia would consider temporary truces along the front line, Peskov told reporters : “For humanitarian purposes, absolutely.”
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
His remarks come ahead of a localized ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky in the Kherson region, intended to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and civilian evacuations.
The agreement, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, is scheduled to take effect on Oct. 29, according to the White House. Russian and Ukrainian officials are coordinating the operation.
However, Peskov made clear that the arrangement would not signal a broader halt to Russia’s war against Ukraine.
“The decision to resume trilateral talks does not imply any restrictions on combat operations,” he said.
“Our armed forces continue to carry out massive strikes on Ukraine’s military-industrial complex,” he added.
Oleshky, a Russian-occupied city on the left bank of the Dnipro River opposite Kherson, has faced a worsening humanitarian crisis, with residents reporting severe shortages of food, clean water, and medicine.
Before Russia’s full-scale invasion, the city had a population of about 24,000. The White House estimates that between 1,700 and 2,000 people remain, including elderly residents and around 50 children.
The temporary truce is intended to allow humanitarian supplies into the city and establish a safe passage for civilians who want to leave. Residents will be able to choose whether to evacuate to Ukrainian-controlled territory or Russia, according to the White House.
Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets, who led Kyiv’s negotiating team, confirmed the agreement and said the operation would be implemented in stages.
Melania Trump said she worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian representatives to coordinate the arrangement. Her involvement builds on previous efforts to reunite Ukrainian children separated from their families during Russia’s war.
The latest diplomatic push follows meetings between US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg on Oct. 21.
The envoys had held consultations with Ukrainian and European officials in Oslo the previous day.
On Sunday, Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov said Moscow was ready to resume trilateral negotiations with Ukraine and the US after Nov. 4, following Russia’s National Unity Day holiday.
“After that, we will be ready to resume negotiations,” Ushakov said, according to Russian state media.
He cautioned against expecting an immediate breakthrough, describing the next round as an opportunity to explore the parties’ positions rather than reach a final agreement.
Working-level delegations could meet in Abu Dhabi or Switzerland to prepare for further discussions.
Previous rounds of negotiations have failed to bring the sides closer to a settlement. Moscow continues to demand additional Ukrainian territory and sweeping restrictions on Kyiv’s military and political independence.
Ukraine and its allies have rejected those demands as unacceptable, warning that concessions imposed under pressure could leave the country vulnerable to another Russian attack.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Redistricting isn't playing out how the GOP hoped. And, Brazil's Lula wins 4th term
body:
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.
North Carolina Republican Congressional candidates, State Rep. Jennifer Balkcom and Laurie Buckhout (R) are embraced by President Trump during an election rally on October 20, 2026 in Greenville, North Carolina. Buckhout is running in North Carolina's 1st District which was redrawn to heavily favor Republicans and is now a toss-up. Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images hide caption
Republicans had a plan to keep control of the House in the midterms: Redraw congressional district lines to favor the GOP and avoid the historical pattern of heavy midterm losses. President Trump began pressuring Republican-led states to do just that last year, but it isn't working out as expected. Republicans could now be spending millions of dollars on House seats that were supposed to be easy wins, and end up losing anyway . Of the 15 districts drawn specifically to favor Republicans, only five are rated by the Cook Political Report as either likely or solid Republican. Most are toss-ups or lean toward a Democratic win.
In a stunning political comeback, leftist Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won a fourth term in the presidential runoff election in Brazil. Lula defeated Flávio Bolsonaro , son of former far-right President Jair Bolsonaro, by more than 4 million votes. It's the first time since Brazil restored democracy in 1989 that a candidate who finished second in the first round has gone on to win the presidency.
Large demonstrations against the government continued over the weekend in France, where more than 100,000 people showed up in Paris, and more than 400,000 came out nationwide. What started with students demanding better conditions has grown into a much bigger movement. Unions and public-sector workers have joined, calling for more public spending and protesting growing inequality. Similar protests have erupted across Europe, from Spain to Serbia.
Out-of-pocket maternity expenses are difficult to predict. A federal requirement for insurers to provide personalized cost estimates under the No Surprises Act was supposed to take effect in 2022, but federal regulators haven't made it happen despite pressure from Congress. Until the cost of maternity care gets more transparent, here are some tips to help you budget for the cost of pregnancy:
A satellite image provided by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) shows Hurricane Isaias approaching the Gulf Coast of Alabama and Florida on Friday, Oct. 9 2026. National Oceanic and Atmospheric/National Oceanic and Atmospheric hide caption
When Hurricane Isaias made landfall in Destin, Fla., as a Category 2 storm, Google DeepMind's AI model outperformed the traditional model, correctly predicting it would hit the Florida Panhandle rather than head west toward Louisiana. Hurricane forecasters say they're increasingly relying on AI technology, and that it's rapidly transforming the field .
This newsletter was edited by Majd Al-Waheidi.

title: Israel Police brace for 'January 6' scenario at Knesset after election, deploy 22,000 officers
body: One day before the elections for the 26th Knesset, police are preparing for the possibility of clashes and public order disruptions on Election Day, particularly in the hours following the release of exit polls.A senior police official estimates that voting day itself is expected to pass relatively quietly, but significant concern centers on 10:00 p.m., when exit poll results are published, and the potential for lingering tensions in the days that follow."I think the day after, as we call it, is no less sensitive," the official said. He noted that exit poll results could bring celebrating or angry citizens into the streets, and police are preparing for potential friction, confrontations, and disorder throughout the night, the following day, and into the weekend. The official emphasized that police cannot limit their focus to securing polling stations and maintaining public order solely during voting hours.Large forces will remain active across the country after polls close, recognizing that election results could trigger sharp reactions among supporters of various parties and political blocs.As part of preparations, police are also slated to secure five major party gatherings: four in Tel Aviv and one for Likud at the International Convention Center in Jerusalem. "Every setup like this, and I am referring to party events, requires a very large number of police forces," he stated.22,000 officers, Netanyahu briefed on securityDespite expectations that Election Day itself may pass without major incidents, police are significantly bolstering their forces.About 22,000 police officers are scheduled to participate in the security operation, up from about 17,000 in the previous election, an increase of roughly 5,000 officers. The senior official shared that as part of preparations, a comprehensive security briefing was presented to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, with National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir in attendance.The meeting covered intelligence assessments, threats of hostile terrorist activity, concerns over public order disruptions, and the operational readiness of the police force.According to the official, police have been preparing for the elections for about three months in coordination with the Shin Bet and the IDF. During the briefing, Netanyahu posed questions focused on security threats and force readiness.The official assessed that the prime minister and his ministry director-general were impressed by the staff work and the seriousness with which the organization approaches the mission.The importance of police independence during the election period was also emphasized during the meeting."The most important organization during elections is the Israel Police. It is completely impossible to hold elections in the State of Israel without an apolitical police force," the official said.He added that even when operating under the responsibility of the National Security Minister, the police must maintain professional independence and remain free from political influence, both in practical conduct and in public perception.Capitol orderConcerns over extraordinary events occurring after polls close are not new. Back in August, Maariv military correspondent Avi Ashkenazi reported that the defense establishment was preparing for what was termed "Operation Capitol", a scenario in which one of the two competing political blocs claims the results were forged, refuses to accept them, and acts to undermine public order.The scenario was crafted following the events of January 6, 2021, in the United States, when supporters of Donald Trump stormed the Capitol building in Washington after his loss in the November 2020 presidential election to Joe Biden. Former head of the Police Operations Directorate, retired Maj.-Gen. Sigal Bar-Tzvi, led the team within the operations division that drafted the "Capitol" order.The plan addresses a situation where a political group in Israel claims widespread fraud in election results and attempts to disrupt the vote count, or a scenario where tens of thousands of people attempt to storm the Knesset building.According to a security official, the primary concern requiring special readiness is the possibility that one of the camps will not accept the election results."If I am Danny Levy, the Police Commissioner, one thing needs to bother me from morning to night. Not the deployment of forces on Election Day; police know how to do that best. The problem is on election night, after polls close and reports begin coming in from exit polls and actual election results," a senior retired police officer said.He noted that "a dangerous scenario that could occur in these elections is that one of the leaders of the two political blocs declares he does not accept the election results and calls on the public to take to the streets. On the other side, the opposing camp will bring its people into the streets to safeguard the democratic process. In such a case, police will require assistance from additional bodies, chief among them the IDF."Former officials warn: 'It would be a massive failure'A series of former police officers and Shin Bet officials believe that the "Capitol" scenario must be placed at the top of the priority list in Election Day preparations. They argue that although it represents an extreme scenario, it must be prepared for through operational plans and advance exercises."It would be a massive failure if it turns out this scenario was not placed at the top of the list of contingencies and responses. An organized order must be issued detailing police force allocations and reinforcement units for police. Exercises must be conducted at National Headquarters, across all districts and units, and commanders should even participate in a war game. This is an extreme scenario, but it must be prepared for with the utmost seriousness," a former security official said.Maariv has learned that Police Commissioner Chief Superintendent Danny Levy held periodic conversations throughout the period with former senior officials in the organization, some of whom raised concerns regarding the scenario.One retired police major general expressed deep concern over the possibility of election results being challenged and criticized the conduct of various figures in the public and security arenas."The Shin Bet and police are the two organizations tasked with safeguarding democracy in Israel. They are responsible for overseeing an orderly transfer of power. Regrettably, today it is difficult to rely on the Shin Bet, and it is unclear to what extent it will act in a professional and statesmanlike manner."We are already witnessing the initial stages of this scenario, where a news channel broadcasts weekly results of absurd polls with figures that do not align with other surveys, serving as a form of preparation for a narrative of stolen elections. This is compounded by a campaign of delegitimization against the Central Elections Committee and the Supreme Court."The retired major general added that he also fears the presence of numerous firearms in civilian hands and the potential for escalation into violent clashes."To all of this, one must add the armed militias established here in Israel over the past four years: regional defense units in Judea and Samaria, standby security squads across the country, and tens of thousands of weapons distributed to civilians. This is definitely a dangerous and violent platform for a civil war. It is the ultimate nightmare. This is a test of leadership, whether leaders are going to create an event around refusing to accept election results, or whether they will act with public responsibility even if they lose," he said.

title: Thessaloniki Celebrates 114 Years Since Liberation from Ottoman Rule
body: Thessaloniki marks the anniversary of its liberation on October 26, commemorating the day in 1912 when the Greek Army accepted the surrender of the Ottoman garrison during the First Balkan War. The historic event took place on the feast day of Saint Demetrius, the city’s patron saint, making October 26 a date of particular significance for Thessaloniki and its Greek Orthodox community. As the First Balkan War unfolded, Greece sought to expand its territory and secure key areas of Macedonia. Prime Minister Eleftherios Venizelos was determined that the Greek Army reach Thessaloniki before Bulgarian forces, which were also advancing towards the strategically important city. According to historical accounts, when asked whether the Greek Army should move towards Thessaloniki, Venizelos insisted: “Θεσσαλονίκη με κάθε κόστος!” meaning “Thessaloniki, at all costs!” The Ottoman authorities negotiated with both the Greek and Bulgarian armies as they approached the city. On October 26, 1912, Ottoman commander Tahsin Pasha surrendered Thessaloniki to the Greek Army. Bulgarian troops arrived the following day. When Bulgarian officials sought entry, Tahsin Pasha reportedly told them: “I have only one Thessaloniki, which I have surrendered.” The city’s incorporation into Greece was subsequently formalised through the Treaty of Bucharest in 1913, following the Second Balkan War. Today, the anniversary remains an important milestone in Greek history, commemorating Thessaloniki’s liberation and its place within the modern Greek state. title: Akku.scm 1.2.0 released
body:
Akku.scm version 1.2.0, the language package manager for R6RS and R7RS Scheme, is now generally available. It can be downloaded from GitLab . The most important change is a fix to the dependency solver, which was running very slowly due to a bug triggered by the many versions of the chez-srfi package.
Akku is a project-based package manager, where each project has its own set of dependencies. You use .akku/env to set shell variables that let your Scheme implementation know where to find everything.
You can upload your own packages to the archive. They go through a review process to ensure nothing malicious is distributed.
Akku also performs automatic conversion from the R7RS define-library form to the R6RS library form. This lets, e.g., Chez Scheme use R7RS libraries. Packages from the Snow package manager, which has many R7RS packages, are also available via Akku.

title: Filipino-Canadian voice actor Eric Bauza dies at 46
body: MANILA, Philippines – Filipino-Canadian voice actor Eric Bauza, best known for voicing iconic Looney Tunes characters Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, died on Sunday, October 25. He was 46. His family announced his death in a statement posted on Instagram on Sunday. They had referred to his passing as “sudden.” View this post on Instagram A post shared by 𝙀𝙍𝙄𝘾 𝘽𝘼𝙐𝙕𝘼 (@bauzilla) Born in Scarborough, Ontario, Canada, on December 7, 1979, Bauza grew up watching Looney Tunes and imitating its characters. He later became one of the franchise’s defining modern voices following in the footsteps of legendary voice actor Mel Blanc. Bauza voiced Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, Tweety, Porky Pig, Elmer Fudd, Foghorn Leghorn, and Road Runner, among other characters. He lent his voice to films like Space Jam: A New Legacy, Super Mario Bros. , and King Tweeny . His latest work before his passing was Coyote vs. Acme, which premiered in August 2026. He had voiced Wile E. Coyote in the Dave Green-directed comedy film. Play Video In a 2021 interview with NBC News , Bauza said the appeal of Looney Tunes crossed cultural and language barriers. “ Looney Tunes transcends all languages and all cultures,” he said. “It doesn’t matter what part of the planet you’re from. You get the comedy.” Beyond Looney Tunes , Bauza lent his voice to hundreds of projects across film, television, and video games, including The Adventures of Puss in Boots, Teen Titans Go!, Ben 10, and The Super Mario Bros. Movie. His career spanned more than 25 years, with over 400 acting credits. He won three Children’s and Family Emmy Awards between 2022 and 2025 for his voice performance. @CoyoteACMEMovie pic.twitter.com/H992Ff6tSO — Eric Bauza (@bauzilla) August 24, 2026 In a statement reported by the Hollywood Reporter , Warner Bros. Television Group chair Channing Dungey paid tribute to Bauza, saying he brought “joy and laughter to millions around the world.” “He followed in the footsteps of giants like Mel Blanc,” Dungey added, honoring Bauza’s 15 years with Warner Bros. animation. – Neo Croox/Rappler.com Neo Croox is a Rappler intern taking up journalism at the University of Santo Tomas.

title: Russia supports gas availability for developing economies
body:
MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. The availability of natural gas is of particular importance for developing countries, as gas infrastructure and modern technologies are essential prerequisites for industrialization and improvement of people's quality of life, Russian Energy Minister Sergey Tsivilyov said at a press conference following the GECF (Gas Exporting Countries Forum) ministerial meeting.
"The availability of natural gas for developing countries, gas infrastructure, modern technologies, investments, necessary conditions for industrialization, creating new production facilities, and improving people's quality of life are of particular significance," he said.
"Natural gas remains the guarantor of global energy security. It ensures the reliability and affordability of energy for millions. One of the main outcomes of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum will be the adoption of the Moscow Declaration, the draft of which was approved today. The declaration is based on three principles: energy justice, technological neutrality, and equal non-discriminatory access to energy resources and technologies," the minister added.
The declaration establishes not only general principles but also specific directions for joint work, Tsivilyov noted. "Among them are the development of new markets, including in Africa and other developing regions; the creation of mechanisms for long-term financing of infrastructure projects; and technological exchange and the implementation of digital solutions, including artificial intelligence," the minister said.
"Our common task is to create the conditions for building long-term and mutually beneficial relationships. This requires predictable market rules, long-term contracts, and a fair distribution of risks," Tsivilyov added.
