title: Anambra govt seeks NMA support in fight against illegal health facilities
body:
The Anambra State Government has called on the Nigeria Medical Association (NMA) to support its efforts to eradicate quack and unregistered health facilities in the state.
Adam Obidike, the commissioner for health in Anambra made the appeal during the closing ceremony of the 2026 Physicians Week and Scientific Conference of the Nigerian Medical Association, Awka Zone in Awka on Sunday.
The theme of the Week, Luncheon and Award Presentation Ceremony was “Securing the Future of Medicine in Nigeria and Sub-Saharan Africa”.
Mr Obidike, a medical doctor, said the NMA was a critical partner and that the government would collaborate with the association to track fake and unregistered facilities.
According to him, “Anambra is going to work with the NMA because they will help us to identify people who are not medical personnel practicing in Anambra.”
“We are determined to shut all of them down because when people go there, they receive treatment that is not proper for their ailment.
“We have a checklist and anybody who wants to set up a facility should go to the department of medical services and get the conditions, including the design of the building,” he said.
In his welcome address, Tim-Uzoma Mbaeri, chairman of NMA, Awka Zone, said this year’s Physicians Week and Scientific Conference was a time to celebrate the profession and reconnect members with each other.
Mr Mbaeri, a professor, said the association used the event to visit sick colleagues, provide free laboratory tests including prostate specific antigens testing, urinalysis among others.
He thanked members and partners of the NMA, Awka branch, whose contributions ensured the success of the physicians’ week.
“We also enjoyed a novelty football match, had an opportunity for friendship, recreation, and strong inter-agency relationships.
“We find satisfaction not merely in the event we organised, but in the lives we have touched, the colleagues we have encouraged, the relationships we have strengthened and the visibility we have given to our profession,” he said.
Mr Mbaeri said three personalities were honoured with awards of meritorious service to the medical profession and the NMA, including Ifeoma Njelita, Emmanuel Umenweke and Amaka Ezeno.
Njelita is an associate professor and a consultant in community medicine at the Chukwuemeka Odumegwu Ojukwu University Teaching Hospital.
Umenweke is a medical doctor with the Nnamdi Azikiwe University Medical Center, Awka while Ezeno, the third awardee is a lawyer, Notary Public and member of the Body of Benchers.

title: From vision to abandonment: Nigeria’s unfinished development, By Dipo Baruwa
body:
…addressing Nigeria’s challenge of abandoned projects demands more than increased funding or renewed political rhetoric. It requires systemic reform anchored in strong authority, effective coordination, well-aligned incentives, and unwavering commitment. By embedding these principles into the country’s development framework, Nigeria stands a better chance of breaking the cycle of unfinished ambitions, both physical and programmatic, and beginning the process of realising the full economic and social value of its investments.
The drive for socio-economic development has seen Nigeria embark on several developmental projects, ranging from physical infrastructure to economic programmes. These initiatives, on the face value, were often well articulated; designed to address strategic gaps in the country’s socio-economic landscape or to deepen the capacity for growth through new opportunities.
Unfortunately, a significant number of these projects have never seen the light of day. Some were abandoned before completion, while others have been left in a state of prolonged inactivity; effectively maintained in a form of ‘suspended animation’. As a result, unfinished structures dot the landscape across the country; some are completed facilities that never became commercially viable, while others remain trapped indefinitely between conception and construction. Several continue to receive annual budgetary allocations, even though they produce little or no public value.
The true cost of these projects, therefore, extends far beyond what was originally budgeted or already spent. It includes the recurring expenses of maintaining dormant institutions, the escalating cost of eventual completion, and the lost productive capacity, employment opportunities, and private investment that these projects were intended, but failed, to generate. Nigeria’s abandoned projects cannot, therefore, be understood through a single headline figure. They represent monumental undertakings that have continued to drain the economy both financially and psychologically, denying the country the benefits of a healthy, prosperous, and development-driven socio-economic environment.
Importantly, this challenge is not limited to physical infrastructure alone. A number of non-physical initiatives – economic programmes, policy interventions, and reform agendas – have also suffered similar fates. Many of these programmes were designed to stimulate growth, enhance productivity, or support vulnerable sectors, but were either prematurely discontinued, inconsistently implemented, or allowed to fade without achieving scale. The consequence is a significant loss of economic gains that could have been realised through scaling effects and multiplier impacts across sectors. In many cases, these abandoned or under-implemented programmes represent missed opportunities for sustained economic transformation, as their intended ripple effects across employment, income generation, and private sector development were never fully realised.
To fully grasp the scale and implications of this challenge, it is important to examine not only the financial outlays but also the systemic issues that have contributed to the persistence of these unfinished ambitions. Weak project planning, inconsistent policy direction, inadequate funding structures, corruption, and poor accountability mechanisms have all played significant roles. In many cases, changes in political leadership have led to shifts in priorities, resulting in the discontinuation or neglect of ongoing projects. A question that naturally arises is: why does the continued allocation of funds to such projects persist? While some may argue that allocation does not necessarily translate to disbursement, it nonetheless represents a diversion of scarce resources from other initiatives that could better align with the objectives of the incumbent administration and may have contributed to the high rate of budget non-completion recently experienced.
… strengthening institutional frameworks for project planning, execution, and monitoring is essential. Here lies the responsibility of the Federal Ministry of Budget and Economic Planning, with the National Infrastructure Integrated Master Plan serving as a central institutional instrument. Transparent procurement processes, clear accountability structures, and consistent policy implementation remain critical to ensuring that future projects and programmes are not subjected to the same fate.
Addressing this issue requires a deliberate and coordinated approach, one that is devoid of political bias. First, there is a need for a comprehensive audit of all abandoned projects undertaken by the government, federal or state, within the last two decades, to determine their current status, viability, and potential for completion or repurposing. This audit should also extend to major economic programmes and policy initiatives that have been discontinued or under-implemented, in order to capture the full spectrum of lost economic value. Projects and programmes that remain economically and socially relevant should be prioritised for completion or revival, while those that are no longer viable should be formally discontinued to prevent further waste of public resources.
Second, strengthening institutional frameworks for project planning, execution, and monitoring is essential. Here lies the responsibility of the Federal Ministry of Budget and Economic Planning, with the National Infrastructure Integrated Master Plan serving as a central institutional instrument. Transparent procurement processes, clear accountability structures, and consistent policy implementation remain critical to ensuring that future projects and programmes are not subjected to the same fate. By adopting a more disciplined and strategic approach to development planning, Nigeria can begin to reverse the trend of abandoned initiatives and unlock the economic potential that these investments were originally intended to deliver.
To better illustrate the scale, diversity, and implications of these unfinished ambitions, the table below presents a selection of notable projects across different sectors. It highlights their intended purpose, estimated costs, current status, and the economic opportunities that have been lost or deferred as a result of their prolonged inactivity.
Beyond the financial and sectoral overview provided above, it is also important to recognise that not all “abandoned” projects are the same. They differ in form, stage of development, and the nature of their failure. The classification below provides a framework for analysing these projects which could help in identifying appropriate policy responses.
At its core, the persistence of abandoned projects in Nigeria reflects deeper governance failures that can be understood through the lenses of authority, coordination, incentives, and commitment. The tragedy of Nigeria’s development is not that it lacks vision, but that it has not built the political and institutional capability to consistently translate vision into completion.
This classification underscores that each category of project failure requires a distinct policy response; while some projects may require renewed funding and completion, others may need restructuring, concessioning, or outright discontinuation. Without such differentiation, policy interventions risk being ineffective or misdirected.
From the tables above, it is apparent that the inglorious act of project abandonment has no boundary or sectoral limitation; it cuts across the fabric of the economy, with no sector or region spared. This reality extends beyond physical infrastructure to include economic programmes whose discontinuation has equally deprived the economy of growth momentum and multiplier benefits. While the figures cited are indicative and based on publicly accessible information at the time of writing, what remains undeniable is the continued accumulation of these colossal costs while the country grapples with severe socio-economic infrastructure deficits. It is also important to note that the projects highlighted exclude the thousands of educational, health, and social infrastructure facilities that have deteriorated due to poor maintenance and inadequate resource allocation, further compounding the scale of the challenge.
At its core, the persistence of abandoned projects in Nigeria reflects deeper governance failures that can be understood through the lenses of authority, coordination, incentives, and commitment. The tragedy of Nigeria’s development is not that it lacks vision, but that it has not built the political and institutional capability to consistently translate vision into completion. In this context, authority speaks to the clarity of institutional mandates and the ability of designated agencies to make and enforce decisions without undue political interference. Coordination highlights the need for alignment across ministries, departments, and agencies, as well as between federal and state governments, to ensure continuity and coherence in project execution. Incentives must be redesigned so that public officials are rewarded for completing projects efficiently and held accountable for delays, cost overruns, or abandonment. Finally, commitment requires a long-term policy orientation that transcends electoral cycles, ensuring that projects and programmes are seen through to completion regardless of changes in political leadership.
In conclusion, addressing Nigeria’s challenge of abandoned projects demands more than increased funding or renewed political rhetoric. It requires systemic reform anchored in strong authority, effective coordination, well-aligned incentives, and unwavering commitment. By embedding these principles into the country’s development framework, Nigeria stands a better chance of breaking the cycle of unfinished ambitions, both physical and programmatic, and beginning the process of realising the full economic and social value of its investments. Development is ultimately about state capability.
Dipo Baruwa is a business climate development analyst.

title: Nigeria has no Ebola case after patient’s evacuation to Switzerland – WHO
body: The World Health Organisation (WHO) Regional Director for Africa, Dr Mohamed Janabi, says Nigeria currently has no Ebola cases following the medical evacuation of the patient and her husband to Switzerland. Janabi disclosed this in a statement on his official X handle on Monday, adding that Nigeria would continue monitoring 52 contacts, while Switzerland would manage the patient and follow up with her husband. He said the evacuation took place earlier in the morning, noting that both the patient and her husband were Swiss citizens. According to him, the patient was clinically stable after Nigerian medical teams successfully managed her through the acute phase of the illness and stabilised her condition. Janabi congratulated the Federal Government, health workers, clinicians, emergency responders and other partners involved in the Ebola response, describing the development as a remarkable achievement. He said the successful management of the patient demonstrated Africa’s expertise, resilience and leadership in public health, particularly when countries worked together to respond to health emergencies. However, the WHO regional director stressed that vigilance remained critical despite the evacuation, urging continued attention to contact monitoring and other response measures. He said Nigeria would maintain close follow-up of 52 contacts, while Switzerland would assume responsibility for the continued management of the patient and monitoring of contact number 53, her husband. (NAN) The post Nigeria has no Ebola case after patient’s evacuation to Switzerland – WHO appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Ukraine to demand review of World Weightlifting Championship in Russia – Bidny
body:
Ukraine is preparing official appeals to the International Weightlifting Federation and the International Olympic Committee regarding the decision to grant Russia the right to host the 2030 World Championship, reported Minister of Youth and Sports of Ukraine Matviy Bidny.
"We call for this decision to be reviewed and for a new, transparent selection of the host country for the championship," Bidny wrote on the social network Facebook.
He added that he also plans to raise this issue with international partners, particularly at upcoming official events with sports ministers of the Council of Europe and EU member states.
"We strive to consolidate the international position – we call on the international sports community to publicly speak out against holding the championship in Russia. As long as Russia continues its war against Ukraine, holding international competitions on its territory is unacceptable. This decision is especially cynical right now, as on the eve of winter Russia intensifies strikes on Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure, kills people, and threatens Europe. And against this background, the international federation invites the global sports community to gather in Moscow, from where orders for these crimes are given. To effectively turn a blind eye to them. For the Kremlin, such a championship will become an instrument of propaganda and political rehabilitation for Putin. This is a dangerous signal that a country can continue war while returning to international sports. This is an encouragement of impunity and disrespect for the principles that global sports must protect," the minister explained.
He emphasized that Ukraine will use all available mechanisms and continue to work with international partners to urge against holding this championship in Russia.

title: Kremlin Signals Desire to Maintain Serbia Ties After Vučić Ousted by Student Movement
body:
The Kremlin said Monday that it wants to maintain and develop ties with Serbia despite the defeat of former President Aleksandar Vučić’s ruling coalition in this weekend’s parliamentary elections, while noting that building those relations will require effort from both sides.
“We deeply value the contribution that Mr. Vučić has made to the development of our bilateral relations,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters at a daily briefing.
“We know that he will remain on the political stage, and we hope that even in opposition, he will continue to contribute to advancing our ties,” Peskov added.
Vučić, who dominated Serbian politics for more than a decade as prime minister and then later as president , conceded defeat on Sunday night following a historic snap election. The vote pitted his ruling coalition against a student-led movement that had spent months protesting against his government.
“Based on a stratified sample, it is clear that we lost these elections,” Vučić told supporters at his party headquarters in Belgrade.
The defeat followed Vučić’s resignation as president in September, a risky political maneuver intended to allow him to reclaim the prime minister post. It also came after nearly two years of anti-government demonstrations triggered by the November 2024 roof collapse at the Novi Sad railway station, an accident that killed 16 people and sparked widespread outrage over state corruption.
During his tenure, Vučić balanced Serbia’s candidacy for EU membership with a refusal to join Western sanctions against Russia over its 2022 invasion of Ukraine. He had remained one of the few European leaders to maintain direct contact with the Kremlin and make official visits to Moscow.
Peskov said Monday that Moscow hopes the incoming government in Belgrade will work “constructively” to preserve bilateral relations since, in its view, doing so would bring “tangible benefits to Serbia itself.”
“For our part, we intend to continue doing everything possible to foster our relations with Belgrade. But as you know, it takes two to tango,” he said.
Jovo Bakić, a representative of the Student List, told the Kremlin-backed broadcaster RT Balkan that the incoming government would not impose sanctions on Moscow or abandon Russian gas supplies despite pressure from the European Union.
He argued that sanctions imposed by a country of Serbia’s size would change little but would send a negative signal symbolically.
“ We respect Russia as a great power and as a historically important partner, and in many cases as a protector,” Bakić said. “ There will be no changes on this issue.”

title: easyJet proceeds with Starlink Wi-Fi despite previous cost concerns
body: easyJet will introduce Starlink Wi-Fi across its Airbus fleet despite stating earlier this year, following talks with SpaceX, that the “economics aren’t quite working for us”. On October 26, 2026, the British low-cost carrier announced that starting from the first half of 2027, Starlink installation will begin across the airline’s Airbus A320, A320neo and A321neo fleet. easyJet said the roll out is expected to be completed by early 2028, allowing millions of passengers to access Elon Musk’s low-Earth orbit satellite powered connectivity. The airline said in a statement that customers will be able to stream, game and browse on their own devices, just as they would when on the ground. There was no mention that the service would be free. London Gatwick Airport easyJet hopes that the move will attract even more business and leisure customers. The introduction will also put clear daylight between the service easyJet and rival budget airline Ryanair offers. Ryanair CEO Michael O’Leary has shown no interest in adopting Starlink and was embroiled in a recent public social media spat with Musk over the cost. In January 2026, easyJet CEO Kenton Jarvis expressed some concerns over the cost of Starlink for the airline but praised the product. “When the time is right, we’ll pick the right service,” Jarvis said. With the latest announcement, it appears that the numbers were now working for easyJet and will proceed with the investment. “Innovation is in easyJet’s DNA and partnering with SpaceX to bring Starlink’s high-speed internet connectivity onboard for the first time will not only further enhance the experience we provide millions of customers, but means we are offering more of the options both business and leisure travellers want when they choose who they fly with,” Jarvis said. He added: “Giving customers the opportunity to get online in the air will mean even greater choice and convenience when you fly with easyJet. Ultimately, it’s yet another way we’re making travel easy.” Low-cost carriers see value in Starlink Other low-cost carriers that have signed contracts for Starlink include Wizz Air, Frontier Airlines, and Volaris. According to ch-aviation data, easyJet currently operates an active fleet of 78 A320-200s, 51 A32neos, and 22 A320neos. The carrier also has 39 A319-100s, but these are gradually being replaced and will not feature Starlink, according to easyJet. The carrier is awaiting delivery of 120 A320neo and 151 A321neo. “We’re proud to bring Starlink onboard easyJet and transform the way their customers stay connected throughout their travels,” Gwynne Shotwell, President and COO of SpaceX, said. “Fast, reliable connectivity from take-off to landing means people can work, stream, or stay in touch without interruption.” RELATED Apollo agrees £5.7 billion takeover of easyJet as Castlelake walks away The post easyJet proceeds with Starlink Wi-Fi despite previous cost concerns appeared first on AeroTime .

title: ‘End the baseless attacks’ – Evacuees defend government over South Africa operation
body: The leader of the Aggrieved South Africa Evacuees, Michael Addo, has called for an immediate end to what he describes as baseless attacks against Ghanaians evacuated from South Africa and the government that facilitated their return. According to him, the ongoing public controversy surrounding the evacuation exercise has subjected returnees to humiliation, despite the trauma and hardship they endured while living in South Africa. “We are here to seek answers and demand an immediate end to the baseless attacks on the government that was sympathetic towards us,” he stated. His remarks come amid heightened scrutiny of the government’s reported GH¢49.72 million expenditure on evacuating 1,964 Ghanaians from South Africa. The evacuation of over 1,900 Ghanaians from South Africa followed renewed xenophobic attacks in the country. The government spent GH¢49.7 million on the evacuation exercise, with each evacuee receiving a GH¢5,000 reintegration grant and GH¢500 transportation allowance. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs, led by Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa, provided a breakdown of the expenditure, which included chartered flights, accommodation, feeding, and medical care. The Minority in Parliament has demanded a detailed breakdown of the expenditure, questioning the amount spent per evacuee. The Minority Caucus on the Foreign Affairs Committee boycotted a planned briefing by the Minister. Mr Addo expressed disappointment that the pursuit of accountability had, in his view, turned into attacks on vulnerable returnees struggling to recover from their experiences. “While we bravely recover from our trauma and pain, the very society we expect to protect us has reduced our pain to humiliation under the guise of seeking accountability,” he lamented. He accused some elements within the Minority, the New Patriotic Party (NPP) and sections of the media of attempting to establish wrongdoing against the government. Mr Addo also questioned allegations concerning financial assistance and relief packages reportedly given to evacuees, urging journalists who witnessed their arrival at the airport to provide an accurate account of the circumstances. He further disclosed that 46 Ghanaians who were expected to be part of the evacuation exercise remain stranded in South Africa, but the ongoing controversy has discouraged the group from seeking additional government assistance. “Currently, we still have 46 people who were supposed to be among the flight, but because of what is currently spreading on social media, we don’t even have the balls to beg the government to go and rescue them,” he said. Expressing appreciation for the government’s intervention, Mr Addo maintained that many Ghanaians had endured xenophobic attacks in South Africa for years without receiving similar assistance. “We have experienced xenophobia for many years, but this is the first time a government has taken our plight into account and come to our rescue,” he added. He consequently urged an end to the allegations and public attacks, stressing the need to protect the dignity of evacuees while addressing the plight of Ghanaians still awaiting assistance in South Africa.

title: NASS Roundup: Ebola, corps member’s death, Abuja rent, other stories from the House of Reps
body:
On Tuesday, House of Representatives urged the federal government to intensify efforts to stop the production and circulation of fake, adulterated, counterfeit and substandard food and drinks in Nigeria.
The resolution followed an urgent motion sponsored by Makki Yalleman (APC, Jigawa) who said unsafe food and beverages posed serious risks to public health, particularly to children, elderly people and other vulnerable groups.
Mr Yalleman cited recent enforcement operations, including the dismantling of an illegal alcohol counterfeiting syndicate at Zamfara Plaza on Lagos Island by the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC) in April and the discovery of an illegal fruit juice factory in Badagry, Lagos State, in September.
The lawmaker said some manufacturers and distributors were falsifying production and expiry dates, batch numbers, manufacturer details and ingredient information, while others allegedly used contaminated raw materials or illegally refilled containers.
The House consequently urged NAFDAC, the Standards Organisation of Nigeria (SON) and the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC), alongside the police, the Nigeria Customs Service, state governments and other agencies, to strengthen surveillance, inspection, sampling, laboratory testing and enforcement.
Relevant House committees were also mandated to examine the scale of the problem and the effectiveness of existing enforcement measures and report their findings within four weeks.
The House also ordered an investigation into the death of a National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) member, Etimbuk Sunday, at the NYSC Orientation Camp in Awgu, Enugu State.
The motion, sponsored by Unyime Idem (APC, Akwa Ibom) on Tuesday, followed concerns about the treatment Mr Sunday received after falling ill during his orientation programme.
Mr Sunday, a former president of the Students’ Union Government of Akwa Ibom State University, reportedly visited the camp clinic on 7 October with symptoms suggestive of malaria or typhoid. He was treated and discharged with oral medication, but his condition later deteriorated. He died on 11 October.
Mr Idem raised questions about the treatment administered to the corps member, the delay allegedly involved in referring him to a hospital and the circumstances surrounding the handling of his remains.
He also raised concerns over reports that the body was handed over to the family naked and with visible bruises, saying the allegations required investigation.
The House thereafter mandated its Committees on Youth Development, Health Care Services, Police Affairs and Human Rights to conduct a joint investigation and report within four weeks.
The development came after the Senate had also called for an investigation, while NAFDAC said it had begun investigating the death, including allegations concerning medicines administered to the deceased.
Following the confirmation of an imported Ebola case in Abuja, the House called for the immediate release of outstanding funds appropriated for health agencies to strengthen the country’s preparedness and response.
The motion, sponsored by Amobi Ogah (LP, Abia), was considered against the backdrop of the confirmed case involving a woman who recently arrived in Nigeria from Uganda.
Health authorities had identified 44 close contacts linked to the case, including healthcare workers, patients, caregivers and travel contacts, for monitoring.
Mr Ogah warned that delays in detecting suspected cases, conducting laboratory tests, isolating confirmed cases and tracing contacts could increase the risk of transmission.
He also raised concerns about gaps in public awareness, infection prevention and control supplies, healthcare workers’ preparedness and emergency response capacity.
The House, therefore, urged the Ministry of Finance to release outstanding appropriated funds to relevant health agencies. It also asked the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare and the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention to assess additional resources required for the response.
The House further called for stronger surveillance involving federal and state health authorities, port health officials, the agriculture ministry and private healthcare providers, while urging collaboration with the World Health Organisation and other international health institutions.
Its Committee on Infectious Diseases was mandated to obtain updates from relevant agencies on the Ebola situation and Nigeria’s preparedness and report back to the House.
The House asked the federal government to review the proposed realignment of sections of the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway and retain the originally conceptualised route through parts of Ondo State and the Escravos–Ogheye–Ugborodo corridor in Delta State.
The motion was sponsored by Thomas Ereyitomi (APC, Delta), who argued that diverting the highway away from coastal communities could undermine the project’s original objective of improving connectivity and unlocking economic opportunities in the region.
The federal government has defended proposed changes to sections of the route on grounds including difficult terrain, flooding, weak subsoil conditions and climate-related risks. Works Minister Dave Umahi has said portions of the existing East-West Road would be used in the affected areas.
Mr Ereyitomi, however, argued that the government should first conduct an independent assessment of the engineering requirements, environmental consequences, socioeconomic impact and lifecycle costs of the alternative routes.
The House has begun consideration of a bill seeking to restrict landlords and agents in the Federal Capital Territory from demanding more than one year’s rent in advance from tenants.
The proposed legislation which passed first reading on Thursday seeks to regulate rent payments for both residential and commercial properties in the FCT. It would also prevent landlords and agents from circumventing the restriction through compulsory service charges, additional payments, artificial tenancy renewals or other arrangements designed to force tenants to pay more than a year upfront.
The Federal Capital Territory Advance Rent Regulation and Tenants’ Protection Bill, 2026 (HB.2839), sponsored by Paul Nnamchi (APC, Enugu), with Ahmed Doro (PDP, Katsina) as co-sponsor, proposes the establishment of mechanisms for registering letting agents, receiving complaints and monitoring rental practices across the FCT, including the satellite towns.
It would also empower the proposed authority to order landlords or agents to refund unlawful payments within 30 days where violations are established.
Individuals who knowingly demand or receive rent above the permitted period could face fines ranging from N500,000 to N5 million, while corporate bodies could face fines between N5 million and N20 million. Courts could also order refunds and compensation for proven losses.
The proposal comes amid rising accommodation costs in Abuja, where tenants have complained of high rents alongside agency, agreement and caution fees.

title: YouTube launches shopping programme in UAE: How influencers can earn money with 500 subscribers
body: YouTube has launched its Shopping affiliate programme in the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Egypt, allowing smaller content creators to earn money from products they recommend to their audiences. The programme, announced on Monday, enables eligible creators with as few as 500 subscribers to tag products in their videos, Shorts and livestreams and receive commissions when viewers make qualifying purchases. Amazon is the first retail partner, with more retailers expected to join the service, according to YouTube. The expansion could provide new ways to to make money for smaller influencers who have not secured lucrative brand partnerships or substantial advertising revenue. It also enables viewers to find products featured in videos and proceed directly to a retailer's website to complete their purchases. How it works Under the programme, creators can tag eligible Amazon products directly in their content using YouTube Studio. When viewers select a product, they are directed to Amazon to complete the purchase. Creators can then earn a commission on qualifying sales. The feature is available across long-form videos, Shorts and livestreams, meaning creators can potentially generate revenue from both new and existing content. Creators can track clicks, estimated revenue and earnings through YouTube Studio, according to YouTube's official Amazon shopping guidance. The platform also allows qualifying creators to earn commissions from international viewers where eligible purchasing options are available. However, earnings depend on qualifying purchases, and refunds can result in previously earned commissions being deducted. Who can apply The lower subscriber threshold is among the most significant changes for smaller creators. YouTube first announced a wider rollout of the programme to eligible US creators in June 2023. In March, the company announced it was expanding its Shopping affiliate programme to eligible members of its Partner Programme who had at least 500 subscribers. But subscriber numbers are only one part of the requirements. According to YouTube's monetisation guidelines, creators seeking access through the expanded Partner Programme must also have uploaded three public videos in the previous 90 days and achieved either 3,000 valid public watch hours over the previous year or three million valid Shorts views within 90 days. Creators must also meet the specific Shopping affiliate eligibility requirements and can check their access through the Earn section of YouTube Studio. Middle East expansion The launch comes as online videos increasingly influence how consumers discover and research products. More than 40 million logged-in users across the UAE, Saudi Arabia , Egypt, Morocco and Algeria conducted shopping-related searches on the platform in June, according to YouTube. The company said viewers worldwide watch more than 40 billion hours of shopping-related content annually. In the UAE and Saudi Arabia, 86 per cent of surveyed viewers considered YouTube to have the most trusted creators for shopping recommendations, according to a survey carried out by international market research and consumer insights company, Kantar. The figures, provided by YouTube, highlight the commercial potential for content that helps viewers make purchasing decisions. The company has also introduced AI-powered tools that can identify products appearing in videos and suggest relevant tags, reducing the time creators spend adding shopping links. Viewers watching YouTube on television can scan QR codes using their mobile phones to access featured products. What does this mean for UAE influencers? For smaller creators in the UAE , the programme offers a way to monetise their audiences without waiting to reach hundreds of thousands of followers. Affiliate commissions could supplement advertising revenue and paid collaborations, although meaningful earnings will depend on attracting viewers who are willing to buy recommended products. Maintaining audience trust will also be important, particularly when creators have a financial incentive to promote certain products.

title: Drone attack sparks fires at industrial facilities in Russia’s Voronezh region
body:
According to Ukrinform, this was reported by ASTRA .
In particular, photographs released by eyewitnesses after the attack show black smoke rising over the grounds of the “Voronezhsintezkauchuk” plant, which is owned by Sibur.
Alexander Gusev, governor of the Voronezh Region, reported that 113 drones had allegedly been shot down over the region, including more than 70 over Voronezh. He confirmed fires at several industrial facilities, without naming them. The governor claims that the fires at these sites have not caused any significant damage.
Voronezhsintezkauchuk’s products are used in the manufacture of automotive and aircraft tires, as well as rubber products. In particular, synthetic rubber is used in the production of tires for military aircraft and heavy wheeled vehicles.
Synthetic rubber is also used in rocket engineering.
Furthermore, according to Astra, a drone struck the 25-story “Chizhov Gallery” business center in Voronezh.

title: Strength vs. Confrontation: Do American Forces in the First Island Chain Deter or Invite War?
body:
“We are not going to get involved militarily in any way on the Island of Formosa,” announced Secretary of State Dean Acheson in January 1950. Taiwan fell outside of America’s security commitment. He further described an American defensive perimeter spanning from the Aleutian Islands through Japan and the Philippines. For the rest of the Pacific, he said that “a [security] guarantee is hardly sensible or necessary within the realm of practical relationship.”
Along with Taiwan, Korea fell outside American guarantees. Concerned about provoking a conflict in Korea, the United States pressed South Korea to build a small, constabulary army that lacked heavy weapons. Without an American security commitment, forward-deployed United States forces, or a capable South Korean army, North Korea saw an opportunity to quickly reunify the peninsula. Five months after Acheson’s speech, North Korean forces invaded. T-34 tanks, invulnerable to South Korea’s light weaponry, spearheaded the attack and almost conquered the South before the United States could deploy forces to halt the communist offensive at the Pusan Perimeter. By October, China entered the war. This deterrence failure cost the lives of 36,516 Americans , hundreds of thousands of Chinese, and over two million Koreans.
After the deterrence failure that led to the Korean War, the United States recognized the necessity of forward presence to prevent war. Within two days of the start of that war, President Harry S. Truman deployed the 7th Fleet to defend Taiwan. In September 1954, the Chinese shelled Taiwan’s Kinmen Island. Two months later, the United States had signed a mutual defense treaty with Taiwan, which deterred further Chinese escalation.
The US Commitment to the First Island Chain
As the risk of a catastrophic war in East Asia has reemerged, the United States must maintain this lesson: When it has defended forward and demonstrated the capability and resolve to make aggression infeasible , it has deterred opponents. When it has not, it has invited war.
With that understanding, the 2026 National Defense Strategy commits the military to “build, posture, and sustain a strong denial defense along the [first island chain],” which includes Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and the Philippines. By focusing on forward-deployed forces, which could immediately respond to Chinese aggression, the strategy reduces the potential for China to achieve its policy objectives in a quick, cheap war. The strategy prioritizes cost-effective, asymmetric capabilities to buttress America’s allies. It prevents war for cheap, so what is the argument against it?
In a recent analysis , Jennifer Kavanagh asks whether America’s commitments to the first island chain “really make Americans safer and more prosperous?” She argues that since the United States has limited interests in the region, it should withdraw to the more defensible second island chain and end its security commitments to the countries of the first island chain. While she leads a worthwhile thought exercise, her recommendations risk Chinese regional hegemony, war, and economic upheaval while precluding an overdue shift by the American military to cheap, asymmetric military capabilities.
At the moment, her argument seems far from becoming policy. Elbridge Colby, head of policy in the Pentagon, recently briefed the Senate on the implementation of the National Defense Strategy, discussing the increasing complexity of Exercise Balikatan in the Philippines, which included a live fire of the new Typhon missile system . He also argued that America’s posture has led to increased commitment by South Korea, Japan, and Australia to regional security.
However, some recent events have raised questions about the endurance of America’s commitment to the first island chain. For example, the United States did not counter a Chinese diplomatic and economic campaign against Japan following Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s statement that a Chinese use of force against Taiwan would constitute an “ existential threat ” for her country. The United States has also postponed missile shipments to Tokyo, paused a planned arms sale to Taiwan, temporarily operated without an aircraft carrier in the region, and scaled back military exercises with South Korea. Whether a critic’s charge that all of this amounts to “ great-power collusion ” or it is just the messy detritus of multifaceted great-power competition is not the point. The point is that perceptions of a weakened commitment could undermine allied confidence and create opportunities for China to expand its sphere of influence within the first island chain.
The US administration would argue that these moves are a part of deterrence as it attempts to navigate the trade-offs of deterring China “ through strength, not confrontation ”—seeking to preserve the capability to deny Chinese aggression while not provoking Beijing—it raises an important question: Where does the balance lie between strength and confrontation?
The Problem with Narrow National Interests
To provide the foundation of her argument for restraint, Kavanagh begins by defining US interests in Asia, which she does more narrowly than either the current and previous administrations. She writes that “The United States has two core interests in Asia worth protecting with military power: defending the US homeland and safeguarding access to key economic markets and trade routes.”
While such an approach can seem intellectually fruitful, the use of national interests to drive policy can be problematic . A narrow list of national interests cannot capture the complexity of American foreign relations.
Kavanagh mentions safeguarding markets, but she sees no core interest in ensuring peace in the region, although the United States traded $2 trillion in goods with Asia in 2025. A war over Taiwan would indefinitely disrupt the world’s supply of advanced computer chips. As the American economy has become reliant on those chips to fuel its economic growth and technological competitiveness, a prolonged interruption in their production would risk an economic crisis.
When Kavanagh does discuss the risk of war, she seems to see the main threat as being unintended escalation. She argues that “The United States should also remove the long-range fire system (the Typhon) currently located in the Philippines, as it’s both unnecessary to support the commitments outlined here and highly escalatory.” Her argument raises a crucial debate on whether forward-deployed forces deter conflict or escalate its risks.
China would certainly argue that the American deployments of Typhon to the Philippines or THAAD to Korea are escalatory. But that is Chinese messaging, not reality. In a similar vein, Xi Jinping regularly cites The Thucydides Trap . Even though that book has several methodological problems , it provides Xi with a means to argue that provocative moves could lead to war.
In contrast to Xi’s self-serving argument, historical experience provides little support for the proposition that provocation through position is itself the primary cause of war. Of course, leaders often cite enemy provocations to legitimize military action, but that does not mean those incitements actually caused a war. Adolf Hitler blamed Polish “ saboteurs ” for war in 1939. Vladimir Putin blamed Ukrainian “ fascists ” for war in 2022. In fact, both Poland and Ukraine, in worrying about provoking war through escalation, delayed military mobilization and so presented tempting targets .
Whatever their public justifications, leaders tend to initiate wars when they gamble that a short war could be a cost-effective means of achieving a policy objective . In addition to the Korean War, modern history is replete with examples of leaders gambling on a short war: the Suez Crisis, the Six-Day War, the Indo-Pakistan War of 1971, the Yom Kippur War, the Cambodian-Vietnamese War, the Sino-Vietnamese War, the Soviet-Afghan War, the Iran-Iraq War, the Falklands War, the Persian Gulf War, the Afghanistan War, the Iraq War, the Russo-Georgian War, and the Russo-Ukrainian War. As with those examples, the risk of war in the first island chain comes not from US provocation but from Xi Jinping betting he could quickly seize Taiwan in a fait accompli before American intervention.
As often in history, Beijing may miscalculate; therefore, the United States should leave little doubt in Chinese leadership’s minds that a short war is infeasible. Forward-deployed forces, which could credibly and affordably contribute to the defense of Taiwan, would weigh heavily on the Politburo’s calculus . American forces in the first island chain can immediately sense, decide, and act against attempts to alter the status quo, creating uncertainty for Chinese planners about whether an initial move can succeed.
While maintaining strategic ambiguity, deterrence by denial involves a strong cognitive component . Units inside the first island chain remain visible and persistent within the adversary’s planning factors. Their presence forces Chinese planners to account for US capabilities immediately rather than treating them as reinforcements that may arrive too late to influence a campaign. The Army’s Typhon system illustrates this dynamic. Its current position in the Philippines, combined with Standard Missile-6’s countermaritime capability, provides the Philippines with a credible means of holding Chinese destroyers at risk if they violate the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone or threaten sovereign claims around island features in the West Philippine Sea. Forward positioning therefore strengthens deterrence not by eliminating strategic ambiguity but by making that response sufficiently credible that China must account for it in its planning.
Kavanagh argues that “the United States should remove most Army and Marine Corps deployments from Asia and cut air and naval power significantly. The remaining US forces should be consolidated at more survivable bases farther from China’s coast and tasked with securing US economic interests and signaling continued US involvement in the Pacific region.” From that distance, any signal would be feeble. Beijing may gamble that political delays, deployment timelines, and Chinese antiaccess/aerial-denial (A2/AD) systems would prevent US forces from intervening before the People’s Liberation Army achieves its objectives.
The Case for Asymmetry and Survivability
Recent conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East have demonstrated how land forces using cheap, asymmetric capabilities can deny the sort of maritime access that China would require for any aggressive campaigns. A second island chain strategy would eliminate US options to pursue similar approaches, including autonomous aerial drones , maritime platforms , antiship missiles , and affordable mass munitions to control maritime gaps . It would increase American reliance on expensive systems required to operate at extended ranges and penetrate Chinese A2/AD.
Kavanagh characterizes forces in the first island chain as “vulnerabilities not assets.” She treats survivability primarily as a function of geographic distance rather than of a force’s ability to survive while remaining relevant in a crisis. The distinction is important. General Charles Flynn, former commander of US Army Pacific, described China’s A2/AD architecture as “primarily designed to defeat [US] air power and maritime power,” while noting that it is less optimized to find, fix, and finish distributed, mobile land forces.
While China’s missile strategy focuses heavily on static US bases and infrastructure, mobile land forces present a distinct targeting challenge . Contemporary conflicts have demonstrated that ground forces can survive months of strikes and still contest access to waterways like the straits of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab . Additionally, compared to the deserts of the Middle East, the thick canopies and dense urban conglomerations of the first island chain provide far more concealment for ground forces.
Small, mobile, distributed, and networked ground formations like the Army’s multidomain task forces and Marine Corps Marine littoral regiments are designed to survive in such environments. They are not simply “ tripwire forces ” to draw the United States into conflict, but rather essential elements in a denial strategy to prevent China from achieving any initial success. Equipped with space and cyber capabilities and with long-range fires, these forces can also disrupt the sensing and strike systems threatening partners and US air and maritime forces. Removing them would reduce broader joint survivability and freedom of action. Meanwhile, the second island chain is no sanctuary . Guam , Tinian , Saipan , Palau , Micronesia , and the Marshall Islands provide strategic depth but face geographic and infrastructure constraints that limit dispersion, concealment, maneuver, and sustainment. Greater distance reduces the number of Chinese systems able to engage US forces but concentrates them in relatively few static locations . And any US systems with the range to operate from those locations will be harder to conceal.
Moreover, distance provides little protection against threats that do not depend on physical proximity. Chinese cyber actors associated with Volt Typhoon penetrated critical infrastructure in Guam, while Salt Typhoon targeted homeland telecommunications infrastructure. Chinese electronic warfare capabilities can now detect and suppress radars at extended ranges, while satellite communications and navigation jamming could have a disproportionate impact on the second island chain’s integrated defense system . China may feel sufficiently confident in its ability to disrupt response times of US forces in the second island chain that it would gamble on a fait accompli.
As a final consideration, the second island chain cannot provide a logistical substitute for the first. The United States has invested decades developing Guam and sites elsewhere in the Marianas, yet infrastructure limitations still constrain force build-ups. The second island chain simply lacks the capacity to absorb the forces and functions currently distributed across Asia . Additionally, the infrastructure on these islands is underequipped to rapidly deploy forces at scale.
Ultimately, survivability must be judged by what the force must accomplish. A force that survives because it is too distant to be targeted is also too distant to shape China’s decision-making.
A withdrawal would risk that our allies no longer feel America’s commitments to them are credible. It would reinforce Chinese cognitive warfare efforts , which seek to establish a sense in the populations of the first island chain that since the United States is unreliable and resisting China alone is futile, it would be best to collaborate with China.
An abandonment would jeopardize recent commitments that America’s partners have made to regional security. South Korea has promised to invest 3.5 percent of its GDP on defense, Japan has increased its capabilities while devoting itself to a “ free and open Pacific ,” Australia signed the AUKUS trilateral security partnership , and Taiwan has invested in its new erosion strategy to better resist a Chinese invasion. Japan and South Korea exercised together in Freedom Edge , while Japan and the Philippines have expanded defense cooperation and increased their surveillance and countermaritime capabilities . The United States should reward this progress while continuing development of integrated intelligence, air defense, and command-and-control systems alongside its partners. Developing and maintaining interoperability cannot occur remotely from the second island chain; it requires constant cooperation.
The United States will never be able to peer inside of Xi’s head, but he must know that gambling on conflict in the Pacific could earn his place in history as the unifier of China or risk defeat, his legacy, and the stability of the Chinese Communist Party regime. Will he be more likely to take that wager with the presence or absence of forward-postured US forces? History points to the answer. The United States demonstrating a strong hand in the first island chain will help Xi recognize that war is a bad bet.
Lieutenant Colonel Ben Blane is a US Army field artillery officer with multiple operational deployments and experience throughout the Indo-Pacific. He holds an undergraduate degree from the United States Military Academy and graduate degrees from Columbia University and John Jay College. He is a research fellow for the Modern War Institute.
Robert G. Rose is the chief research officer at the Modern War Institute. He holds an undergraduate degree from the United States Military Academy and graduate degrees from Harvard University and, as a Gates Scholar, from Cambridge University.
The views expressed are those of the authors and do not reflect the official position of the United States Military Academy, Department of the Army, or Department of Defense.

title: Woman allegedly poisons stepson in Bauchi
body: The Bauchi State Police Command has arrested two suspects linked to the tragic deaths of two children in Alkaleri and Ganjuwa, local government areas. The Police public Relations Officer, SP Nafi’u Habib, disclosed this to newsmen on Monday in Bauchi. He said the two children’s lives were cut short in the most painful way. Nafi’u said the first incident occurred in Kwaimawa community in Alkaleri Local Government Area a six-year-old child, Mubarak Ibrahim, allegedly died after he took a drink given to him by his stepmother, Fatima Ibrahim. Borno NDC sanctions assembly candidate over alleged pro-Atiku campaign FCTA urged to establish funding mechanism for primary education He said moments later the cheerful boy started vomiting uncontrollably. His family panicked, rushed him to PHC Kwaimawa and then to the Federal Medical Centre (FMC), Gombe, where doctors battled to save him, for eight days. On October 24, 2026, he was confirmed dead by doctors. According to the PPRO, following a report by the Village Head of Kwaimawa, detectives swung into action and arrested the suspect. She is now in custody as the investigation continues. The police spokesman said the second incident occurred in Zaila Community of Ganjuwa Local Government Area of the State, where the five-year-old Jabiba Abubakar, who was staying with her aunt in Zaila Village and her grandfather, in Badaromo Village, was reported missing. Nafi’u said, “On 24th October, 2026 at about 7am the community’s hope turned to horror as her tiny body was found abandoned in a small pit behind the village.” He said upon receiving the report, Police operatives from Soro Division cordoned off the scene and arrested one Sadiku Musa in connection with the heinous act. He said both cases have been transferred to the State Criminal Investigation Department (SCID), Bauchi for discreet and thorough investigation. He said the Commissioner of Police, CP Sani-Omolori Aliyu, described the incidents as heartbreaking and inhuman. “These are innocent souls. Children who looked up to adults for protection. We will ensure that justice speaks for Habiba and Mubarak,” the CP vowed, while commiserating with their families. He urged parents, guardians and community leaders to watch over their children more closely and to promptly report strange persons or suspicious movements.

title: BoG researchers propose AI-powered system to track inflation in real time
body: Researchers at the Bank of Ghana (BoG) have proposed an artificial intelligence-powered framework to track consumer prices and estimate inflation in real time. The system, called e-Inflation, uses Big Data and AI tools to collect large volumes of price information from websites. It aims to provide timely estimates ahead of official inflation releases. The proposal is outlined in a working paper by Francis Mawuli Abude, Collins Kwesi Appiah and Julius B. Dasah, published on the central bank’s website. The authors say preliminary results suggest the framework can estimate current inflation rates more accurately and at a lower cost. They also report that it can capture price movements during both stable and unstable economic conditions. However, the Bank of Ghana notes that working papers reflect the authors’ views and do not necessarily represent those of the bank, its board or management. The papers present research in progress to encourage comments and debate. How the proposed framework will operate The e-Inflation framework draws price data from electronic sources to estimate the Consumer Price Index (CPI), headline inflation, food inflation and non-food inflation. The authors say the approach could help reduce delays in traditional price collection and publication. According to the paper, official inflation figures are published after the reference month ends. This requires policymakers to estimate current price movements before official data becomes available. Central banks use statistical models, econometric models and machine learning to produce these estimates, a process known as nowcasting. The researchers argue that existing methods can be costly and do not always deliver accurate, real-time estimates. They therefore argue for “more innovative and cost-efficient methodologies, leveraging Big Data and Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques, tools, and technologies”. The paper says the Bank of Ghana has been conducting work involving Big Data and AI since May 2021. This includes identifying alternative sources of consumer prices and comparing their coverage with the official basket of goods and services. The research also involves constructing overall, food and non-food consumer price indices. “The e-Inflation framework is capable of collecting price data every week for monetary policy decision-making and for general economic policy analysis,” the authors state. They argue that the system could provide more frequent information to support policy decisions. “More importantly, relative to the traditional approach of compiling price data, the e-Inflation framework has the unique advantage of providing real-time CPI statistics as needed.” It also added that the Working Papers describe research in progress by the author(s) and are published to elicit comments and encourage debate. Our special appreciation also goes to Dr Philip Abradu-Otoo, the former Director of the Research Department, for his interest in the study from its inception and for providing the necessary resources and technical guidance,” the Working Paper acknowledged. Challenges and concerns A key concern is whether online prices accurately reflect those charged in physical shops. The authors acknowledge that “whether online prices are identical to those in physical shops remains the main concern of this research”. However, they say a survey found online and offline prices in Ghana to be statistically identical, supporting their confidence in the data. “Based on this, we are confident in the representativeness of the price data extracted from online sources and in its use in computing the CPI and inflation rates for Ghana.” The framework’s reliability also depends on businesses keeping their online prices current. “Despite these advantages, the accuracy of e-Inflation statistics depends largely on the availability of current price data on the websites of the selected e-commerce shops and institutions.”

title: Mitsotakis Attends Saint Demetrius Feast Day Liturgy in Greece
body: Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis attended the Divine Liturgy at the Church of Saint Demetrius in Agios Dimitrios, Attica, on Monday, October 26, joining Orthodox faithful in celebrating the feast day of the revered saint. The service was presided over by Archbishop Makarios of Australia, who is visiting Greece. Saint Demetrius is one of the most venerated saints in the Orthodox Christian tradition, with his feast day celebrated annually on October 26. Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis attends the Saint Demetrius feast day Divine Liturgy in Agios Dimitrios, presided over by Archbishop Makarios of Australia. Mitsotakis’ visit to Agios Dimitrios comes ahead of a series of official engagements culminating on Wednesday, October 28, in Thessaloniki, where he is expected to take part in events marking Greece’s national holiday, Ohi Day. title: Iraqi court seeks arrest of Maysan provincial leader for defying Iran border closure
body: Iraq's Karkh Court in Baghdad on Monday ordered an investigation into the head of Maysan's provincial council after Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi called for a probe over his calls for civil disobedience if the Al Sheeb border crossing with Iran is not reopened. Last week, Iraq closed the crossing in Maysan to travellers and goods, with the decision escalating tension with Iran and pro-Tehran Iraqi politicians. The decision was made due to security concerns at the border. On Sunday, Mustafa Duair Abdulhassan, the head of Maysan's provincial council, said that people would have to “resort to civil disobedience and cut Maysan off from the rest of Iraq” if the crossing was not reopened. Mr Abdulhassan is affiliated with Sadiqoun, the political wing of the Iran-aligned Asaib Ahl Al Haq, led by Qais Al Khazali. Mr Al Zaidi's office said the investigation was in response to “threats” and “inappropriate language”. Other politicians have also criticised the closure, with some joining dozens of lorry drivers and workers who demonstrated last week, calling on the government to reverse its decision to shut the crossing, which is a vital land route for commercial and civilian vehicles. Protesters said their livelihoods depended on cross‑border traffic. Mr Al Zaidi called on security forces to ensure a safe environment for demonstrators. The Prime Minister chaired a meeting of the Ministerial Council of National Security that underscored the need to “secure peaceful demonstrations” and to treat protesters with respect, his office said in a statement. Maysan Governor Habib Dhahir Al Fartousi called on Mr Al Zaidi to reopen the crossing and warned the closure would drive up prices and disrupt trade. Others have defended the decision . Abdelamir Taiban, a senior adviser to Mr Al Zaidi, told local media that Iran had “deliberately undermined Iraq’s security”, and alleged that Iranian-linked people were entering the country without authorisation and causing “chaos” along the border. Mr Taiban said Iraq’s most serious border problems involved Iran. One of the biggest challenges was the flow of drugs and counterfeit currency from Iran, which he said had inflicted economic damage “greater than what ISIS caused”. Iran's embassy in Iraq issued a statement on Saturday describing Mr Taiban's claims as “false allegations” and called on Iraqi authorities to take a position on remarks it said could damage relations between the countries. Iran had already criticised the border closure. Iranian state media reported that Tehran was not given advance notice that the Al Sheeb crossing would be closed. The matter is under review, Iranian Interior Ministry spokesman Ali Zeinivand was quoted as saying. Mr Al Zaidi, who took office in May, has sought to maintain balanced ties with both Iran and the US while moving to bring armed factions under state control. Some Iran‑aligned groups have complied, while others have resisted. Many of these groups have been accused of carrying out crimes and killings, particularly during anti-government protests in 2019. Thousands of protesters gathered on Sunday in Baghdad to commemorate the anniversary of the demonstrations that became known as the Tishreen movement, demanding accountability.

title: Ukrainian Attack Targets Russian AVISMA Plant Which Produces Country s 96 of Titanium Sponge
body:
Russia’s AVISMA Chemical and Metallurgical Plant in Berezniki, Perm Krai, a major global producer of titanium sponge used in aircraft, engines and missile manufacturing, was reportedly targeted in an attack.
Footage of the attack was published by the Exilenova+ community on X . Perm Krai Governor Dmitry Makhonin confirmed an attack in the region, saying air defenses intercepted 11 drones and an unnamed industrial facility in the north sustained minor damage. Five employees were reportedly injured, according to preliminary information. The governor did not publicly identify the damaged facility as AVISMA.
AVISMA belongs to VSMPO-AVISMA, which operates an integrated titanium production chain, including a major facility in Verkhnyaya Salda, Sverdlovsk Oblast. According to the United States Geological Survey (USGS), the corporation produced approximately 33,500 tonnes of titanium sponge in 2024, representing about 96% of Russia’s output.
The company has historically been a major supplier to global aerospace manufacturers. By 2021, it exported approximately 70% of its titanium production, supplying Boeing, Airbus, Embraer, Rolls-Royce and Safran. USGS figures indicate its output covered about 35% of Boeing’s titanium requirements, 65% of Airbus’s and 100% of Embraer’s at the time.
A July 2023 investigation by the independent Russian publication Proekt identified dozens of contracts between VSMPO-AVISMA and Russian defense enterprises involved in manufacturing aircraft, missiles, armored vehicles and ships.
Its reported customers include the Votkinsky Plant, which manufactures missiles for the Iskander operational-tactical systems and Yars and Topol-M intercontinental ballistic missile programs. Ukrainian authorities have also reported that titanium raw materials supplied through structures associated with VSMPO-AVISMA were used in Kalibr cruise missile production.
In aviation, the corporation supplies titanium alloys to manufacturers associated with the Su-30, Su-34 and Su-35S combat aircraft, as well as Tupolev’s Tu-95MS, Tu-160 and Tu-22M3 bombers. Ukrainian military intelligence has documented links between its titanium products and Su-34 and Su-35S production. Other reported customers include Aviastar-SP, which manufactures Il-76 transport aircraft and Il-78 aerial refueling tankers, and the Voronezh Joint Stock Aircraft Manufacturing Company.
The corporation also supplies Russian naval and armored vehicle industries. Reported customers include Admiralty Shipyards, Amur Shipyards and the Zvezdochka Ship Repair Center, which build, repair or modernize warships and submarines. Admiralty Shipyards manufactures Project 636.3 diesel-electric submarines capable of carrying Kalibr missiles. VSMPO-AVISMA also supplies Uralvagonzavod, the manufacturer of T-72B3 and T-90M tanks, with products including metal forgings, stamped parts and hatch covers.
