title: AY apologises after payment dispute disrupts UK comedy show
body: By Wasiu Rokibat Nigerian comedian and actor Ayo Makun, popularly known as AY, has apologised to fans disappointed that the Cardiff leg of his “AY Live: Single and Not Searching” UK tour failed to go ahead as expected. The event, scheduled for Sunday, October 25, 2026, at Valegate Retail Park in Cardiff, Wales, reportedly saw hours of delays and confusion, leaving many ticket holders unable to see any of the advertised performers. AY, in a statement shared on Monday on Instagram, said he and the other comedians on the bill had travelled to Cardiff and arrived at the venue but could not perform because of unresolved payment commitments with the organisers. “My fellow comedians and I travelled to Cardiff to perform and eventually entered the venue. Unfortunately, unresolved payment commitments delayed our appearance, and by the time we arrived at the hall, most of the audience had left,” he said. The comedian expressed regret over the experience, acknowledging that fans who paid to attend the show deserved better treatment. “You deserved a properly organised show and timely information. You should never have been caught in the middle of a payment dispute,” AY stated. He also appealed to fans to hear his account of the incident before reaching conclusions about what transpired, saying he had explained the circumstances in a video. Addressing the issue of compensation, AY called on the organisers and the UK tour management to provide a clear resolution for affected ticket holders, including information on refunds. “I am calling on the organisers and our UK tour management to provide a clear resolution for ticket holders, including refund information,” he said, adding that verified updates would be communicated through his official channels. The incident had triggered complaints from attendees on social media, with reports of prolonged waiting, heated exchanges and police presence at the venue. As of the time of filing this report, the organisers had yet to publicly explain the circumstances surrounding the disruption or announce refund arrangements. The post AY apologises after payment dispute disrupts UK comedy show appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Mugwo Community mobilizes resources to build a maternity ward
body: Residents of Mugwo Payam in Central Equatoria State’s Yei River County are pooling their own resources to improve maternal healthcare at a local health facility that serves patients from neighboring areas and the Democratic Republic of Congo. Through the Mugwo Community Health Initiative, residents are financing the construction of an eight-room maternity ward at Mugwo Primary Health Care Centre (PHCC), hoping to improve services for pregnant women, mothers and newborns. Speaking on Sunday during a fundraising event meant to raise funds for the completion of the building, Betty July Araba, chairperson of the initiative, said the facility faces challenges meeting the needs of a population larger than the one for which its services and supplies are allocated. “The unique thing about Mugwo PHCC is that the population of Mugo Payam is smaller than the population that comes to services in that facility,” Araba told Radio Tamazuj on Sunday during a fundraising gathering for the construction project. “The drugs that are provided by the government and the partners to that facility get finished even before the end of the month, the allocations that are given to us.” She said patients travel to Mugo from as far as Morobo, parts of Lainya County and neighbouring areas of the Democratic Republic of Congo to seek medical care. She cited the death of a close cousin during childbirth as one of the experiences that motivated her to take up the leadership role. Araba said the maternity ward is intended to help women access maternal healthcare closer to their communities and improve the care available to mothers and newborns. Accountability builds community trust According to Araba, transparent financial reporting and accountability have helped build trust among residents and encouraged more people to contribute towards the project. “The biggest challenge is trust,” she stated. “This is a hard-earned money so nobody wants to give the money and just lose it and for us consistently we have told them your money is safe.” She said contributions are accepted regardless of a person’s position or financial capacity, with some residents giving as little as 1,000 South Sudanese pounds while others contribute larger amounts. According to the chairperson, the initiative has raised about $15,000 in total contributions, including cash and in-kind support, noting that the amount had been calculated by assigning values to materials, labour, and other contributions made towards the construction. The eight-room ward building has currently reached beam level, awaiting roofing. The community has provided labour, collected stones, excavated sand and moulded bricks, while engineers from the area volunteered to design the building. Call for community-led development Araba called on other communities in South Sudan to organise themselves and contribute towards improving essential services, saying residents can play an important role alongside government and development partners. “This is a community-grown initiative, and my main message about this is that community has power. Community is a contributor, a partner in any development,” she said. Araba said local leaders, the Payam administrator and Yei County authorities were aware of the project, adding that the initiative had invited county commissioners to its fundraising activities to explain the community’s needs. “Thirdly, we have reached out to the government and said it is your responsibility to support this community,” she said. “We know you’ve done a lot, but we would like to tell you that we have gaps.” The initiative organises fundraising activities and community gatherings known locally as “Tukaro”, where residents meet to share a meal, discuss challenges and plan the next steps for development. Araba urged residents and well-wishers to continue supporting the project so that construction could proceed and the maternity ward could eventually serve women and newborns in Mugwo and surrounding communities. The post Mugwo Community mobilizes resources to build a maternity ward appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: Rada extends martial law for 90 days
body:
The Verkhovna Rada has supported President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's decree to extend the period of martial law in Ukraine for 90 days.

As reported by an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent, 293 people's deputies voted in favor of the relevant draft law No. 16182 as a whole during a plenary session of the Verkhovna Rada on Monday.

According to the draft law, martial law is extended for 90 days starting from 5:30 a.m. on October 31, 2026.

title: South Africa evacuees condemn public humiliation, seek rescue of 46 stranded Ghanaians
body: The leader of the Aggrieved South Africa Evacuees, Michael Addo, has condemned what he describes as the public humiliation of Ghanaians evacuated from South Africa, accusing sections of society of disregarding their trauma under the guise of demanding accountability. According to him, the ongoing controversy surrounding the evacuation exercise has compounded the emotional distress of returnees and discouraged further appeals for government assistance. “While we bravely recover from our trauma and pain, the very society we expect to protect us has reduced our pain to humiliation under the guise of seeking accountability,” he lamented. His concerns come amid growing public scrutiny of the government’s reported GH¢49.72 million expenditure on evacuating 1,964 Ghanaians from South Africa. Mr Addo disclosed that 46 Ghanaians who were expected to be part of the evacuation exercise remain stranded in South Africa, but the controversy circulating on social media has made it difficult to seek further government intervention. “We have other brothers and sisters who are still over there who are willing to come. Currently, we still have 46 people who were supposed to be on the flight, but because of what is currently spreading on social media, we don’t even have the balls to beg the government to go and rescue them,” he stated. He further accused some elements within the Minority, the New Patriotic Party (NPP) and sections of the media of attempting to establish wrongdoing against the government. Mr Addo also questioned allegations surrounding financial assistance and relief packages reportedly provided to the evacuees, insisting that journalists who witnessed their arrival at the airport could attest to their circumstances. He consequently demanded an immediate end to what he described as baseless attacks against the returnees and the government. “We are here to seek answers and demand an immediate end to the baseless attacks on us and the government that was sympathetic towards us,” he declared. Expressing appreciation for the government’s intervention, Mr Addo said many Ghanaians had endured xenophobia in South Africa for years without receiving similar assistance. “We have experienced xenophobia for many years, but this is the first time a government has taken our plight into account and come to our rescue,” he added. He maintained that the pursuit of accountability should not come at the expense of the dignity and well-being of evacuees, particularly when other Ghanaians remain in need of assistance.

title: Nigeria’s Index Ebola Patient Evacuated Abroad By Air Ambulance
body: Ayodeji Ake Nigeria’s index Ebola patient, a 42-year-old Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat, has been evacuated from Abuja aboard an air ambulance, according to a report by ARISE News, the sister media company of THISDAY Newspapers. The medical evacuation took place early Monday morning through the private jet wing of the Nnamdi Azikiwe International Airport in Abuja, where heightened security measures were reportedly put in place ahead of the aircraft’s departure. It was reported that its crew deployed to the airport’s General Aviation Terminal obtained photographs showing a convoy of ambulances and diplomatic vehicles arriving from the Abuja city centre. The three-vehicle convoy reportedly included a vehicle belonging to an international agency, which proceeded into the airport’s private aviation section. Airport officials subsequently cordoned off the private wing as arrangements for the medical evacuation continued. ARISE News also obtained video footage showing the medical evacuation aircraft and members of its crew involved in transporting the passenger, whose reported status as Nigeria’s index Ebola patient had drawn significant attention to the operation. A source cited by ARISE News disclosed that the Federal Government planned to announce the evacuation only after the aircraft had taken off and exited Nigerian airspace. The reported evacuation comes amid heightened public attention to Nigeria’s Ebola preparedness and response measures, particularly concerning the management and movement of suspected or confirmed cases. As of the time of the report, further official details about the patient’s destination, medical condition and the circumstances surrounding the evacuation had not been disclosed.

title: Trade Pathways launches Nigeria coverage as US tariffs weigh on small business exporters
body: New US import tax falls hardest on processed goods, the core of Nigeria’s small-business export economy. For Nigeria’s small businesses, selling to the United States has become a moving target. Tariff costs for buyers have changed four times in the last 18 months, and the latest change brings new challenges for entrepreneurs and business owners. The recent volatility began in April 2025, when the US placed a 14 per cent tax on most Nigerian goods. Four months later, the tariff rate rose to 15 per cent. Then, in February 2026, the US Supreme Court ruled these taxes unlawful, and a temporary 10 per cent tax was put in their place. For many exporters, it became difficult to know which rate applied, or for how long. That temporary tax expired in July 2026 and was replaced by the one in place today: a 12.5 per cent tax on goods from countries that, according to the US government, have not banned imports made with forced labour. Nigeria is one of the few African countries on that list. A key concern with the latest tariff is that it falls hardest on small businesses. Nigeria’s largest exports to the US, such as crude oil, gas and fertiliser, are exempt, and those are mostly handled by large enterprises. Beyond these exports, the dividing line tends to fall between raw and finished goods. Most raw commodities, like cocoa beans and raw cashews, are exempt, while finished goods such as roasted cashews, chocolate, shea butter, leather goods, cosmetics, packaged foods and crafts are taxed. These finished goods tend to be items that Nigeria’s small and medium-sized businesses most commonly export. “The greater challenge lies not in the immediate loss of export opportunities, but in navigating an increasingly fragmented and protectionist global trading environment,” Dr Muda Yusuf, Chief Executive Officer of the Centre for the Promotion of Private Enterprise (CPPE), said in a policy brief issued after the tax was announced. This growing challenge for small and medium-sized businesses is why Trade Pathways, a US-based, student-run organisation, was founded. Its goal is to create opportunities for small businesses in Africa by giving them free access to the same clear, up-to-date picture of US trade policy that multinationals and large enterprises get from legal teams and policy experts. The platform tracks every US trade policy change and explains the structure in simple terms, so business owners can keep up with the constant shifts and understand buyer behaviour. Having initially served businesses in Kenya and Ghana, Trade Pathways is now launching full coverage for Nigeria, driven by recent trade policy changes and the potential adverse impacts on Nigerian business owners. “Small business owners should be spending their time making and selling great products, not on interpreting US government trade notices,” noted Keshav Suman, the platform’s founder. “The information is public, but it changes constantly and is written for lawyers and policy experts, not for the business owners it affects most.” The timing reflects growing activity among smaller Nigerian exporters. Non-oil exports reached a record $6.1 billion in 2025, and the Nigerian Export Promotion Council (NEPC) registered 1,129 new exporters during the year. NEPC’s Executive Director, Nonye Ayeni, has said the council is focused on “reducing dependence on large exporters by supporting small and medium-scale enterprises.” What Nigerian exporting businesses should know now Which party pays the tariff. The US import tax is paid by the American buyer when the goods arrive, not by the Nigerian supplier. Suppliers are still impacted indirectly, however, as buyers ask for lower prices, order smaller quantities, or move part of their orders to suppliers in countries that pay less. The exception is when a seller agrees to deliver goods with all import duties already paid, an arrangement that is common when shipping parcels directly to US customers. In that case, the seller would be responsible for the tax. Product classification. Exemptions from the new tax are set based on product and further classified by process, so two closely related goods can be treated very differently. Raw cashews, for example, are exempt, while roasted cashews are not. Before agreeing on a price, exporters should confirm exactly how their product is classified, so a buyer is not surprised by a higher cost after the order is placed. Refunds of the 2025 tariffs. The emergency tariffs the US charged on imports from around the world in 2025, including the 14 and 15 per cent rates on Nigerian goods, were ruled unlawful by the US Supreme Court in February 2026. US Customs has been refunding importers since April 2026, and on October 8, a US court ruled that importers who have not filed their own lawsuits are covered under a single group claim. Although refunds benefit US buyers, Nigerian export businesses that lowered prices to help buyers absorb the tariff can reasonably negotiate in future pricing discussions. AGOA and duty-free entry. The African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), a US programme that removes the standard import tax on qualifying goods from sub-Saharan Africa, was extended in September 2026 and now runs until December 2028. It covers thousands of products, including several forms of clothing, footwear, leather goods, processed foods and wooden crafts. Nigeria has also been certified since 2005 to export handloomed and ethnic printed fabrics such as aso oke, Akwete cloth and Ankara prints under AGOA, a benefit that many business owners are not aware of. AGOA does not, however, cancel the new 12.5 per cent tax rate in place for Nigeria. US travel restrictions. Since January 2026, the US government has suspended new business and tourist visas for Nigerian nationals, which makes US trade shows difficult to attend. Video meetings, product samples sent ahead of a call, and US-based sales representatives or partners in the Nigerian diaspora can all help maintain buyer relationships through the absence of physical visits to the US. Alternative markets and customers. Selling to more than one market reduces the risk of depending on a single country’s trade rules. Europe is already Nigeria’s largest buyer of non-oil goods, and many Nigerian products receive reduced import taxes there. Since May 2026, China has charged no import tax on Nigerian goods, an arrangement that runs until April 2028, though food and agricultural exporters must still register with Chinese customs and meet its product standards. Closer to home, the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) is gradually lowering import taxes between African countries, opening regional markets that are often easier to reach than the US. What comes next Several US developments could change the picture in the coming months. American importers and 25 US states are challenging the current 12.5 per cent tariff in a US trade court, which heard the case on September 30. A potential ruling could reduce or remove the tax entirely, though an appeal is expected on either side. The US government is also expected to announce its annual decisions on which countries remain eligible for AGOA near the end of the year. Trade Pathways noted it is currently tracking each of these policy movements and will update guidance as announcements come. Trade Pathways’ resources for small business owners Trade Pathways provides tools and services that are free for business owners in Kenya, Ghana, and now Nigeria. One such tool is a cost estimator, which calculates what a US buyer would pay at the border for a given product and shipment by country. On a $10,000 shipment, for example, Nigerian cocoa butter costs the buyer about $47 in customs fees, because it is exempt from the current tariff. The same shipment of wooden carvings costs about $1,297, almost all of it the 12.5 per cent tax. This allows sellers to anticipate how a buyer might respond to the tax, and to go into pricing conversations better prepared. The platform also offers guidance on labour management, an area where US buyers are paying closer attention than ever. Because US law bans imports made with forced labour, American buyers increasingly ask their suppliers for proof of fair employment, such as written contracts, payroll records and confirmation that workers keep their own identity documents. Trade Pathways provides a checklist of these records so businesses can respond to buyer requests quickly. Suman, a US-based high school student, started Trade Pathways in 2025. For years, he had bought home decor from sellers in Africa through platforms such as Etsy and TikTok Shop. When US tariffs took effect, he noticed several of those sellers begin to raise prices, pause shipments to the US, or announce closures of their operations. Realising that small businesses had limited ability to absorb or ride out sudden policy changes, he built Trade Pathways to give them clearer information to make informed decisions. US trade policy is likely to remain unpredictable, and the businesses best placed to adapt will be those that understand the rules early. With its launch in Nigeria, Trade Pathways aims to make sure that knowledge base is available to every small business owner. The post Trade Pathways launches Nigeria coverage as US tariffs weigh on small business exporters appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Thales opens new facility to support sonar production
body:
Thales Australia has opened a new sonar manufacturing facility in Rydalmere, Western Sydney, to support the design, production, integration and sustainment of undersea acoustic systems.
The facility was jointly funded by Thales Australia and the Commonwealth of Australia and will support the supply chain for the towed-array sonar system used on the Royal Australian Navy’s Hunter-class frigates.
Thales Australia and the Commonwealth of Australia jointly invested in the multimillion-dollar facility at Rydalmere, which has been built within the wider Thales Australia Acoustics Centre of Excellence.
According to Thales, the hall is 100 metres long and is designed to facilitate the end-to-end manufacture of towed array sonar systems that act as the ‘ears’ of submarines, surface ships and autonomous maritime systems.
The Rydalmere facility has supported the Royal Australian Navy’s sonar requirements for more than 30 years, providing technologies for anti-submarine warfare (ASW), maritime surveillance and undersea domain awareness, including for the Collins-class submarines.
The new facility will boost this Australian-made deterrence by ensuring end-to-end sovereign manufacturing capability for next-generation towed array sonar systems that support submarines and surface combatants, and thin-line towed arrays for uncrewed maritime systems serving both Australian and export markets.
In particular, the towed array facility will deliver:
“Through this new co-invested manufacturing facility, Australia is strengthening national security, creating high-value jobs and establishing a sovereign centre of excellence for advanced acoustic systems that will support both Australian Defence and export opportunities for decades to come," Pat Conroy , Minister for Defense Industry, said.
"The capabilities developed and manufactured at Rydalmere demonstrate Australia's ability to deliver sovereign undersea warfare technology, from the Collins Class submarine fleet of today to the Hunter Class frigates and autonomous BlueSentry surveillance systems of the future," Jeff Connolly , CEO, Thales Australia and New Zealand, stated.
