In an earlier Facebook post reported by PREMIUM TIMES, Marshall called on the minister to submit to a DNA test, insisting that the exercise would settle questions about their relationship.
“Dear Father, if you truly believe in your integrity, then let us settle this once and for all through a DNA test. Truth does not fear examination, and facts will speak for themselves,” he said in the earlier post.
The controversy around paternity followed comments attributed in now deleted reports to the minister’s spokesperson, Louis Ibah, who was quoted as saying that none of the minister’s sons was contesting an election. The reported remarks fuelled questions about whether the minister was disputing Marshall’s paternity or distancing himself from his political activities.
PREMIUM TIMES reported in June that it could not independently verify whether the minister personally made the statement attributed to him. The newspaper also said it found no official statement issued directly by the minister expressly denying that Marshall was his son.
The minister is yet to react to the latest Facebook post by Marshall.
Marshall’s latest comments frame the forthcoming elections as a contest between the influence of government officials and the electorate’s power to choose its representatives.
The 2027 general elections are expected to test political parties, candidates and alliances across Nigeria, including in Akwa Ibom State.
Marshall’s declaration remains a political vow. Whether the position he has articulated resonates with voters will become clearer as political activities ahead of the elections intensify.

title: Ghana is restoring nature, but is nature recovering?
body: Included is an opinion feature told through the imagined voice of Auntie Mansa, a Ghanaian woman whose livelihood depends on the land. “Aaah, my son, when the people come to our community, they tell us they have come to restore the land. They bring seedlings, take photographs, call us for meetings, and tell us that things will be better.” “Of course, we are happy. Who does not want good land, clean air, clean water, and enough food for the family? If the land is healthy, we can farm. If the water is clean, we can drink and do our work. If the trees grow well, the children coming after us will also benefit. But, my son, I have one small question. When the visitors leave, who will take care of the land? Who will water the seedlings when the rains delay? Who will protect them when animals start feeding on them? And if the land we depend on has been damaged by galamsey, how soon can we farm there again? I am not against planting trees. Not at all. But I also have children to feed today. I cannot tell them to wait twenty years because somebody has planted a tree.” Auntie Mansa’s questions may sound simple, but they expose one of the most important challenges facing Ghana’s environmental restoration agenda. From degraded mining landscapes to threatened mangroves, Ghana has made important commitments to environmental restoration. Across Africa, governments, research institutions and development partners are investing in initiatives intended to restore ecosystems, strengthen climate resilience and improve livelihoods. Yet a fundamental question remains: Are we restoring nature, or are we becoming better at reporting the activities we undertake in nature’s name? The distinction matters, as a seedling planted is not necessarily a tree established, and a tree established does not necessarily mean a functioning ecosystem has recovered. An ecosystem showing signs of recovery does not automatically mean that the people living around it are better off. For Ghana, these are not merely academic questions. They concern the rivers we depend on, the land we farm, the wetlands that support fisheries and the livelihoods of communities bearing the consequences of environmental degradation. Nature-based solutions offer a promising way forward. They involve protecting, sustainably managing, and restoring ecosystems to address societal challenges while benefiting biodiversity and human well-being. But what does this mean for ordinary people? Ghana has made progress, but what does the evidence tell us? Let us begin with what the country has achieved. Ghana’s restoration achievements: What does the data tell us? Ghana’s Landscape Restoration and Small-Scale Mining Project, launched in 2022, showed by October 2024 that it had restored 25,181 hectares of agricultural land and reached nearly 58,000 farmers across 26 districts in eight regions. The programme combines landscape restoration with agricultural support and efforts to address the environmental consequences of small-scale mining. Ghana’s 2025 Voluntary National Review reported a cumulative 748,941.6 hectares under the Ghana Forest Plantation Strategy for 2017–2023. Of this reported area, 587,340.8 hectares, or 78.5%, were classified as trees on farms. These are significant implementation figures and deserve recognition. They suggest that restoration is being connected to agriculture and rural livelihoods and was not treated solely as a forestry activity. But let us pause here. What do these figures tell us about the condition of the land today? How many planted trees survived? How much of the restored agricultural land remains productive? Have farmers experienced lasting improvements in soil fertility, water availability, and income? And what happens when project funding ends? These questions do not diminish the reported achievements. They help us understand their real value. Imagine a farmer who joins a restoration programme. She was part of the tree planters, attended the training sessions and followed the instructions. When the project ended, the vehicles drove away, the officers returned to their offices, and the farmer was left to manage the work alone. Two rainy seasons later, she found some seedlings dead, rains becoming less predictable, her own resources running low, and struggling to keep the remaining trees alive. Can we still call the intervention a success simply because the seedlings were planted? Auntie Mansa would probably put it differently. “My son, if you say you have restored the land, please come and show me the land. Do not only show me the photographs you took when we planted the trees.” That is the kind of accountability Ghana needs. 2025–2026: Ghana is scaling up. Will the results last? Ghana’s restoration agenda has gathered further momentum. Recent initiatives show growing interest in linking tree planting, coastal protection, water security and climate-resilient agriculture. The challenge is to ensure that this momentum translates into lasting ecological and social benefits. Consider the Tree for Life Reforestation Initiative. A July 2026 government update reported that the 2025 programme had planted approximately 31 million seedlings across about 23,600 hectares of degraded landscapes. Seedling success rates ranged from 50 to 78% in the northern savannah zone and 65 to 85% in the High Forest Zone. A further target of planting 30 million seedlings was set for 2026. These figures provide a useful starting point. But what exactly do the reported success rates measure, and at what point were they assessed? How many seedlings remain alive after successive dry seasons? How many will develop into established trees? And are the restored landscapes showing measurable improvements in biodiversity, soil condition and water regulation? The initiative deserves recognition for its scale. Its lasting contribution, however, will depend on nurturing, protecting and monitoring the trees beyond the initial planting period. The country’s coastal restoration agenda is also expanding. In November 2025, the Water Resources Commission convened a national dialogue on solutions for coastal protection, bringing together experts, policymakers and other stakeholders to explore more sustainable approaches to protecting vulnerable shorelines. In March 2026, the Forestry Commission signed an agreement with Terraformation to restore up to 6,000 hectares of mangroves in the Volta Region under the Keta Lagoon Blue Carbon Project. The agreement envisages planting 12 million native mangroves, with anticipated benefits for coastal resilience, biodiversity, employment and livelihoods. The project is built on earlier restoration activity. Planting began in 2024 with more than 3.2 million mangroves planted across nearly 1,000 hectares by August 2025. These reported achievements are encouraging. However, further monitoring is needed to establish how many seedlings survive, whether the ecosystem is recovering, and whether communities experience lasting benefits. Another coastal initiative led by ActionAid Ghana and its partners under the Improved Resilience of Coastal Communities Project is targeting approximately 410 hectares of degraded mangrove ecosystems across communities in the Volta and Greater Accra regions. By July 2026, the project had reported planting 95,300 mangrove seedlings in its first phase. Further inland, the Water Resources Commission reported in May 2026 that it was working with The Nature Conservancy and the Nature for Water Facility to expand watershed investment programmes. Initiatives for the White Volta and Black Volta basins are intended to connect ecosystem protection with water security and longer-term financing. In September 2026, Ghana launched the seven-year Climate-Resilient Landscapes for Sustainable Livelihoods in Northern Ghana project, valued at US$63 million. The initiative aims to restore approximately 14,000 hectares across the North East, Upper East and Upper West regions while strengthening climate resilience and agricultural livelihoods. These developments matter as they show that nature-based solutions are increasingly being connected to forestry, coastal protection, water management and climate-resilient agriculture. But we must distinguish between a target, an agreement, an activity completed and an outcome demonstrated. Each represents a different stage of implementation. Auntie Mansa would have something to say about this. “If they say they will plant millions of trees, that is good news. If they say they will restore our mangroves and protect our water, we are happy. But please, do not stop at telling us what they plan to do. Come back and tell us what has happened. Are the trees growing? Is the water getting better? Are our farms becoming more productive? Are the people who live here finding better ways to earn a living? And when the project finishes, who will continue the work? We do not want to wake up one day and realise that the money has finished, the visitors have gone, and the land is still waiting for us to rescue it.” Her questions capture the distinction Ghana must now confront. Announced targets, signed agreements, planted seedlings and hectares earmarked for restoration are important indicators of implementation. They are not by themselves proof that the promised ecological and social benefits have been achieved. Keta Lagoon: Restoration must be measured against the wider ecosystem Consider the Keta Lagoon Complex Ramsar Site along Ghana’s eastern coastline. In May 2023, the Ghana News Agency reported that six communities had restored 27 hectares of degraded land, including mangroves and woodlots, with approximately 84,000 seedlings planted. The initiative was linked to concerns about declining fisheries resources and the need to protect local livelihoods. This is encouraging. Mangroves provide habitat for wildlife, support fisheries, store carbon and contribute to coastal ecosystem stability. However, a peer-reviewed study published in 2021 documented substantial changes in land cover within the Keta Lagoon Complex between 1991 and 2020. Mangrove and dense vegetation accounted for 38.34% of the mapped area in 1991, compared with 27.12% in 2020. The picture was not one of uninterrupted decline. The study documented both gains and losses in vegetation across different periods and land-cover categories. The overall 2020 share of mangrove and dense vegetation nevertheless remained below the 1991 level. This matters because ecosystems can experience local recovery while continuing to face broader pressures. A separate study published in 2025 identified fragmented institutional responsibilities, limited institutional capacity, and dependence on external funding as barriers to implementing wetland-based nature-based solutions effectively. What should we make of this? The restoration of 27 hectares is a meaningful local achievement, but it must be understood within the context of the wider ecosystem. Planting seedlings in one location cannot by itself reverse degradation across an entire wetland. Mangroves need suitable hydrological conditions, appropriate sediment environments, and protection from destructive pressures. Communities also need practical incentives and the authority to help safeguard restored areas. For the woman who depends on the lagoon, the issue is not simply whether seedlings have been planted. She wants to know whether the ecosystem is recovering, whether fisheries can be sustained, and whether her livelihood will become more secure. “Ei, if the trees are growing but our problems remain the same, then let us sit down and find out what is missing. We are not saying the work is useless. We are asking whether the work is giving us the results we were promised.” That is a reasonable demand. Galamsey: Can nature repair what we have damaged? The question becomes even more urgent when we turn to mining-affected landscapes. Illegal mining can remove fertile topsoil, disrupt soil structure, contaminate water, and leave land unsuitable for conventional agricultural production. In some locations, the damage is so severe that ordinary farming cannot resume without substantial intervention. Can nature-based solutions help? Potentially, yes. But the approach must be scientifically appropriate to the damage. A study published in Advances in Bamboo Science investigated the growth and root development of Bambusa vulgaris on galamsey-degraded soil. The researchers found that combining biochar and poultry manure improved bamboo root density and average root diameter under the experimental conditions. This offers a promising research direction. Appropriately selected plants, soil amendments, and other restoration techniques may help rehabilitate degraded land under suitable conditions. However, we must not overstate what the study demonstrates. Improved bamboo growth is not proof that contaminated mining land has been made safe, nor does a controlled experiment establish that the method will restore mining landscapes at scale. Sites affected by mining require appropriate assessments of soil and water conditions. Near-real-time monitoring can help track changing environmental conditions and the progress of rehabilitation. It should complement field inspections, laboratory testing and assessments of contaminant risks. Where contaminants pose risks to people, crops or ecosystems, remediation and exposure prevention must be addressed explicitly. And here is where Auntie Mansa’s voice becomes important again. “My son, suppose you tell me the land is ready for farming. How do I know it is safe? If I plant cassava there, can my children eat it without danger? If the water looks clean, does that mean it is clean? Please, let somebody test it and explain the results to us.” This is not a rejection of science. It is a demand for science that protects people. Restoration should not end when vegetation returns. It should establish whether the land is functioning, whether environmental risks have been addressed, and whether the community can safely benefit from it. Africa has lessons for Ghana. Let us learn before we scale up. Ghana does not need to learn every lesson through expensive mistakes of its own. Other African countries provide valuable evidence of what nature-based solutions can achieve, as well as the limitations we must take seriously. In Niger, farmer-managed natural regeneration has enabled farmers to encourage trees to regenerate naturally within agricultural landscapes. Published research describes the approach as affecting approximately five to six million hectares. Farmers can benefit from trees that provide fuelwood, construction materials, food, and fodder while integrating tree management into existing farming systems. The principle is important: restoration does not always require planting new trees everywhere. In suitable landscapes, protecting existing vegetation and supporting natural regeneration may be more practical than starting from scratch. For Ghanaian farmers, this raises a useful question: are we making the best use of the trees and natural vegetation that already exist on our farms? Senegal’s experience with the Great Green Wall offers a different lesson. A 2025 study examining 36 planting parcels in northern Senegal found statistically significant greening trends in only two parcels, with just one showing greening beyond what rainfall changes would explain. These findings do not establish that the Great Green Wall has failed as a whole. They show that implementation achievements and ecological outcomes are not the same thing. The study also identified economic and social benefits for communities, including employment and services, although these benefits were described as periodic and often short-lived. That distinction is important. Employment and community services are valuable, but they should not be presented as substitutes for successful ecological restoration when restoration is the stated objective. In Ethiopia, landscape restoration has demonstrated potential for vegetation recovery. Yet restrictions on grazing and access to natural resources can create difficulties for households that depend on those resources. The lesson is not that restoration is inherently harmful, but that ecological objectives must be balanced with community needs and the availability of alternative livelihoods. Across these experiences, one message stands out. Successful nature-based solutions require ecological suitability, credible monitoring, long-term management, and meaningful community participation. “If something works in Niger, why can we not learn from it? But, my son, will the same method work on our land? Have the scientists checked? Have the farmers tried it? And if it does not work, who will help us find another way? “And when an intervention succeeds or fails in our community, who can we hold responsible?” These are precisely the questions that should guide the transfer of restoration approaches from one country to another. What happens to people when the project ends? This is perhaps the most important question of all. Environmental restoration is often discussed in terms of hectares, seedlings, carbon stocks and biodiversity indicators. These are important measurements. But the people who live with the consequences of environmental decisions must also be part of the assessment. If a community is asked to protect a wetland, how will its members sustain their livelihoods? If farmers are encouraged to establish trees, what happens to the land they need for food production? If mining has destroyed their farmland, what support will help them rebuild their livelihoods while restoration takes place? Women deserve particular attention because environmental degradation can affect the resources, agricultural activities, and local enterprises on which they depend. Young people also need meaningful opportunities to participate in restoration, monitoring, nursery enterprises, agroforestry and other viable green economic activities. Participation should mean more than inviting people to meetings or asking them to plant seedlings. Communities should help identify priorities, select appropriate interventions, monitor results and determine how benefits are distributed. Their observations should inform decisions, while scientific assessments should help establish what is changing and why. And when the project ends, the community should not be left holding responsibilities without the resources to fulfil them. “My son, do not call us only when you need labour. Call us when you are planning. Call us when you are making decisions. Call us when you are checking whether the work has succeeded. We live here. We see the land every day.” Five questions Ghana must answer First, what survives and recovers? Restoration programmes should measure seedling survival, natural regeneration, vegetation condition, soil health, water quality and biodiversity, where relevant. Planting numbers and hectares covered are useful, but they cannot stand in for ecological recovery. Second, who benefits? We must establish whether communities experience lasting improvements in livelihoods and whether women, young people, people with disabilities and vulnerable households share fairly in the benefits. Third, what happens after project funding ends? Restoration requires maintenance, protection and monitoring. Long-term financing and local ownership must be considered from the beginning. Fourth, are we restoring the right ecosystem in the right way? Wetlands, forests, agricultural landscapes and mining-degraded soils have different ecological requirements. A solution suitable for one environment may be inappropriate for another. Restoration must respond to the actual problem rather than follow a fashionable method. Finally, who verifies the results? Research institutions, government agencies, development partners and implementing organisations should establish baselines, publish monitoring findings and assess whether observed improvements can reasonably be attributed to the interventions. Remote sensing, environmental sensors and artificial intelligence can strengthen monitoring, but these tools must be combined with field measurements, sound scientific methods and local knowledge. Auntie Mansa does not need to understand every technical detail of these methods. She needs the results explained in a way she can understand, question, and use. “If the scientists say the land is improving, let them show us. If the water is safe, let them explain how they tested it. If the project has succeeded, let us know what has changed. And if it has not succeeded, please do not hide the truth from us.” That is what transparent science should look like. Ghana needs an implementation revolution, not another environmental slogan Ghana has an opportunity to build on its restoration achievements and strengthen the evidence, institutions and partnerships needed to sustain them. This means documenting both successful and unsuccessful interventions, comparing costs and benefits, identifying the conditions under which solutions work and sharing lessons across districts and ecological zones. It also means recognising that nature-based solutions cannot replace effective environmental regulation. Restoring a river catchment while allowing continued pollution upstream is unlikely to deliver lasting results. Restoration must go hand in hand with preventing further environmental damage. We must therefore ask every major restoration investment a few straightforward questions: What problem is being addressed? What has changed? Who has benefited? What has it cost? Will the benefits last? The answers should not remain in technical reports that few people can access. They should inform public debate, government decisions and the choices communities make about their own landscapes. Our ambition should not be to plant the most trees, announce the largest restoration area or launch the greatest number of environmental projects. It should be to leave behind healthier ecosystems, more resilient communities and stronger livelihoods than we inherited. That is the standard by which Ghana’s nature-based solutions should ultimately be judged. Return after the cameras leave “My son, the people in the media have a very important job to do. When the government announces a project, please do not only report the launch and the number of seedlings they say they will plant. Come back after one year, two years, or five years. Ask what has happened to the land. “If they say they have restored a river, ask whether the water is cleaner. If they say they have restored a forest, ask whether the trees are surviving and the wildlife is returning. If they say they have helped farmers, ask the farmers themselves whether their lives have improved. Please give us the chance to speak. Do not allow only the big people to talk about our land while those of us who live on it remain quiet. When you meet the policymakers, ask them who is responsible for maintaining the projects after the funding ends. Ask them how communities will be supported. Ask them how they will make sure that the land is safe, that the benefits reach the people, and that the same environmental damage does not happen again. And when they answer, please bring the answers back to us. We want to know what they have promised, what they have done, and what remains to be done. If something is working, tell the whole country so others can learn. If something is not working, report it fairly so we can correct it. Do not wait until the land is completely destroyed before you come and ask questions. We are not asking for miracles. We are asking for honest answers and people who will remember us after the cameras are gone. Because when the land suffers, we suffer with it. And when the land recovers, we should recover with it. That is what I want you to tell the policymakers for me.” Author Dr Caleb Melenya Ocansey President, AINAS (African Initiative for Nature-Based Solutions)

title: 8 arrested for repackaging allegedly expired food in Juba
body: Eight suspects have been arrested for repackaging allegedlyexpired flour for resale at H Brothers General Trading and Investment Co. Ltd. in Gumbo, Juba County, Central Equatoria State. Juba County authorities said on Saturday that security personnel caught the suspects transferring expired maize flour into new sacks. The company was closed, and the suspects were taken into custody pending legal proceedings. Caretaker County Commissioner Kalisto Lado Faustino warned businesses against selling expired food products, saying “public health and consumer safety remain a priority for the county administration.” On Sunday, Caretaker Governor Augustino Jadalla Kamilo visited the premises alongside the commissioner. The state government said the inspection uncovered expired flour, biscuits, cooking oil, sugar, and other food items allegedly being repackaged into new sacks, jerrycans, and boxes with altered expiry dates. Jadalla directed the commissioner to pursue legal action through relevant authorities, including the South Sudan National Bureau of Standards (SSNBS) and security agencies, to hold those responsible accountable. “The state government reiterates that public health remains a top priority and must not be taken lightly,” the government said, pledging legal action against any company found repackaging expired goods. The governor also urged residents to report suspicious or expired goods in markets and shops, stressing the importance of cooperation between the public and security agencies. In a statement on Sunday, the SSNBS commended Juba County authorities for their action and reminded businesses of their responsibility to comply with food safety standards. “As the national institution mandated to promote standardization, quality assurance and consumer protection, the SSNBS emphasizes that all businesses involved in the production, processing, packaging, distribution and sale of food products must uphold applicable standards and regulatory requirements,” the bureau said. The SSNBS urged traders to check expiry dates regularly, separate expired products from goods intended for sale, and ensure non-compliant items are handled and disposed of according to applicable requirements. It also advised consumers to check product labels and expiry dates before buying food and to report suspected cases of expired or tampered-with products. “Consumer protection is a shared responsibility,” the bureau said, calling for stronger cooperation among authorities, businesses and the public to prevent unsafe food from reaching consumers. The post 8 arrested for repackaging allegedly expired food in Juba appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: Patriot getting closer to 'over-the-shoulder' shooting
body:
Lockheed Martin has reported on the subsequent stages of development for the RIG-360, a device providing omni-directional connectivity with PAC-3 family missiles used in Patriot systems during flight. In less than two months, a critical design review, a series of flight trials, and a missile launch test were conducted.
According to a statement from Lockheed Martin, the trials were successful, and the programme is ahead of schedule for delivery and implementation within the U.S. Army.
The RIG-360 is designed to enhance the operational capabilities of PAC-3 missiles by making the transmission of in-flight data independent of the Patriot system’s radar. Target information can originate from other sensors operating within the IBCS command system and then reach the missile via a separate link. This allows for complete freedom in selecting sensors and launchers tailored to the specific conditions of an intercept, utilising information available in the integrated air defence network without the need to rely on the communication assets of Patriot radars.
The PAC-3 missile launch test was preceded by three captive-carry trials . These involved an aircraft carrying the missile’s communication device to verify data exchange with the RIG-360 without launching a rocket. According to the manufacturer, full 360-degree connectivity was confirmed, as was the fulfilment of maximum transmission range requirements.
A few weeks later, a PAC-3 test firing was conducted, during which data exchange between the flying missile and the RIG-360 was confirmed. This allowed for the verification of the link’s performance during an actual missile flight, supplementing the results of the earlier aircraft-based tests.
The RIG-360 is set to increase the utility of PAC-3 missiles by separating the Patriot radar from the transmission of data to the flying missile. Today, even if a Patriot battery features the IBCS system and uses another sensor for target tracking , the update of data for that object (the so-called uplink) takes place via the Patriot radar (even if this radar does not „see” the target itself).
Thanks to the RIG-360, information acquired by sensors collaborating with the IBCS will be able to reach the missile via a separate link, without the need to use the Patriot radar’s communication equipment . This increases the flexibility of using radars and launchers operating within a single network and enables intercepts based on data from various sources.
PAC-3 , currently produced in the modernised PAC-3 MSE version, is an active radar-guided missile used for defence against the most complex threats (ballistic and cruise missiles, aircraft). The PAC-3 MSE constitutes the primary armament for newer configurations of Patriot systems, including the Polish Wisła system. During the war in Ukraine, it has been used to engage Iskander and Kinzhal aeroballistic missiles, which are considered the greatest threat to critical infrastructure. Meanwhile, the IBCS is a command system developed by Northrop Grumman for the US Army, connecting various layers of air defence into a single network. It is used by the US Army and in Poland within the Wisła programme, and it will also be utilised in the target configuration of the Narew system. New sensors are to be integrated with the IBCS, including F-35A fighters and – in the Polish configuration – the domestic Sajna and Bystra radars.

title: Campaign Council: Of NDC’s Authority, O-K Movement and Race against Time
body: As the January 16, 2027 presidential poll approaches, the Nigerian Democratic Congress faces a defining test: reconcile competing campaign structures, resolve support-group tensions and translate political enthusiasm into coordinated electoral strength, writes Sunday Aborisade . The Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) is approaching a critical moment in its preparations for the January 16, 2027 general election. With Peter Obi as its presidential candidate and Senator Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso as his running mate, the party has assembled a ticket with potential cross-regional appeal. Yet, beneath the enthusiasm surrounding the alliance lies an organisational challenge that could determine whether its electoral promise translates into success: who controls the campaign, how competing interests are accommodated and how quickly a coherent national structure can emerge. The delayed inauguration of the National Campaign Council (NCC), uncertainty surrounding the party’s manifesto and friction with support groups, particularly the Obi-Kwankwaso movement that established a Presidential Campaign Council (PCC) outside the party’s approved framework, have raised questions about NDC’s preparedness. These are more than administrative disagreements. They concern the relationship between political parties and the movements supporting their candidates, the balance between institutional authority and grassroots mobilisation, and the ability of an opposition platform to manage competing expectations under a demanding electoral timetable. The central question is whether the NDC can resolve these differences or allow disputes over recognition, appointments and authority to consume valuable campaign time. The NDC leadership has attributed the delay in constituting its campaign council to consultations, due diligence and the need to involve its presidential candidates in selecting key officials. Following a two-day meeting of the National Working Committee (NWC), National Chairman, Senator Moses Cleopas announced October 20 as the proposed inauguration date, explaining that the party had been developing its campaign blueprint since August. “The constitution and inauguration of the presidential campaign council is a responsibility of the party at the highest level. But the party itself cannot do that without recourse to the presidential candidate and the vice-presidential candidate,” Cleopas said. He disclosed that Obi and Kwankwaso were consulting on appointments to strategic positions, including director-general, deputy director-general, finance director, mobilisation director and media director. “It is better to get it right. It is a sensitive election that we are going into, and we must check characters,” he added. The October 20 inauguration was subsequently postponed to October 26, with the party citing Obi’s overseas engagement. National Publicity Secretary, Osa Director attributed the decision to “the very tight schedule of our presidential candidate” and an important overseas engagement. The party later announced that its third National Executive Committee (NEC) meeting, scheduled for October 26 in Abuja, would feature the unveiling of the NCC, presentation of certificates of return to candidates and disclosure of its financial accounts. Although consultation and scrutiny are legitimate, repeated adjustments to the inauguration timetable risk creating an impression of uncertainty. The leadership must demonstrate that consultation has a definite endpoint and will not become an obstacle to implementation. The candidates deserve meaningful input into the composition of their campaign council. They will defend the party’s policies, lead public engagements and bear the greatest political responsibility for the election. However, consultation must not translate into the indefinite concentration of campaign decisions in the hands of two individuals. A presidential campaign council is the operational machinery through which a party coordinates communications, finances, policy, state organisations, mobilisation and electoral protection. The NDC must therefore reconcile the candidates’ preferences with its institutional responsibilities. Cleopas has warned against appointing officials whose loyalty is uncertain, arguing that divided political commitments could undermine the campaign. While understandable, such screening must not become an open-ended exercise or reduce appointments to questions of personal loyalty rather than competence and clearly defined responsibilities. The party needs transparent appointment criteria, firm deadlines and a mechanism for resolving disagreements. If the candidates and leadership cannot agree on every position, they should settle essential appointments first and establish a deadline for completing the remaining arrangements. In an election campaign, the cost of prolonged vacancies may exceed the benefits of pursuing ideal appointments. The more complicated issue concerns the relationship between the party and the support groups associated with its candidates. Obi’s political appeal has been sustained by the Obidient Movement and networks of volunteers, professionals, young people, diaspora supporters and community organisers. Kwankwaso also brings an established political constituency and mobilisation networks that the NDC needs to incorporate into its national strategy. These groups can provide campaign resources, grassroots contacts, volunteers and visibility beyond conventional party structures. However, the Obi-Kwankwaso movement’s creation of a separate PCC raises a fundamental question: can a support group establish a parallel campaign structure while the party is constituting its own NCC? Cleopas has insisted that the NDC welcomes support groups but expects them to operate within its approved framework. “Why wouldn’t we be here and love an OK Movement? Why wouldn’t we be here and love an obedient movement?” he asked. He added: “We are not against support groups. We know their relevance. We need them, we love them, and we see them as our helpmates.” The chairman identified the Directorate of Mobilisation under the Office of the National Organisation Secretary as the channel through which support groups should register and coordinate their activities. His position reflects a legitimate concern about accountability. Multiple bodies issuing competing directives, organising overlapping programmes or claiming authority over the same resources could undermine campaign coordination. Nevertheless, support groups also have legitimate interests in preserving their identities, networks and operational independence. Many volunteers have invested personal resources and spent years mobilising supporters before the emergence of the NDC as their preferred political platform. The solution is neither unrestricted parallel authority nor the wholesale absorption of every group into the party hierarchy. It is a negotiated division of responsibilities. At the heart of the disagreement is whether the campaign belongs primarily to the party, its candidates or the movements mobilising support for them. The party must retain authority over its official electoral machinery, compliance with electoral requirements and formal campaign coordination. The candidates must exercise substantial influence over political messaging, public engagements and strategic direction. Support groups should retain room to mobilise volunteers, organise community outreach, engage professional associations and develop innovative ways of reaching voters. These responsibilities are complementary, not mutually exclusive. A group’s ability to attract thousands of supporters does not automatically confer authority to appoint national campaign officials. Equally, the party’s formal control of its structures does not justify disregarding the experience, resources and grassroots relationships of its supporters. The NDC should establish a joint coordination mechanism involving party leaders, representatives of Obi and Kwankwaso, and recognised support groups. The body should meet regularly, document decisions and resolve disagreements before they escalate publicly. The leadership should also review the existing Obi-Kwankwaso PCC, examining its personnel, activities and objectives to determine which elements can be incorporated into the official campaign. Where appointments or responsibilities conflict with the party’s constitution, the leadership should explain the problem and propose an acceptable alternative. This would defend institutional authority without unnecessarily alienating supporters whose contributions could prove decisive. Parallel campaign structures can produce conflicting instructions to state coordinators, contradictory media statements, overlapping fundraising activities and competing demands for candidates, venues and volunteers. Disputes could become particularly damaging if separate groups claim authority over campaign appointments, polling agents or official communications. Beyond administrative inconvenience, public disagreements could undermine voter confidence, reinforce perceptions of unpreparedness and distract the candidates from communicating their policies.o However, the leadership must not assume that every disagreement represents disloyalty. In a coalition involving established politicians, newer party officials and independent movements, disagreements are inevitable. What matters is whether credible mechanisms exist to manage them. Cleopas has maintained that elected party officers cannot be removed arbitrarily and that disputes must be handled in accordance with the party’s constitution. The same commitment to rules should guide relations with support groups. Procedures must be clear, consistently applied and flexible enough to accommodate legitimate differences. A party demanding discipline from supporters must demonstrate fairness in exercising its authority. The campaign council is not the only outstanding issue. According to statements from the party leadership, the NDC has yet to establish a firm timeline for releasing its manifesto. Osa Director previously explained that the candidates and party were conducting due diligence to ensure that the campaign reflected competence, unity and the national interest. However, organisational preparation and policy communication should proceed simultaneously. A manifesto should explain the party’s priorities, how its proposals would be implemented and how voters can assess its candidates. The Obi-Kwankwaso ticket must articulate credible plans for addressing economic hardship, insecurity, education, healthcare, employment and institutional reform. It must also demonstrate how the candidates’ different political experiences and constituencies translate into a coherent governing programme. The NDC should establish a policy committee comprising professionals, researchers, sectoral specialists and representatives of relevant support groups to consolidate the candidates’ positions into a clear, cost-conscious and measurable manifesto. The document should be published within an announced timeframe, with accessible summaries for young people, traders, workers, farmers, professionals and other constituencies. The campaign cannot afford to spend its limited time debating appointments while leaving voters uncertain about what the party intends to accomplish. The NDC chairman’s emphasis on recruiting polling agents early offers another important lesson from Nigeria’s recent electoral experience. Cleopas has argued that winning votes is insufficient unless parties ensure that results are accurately recorded and transmitted through the collation process. “It is vote protection. It is vote protection legitimately, and the vote protection starts from awareness that must be created among our voters,” he said. The party has begun preparations to recruit polling agents through its state structures rather than wait until the final stages of the electoral process. This should be expanded into a comprehensive electoral-readiness programme involving trained agents, reliable communication channels, legal support, incident-reporting procedures and a central system for collating polling-unit results. Support groups could help recruit volunteers, identify training needs and educate voters about participation and lawful vote protection. However, the party must retain responsibility for official nominations, compliance with Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) requirements and coordination of electoral agents. Vote protection must mean lawful observation, accurate documentation, prompt reporting and appropriate legal action, not intimidation, obstruction or vigilantism. The objective should be a single, accountable electoral system supported by multiple mobilisation networks. The campaign council dispute also reflects the NDC’s wider challenge of managing internal disagreements. Cleopas has disclosed efforts to reconcile prominent Adamawa politicians, including former Secretary to the Government of the Federation, Babachir Lawal, and the party’s governorship candidate, Aishatu Binani. “Even as you have mentioned Babachir and Binani, the party will not allow them to disintegrate. We need one another,” he said. The proposed reconciliation recognises that a national campaign cannot succeed if its constituent political interests remain divided. The same approach should govern disputes involving support groups, state executives and campaign appointments. The leadership should establish a rapid dispute-resolution mechanism with clear timelines for complaints, mediation and decisions. Where disagreements involve the presidential candidates, the chairman and designated representatives should convene structured consultations rather than allow grievances to escalate through the media. Party officials must avoid using disciplinary procedures to silence legitimate criticism, while support-group leaders should not interpret every disagreement as evidence that their contributions are being disregarded. Both sides must distinguish genuine organisational concerns from struggles for influence. With January 16, 2027, designated as election day, the NDC cannot afford prolonged uncertainty over its campaign machinery. The October 26, 2026 unveiling should be treated as a critical operational milestone rather than a ceremonial event. First, the party should publish the names and responsibilities of campaign officials, clarify reporting lines and establish a timetable for operations across the states. Second, Obi and Kwankwaso should jointly endorse the agreed structure to reassure supporters that the ticket is united. Third, the party should register support groups under transparent criteria, distinguishing independent mobilisation from official campaign responsibilities and constitutional party functions. Fourth, representatives of the Obi-Kwankwaso movement should negotiate the future of its existing PCC, with the aim of integrating useful personnel and programmes without unnecessarily destroying its identity or grassroots capacity. Fifth, a campaign coordination committee comprising the party, candidates and recognised support groups should harmonise communications, schedules and mobilisation activities. Sixth, the manifesto should be released on a definite date, accompanied by policy engagements and public consultations. Seventh, the NDC should accelerate polling-agent recruitment, voter education, financial transparency and legal preparedness. Finally, all parties should commit to internal dispute resolution and regular progress reviews to identify bottlenecks before they threaten the campaign. The NDC’s difficulties present both a risk and an opportunity. If the leadership insists on control without consultation, it could alienate the support networks needed to expand its electoral reach. If support groups operate independently of agreed structures, they could create competing centres of authority. If the candidates delay decisions while awaiting perfect agreement, the campaign could lose valuable preparation time. Conversely, rushing appointments without adequate scrutiny could create avoidable problems. The way forward requires a balance between institutional discipline, political inclusion and administrative urgency. The leadership must recognise that consultation and transparent procedures strengthen party authority. Obi and Kwankwaso must demonstrate that their alliance extends beyond sharing a presidential ticket to a common commitment to organisational success. Support groups, in turn, must understand that enthusiasm, personal sacrifice and grassroots influence confer political value but do not automatically supersede the party’s formal responsibilities. Their greatest contribution would be to bring their organisational strengths into a coordinated campaign capable of reaching communities where conventional party structures may be weak. Ultimately, the contest is about whether the NDC can demonstrate the competence required to compete for national power. Its promises of transparency, internal discipline and early electoral preparation will carry greater weight if reflected in how it manages its affairs. The coming weeks should therefore be a period of consolidation rather than confrontation. The campaign council must be inaugurated, the manifesto published, support groups accommodated within a clear framework and electoral preparations accelerated. The election will ultimately be decided by voters, not the number of meetings held or titles assigned to campaign officials. But voters must first have compelling reasons to believe that the party is organised, prepared and capable of translating promises into action. The real test of the Obi-Kwankwaso alliance is not simply whether supporters can mobilise crowds or the NDC can announce a campaign council. It is whether both can convert political enthusiasm into a disciplined, inclusive and credible national campaign. The NDC still has an opportunity to get this right. Whether it succeeds will depend on its ability to replace uncertainty with decisions, rivalry with cooperation and parallel structures with a shared electoral purpose.

title: Phone-tapping charge: Court rejects El-Rufai’s no-case submission
body: …orders him to open his defence By Ikechukwu Nnochiri The Federal High Court in Abuja on Monday held that the detained former Kaduna State governor, Nasir El-Rufai, has a case to answer over an allegation that he unlawfully intercepted the phone communications of the National Security Adviser (NSA), Nuhu Ribadu. The court, in a ruling delivered by Justice Joyce Abdulmalik, dismissed as lacking in merit a no-case submission that the embattled former governor filed to be discharged and acquitted of the charge against him. El-Rufai, who was governor between 2015 and 2023 and also served as Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) under former President Olusegun Obasanjo’s administration, is facing trial over comments he made when he appeared as a guest on Arise Television on February 13. He is answering to a five-count amended charge that the Federal Government preferred against him through the Department of State Services (DSS). It was alleged that the defendant, during his appearance on Arise TV’s Prime Time programme in Abuja, admitted that he knew and was associated with an individual who had illegally intercepted the NSA’s telephone communications. Aside from the allegation that his action breached national security and public safety, an offence punishable under Section 12(1) of the Cybercrimes (Prohibition, Prevention, etc.) (Amendment) Act, 2024, the former governor was also charged with failing to report the crime to the relevant security agencies. The defendant had, during the TV interview, reacted to what he described as an attempt by DSS operatives to “abduct” him at Nnamdi Azikiwe International Airport in Abuja on February 12, 2026, upon his return from Cairo. He insisted that the security agency was being instigated by the ICPC, which he said had received a directive from the NSA, Ribadu, to detain him. The former governor claimed the information reached him through someone who had listened in on the NSA’s telephone conversations. Meanwhile, after the prosecution closed its case with the evidence of two witnesses who testified before the court, the defendant applied to be discharged and acquitted. El-Rufai, through his team of lawyers led by Mr. Paul Erokoro, SAN, insisted that the prosecution had failed to establish a prima facie case to warrant the court compelling him to enter a defence to the charge, which he described as incompetent. However, the prosecution counsel, Mr. Oluwole Aladedoye, SAN, urged the court to dismiss the application and order the defendant to open his defence to the charge. Aladedoye, SAN, maintained that the oral and documentary evidence laid before the court was sufficient to tie the defendant to the allegations against him. In her ruling on the matter, Justice Abdulmalik said the court was satisfied that the evidence laid by the prosecution was strong enough to warrant explanations from the defendant. Even though the court had yet to ascertain the defendant’s culpability or otherwise, it dismissed the no-case submission and ordered him to open his defence to the charge. It will be recalled that shortly after being accused of admitting that he used “technical equipment” to illegally intercept the NSA’s calls, El-Rufai filed a motion to stop his trial. He gave 17 reasons why the charge, marked FHC/ABJ/CR/99/2026, should be quashed by the court. He argued that the charge was incompetent and legally defective, insisting that the DSS had no legal basis to elevate a “casual remark” he made during a television interview into “a confession” that he had indeed tapped the NSA’s telephone line, as alleged. He argued that the statement he made on Arise TV did not constitute a confessional statement in law, saying that for a statement to be admissible as a confession, it must be made under caution, voluntarily, and in circumstances that satisfy the Judges’ Rules. El-Rufai maintained that the statements he made during his television interview were made without caution or warning, in a voluntary public discussion, and without the protections afforded to suspects in custody. “A casual remark on a television programme cannot be elevated to a judicial confession,” he further argued. However, the court declined to quash the charge and ordered an accelerated hearing of the case. El-Rufai who has been in detention since February is standing trial before courts in both Abuja and Kaduna state. Justice Abdulmalik had, on July 23, dismissed as lacking in merit an application that the former governor filed for the variation of his bail conditions, which he described as very stringent and difficult to fulfil. According to El-Rufai’s lawyer, the bail conditions sought to be varied included the requirement that the defendant produce level 17 civil servants with properties in Maitama or Asokoro, as well as verification and attestation letters from the Kaduna State traditional council. However, the prosecution opposed the variation request, insisting that qualified public officers who could meet the conditions existed and could easily be secured by the defendant. It persuaded the court to reject the application. The post Phone-tapping charge: Court rejects El-Rufai’s no-case submission appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: IN BRIEF: What is known about FSB’s thwarted attack on Moscow air defense site
body:
MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) detained two men from the South Caucasus who, acting on orders from the Ukrainian State Security Service (SBU), were preparing an attack using FPV drones against one of the key components of Moscow’s air defense system and an electric power facility, the FSB press office reported.
TASS has compiled the key information known at this time.
- The FSB thwarted the sabotage and terrorist activities of two men from the South Caucasus, born in 1991 and 1998, the press office reported.
- According to the Federal Security Service, the men were going to prepare attack drones obtained from hidden stashes, transport them to the Moscow Region for launch, and activate them before takeoff.
- It was specified that the drones were to be controlled remotely from Ukrainian territory.
- While preparing to carry out a terrorist attack on an electric power facility and one of the key components of Moscow’s air defense system, the suspects were detained by FSB officers, the press office said.
- The FSB released a video showing the FPV drones that the two detainees, natives of the South Caucasus, were using, on orders from the SBU, to prepare an attack on one of the key components of Moscow’s air defense system and an electric power facility.
- A video provided by the FSB press office shows the suspects assembling the drones and getting them ready for use according to instructions from their handler.
- The video shows two drones, both disassembled and assembled, as well as the communication devices used by the agents and instructions for assembling the drones.
- According to the FSB, one of the detainees was recruited by an SBU officer. Acting on his orders and in exchange for a promised monetary reward, the detainee traveled to Russia to plan a terrorist attack.
- To this end, he enlisted the help of a close acquaintance. Together, they retrieved FPV drones and components for homemade explosive devices from hiding places in the Smolensk and Kaluga Regions.
- The FSB had prior intelligence indicating that individuals from the South Caucasus were preparing an FPV drone attack on air defense and energy facilities in Moscow on behalf of the SBU. These individuals were agents of the Ukrainian special services, just like their handler, an FSB officer reported.
- The operation involving the handlers is ongoing, he noted.
- A criminal case has been initiated against the detainees under Article 205.4 of the Russian Criminal Code (Participation in a Terrorist Organization).
- The Federal Security Service is conducting the necessary investigative and operational measures to establish all the circumstances of the suspects’ illegal activities and their possible connections, the press office noted.

title: Uganda imposes 21-day quarantine on citizens returning from DR Congo over Ebola fears
body: Ugandans returning from neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo will be quarantined for 21 days, the health ministry has said, as the country tightens restrictions to contain the spread of the Ebola virus. More than 4,800 people have died in DR Congo since May – the country’s deadliest outbreak of the disease – and it has since spread to several other countries. Uganda’s restrictions follow questions after two people who had travelled through the country tested positive for Ebola in Kenya and Nigeria. The health ministry on Sunday said the 60 people who were being monitored after coming into contact with the Kenyan Ebola patient had all been discharged. Announcing the new measures on Sunday, the health ministry said travellers who had been to DR Congo would not be allowed to transit through Uganda. It said returning Ugandans would “undergo 21 days of quarantine at their own cost”. Uganda has also “intensified traveller screening at Entebbe International Airport and all land border crossings, supported by screening at designated road checkpoints”, it added. Uganda’s Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi told the BBC’s Newsday programme that only essential travellers from DR Congo would be allowed in but would be subjected to “intense public health measures”. “All these are measures to ensure that we keep Uganda free of Ebola,” he said. Since the two cases were reported in Kenya and Nigeria this month, Uganda has repeatedly stressed that no cases have been reported within its borders. Uganda recorded 20 Ebola cases, and two people died shortly after the outbreak started in DR Congo, but the World Health Organisation declared the country free of the disease in August. Concerns have, however, persisted after the two passengers tested positive after passing through Uganda’s Entebbe airport on the same day. The patient in Nigeria is the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat who had travelled to the Ugandan capital for a holiday, according to the head of Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, Jean Kaseya, while the Kenyan had travelled from the DR Congo, where he had business interests. Diana Atwine, the health ministry’s permanent secretary, said CCTV camera footage showed no physical interaction between the two patients. The Kenyan businessman died two days after arriving in Nairobi, and the country has since confirmed eight other cases of Ebola. A second woman, related to the businessman, died over the weekend. Ugandan officials had previously said the patient in Nigeria had travelled to eastern DR Congo, only transiting through Uganda. On Sunday, however, the health ministry said Uganda and Nigeria were both working to establish her movements, complete travel history and possible routes of exposure. The Ugandan health minister said the recent cases meant the risk had not ended and further underscored the need to “remain vigilant”. “We share a border with [DR Congo], where transmission continues, and our communities remain closely connected through trade, travel and family ties,” Baryomunsi said. The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit. The Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind this outbreak is relatively rare, and there is still no vaccine or specific treatment – though trials are under way.

title: Israeli rehabilitation village prepares adults with disabilities for Election Day voting
body: Ahead of Tuesday's election, more than 200 adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities at a Perach Israel village are learning about their right to vote and practicing how to cast their ballots.As millions of Israelis prepare to head to the polls, residents of a Perach Israel-operated rehabilitation village are getting ready for Election Day with a special initiative to help them exercise one of their most fundamental democratic rights.The village, home to more than 200 adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities, has set up a mock polling station, complete with a voting booth, envelopes, and ballot slips, allowing residents to familiarize themselves with the voting process ahead of the October 27 Knesset election.Staff members are guiding residents through the process, explaining their right to vote and helping them practice selecting a ballot and placing it in an envelope, as they would at an official polling station.Right to choose is important element of rehabilitation village"The right to choose is part of everyday life in our village," said Moshe Stein, CEO of Perach Israel."We work to teach our residents the importance of making their own choices, from deciding what color clothes to wear to choosing how to spend their free time. The ability to make their own decisions plays a significant role in their quality of life."For residents, the exercise offers a chance to learn the practical aspects of voting in a familiar environment, ahead of an election in which millions of Israelis will choose their representatives in the next Knesset.With Election Day just around the corner, the practice sessions are helping ensure that residents who are eligible to vote have the opportunity to make their voices heard alongside the rest of the country.

title: 2027: Northerners urged to re-elect Tinubu
body: A chieftain of the All Progressives Congress (APC) Anas Adamu Galadima, popularly known as Zam Zam, has urged Northerners to re-elect President Bola Ahmed Tinubu in 2027. Galadima made the call while speaking to journalists on the sidelines of the APC presidential campaign launch in Kaduna, on Saturday. He identified political reciprocity, continuity, economic reforms and improved national security as three reasons for the North to support Tinubu’s second term. He said Tinubu’s role in Buhari’s victory in 2015 and the need to consolidate economic and security gains are reasons for his re-election. Ebola: No case in Yobe, govt activates emergency response system Tongues wagging as Dankwambo’s name appears on Gombe APC campaign list He said Buhari had lost presidential bids in 2003, 2007 and 2011 before Tinubu deployed his political structures, grassroots networks and resources in support of the APC candidate in 2015. Galadima said, “President Buhari’s victory in 2015 was a defining moment in Nigeria’s democratic history. Before that election, he had contested three times without winning. The political support, structures and resources that His Excellency, President Asiwaju Bola Ahmed Tinubu brought into the contest were instrumental in building the coalition that eventually secured victory.” He maintained that reciprocity should guide political relationships, saying Tinubu and the South-West deserve two terms, just as Buhari had. He said, “Politics should not be about taking support when you need it and abandoning the principle of reciprocity when it is time to return that support. “In the spirit of fairness and mutual respect, the South-West should also be allowed to complete its two-term.” Galadima said his second reason for supporting Tinubu’s re-election was to sustain the economic reforms, arguing that fundamental economic changes require time and policy consistency to yield results. He cited foreign-exchange reforms, saying sustained implementation was necessary to achieve lasting results. While acknowledging the short-term hardship of the reforms, he warned that abandoning them prematurely could undermine efforts to build a stable and productive economy. He said, “The reforms being undertaken are significant, and their long-term benefits will depend on consistency, effective implementation and the ability to address the difficulties Nigerians face during the transition. We need to consolidate the gains, improve the implementation and ensure that the benefits reach ordinary citizens.” He said that a second Tinubu term would deepen reforms, boost investor confidence, and deliver tangible results. On security, Galadima recent changes to security leadership and structures offered an opportunity to strengthen the fight against terrorism, banditry and kidnapping. He said the North has a particular interest in supporting measures that could deliver lasting peace, protect lives and property, urging the APC to intensify engagement with citizens across the North. He said, “We cannot afford to treat national security as a short-term political issue. The recent adjustments in the security architecture must be given the necessary support, time and resources to deliver results. A second term would provide an opportunity to consolidate the efforts and pursue a more sustained response to insecurity.” On Kwara politics, Galadima urged residents to support the candidature of Hon. Salihu Yakubu Danladi (SYD), commending Governor Abdulrahman Abdulrazaq for promoting power rotation in the state for the first time since 999.

title: EFCC arrests 14 Chinese nationals, one Nigerian over four illegal lithium processing plants
body:
The Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) has arrested 15 people comprised of 14 Chinese nationals and a Nigerian, over alleged illegal lithium-processing operations at four plants in Ogere, Ogun State.
The suspects were arrested on Friday, (23 October) by operatives of the commission’s Lagos Zonal Directorate 2 following intelligence gathering and surveillance.
In a statement on Monday, the commission’s Head of Media and Publicity, Dele Oyewale, said operatives recovered bags of lithium rocks, 18 mobile phones, four laptop computers, two decoders, a television remote control and a trailer truck during the operation.
“The suspects will be charged to court upon conclusion of investigations,” the statement read.
The commission did not disclose the identities of the suspects or the quantity of lithium recovered. It also did not explain how the plants were operating illegally.
The arrests come amid growing interest in lithium, a mineral used in rechargeable batteries for electric vehicles and electronic devices. Nigeria has deposits of the mineral and has been seeking to develop its solid minerals sector as part of efforts to diversify the economy beyond crude oil.
However, the circumstances surrounding the four facilities, including the source of their raw materials and whether they possessed the required licences and regulatory approvals, remain unclear.

title: We do not just want to sell to Africa; we want to build with Africa – ADSL
body:
Indian defence company Airbornics Defence & Space Pvt Ltd (ADSL) is bringing its joint-development model, legacy-fleet modernisation capabilities and latest defence solutions to the inaugural Africa International Defence Exhibition (Afridex) 2026 in Lagos, Nigeria, emphasising its ambition to establish a permanent presence in Africa rather than pursue one-off sales.
“Our ambition extends beyond supplying products to the African market. We aim to establish a sustained presence through long-term partnerships and a strong regional network.”
This long-term vision for the African market was among the key themes discussed by Rishi Aggarwal, Managing Director of JCBL Group, and Raj Kumar Pandey, Joint Managing Director of ADSL, in a conversation with DefenceWeb ahead of Afridex 2026.
The discussion explored ADSL’s capabilities, its evolution, and its ambitions to become a trusted long-term partner to Africa’s defence and security forces.
Established with a vision to advance indigenous aerospace and defence capabilities, ADSL serves as the dedicated aerospace and defence arm of the JCBL Group, which brings over four decades of industrial experience across diverse sectors, including defence. After gradually building up its capabilities, ADSL now works across what Pandey described as four verticals: Maintenance, Repair & Overhaul (MRO) and Sustenance; Aerial Delivery Systems; Land Systems; and Combat System Technology.
The company counts the Indian Ministry of Home Affairs, Ministry of Defence, Indian Army, Indian Navy, Indian Air Force, and State Police forces among its growing customer base. ADSL’s international growth has seen sustained momentum in recent years, following a landmark MoU between the company and Slovakia which includes the joint development and production of advanced military technologies such as turrets, remote-controlled weapon stations, and active protection systems.
As ADSL increasingly turns its attention to international markets, it has identified Africa as a strategic priority, not only for future sales but also for long-term partnerships. Pandey said ADSL had spent more than a year exploring the continent’s security landscape and engaging with experts and potential partners in North and West Africa.
Accordingly, Pandey said that the continent’s terrain, shared reliance on Russian military systems, and growing appetite for localisation and force modernisation in light of contemporary and future threats not only mirror India’s own experience but also align with ADSL’s expertise, making the company a natural partner for the continent.
ADSL has built up considerable experience and intellectual property in maintaining, refurbishing and modernising Russian-origin and other legacy systems for the Indian military, including T-72 tanks, BMP infantry fighting vehicles and Shilka air defence systems. Pandey explained that the company could apply this expertise across Africa.
Pandey added that geopolitical disruptions had left many African countries struggling to obtain adequate support for their Russian-origin military systems. “They are not getting the right kind of support. So, we are there to support them, because we understand these technologies,” he said.
Modern warfare requires modern solutions
ADSL’s capabilities extend well beyond the MRO of legacy systems. In 2025, the company acquired a Slovakian company specialising in remote weapon stations, fire-control systems and stabilisation systems.
It now offers 7.62 mm, 12.7 mm and 30 mm remote weapon stations that can be fitted to both Russian and non-Russian platforms and configured to accommodate a range of anti-tank guided missiles or loitering munitions.
Indeed, the company has gone further, developing its own sophisticated anti-unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) system capable of detecting and neutralising threats through both soft-kill and hard-kill options.
Pandey said much of the company’s products sit at Technology Readiness Level 9 to 10 and have been certified and brought into service by the Indian security forces.
ADSL’s wider offering includes aerial delivery systems for C-130, C-295 and C-17 aircraft, handling loads of about eight to 20 tons, along with strategic trailers, command-and-control and container-based solutions such as field offices, firing ranges and even data centres.
ADSL’s value proposition rests on three pillars: customisation, localisation and long-term support. “We are not there just to push our products. Our idea is to understand the issues of African markets and give them the product which is apt for them,” Pandey explained.
It is an approach that has been built on decades of experience across the Indian defence industrial landscape. Pandey argued that “it is better to have a joint development along with the customer”, adding, “we started with a product-only approach, but we realised that is not the right approach.”
ADSL has actively sought to localise around 60 to 90 per cent of its products in India. Pandey told DefenceWeb, “The way we did it, we took the technologies, and we customised it for the Indian markets, the same thing, we want to do it for the African markets.”
Moreover, both Pandey and Aggarwal emphasised ADSL’s long-term commitment to its customers. “No product normally fails because of its performance; they fail because of the after-sales support,” Pandey said, explaining that ADSL is actively seeking local partners to train and equip to provide reliable, cost-effective, long-term support. This could include local maintenance and systems integration and, where financially viable, local manufacturing.
Aggarwal emphasised that providing reliable, affordable solutions to customers’ actual problems is part of the company’s DNA. “Our focus is on building a lasting presence in Africa through strong networks and long-term partnerships. We see the opportunity as much bigger than individual contracts, with our sights set on sustained collaboration and a long-term commitment to the region.”
For more information, visit https://adslglobal.com/

title: We have no additional funds to support GBA elections – Sports Ministry
body: The Ministry of Sports and Recreation say there’s no funds to support the Ghana Boxing Interim Management Committee (GBIMC) to organise elections on October 31, 2026. The Committee had scheduled October 31 as the deadline for the Ghana Boxing Authority to return to elected leadership, but now face fresh uncertainty as a funding dispute between theSports and Recreation Minister Kofi Adams. The Samir Captan-led committee says it is awaiting government funding to complete the electoral process, but the minister has ruled out additional financial support, insisting that the exercise can be financed through nomination fees and contributions from candidates. The impasse comes amid a separate High Court challenge to the committee’s continued stay in office following the expiration of its original mandate. In a statement dated October 20, Mr Captan said the committee was still awaiting promised government funding to complete its outstanding assignments and organise elections, tentatively scheduled for October 30. However, Adams had earlier insisted that the elections must be held by October 31, making it clear that the government would not provide additional funds. “We have told the Director-General of the NSA we have no additional funds,” Mr Adams is quoted by Graphic Sports to have said, arguing that proceeds from nomination forms and filing fees should be sufficient to finance the exercise. The minister added that candidates could make additional contributions if necessary. Funding assurances at the centre of dispute The GBIMC maintains that its expectation of government support followed assurances communicated through the National Sports Authority (NSA). According to the committee, the NSA requested an update on September 3 regarding operational funding and progress towards the elections. The GBIMC subsequently proposed October 30 as the election date, subject to the availability of funds. On September 29, the NSA reportedly informed the committee that the Sports and Recreation Ministry would provide the necessary financial support. Relying on that communication, the committee submitted a formal funding request on October 8 to complete its outstanding assignments, finalise electoral arrangements, and facilitate a smooth handover to an elected GBA executive board. With the funds yet to materialise, the committee says it has written to the minister and the acting NSA Director-General seeking further engagement. Despite the uncertainty, the GBIMC says preparations are progressing, with candidate vetting completed, stakeholder validation ongoing, and petitions concerning delegate eligibility and representation still under consideration. Questions over election revenue The committee’s insistence on government funding has raised questions about the revenue generated through nomination and filing fees. Presidential aspirants were charged GHC10,000 each, while vice-presidential candidates paid GHC 5,000. Candidates for treasurer and executive board positions were charged GHC 3,000 each, with an additional GHC 500 for nomination forms. Although these fees do not establish the total amount collected, they raise questions about the overall cost of the election, the revenue already available to the committee, and the precise funding shortfall. The GBIMC has yet to establish publicly, in the information provided, how much it has collected and how much additional funding is required to complete the process. High Court challenge adds to pressure The funding dispute is unfolding against the backdrop of a legal challenge to the committee’s continued authority. On October 12, ten boxing stakeholders filed a suit at the Accra High Court challenging the GBIMC’s continued stay in office, arguing that its mandate had expired. The plaintiffs are seeking judicial intervention to end the interim administration and establish a process for restoring elected leadership to the Ghana Boxing Authority (GBA). The committee was inaugurated in September 2025 following the dissolution of the previous GBA board and the suspension of professional boxing after two ring-related deaths. Since taking office, it has overseen safety reforms and the resumption of professional boxing. However, repeated delays in holding elections and its prolonged tenure have intensified concerns over the sport’s governance. With the October 31 deadline approaching, the minister ruling out further funding and a court challenge hanging over its authority, the GBIMC faces mounting pressure to resolve the impasse. For Ghana boxing, the immediate question is whether the committee can complete the electoral process on time and pave the way for a return to elected leadership.

title: US forces support transit of 3,000 ships through Strait of Hormuz — CENTCOM
body:
