WASHINGTON, October 26. /TASS/. More than 3,000 commercial vessels have successfully passed through the Strait of Hormuz with support from US Central Command (CENTCOM) forces over the past six months, CENTCOM reported.
According to the command, US forces reached the milestone of assisting Gulf partners in exporting more than 1.5 billion barrels of crude oil through the Strait of Hormuz since summer. In recent months, CENTCOM noted, over 95% of ships navigating the Strait of Hormuz have sailed through safely.
The United States and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28. In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding providing for an immediate cessation of hostilities on all fronts, including in Lebanon. However, in the early morning hours of July 8, the US resumed large-scale strikes against Iran, accusing it of violating the terms of the agreements reached on the Strait of Hormuz. Approximately 25% of global oil trade and about 20% of liquefied natural gas trade pass through the strait. Later, the US administration effectively indicated that it was halting large-scale military action against Iran and pursuing economic strangulation through stricter sanctions.

title: Kallas at E5 defense ministers' meeting
body:
High Representative of the European Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas will participate in a meeting of defense ministers of the E5 group – a group of European countries with the largest defense budgets, including Germany, Poland, France, Italy, and the United Kingdom.

A corresponding announcement was distributed by the European External Action Service in Brussels on Monday. The meeting will take place in Paris. Kallas is expected to hold a press conference following the conclusion of the event.

The E5 group, also known as European Five (E5), was launched in November 2024 in response to growing calls for European rearmament and the strengthening of its leadership role in providing support to Ukraine.

title: Pentagon Prepares U S Military Bases to Operate Independently for 90 Days Report
body:
The U.S. Department of Defense is preparing major military installations across the continental United States to operate independently for at least 90 days during a major war, according to Fox News .
The FORTRESS initiative aims to reduce reliance on civilian infrastructure by ensuring independent access to electricity, water, fuel and communications. Proposed energy measures include portable small nuclear reactors, large-scale energy storage systems and local power grids to keep bases operational if civilian power networks are disrupted.
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said the United States could no longer rely solely on the protection of the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. “We do not want to rely on standard civilian municipal infrastructure to support our national defense. That is an unacceptable risk,” he said.
The plan also calls for strategic reserves of ammunition, fuel, critical minerals, electronics, spare parts and medical supplies. The Pentagon aims to establish at least two independent supply or production channels for critical defense components, reducing dependence on individual factories or suppliers.
Under the Civil Reserve Manufacturing Network, the Pentagon plans to identify civilian companies capable of switching rapidly to defense production during wartime. Preparations would include technical requirements, contracts, production-conversion procedures, cybersecurity measures and regular exercises to test industrial capacity and mobilization readiness.
The initiative is designed to help U.S. forces sustain operations during a major conflict, even if civilian infrastructure, transportation networks or commercial supply chains are disrupted.

title: French political turmoil may affect olim with restrictions on transferring money out of country
body: Israel's Aliyah and Integration Ministry is preparing for the possibility that political and economic turmoil in France could lead to restrictions on transferring money out of the country, potentially complicating plans by French Jews to immigrate to Israel, ministry director-general Dganit Sankar-Langa told Walla on Monday.The concern centers on the possibility that, following elections in France, the government could impose restrictions on capital transfers that would make it more difficult for Jews seeking to move their lives to Israel to bring their savings with them."We are preparing for the possibility that, following the elections, a government decision will be made that will make it more difficult to transfer money out of France," she said.According to Sankar-Langa, France's economic crisis is a significant factor behind growing interest in aliyah, no less than antisemitism."France's debt-to-GDP ratio is among the highest in OECD countries, and we are seeing the economic protests. That is why we are also examining this aspect and preparing to assist immigrants with tax advice, pension advice, and financial guidance."Sharp increase in immigration from FranceThe ministry stressed that the concern relates to a possible scenario, not a decision that has already been made in France.The remarks come amid a sharp increase in immigration from France. According to Aliyah and Integration Ministry figures, approximately 3,400 Jews immigrated to Israel from France in 2025, while more than 4,000 have already arrived since the beginning of 2026, an increase of nearly 50% compared with the corresponding period last year.By comparison, North America, home to nearly eight million Jews, is expected to send only about 4,000 immigrants to Israel this year, according to the most optimistic forecasts. France has a Jewish population of approximately 440,000.This month, the Aliyah and Integration Ministry, the Jewish Agency for Israel, and Ofek Israeli held three aliyah fairs in Paris, Marseille, and Lyon.More than 600 households, representing approximately 2,000 people, attended the Paris Fair. According to ministry figures, about 90% of those expressing interest at the fair said they wanted to immigrate to Israel immediately or during 2027.Sankar-Langa, who has worked at the ministry for approximately 12 years and also served as director-general during the Russia-Ukraine war, said she had never encountered such determination among prospective immigrants."We held large fairs a year and two years ago as well, but this time people are arriving with clear decisions. They say they are immigrating in the summer of 2027, approach the Education Ministry booth, and ask where their children will study. This is a level of certainty I have never experienced before. These are not questions of 'maybe' or 'let's see,' but questions about the here and now. There is a real sense of urgency."Roni, a 75-year-old French-Israeli who has lived in Paris since 1975 and spent his career in senior management positions working with numerous public-sector clients, is well acquainted with the change.For decades, he saw no contradiction between his Israeli identity and his life in France. Now, he says, everything has changed."We used to be proud to say we were Israelis, that we had served in the IDF. People were impressed. Now it has become something negative," he told Walla.Antisemitism affecting day-to-day life of French Jews"In the past, we wouldn't even think twice before speaking Hebrew in the street or telling people in a business setting where our roots were. Now it's better to keep quiet. Now we're careful. My wife no longer speaks Hebrew as freely in a taxi as she once did. When we're asked at the airport where we've arrived from, we're no longer quick to say Israel. There are restaurants where we prefer that people not know we're Israeli or Jewish. There are restaurants we simply don't go to anymore."The change is evident even at the entrance to their home."We have a mezuzah, but we moved it from the outside doorpost to the inside several years ago."According to Roni, many Jews now avoid wearing a kippah in public, even on their way to synagogue and even on Yom Kippur."The atmosphere is very worrying. People tell you, you're Jewish, so you must be a Zionist, so you defend the killing of Palestinians. We used to speak enthusiastically about Israel, about its technology and the IDF. Now people look at you differently. You can speak, but they don't want to listen or understand."He said concern about the future is especially pronounced among younger French Jews in their 30s and 40s, many of whom have children."Their parents, who came to France from Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia and managed to build good lives here, weren't necessarily thinking about leaving. But their children have started asking themselves where their future lies. This phenomenon began several years ago, long before the war, but now the questions have become much harder."Even Jews with successful careers in France's high-tech industry are reconsidering their futures, he said."They ask what will happen in one, two, or three years, and whether their future is still in France."Roni is also troubled by the country's political polarization and the growing strength of Marine Le Pen's nationalist right and the radical left led by Jean-Luc Mélenchon, a fierce critic of Israel."Jews are caught between a rock and a hard place, between the far Right and the far Left. Even well-established Jews, business owners, and people who have already built entire lives here are beginning to ask themselves where their future and their children's future lie."Roni and his wife have already purchased an apartment in Herzliya and visit Israel three or four times a year, sometimes staying for a month or longer.On this occasion, he came specifically to vote in Tuesday's elections."I'm trying to convince my wife to move permanently. She's still worried about the security situation in Israel. I actually feel safe here. Even with all the chaos in the country, I prefer to be here."He can also see the change in Herzliya."Every time I come, I hear more and more French, in shops, in cafés, and even on the padel courts. Sometimes I feel as though I'm still in France."His dream is to reverse the living arrangement he has become accustomed to over the past five decades: to live in Israel and visit France, rather than live in Paris and visit Israel.Immigrants from France arrive in Israel with high hopes. Many are deeply committed to Zionism, speak Hebrew, and are religious or at least traditional.Even those who do not wear a kippah regularly tend to send their children to state religious schools.Many operated small businesses in France and intend to open similar businesses in Israel. They arrive with relative financial independence, a willingness to integrate into Israeli society, and an interest in volunteering for community activities.Another prominent characteristic is their preference for living in close-knit communities near other families who have immigrated from France.While French immigrants previously concentrated primarily in Netanya, Tel Aviv, and Ashdod, new communities have emerged in recent years in Nahariya, Afula, Hadera, and Haifa's Neve Sha'anan neighborhood.In Or Akiva, for example, approximately 200 immigrants from France have settled in recent years.These communities provide immigrants with supportive social networks, help them cope with the challenges of integration, and allow them to preserve the language and culture they brought with them.Yet moving is not straightforward, even for those who have already decided to immigrate.Israel's cost of living, housing prices, and the need to find employment are significant obstacles.According to Sankar-Langa, many French Jews live in high-quality subsidized housing, sometimes in spacious apartments in desirable areas, and moving to Israel means making financial sacrifices.Leading company reps. join Paris FairTo address one of the main obstacles, representatives of leading Israeli companies and organizations joined the Paris Fair for the first time this year.They included Israel Aerospace Industries, Elbit Systems, Mekorot, Bank Mizrahi-Tefahot, and the National Artificial Intelligence Headquarters.The goal was to begin recruiting employees even before they immigrated to Israel.During the fair, company representatives met with approximately 200 prospective immigrants, more than 50 of whom were found to be potentially suitable for available positions."People didn't come just to find out what the options were and what the salaries were. They came to look for work," Sankar-Langa said."By the very next day, advanced interviews were being held with candidates who had been found suitable."At the same time, approximately 200 families received guidance and information from ministry and Jewish Agency representatives, led by delegation head Erez Cohen.Defense Ministry representatives who joined the delegation also met with parents of lone soldiers serving in Israel.Following the developments, the prime minister instructed officials to formulate a dedicated government plan to encourage immigration from France and integrate the new arrivals.Ministry officials are careful not to describe the preparations as an "emergency plan," a term that evokes previous events, particularly the wave of immigration following the outbreak of the Russia-Ukraine war."Back then, people landed here carrying bags, sometimes without medication," Sankar-Langa recalled.This time, she said, the goal is to prepare in advance for large-scale immigration, remove economic and bureaucratic obstacles, and ensure that immigrants not only reach Israel but also integrate successfully and remain in the country."Immigration from France is at its highest level in years, and we are preparing to absorb thousands more,” Aliyah and Integration Minister Ofir Sofer said. “This year, for the first time, we brought the major companies in the Israeli economy to France, based on the understanding that quality employment is one of the central keys to successful immigration and optimal integration."Sankar-Langa also sees immigration as an opportunity for the Israeli economy, which faces shortages of engineers, doctors, teachers, and artificial intelligence professionals."We increasingly understand that the Aliyah and Integration Ministry is, in effect, the human resources department of the State of Israel," she said.

title: Lula wins historic fourth term as Brazilian president
body: Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has secured a historic fourth term in office after defeating his far-right challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro, in a dramatic election comeback. With 100 per cent of the votes counted, Lula, 80, secured 51.79 per cent of the vote, defeating his 45-year-old rival, who polled 48.21 per cent. The final results showed that Lula received 4.4 million more votes than Bolsonaro, confirming his victory in the presidential election. However, shortly after Brazil’s electoral authority confirmed the outcome, Bolsonaro refused to concede defeat and called for the results to be annulled. Ebola: No case in Yobe, govt activates emergency response system NIGERIA DAILY: APC’s Road To 2027 — Can Tinubu Turn Economic Reforms Into Relief For Nigerians? Lula’s victory marked a remarkable political turnaround after he narrowly lost the first round of voting to Bolsonaro in early October, raising questions about his political future and leaving his supporters among Brazil’s progressive movement facing three weeks of uncertainty. Since Brazil returned to democracy in the 1980s, no candidate who finished second in the first round of a presidential election had gone on to win the second round. Lula broke that pattern on Sunday, triggering celebrations in the streets of São Paulo, where he had been following the election developments, and at the hotel where he watched the vote count. Addressing a packed conference hall filled with jubilant supporters in São Paulo, the president-elect said his victory would usher in a change in the country’s governance. “We are going to change the way that this country is governed,” Lula said. Describing the outcome as a rejection of denialism, he added: “This election was a defeat for denialism.” Lula also expressed gratitude to God and the Brazilian electorate for supporting his return to office. “I want to thank God and to thank you, Brazilian men and women of this country … it was democracy that made this happen,” he said. The victory also drew praise from Lula’s health minister, Alexandre Padilha, who described the result as a significant triumph for the Brazilian people. Padilha said the election had given voters an opportunity to consider the implications of Lula’s leadership for the environment, the country’s national health service, its education system and the constitution. “This is a huge victory for the Brazilian people who in the second round had the chance to think about what President Lula means for the environment, for the defense of our national health service and our education system and the Brazilian constitution. And the risks that the extreme right candidate entailed,” he said. Padilha further described the outcome as significant beyond Brazil, saying it carried an important message for other countries in the region and the international community. “It’s a massive victory – not just for Brazil. It’s also an important signal to the rest of Latin America and to the world,” he added.

title: Incomar invests in the next generation of flight test engineers
body:
South Africa’s defence and aerospace industry continues to lose specialist engineering skills to opportunities abroad, with local companies reporting that top engineering graduates often leave the country a few years into their careers for markets such as the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Canada, the United States and the United Kingdom. Flight test engineering, a small and highly specialised discipline, and flight test engineers (FTEs) trained in South Africa are highly sought-after by overseas companies.
Centurion-based Incomar is addressing that gap directly through its Graduate Flight Test Engineer programme, which trains candidates across the full flight test lifecycle: preparation, execution and reporting. Graduates learn to define test objectives, build flight test plans and identify applicable requirements; support and conduct testing covering aircraft performance, flying qualities and systems; and then analyse results, document findings and help determine whether a system meets its technical and operational requirements — all under Incomar’s Flight Test Process, Quality Management System and Safety Management System.
The role sits at the interface between engineering and operational reality. While design and systems engineers build a solution, the FTE determines whether it actually delivers the required operational capability, working daily alongside systems engineers, design engineers, pilots, operations personnel and clients, and gaining early exposure to configuration control, safety review boards and project reporting. Incomar is currently running its fourth course, which takes the number of graduates up to 10, eight of them under the facilitation of Flight Test Engineer Peter Chaplin.
Crucially, the training is backed by real infrastructure rather than classroom theory, the company said. Graduates work across manned and unmanned systems using a fleet that includes a Learjet 35A and Cessna Grand Caravan as systems test beds, an Aermacchi AM-3C for weapons testing, and a Van’s RV-7A for practical training on Incomar’s in-house professional flight test course, alongside unmanned aerial system (UAS) testing work spanning both aircraft and supporting subsystems. Graduates often go on to help deliver that same in-house course to the next intake, lecturing, compiling material and assessing submissions.
This sits within a broader pattern of investment at Incomar, which was established in 2000, now employs close to 600 people, and operates from two hangars at Wonderboom National Airport, three offices in Gauteng, Jaffie Aviation Training in Robertson and the Incomar Aeronautical Academy. The company has continued to grow its fleet alongside its flight test workload and is a member of AMD, the Aerospace, Maritime and Defence Industries Association of South Africa.
“Every graduate who comes through this programme without having to leave South Africa to get that experience is a win for the entire industry, not just Incomar,” said Incomar Flight X CEO, Lance Wellington. “Flight test is one of the scarcest skills in aerospace and defence anywhere in the world, and if we don’t grow it locally, we will keep losing it to countries that are willing to invest in their engineers.”
South Africa’s Aerospace and Defence Masterplan identifies skills availability as central to unlocking the sector’s growth. By pairing structured mentorship and continuing professional development with hands-on access to live manned and unmanned flight test programmes, Incomar’s Graduate FTE programme offers a homegrown route to that experience, the company said — helping keep flight test capability, and the skills base behind it, rooted in South Africa.

title: Call for Articles: Naval Applications and Dangers of Artificial Intelligence
body:
Articles Due: January 18, 2027 Series Dates: February 15-19, 2027 Article Length: 1,5000-3,000 Words Submit to: Content@cimsec.org
The rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the maritime domain and naval warfighting. From automated target recognition systems enabling autonomous swarm attacks in the Black Sea and the Red Sea, to predictive maintenance models keeping aging surface combatants mission-ready, artificial intelligence is expanding across naval operations.
Yet, as AI transitions into a core instrument of naval power, it introduces structural vulnerabilities and escalation risks that military leaders and policymakers are only beginning to grapple with.
These vulnerabilities have drawn sharp attention on Capitol Hill. In debates over recent defense legislation, U.S. congressional leaders and defense committees expressed rising alarm regarding the unvetted deployment of military AI. Lawmakers warn that rushing unverified algorithms onto the digital high seas could result in unintended escalation, catastrophic system failures, or friendly-fire events. These risks have led Congress to demand strict AI assessment frameworks, mandatory cyber-governance rules, and sandboxed testing environments before systems are fielded.
Whether considering opportunities or risks, the operational integration of AI offers profound implications for naval operations and doctrine. Given the many promises and dangers of AI to naval warfare, how should leaders respond?
How should the Navy balance the operational demand for rapid fielding of AI with the rigorous testing and sandboxed environments necessary for safe deployment as mandated by Congress? How should adversary AI deployments and escalations affect our own escalation calculus and rules of engagement? How do we reform the training of our warfighters to prevent a dangerous gap between rapid AI adoption and actual warfighter understanding, ensuring operators at the tactical edge have the readiness to effectively trust, override, or troubleshoot autonomous actions in combat circumstances?
Authors are invited to consider these topics and more as they explore the benefits and dangers of naval AI. Authors can cover matters of technology, strategy, ethics, policy, or any other related area. Authors should strive to go beyond solely identifying risks and propose thought-provoking, concrete solutions to the issues they raise.
Send all submissions to Content@cimsec.org .

title: ‘They buy because it’s easy’: Legal shops want more than enforcement to fight illegal pot
body:
Though the Ford government says it’s planning to introduce new measures to crack down on illicit cannabis sales, legal retailers are questioning why it took eight years following legalization for enforcement tools to be bolstered.
Several legal sellers told Global News they want Ontario to take the new rules a step further, by allowing the legal market to innovate and modernize cannabis sales by lifting some restrictions on how and where pot can be sold.
Increasing the appeal and ease of the legal product is what the industry truly needs to combat illegal enterprises, said Mike Dunn, the owner and founder of 1922 Cannabis in Toronto, a licensed cannabis dispensary.
“People don’t buy illegally because they want to break the law. They buy because it’s easy,” said Dunn.
On Monday, the Ministry of the Attorney General announced the Ford government will introduce new legislation to “strengthen enforcement” against illegal cannabis sales by providing “new tools” to the Alcohol and Gaming Commission of Ontario to tackle unauthorized sellers.
The legislative changes would include “the authority to conduct inspections, seize illegal cannabis products and equipment and issue administrative monetary penalties,” said the attorney general in a news release this week.
The illegal market for cannabis sales in Ontario has been prolific. When cannabis was legalized in October, 2018, the legal market was only responsible for 5.4 per cent of purchases, according to the Canadian Press. Legal sales only overtook illegal sales for the first time at the end of 2021.
Now, illegal cannabis retailers make up about 30 per cent of cannabis sales in Ontario, according to the ministry.
Omar Khan, with High Tide, the parent company of retail chain Canna Cabana, said the new legislation will allow the Alcohol and Gaming Commission to seize products and issue fines without the burden of proof needed for criminal prosecutions.
Anytime a new illegal seller emerges near any store, legal enterprises are threatened, he said. There are about 1,800 legal retailers across the province, according to the Ministry of the Attorney General.
“We’re encouraged by this move,” he said. “Every indication that I’ve heard says that the government is taking this seriously.”
But the province has faced criticism for its approach to shutting down illegal pot shops over the last few years.
In early 2025, Carleton Grant, Toronto’s executive director of municipal licensing and standards, said the city hadn’t been given adequate municipal funding to enforce rules against illegal stores.
Ford should have shored up enforcement on illegal retailers soon after cannabis was legalized, according to some legal sellers. Now, they say, the government has an opportunity to make legal sales more appealing and further discourage illegal sales.
Some illegal vendors offer late night delivery options, with cannabis products just a text away on a customer’s phone. Cannabis can be delivered legally in Ontario but hours are restricted from 9 a.m. to 11 p.m. Dunn’s retailer, 1922 Cannabis, does offer delivery using bike couriers to try to tap into the ease customers are looking for.
“Enforcement can close doors. It can’t make the legal option easier,” said Dunn.
Khan said the new tools will only work if the Alcohol and Gaming Commission is provided with enough resources. He also agrees with Dunn that Ontario’s retail framework for cannabis needs modernization.
“Whetheter that’s looking at the potential for consumption spaces, consumption lounges for cannabis drinks or cannabis edibles,” he said. Ontario could follow Alberta, which allows temporary cannabis store licences for adults-only music festivals, he said.
“A lot of provinces are letting cannabis stores sell munchies and snacks and a few other things to increase revenue lines. We hope and encourage the Ontario government to take a look,” he said.
Ontario NDP Leader Marit Stiles said she wants to see what the Ford government firmly proposes before determining if the legislation will be effective.
“They talk a lot before they come back to the legislature, but we need to see the details of what they’re proposing,” she said.
The planned new legislation has not been released yet. The legislature is not sitting, as it was put on a 21-week long summer break that began in June. MPPs are scheduled to return on Oct. 27.

title: MTN Ghana rewards over 30,000 customers as nine others win Toyota Land Cruiser Prados
body: MTN Ghana has rewarded more than 30,000 customers with cash prizes, while nine subscribers have won brand-new Toyota Land Cruiser Prados as part of activities marking the company’s 30th anniversary. The rewards form part of MTN’s Mega Promo, introduced to appreciate customers for their loyalty and continued support over the past years. At a presentation ceremony in Accra, Senior Manager for Consumer Marketing at MTN Ghana, Sandra Adu Antwi, said the promotion was designed to give back to customers as part of the company’s anniversary celebrations. She explained that customers accumulated points through their regular use of MTN services, including voice calls, internet browsing, social media, mobile money transfers and payments. “This is our birthday, but we said that let’s give back to our customers, let’s give something to them,” she said. She added that the promotion was deliberately made simple to allow customers to participate through their everyday activities without undertaking any extra tasks. Under the promotion, customers with the highest accumulated points were selected for the monthly car prizes, while others received cash rewards. One of the Prado winners, Benedicta Obeng Asare from Sowutuom in Accra, described her win as a dream come true. She said she was in a car when she received a call from MTN informing her that she had won the Toyota Land Cruiser Prado. “I wasn’t expecting it. I was super, super glad. It’s a dream come true that I’ve gotten this Toyota Land Cruiser,” she said. She encouraged other MTN subscribers to participate in MTN promotions, assuring them that the rewards were genuine. The anniversary promotion forms part of MTN Ghana’s customer appreciation efforts as the telecommunications company celebrates 30 years of operations in the country.

title: Voters head to the polls across Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area
body:
Toronto voters have re-elected Olivia Chow as mayor of Canada’s largest city.
Unofficial results Monday night placed Chow ahead of her main challenger, Brad Bradford, and 50 other mayoral candidates in the Oct. 26 municipal election. She had 54 per cent of the vote as of 11 p.m., compared to Bradford’s 41 per cent. Chow will now serve her first full term as mayor after winning the 2023 mayoral byelection.
Unofficial results included vote totals from advance voting, voting by mail and election day. The official election results are anticipated to be certified by the City Clerk later in the week.
“Every person who calls Toronto home, whatever your background, whatever you believe, whoever you love, wherever you live. I will listen to you,” Chow told the crowd at her election night headquarters.
“I will listen to you. I will stand up for you, and I will work every day to earn your trust because that’s what being mayor means to me – it means serving everyone.”
Chow ran on a platform to protect city services, expand transit-signal priority for TTC vehicles and increase funding for youth-violence-prevention programs.
Her key promises included measures to lower grocery prices, provide free school lunches and build more affordable homes.
During her first term as mayor, Chow supported property tax increases of 9.5 per cent in 2024, 6.9 per cent in 2025 and 2.2 per cent in 2026. She also implemented a TTC fare freeze and secured a deal with the Ontario government that will see Queen’s Park take ownership of the Gardiner Expressway and Don Valley Parkway.
Chow, 69, has spent decades in politics and is a prominent figure on the political left. She first moved to Canada from Hong Kong at 13, living with her family in an apartment in St. James Town.
She was introduced to politics after working for NDP MP Dan Heap, whom she credits as her mentor. She was elected as a TDSB trustee in 1985, a position she held for six years.
Chow was elected to Toronto council in 1991, where she served alongside her late husband, Jack Layton, who later became federal NDP leader. In 2006, she was elected to the House of Commons as an NDP MP for Trinity-Spadina.
In 2014, Chow ran against former mayor John Tory and now-Premier Doug Ford in the Toronto election but came in third place.
She unsuccessfully sought a return to Parliament in 2015 and stayed out of politics until the mayoral byelection.
Chow is Toronto’s fifth mayor since amalgamation on Jan. 1, 1998.
“I have never forgotten what Toronto gave my family and I have spent my life trying to give back. Because Toronto is a city that believes in people. A progressive city, a city of compassion, a city that welcome newcomers,” she said.
“A city that stands up for working people, celebrates our differences and believes everyone deserves a fair chance – not because we always agree, we don’t, but because deep down we understand something important. We are stronger when we care for each other, and that is the Toronto I believe in. That is the Toronto we voted to keep building tonight.”
Bradford, a 40-year-old, two-time Beaches East-York councillor, ran in the 2023 mayoral byelection and finished eighth. During Chow’s term, he became one of her most vocal critics.
Both frontrunners hit the pavement daily in the final week to reach undecided voters. Chow and Bradford were quick to trade barbs throughout the campaign, with Chow last week accusing her opponent of neglecting residents in his own ward during his time as a city councillor. Bradford has claimed Chow has failed to address the city’s traffic and transit woes.
He ran on a platform that prioritized tackling crime, congestion, cost of living, cleanliness and economic competitiveness.
Bradford told the crowd at his election night party he wishes Chow success.
“When the mayor succeeds, whether that’s mayor Bradford or mayor Chow or anybody else, Toronto succeeds,” he said.
Bradford added his campaign was one of “hope and energy.”
“This was a positive campaign, not a negative campaign because you folks are positive people and that’s what Toronto deserves,” he said.
“I implore all of us, everybody in a leadership position here in Toronto, to make sure that we spend the days, weeks and months ahead bringing this city back together, healing this city, making sure that this is a city for everybody, a city that’s safe for everybody, and a city where nobody is left behind.”
Chow said Bradford brought “new energy” and ideas to the race and thanked him for his candidacy.
She added she will begin working on to deliver her promises as soon as possible.
“Tomorrow we get back to work because an election victory isn’t the finish line: it is a responsibility,” Chow said.
“We’ve come a long way together and we have so much more to do, so let’s keep moving forward together with each other for every neighborhood, every community, every person. Let’s get to work building the Toronto we love.”

title: How the war in Iran could impact your home heating oil bill this winter
body:
The Iran war isn’t just making it costlier to fill up the tank of your car at the pump, it may also be making the cost of heating your home go up this fall.
Heating oil is similar in composition to diesel fuel, the price of which has hit records above US$6.50 per gallon following disruptions in the Middle East caused by the Iran war. The Trump administration also blames high prices on Ukrainian attacks on refineries in Russia.
Canada, too, has been hit with higher heating oil prices.
Since the start of the war, heating oil prices have jumped 42 per cent in most of the country. Average retail price for furnace oil in Canada was just under $2.50 per litre on Tuesday, according to Natural Resources Canada, a sharp jump from the $1.76 just before the Iran war began and almost a full dollar higher than the $1.56 per litre seen in January.
There is “no question” that the higher prices are “linked to the war,” said Behrouz Bakhtiari, a supply chain expert and professor at McMaster University’s DeGroot School of Business.
“There are other aspects also. There may be some panic in the market. There may lower inventories, but really the link is directly tied to the Strait of Hormuz,” he said.
Adding to the pressure is the fact that many refineries close down temporarily for the fall, Bakhtiari said.
While in most years it is a routine shutdown, this year it could add pressure to prices.
“This year, because there was already shortage in the market, those maintenance schedules would add to the pain,” he said.
The Trump administration is offering to loan up to nearly a third of the one-million-barrel U.S. emergency heating oil reserve, the Department of Energy said on Wednesday, in a bid to tame surging prices.
U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the administration was “committed to doing everything in our power to lower energy costs.” The department said there would be a competitive bidding process for the loans for both fuel retailers and terminal holders to allow the fuel to flow into areas facing shortages.
The U.S. has only tapped the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve once since Hurricane Sandy struck the region in 2012. The emergency stockpile is held at sites in New Jersey, Connecticut, Massachusetts and Maine.
About one-third ​of New England homes use heating oil, including about half of homes in Maine.
In Canada, the pain is likely to be concentrated in Atlantic Canada, Bakhtiari said. As of 2022, 305,900 homes in Atlantic Canada used oil to heat their homes, according to Environment and Climate Change Canada.
Earlier this month, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced that the federal government will launch a new heat pump rebate program early next year as part of ongoing work over recent years to get consumers onto alternative heating options, but program details haven’t been finalized.
Ottawa is in the process of winding down an existing program to subsidize purchases of heat pumps for homes heated with oil.
Last month, Finance Minister Francois-Phillipe Champagne said the current pause on the federal excise tax on fuel would be extended until February.
For Atlantic Canada with its long winters, this would mean that heating oil costs could rise further in March.
A single cold snap could mean an additional $600-$700 per household for that period, Bakhtiari estimates.
Higher heating oil prices, along with the end of the fuel tax holiday, would mean “$3,000 to $4,000 dollars added to the cost of the energy bill,” he said.
In his announcement, Carney announced $2 billion in spending to retrofit one million homes across Canada with heat pumps, which he said would mean $1,400 in annual savings on energy bills for households heating with oil, propane and electric resistance.
–with files from Reuters and Canadian Press

title: [Rappler’s Best] Yes, Marcos still shuffling his Cabinet
body: Vince Dizon , pulled out from the transportation department a little more than a year ago to head the scandal-ridden Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), is back in his old gig as transportation czar, Malacañang announced on Monday, October 26. He swaps posts with the man who replaced him as transport secretary, Giovanni Lopez , now the new DPWH secretary. Until his latest transfer, Dizon’s appointment as DPWH secretary had yet to be confirmed by the Commission on Appointments, and this showed in an awkward exchange between him and estranged presidential sister Senator Imee Marcos last month. Dizon’s transfer also came on the heels of a spat with Senator Panfilo Lacson over the latter’s allegations that he seemed to be covering up for Senator Alan Peter Cayetano, who is being accused by Lacson of having anomalous flood control projects in Taguig. Dizon and Cayetano are longtime allies, having both served under the previous Duterte administration after playing key roles in the strongman’s successful 2016 presidential run. Indeed, ghosts from the past continue to haunt. On Saturday, October 24, we were disrupted by the news that a team of Quezon City cops, showing uncanny efficiency, arrested a 72-year-old veteran journalist while he was attending a media forum, over a warrant issued by a judge from Davao City, and in relation to an unknown case filed by an unknown complainant. Philip Lustre Jr. is known to journalists of my generation as a savvy and prolific political reporter who did the rounds and made waves in his heyday, poking fun at power and unmasking its unholy alliances. For all his acerbic posts on social media especially against the Dutertes, he did not see this coming — a warrant bare in substance and brazen in form. It broke the norm that journalists and newsrooms are used to: when they are charged with libel or cyber libel, they get notified of the complaint and have the right of reply. Lustre said he was clueless about who filed a cyber libel complaint against him, and what about. That it reached the court meant it already passed the desk of a prosecutor who should have informed him about it. The arrest warrant, dated October 2, came from Davao City Judge Retrina Fuentes, and this gives room for a reasonable assumption that this had something to do with the Dutertes. Fuentes is the same judge who issued a warrant in 2022 against public intellectual and former vice presidential candidate Walden Bello, who was also arrested in Quezon City over two counts of cyber libel filed by a longtime aide of Vice President Sara Duterte, Jefry Tupas. Unlike Lustre, Bello knew that a prosecutor had indicted him and that an arrest would follow. He spent the night at a police headquarters and was released the following day after posting bail . Lustre’s arrest came in the same week that Davao City 1st District Representative Paolo Duterte, a brother of the Vice President, filed a cyber libel complaint against executives and staff of media giant, GMA Network, over stories linking him and his sister to bribery. Included in the complaint were National Bureau of Investigation Director Melvin Matibag and whistleblower Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. Read about Gracioso’s claims here . Philippine journalists and media organizations have been pushing for the decriminalization of libel and, shortly after the cybercrime law was enacted in 2012, they have moved to declare it unconstitutional. The High Court eventually declared the cybercrime law constitutional, but struck down some controversial provisions. Still pending for justices to decide on, however, is a petition filed by Bello in 2023, that essentially asked the Tribunal to decriminalize libel. The criminal aspect means that one who is charged with libel faces arrest and will be freed only after posting bail. To decriminalize libel does not absolve journalists of accountability; it simply turns it into a civil case that will still be litigated on top of the constant hurdles that powerful people in the Philippines throw at them — threats and harassment, reputational attacks, killings, bribery, closed access to information that the public needs to know. The Philippines remains to be one of the most dangerous places for journalists globally, ranking 114th out of 180 countries and territories. “Despite its extremely dynamic media landscape, the Philippines is one of the most dangerous countries in the world for journalists,” according to the 2026 World Press Freedom Index . Because in plain truth, beyond the reach of libel are those in power, who are already gifted with all means fair and foul for their so-called grievances. Former president Rodrigo Duterte’s words, for instance, killed. And he’s proven it, as we wrote in this piece . From 2012, when the cybercrime law was enacted, up to 2022, nearly 4,000 cases were filed in various agencies, with the national police saying that cyber libel makes up 20% of the crimes they investigate. Just imagine the other crimes that need more police attention. Simply for practical reasons, decriminalizing libel “will free our public prosecutors to allocate their time… to prosecuting criminal cases that affect the national interest and our territorial integrity,” said lawyer Gilbert Andres in this story . Speaking of territorial integrity: China’s agent-provocateur in Manila, Ambassador Jing Quan, also knows how to weaponize language, as we’ve seen in the past days as he fired volleys of criticism against Philippine officials. How do we make sense of this gutter talk from the Chinese envoy? Bea Cupin weighs in in this piece . But still a happy Monday to you! In a dramatic victory , Brazil President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva fended off a rally by far-right candidate Flavio Bolsonaro, winning a historic fourth term. Here are some of Rappler’s bests that you shouldn’t miss: Dwight de Leon tells us the practical effects of a landmark Supreme Court ruling declaring the 2024 and 2025 national budgets unconstitutional , which the Solicitor General said it would ask to reconsider . Jelo Ritzhie Mantaring looks into how prepared the education department is for El Niño. Jairo Bolledo asks , where in the world is Atong Ang? Our culture desk and creatives team have a quiz for you as Halloween approaches: Would you survive a Filipino horror movie? Lance Spencer Yu reminds us that before the Philippines even had a name, it had gold. New DICT chief faces task of putting house in order amid digital ambitions Inside story: Politician behind 521-kilo shabu shipment bound for Manila ‘No person is walang kwenta’: Groups, friends defend Josh Aquino amid podcast controversy Scientists call for international body to oversee advanced AI At #MoveCebu forum, Cebuanos define what a liveable city should be Rappler’s Best is a weekly Rappler+ exclusive newsletter of our top picks delivered straight to your inbox every Monday. Visit rappler.com/newsletters to subscribe. The views expressed by the writer are his/her own and do not necessarily reflect the views or positions of Rappler .

title: Press review: Alyoshki ceasefire tests peace hopes as US restores Ukraine’s strike ability
body:
MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. A local ceasefire in Alyoshki could open the door to renewed Russia-Ukraine-US peace talks in November; Ukraine continues long-range strikes on Russia as Starlink/Starshield operations reportedly resume; and Europe and Asia are vying for scarce LNG supplies, driving gas prices to four-year highs ahead of winter. These stories topped Monday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.
The ceasefire in Alyoshki will test Russia and Ukraine’s ability to reach agreements and compromise. The ceasefire will take effect on the morning of October 27. Success on the humanitarian front would create a favorable atmosphere for resuming trilateral negotiations involving the United States. The next round of talks will take place after November 4, most likely in Abu Dhabi.
However, Switzerland, which hosted the last meeting of this kind, is also ready to host all parties to the conflict, Izvestia has learned. Europe could also take part in the negotiations this time, a move supported by the Kremlin, Izvestia writes.
Following the mutual cessation of hostilities on the morning of October 27, combat engineering reconnaissance teams will first have to inspect the routes to be used by the humanitarian convoy, military expert Vasily Dandykin told Izvestia. If necessary, they will clear the roads of mines and burned-out military vehicles.
"A contact group has already been established to monitor compliance with the ceasefire. Its members on the Ukrainian Armed Forces’ side will have to ensure that firing stops and prevent UAV flights," Dandykin explained. "Apparently, US mediators will also be involved in monitoring compliance. We should assume that our combat engineering reconnaissance teams will carry out work not only along the routes taken by vehicles carrying humanitarian supplies, but also throughout the city itself and the surrounding area," he added.
After that, staff from the offices of the Russian and Ukrainian human rights commissioners will apparently join the process.
Alongside humanitarian cooperation, political negotiations on Ukraine are also gathering pace. Switzerland is currently ready to host another round of talks on its territory, the country’s Foreign Ministry told Izvestia. "The Swiss Federal Department of Foreign Affairs maintains contact with all parties and continually offers its mediation services to help find a path to peace," the ministry said.
Nevertheless, Abu Dhabi remains the most likely venue, Izvestia writes.
The outcome of the US congressional elections will also influence the peace process. Experts warn that if Republicans lose control of even one chamber of Congress, Trump will be forced to devote more attention to domestic disputes with Democrats, potentially hindering his international diplomatic efforts. Russia’s territorial conditions must also be taken into account, as the conflict is unlikely to be resolved without them. The Kremlin has repeatedly stressed that it will agree to a deal once Ukrainian forces withdraw from the Donetsk and Lugansk People’s Republics and the Zaporozhye and Kherson regions.
Kiev has continued launching long-range strikes on Russia, confirming the renewed operation of the US Starlink/Starshield satellite communications system in support of the Ukrainian Armed Forces, Nezavisimaya Gazeta writes. Ukrainian attacks the previous day left Crimea and other new Russian regions almost entirely without electricity, while Ukrainian drones struck civilian facilities in Central Russia, the Volga region, and Western Siberia. Retaliatory strikes by the Russian military have so far failed to critically weaken Ukrainian forces’ capabilities, which experts attribute to substantial military assistance to Kiev from NATO countries, the Pentagon, and the CIA.
Against this backdrop, Moscow appears to be preparing for negotiations with Ukraine mediated by the United States. The first trilateral meeting on settling the Ukraine conflict, which could take place in Abu Dhabi around November 10-19, will be an "exploratory" meeting, Russian Presidential Aide Yury Ushakov said.
The long-range strikes carried out on Saturday and Sunday suggest that the United States has restored Ukraine’s access to Starlink satellite communications and its military version, Starshield.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, who developed the Starlink system, said satellite communications remain crucial to Ukraine’s defense and that if Starlink is switched off, the Ukrainian Armed Forces’ front line will immediately collapse.
"Judging by Musk’s statements, the Americans have leverage they could use to pressure Ukraine," retired Colonel and military expert Nikolay Shulgin told Nezavisimaya Gazeta. "But Starlink is operating, and Ukrainian forces are using it to strike targets in Russia. This raises doubts about whether Trump and his team genuinely want to end the conflict in Ukraine as quickly as possible," he added.
The expert believes Trump’s team has relaxed its pressure on Zelensky for political reasons. "Many US voters sympathize with Ukraine, the US congressional elections are on November 3, and there is a possibility that the incumbent president’s supporters will lose," Shulgin said. "The slowdown in Starlink operations displeased not only many politicians in Europe but also those in the United States. Criticism of Trump intensified, and he decided, as the saying goes, not to stir up trouble," Shulgin said.
If Trump’s political influence declines after the congressional elections, it will benefit Zelensky’s team in the negotiations, according to Oleg Tsarev, a political analyst and former member of Ukraine’s Verkhovna Rada. The new Congress will take office in 2027, meaning Zelensky’s team has an incentive to prolong the process.
Bratislava wants to continue importing energy resources from Russia. Slovakia intends to seek solutions that would allow it to fulfill its existing contracts with Russia, Tibor Gaspar, deputy speaker of the Slovak parliament, told Izvestia. Slovakia currently receives Russian gas via the TurkStream pipeline under a contract running until 2034. However, the European Union intends to stop imports as early as next year. Experts believe Slovakia could obtain a delay from Brussels or purchase gas through intermediaries.
The Slovak government is interested in pragmatic relations with Russia, and the two sides will discuss the continuation of Russian energy supplies during the negotiations, Gaspar told Izvestia. "Energy, natural gas supplies, and the continuation of oil deliveries will be particularly important, as energy stability directly affects the Slovak economy and its citizens. Negotiations on oil and gas supplies have been officially confirmed, and the Slovak government has expressed interest in pragmatic relations with Russia. It is therefore entirely reasonable to expect efforts to achieve concrete results in the energy sector," Gaspar said.
According to him, a positive outcome of the negotiations would tangibly strengthen Slovakia’s energy security. "Our country has a legitimate interest in protecting its energy and economic interests, ensuring predictable trade relations, and finding solutions that will allow existing contractual obligations to be fulfilled in accordance with the law," Gaspar said.
Bratislava currently receives Russian gas through the TurkStream pipeline under a contract that expires in 2034. Slovak Economy Minister Denisa Sakova recently said that the country had secured adequate gas supplies for the coming winter thanks to its contract with Gazprom.
The resumption of the intergovernmental commission’s work with Russia may be linked to the approaching parliamentary elections in 2027, Mikhail Vedernikov, a senior research fellow at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute of Europe, told Izvestia. Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico’s position is currently rather vulnerable: the economy is not performing well, while support for the opposition is growing. Fico probably wants to secure guarantees of continued supplies from Russia and obtain a favorable gas price for Slovak consumers, the expert believes.
Vedernikov also believes Brussels could grant Slovakia a temporary exemption to allow it to continue importing Russian gas. At the same time, Bratislava is seeking alternatives to Russian gas. In July, the Slovak government officially announced plans to sign a major 10-year contract with Azerbaijan for annual supplies of 1.2 bln cubic meters.
The United States and Israel could use airports in neighboring Afghanistan to launch fresh strikes on Iran. The possibility is being actively discussed in informal conversations among representatives of regional intelligence agencies and concerned experts, Nezavisimaya Gazeta writes. Tehran’s adversaries have the technical capabilities to take control of Afghan airports. The question remains which side the Taliban will support if Washington and Tel Aviv decide to attack the Islamic Republic again.
In recent weeks, Afghan and regional experts have been actively discussing the likelihood of another US-Israeli attack on Iran. Sources in countries across the region describe a new attack on Iran as a foregone conclusion, the newspaper writes. Meanwhile, increased activity by US, Israeli, and other intelligence agencies has been reported in Iraq, Pakistan, and the South Caucasus. Various Arab, Kurdish, and Baloch groups opposed to Tehran are obtaining increasing amounts of weapons and ammunition, while militants from these armed groups are testing the response of Iranian security forces through provocations along the border.
Against this backdrop, Afghanistan, which also borders the Islamic Republic, is attracting particular attention. This is not only because of its long land border with Iran, which is not particularly well protected, according to Nezavisimaya Gazeta. Afghanistan has major airports built during the period of US and NATO military presence that, according to some specialists, could be used by an anti-Iran coalition to plan another attack on Tehran.
According to information from the Amrullah Saleh movement, GAAC, which operates in Kabul and is registered under the Taliban administration, is handling two key contracts. The first covers ground handling services at the airports in Kabul, Kandahar, and Herat. The second involves providing security at the airports in Kabul, Kandahar, Mazar-i-Sharif, and Herat. Herat Airport is particularly significant in the current situation because of its proximity to the Iranian border. The prospect that effective control of the strategic Herat airport hub could pass into the hands of forces belonging to an anti-Iran coalition amid expectations of another US-Israeli strike is unlikely to reassure Tehran, the newspaper writes.
Of course, it is far from certain that the runways at the airports in Herat, Kabul, and Kandahar would be used by the US military in the event of another attack on the Islamic Republic. As specialists point out, the United States and Israel have other infrastructure available to carry out their military plans, ranging from aircraft carriers to secret bases in Iraq and the South Caucasus.
Nevertheless, Afghan airports clearly have strategic value for the United States; otherwise, Washington’s representatives would not be conducting confidential negotiations with the Taliban and continuing to provide financial support to its regime, according to Nezavisimaya Gazeta.
Gas prices at major trading hubs in Europe and Asia are hovering near $1,100 per 1,000 cubic meters, their highest levels in four years. The two regions have entered a bidding war, pushing prices higher to attract available shipments of liquefied natural gas (LNG) ahead of the coming winter, Rossiyskaya Gazeta writes.
The main reason for rising gas prices this year is the conflict in the Middle East. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has virtually stopped LNG supplies to the global market from Qatar and the UAE. According to Giignl, the two countries accounted for 20% of global LNG trade in 2025, with Qatar contributing 19% and the UAE 1%. By early September this year, LNG exports from Qatar, the world’s second-largest supplier after the United States, had plummeted by 96%.
Valery Andrianov, associate professor at the Financial University under the Russian Government, told Rossiyskaya Gazeta that further gas price movements would depend primarily on the situation in the Strait of Hormuz. The closure of this vital shipping route is causing a gas shortage that simply cannot be made up for by supplies from other sources. Compared with the oil market, the LNG industry is relatively inflexible. There is no way to rapidly bring new production capacity online. When a shortage emerges in one market, supplies can only be redirected from other markets through significant price increases.
This is precisely what is now happening in Europe, which is being forced to compete with Asia for scarce LNG supplies, primarily from the United States and Norway. Therefore, if the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz continues, winter peak gas prices will exceed $1,150 per 1,000 cubic meters.
Against this backdrop, Russia is once again drawing attention. On the one hand, Russia was previously Europe’s largest gas supplier. For decades, its gas deliveries effectively supported economic growth and prosperity across European countries. On the other hand, China, Asia’s largest gas consumer, is boosting imports of both pipeline gas and LNG from Russia.
Andrianov believes Beijing continues to maintain a strong position in negotiations over the gas pipeline. Its bargaining position is strengthening because Europe intends to completely abandon Russian gas from 2027 and will most likely stick to that decision despite the severe energy crisis. This would leave Russia with virtually no alternative to China as a destination for its pipeline gas exports. At the same time, Russian LNG previously shipped to Europe, totaling 14.7 mln metric tons in 2025, will have to find alternative markets and will most likely be redirected to China as well.
TASS is not responsible for the material quoted in these press reviews

title: The city that fought Flock
body:
It was about to be a long night in Huntington, West Virginia.
Mayor Patrick Farrell stood before 10 members of city council in a white dress shirt and dark blazer studded with an American flag pin. Behind him sat his constituents and residents from neighboring towns. Some had their arms crossed, while others held a steady glare in his direction. Less than a week before the July 13th meeting, a 33-year-old named Jackie Harper had been shot and killed in Huntington. It was the kind of crime Farrell had promised to get under control. But a breakthrough in the case just days after the killing suggested something promising to Farrell. Harper’s suspected killer, said the mayor, had been found in another state — and it was Flock cameras that helped track him down.
The network of automated license plate reader technology, Farrell said, had also helped find a suspect in another tragic double killing earlier in the year of a beloved middle school basketball coach and his brother, a city worker. “Take that in just this year, and then take it back to all of the cold cases that we have,” Farrell said, referencing an unsolved case from more than 20 years ago where four teens were killed in Huntington on their prom night. Shortly after the gruesome shooting, police said they suspected it was linked to crack cocaine dealers from Detroit. To this day, officials still point to a stubborn flow of drugs from Michigan as the central scourge of the community. The prom night murders remain unsolved. “Think about what might have happened had we had this technology,” Farrell pleaded.
For the next seven hours, that’s what dozens of residents of Huntington and surrounding areas imagined as they stepped up to the microphone to address the city council. Their vision of a Flock-filled future sounded far more bleak. Individuals’ rights to privacy would be trampled. They would be stalked and surveilled. Perfectly legal day-to-day activities could be subject to abuse by Flock itself or rogue police officers with access to its recordings. Sometime after 2AM, a few speakers simply read from George Orwell’s 1984, passing a copy of the book back to the next person in line who wanted it, committed to keeping councilmembers up and looking into their own crystal ball as long as they could.
Several members of the city council shared their concerns. Language in the proposed contract was not as tight as they would have liked to protect the city, potentially opening it up to lawsuits, a few warned. And given how strongly opposed so many residents seemed to be — both at the meeting and in private outreach in the days leading up to the vote — even if the technology might be helpful, was it really necessary to vote right now?
[Image: Noah Jasper Gibson poses for a portrait outside Po-Boy’s Tires. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268752_Flock_camera_photos_CAlo_41.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]
Farrell told the officials that he was inspired to bring Flock to Huntington after speaking with other mayors at a conference who said the tool was the key thing that helped them to reduce crime. “Have you spoken with the mayors of any cities who have canceled their contracts with Flock?” one councilmember asked. “I have not,” said the mayor.
But amid hours of argument against the contract, the majority of the council remained unconvinced. They approved the resolutions that would let Farrell enter Huntington into business with Flock, 6-4. After an initial vote rejecting a motion to table the contract indefinitely, a camera recording the live stream of the meeting began to shake. “Is that thunder?” the council chair asked. Someone off-screen responded, mentioning the constituents watching in an upstairs auditorium. “That’s your taxpayers.”
Huntington, several locals tell me, is a place where people would give you the shirt off their back. Every interview during my visit seems to end with a lengthy list of restaurants to try and a firm request that I reach out if I need help with anything else at all.
It’s a fairly spread-out city dotted with a popular downtown food hall, quaint shopping areas, a city park, and anchored by Marshall University, which is led by the former CEO of Intuit. A state delegate I meet, Ryan Browning, describes it as a “small town” with a “big city feel,” and he lights up talking about the local summer concert series and his favorite cafe that turned him into a coffee drinker. On the weekend I visit, everyone seems to be walking around in kelly green in preparation for Marshall’s Division 1 NCAA football team’s home opener, at a stadium that can host more than 38,000 people — just about 7,000 shy of the city’s own population. “I think what makes Huntington a very special little pocket of West Virginia is the people in the community and how they’re just ready to roll up their sleeves,” Holly Smith Mount, a Marshall alumna and city councilmember who voted against the Flock contract, tells me.
Part of that is the fact that the city has “had our share of tragedies,” she says. It’s grappled with a series of large floods, a plane crash in the ’70s that killed 37 members of the Marshall football team alongside coaches and staff (and became the subject of the movie, We Are Marshall, starring Matthew McConaughey), and a drug epidemic that has rattled the community for years. The Cabell-Huntington Health Department found in 2015 that drug overdose was the third-leading cause of death in Cabell County, which encompasses much of Huntington. Following a 2018 study, Johns Hopkins University researchers said the county had the highest opioid overdose rate in the state.
But because of that, it’s also a place with a lot of tenacity. “I know a lot of people who are barely making it, even including myself, a lot of Gen Z people,” says Noah Jasper Gibson, a young musician I meet while he’s protesting Flock. “Even though their situation’s hopeless, they’re still making the best of it. They’re still out protesting after working 12 hours. They’re still donating their money when they have almost nothing left to give … I think it’s the spirit of those who strive for more that makes Huntington what it is.” Longtime Huntingtonian Brian Trippett, who goes by the moniker “The Front Porch Conservative” on his local streaming talk show, says there’s “a certain amount of lovable curmudgeoniness to our city.”
That might explain why Farrell, when asked after the vote on the Flock contract about his constituents’ reactions, described those who opposed it as part of “a very loud and vocal minority.” On the other side, he added, “is the silent majority.” He said he’s heard from hundreds who support the contract.
There may well be hundreds, if not thousands, of Huntingtonians who’d rather bring Flock to town than not. But on my brief visit, I see far more than a few people who oppose it, and most people I meet struggle to put a finger on who this silent majority is. A councilmember who voted in favor of the resolutions, Rob Archer, tells me that he encounters more Flock supporters in person than he sees online, but he also regularly meets constituents who disapprove of it. One group of Huntingtonians is betting they can prove Farrell wrong by putting it to a vote. They’re aiming to get enough signatures — at least 10 percent of registered voters — for a ballot initiative that would effectively void the Flock contract and bar the government from replacing it with a competing service.
[Image: Flock automated license plate reader cameras have been popping up across the country. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/GettyImages-2295097164_cc650c.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
As of mid-September, the Huntington Community Action Group (HCAG) said it had 1,600 signatures after a little over a month of canvassing. It aims to collect 4,000, giving it some buffer for the roughly 2,700 needed to force a city council vote on their proposal. Success would start a clock on a process that could put the proposed ban to a citywide vote. If the city council rejects or alters the ordinance, as expected, it will get put to a vote within a year. If there’s no election that year, it would get its own ballot.
It’s “one of those popcorn emoji moments,” Mount says. She finds it exciting to see the democratic process in action. “I don’t want to sit there ‘til four in the morning again,” she says, “but I will if I have to. I absolutely will if I have to.”
It was the first Tuesday of July, less than a week before the marathon city council meeting, and Mount paid a visit to the Huntington Police Department with her fellow Democratic councilmember Tia “Fix” Rumbaugh.
Mount and Rumbaugh, alongside other city councilmembers, had been invited to the police department for a tech demonstration. In a letter from the city’s chief data officer on June 25th, Flock’s name was not mentioned. It invited the members to “an informational meeting” about two resolutions dealing with the “proposed purchase” of a suite of devices for the police force. Members would receive a “detailed overview” of what the tools could do, and the anticipated data security and privacy protections that would come with them.
By the time of the demonstration, there had been reports about police misuse of the database, and neighboring cities employed the technology, but the nationwide crescendo of pushback that broke out this summer had not yet peaked. So on Tuesday, July 7th, Mount and Rumbaugh went in relatively fresh to the demo, where they were joined by Republican councilmember Todd Sweeney, Police Chief Phil Watkins, his deputy, and a screen full of Flock employees ready to present how their technology could help Huntington fight crime.
Over a slide deck, Flock representatives discussed the scale of its reach in other police departments and described the basics of each of its technologies. Flock’s most well-known tool is its automated license plate reader (ALPR), which uses AI to help identify vehicles by specific characteristics, as well as partial or full license plate numbers. What makes Flock’s offering unique is its nationwide network, which lets local police departments search not only their own cameras, but those of others who have opted in. Police can track a single vehicle often in real time, which they say can be a valuable tool, especially in time-sensitive cases like kidnappings. The city didn’t pursue a bidding process for the contract, Rumbaugh recalls being told, because no other tool can replace what Flock offers.
But as reports at law enforcement agencies across the country have demonstrated, Flock’s unique selling point can also make it uniquely vulnerable to abuse. Officers have been reportedly caught using Flock to track exes or harass residents who have not been suspected of committing a crime. Following a national uproar, Flock updated some of its policies and defaults to safeguard its systems from this kind of abuse. But critics like the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) say the protections do not go nearly far enough, and that the expansive use of such tools threatens to degrade civil liberties.
Still, as Flock shared the crime-fighting possibilities in Huntington, the promise seemed almost irresistible. “The picture that was painted in the presentation was beautiful,” Mount says. She coached at the middle school and was friends with the fellow coach who was killed in the shooting earlier this year. “I couldn’t help but think, If we had this, would that not have happened?” she says. She got choked up during the presentation. Flock, she says, assured her they could absolutely help prevent such crimes. “And I thought, if this is the silver bullet that we need to fix the problems with drug trafficking … show me where to sign.”
Rumbaugh, however, had begun typing on her phone under the table, trying to find out more about the company. She saw reports about vandalism of the cameras, and anticipated residents furthest to the political left would be most upset. This was about to be a partisan fight, she thought. Yet seeing Mount, a fellow Democrat and ally on city council, have such a visceral positive reaction made Rumbaugh worry she was out on her own. “My state of mind was, ‘This is going to be a problem,’” Rumbaugh says. “‘Everybody is going with it, and I am outnumbered.’”
When, Rumbaugh recalls asking the city and police officials, would this technology come up at city council? If it were up to Farrell, she recalls them answering, it would have already been done. The next day, the council released its agenda for the following Monday’s meeting, and the Flock resolutions were on it. If passed, they’d allow the city to enter into a contract.
Though Mount left the tech demo dreaming of what-ifs, more practical questions soon settled in. As a self-described “data and tech nerd” with a nursing informatics degree, she began researching the company and its claims about resolving and deterring crimes. She was unimpressed by Flock’s own studies of its impact, wanting a longer observation period and independent, peer-reviewed assessment. Could it have really caught her friend’s alleged killer before the act? The suspect had a criminal history but wasn’t currently wanted for a crime, so he was unlikely to be on a hot list flagging his whereabouts before the shooting. “So how would they have known?” Mount asks.
[Image: Huntington Community Action Group members setting up their table for a drive-through canvassing event at Po-Boy’s Tires. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268752_Flock_camera_photos_CAlo_1.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]
”Flock has consistently responded to requests from West Virginia State Delegates and Huntington city leaders to explain how Flock LPR technology works and to address common questions and concerns. We have been transparent about what the technology does and does not do, and we will continue providing factual information to lawmakers and the public,” Flock spokesperson Courtney Terlecki said in a statement. Terlecki called Flock’s technology “an investigative lead” that “captures point-in-time images of vehicles in public places,” and said that in West Virginia this year, its automated license plate readers sent alerts about 21 missing people and over 900 stolen plates or vehicles. Terlecki also pointed to two other cases in West Virginia where Flock was credited with finding a missing child and locating a murder suspect in another state.
As Mount’s analytical side began sowing skepticism, she and Rumbaugh were also hearing from constituents. First, from the regulars who are highly engaged in local politics. Then, from constituents who rarely reach out. “The floodgates opened,” Mount says. “I have never received as many correspondences from constituents on any other topic.” Though she eventually stopped counting, Mount estimates she got over a hundred messages on the subject, with “less than a handful” in favor of Flock. Rumbaugh says the level of fear reminded her of the pandemic. “I think our residents feel like they just have no control over it, and not having control is terrifying,” she says.
Rumbaugh, meanwhile, was poring over the initial contract language with growing trepidation. “I was like, ‘Red flag, red flag, red flag,’” she says. The privacy policy pointed to a URL that she worried could be changed at any time, rather than a static commitment. Legal conflicts would be resolved on Flock’s home turf of Atlanta, rather than in West Virginia where the technology would be installed. And while the city attorney addressed some of her concerns, she still worried about the impact of the technology and the safety of her constituents’ data.
At some point between the demo and the city council meeting, Mount and Rumbaugh spoke on the phone. Rumbaugh recalls Mount sounding distressed. She felt misled by Flock. Rumbaugh realized she may no longer be alone in her fight, but the resolutions were still likely to pass. “It felt like entering a losing battle,” Rumbaugh says. “But that doesn’t mean that you stop.”
Shortly after 4PM the Friday before the vote, a Facebook post from ACLU-WV investigative reporter Kyle Vass lit another match. Through Freedom of Information Act requests, Vass had obtained hundreds of pages of emails between the police department and Flock, going back months. About to leave for a music festival, Vass pored over what he could and posted the rest to his Facebook page for others to mine. It was reshared nearly 700 times.
For Mount, “the glass started to crack” with those documents. She realized the city was already talking to Flock by the time the council approved a line item for public safety capital expenditures — the one that would be used to fund the contract. Farrell’s budget requested $1.5 million for “other equipment” pertaining to public safety, on a line that had been blank in the 2026 budget, and just $169,000 the year before. And as Rumbaugh spent hours reading and answering comments on Vass’ post and on her own page, she noticed some of her usual right-wing “trolls” sounding a note of agreement. “When I noticed that these MAGA conservatives were equally upset about Flock, it made me sit up,” she says. “That’s when I knew it was bigger than I had previously thought.”
The vote was barreling ahead on Monday. Mount planned to raise a motion to table the discussion altogether. At the meeting, Rumbaugh supported the motion, but it failed. Both were left wondering: What’s the rush?
The empty lot of Po-Boy’s Tires didn’t strike me as the ideal place to collect signatures. The used tire shop is on the corner of a residential block and is made up of two structures reminiscent of converted shipping containers painted red. “Po-Boy’s Used Tires” is spray-painted on their sides in big bubble letters in black with a white shadow, and piled-up tires mark an entrance of sorts.
Soon after I arrive, some of the HCAG volunteers I’m shadowing begin to trickle in, some wearing bright yellow T-shirts that say “GET THE FLOCK OUT.” They set up a table with fliers and distribute clipboards on which they’ll collect signatures. Then, they get to work.
[Image: Dennis Gibson, who describes himself as a “huge conservative,” is no fan of Flock. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268752_Flock_camera_photos_CAlo_31.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]
As the evening traffic picks up, I begin to understand the logic behind this spot. For the next two to three hours, nearly a dozen volunteers stand by the side of the road with signs and clipboards, waving down cars to sign their petition. “Stop Flock, sign here,” one sign says. Another has a cut-out picture of Farrell’s face with a speech bubble that says “Let us spy on you!” On the wide thoroughfare, there’s consistent honking by drivers cheering on the effort. At one point, a police officer on a motorcycle looks bemused as he drives by. Volunteers begin directing a steady stream of cars into the Po-Boy’s lot, handing the clipboards through car windows after asking if they’re registered to vote in Huntington.
Signatories come from all kinds of backgrounds. Dennis Gibson is an Army veteran with a long white beard and leather jacket full of patches celebrating the US Army, the Second Amendment, and Harley-Davidson. Standing next to his sleek black motorcycle, he tells me he’s a “huge conservative” who actually voted for Farrell.
