Now, he believes the mayor to be “a Democrat in sheep’s clothing” due to his support of Flock. Gibson says he’s “totally against” Flock and worries about degrading residents’ privacy rights. For the $2.1 million the city is spending on the technology, he says, they could likely solve more crimes by getting more cops on the street, though several councilmembers have warned me police recruitment has gotten harder.
At some point in the evening, a man wearing sunglasses and long hair tied back shows up with what looks, at least from a few feet away, like a cut-down Flock camera. On closer inspection, it’s a hyper-realistic replica that its maker, a carpenter named Josh Pickens, says he constructed in 30 minutes from PVC pipe, cardboard, duct tape, and spray paint. There’s a real solar panel attached to the top, that is actively charging his phone. “The cell phone’s zip-tied to the whole thing so that it can’t be ripped away or anything,” he tells me while standing on a platform where he can hoist the pole into view across the street. “So I can actually record stuff if I wanted to.”
Pickens wears a cardboard sign strung around his neck that reads “FUCK FLOCK,” recognizing his craft project might be mistaken for the real thing otherwise. “I figured people need to see what they’re mad at.” Pickens, who lives in a neighboring town, describes himself as apolitical; his last major protest was an encampment for the Occupy movement around 2011. He first learned about Flock last winter, when he saw the cameras in his hometown in Illinois. “I have firsthand experience of feeling uncomfortable as shit,” he says. So when he learned about the vote in Huntington, he says, “I was just like, ‘No, you can’t have that. Not here.’ West Virginia’s supposed to be too wild and wonderful to have this surveillance crap.”
Candy Tapp, one of the volunteers in the yellow HCAG shirts, tells me between her clipboard duties that she just recently registered to vote, motivated to sign the petition. “I’m really totally for this,” she says. “I want the police to get off their butts and do their job. They don’t need these cameras to do their job.” When it’s time, she says, “by George, I’m ready to vote.”
A few of the volunteers are musicians; they’re holding a “Rock Against Flock” concert the next day, organized to raise awareness for the petition. Michael “Roofus” Riley Jenkins wears a T-shirt littered with holes — I’ll later watch him rip it off his chest mid-performance with his band, Roofus and the Rex. At the canvassing event, he tells me he’s occasionally recognized around town for his sign-off at the marathon city council meeting: “I’m not going to waste your time — I’m kind of hungry. But one last thing. Every single Flock camera has about two to three pounds of copper and about one to two grams of gold. Do with that information what you will.”
Jenkins says he doesn’t really have a political affiliation but that his philosophy is best described as “killdozer-esque libertarian socialist.” Or, put another way, “I believe in having gay Muslim immigrants protect their weed farms with guns.” Still, he says the Flock vote was the first city council meeting he showed up to. “This whole situation just kind of lit a fire up under my ass,” he says. One silver lining? He’s found something in common with his Trump-supporter parents. “The only good thing to come out of this is the fact that I can talk to Republicans again.”
After the meeting, Jenkins posted a song he wrote on Instagram. “The mayor thinks he sees a vocal minority, but I think we all know the truth,” he sang. “It’s about the money in his pockets. Flock you.” When I attend the concert the next day, he and his band perform from the side of his front porch to a crowd of at least a couple dozen people in what feels like some combination of a backyard party, performance, and protest. “We’re here because the government decided against what the people want,” he shouts into the microphone, punctuated by a drum and shouts in response from the crowd. “And we the people are the ones who are going to take the power back.”
[Image: Josh Pickens created a faux-Flock camera with PVC pipe, cardboard, duct tape, and spray paint. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268752_Flock_camera_photos_CAlo_37.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]
Jasper Gibson, who also sings at the concert, tells me he wanted to communicate that all hope is not lost just because of the city council vote. “You have a purpose. There’s a fight that can be had. We can make stuff happen,” he says. From the porch, he introduces a song he says he wrote when he was 14 about “helicopter parents” who are always watching, telling you what you can or can’t do. It applies nicely to the current situation, he says. “You call it backtalk, I call it free speech,” the song goes.
Back at Po-Boy’s, the steady honking throughout the evening is certainly loud. The volunteers and signatories are vocal. “I don’t know too many that are for it,” Gina Carr tells me through her window after signing the petition. The volunteers fold up their table and collect their clipboards as the traffic finally dies down. They estimate they collected well over 100 signatures tonight. If they reach their goal of 4,000 signatures, they’ll get the chance to show if they’re the majority, too.
“I don’t want my kids to grow up with stories of, ‘Oh, this used to be a great place 50 years ago,’” Jenkins tells me. “I want my kids to experience this as a great place to live now. Because I am a West Virginian. I’m a proud West Virginian. I want to die a proud West Virginian, and I want to raise hell and praise Dale until people actually start to fucking listen to what West Virginians have to say.”
Making Huntington safer was always a core pillar of Farrell’s pitch to become mayor. “Public safety is priority number one, and it begins with strong support for law enforcement,” he wrote in a Substack post while running for office in 2024. That includes focusing on the drugs that flow into the city and have fueled addiction among some residents. Earlier this year, while the Huntington Police Department was engaging in talks with Flock, Farrell released a public safety dashboard on the city website. “The people of Huntington should be able to see the same trends and patterns city leaders use to understand what is happening in our community, while understanding that some information must remain confidential for public safety,” he wrote on his Substack. “Transparency should not be an afterthought. It should be the starting point.”
Farrell is a clean-cut Huntington native, whose tie-less blazer and button-down look at city council is still a touch more formal than the councilmembers’ attire. He’s the son of a nurse / hospice executive and a judge. “I was raised by a nurse’s heart and judge’s sense of justice,” Farrell told the West Virginia Chamber. Farrell served almost a decade in the Air Force and then pursued his MBA at Duke University, becoming optimistic about the impact he could make through running businesses. When he returned to Huntington, he ran a clean water solutions company and joined several boards, including Marshall University’s board of governors, where he helped recruit former Intuit CEO Brad Smith to lead the institution. City Hall spokesperson Chrisa Hayes declined The Verge’s request to interview Farrell for this article, saying he wouldn’t be commenting on the ballot measure effort. Hayes did not respond to a detailed list of questions seeking comment on this article.
Farrell’s vision for Huntington, according to past interviews and campaign materials, is for the city to become a thriving, safe place, where residents feel they need not look elsewhere for opportunity. So when Farrell attended a conference for newly elected mayors in December 2024, just before taking office, he was keen to figure out what other cities were doing to improve public safety. This, he’s said, is the first time he learned about Flock.
[Image: HCAG member Candy Tapp talks about how many signatures she collected. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268752_Flock_camera_photos_CAlo_14.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]
To Farrell, it seemed, the thing that cities lowering their crime rates had in common was this networked surveillance technology. He heard about it again at another meeting of the mayors in the summer of 2025, the first year he was officially in office. Around that fall, he told local TV station WSAZ in an interview that he approached Watkins, the Huntington police chief, about exploring using Flock’s technology.
Farrell told WSAZ that Watkins did nine months of due diligence, rebuffing the idea that the process was rushed. In a lawsuit filed after the city council vote, the ACLU claimed City Hall had still skipped relevant steps to put the process in place.
But the mayor maintains that he’s been listening. “I am not surprised that people have very sincere concerns about privacy,” he told WSAZ. “For eight and half hours I had ears open” at the city council meeting, he said, hearing 50 people speak out. But “just because you come to city council and you speak out, doesn’t mean you speak for the majority of the city,” he said. Throughout the interview, he referred to a separate group of constituents: the silent majority.
Farrell said he’d privately heard from religious leaders and business people who perhaps find the technology “creepy” but understand its potential benefits and accept the trade-offs. But when I speak to even supporters of the mayor, they don’t seem to personally know many of those people. “I haven’t heard anybody really clamoring for this,” says David Williams, better known around Huntington as Alligator Jackson, the moniker of a popular Facebook page where he posts updates about local happenings. He can’t think of many people who support the contract, except for “one guy who messaged me all the time. He ain’t that silent.”
Williams describes himself as a friend of the mayor’s and initially says he’s neutral on Flock coming to Huntington. He sees the fight as a continuation of past squabbles between the mayor and more liberal residents over issues like funding a homeless shelter or an animal refuge. “I think it more or less threw the proverbial gasoline on the fire and ignited it,” he says.
But as we speak, Williams, too, admits he’s “not in favor” of the technology. “We’ve been getting by without it,” he says. “I think it’s a little bit overkill, especially with everything that’s going on… why do we want to get into something that everybody else is trying to get out of?”
Williams, like many others I spoke with, worries about a slippery slope of allowing expansive surveillance to become the norm. His first concern was that Flock could be used to track down residents for minor traffic violations in an effort to raise money through tickets. Williams said Farrell assuaged this concern in a private meeting, saying he was laser-focused on using the cameras to crack down on “cartel-level drug activity” in the city. Flock could be used to track down drug traffickers as soon as they cross into Huntington. “It just seems all iffy to me,” Williams says. “It’s just a slippery slope.”
He and many others wonder: Why the rush? Williams is a recreational therapist who works regularly with people experiencing addiction, and he says Huntington’s problems with drugs span well over a decade. While his “Alligator Jackson’s Inside Huntington WV” page now shares a mix of local news, restaurant openings, and community events, he started it around 2011 to warn residents about an addiction epidemic he’d seen firsthand. “They’re acting like there’s a keen sense of urgency, and I don’t understand what the sense of urgency is because that would’ve been great 10, 15 years ago. But now it’s not as bad as what it was,” he says.
Jason Arthur, chair of the city council’s public safety committee who voted to approve the contract, believes “not as bad” is still unacceptable. “My mindset is operation zero,” he says. Yes, the city’s own public safety dashboard shows violent crime was down 30 percent in the first six months of the year compared to 2025, but that’s not good enough. “Is one murder better than five murders? Absolutely, but it’s still a murder.”
Farrell insists that though the Flock contract is multiyear, it’s funded annually, so the city council could simply choose to stop funding it after one year if it doesn’t work as expected. But at least under the current budget, the money allocated for the Flock contract couldn’t simply be rerouted to other issues like funding the animal shelter, says Arthur, because it was set aside specifically for law enforcement equipment.
Arthur and Archer, the city council vice chair who also voted in favor of the contract, both say they’ve heard from this quiet faction that Farrell insists exists. Arthur says he listens to the residents who show up at city council, but like the mayor, cautions they aren’t necessarily representative of all of Huntington. “When I make decisions like this, especially with public safety, I think of the people that are voiceless,” Arthur says. “So I’m thinking of our elderly, I’m thinking of our children.”
[Image: Noah Jasper Gibson, Michael “Roofus” Riley Jenkins, and Bobby Adkins III pose with their guitars. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268752_Flock_camera_photos_CAlo_10.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]
Archer says most of the emails he’s gotten about Flock have been negative, but the opinions of people who approach him in person are varied and often lean more positive. As an associate principal and wrestling coach at the local high school, Archer says he can instantly tell when someone approaches him at a game or event to bring up Flock. “They walk up and say, ‘Hey, man.’ I’m like, ‘Oh, here it comes,’” he says. But he’s often surprised by where they stand. “It is not a Democrat-Republican issue. It is a personal issue ... You don’t know what you’re going to get, who’s for it and who’s against it. You can’t tell.”
But for all his conviction, Archer says he, too, has concerns. When I ask about the people who read from 1984 at the city council meeting, worried that they were about to bring “Big Brother” to town, Archer doesn’t resist the analogy. “I worry about it too,” he says. “I’m not sitting here saying ‘I 100 percent back this.’” Even so, he thinks Flock could be a “force multiplier” for the dwindling number of police hopefuls he watches try out on the high school track field every year. He believes it might have helped catch the prom night killer, whose impact still ripples through the schools. With some safeguards in place, Archer believes, it’s worth a shot.
About a month after Huntington approved its contract with Flock, the company was in the hot seat again in West Virginia — this time, though, it had a far colder welcome from the jump. Flock’s director of government affairs Kevin Kane faced a skeptical crowd at the state capitol building in Charleston, where he sought to address state lawmakers’ concerns about the technology during an interim session hearing. By the end, lawmakers seemed to only walk away with more concerns.
“I remember going like, ‘Why is he not answering the question?’” Republican state Sen. Patricia Rucker tells me at her office in Charleston in September. She pulls out a sheet of scribbled notes from the hearing. “Require warrant to access certain info. With exceptions for emergencies,” she’d written beneath a cursive header titled “Model Legislation.” “I personally do not want this used for speed checks!”
A few days after the hearing, Flock released its policy updates, including newly mandated multi-factor authentication across its user base. That statement, three state lawmakers charged in a letter to Flock’s CEO, appeared to contradict Kane’s sworn testimony. “Do you guys require two-factor authentication to log into the system?” Republican delegate Ryan Browning asked. “Yes,” Kane answered, saying he didn’t know when that began, but “it’s been a standard practice for a long time.”
That was one of several alleged inconsistencies or misleading statements. The lawmakers requested a detailed list of information about Flock’s policies, safeguards, and technical capabilities. Flock gave a lengthy response that defended Kane’s answers as “the conduct of a witness drawing an accurate distinction, not obscuring one.” But the lawmakers again slammed it as “a two-page exercise in corporate reframing.” After another tense round of letter exchanges, the lawmakers told Flock they expect a prepared witness to testify under oath at their next public meeting on November 9th. Republican delegate Tristan Leavitt tells me at his office in the Charleston capitol building that it’s “extremely likely” the state will pass legislation around surveillance technology next year.
“We have responded to West Virginia lawmakers’ questions in writing, promptly, and remain committed to working directly with state officials,” Flock’s Terlecki said in a statement. “Flock has offered to participate in the November 9 briefing, and we welcome the opportunity to address questions openly and correct any misunderstandings.”
Among the three Republican state lawmakers I meet, each has a different core reason for their skepticism of Flock. Browning sees the ability to track vehicles across locations as a tool that could encroach on civil liberties and privacy, including Second Amendment rights if, say, a camera tracked the comings and goings at a gun shop. “If it’s used to gather data on a high crime area, et cetera, then it could be used as a valuable tool,” he says. “But if you’re using it to just constantly collect and store data that could then be later used to target groups, then it’s a problem. And whether that be the LGBTQ community, or gun owners, or whatever the ideological change is, then it can be a massive problem.”
[Image: A HCAG member reaches out to commuters in the community. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268752_Flock_camera_photos_CAlo_22.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]
Rucker is staunchly opposed to allowing a tool to perform searches that in other contexts would require a warrant under the Fourth Amendment. As a first-generation American citizen born in Venezuela, Rucker says she knows government surveillance first-hand. Some of her relatives there will only communicate with her in “coded language,” she says. Flock’s lofty aspirations of eliminating crime strike her as less rosy than the company likely intends. “If we want to consider a society where no one would ever get lost, and no one would ever get hurt, and there would be no way that someone could hurt another individual, what type of surveillance would that take?” she asks. “I’m not going there.”
Leavitt is more confident that the Fourth Amendment concerns could be addressed through careful policy and isn’t even particularly concerned with Flock’s (since-disbanded) pilot with federal agencies, though he asked about it in his initial letter. He’s more concerned about what he sees as purposefully obtuse answers from Flock. “It doesn’t matter what my ideological views are or your ideological views are. If they are going to legislative bodies or public bodies who have a responsibility because they’re entrusted by the voters of their area to make decisions, you give them straightforward information,” he says.
As the legislature waits to officially regroup in January, Browning says nothing is stopping Flock from taking more action on its own. “If you were really genuine about wanting to be a good company, you would be the ones trying to model your technology around the rights of our citizens, not waiting for a legislature — which meets 60 days out of the year and makes laws 60 days out of the year — to come in and regulate.”
By mid-September, it’s been two months since Huntington’s city council approved the city’s Flock contract. The company has since faced national scrutiny over a relentless drip of stories about alleged police misuse, prompting the company to update its data access and retention policies, and its CEO to issue a mea culpa over his past approach. Flock planned to cut about 18 percent of employees as of October, according to Reuters, after an earlier voluntary buyout program.
But some cities that have ousted Flock have simply replaced it with similar surveillance systems from competitors like Axon. At this point, the fight isn’t just about one company — the path forward for an entire technology is at stake.
As Huntington’s city council reconvenes, Farrell still hasn’t signed the contract with Flock, even though he’s been given the power to do so. First, he says, he’d like the government to pass guardrails on the technology’s use. That’s what the council assembled to discuss on this late summer day, with a scheduled vote on an ordinance proposed by the mayor. If passed, it would lay out the acceptable and prohibited uses of data collected by Flock or similar technologies. Authorized uses: homicide, missing persons, stolen vehicles, active warrants, officer safety, and more. Prohibited uses: traffic enforcement, immigration enforcement not required by a federal warrant or court order, “Revenue generation,” and “Personal curiosity,” among others.
The police chief would be expected to maintain a list of authorized users, and officers would be prohibited from sharing accounts. The data would be deleted after 30 days, and there would be quarterly audits for compliance. Officers found to misuse access could face administrative sanctions, which could include a referral for criminal investigation.
[Image: Mayor Patrick Farrell has been key to Flock’s entrance into Huntington. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268752_Flock_camera_photos_CAlo_7.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]
“I am assuming good intentions by everybody, and I’d like all of you to as well,” Farrell begins his remarks, clarifying that it would apply to all public safety technologies, not just Flock. He shares residents’ concerns and disdain for mass surveillance, and this ordinance will help safeguard their privacy. Huntington is lucky, actually, he says. Other cities had to enact safeguards after the fact. Huntington is getting to craft them before. This time, he’s read up on those mayors who paused their Flock contracts. Several of them did so to put those guardrails in place, he says, but intend to resume them.
Democratic councilmember Sarah Walling grills Farrell on terms of the contract and ordinance. How could consistent tracking of public locations that can be strung together not be considered warrantless surveillance? Farrell says all of the cameras will be pointed at public places, and the courts would agree that’s okay. “We’ll see,” says Walling.
Rumbaugh asks why the ordinance doesn’t include the ability to charge officers who abuse the system with a misdemeanor. Will officers who abuse the system really go from zero to 100 by committing a felony? Walling doubles down on the point: Is one unauthorized search a felony? Five? Farrell says he doesn’t determine that as the mayor.
He leans on a standard line, that “if we can trust these men and women that have sworn an oath to protect us with firearms, I think we can trust them with cameras.”
“This is a company that lies,” Walling objects. “It lied to our legislatures, it’s lied to cities across the country, we have at least two states that have said that state money can’t be used for them. It can’t be used on public highways. How on Earth is Huntington, West Virginia, able to make the assurances that Flock is not going to misuse our data when it’s absolutely done it in other places without any repercussions whatsoever?”
The meeting is shorter than the one back in July, but the result is similar. After roundly negative comments from the public, the ordinance passes 7-2. Walling had earlier said the ordinance was “better than nothing,” but apparently changed her mind and votes no. Rumbaugh also votes no, and Mount isn’t present.
When the vote is finished and the floor opens for general comments from the public, a 67-year-old Army veteran eventually steps up to the microphone. “It’s my very first time ever doing this,” says Steve McDilda, wearing a yellow “Get the Flock Out” shirt and gripping both sides of the podium. His tone is that of a father trying to talk some sense into a child. “You really have no idea what you’re about to do. You’re about to give away your rights.” He’d heard that there’d been some talk of a “silent majority.” He says we’ll see about that. Once the people of Huntington get the chance to vote, he says, “you’re going to really find out.” In fact, he says. “You’re going to have an awakening.”

title: Scale AI establishes Dubai office
body: US technology company Scale AI announced on Monday that it has established a UAE office at the Dubai International Financial Centre . Scale AI , founded in 2016, is valued at $29 billion and has more than 1,000 employees. The official announcement that it is to have a presence in the UAE was made at a signing ceremony during the Dubai AI Festival. Trevor Thompson, global managing director at the AI infrastructure company , reflected on the company's decision to expand into the country, saying it has set a "clear, ambitious vision for AI and is now putting it to work across government and the economy". He added that Scale AI's plans will work well with the UAE's ambitions for the technology. "Making our home at DIFC is a long-term commitment," he said. "We are here to help UAE institutions build AI they can trust and use for their most critical use cases and important decisions." The company lists Meta, Cisco, Instacart, Nvidia, Cohere, OpenAI, Microsoft and Time, as well as the US Air Force and US Army, among its clients. Scale AI makes the tools other technology companies use to increase the reliability of their AI solutions. Its software assists with identifying items in images, tagging subjects within large amounts of text and labelling that information so it can be used in AI apps and chatbots. The company says its largely automated software allows humans to easily review and make changes to ensure accuracy. Scale AI’s footprint continues to grow as buzz surrounding the self-described "data-centric end-to-end solution" AI infrastructure company shows no sign of slowing. Essentially, if a company needs reliable and well-organised data to help create a large language model, Scale AI has become the go-to expert. It was founded by Alexandr Wang shortly after he dropped out of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology when he saw AI developments creating the need for ways to provide and manage high-quality training data for technology companies and other large businesses. Scale AI’s rapid rise has also carried Mr Wang into the rarefied air of AI tech entrepreneurs including Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and OpenAI’s Sam Altman. Mr Wang has graced the cover of magazines and testified before the US Congress. In June, he left the company for Meta after the social media company announced a significant investment in Scale AI. Mr Wang officially serves in the capacity of chief AI officer for Meta and has since been charged with developing its consumer-facing AI products such as Muse, Muse Image and various language models. After Mr Wang's departure, Scale AI named Jason Droege as the company's interim chief executive before announcing in July that Francis deSouza, Google Cloud's former chief operating officer, would be Mr Wang's official successor. According to Scale AI's media release, the company's UAE branch is based in the Dubai AI Campus at DIFC, part of the Dubai Universal Blueprint for Artificial Intelligence, "which brings together infrastructure, business support and international connections for AI companies building in Dubai".

title: [UPDATED] Alleged Wire Tapping: Court Orders El-Rufai To Enter Defense
body: Justice Joyce Abdulmalik of the Federal High Court, Abuja, has ordered the former governor of Kaduna State, Nasir El-Rufai, to enter his defence if he so desires in his ongoing trial over his alleged unlawful interception of the telephone communications of the National Security Adviser (NSA), Nuhu Ribadu. Justice Abdulmalik issued the order while ruling on a no-case submission made by El-Rufai on Monday. The Judge dismissed the no-case submission because there is sufficient evidence furnished by the prosecution to warrant the court calling on the defendant to enter his defence if he so desires. The judge adjourned till November 25 for defense. The post [UPDATED] Alleged Wire Tapping: Court Orders El-Rufai To Enter Defense appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Armscor not inviting bids for soldier-worn body cameras
body:
Armscor, the State-owned defence acquisition and project management company, maintains a May body camera Request for Information (RfI) was not intended to be the basis of a technical specification.
It was, according to Armscor Senior Manager: Corporate Communication, Liziwe Nkonyana, part of efforts to “understand the latest technology trends and prices thereof for future possible integration into a smart soldier solution and other applications”. This, she said in response to a DefenceWeb inquiry, would form part of an RfI analysis report for record purposes.
“Armscor,” she said further “will not be issuing a Request for Bids (RfB) because this RfI was not based on any particular requirement from the Department of Defence (DoD). If ever the DoD in the near future decide to generate such a requirement, Armscor will be in the position to issue an RfB”.
The RfI (RFI/1/2026), again according to her, was for body cameras for the SA National Defence Force (SANDF) as part of “border optimisation”.
“Border optimisation” applies directly to Commissioner Michael Masiapato’s Border Management Authority (BMA) where 40 body cameras are reportedly in service with more to come. The SANDF is also acquiring additional equipment for border safeguarding, such as radars and armoured vehicles.
Acting National Police Commissioner Puleng Dimpane and Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia also have body cameras on their wish list with currently no firm timeline for acquisition in what appears to be another example of bureaucratic overkill. Instead of going to Armscor, as government’s approved acquisition agency for its defence and security agencies, it will fall to the State Information Technology Agency (SITA) to oversee the acquisition. This is not cast in stone with Cachalia earlier in September saying SITA has yet to make the bid public. Once a service provider is chosen, the SA Police Service (SAPS) will develop a comprehensive national rollout plan, which will determine the timeline for full implementation.
The SITA involvement is reportedly because body cameras are no longer standalone items of equipment. They rely on software, storage, security and digital evidence management systems, placing them in the information and communications technology procurement environment where SITA resides.
With no request for acquisition of body cameras for specifically for soldiers deployed on the border protection tasking Operation Corona, the Armscor RfI is interpreted as a preparatory measure in anticipation of an official ask from the SANDF. This is illustrated by part of Nkonyana’s response to DefenceWeb. It reads: “No date has been set for bid publication as this RfI was not based on any particular requirement from the DoD. If the DoD in the near future decide to generate such a requirement, Armscor will be in the position to issue an RfB based on the research already done”.

title: Russian shelling causes new power outages in six regions, Ukrenergo says
body:
According to Ukrinform, this was reported by NEC “Ukrenergo” on Facebook .
“Over the past 24 hours, the enemy continued to carry out attacks on Ukraine’s civilian energy infrastructure. As a result, as of this morning, there are new power outages in the Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Chernihiv, Kharkiv, and Sumy regions,” the statement reads.
Power utility workers have begun restoration work wherever the security situation allows.
Due to the consequences of Russian attacks in some regions, power restriction schedules for industry and hourly blackout schedules of up to two rounds are being enforced until the end of the day.
As of 9:30 a.m. on Monday, electricity consumption was 5.8% lower than on the previous business day—Friday, October 23. Ukrenergo urges the public to limit the use of high-power electrical appliances from 4:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m.
As previously reported, Andrii Herus, chairman of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Energy, Housing, and Utilities, stated that the switch to daylight saving time no longer has a significant impact on the country’s power grid or electricity consumption levels.

title: About the compromised eMudhra intermediate CAs
body:
Apple is blocking the compromised certificates automatically. Mac administrators can take optional steps for some command-line tools.
Since 19 October 2026, Apple has been blocking the certificates of the compromised eMudhra intermediate Certification Authorities (CAs) that issue TLS certificates, and is making additional updates to this block.
If you don't use Terminal as part of your workflow, you don't need to do anything. Your Apple devices now automatically block these certificates in Safari, Mail, and apps that use Apple's networking and security frameworks.
If you use Terminal as part of your workflow (such as system administrators or developers), you might use command-line tools that can still accept these certificates. Some tools included with macOS or the Xcode Command Line Tools — like curl and git — check certificates against /etc/ssl/cert.pem and can still accept these certificates until a future software update. To stop those tools from accepting them sooner, you can remove root CA certificates from the file.
The private keys of eight intermediate CAs operated by eMudhra were compromised. Two of these CAs issue code signing certificates, which Apple's frameworks don't trust. The other six issue TLS certificates. Someone with keys from these six CAs could create certificates that appear valid for any website. eMudhra and Sectigo have revoked the affected certificates.
Each of the 6 TLS intermediate CAs has two certificates, for 12 in total:
A certificate issued by emSign Root TLS CA - G3, which chains to emSign ECC Root CA - G3
A certificate cross-signed by Sectigo, which chains to AAA Certificate Services
On 19 October 2026, Apple began blocking these 12 certificates on Apple devices. Updates to certificate configuration data are sent to devices automatically and as needed, so you don't need to install a software update to get this change. Apple is making additional updates to this block, which will also be delivered automatically. On 23 October 2026, Apple also began blocking the emSign ECC Root CA - G3.
Apple is making further changes to block these certificates in other places on Mac where software checks certificates, such as the command-line tools included with macOS or the Xcode Command Line Tools that use /etc/ssl/cert.pem. These changes will be available in a future software update, and you won't need to edit any files to get them.
Most users don't need to edit /etc/ssl/cert.pem. Safari, Mail, and apps that use Apple's networking and security frameworks don't use this file, and your Apple devices block these certificates in them automatically.
On Mac, some command-line tools included with macOS or the Xcode Command Line Tools (including curl, git, python3, ruby, perl, and openssl) check certificates against /etc/ssl/cert.pem. For certificates that chain to a root CA certificate in this file, these tools don't check Apple's block or whether the certificate has been revoked. This file will be updated in a future macOS update. If you use these tools and don't want to wait for the update, you can remove root CA certificates from the file.
Some apps and tools include their own list of root CA certificates and don't use Apple's block or /etc/ssl/cert.pem. For those apps or tools, contact the developer .
Rather than wait for the upcoming software update, administrators can choose to remove the root CA certificates to which the blocked certificates chain from /etc/ssl/cert.pem.
These steps affect every tool that uses /etc/ssl/cert.pem. Afterward, tools that use only this file might not be able to verify some websites whose certificates chain to these root CA certificates through intermediate CAs that weren't affected.
A macOS software update can replace /etc/ssl/cert.pem with Apple's version. Until you install the software update that includes Apple's changes, run the command in step 4 after each software update. If it lists a root CA certificate that you removed, the update replaced the file. Delete the old backup using sudo rm /etc/ssl/cert.pem.orig , then repeat these steps. After you install the update that includes Apple's changes, you don't need to repeat these steps for the command-line tools included with macOS or the Xcode Command Line Tools.
You need an administrator account, or you can deploy the commands with your device management solution. Copy each command exactly as written. Learn what to do if you get an alert about possible malware when pasting the command into Terminal.
To remove root CA certificates from /etc/ssl/cert.pem:
Back up the file. If a backup already exists, this command keeps it:
[ -e /etc/ssl/cert.pem.orig ] || sudo cp -p /etc/ssl/cert.pem /etc/ssl/cert.pem.orig
Remove emSign ECC Root CA - G3. This command makes a copy of the file without emSign ECC Root CA - G3, checks that the copy isn't empty, and replaces the original. It shows nothing when it succeeds:
t=$(mktemp) && awk -v s='=== /C=IN/OU=emSign PKI/O=eMudhra Technologies Limited/CN=emSign ECC Root CA - G3' '/^(===|###) /{skip=0} $0==s{skip=1} !skip' /etc/ssl/cert.pem > "$t" && [ -s "$t" ] && sudo install -m 0644 -o root -g wheel "$t" /etc/ssl/cert.pem; rm -f "$t"
Optional: Removing emSign ECC Root CA - G3 doesn't block the six certificates that Sectigo cross-signed, because these tools can still verify them through AAA Certificate Services. To stop these tools from accepting those six certificates through the file until you install Apple's software update, you can also remove AAA Certificate Services. This command works the same way as the one in step 2:
t=$(mktemp) && awk -v s='=== /C=GB/ST=Greater Manchester/L=Salford/O=Comodo CA Limited/CN=AAA Certificate Services' '/^(===|###) /{skip=0} $0==s{skip=1} !skip' /etc/ssl/cert.pem > "$t" && [ -s "$t" ] && sudo install -m 0644 -o root -g wheel "$t" /etc/ssl/cert.pem; rm -f "$t"
Check the result. This command lists either root CA certificate if it's still in the file. If you removed both, it shows nothing. If the command shows an error, restore the backup from step 1.
openssl crl2pkcs7 -nocrl -certfile /etc/ssl/cert.pem | openssl pkcs7 -print_certs -noout | grep -E 'emSign ECC Root CA - G3|AAA Certificate Services'

title: ‘Astronomical’ Arab turnout could reshape Israeli politics in key election
body: An “astronomical” turnout of Arab voters is expected in the Israeli elections on Tuesday, with the possibility that their politicians could significantly influence the next government, political sources have told The National . Senior opposition officials have also said there is a possibility of a coalition or agreed minority government with the Arab parties, if the mainstream parties do not win an outright majority. Opinion polls have now closed under Israeli law, with the final ones showing the opposition with a potential 56 seats, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party on 50 with the Arab parties taking 14 in the 120-seat Knesset. With 61 seats needed to form a government, the opposition led by Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot could either form a minority government with tacit Arab party support or go into a coalition with the Ra’am party, led by Mansour Abbas. Arab influence could also be strengthened by a surge in votes for its two main parties – Ra'am and the Joint List – with turnout expected to rise from about 50 per cent to 70 per cent of the two million people who make up 20 per cent of Israel ’s total population. “After what they have witnessed over the past three years, they have understood the difference between bad and worse,” said an Israeli political observer, referring to the hard-right parties that have influenced politics. If the bloc against Mr Netanyahu takes power, then significant steps would be taken to halt the settler violence and illegal dwellings in the occupied West Bank , an opposition source said. “We will clamp down on settler violence, which has gone on for too long, because it is a disgrace to the country and because it is wrong," he said. "We will also stop wildcat home building because we believe in law and order.” A coalition involving Ra’am is one of three possible outcomes from the election. The other two are either a coalition between the centre-right and ultra-orthodox parties or a “government of unity” that would be likely to have Mr Eisenkot as prime minister, but would also include Mr Netanyahu ’s Likud. There are also many unknowns and other factors at play that could still affect the outcome. About 700,000 young people will vote for the first time – the last election was in 2022 – and it is not known which way the group that went through Covid, Israeli judicial reforms, the October 7 attacks and military service will vote. There are up to 70,000 Israelis living abroad who have flown back to the country to vote – the majority are understood to be against Mr Netanyahu – alongside a similar number of Russian emigres, who fled after the 2022 Ukraine invasion, who are thought to be in the more liberal camp. Key issues for Israel, which observers say are existential, are also at play. Some officials believe getting the ultra-Orthodox into conscripted military service is important to Israel’s security, but their parties object. There are 72,000 ultra-Orthodox young men aged 18 to 21 who are listed as “deserters” for not joining up. There is also talk of a “declaration of independence” that would give the country a written constitution, alongside term-limits for prime ministers. Mr Netanyahu has served for almost 20 years over three spells in office. Israel also faces other crises, including the imposition of international sanctions from European countries and a plummeting birth rate, except among the Arab and ultra-Orthodox population. About 50 per cent of school children are from those two groups. But some observers believe that, come dawn on Wednesday, Israel will simply resume the status quo, with the idea of Zionist parties working with Arab groups unacceptable to too many people. “My concern is that they will opt for the unity government [with Mr Netanyahu] because they are cowards and it is politically convenient,” one opposition figure said.

title: Pentagon Prepares US Military Bases to Operate Independently for 90 Days in Major War
body:
The Pentagon is preparing US military bases to operate for at least 90 days without outside support if a major war disrupts power grids, supply chains and critical infrastructure, Fox News Digital reported , citing documents it reviewed.
The plan, known as FORTRESS, would require major military bases in the continental US to secure their own electricity, water, fuel, and communications.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“We don’t want to rely on standard civilian municipal infrastructure to run our national defense. We just simply can’t. It’s an intolerable risk,” Pentagon chief spokesperson Sean Parnell told Fox News Digital.
“Power is combat now. Without electricity, you lose communications, water, logistics, assembly lines, and just basic military command structures,” he said.
FORTRESS calls for portable nuclear reactors, large-scale battery storage and microgrids to keep bases running during prolonged power outages.
The Pentagon also plans to stockpile weapons, fuel, spare parts, and other essential supplies, while preparing civilian factories to switch to military production during a crisis.
“The next conflict will likely be fought on multiple fronts. Look at the geopolitics behind any major war. When that happens, global supply chains will break,” Parnell said.
The plan would require at least two qualified supply or production sources for critical military needs to reduce reliance on any single supplier or factory.
It also includes measures to protect military communications, navigation, and satellite systems against GPS jamming and disruptions to space-based infrastructure.
The initiative reflects a shift in US military planning toward the possibility that a major conflict could disrupt infrastructure supporting military operations inside the country.
“I realized that a lot of the way we think about homeland defense was built around the antiquated assumption that two oceans would protect us,” Parnell said.
“President Trump understands that world is gone, and he’s already paved the way for new thinking: Golden Dome, a renewed focus on the Western Hemisphere, Greenland, Panama,” he added.
The Pentagon has already announced plans to reduce major military installations’ dependence on civilian power grids. FORTRESS extends those efforts to water, fuel, communications, industrial production, and other essential services.
Parnell described the initiative as insurance against a major conflict disrupting the infrastructure and supply networks on which US forces rely.
“You don’t want to be making these decisions in the middle of a global multi-front conflict. We have to have a plan,” he said.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Masondo to end his Military Ombud tenure at annual symposium
body:
This year’s South African Military Ombud symposium is a significant one in that it will mark the end of tenure for retired SA Army lieutenant general Vusi Masondo.
The former SA Army Chief was moved to Defence Headquarters in 2016 as SA National Defence Force (SANDF) Chief of Corporate Staff (CoCS), now sans the “Corporate”, before exiting active service. His retirement didn’t last long with him named to replace first Ombud, also a retired lieutenant general, Temba Matanzima, in November 2019. Like his predecessor, Masondo will complete a seven-year term of office.
Looking back – and ahead to the symposium set down for Friday 30 October at the CSIR International Convention Centre in Pretoria – Masondo said it is an important platform to reflect on the role of independent military oversight in strengthening accountability and ensuring complaints are addressed fairly and effectively.
“As the Office concludes this seven-year term, it is an opportunity to take stock of our progress, recognise the value of collaboration with our stakeholders and reaffirm our commitment to strengthening trust within the defence environment.”
The symposium will see senior government representatives, military leadership, ombud institutions, academics and security sector governance experts gather to explore its theme of “Strengthening Trust and Accountability: Enhancing Complaints Resolution Mechanisms within the Civil-Military Relations Framework”. Among others delegates will discuss improved complaints resolution, reinforcing institutional integrity and how best to build public confidence.
Deputy South African Public Protector, Advocate Dinkie Dube, is the symposium programme director and she has the distinction of introducing Masondo ahead of his final public appearance as Military Ombud.
Others on the speaker list are Caroline Sekoni, Zambian Public Protector and African Ombudsman and Mediators Association (AOMA) Secretary-General; Velile Jonas, Director: Investigations at the South African Military Ombud; and Dr Hans Born, Research and Training Head at the Geneva Centre for Security Sector Governance (DCAF).
Associate Professor in the UNISA Department of Political Science, Professor Moses Khanyile will moderate a panel discussion titled “From democratic accountability to sustainable complaints resolution”. Named participants are SA National Defence Force (SANDF) Adjutant General, Major General (Dr) Eric Mnisi; Professor Extraordinarius at the Thabo Mbeki African School of Public and International Affairs, UNISA, Professor Dries Velthuizen; Health Ombud Professor Taole Mokoena; and Professor Thuli Madonsela, Director Centre for Social Justice, Faculty of Law, Stellenbosch University.
The symposium wraps up with an evening session celebrating the end of Masondo’s tenure along with the launch of a commemorative coffee table book “Strengthening Trust and Accountability: A Seven-Year Review (2019-2026)”.

title: Europe’s top five defence powers to name Russia as greatest threat
body: Europe’s five largest defence spenders are set to warn that Russia represents the most acute and long-term threat to the continent’s security as they pledge unflagging support for Ukraine. “Russia’s ongoing war of aggression against Ukraine, on the one hand, and its continued violations of Allied airspace, acts of sabotage and growing use of multi-domain hybrid attacks, on the other, do not undermine our unity, solidarity and cohesion,” said a draft joint statement from France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the UK , or E5, according to Bloomberg News. The ministers also plan to say that Europe “must assume greater responsibility for its own security.” The statement, whose language could change before publication, is expected to be released after a meeting in Paris on Monday hosted by French Defence Minister Catherine Vautrin and attended by her counterparts from the other four countries. Ministers will also be discussing "security challenges in the Middle East," Ms Vautrin's office said. Their meeting comes as Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman heads to Iran with other officials from countries in the Makkah Agreement to push forward a diplomatic solution to the crises in the region. The European ministers' message is a response to Russia intensifying a campaign of hybrid attacks across Europe, including suspected sabotage, cyber attacks, arson, drone incursions and threats to critical infrastructure and defence companies. Testing Nato European officials see the activity as an effort by Moscow to test Nato's limits , disrupt support for Ukraine and exploit uncertainty over how the alliance should respond without triggering a broader conflict. While highlighting that the US will remain an “indispensable ally,” the draft said that “this greater responsibility must begin with the empowerment of European Allies within Nato”. The European leaders are expected to say in the statement that they will assume greater political and military leadership to modernise their forces and capabilities, strengthening Nato’s collective defence to “adapt to current and future challenges” and also bolstering Europe’s defence readiness. The EU’s regulatory and financial resources can help support member states’ defence ambitions, according to the draft, while stressing that the bloc’s defence efforts should reinforce Nato rather than duplicate its work and should remain open to members outside the military alliance. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned last week that Russia’s threat to Europe extends beyond the war in Ukraine, arguing that Moscow is increasingly seeking to destabilise European democracies through pressure, interference and hybrid attacks. In an interview on Bloomberg Television on October 19, Mr Merz said Europe must take the threat more seriously, strengthen its defences and reduce its reliance on the US while continuing to support Ukraine. This step by European leaders comes after rising tension between America and Ukraine, following US President Donald Trump’s deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin, in which Washington agreed to refrain from imposing further sanctions in exchange for Moscow supplying diesel to the global market in a bid to reduce rising energy prices. The agreement was met with a strong backlash from US politicians allied with Mr Trump, as well as from Ukraine and European leaders. “We will maintain our unwavering commitment to supporting Ukraine in its fight back against Russian aggression,” the draft said, emphasising the combating of Russia’s shadow fleet and its continued violations of European airspace. “Ukraine’s ability to defend itself now and in the future is critically important to Euro-Atlantic collective security.” Agencies contributed to this report

title: These key Senate races will determine which party controls the body next year
body:
Several appear neck-and-neck in the last week before Election Day.
Thirty-five Senate seats are up for grabs when Americans head to the polls on Nov. 3. A key handful of them will be critical in determining whether Democrats or Republicans control the chamber next year.
Republicans currently control the Senate with 53 seats. Democrats and two independents make up the Senate minority with 47 seats.
In order for Democrats to take the chamber back, they’ll have to net four seats in the upcoming election. Republicans can afford to lose up to three and still be considered the Senate majority with the tie-breaking vote of Vice President JD Vance.
Some of the races that were closely watched earlier this year have slid from the spotlight as the election grew near. Republicans seem to have abandoned efforts to unseat incumbent Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia and have pulled out of spending in North Carolina, where former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper now seems poised to best former Republican National Committee Chair Michael Whatley to fill retiring GOP Sen. Thom Tillis' seat.
As both parties prepare for the final leg of the campaign, here are some of the most closely watched Senate races.
Republican nominee Mike Rogers is no stranger to Senate races -- the former congressmen lost his 2024 bid to now-Sen. Elissa Slotkin by less than 20,000 votes.
Rogers is squaring off this time against progressive Abdul El-Sayed, a former health executive who bested a moderate candidate in the Democratic primary.
Republicans have gone to great lengths to frame El-Sayed as “radical" over his support for Medicare for all and his positions on immigration. They've also attacked him for his faith and ethnicity. Rogers has falsely linked him to terrorist groups and President Donald Trump has gone as far as calling him a "vicious, violent jihadist" while urging voters to reject him to "preserve our religion, our values, and our heritage."
El-Sayed, who was born to Egyptian immigrant parents in Rochester Hills, Michigan, has denied ties to terrorism and called those characterizations Islamophobic.
El-Sayed told ABC News Live anchor Linsey Davis last week, "They think they can point to my name and my faith and distract us from the fact that we can't afford our gas and we can't afford our groceries."
Rogers told Davis in a separate interview the he thought he was making inroads with traditionally Democratic Jewish and Black voters who are wary of El-Sayed.
Michigan has voted for Trump in two of the last three elections, yet Democrats have prevailed in every Senate race since 1994.
Texans have not been represented by a Democrat in the Senate for 33 years, but Democrats say this could be the year that changes.
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton beat long-time incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in a costly GOP primary runoff thanks to Trump's late endorsement. Paxton, a hardliner and ally of the president, is seen by many Republicans as a harder sell in the general election than Cornyn would have been.
Paxton has had several scandals in his time in the public eye. He was impeached in 2023 on allegations of abuse of office, bribery and corruption but was acquitted by the state Senate. He was indicted on securities fraud charges in 2015 but reached a pretrial agreement with prosecutors just weeks before trial in which he agreed to community service, legal ethics courses and pay $300,000 in restitution in return for not having to admit guilt.
Democrat James Talarico is a former state representative and Presbyterian seminarian. Republicans have tried to paint the 37-year-old progressive as far-left and radical.
Democrats hope Paxton’s lack of favorability coupled with larger concerns about affordability could be enough to end their three-decade Senate drought.
Republicans are taking no chances, pouring millions into this race and even opted to hold their inaugural midterm convention in Dallas.
The race is the most expensive Senate race in history: Outside groups have contributed more than a quarter-billion dollars to elect Paxton. Over $500 million has been spent on ads in the state, according to AdImpact.
Incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan will square off against former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola and another candidate with the same name in another surprisingly close race.
Alaska’s ranked-choice voting sends the top four vote-getters in primaries to the general election. Peltola is advantaged by being the only Democrat to advance.
In addition to Peltola, Sen. Sullivan faces another opponent on the ballot also named Dan Sullivan, an independent, and Republican Gerald Heikes, who made the final four when the fourth-place finisher dropped out.
Republicans, including Trump, have made a point of reminding voters to check that they’re casting their ballot for the “real Dan Sullivan,” and on Oct. 23 he directed the Justice Department to preemptively sue to block certification of the results if the incumbent narrowly loses.
The Ohio Senate race features two candidates fighting for their chance to return to the Senate: incumbent Republican John Husted and former Sen. Sherrod Brown, who lost his 2024 reelection bid to Bernie Moreno.
Husted was appointed by Ohio GOP Gov. Mike DeWine in 2025 to fill the Senate seat left vacant by Vice President JD Vance. This race will determine who finishes out the remainder of Vance’s term until 2029.
This is Husted’s first time on the statewide ballot. Though Ohio has been moving increasingly toward Republicans in recent elections, Husted faces a tough race amid growing concerns about affordability and data centers in his home state.
Brown lost his reelection bid against newcomer Moreno by about four points in 2024, though he outperformed Democratic nominee Kamala Harris in the state. The three-term senator is making a pitch to working-class voters concerned about cost-of-living issues.
The Kansas Senate race was not expected to be competitive -- Trump won the state by 16 points in 2024 and Republicans have held both Senate seats in Kansas for nearly a century. Yet even incumbent Republican Sen. Roger Marshall has conceded that it's “quite a close race” this cycle.
Marshall, a medical doctor who served in the House before being elected to the Senate in 2020, has largely supported Trump’s policies during his time in Congress. His opponent, Adam Hamilton, has sought to emphasize Marshall’s ties to the unpopular policies that have created economic challenges for voters.
Hamilton is reverend of the largest United Methodist congregation in the nation. He has tried to brand himself as an “independent-minded” Democrat but Marshall has said Hamilton is “too woke” to represent the people of Kansas.
Longtime Maine Republican Sen. Susan Collins has repeatedly defied the odds, and kept her seat even after being counted out. She’s a moderate Republican who has been more willing than most in her party to break with the president on some issues.
But Democrats think Troy Jackson, a former Maine Senate president and majority leader, could put an end to Collins’ nearly-30-year Senate career.
Jackson was a late entry into the race after Graham Platner, the original nominee, dropped out following sexual assault allegations.
Collins, the chair of the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee, has name recognition and a long record of serving Maine on her side and has tried to highlight her willingness to vote against her party.
Jackson has tried to show Collins failed to when it counted -- notably, Jackson has accused her of "paving the way" for the Supreme Court to overturn Roe v. Wade by casting the deciding vote for Justice Brett Kavanaugh.
Trump has been rallying in Iowa to support Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson’s bid to replace retiring GOP Sen. Joni Ernst in a race that few thought would be competitive at the beginning of the cycle.
There are no Democrats in Iowa's congressional delegation and Trump won the state by a commanding 13 points in 2024. Iowa has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 2008.
But rising costs caused by the Iran war have hit Iowa farmers hard. Many see moderate Democratic nominee Josh Turek, a state representative and two-time Paralympics gold medalist in wheelchair basketball, as a formidable candidate against Hinson.

title: Avior Labs unveils Callisto, its next-generation AI-driven autonomous VTOL drone
body:
South African UAV developer Avior Labs is expanding its unmanned aircraft portfolio with Callisto, an all-electric vertical take-off and landing (VTOL) platform designed to combine extended endurance with onboard artificial intelligence and autonomous mission management.
Avior Labs, based in Irene, Gauteng, showcased the Callisto at the recent Africa Aerospace and Defence (AAD) exhibition in September. The aircraft represents a new approach to persistent surveillance, surveying and intelligence gathering, with an emphasis on onboard processing and reduced operator workload.
Founded in 2019, Avior Labs applies a defence aerospace engineering background and a simulation-led development philosophy to its aircraft. Founder and Managing Director Dr Bennie Broughton said this approach enables the company to predict performance before committing to hardware development.
“We don’t fly anything without simulating it first,” he clarified. “We can predict with a very high level of accuracy what performance we are going to get out of the system long before we build it.”
Callisto is intended for border security, coastal and maritime patrol, search and rescue, and protection of pipelines, powerlines and railway infrastructure. Its surveying applications include wildlife management, game counting and vegetation monitoring across extensive areas, potentially exceeding 2 000 hectares per mission.
Callisto builds on lessons learned from the company’s hugely successful smaller Elevation platform but represents a fundamental shift in design philosophy.
“Callisto is built to a large extent around its AI mission computer,” Broughton explained. “On Elevation, the AI that it does have on board, like object detection, is a payload function. In the case of Callisto, it’s an aircraft function.”
At the heart of Callisto is a dedicated FPGA-based mission computer, supported by a proprietary software stack developed over several years. The architecture is designed to process sensor data, identify objects and prioritise information in real time, reducing reliance on continuous operator intervention and high-bandwidth communications.
Avior Labs has developed its own object-detection algorithms for aerial imagery, alongside software that monitors the aircraft’s health. This includes identifying changes in vibration that could indicate a deteriorating motor or damaged propeller, as well as detecting certain control-system failures and reallocating control functions to compensate where possible.
Callisto’s autonomy extends to mission planning. Rather than requiring operators to programme individual waypoints, the system allows them to designate an area of interest and specify a task, such as surveying terrain, patrolling a perimeter or monitoring an area for particular activity.
“We designate an area of interest on a map, and then we task the drone,” said Broughton. “We tell it what we’d like it to do in that area.”
The aircraft then determines how best to execute the mission, taking account of terrain and communications coverage.
An encrypted mesh datalink allows Callisto to communicate with other aircraft, ground units and network relays. Multiple drones can share information and coordinate their activities, enabling one aircraft to concentrate on a detected target while another expands its patrol area to cover the resulting gap. A reserve aircraft could also be tasked to launch when additional coverage is needed.
“The whole idea is it’s all done in an automated way so that to the operator all of this is transparent,” Broughton noted. “He can focus on getting his ground units to deal with the target.”
Callisto has a wingspan of 3.6 metres and a maximum gross take-off weight of 15 kg, compared with Elevation’s 2.5 metre wingspan and approximately 4.5 kg weight. Its modular mission bay is designed for a two kilogram payload, with scope for heavier configurations when an optional battery extender is removed.
Avior Labs is targeting flight times of four to eight hours, depending on the battery configuration, and a range of up to 580 km. These figures are intended to support missions requiring substantially longer persistence than conventional multirotor drones can provide.
Callisto was initially conceived as a hybrid-electric aircraft, as endurance requirements for missions such as border patrol and search and rescue have traditionally favoured platforms with combustion engines. Recent improvements in battery technology and propulsion-system efficiency, however, prompted a rethink.
“When we started running the numbers using our own design capability and what we can push in terms of efficiency, it became clear to us that we can actually achieve sort of an entry-level hybrid type of performance, but with an all-electric,” Broughton said.
Different battery options will allow customers to balance endurance against acquisition and operating costs. A higher-energy-density battery is intended to support the upper end of the endurance range, although its cost and cycle life may not suit every operator.
The design also leaves open the possibility of a hybrid configuration for customers prioritising maximum endurance and already equipped to support combustion engines.
The aircraft’s three-lift-rotor VTOL arrangement, featuring what the company describes as an over-actuated configuration, is intended to improve stability and control in demanding conditions. Avior Labs targets operation in ground-level winds of approximately 12–14 m/s and specifies IP55 protection against dust ingress and water. Actual mission capability will also depend on the environmental limits of the selected payload.
Broughton said this resilience is particularly important for time-critical missions: “The last thing you want is someone is in a capsized yacht off a coast, but you have to wait for the storm to pass before you can go look for the guy.”
Avior Labs is developing two configurations using the same basic airframe. One is intended for civilian and commercial operations; the other incorporates additional systems and software hardening for military environments.
Callisto remains at the prototype stage and is not yet in production. Broughton saids the company’s experience establishing production processes for Elevation should help accelerate the transition once development and validation are complete.

title: No rift between Netanyahu, army chief on Iran – Israel defence minister
body: Defence Minister Israel Katz said Monday that reports of a rift between Israel’s army and its civilian leaders over fresh action in the war with Iran were “entirely baseless”. Israel’s Channel 12 reported on Sunday, citing unnamed sources, that there had been a confrontation between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and army chief Eyal Zamir over an unspecified new directive. The premier dismissed the report as “rubbish” during a TV appearance, and Katz characterised it as an effort to cast doubt on the Netanyahu bloc’s judgement on the eve of close elections. “The reports about gaps between the political echelon and the IDF (army) on the Iran issue are entirely baseless and false,” Katz said on X, insisting there was “complete” coordination between the two. In its report, Channel 12 said Zamir had demanded a detailed discussion as well as legal guarantees and the signatures of the political leadership before carrying out the directive he had received. The outlet did not offer details of the directive, but cited sources saying there were concerns within the army that the war might be exploited for political gain. Katz stated “unequivocally that there was no intention on Israel’s part to initiate an attack on Iran before the elections”. Opposition leader Yair Lapid referenced the report in a post on X Sunday, accusing Netanyahu of seeking to put off the vote. “Tonight it was published that he wants to set off an escalation and a confrontation with Iran, just to postpone the elections,” he said. “This man has lost his grip. We absolutely must send him home.” Netanyahu has campaigned heavily on his security credentials, arguing that only he can finish the job in the US-Israeli war against Iran. AFP The post No rift between Netanyahu, army chief on Iran – Israel defence minister appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Ebola: No case in Yobe, govt activates emergency response system
body: The Yobe State Government has said no case of Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) has been recorded in the state, but it has activated its emergency response system following the confirmation of an imported case in the country. The state Ministry of Health and Human Services stated this on Monday during a press briefing at the State Emergency Operations Centre (EOC) in Damaturu. The Permanent Secretary of the ministry, Hajiya Hadiza Sabo, said the briefing was necessitated by the confirmation of an imported case of EVD in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Abuja, by the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) on October 20, 2026. She said the case involves a diplomat who travelled into Nigeria from Uganda and tested positive for the Bundibugyo strain of the virus. Woman allegedly poisons stepson in Bauchi Petrol consumption hits record low amid rising prices She said the patient is in isolation and receiving care, while the NCDC has activated its national Incident Management System. She said as of October 24, 53 close contacts, including health workers, patients, caregivers and travel contacts, have been identified and are being monitored, while 46 exposed persons have been placed on a 21-day no-fly list as a precautionary measure. She said the NCDC has classified the risk of Ebola importation into Nigeria as HIGH due to increasing regional transmission, international travel and porous borders, but there is currently no evidence of community transmission in the country. She said in line with the national directive and NCDC guidelines, Governor Mai Mala Buni has directed the activation of the Public Health Emergency Incident Management System (IMS) and the development of a comprehensive Emergency Preparedness and Response (EPR) plan. Sabo said Yobe is among the states that have fully activated emergency response teams, established isolation facilities and intensified contact-tracing for EVD. She said the preparedness is built on the six technical pillars recommended by the NCDC. She said the State EOC has been placed on high alert and multi-pillar coordination meetings have been convened to review the epidemiological situation and ensure a unified command structure in collaboration with NCDC, WHO and UNICEF. Sabo said surveillance has been intensified across the 17 local government areas, with Disease Surveillance and Notification Officers placed on high alert to investigate and verify any rumour or alert, while the contact-tracing system has been strengthened to monitor contacts for 21 days. She said designated isolation and treatment facilities across the three senatorial zones have been equipped with medicines and Personal Protective Equipment (PPE), while frontline healthcare workers have been retrained on IPC protocols, safe sample collection and clinical management. She also advised residents to practise good hygiene by washing hands frequently with soap and water or using alcohol-based sanitiser, to avoid direct contact with blood or bodily fluids of anyone who is sick, and to avoid traditional burial practices that involve direct contact with the deceased. She urged citizens to shun rumours and rely only on verified information from the state Ministry of Health and NCDC, and not to stigmatise persons identified as contacts, saying being identified as a contact does not mean a person has Ebola. She said Yobe State has no case of Ebola but its IMS is fully active and operational to protect the people of the state.

title: Russian attacks across Ukraine kill 2, injure 35 over past day, as repeated strikes hit Zaporizhzhia
body:
Russian attacks across Ukraine have killed at least two and wounded 35 others over the past day, local authorities said on Oct. 26, as Russia repeatedly struck the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia.
Eight people were injured over the past day by Russian attacks on the city of Zaporizhzhia in Zaporizhzhia Oblast , Ivan Fedorov, co-head of the regional Defense Council, said . In total, Russia launched 857 strikes on 52 settlements of the Zaporizhzhia region, fedorov said, including two missiles at Zaporizhzhia. In the morning of Oct. 26, a Russian strike hit a shopping mall which had been "no longer in operation," according to Mykhailo Semikin , the acting regional governor. There were no injuries reported.
Russian forces attacked Ukraine with a Kh-31P anti-radar missile, three Kh-59/69 guided air-to-ground (air-to-surface) missiles, and 140 attack drones overnight, the Air Force said. It reported shooting down three Kh-59/69 missiles and 112 drones.
In eastern Donetsk Oblast , at least one person was killed, and 10 others were injured by Russian attacks over the past day, regional governor Vadym Filashkin said .
In northeastern Kharkiv Oblast , four people were injured by Russian attacks over the past day, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said . He said the victims include two women, aged 51 and 71, and two men, aged 52 and 72.
In southern Kherson Oblast , a person was killed, and eight others were injured by Russian attacks over the past day, regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin said .
In northern Chernihiv Oblast , a 33-year-old man and a 54-year-old woman were injured by Russian drone attacks over the past day, regional governor Viacheslav Chaus said .
In northeastern Sumy Oblast , three people, a 63-year-old man and two women, aged 56 and 76, were injured by Russian attacks over the past day, the regional military administration said .

title: Fire Point confirms FP-1 drone strike on Russian Voronezhsyntheskauchuk plant
body:
Ukrainian missile and drone manufacturer Fire Point has confirmed a strike on the Voronezhsyntheskauchuk plant in the Russian Federation using its self-developed FP-1 long-range kamikaze drone.

"We confirm, Voronezhsyntheskauchuk has once again hosted the FP-1," the company stated in a Telegram message on Monday.

According to Russian Telegram channels, the city of Voronezh came under a drone attack on the night of October 26. Preliminary reports indicate that fires broke out in several districts of the city. Likely damage was also reported to the Pivnichny (Northern) Bridge, the Voronezhsyntheskauchuk plant, and the Voronezh Aircraft Production Association (VASO).

It is noted that a drone threat was declared in the region around 3:00 a.m., followed two hours later by a missile alert. Local residents reported a series of explosions and air defense activity, after which plumes of black smoke rose in several areas of the city.
