title: Iran says outcome of Israeli elections ‘makes no difference’
body: Iran’s foreign ministry said Monday that the outcome of the Israeli elections in which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is facing a tight race will make “no difference”. “It makes no difference to us who, in these elections, takes the helm of a regime that has brought nothing but violence and massacres to our region,” said ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei in a weekly press briefing. Tuesday’s legislative elections will take place amid mounting threats by Israel and the United States to renew attacks on Iran after they launched their war in late February. Netanyahu has in recent days repeatedly said the only way to remove the threat posed by Iran is to topple its government. On Sunday, he told Israel’s Channel 14 that he had “instructed the Mossad and the IDF to overthrow the Iranian regime”. Baqaei dismissed Netanyahu’s remarks as “empty threats” and a “sign of desperation”. The post Iran says outcome of Israeli elections ‘makes no difference’ appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Trump-Netanyahu team suited to removing Iran’s regime, Netanyahu adviser tells ‘Post’
body: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's foreign policy adviser, Ophir Falk, called for the removal of Iran's regime and said Netanyahu and US President Donald Trump were suited to achieving it, in written remarks to The Jerusalem Post ahead of Tuesday's Israeli election.“Removing the genocidal Ayatollah regime in Iran is in the best interests of America, Israel, and civilization,” Falk said. “The Trump-Netanyahu team has shown to be suited to do so.”Falk argued that the decisive question for voters was who would lead Israel during the final two years of Trump's presidency.“Who will best cooperate and coordinate with the President to finish the job in Iran and expand peace in the region?” he asked.Trump renewed his endorsement of Netanyahu on Sunday evening, urging Israelis to back him in the October 27 vote.“Vote for Bibi Netanyahu for Prime Minister; we have to finish the job that we started!” Trump wrote on Truth Social.Falk contrasted that support with what he said were the preferences of Israel's adversaries.“Trump wants to work with Netanyahu,” he said. “At the same time, Israel's enemies – Hamas, Hezbollah, the Houthis, and, of course, Iran - want Netanyahu to lose.”“Israel and the American-Israeli alliance have never been stronger, and Iran and its proxies have never been weaker,” he added.Israel 'very close' to creating regime change conditions in IranIn an October 15 interview with the Post, Falk said Israel was “very close” to creating conditions for regime change, while stressing that Iranians would have to determine their country's future.“Regime change in Iran is up to the Iranian people,” he said in that interview.His written remarks ahead of the election did not specify how the US and Israel should pursue the regime's removal or provide a timetable.

title: Serbia protests timeline: how students brought Vucic’s 12-year rule to end
body: The end of Vučić’s rule Aleksandar Vučić, Serbia’s former president and the ruling party’s candidate for prime minister, conceded defeat in the snap parliamentary election held on 25 October. He said the “Student List” had won. “Judging by the preliminary results, it is clear that we have lost this election. The Student List has won — they will get between 135 and 140 seats, while we will have around 105,” Vučić said. The snap election, which Vučić called before stepping down as president, followed a wave of student-led protests that had lasted for almost two years. The demonstrations began after a disaster at the railway station in Novi Sad in 2024 that killed 16 people. Protesters blamed corruption and negligence for the tragedy and demanded that those responsible face justice. Vučić’s party had been in power in Serbia for 12 years. Here is a chronological account of how the protests began, grew into a student movement, challenged Aleksandar Vučić’s government and brought Serbia to the 25 October 2026 election, in which Vučić conceded defeat. From a spark to a change of government Aleksandar Vučić and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) have dominated Serbian politics since 2012. Vučić became prime minister in 2014 and was elected president in 2017. Government supporters portrayed him as a guarantor of stability, economic development and a foreign policy that balanced relations with the West and Russia. Critics, however, pointed to the concentration of power, the ruling party’s influence over the media, corruption and concerns about the independence of state institutions. Public discontent periodically spilled onto the streets. Protests included demonstrations over electoral fairness and rallies against a proposed lithium mining project. Until 2024, however, the government had largely managed to prevent the emergence of large-scale, sustained protest movements. Goodbye, Orbán! How did the 16-year rule of the Kremlin’s best friend in the European Union come to an end? About how the election campaign unfolded and what consequences its results led to 1 November 2024: the tragedy that changed everything On 1 November 2024, a concrete canopy collapsed at the railway station in Novi Sad, a city in northern Serbia, killing 16 people. The station had undergone renovation shortly before the disaster, prompting immediate questions. How could recently refurbished infrastructure collapse? Who was responsible for the quality of the work? How transparent were the public procurement procedures and the renovation project itself? Authorities opened an investigation, but for many people, the fact that an investigation had begun was not enough. Suspicions grew that the collapse might not have been merely a technical failure, but could also involve corruption and attempts to evade accountability. Further concerns over access to project documents only deepened those suspicions. Protesters demanded that those responsible be identified. The tragedy, which claimed 16 lives, became more than a moment of mourning. It turned into a test of accountability for state institutions. People wanted to know not only what caused the canopy to collapse, but also who had allowed potential wrongdoing to take place and why the oversight system had failed. November 2024: students take to the streets On 22 November, students at the Faculty of Dramatic Arts in Belgrade were attacked during a silent protest in memory of those killed in the disaster. The incident gave the protests a new focus: students demanded that authorities identify the attackers and hold them accountable. University students soon began disrupting classes. The movement spread from Novi Sad and Belgrade to other cities across the country. The way the protests were organised was also significant. Students made decisions at general assemblies known as “plenums”. From the outset, the movement had no single central leader whose removal would have allowed the authorities to bring the entire campaign to a halt. What were the students demanding? Make all documents related to the station’s reconstruction publicly available; Identify those responsible for the disaster and hold them accountable under the law; Punish those involved in the attacks on students and drop charges against detained protesters; Increase funding for higher education by 20%. In other words, the movement was never solely about calling for the government to resign. Its main goals were transparency, justice and accountability from state institutions. By December, the protests had evolved beyond a reaction to the Novi Sad tragedy. University blockades, daily demonstrations and public support for the students had turned the movement into a nationwide campaign. One of its most powerful symbols was the minute of silence. Every day at 11:52 — the exact time the canopy collapsed — protesters stopped to honour the victims. They also held 16-minute silences in memory of the 16 people who died. The movement drew its strength from the fact that it differed from a typical political opposition campaign. Students stressed that political parties should not dictate their demands. This helped bring a wide range of social groups into the protests. January 2025: the first major political outcome On 28 January 2025, Prime Minister Miloš Vučević announced his resignation. Around the same time, the mayor of Novi Sad also stepped down. This marked a significant political concession. The authorities could no longer maintain that street protests were failing to achieve any tangible results. However, the students continued their protests. In their view, the resignation of individual officials did not answer the key questions: who was responsible for the disaster, how independent was the judicial system, and how should the system of government be reformed? This marked an important turning point. The protests showed that a sustained, organised mass movement could impose significant political costs on the authorities. The students adopted a new strategy. Rather than limiting their demonstrations to the capital, they began organising marches, cycle rides and meetings with local residents across the country. This strategy was important for several reasons: The protests spread beyond the capital. The movement built ties with residents of smaller towns and regional communities; Students positioned themselves as representatives of society as a whole. They won support from university staff, teachers, ordinary citizens and people from a wide range of professions; The movement built its own communications network. Citizens critical of the government ensured that the flow of information no longer depended solely on traditional media. By this stage, the student protests had become one of the largest popular movements in Serbia’s recent history. Miloš Vučević 15 March 2025: the historic rally in Belgrade The rally on 15 March 2025 marked a pivotal moment for the movement. Hundreds of thousands of people gathered in Belgrade. The independent organisation Archive of Public Gatherings estimated that between 275,000 and 325,000 people took part. Serbia’s Interior Ministry gave a significantly lower figure. The discrepancy itself became a subject of debate. Why was this event important? First, it showed that the students enjoyed support well beyond university campuses; Second, the government faced a challenge not only from the traditional opposition, but also from a broad coalition of citizens united by a common demand for justice and state accountability; Third, the movement had grown so powerful that the question of Serbia’s political future could no longer be ignored. Once again, the protest showed that calls for a change of government were coming from beyond political parties. A sense emerged across society that the existing system could be changed. Ten years after Brexit: Why are Britons looking back toward Europe? Nearly Half of Britons Want a New Referendum. What Has Happened Since Brexit? Spring and summer 2025: when the demands turned into a political struggle On 5 May 2025, the student movement called for snap parliamentary elections. This broadened the scope of the protests. Vučić’s government, meanwhile, said the demonstrations aimed to destabilise the state and alleged that foreign powers were involved. The student movement rejected these accusations, identifying its main goals as fighting corruption, establishing independent institutions and holding fair elections. Tensions continued to rise throughout this period. Reports emerged of arrests, clashes and acts of violence against protesters. Government opponents accused the authorities of controlling the media and weakening democratic institutions — allegations the government denied. One of the movement’s most significant decisions was to create a political alternative from within the protest movement. Students began selecting candidates to represent them in the parliamentary election. They formed an electoral list called “Student List — Students Win”. The aim was to broaden the movement’s representation by including people from different professions and social groups. On 9 September 2026, Vučić called a snap parliamentary election for 25 October. He made the announcement amid a prolonged political standoff, as the student movement was already preparing to contest the election. 22 октября 2026 года: сотни тысяч сторонников движутся к предвыборной финишной прямой За несколько дней до выборов, назначенных на 25 октября, студенческое движение провело в Белграде масштабный заключительный митинг. Сторонники из разных городов страны направились в столицу. Согласно данным, опубликованным накануне выборов, между студенческим списком и правящей партией развернулась упорная борьба. Вучич предрекал победу, хотя и признавал, что она достанется нелегко. Это стало кульминацией движения, которое продолжалось почти два года: протест, начавшийся с требований справедливости после гибели 16 человек, теперь стремился обеспечить себе большинство в парламенте. 25 October 2026: Vučić concedes defeat On election night, something that many in Serbian political circles had long considered unthinkable happened. Vučić announced that his political camp had lost the election and that the Student List had won. He estimated that the Student List would secure between 135 and 140 seats in parliament, while his own camp would get around 105. According to Reuters , preliminary projections gave the Student List 138 seats in the 250-member parliament, compared with 104 for Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party. The Student List had therefore secured a parliamentary majority. Voter turnout stood at around 70%, one of the highest levels since 1992. According to Serbian political sociologist Gazela Pudar Draško , writing in The Washington Post , the student movement had taken the protests to a new level: citizens had moved beyond simply expressing discontent and begun taking direct part in political change. Students across the country had created an alternative model of political mobilisation by building relationships with local communities and making decisions collectively. Radomir Šajčić , a professor at the University of Belgrade, commented on the victory at the students’ campaign headquarters. “Tonight we celebrate our victory, and tomorrow we will start building the future!” he said, Reuters reported . title: How to check your polling unit
body: By Adegboyega Adeleye Voters can use the Independent National Electoral Commission’s (INEC) online Polling Unit Locator to find their assigned polling unit ahead of the 2027 general elections. According to INEC, the directions shown by the locator are approximate, so voters should confirm the location before election day. The presidential and National Assembly elections are scheduled for January 16, 2027 while Governorship and State House of Assembly elections in participating states are scheduled for February 6, according to INEC’s election calendar. How do you find your polling unit? Visit INEC’s Polling Unit Locator and follow the instructions on the portal to look up your polling-unit location. Check the location and any directions shown, bearing in mind that INEC describes those directions as approximate. What if you cannot find your details? Check your information using INEC’s official voter services and follow the instructions available there. If you still cannot confirm your polling unit, seek guidance through INEC’s official channels before election day. The exact steps for resolving a missing or incorrect record should be confirmed with INEC. What should you remember on election day? Go to the polling unit where you are registered and take your physical Permanent Voter Card (PVC). INEC’s current voter guidance says voters must be physically present and verified through BVAS before voting. The election calendar currently lists accreditation and voting from 8:30 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. Voters are advised to check INEC’s announcements for any updates. The post How to check your polling unit appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Ebola death count in Congo tops 4,800 people
body:
PRETORIA, October 26. /TASS/. The number of laboratory confirmed deaths from the Ebola fever in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has exceeded 4,800, according the National Institute of Public Health, part of the DRC Health Ministry.
"The number of deaths from Ebola has reached 4,803," it said in a statement. "The number of infected people stands at 9,876. The mortality rate amounts to 48.6%."
The Ebola outbreak began on May 15 in the DRC and Uganda and became the second deadliest in the entire history of observations in Africa. Cases and deaths from Ebola were identified in eight DRC provinces.
Uganda said on July 28 that the outbreak had ended. On August 25, the World Health Organization confirmed this.
On October 6, Kenya registered the first Ebola case. Then, Nigeria reported the first case on October 20.
During the current Ebola outbreak, 9,907 people contracted the disease, and 4,807 died.

title: Prem Watsa: How the Canadian Billionaire Became One of Greece’s Biggest Investors
body: Prem Watsa, the Indian-born founder of Canada’s Fairfax Financial, arrived in Canada in 1972 with, by his own often-told account, just eight dollars to his name. Today, at 76, he is worth about US$2.8 billion, according to Forbes . Through Fairfax, he has also quietly become one of the most important foreign investors in the Greek economy. From Hyderabad to Toronto Watsa was born in Hyderabad, India, on 7 August 1950, according to The Canadian Encyclopedia . He graduated in chemical engineering from IIT Madras in 1971. The following year, he moved to London, Ontario, to live with his brother and study for an MBA at the University of Western Ontario. He paid his way by selling stationery, gifts and appliances door to door, the Financial Post reported. In 1985, he took control of a struggling insurer and turned it into Fairfax Financial Holdings, which he still chairs and runs as chief executive. His long-term, value-driven approach has long earned him the nickname “Canada’s Warren Buffett”. Betting on Greece when others fled Fairfax first came to Greece in 2012, at the height of the debt crisis, when it bought into Eurobank Properties, the real estate company later renamed Grivalia. Then, in April 2014, Fairfax led a group of investors that backed Eurobank’s €2.864 billion recapitalisation, committing €400 million of its own, Carrier Management reported . By May that year, it held 8.77% of the bank, at a time when many foreign investors were heading for the exit. Two years later, in 2016, Fairfax and Canadian pension fund OMERS bought 80% of Eurobank’s insurance arm, Eurolife. Grivalia, meanwhile, was later merged into Eurobank, adding to Fairfax’s position in the bank. Cashing in, and reinvesting The patience has paid off. In January 2025, Fairfax sold 80 million Eurobank shares, about 2.2% of the bank, at €2.33 each, Eurobank announced . The sale raised about €186 million. However, Fairfax described the placement as a “mandatory technical adjustment” to keep its holding just below 33%. It added that it would remain a “long-term, committed reference shareholder” of the bank. Later in 2025, Fairfax sold DIY chain Praktiker Hellas to Romania’s Pavăl Holding, the owner of Dedeman, ot.gr reported . Then, in May 2026, Eurobank agreed to buy the 80% of Eurolife Life it did not already own from Fairfax-controlled entities, for about €813 million, the bank said . Fairfax keeps its 80% of Eurolife’s general insurance business. A second wave: Metlen and ANT1+ Rather than taking his money out, Prem Watsa has kept investing in Greece. In March 2023, Fairfax agreed to take a 15% stake in ANT1+, the streaming platform of Antenna Group, through a share capital increase, Naftemporiki reported . Fairfax has also built a holding in energy and metals group Metlen. In March 2025, it agreed a €110 million exchangeable bond with the company. “We are excited to further increase Fairfax’s investment in METLEN,” Watsa said at the time, according to Metlen . Goody’s, Everest and Flocafe Most recently, on 14 October, Vivartia announced it would sell 100% of Evergood, its food services business, to Recipe Unlimited Corporation, Kathimerini reported . Recipe, Canada’s largest full-service restaurant company, has been wholly owned by Fairfax since October 2022. Evergood runs more than 575 restaurants under the Goody’s Burger House, Everest, Flocafe Espresso Room, La Pasteria and Jackaroo brands, Recipe said . Its outlets range from high streets and shopping centres to airports, motorways and ferries. In 2025, Evergood’s sales rose 13.1% to €299.6 million. Neither side disclosed the price, but Capital.gr put the deal at around €300 million. The sale still needs the usual regulatory approvals before it can be completed. Eurobank remains the crown jewel Eurobank is still the centrepiece of Fairfax’s Greek portfolio. Fairfax holds 1,186,363,895 shares, or 32.67% of the bank, according to Eurobank’s shareholder data . At Friday’s closing price of €4.148, that stake is worth about €4.9 billion. In Metlen, Fairfax holds about 8.35%, or 11,938,047 shares, according to its latest notification to the company . At Friday’s close of €46.94, that holding is worth about €560 million. Prem Watsa, “Canada’s Warren Buffett” It is easy to see why the Buffett comparisons have stuck. Watsa modelled Fairfax on the success of his idol, according to Forbes. Moreover, in Greece, he bought when others were selling, held on through the crisis, and is now reinvesting the profits in the country’s economy. title: Germany intends to purchase Ukraine’s Bars cruise missiles — newspaper
body:
LONDON, October 26. /TASS/. German authorities are expected to finalize a deal in the coming weeks to purchase the initial batch of Ukraine’s Bars cruise missiles, The Financial Times reported, citing sources.
According to the sources, the Bundeswehr could conduct technical tests of the missiles early next year. If the tests yield "satisfactory results," Germany could purchase hundreds more of these missiles, the newspaper writes. According to the newspaper, this would mark the first known purchase of an offensive weapon developed in Ukraine for the Bundeswehr’s own use.
According to the publication, the Bars is a jet-powered weapon with a range of up to 1,000 km and a payload of up to 105 kg, depending on the variant. While Ukrainians sometimes refer to it as a "drone missile", Germany calls it a low-cost cruise missile. In recent months, Bars missiles have been manufactured in Germany at a Ukrainian-German joint venture established as part of the Build with Ukraine program. Initially, this initiative was aimed at organizing the production of weapons for Ukraine abroad.

title: Wall Street's fastest traders are building data centers and backing chip startups to stay ahead in AI
body:
High-frequency traders like Jane Street and Hudson River Trading are now racing each other for AI computing power. The biggest firms are spending billions on cloud contracts, startups, and their own data centers, Bloomberg reports. Part of the reason is that they increasingly rely on machine learning to predict market moves.
One executive estimates that compute spending is now ten to twenty times higher than it was before ChatGPT launched. XTX Markets is building a data center in Finland, and Jane Street runs one in Texas with more than 4,000 Nvidia GPUs. Hudson River spends $1 billion a year on AI, according to AI chief Iain Dunning, and signed a multiyear deal with CoreWeave. Jane Street went a different route. It invested $1 billion directly in CoreWeave and committed $6 billion to its computing services.
Jane Street also led a funding round for chip startup Etched and became the first customer for its AI chip, which is supposed to deliver more performance by running at a lower voltage. According to Bloomberg, the industry sees rising costs and fast-aging chips as real risks. Executives like Jan Boomaars, CEO of Amsterdam-based high-frequency trader Optiver, still think doing nothing is more dangerous. Ad Ad

title: Oman, South Africa discuss regional de-escalation
body:
Muscat: Sayyid Badr bin Hamad al Busaidi, Foreign Minister, received a phone call on Monday from Ronald Lamola, Minister of International Relations and Cooperation of the Republic of South Africa. During the call, the two sides underscored the relations of friendship and cooperation between the two countries. They also discussed a number of issues of mutual interest, foremost among which are the situations in the Middle East and the Gulf. The two ministers exchanged views on current developments. They also underlined the importance of supporting diplomatic efforts aimed at de-escalation, as well as regional cooperation among countries of the region to reach understandings and sustainable solutions for issues and conflicts, based on the principles of international law, respect for the sovereignty of states, and non-interference in internal affairs, in order to establish stability and security for all and to support common interests and the security of supply lines and navigation.

title: Airbus says it can deliver A400Ms to Poland before 2030
body:
Airbus could deliver A400M military transport aircraft to Poland before the end of the decade if Warsaw makes a procurement decision soon, according to the manufacturer's top executive in Europe.
Airbus Europe President Johan Pelissier told Polish news outlet RMF24 that production capacity would allow deliveries before 2030. Poland has been evaluating the A400M as it seeks to expand its airlift capability beyond its existing C-130 Hercules and C-295 fleets.
The potential acquisition is not new . Polish Deputy Defense Minister Paweł Zalewski confirmed in August that the government was negotiating a possible A400M purchase, with financing potentially available through the European Union's Security Action for Europe (SAFE) program.
Unofficial estimates have previously suggested a fleet of between eight and 15 aircraft. Polish Air Force officials have separately indicated a requirement for around 10 heavy transport aircraft.

Airbus' latest statement adds a potential timeframe to those discussions, suggesting that Poland could begin receiving the aircraft before 2030 rather than waiting until the following decade.
Poland also joined a NATO initiative in July aimed at expanding cooperation around the A400M. Belgium, Croatia, France, Germany, Spain, Turkey and the United Kingdom are also involved.
The initiative is designed to explore different levels of cooperation, including joint procurement, shared aircraft, training, maintenance and infrastructure. Poland and Croatia are the only participating countries that do not currently operate the A400M.
Participation does not prevent Poland from acquiring its own fleet. A national purchase could operate alongside multinational arrangements intended to improve aircraft availability and reduce support and training costs.
Warsaw has already held discussions with Spain and Airbus over both transport and aerial refueling capabilities. Polish officials visited Airbus facilities in Getafe in June, including the A400M maintenance center and the A330 Multi Role Tanker Transport (MRTT) conversion line.
An A400M acquisition would address Poland's heavy airlift requirement and is separate from its search for a new medium transport aircraft.
The Polish Air Force is also evaluating replacements for its older C-130 Hercules fleet, with the Embraer C-390 Millennium and Lockheed Martin C-130J Super Hercules among the aircraft associated with that requirement.
The A400M occupies a larger category, with a maximum payload of 37 metric tons (81,600 lb) and the ability to transport oversized military equipment that cannot fit inside smaller tactical transports.
Poland is simultaneously pursuing an aerial refueling capability. The country is expected to acquire four Airbus A330 MRTTs through a cooperative European procurement, giving the Polish Air Force a dedicated tanker capability as its fleet expands to include the Lockheed Martin F-35A.

title: EBOLA: The Bundibugyo Strain Does Not Show Symptoms Early In Patients, Virologist Warns
body: A United Kingdom (UK) Virologist at the University of Lancaster, Muhammed Munir, has warned of a major challenge of the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, saying the incubation period is long, so an infected person might not show clinical signs until after two weeks or more. Munir made this known during an interview on Channels Television’s The Morning Brief on Monday “One of the complex things with the Ebola virus compared to many other infections that we currently are dealing with is that it has a very long incubation period, which means that if a person is infected today, the clinical signs could turn out to be in two weeks or at the end of the three weeks’ time”. “So, because of this long incubation period, people think, oh, they have been in DRC like three months before or two weeks to three weeks before they might have not really contracted that infection from there, but because of this longer incubation period of up to two weeks, the person could still be carrying the infection but not showing the clinical signs; the clinical signs would only start coming in the second week or so”, he added. His comment comes amid the strain of Ebola detected in a 42-year-old woman in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Abuja, who was said to have returned from Uganda through Addis Ababa on October 3rd through an international flight to Abuja. The woman was said to be symptomatic four days later and was admitted to a private health facility on October 10, where she was receiving treatment and the contacts linked to her were placed under observation. In an update on Sunday, the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) said the number of contacts linked to the index case recorded had risen to 53. Munir also spoke about the debate of the index case coming from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), stating that it required questioning “However, I must say that if the person who has been considered as the index case hasn’t been to DRC and has only been to Uganda, that really raises some of the serious questions: that Uganda can be reporting the cases, but if somebody caught the infection within the country, that means that the disease is not considered free from Uganda, so the disease is still prevalent over there”. Speaking further on the breakfast show, Munir advised against infected patients feeling shy to report themselves at health centres, saying that early detection could help tackle the case. “So, one should not feel shy about accepting those facts because until we really look at those cases, we are not going to have a good handle on the infection,” he said. title: Historic Ermoupoli at 200: Hidden Corners of Syros’ Past
body: Historic Ermoupoli marks 200 years since it took its name in 1826, and a local festival chief has picked the places that tell its story. This year the international animation festival had an extra reason to celebrate. Ermoupoli, the capital of Syros, has hosted it for 19 years. For its president, lawyer Vasilis K. Karamitsanis, Syros began as a teenage love during family summer holidays. It became a lifelong bond when he and his colleague Maria Anestopoulou chose the island as the home of Animasyros. Today Anestopoulou serves as the festival’s artistic director. Why historic Ermoupoli stands apart Festival events, held with the Municipality of Syros-Ermoupoli, honoured the 1826 naming. Karamitsanis also named the landmarks that best explain the past and present of historic Ermoupoli. Its story, along with its well-preserved mansions , still lives in every building and laneway. The town offers a taste of how much more beautiful other Greek towns could be. However, unchecked development spoiled many of them. Karamitsanis also explained what makes the capital of Syros unique. “There is no other town in the country with this architectural structure and its undisturbed character. We had very beautiful towns, including the capital, which lost much of their identity with the land-for-apartments system and the rapid building of the 1960s and ’70s.” Vasilis K. Karamitsanis, Animasyros president By contrast, he said, the state protects historic Ermoupoli. Animasyros learned this first-hand while creating Animasyros Espace. The new venue behind the Metropolis will also host artist residencies. Ziller’s Town Hall and an El Greco icon At first, Karamitsanis found it hard to single out corners of the town, “because the whole of it is a monument.” Still, he chose “the supremely beautiful right atrium of the Town Hall with its mosaic.” The landmark building is the work of Ernst Ziller . Inside, outside the office of the Aegean prosecutor, stands a sculpture of the festival mascot, Animaspyros. Illustrator, comic creator and painter Petros Christoulias made it. For the anniversary, the mascot turned into the god Hermes and flew over historic Ermoupoli. Karamitsanis recommends a tour of the churches of historic Ermoupoli, which he called “a very fine chronology of its evolution.” The more lavish they are, the closer the town stood to its economic peak. Humbler churches mark times of decline. In particular, he highlights the Church of the Dormition of the Virgin. Its icon in liturgical use is a work by Domenikos Theotokopoulos, known as El Greco . Refugees from Psara brought it to Syros. A new museum in an old mansion Any journey back in time in historic Ermoupoli also calls for a visit to the new Historical Museum of Ermoupoli. It sits in the former Rethymnis mansion. State funding paid for it. Even so, Karamitsanis pointed out that the museum is an initiative of the Syros branch of the Lyceum of Greek Women . He described the branch as the second most important after Athens, based in “an excellent building.” Inside, the exhibition presents the interior of an old Syros home “in a very fine way.” He credited the curatorial work of Pavlos Chatzigrigoriou, a newcomer from Thessaloniki. Chatzigrigoriou works to preserve the heritage of the island. Resistance, famine and the Statue of Victory Many visitors may walk past a monument with powerful symbolism. The Statue of Victory stands at the end of Eleftheriou Venizelou Street, on the coastal road of historic Ermoupoli. “Syros is one of the few islands this small that had a National Resistance,” Karamitsanis said. During the Occupation , he added, the island lived through a famine like the one in Athens . Residents died of hunger because wheat and other basic goods ran short. So resistance was, quite literally, a matter of survival. Syros and the first mixed bathing in Greece Finally, the trip into the past of Syros leads to the sea. Like the whole island, it suits every season. Even when the weather rules out a swim, the waterfront mansions reward visitors. Here, Karamitsanis suggests the swimming platform at Asteria. It is where “shortly before the Second World War, the first mixed bathing in the country was allowed.” Specifically, men and women could swim at the same beach, in swimsuits rather than clothes. Women’s rights became a topic of debate in Hermoupolis very early. According to Karamitsanis, Syros was where the need for two years of compulsory schooling for women was first discussed. That progressive spirit spread to leisure as well. Mixed bathing started in France, and close ties with France helped it reach historic Ermoupoli before anywhere else in Greece. Today the Asteria platform blends “everyday lifestyle and understated cosmopolitanism” with “a piece of hidden history,” Karamitsanis said. When a ship passes, its waves sweep away your towel, your shoes and everything else. “It is a very beautiful place,” he concluded. title: Kazakhstan, Belgium Look to Expand Cooperation Following Royal State Visit, Kazakh Ambassador Says
body: The Astana Times provides news and information from Kazakhstan and around the world. ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Belgium are looking to expand cooperation in trade, transport, critical minerals, education and advanced technologies, following the recent state visit of Belgium’s King Philippe and Queen Mathilde to Kazakhstan, Kazakhstan’s Ambassador to Belgium and Luxembourg and Head of Mission to the European Union Roman Vassilenko said at a briefing in Brussels. Kazakhstan’s Ambassador to Belgium Roman Vassilenko outlines prospects for expanding Kazakhstan-Belgium and Kazakhstan-EU cooperation during a press briefing at the Press Club Brussels Europe. Photo credit: MFA. Speaking at the Press Club Brussels Europe, Vassilenko outlined the outcomes of the royal visit , which took place on Oct. 12-14, and discussed prospects for bilateral cooperation and Kazakhstan’s partnership with the EU, reported the Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ press service. The briefing brought together Deputy Director of the Central Asia and Caucasus Department at the Belgian Ministry of Foreign Affairs Gommaar Dubois, Foreign Policy Adviser to the President of the European Council Marilyn Josephson, as well as representatives of the diplomatic corps, media and expert community. Vassilenko described the first-ever state visit by a Belgian monarch to Kazakhstan as historically significant, highlighting its role in strengthening political dialogue and expanding trade and economic ties between the two countries. The ambassador outlined the visit’s outcomes, including a joint statement adopted by the two heads of state and a roadmap for cooperation for 2027-2029 signed by the two countries’ foreign ministries. A total of 40 documents were announced during the visit, including 16 commercial agreements and 22 agreements between universities and research institutions. Trade, investment cooperation and EU partnership Roman Vassilenko. Photo credit: MFA. Vassilenko highlighted opportunities to implement the agreements reached during the visit in transport and logistics, critical minerals, agriculture, healthcare, education and advanced technologies. He pointed to potential cooperation between the Port of Antwerp-Bruges and Kazakhstan’s ports of Aktau and Kuryk, as well as joint projects in critical raw materials processing, scientific research and artificial intelligence. Turning to relations with the EU, Vassilenko emphasized Kazakhstan’s role as the EU’s key trade and economic partner in Central Asia as trade between Kazakhstan and the EU exceeded $45 billion in 2025. Vassilenko also highlighted the significance of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s visit to Brussels in June and the first Central Asia-EU Summit, held in Samarkand in April 2025. Belgian and EU perspectives Dubois, representing Belgium’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, commended the outcomes of the state visit, noting its extensive political, economic and academic program. He said the participation of a 115-member Belgian delegation, alongside events held in Astana and Almaty, helped establish direct contacts between the business and scientific communities of the two countries. Dubois also highlighted the agreement between the Benelux countries and Kazakhstan on visa-free travel for holders of service passports, which is set to enter into force on Nov. 1. He said the agreement would facilitate more frequent official contacts, including with EU institutions. Foreign Policy Adviser to the President of the European Council Josephson said diversifying economic ties and strengthening connectivity remain key priorities for the EU’s partnership with Kazakhstan. She highlighted opportunities for cooperation in digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence, energy security, renewable energy, green hydrogen and critical raw materials. Josephson also emphasized the Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor, designated a flagship project under the EU’s Global Gateway initiative. Unlocking its full potential, she said, requires investment in railway and port infrastructure and logistics hubs, as well as simpler border-crossing and trade procedures. Participants also discussed next steps for implementing the agreements reached, attracting investment, improving transport connectivity and expanding cooperation between businesses, universities and research institutions in Kazakhstan and Belgium. The post Kazakhstan, Belgium Look to Expand Cooperation Following Royal State Visit, Kazakh Ambassador Says appeared first on The Astana Times .

title: Moldovan PM arrives in Kyiv to meet Zelensky, Ukrainian officials
body:
Editor's note: This story was updated with additional comments by President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Ukraine and Moldova signed a military-technical cooperation agreement on Oct. 26 during Moldovan Prime Minister Vasile Tofan's visit to Kyiv, where he met President Volodymyr Zelensky.
"We support Moldova, your sovereignty, and territorial integrity. We are always happy to help and provide support. We have very good relations and communication at the presidential level," Zelensky said .
"The agreement opens the way for an exchange of experience," Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi told reporters.
In addition to the agreement, Zelensky and Tofan discussed Ukraine and Moldova's EU accession and the security situation in eastern Moldova's Russian-occupied Transnistria region.
Tofan arrived in the Ukrainian capital alongside Infrastructure and Regional Development Minister Vladimir Bolea, Defense Minister Anatolie Nosatii, and Energy Minister Dorin Junghietu for a working visit.
Zelensky reiterated that the EU accession process of both countries should not be separated and condemned any efforts to do so.
"Moldova and Ukraine are certainly stronger when we move forward on this track together. And it is important that we carry on together, because it is fair," he said.
Tofan's visit comes after Zelensky's recent push to keep Ukraine's and Moldova's EU accession processes linked. The two countries have so far pursued EU membership together, but the arrangement could slow Moldova 's progress as it advances faster than Kyiv on reforms required for accession.
"I am in Kyiv today to reconfirm Moldova's support for our Ukrainian neighbours and friends, as well as to discuss joint projects in infrastructure, energy, and security," Tofan wrote on social media.
Ukraine proposed resuming Solidarity lanes that allow for easier trade with Europe, a lifeline for Ukrainian exports as Russia targets Black Sea ports.
Zelensky also thanked Moldova for supporting a Vertical Gas Corridor and for offering a discount on gas transit via the Trans-Balkan route.
Earlier in the day, the Moldovan prime minister and his Ukrainian counterpart Koretskyi paid tribute to fallen Ukrainian defenders at the Wall of Remembrance in Kyiv.
"The prime ministers will discuss strengthening bilateral relations, developing economic and trade cooperation, regional security, and the two countries' European path," the Moldovan government said .
According to Koretskyi, Kyiv proposed expanding cooperation with Chisinau through the demining coalition.
Ukraine and Moldova cooperate on regional security and efforts to counter Russian hybrid threats. Moldova's airspace has been violated by Russian drones on multiple occasions, while Russian attacks on Ukraine have also affected areas near the Moldovan border.
Last week, Moldovan President Maia Sandu declared a member of the Russian embassy in Moldova persona non grata after a Russian drone violated Moldova's airspace and fell near homes in the country's center.
Tofan said on Oct. 26 that Moldova's airspace had been violated more than 100 times since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, prompting Chisinau to seek Ukraine's expertise in air defense.

title: Middlesex Regiment soldier laid to rest on the Somme
body:

Private (Pte) Percy Tolliday, from Camberwell, London, buried on the Somme alongside two unknown soldiers. Identification was made through DNA testing 110 years after Pte Tolliday went missing in action during the Battle of the Somme.
The Reverend Fiona Beale CF conducts the service (Crown Copyright)
Pte Percy Tolliday, of 11th Battalion The Middlesex Regiment, was laid to rest on the Somme on 21 October 2026 alongside two unknown comrades, at a burial service organised by MOD ’s Joint Casualty and Compassionate Centre ( JCCC ), also known as the ‘War Detectives’. The service took place at the Commonwealth War Graves Commission’s ( CWGC ) Warlencourt British Cemetery.
Richard Tolliday, the great nephew of Pte Tolliday, had travelled from Atlanta, USA to attend the burial service with his wife and nephew. It was Richard who had provided the DNA sample that made identification of Pte Tolliday possible.
Richard Tolliday stands at the graveside with his wife, nephew and members of the military party (Crown Copyright)
Richard Tolliday, great nephew of Pte Tolliday said:
We are deeply grateful to the JCCC for their extraordinary dedication, expertise, and professionalism that enabled the identification of the remains of our Great Uncle, Pte Percy Tolliday, 110 years after his death in the Battle of the Somme. In 1916, Percy was a soldier but also a son and a brother. It has been an honour to be able to assist in this process and to attend his burial service that so movingly and impressively brings an appropriate recognition and closure for Percy and his family, past and present.
Pte Tolliday and the two unknown soldiers were uncovered during the installation of wind turbines near Gueudecourt. They were found lying in a shell hole, suggesting that they may have died together, possibly having been hit by the same shell. Work continues in an attempt to identify the unknown soldiers.
It has been a privilege to have played a part in the identification and burial of Pte Percy Tolliday and to have provided answers for his family. He and these two unknown soldiers were killed in the most awful conditions in heavy rain, deep mud and under continuous shelling. The worst extremity of World War 1 conditions. JCCC will continue to do all it can to work to identify Pte Tolliday’s comrades and hopefully bring further closure to other families.
The service was supported by serving soldiers from The Royal Regiment of Fusiliers, The Princess of Wales’s Royal Regiment and The Regimental Band and Corps of Drums of The Royal Welsh.
Pte Tolliday's coffin is carried to the graveside by serving soldiers of the Royal Regiment of Fusiliers (Crown Copyright)
The service was conducted by the Reverend Fiona Beale CF, Chaplain to 1st Battalion The Royal Regiment of Fusiliers.
Being the Padre to 1st Battalion The Royal Regiment of Fusiliers, I find it a deeply moving and humbling privilege to conduct the burial service for Pte Percy Tolliday and two unknown soldiers, presumed to also be of The Middlesex Regiment. It is a sacred duty and profound honour to lay to rest these World War 1 heroes who endured the unimaginable horrors of the trenches.
The graves of all three men will now be cared for by the CWGC in perpetuity.
Dr Daniel Seaton, Commemorations Case Officer at the CWGC , said:
The three casualties now laid to rest were recovered by the Commission’s specialist Recovery Unit, not far away from where today’s ceremony has taken place. I am delighted that, following research conducted by ourselves and the JCCC , Private Tolliday has been identified, and remain hopeful that it may also be possible to identify the two Unknown Soldiers in the future. All three are now remembered with honour in the Commission’s Warlencourt British Cemetery.

title: Bedfordshire soldiers laid to rest on the Western Front
body:
Pte
George McIntosh, of 8th Battalion The Bedfordshire Regiment, was laid to rest in France on 20 October 2026 alongside one of his comrades, at a burial service organised by
MOD
’s Joint Casualty and Compassionate Centre (
JCCC
), also known as the ‘War Detectives’. The service took place at the Commonwealth War Graves Commission’s (
CWGC
) Loos British Cemetery Extension.
The coffin of Pte McIntosh is carried to the graveside as his family looks on (Crown Copyright)
JCCC
Caseworker, Rosie Barron said:
It has been an honour to have met
Pte
McIntosh’s family today and to have seen him laid to rest alongside his comrade. His family has travelled a long way to be here, and this shows the depth of what these men still mean to their families even 110 years on. Their sacrifice and commitment to the cause of obtaining freedom and peace must never be forgotten.
Pte
McIntosh and the unknown soldier were some of around 100 sets of British and Canadian remains recovered during the construction of a hospital on the outskirts of Lens. They are the final British casualties from that site to be laid to rest. DNA testing, coordinated by
JCCC
, confirmed the identity of
Pte
McIntosh. Work continues to identify the unknown Bedfordshire Regiment soldier.
Ten members of
Pte
McIntosh’s family attended the burial service including his great nephew, Jeff MacIntosh, who had travelled from the North Carolina, USA to be in attendance. It was Jeff who had provided the DNA sample that made identification of
Pte
McIntosh possible.
Jeff MacIntosh, great nephew of
Pte
McIntosh said:
The work that
JCCC
and
CWGC
do is simply remarkable. While we knew that we had a great uncle George MacIntosh we knew very little about the details of his life and death in WW1. The work of
JCCC
in connecting George to us via DNA has allowed us to explore his life, what his loss meant to his mother and family, as well as gain a better understanding of the horrors of WW1. Our family sincerely thanks
JCCC
for the work that you all do. His story has now been shared with our entire clan, and we are honoured to be in attendance at the ceremony.
Pte
George McIntosh was born in 1883 in Ilford, Essex to Scottish parents. He grew up in Barnet. Before enlisting into the Army, he worked as a gardener and a florist. Having enlisted,
Pte
McIntosh was posted to 8th Battalion The Bedfordshire Regiment.
The Battle of Arras started on 9 April 1917. Following the successful capture of the high ground at Vimy Ridge by Canadian forces, the Douai Plain was open to the Allies. On the morning of 18 April 1917, 8th Battalion The Bedfordshire Regiment found themselves south of Loos-en-Gohelle. They moved into the frontline and spent the next two days fighting over the location where the new hospital is being built. It was during this fighting on 19 April 1917 that
Pte
McIntosh was killed. He was 34 years old. It is highly likely that the unknown Bedfordshire Regiment soldier was also killed during this period. As they were missing, both men would have been commemorated on the Loos Memorial.
The coffin is lowered to the grave (Crown Copyright)
The service was supported by serving soldiers from The Royal Regiment of Fusiliers, The Princess of Wales’s Royal Regiment and The Regimental Band and Corps of Drums of The Royal Welsh and was attended by staff of The Royal Anglian Regiment Headquarters. The service was conducted by the Reverend Fiona Beale CF, Chaplain to 1st Battalion The Royal Regiment of Fusiliers.
Reverend Fiona Beale CF said:
It is a privilege and an honour to be chosen to conduct the burial of
Pte
George McIntosh and this unknown soldier—known only to God—both of The Bedfordshire Regiment. The mere anticipation of standing before these World War 1 heroes’ final resting places brought an overwhelming wave of profound gratitude and solemn reverence.
The graves of both men will now be cared for by the
CWGC
in perpetuity.
David Royle, Recoveries and Ceremonies Manager at the
CWGC
, said:
> Nearly 110 years after they fell in action, and less than a mile from where they were recovered, it is a privilege to lay these two Bedfordshire Regiment soldiers to rest with the care and dignity they deserve. We are proud to have worked alongside the
JCCC
to restore Private George McIntosh’s name, and although the identity of the second soldier remains known only unto God, he is no longer lost or forgotten. Both men now rest among their comrades ensuring future generations can pay their respects and remember their stories in perpetuity.

title: Airbus to discuss GPAC fighter opportunities with BAE Systems: FT
body: Airbus and BAE Systems are set for talks over possible opportunities for the European planemaker to play a role in the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP), according to the Financial Times. The GCAP fighter jet program is currently jointly led by the United Kingdom, Italy and Japan, but could also welcome Germany into the fold, after its own fighter project with France reached the end of the line earlier this year. According to the Financial Times , talks between Airbus and the UK’s BAE Systems will take place in the following weeks, and include discussions around several options for potential collaboration. Sources told the British newspaper that uncrewed autonomous Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) would also be an area of discussion. AeroTime GCAP is a joint venture led by BAE, Leonardo and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries along with companies such as Rolls Royce, MBDA and Avio Aero. In an interview this month with Handelsblatt, Mike Schoellhorn, CEO of Airbus Defence and Space, said the company would want to take a “key role” in the project and “won’t just be making the fin or a wing”. Some industry commentary has suggested that the program could be disrupted if Berlin pushed hard for a large design role, and a collaboration would need to be carefully managed. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on October 8, 2026, that the UK was open to Germany joining GCAP. “I’ve indicated to the chancellor our openness to Germany joining GCAP,” Burnham said, during a joint press conference with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Prime Minister Burnham said he would seek to move the idea forward “in the coming period” with Italy and Japan. An alternative option for Germany and Airbus is to partner up with Sweden’s Saab which builds the Gripen jet. title: It’s About Security, Stupid!
body:
Transitioning from Ukraine to the West exposes significant shifts in perspective. My most recent reentry into Europe and the US, after a stint in Ukraine, brought to light a perceptual disconnect around one crucial issue – especially as peace talks and potential deals appear in the news. That issue is security.
Outside of Ukraine I’m often asked the question: “Would Ukrainians accept a land-for-peace deal?”
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The simple answer is: “Yes, definitely. As long as they get a real security guarantee.”
In an interview with CNN’s Christiane Amanpour aired on Thursday, Oct. 22, President Volodymyr Zelensky insisted: “The most important thing [is] security guarantees.”
Of course, the full answer to the question of “land-for-peace” is very complex.
A recent poll by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology indicated that 61 percent of Ukrainians consider handing Moscow all of eastern Ukraine’s Donbas region in exchange for security guarantees completely unacceptable.
However, like all such polls, the survey needs to minimize the contingencies surrounding any given issue. In this case, giving up the so-called “fortress belt” of cities in the remainder of the Donbas region that Ukraine still controls would be “unacceptable,” as it would require Kyiv to pull troops away from what constitutes its “Maginot line” against a Russian blitz toward Kyiv. In terms of security, such a land giveaway would be tantamount to capitulation – something obvious to Ukrainians on the ground there.
When I consider the question, I keep hearing the refrain of Bill Clinton during the 1992 US presidential elections, when he was running against the incumbent George H.W. Bush.
Bush had just won a quick war, liberating Kuwait and manhandling the Iraqi army, which was supposed to be the third strongest in the world. Yet, despite his undisputed foreign policy success, economic figures were beginning to hint at recession, and the young candidate Clinton jumped on them with the rally cry: “It’s the economy, stupid!”
Clinton’s success lay in his ability to simply focus on the obvious, rather than getting sidetracked by ancillary issues and spectacles.
In a sense, that’s how Ukrainians feel. Everything depends on security. And security for Ukrainians has never been easy.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion, Ukraine has sought three basic types of security guarantee.
The most desirable for Kyiv, at least initially, was NATO. But as Zelensky pleaded for some sort of NATO membership, it became clear that this would never happen as long as Ukraine was under attack. And even after a ceasefire, opposition to Ukraine’s full membership would be virtually insurmountable.
That left Ukraine with the hope of a watered-down alternative to NATO: separate bilateral security agreements with partners that could help in the event that any future peace deal were breached by Moscow. Preferably, the partner should be a NATO member with nuclear capabilities. (Only the US, the UK, and France fit that bill).
The key to any such agreement would be what’s referred to as an “Article 5-type” clause that would oblige the partner to come to Ukraine’s assistance in case of attack. But Article 5 is ambiguous enough to have even NATO members questioning what would happen if Russia attacked (ironically, the very scenario that NATO was designed to deter and/or defend against).
This second scenario is fraught with problems. What about foreign boots on the ground to monitor the ceasefire? What about foreign military bases in Ukraine? What about tripwires? It’s not surprising that most nations have diplomatically eschewed committing to Ukraine’s security beyond money and materiel.
The third scenario – at least from the perspective within Ukraine – is fast proving to be the only viable solution: Ensure that the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) become so strong and capable that any invasion of Ukrainian territory would be too costly for the aggressor. And this is exactly what’s happening.
As with any promising solution to an intractable problem, the positives tend to snowball with momentum. As the nature of warfare becomes increasingly determined by drones and artificial intelligence, all the world’s military powers are studying the tactics and technologies employed in Ukraine. Even NATO military officers understand that in order to defend against a hypothetical attack, Ukraine’s know-how – acquired and developed out of necessity – is essential.
At this stage, though, Ukraine still can’t go it alone. Kyiv is currently parlaying its battlefield experience and willingness to sacrifice blood into a flood of treasure coming from the rich countries to its west. Security autonomy will take time, so Ukrainians have little choice but to hold the line, have faith in the AFU, and hope for the best in the West.
As Zelensky continually insists: It’s about security. All the mineral and gas deals, all the talk of Donbas lines and territorial integrity, these are sideshows – important only inasmuch as they determine Ukraine’s security.
The Donbas issue – which US Secretary of State Marco Rubio disingenuously claimed on Oct. 22 was what “the war is about” – offers a perfect example:
It’s not that Ukraine is so attached to some holy notion of land or the mineral wealth beneath it. Zelensky has publicly repeated that he would accept a ceasefire on the current line of contact. But to give away land Russia has been unable to grab in 12 years for the sake of a dubious guarantee? That would be worse than naiveté – it would be disastrously criminal negligence on the part of Ukraine’s negotiators – especially as US President Donald Trump and his cohort, most notably Elon Musk, are so quick to double-cross friends for the sake of personal (not even national) interest.
As such, any proposed peace deal, if it is to be taken seriously, must offer real security guarantees. Given the current climate of distrust, “Article 5-like” guarantees will and should be met with a politely diplomatic “Thank you very much, but…” followed by hardnosed inquiries into details of commitments and tripwires.
The view from Ukraine, now nearly five full years into Moscow’s failed full-scale invasion, is rather clear. From the front line, where Russians are dying at a 10:1 ratio in many places and being fed into a drone buzzsaw in a maniacal effort to claim ruined Donbas villages as “conquered,” to cities such as Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa, where inhabitants are bracing for a winter rife with power outages and ballistic missile attacks, no one is talking about surrendering, which is what Trump is effectively trying to coerce.
With each passing day, Ukraine’s only real security hope grows in strength, and many of its European partners have begun to realize that in terms of security they cannot do without a strong Ukraine.
Ultimately, though, Ukrainians know their security will hinge on two ineluctable facts – one biological, the other political – all dictators die, and all empires disintegrate.
This is a generational fight that can’t be framed by American or European election cycles. And the existential security problem Ukraine has with Moscow is centuries old.
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.

title: Poultry products to witness 15% rise in prices ahead of Christmas – farmers warn
body: The Greater Accra Poultry Farmers Association is projecting at least a 15 per cent increase in poultry prices ahead of the Christmas festivities, citing rising costs of animal feed and imported production inputs. Chief Executive of the Association, Mohammed Ali, said the increasing cost of maize, soya and other feed ingredients, coupled with higher freight charges, is putting pressure on poultry production costs. Speaking to Joy Business during an outreach to schools in Dansoman to mark World Egg Day, he said consumers should expect some price adjustments by Christmas. “Maybe not less than 15 per cent; we must see some price change,” he said. Mr Ali explained that most of the ingredients used in poultry feed are imported, leaving local farmers exposed to international price movements and rising transportation costs. He called on the government to address the high cost of feed inputs by supporting increased local production of maize and soya. “When we are able to have an abundance locally, the feed price will surely come down. But without them, we can’t do anything about poultry feed,” he added. Meanwhile, the association is calling for stronger measures to address price disparities between poultry farmers and retailers, particularly in the egg market. Mr Ali said the difference between farm-gate prices and what consumers pay at retail outlets is excessive, with some traders allegedly adding as much as GH¢20 to the price of a crate. He disclosed that farm-gate prices currently range between GH¢40 and GH¢45, arguing that retail prices should not exceed GH¢50. “We don’t expect an egg to go beyond 50 cedis. Take or leave,” he stressed. He also called for the Ministry of Trade and Agribusiness to introduce measures to bring discipline into the market and address practices that prevent traders from selling eggs at lower prices. On the Association’s World Egg Day activities, Mr Ali said it had reached five clusters of schools in the Dansoman enclave to educate pupils on the nutritional benefits of eggs. He said the initiative was aimed at encouraging children to make egg consumption part of their daily meals. “Eggs have some special protein content for every child from zero to, say, eight that they need. And we want to inculcate this habit into their meals, for daily meals, consumption of eggs,” he said. According to him, the association distributed more than 100,000 eggs to schools as part of the exercise, adding that early education would help children develop healthy eating habits. Mr Ali also urged the association to extend the Nkokor Nkitinkiti initiative to improve its implementation and deliver greater benefits to local poultry farmers, whose production volumes have a greater impact on market supply and prices. He said targeting larger-scale farmers with support could produce more significant changes in the poultry market.

title: Nigeria temporarily free of Ebola
body: Nigeria is temporarily free of Ebola patients following the evacuation of the country’s only confirmed case to Switzerland for further medical care. According to the coordinating minister of health and social welfare, Ali Pate, the patient departed Abuja with his approval, accompanied by her spouse, who has remained asymptomatic. In a post via X, Pate said the patient’s clinical condition had improved significantly before the evacuation, adding that she was stable, conscious and able to communicate, while her laboratory test results were approaching baseline levels. However, the minister cautioned that the improvement did not necessarily mean the patient was no longer infectious, stressing that strict public health protocols remained in place.
