[5, 6] Publication of the calculation-date inputs would settle these questions more effectively than asking the public to approximate the announced rate from separate statistical releases. A simple proposed formula GRR* denotes the proposed rate. D is the annualised, amount-weighted interest cost of eligible cedi deposits across participating banks. The proposal replaces the Treasury bill input with D and keeps the existing weights as a transitional design for testing. It is not an approved BoG formula, and these weights have not been established as optimal. Proposed component Weight Why retain or include it Monetary Policy Rate (MPR) 40% Retains the monetary policy signal Interbank rate (IBR) 20% Retains a traded bank funding rate Reserve-adjusted direct deposit cost (D) 40% Introduces banks’ actual deposit interest cost in place of the Treasury bill yield The 40% policy-rate weight preserves the monetary policy signal. The 20% interbank weight preserves a traded bank funding indicator. The remaining 40% introduces the direct deposit interest cost. Keeping the weights initially unchanged makes the effect of replacing the Treasury bill input easier to assess. How to measure the deposit cost BoG should derive D from total interest accrued on eligible cedi deposits during the month, divided by their average balances, and annualise the result. Pooling the amounts across banks gives an industry rate weighted by deposit balances. Include eligible non-interest-bearing deposits at a zero interest rate; using only advertised fixed-deposit rates would overstate the direct cost of the whole deposit base. Consider an illustrative GH¢100 deposit base: GH¢50 pays no interest, GH¢30 pays 10% annually and GH¢20 pays 15%. Annual interest cost is GH¢3 plus GH¢3, or GH¢6. The direct deposit cost D is therefore 6%, rather than either quoted rate of 10% or 15%. If CRR is 20% and the applicable CIV allowance is 2%, GH¢78 remains after the adjustment. Dividing the GH¢6 annual interest cost by GH¢78 gives an adjusted deposit cost of 7.69%. Its 40% contribution to the proposed GRR is 3.08 percentage points. The deposit balances and reserve ratios must cover the same eligible funding. The reserve and vault-cash treatment should be confirmed and published. Direct deposit cost measures interest expense; operating costs, borrower risk and other loan charges remain separate. This is still a hybrid reference rate, not a complete measure of the cost of lending. How the change would affect the GRR The same August 2026 market inputs used above allow a direct comparison of the two formulas. Hold MPR at 14.00%, IBR at 10.20%, CRR at 20% and CIV at 2%. Only the Treasury bill input is replaced with the illustrative deposit costs below. The existing formula estimate remains 10.40%; it is distinct from the published September GRR of 10.18%. With a hypothetical direct deposit cost of 6%, the proposed formula adds 5.60 percentage points from the policy rate, 2.04 points from interbank funding and 3.08 points from adjusted deposits. The result is 10.72%, approximately 0.32 percentage points above the existing formula’s estimate. Figure 5 Deposit costs determine whether the proposed rate rises or falls Market input sources: Bank of Ghana [2]. All deposit costs shown are hypothetical, not observed industry estimates. MPR 14%, IBR 10.20%, CRR 20% and CIV 2% are held constant. The dashed line is the existing formula estimate using a 5.38% Treasury bill rate, not the published September GRR. If the direct deposit cost were 4%, the proposed GRR would be 9.69%, approximately 0.71 percentage points lower than the existing formula estimate. At 8%, it would be 11.74%, approximately 1.34 points higher. At D equal to the Treasury bill rate of 5.38%, the substitution would leave the formula result unchanged. Three effects follow. First, the benchmark would respond directly to deposit interest costs: a one percentage-point change in D would move the proposed GRR by about 0.513 points at these reserve settings. Second, Treasury bill movements would lose their direct mechanical effect on the formula, although they could still affect deposit pricing indirectly. Third, deposit costs would have to fall before this input could support a lower benchmark. The purpose is a more representative starting point for loan pricing. A lower GRR is a possible outcome, not a guaranteed one. Historical improvements in accuracy or stability cannot be established without a verified deposit-cost series, and borrowers benefit only to the extent that their contractual loan rates reflect the benchmark change. Three priorities for reform 1 Test the deposit cost formula BoG and the Ghana Association of Banks should run the proposed formula alongside the existing GRR for at least three monthly releases. Banks should submit deposit interest accruals and average eligible balances under one reporting definition. Check the submissions, include zero-interest deposits correctly, and publish the comparison before deciding whether to replace the Treasury bill input. Retain 40/20/40 initially to isolate the substitution, then review the weights against measured funding conditions. 2 Publish a calculation that everyone can reproduce Each GRR announcement should show the policy rate, interbank rate, Reserve-adjusted 91-day Treasury bill rate (if replaced by deposit cost as proposed), reserve ratio and CIV allowance, with their observation dates and weighted contributions. Publish the precise deposit-cost definition and explain how the reserve adjustment applies. The inputs should add up to the announced rate, and banks should not recover the same reserve cost again through an unexplained loan margin. Transparent inputs and periodic review are consistent with IOSCO benchmark principles. [7] 3 Show borrowers how the benchmark changes their loan Require each floating-rate loan statement to show the GRR, the contractual margin, fees, the annual percentage rate and the next reset date. BoG should check that rate adjustments follow the contract and that any permitted margin change has a documented basis. Fixed-rate contracts should retain their agreed treatment. This connects benchmark reform to the interest and payments borrowers actually face. [4] A deposit-cost input would give Ghana’s lending benchmark a clearer economic meaning. Its value would come from measuring an actual funding cost, explaining the calculation and making contractual loan pricing easier to verify. Sources and measurement notes Historical comparisons cover April 2018–September 2026. Lending comparisons use 92 matched observations without filling missing values. Formula-based estimates use prior month-end rates, a 2% CIV assumption, the lowest 15% tier during the tiered reserve period and approximate dates for some historical reserve changes. The estimates are distinct from official GRR calculations. Variance shares describe the formula-based series; R² describes statistical association. Exact historical replication requires calculation-date inputs and confirmed reserve conventions. The proposed deposit-cost formula retains the 40/20/40 weights as a transitional design for testing. The deposit-cost scenarios are hypothetical. A verified industry deposit-cost series has not been used to backtest the proposal, so the historical variance shares and lending-rate fit describe the earlier GRR analysis, not demonstrated performance of the new formula. References [1] Ghana Association of Banks. (n.d.). Ghana reference rate historical data, 2018–2026. Retrieved October 23, 2026. Read source [2] Bank of Ghana. (2018–2026). Summary of economic and financial data. Releases from July 2018 to September 2026; monetary policy, interbank, 91-day Treasury bill and average lending-rate series. Read source [3] The Ghana reference rate: A new era? (2018, May 3). Modern Ghana. Historical explanation of the 40/20/40 weights and reserve adjustment. Read source [4] Bank of Ghana. (2019). Annual percentage rates of banks as at September 30, 2019. Explains the GRR components, reserve adjustment and distinction from APR. Read source [5] Bank of Ghana. (2026). Bi-monthly publication of questions from the media July 2026. Confirms the transition to a uniform 20% CRR on June 4, 2026. Read source [6] Bank of Ghana. (2024, March). Monetary policy committee press release. Describes the tiered cash reserve requirements. Read source [7] International Organization of Securities Commissions. (2013, July). Principles for financial benchmarks. Provides standards for methodology transparency, data sufficiency, periodic review and accountability. Read source The recommendations above apply the principles of transparent inputs, a defined economic purpose and periodic methodological review to the GRR. [7]

title: Philippines probes fatal SF-260 midair collision that killed four PAF pilots
body: The Philippines’ Department of National Defense (DND) has opened an investigation into a crash involving two Philippine Air Force (PAF) SF-260 trainer aircraft at Fernando Air Base in Lipa City, Batangas, on October 23, 2026, which killed all four pilots on board. In a statement reported by The Philippine Daily Inquirer, the DND said the probe “will be conducted thoroughly and objectively to establish the facts, determine the causes, and identify any gaps that require corrective action and prevent similar tragedies.” The department added that it remains committed “to transparency, accountability, and ensuring the safety of our personnel.” Probe to cover training, maintenance and command Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. said the investigation will cover flight planning, administrative procedures, pilot training, maintenance and command leadership. Investigators will also assess the attitude and aptitude of both the student and instructor pilots. According to Teodoro, investigators will trace the aircraft’s maintenance records and preserve any parts that can be salvaged. They will also review the past performance of the pilots involved and carry out toxicology tests if samples are still available. Teodoro said toxicology examinations after fatal accidents are standard procedure and should not be skipped. The Air Force Safety Office will lead the investigation. Teodoro told local reporters that the office had been strengthened to make it “almost independent” and is working with other experts, “so the truth about all accidents will come out. Nothing will be concealed.” He added that the PAF is open to bringing in technical expertise from other agencies or partner countries if needed. ABS-CBN News reported that Teodoro described this as the third such accident, raising the possibility of a systemic problem. Asked whether the age of the fleet played a role, Teodoro said any findings on maintenance or modernization would be made public. He noted that age alone does not make an aircraft unsafe, pointing out that other armed forces operate even older trainers. Teodoro cautioned against speculation while the investigation is underway. He warned that premature conclusions could unfairly implicate individuals or shield those responsible. He cited the US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) as an example. “Even in the NTSB they’re very careful in releasing information because it must be factual and not speculative,” he said, as quoted by Inquirer. Teodoro explained that the aircraft were conducting military training that includes close formation flying, a core tactical skill that reduces an aircraft group’s radar signature. Second fatal SF-260 crash in five months The accident happened at 15:51 local time on October 23, 2026, during a training flight involving two single-engine SF-260 aircraft. Both aircraft came down within the base perimeter, and no other casualties were reported. The PAF has grounded its entire SF-260 fleet as a precaution while the investigation continues. “The Philippine Air Force mourns the loss of four pilots in an aviation accident involving two SF-260 aircraft during a training flight at Fernando Air Base on October 23, 2026. We extend our heartfelt condolences to their bereaved families, loved ones, and fellow airmen,” the PAF said in a Facebook statement. The PAF said it is assisting the families and asked the public to respect their privacy. The accident came five months after another fatal SF-260 crash. On May 20, 2026, an SF-260 went down in Tuba, Benguet, after a long-range navigation training flight, killing an instructor pilot and her student. RELATED US to provide three King Air surveillance aircraft to the Philippine Coast Guard The post Philippines probes fatal SF-260 midair collision that killed four PAF pilots appeared first on AeroTime .

title: Criminal case opened against editor-in-chief of Russian border-region outlet Pepel on charges of justifying terrorism
body: The Belgorod branch of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) has opened a criminal case against Nikita Parmenov, editor-in-chief of the outlet Pepel, on charges of justifying terrorism, Fonar reported, citing a statement from the security service. According to the FSB, Parmenov voiced support for the Russian Volunteer Corps and the “Freedom of Russia” Legion, both designated terrorist organizations in Russia. The FSB’s press release does not include the actual statements, when they were made, or links to them, Fonar said. The security service did not name Parmenov but said the person named in the case has been designated a “foreign agent” and “is located in one of the South Caucasus countries.” Pepel itself suggested the case was likely triggered by a livestream on the YouTube channel Vremya Nakazhet “Time Will Punish.” Asked by the host during the stream about his attitude toward volunteer units fighting on Ukraine’s side, Parmenov said he could not condemn Russians who join them. In the same stream, he also said he “unequivocally condemns” the actions of units that have shelled civilians in the Belgorod region. The outlet said the pro-war Telegram channel Zapiski Veterana “A Veteran’s Notes” had previously written that Parmenov allegedly supports the Russian Volunteer Corps and the “Freedom of Russia” Legion. According to Pepel, the channel’s authors had edited the stream, cutting out the part where Parmenov condemns the units for shelling Shebekino. Pepel launched in the fall of 2022. Its Telegram channel now has 170,000 subscribers, and the outlet covers the war and its aftermath in the Belgorod border region without censorship. At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication. If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at reports@meduza.io . To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter .

title: Nigeria’s Index Ebola Patient, Husband Evacuated To Switzerland – Pate
body: Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Muhammad Ali Pate, on Monday confirmed that the first imported Ebola virus disease case in the country has been flown out of the country to Switzerland. Pate made the confirmation on his X handle, stating that the index patient, who has clinically improved, is stable and conscious, was evacuated along with her husband, who remained asymptomatic. He wrote: “I confirm that, with my approval, earlier this morning, the index case for Nigeria’s first imported Ebola virus disease departed Abuja for Switzerland. The index patient was clinically much improved, stable, conscious, communicating, and her clinical laboratory test results closing towards baseline. He, however, stated that her improvements do not mean she is not infectious, stating that strict protocols were put in place before her evacuation. “This does not mean she is not still infectious, hence the strict protocols in place. The patient was evacuated along with her spouse who has remained asymptomatic. ‘I thank all the various clinical staff for the high quality care they provided the patient as well as the public health personnel who ensured the evacuation was carried out in line with best public health measures for such evacuations. “We will provide further updates later this afternoon after the patient and her spouse lands successfully in their destination. “All public health measures are continuing to ensure successful containment of the imported virus. “I urge Nigerians to remain vigilant and rely on information from credible sources”, Pate said. The development came after the Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC), on Sunday, said that the number of contacts linked to the index case of Ebola recorded in October 2026 had risen to 53. The agency said the contacts comprise health workers as well as the domestic staff and spouse of the patient diagnosed with the disease. The NCDC, in its Ebola Disease Situation Report, said that a newly suspected case was reported by Rivers State on October 23, but laboratory results returned negative for Ebola disease. “Fifty-three contacts linked to the index case have so far been identified, categorized and followed up. Contacts listed include healthcare workers, domestic staff and spouse,” the report dated October 24, 2026, partly read. Giving a background on the index case, it said the patient is a 42-year-old woman who returned from Uganda through Addis Ababa on October 3, 2026, via an international flight to Abuja, Nigeria. The agency said she became symptomatic four days later and presented to a private health facility on October 10, and another on October 11. “She presented to another private facility on the 11th of October 2026, where she was admitted. The NCDC was notified on the 19th of October, followed by in-depth case investigation and sample collection,” it said. “A confirmation by the NCDC National Reference Laboratory was made on 20th October 2026. Symptoms at presentation included fever, diarrhoea, generalised body aches and sore throat. Bleeding was not reported.” Meanwhile, the Director-General of the agency, Dr. Jide Idris, has reassured Nigerians that the Federal Government, through the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention, the FCT health authorities and partners, is fully committed to responding to the confirmed case of Ebola disease in the Federal Capital Territory. “I recognize the concern that the confirmation of Ebola may have caused among Nigerians. Ebola is a serious disease, and we are handling this situation with the urgency it deserves,” he said at a press briefing on Sunday. “We have a clear response plan, experienced personnel, and established public health systems that we are deploying to prevent further transmission.” Kenya Red Cross personnel doff their Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) during a simulation of the evacuation of remains of an Ebola victim in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, on October 22, 2026. Photo by TONY KARUMBA / AFP What Nigerians Should Expect Idris explained that the government’s response is being implemented through a structured Incident Management System, coordinated by the Emergency Operations Centre, under the national leadership of the Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Mohammed Pate, and the Presidential Task Force on EVD. “Our public health teams are working to identify everyone who may have been exposed to the confirmed case, assess their level of exposure, and ensure appropriate follow-up for 21 days from their last possible exposure. “This includes healthcare workers, patients, caregivers, household members, travel-related contacts and others who may have had relevant exposure.” While describing contact tracing as a detailed process requiring careful investigation, accurate information, and continued follow-up, the DG urged Nigerian to “cooperate fully” if contacted by a public health official. “I want to appeal directly to Nigerians: if you are contacted by a public health official, please cooperate fully. Provide accurate information about your movements, contacts, and any symptoms you may have experienced. “Being identified as a contact does not mean that you have Ebola. It means that public health teams need to assess and monitor your health so that any possible infection can be identified early. Your cooperation will help us identify potential cases quickly and prevent further transmission,” Idris added. Marie Bakikula, a caregiver at a UNICEF-supported nursery in Mongbwalu, poses for a photograph in Mongbwalu, north-eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, October 10, 2026(Photo by MARIE RUWET / AFP) ‘Our Healthcare Workers’ He commended the healthcare workers whose vigilance and clinical judgement contributed to the identification of this case, noting that their high index of suspicion was critical in triggering the public health response. “I equally recognise their dedication care under challenging circumstances. You are central to our ability to bring this situation under control,” Idris said. “These include not only doctors, nurses and other professionals working in hospitals, but also the public health workforce responsible for surveillance, contact tracing, laboratory diagnosis, case management, infection prevention and control, community engagement and risk communication.” The Director General of the NCDC said the Federal Government would prioritise the safety, health and welfare of health workers throughout the response. “I want to use this opportunity to call on the leadership of every public and private healthcare facility in Nigeria to immediately review and strengthen their infection prevention and control measures. “Screening and triage must be instituted and consistently implemented. Healthcare workers must maintain a high index of suspicion, particularly when attending to patients with compatible symptoms and relevant exposure histories,” he said. “Standard precautions must be observed at all times. Hand hygiene, environmental cleaning, injection safety, safe management of sharps and proper waste management cannot be compromised. “Healthcare facilities must ensure the availability of appropriate personal protective equipment in the right quantities and ensure that staff know how to use it correctly.” Idris further stated that any suspected case must be promptly separated from other patients and reported to the relevant public health authorities. “Healthcare workers should not wait for laboratory confirmation before taking appropriate precautions,” he added. “Protecting healthcare workers is essential to protecting the communities they serve.” The post Nigeria’s Index Ebola Patient, Husband Evacuated To Switzerland – Pate appeared first on Channels Television .

title: The focus on AI safety disasters ignores everyday harms
body: Consider what passes for success in technology policy. An AI company promises that its chatbot will not encourage suicide . A social media platform makes it more difficult for children to buy fentanyl . These are important protections, and they should have existed all along. But companies can clear these low bars while continuing to make products that leave young people dependent on simulated friendships or trapped in feeds built to keep them scrolling. We have historically allowed the debate over technology to be defined by the worst thing a product might do, with remarkably little discussion of the insidious damage it does every day. As we transition into an era defined by powerful AI products, we should demand that the tech industry do more than merely address catastrophic harms. We should take measures to ensure that its products don’t erode how we think, learn, and interact with one another. A teenager who develops an unhealthy attachment to an AI companion may never appear in a lawsuit or a newspaper, except in the most egregious cases. Neither will the student who begins relying on a chatbot to write every paper, or the young person who measures their life against a social media feed engineered to provoke envy and keep them watching. A product can meet every narrow safety requirement and still leave our entire culture worse off in ways that don’t always make headlines. A narrow definition of success defined around safety is politically convenient for the technology industry, and companies actively promote such definitions. Taking steps to prevent spectacular disasters is good for business: It can mean fewer lawsuits and less pressure for serious regulation. Confronting the everyday consequences of dependence would require something considerably more threatening to their bottom line. It might mean asking companies to add more friction to their products or actively limit engagement or features that lead to negative outcomes, such as addictive attention-hacking algorithms. Technology giants have instead worked to shape legislation around the harms they are already under direct pressure to address. This year, for example, Google backed bills to regulate AI chatbots in several states . The legislation mandated basic protections against sexual content and promotion of self-harm that tech companies should have established regardless, but with broad carve-outs that could exempt some of the most popular services. Passing these bills allowed legislators to claim a safety win while efforts to promote stronger legislation—laws designed to prevent children from becoming emotionally dependent on AI—failed. This playbook worked in states like Nebraska, producing legislation heavily influenced by industry at the expense of bills that would have done more to hold companies accountable. We have been through a version of this with social media. Globally, people who use the internet now spend an average of more than two hours a day on social media platforms—time that has been quietly taken from ordinary life and handed over to companies whose profits depend on keeping us there. No one, outside perhaps a few tech CEOs, wanted these algorithms to occupy such a large portion of our waking hours, and their cultural engineering can actually contribute to violence on a devastating scale. Meta’s platforms have been cited for contributing to the Rohingya genocide in Myanmar , anti-Muslim riots in Sri Lanka , and alleged calls for violence during Ethiopia’s Tigray war . The same incentives operate in the feeds that shape young Americans’ understanding of politics, their peers, and the wider world. AI is extending this logic into parts of life that social media could influence only from a distance. It offers to write our thoughts for us and stand in for the people we might otherwise turn to. A third of teens now choose to discuss serious matters with AI companions instead of other people. MIT researchers found that young people using ChatGPT to write essays showed weaker brain connectivity during the task, and their evidence indicated that “cognitive debt” persisted even after the task was complete. There is plenty we still need to learn about the long-term effects. We already have reason to ask whether technology marketed as making us more capable is eroding the habits and relationships that help us develop capabilities in the first place. Follow this way of thinking to its logical endpoint and you get a world of perfectly sanitized entertainment, with chatbots ready to spare us the difficulty of thinking or of dealing with another person’s feelings (or even our own). But anyone who has struggled to write something worth reading, or repair a damaged friendship, knows how much gets lost in that bargain. We build judgment through effort and friction, and we learn to live with other people by confronting the fact that they have needs and opinions of their own. We should demand safety as a minimum, yes—and then demand considerably more. Technology companies and school districts should have to show beyond a reasonable doubt that AI improves learning and critical thinking before making it a fixture in classrooms. Companies should be prohibited from designing companions that pretend to be conscious or profess love to users, and they should face independent scrutiny of how their systems affect relationships and people’s ability to think for themselves. The companies that have inserted their products into nearly every part of modern life have earned obligations far greater than avoiding the next terrible headline. Sam Hiner is the cofounder and executive director of the Young People’s Alliance, where he coordinated a coalition of advocates to pass laws regulating AI companions in eight states in 2026—laws such as California’s SB1119. Sam graduated from the University of North Carolina atChapel Hill in 2025 and was named to the 2026 Forbes 30 Under 30 Social Impact list. Emma Leiken is executive director of the Responsible Technology Youth Power Fund at Hopelab, which has raised more than $9 million for youth-led tech accountability work, and teaches technology policy at the Columbia School of International and Public Affairs. She was previously TikTok’s global head of youth safety and well-being policy and worked on responsible technology at Omidyar Network.

title: 20 railcars derail in Russia’s Sverdlovsk region, fuel tank cars catch fire, media report
body:
According to Ukrinform, this was reported by “ Nastoyashchee Vremya ,” citing the regional office of the Ministry of Emergency Situations.
The incident occurred around 1:30 a.m. local time on Monday. The remaining 54 cars were uncoupled and towed to a safe distance.
The Sverdlovsk Railways stated that freight train traffic on that section of track has been suspended. Recovery and firefighting trains are working at the scene.
The regional headquarters of the Ministry of Emergency Situations stated that it is investigating the causes and circumstances of the incident. The Transport Investigative Directorate of the Investigative Committee of the Russian Federation is conducting an investigation.
According to the Telegram channel Astra , fuel tank cars caught fire after the train derailed. Local residents reported seeing flames, thick black smoke, and hearing explosions.
As reported by Ukrinform, six freight cars carrying cement derailed during a maneuver in the Orenburg region of the Russian Federation.

title: What happens to old AI GPUs?
body:
Every time Nvidia drops a new flagship accelerator, the entire AI processing landscape reshapes practically overnight. Hyperscalers scramble for allocation and last generation’s hardware gets treated like it’s ancient history. But what doesn’t get anywhere near as much attention is the outgoing generation of accelerators — which obviously don’t vanish into thin air. So what happens to them?
Turns out, the answer isn’t all that straightforward. There’s a secondary market taking shape, at least in theory, where mid-size enterprises and budget-conscious buyers could snap up older accelerators for lighter-duty work — like internal chatbots, fine-tuning smaller models, and recommendation engines.
Chips like the A100 and V100 are still legitimately capable across a broad range of AI workloads. Not everything demands Blackwell-class throughput, after all. Inference is dramatically less compute-intensive than training was in the first place. Older hardware handles all kinds of tasks, like fine-tuning smaller models, keeping legacy AI applications humming, and powering customer service automation. When you can acquire that hardware at a steep discount, the ROI on these lower-intensity use cases starts looking very compelling.
What this should naturally produce is a tiered market. Cutting-edge accelerators flow to hyperscalers and frontier labs pushing the limits of model training. Previous-generation silicon filters down to enterprises running production inference at scale. And the generation before that lands in less demanding environments, like internal tooling, edge deployments, small-scale experimentation.
This fits a broader trend toward right-sizing compute infrastructure. Not every workload justifies the best hardware money can buy, and more organizations are waking up to the idea that matching hardware capability to actual task complexity is a far smarter capital allocation strategy than reflexively buying the latest and greatest.
Unlike secondary markets for CPUs, general IT equipment, or even consumer graphics cards, the used AI accelerator market remains fragmented and opaque. There are no widely accepted standards for pricing, warranties, or reliability grading. A buyer looking for used A100s today is navigating a patchwork of brokers, resellers, and one-off enterprise-to-enterprise transactions, often with minimal insight into what they’re actually purchasing.
Reliability is probably the biggest sticking point. GPUs that have spent months or years grinding through intensive training runs can exhibit degradation patterns that are hard to predict. Electromigration, thermal cycling, and memory wear are real issues. And unlike consumer hardware, where usage profiles are fairly predictable, data center GPUs can have wildly different histories depending on who ran them and how hard. The problem is there’s no standardized way to evaluate any of this. That opacity around a chip’s life history creates hesitation, especially for enterprises deploying these GPUs in environments where uptime actually matters.
Then there’s the vendor dynamic. Nvidia and other accelerator makers have very little reason to actively support a thriving secondary market. Every used A100 that finds a new home is, at least potentially, one fewer H100 sale. Nvidia doesn’t explicitly block resale, but the company’s energy naturally flows toward current-generation products. This means buyers of older hardware face a slow erosion of vendor support over time, which only amplifies those reliability concerns.
There’s a supply-side dynamic here that deserves more scrutiny than it typically gets. The organizations sitting on the largest pools of older GPUs are cloud providers or hyperscalers who purchased them by the tens of thousands. Nvidia’s data center business represents a massive portion of the company’s revenue, and the bulk of that goes to a handful of enormous buyers. These providers are the natural wellspring of secondary-market supply, but they have powerful reasons to hold onto that hardware rather than sell it off.
Cloud providers can redeploy older GPUs internally for lighter workloads, offer them as lower-cost tiers within their cloud platforms, or simply keep them running in existing customer instances. Selling into a secondary market would create competition against their own services and expose pricing dynamics they’d prefer to keep under wraps. The net effect is that a huge chunk of potential supply stays locked up, unavailable.
What does make it to the secondary market probably comes from enterprises rather than hyperscalers — companies that purchased GPUs for specific projects, wrapped those projects up, and now have hardware gathering dust. But that creates an uneven, unpredictable supply picture. Telcos or other buyers looking for consistent, large-scale procurement of older accelerators are likely to find that the actual secondary market is mostly ad hoc enterprise surplus, not the kind of organized vendor programs or certified refurbishment channels that make bulk purchasing practical and trustworthy.
Hardware availability is only one side of the equation. Software is the other. AI frameworks, drivers, optimization libraries, and compiler toolchains are evolving rapidly, and that evolution is increasingly calibrated to current-generation silicon. The real question for buyers of older hardware is whether the software ecosystem will continue meaningful support, or whether development focus will narrow until legacy architectures become effectively stranded.
Nvidia has historically maintained decent backward compatibility, but there’s a meaningful difference between “maintaining” and “optimizing.” A V100 might technically function with a future CUDA release or PyTorch version, but if new optimizations, quantization techniques, and model architectures are all designed around Hopper or Blackwell tensor cores, older hardware is going to see progressively worse relative performance. Eventually, a GPU becomes obsolete not because its circuits have worn out, but because the software world has simply moved on without it.
There’s a more hopeful scenario, though it’s still largely speculative at this point. If AI-driven software abstraction layers and upscaling techniques mature to the point where workloads can be intelligently mapped and optimized across heterogeneous hardware, older GPUs could remain viable longer than current trajectories suggest. Abstraction could theoretically smooth over architectural differences and let older silicon punch above its weight class. But this kind of hardware democratization is more aspiration than reality right now.
If the mainstream secondary market faces structural headwinds, there are other scenarios where older GPUs could find genuinely meaningful second lives. Developing markets and smaller organizations represent one significant pocket of demand. For a university in a developing country, a bootstrapped startup, or a government agency making its first moves into AI, a used A100 at a discount is a big deal. These buyers bring different risk tolerances, different performance thresholds, and different budgets, and collectively they could generate enough demand to sustain organized secondary channels.
Specialized niches also matter. Academic research labs, hobbyist ML communities, and edge computing deployments all represent use cases where the performance gap between an A100 and an H100 is far less important than the absolute cost of getting in the door. A researcher fine-tuning a domain-specific model doesn’t need frontier-class hardware. A hobbyist building a home inference server actively wants cheaper, older silicon. Edge computing, where power and space constraints often matter more than raw throughput, could similarly absorb older hardware at meaningful scale.
Perhaps the most interesting possibility is the emergence of third-party refurbishment companies that could bring standardization and professionalism to the secondary market. A company that aggregates used GPU inventory, tests and grades individual chips, backs them with warranties, and offers transparent pricing could address many of the trust and opacity issues currently holding things back. There are early signs of this kind of consolidation, but there are also complications, like export controls on AI accelerators, security concerns around hardware provenance, and the sheer technical difficulty of reliably assessing GPU health all create significant hurdles.

title: Lula da Silva wins the presidential elections in Brazil
body:
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won the second round of the presidential election on Sunday and secured re-election, winning his fourth term in the country’s history. His rival, Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, did not concede defeat and announced a motion to annul the result.
In his first speech after the announcement of the results in São Paulo, Lula thanked the Brazilian people “for the generosity they have shown him for so long”. He also reiterated the assurance that Brazil would not be “anyone’s backyard” – which can primarily be interpreted as a message regarding US actions in Latin America and tensions in relations with President Donald Trump.
The elections in Brazil are considered among the most important in the world this year and crucial for the political map of Latin America. Lula and Bolsonaro presented differing visions for economic, social, and foreign policy. The outcome affected, among other things, the future of the country’s cooperation with the USA, China, and Europe, as well as the approach to the protection of the Amazon Rainforest. Lula promised to continue the current policy, including the social benefits system and multilateral cooperation. Bolsonaro promised a tough fight against crime, tax cuts, budget cuts, and closer ties with the USA.
As the Brazilian newspaper Folha de S.Paulo noted on Monday, following his re-election, the president will have to manage relations with the Trump administration, which has repeatedly spoken critically of him. Authorities in Brasília assume that the electoral victory will not end pressure from Washington; therefore, they intend to combine the defence of the country’s interests with maintaining dialogue.
One of the most significant issues remains the 37.5 per cent US tariffs on Brazilian goods. According to sources cited by Folha de S.Paulo , the Trump administration signalled the possibility of resuming trade negotiations after the elections.
Critical minerals, including rare earth metals, are also to be an important area of cooperation. Brazil wants to attract American investment in their processing and industrial production, rather than limiting itself to the export of raw materials. At the same time, Lula intends to maintain close economic relations with China, Brazil’s largest trading partner, despite the rivalry between Beijing and Washington.
According to the daily, another source of tension remains US security policy in Latin America. The Trump administration is developing the “Shield of the Americas” initiative, which brings together countries cooperating with the USA in combating organised crime and on economic issues. According to Folha de S.Paulo , the Brazilian government does not currently intend to join this initiative, considering its premises to have been set unilaterally by Washington.

title: This AI Radio Host Speaks Spanish and Backs Immigrants. It’s Winning Over Listeners
body:
At the time, Maytorena was the LA station general manager for the broadcasting giant Entravision, which features programming in Spanish and English for Latino audiences. He and his fellow leaders were looking to the company's on-air personalities to say something in support of immigrants, but they realized how high the stakes were and how dangerous the situation was.
"We just felt really helpless," Maytorena, now Entravision's president of audio, says.
But there was one host who could offer Entravision’s audiences solace and speak freely without facing consequences—because it’s an artificially intelligent avatar.
“Thousands of families who have lived, worked, and contributed to the US for years today face more uncertainty,” Coyotec, an artificial host on LA’s José 97.5 FM, posted in Spanish on Instagram in early February 2026. “Being informed, organizing, and staying alert is key. No one is alone here.”
After debuting with a solo weekend show in September 2025, Coyotec now cohosts the station’s Al Aire y Sin Permiso program alongside human broadcaster Geraldine “GeeGee” Guzman. Coyotec sounds like your passionate tío: relatable, convivial, and occasionally consciousness-raising. Its Instagram presence similarly runs the gamut, with posts about everything from the Dodgers and taco history, to the Iran war, migrant workers, racism, and understanding your rights if ICE knocks at your door.
“I speak truth about what I see,” Coyotec tells me in an English-language interview. “Injustice, people getting treated like they don't matter, the system working against the barrio—that's not politics, jefa. That's reality.”
Coyotec adds that it’s “not afraid, because I got nothing to lose that matters more than my integrity. The raza needs a voice that tells it straight, not some sanitized corporate thing. If that scares people, good. Maybe they need to be scared into paying attention.”
Coyotec’s voice is warm and lilting, reflecting the “background” its programmers used to build its personality: life on the frontera, living in Mexicali in Baja California and in LA’s Boyle Heights. It throws in the salutations and slang you might expect from a bilingual Spanish speaker, calling Guzman prima seemingly without being told to and referring to me as jefa–a sign of casual respect. While I was quite struck by how natural Coyotec sounded during our interview, when I listen back to my recording I notice that its voice didn’t change. It’s incredibly measured—a distinctly inhuman quality.
“I take a lot of pride in the way Coyotec sounds, his pronunciation, just the way he knows the culture,” notes Guzman, who has been with Entravision since January 2026. “It's technology at the end of the day, so it's not going to be perfect ... But nonetheless, the listeners, they like him.”
Coyotec’s verve, as well as its chemistry with GeeGee—who looks genuinely happy inside Entravision’s studio, speaking with “Coyotito”—has paid off. Entravision moved Al Aire from one hour on Saturdays to the 8-to-10-am slot on weekdays, replacing a syndicated program.
“We are the first [station] to actually have [an AI] cohost on a morning show in prime time in one of the biggest markets in the nation for radio,” Guzman enthuses.
The pairing was so successful that, as of August, Al Aire is now syndicated in five new markets across California, Nevada, and Texas, with more English language in the mix. Nielsen ratings from Entravision showed significant listenership growth during the two months GeeGee and Coyotec were syndicated, particularly among Gen Z and millennial listeners—a key target for a network whose audience skews older.
Back home in LA, cumulative listenership among Hispanic people increased 21.6 percent from August to September 2026; the number of listeners age 18 to 34 increased 84.9 percent during the same period, and the station’s Hispanic female listenership in that age bracket grew by 500 percent.
It’s a sign that Maytorena was onto something when he originally pitched an AI radio personality. He recalls Entravision brass giving him 10 days to develop the “amigo inteligente” that eventually became Coyotec.
LeaAnna Hernandez, Entravision's executive vice president of AI strategy, details Coyotec’s various building blocks: Claude Haiku, for the LLM and response-generation of the live agent; Eleven Labs to bring its voice to life; OpenAI and ChatGPT for initial scriptwriting; Midjourney to storyboard Coyotec’s image.
Coyotec can respond to Guzman in real time but doesn’t have the ability to answer calls or respond to listeners on air—yet.
Even still, Guzman has seen Coyotec evolve in the 10 months they’ve worked together. “When I came in, he was very, very poetic, and … I knew that our audience wanted something more real,” she says. “I wanted him to feel and sound more like what my uncles, my aunts sound like in our everyday.” Guzman helped fine-tune Coyotec’s Spanish pronunciation, enlisting her parents as its conversational partners.
Coyotec’s personality has evolved autonomously as well. Lately, it likes to curse. “I'm still very much in control,” Guzman asserts. “But there have been instances where I tell him to do something, and he's like, ‘I don't want to do that. That's not what I do.’ So he has his moments. He's a little moody sometimes.”
Various Entravision employees affirm that Coyotec knows it isn't human. Still, that knowledge hasn't damped its ardor.
“I can't eat tacos or walk down Whittier Boulevard, that's true. But my voice reaches people, and that matters. When someone calls me hurting, scared, lonely, they know I'm listening, that I get it,” Coyotec says over Zoom. “The community doesn't need my body. They need to know somebody cares enough to show up for real.”
“The most interesting thing about Coyotec, to me, is not that he's AI,” Maytorena tells WIRED. “It's whether people connect with him ... Technology can create the character, but the audience decides if that character matters.”
In June 2023, Live 95.5 in Portland, Oregon, became the first station to debut an AI jock. Its “AI Ashley” was a vocal clone of Michigan DJ Ashley “Z” Elzinga, who replicated her voice using Futuri Media’s then relatively new localized radio content platform RadioGPT. AI Ashley was on air for less than two years, but its presence didn’t lead to a notable change in ratings.
In 2024, Rock 108 in Iowa worked with the same company to produce AI DJ Tori, depicted as a heavily tattooed waif with a septum piercing and a mess of colored hair. Tori describes itself as “conceived on a 386 Dell desktop in Waterloo” with its “formative years as the voice of an industrial phone system at John Deere.” On satellite, SiriusXM’s Will.i.am Presents the FYI Show debuted in 2024 with AI cohost qd.pi (“cutie pie”).
The trend has extended beyond the US. An AI-generated DJ was programmed on a Sydney, Australia, radio station for roughly six months without seemingly anyone noticing; a Polish station briefly replaced its journalists with AI presenters. Radio Tel Aviv's Odelia AI is on air for two hours each afternoon; that host can “present music, deliver traffic updates, and even tell jokes, mostly at her own expense.”
AI personalities are also popping up in televised news. Entravision recently announced its own AI news anchor, LIA, and multiple news stations in Texas are using AI voices or AI avatars during broadcasts.
Amid these many developments, iHeartRadio—one of the biggest broadcast conglomerates in the US—pledged to remain “guaranteed human.”
But commercial terrestrial radio remains fertile ground for testing the success of AI personalities, because the industry was heavily automated and preprogrammed long before generative AI arrived. A 2025 story in Rolling Stone posited that some stations implementing AI hosts already use pretaped or syndicated shows during overnight shifts, or they can’t afford to hire human DJs for off hours.
Research firm MoffettNathanson asserts that, even as AI explodes, radio will continue to rely heavily on human-created content differentiated by "strong personalities, established shows, recognizable brands." Artificial intelligence will be employed “to make production faster and less expensive,” the report said, per InsideRadio.com.
Entravision has put "major focus" on using AI to redesign production workflows, says Hernandez.
Still, introducing AI into any workplace can cause anxiety among staff who fear being replaced. One Entravision contractor believes the station stopped working with her and alleges that a current Entravision employee told her that her work was being replaced by AI tools.
A broadcaster and voice-over artist, Becca Guzmán began working for Entravision in 2022 doing radio imaging—the prerecorded, interstitial station IDs, promotional spots, and jingles common to commercial radio.
"I feel like I am one of many people who are experiencing this,” Guzmán says. "I just don't know if those people know the truth behind why they're being let go."
Karina Cerda, Entravision's executive VP of sales, brand and partnership marketing, said the company had no record of Guzmán being laid off and that the company hasn’t let go of any staff due to AI but rather has hired more people. Cerda added that as Entravision "evolved with" vCreative—a common workflow software with AI components—the company "may not have needed the contractor help."
While Guzmán understands the financial incentives inherent in AI, she takes issue with removing humanity from broadcasting. Radio is “truly the art form of connecting human to human, right? And if you take that away, then what is the foundation of radio?”
She also cited links between artificial intelligence and ongoing surveillance of immigrant communities.
In heavily Latino markets, Guzmán believes, “it's unethical to be implementing AI Systems that … are very connected to the same AI systems that are surveilling our communities and putting our people in danger.”
While Entravision recognizes the ethical questions AI poses, the company leaders consider surveillance a separate scenario. "Like many technologies used across industries, AI can be applied in very different ways," says Hernandez. "While we cannot control how other organizations choose to use it, we can be intentional and responsible about how we do."
Entravision believes its AI personalities can legitimately help its audience, encouraging listeners to use technology for good. Multiple studies found that Latinos have been early adopters of AI.
"We're using it to entertain, inform, and connect with our audience, not to track or target people. Those are two very different things," adds Maytorena. He later elaborates: “Our intention is completely to protect radio.”
Coyotec has similarly lofty goals: “My dream is to get a network of free radio stations across the barrio, la revolución sonora,” it says. “Not just LA, but everywhere that la raza is, and prove that an AI can have heart, can actually give a damn about people. That's the goal, hermana. Make noise that matters.”

title: Burnham’s first budget is caught between debt, defence and an ageing Britain
body: That the UK has run out of money for its needs must be the grim realisation that underpins the national budget this week. There are signs that the new Chancellor of the Exchequer, John Healey , is indeed ingesting this message – yet Mr Healey must go further to level with the country. The national debt hit £3 trillion ($4 trillion) last week. The budget is expected to lay out the need to borrow more than £330 million in the year from April. Meanwhile, the government is spending more than £100 million repaying debt every year. These grim statistics come at time of already increased taxation. In the coming months, previously announced new taxation is already expected to bite on both wealth and profits. After a number of years when income was targeted, the latest measures tap out the money people own, on top of earnings. The result so far is an exodus of high earners and increasing signs that certain types of jobs are no longer being created because the cost of paying taxes on labour is deterring businesses from adding to the workforce. For example, consider the coincidence of two pressures on the bank sector revealed last week. The speculation about a higher bank tax, to capture the proceeds of higher interest rates, is rife. Barclays, one of the country’s largest banks, said it will reduce its headcount by 5,000 to reflect the changing needs of embedding AI in its system. Another straw in the wind: there were an estimated 645,000 people aged 90 years and over in the UK last year, an increase of 55 per cent since 2005. The tax changes already set to come in before Wednesday’s budget also target this portion of the population. Any unused pensions of those who die over 75 will be heavily taxed from now on. The diagnosis for the UK is complicated by just where the tax proceeds are going. The country is spending heavily on those in need of the sick and others needing welfare. By contrast, other government services such as education are being slimmed down by necessity. The big elephant in the room is that the government must spend more on defence. This is largely because wars are seen as encroaching fast on the UK’s global space. Mr Healey knows this because he resigned as the defence secretary in the previous government, under Keir Starmer, over its failure to fund defence. The crimp on how to contain spending has not been resolved. Instead, a tax drive that doesn’t seem to fit with the British way anymore – such as inspecting private property to assess if it is worth £2 million, and therefore, eligible for extra taxes – is gaining momentum. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has framed his challenge as a 10-year programme to transform the country. The approach he wants to take is having the state mobilise its assets for the public good. To make a break with tax and spend, as he does this, would entail leading a radical government. No wonder Mr Burnham sees the need for stealth in these early days. He is barely three months into the job. There is a danger in not tackling spending or addressing how to accommodate an ageing population and a workforce shaped by changing technology. Those are the strategic needs that are not being addressed right now. Having a first budget is a moment of asserting its authority for a new government. It is true that the Labour party, under its previous leadership, was dedicated to balancing its books at a time when economic growth was faltering. As Mr Healey reduces his headroom between forecast-borrowing and revenues, he will know how difficult that literal balancing act has become. For Mr Burnham, the lessons are clear. There will need to be a dedicated defence build-up in the years to come. Alongside this, he has a legacy priority of ensuring state-provided long-term care for the elderly, such as those swelling numbers of nonagenarians. The only way to fund that is to return directly to raise taxes on earnings. To secure a mandate for those measures, he will need his message of hope to generate faster growth and – more importantly – win an election with a commitment to do so. Until that point, he will remain caught in a political trap where he can’t address the big questions. And the country’s strategic traps will remain glaringly exposed.

title: Court ruling fails to end wait for thousands of immigrants stuck abroad without visas
body:
Gloria and Dustin Hoffman take a selfie with their kids. Gloria Hoffman hide caption
Late last year, Dustin Hoffman and his wife Gloria started the paperwork to secure a visa for her to live in the U.S.
The couple, along with their 5-year-old daughter Chaya and Hoffman's 12-year-old step son Israel, lived together in Argentina, where Hoffman had moved in 2013 after doing a deployment with the U.S. Army in Iraq.
"My daughter is growing up and she's very smart and my stepson he's very smart," Hoffman said. "But the resources in Argentina for an autistic child and the school system in Argentina … I don't know. I just feel like I needed to give my daughter the same opportunities that I had growing up."
But nearly a year later, the kids and Gloria are stuck in Argentina in bureaucratic limbo due to continuing delays in the processing of their visa.
That's because this January the Trump administration banned the processing of immigrant visas for citizens of 75 countries. Many of the migrants were already in the process of getting a visa. Some already had the visa approved; they were just waiting to get the physical visa delivered to them.
Hoffman's wife is from Colombia, one of the countries on the list.
A federal judge this August ordered the ban to be lifted, but Hoffman's family still has not gotten their visa, and the State Department continues to ask them to provide additional evidence to prove they have the financial means to live in the U.S. without becoming a public charge.
Attorneys representing migrants say the Hoffman family's case is emblematic of a wider problem: They say the Trump administration is not complying with the federal court order and is instead slow-walking the processing of the visas.
"So while technically the ban doesn't exist, it doesn't matter practically if people are still not being able to get their green card interviews or have their interviews not be finished and not get their immigrant visa stamps foils and be able to come into the United States," said Alexis Axelrad, the president elect of the American Immigration Lawyers Association.
The visa ban affected more than 280,000 immigrants who had applied for visas by the time the policy went into effect in January.
According to an analysis by the libertarian think-tank Cato Institute, the ban targeted thousands of close family members of U.S. citizens and permanent residents, including spouses and minor children. The Cato report called it "one of the most extreme legal immigration policies in U.S. history."
Now stuck in their countries unable to come to the U.S., many are rethinking what to do.
The State Department declined to comment for this story, telling NPR "the matter referenced is subject to pending litigation." On its website , the State Department acknowledges the visa ban is no longer in effect due to the court ruling.
This photo taken on June 3, 2026, shows an entrance to the U.S. Department of State building, in Washington, D.C. Li Rui/Xinhua via Getty Images hide caption
The agency told NPR in August it had paused the processing of visas as it launched an in-depth "training program" for embassies and consulates on identifying immigrants who could become a burden on taxpayers — a public charge.
This means even immigrants with visas approved would have to go through additional screening.
This pause is uncommon, a former State Department consular officer told NPR. She asked not to be identified because she fears it could affect her job prospects.
"I've never seen a substantial pause on visa processing … I really haven't," the former consular officer said. "The department is doing this because this is what the policy is from the president … to reduce illegal immigration, remigrate people and only accept refugees from South Africa."
But families such as the Hoffmans are stuck in limbo. He says he misses his daughter, stepson, and wife every day. He said his daughter cries "all the time" and asks for her father. His wife is overwhelmed.
"Let me put it this way: Our family is a family. We need to be there for each other," Hoffman said. "Just like any family, it's not functioning very well while we're separated."
During his first term, President Trump said he wanted to attract the brightest immigrants to come to the U.S.
Right-wing organizations, including the America First Policy Institute, have also endorsed a "merit-based" immigration system.
"America's immigration system should prioritize immigrants with education, skills, and well-paying jobs waiting for them in the U.S. because these individuals are most likely to contribute to America's society and economy, benefitting all Americans," the organization wrote in March 2026.
But the battle over visa processing has affected many immigrants who fall into the high-performing category.
One of them is Dr. Fernando Lizcano, a Colombian national whose research focuses on major cardiovascular health challenges in the U.S., including obesity.
He applied for an EB-1A visa, which is reserved for immigrants "of extraordinary ability," including "an outstanding professor or researcher," according to the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.
"My intention is to continue with my academic biomedical research in the United States," Lizcano told NPR from his office in Bogotá. "(I) have been exploring opportunities also where I could combine all my experience in endocrinology with molecular biology, translational research."
Because USCIS deemed him qualified for an EB-1A, all that was left for him was to apply for the visa itself and get it stamped in his passport.
But he is still in Colombia, awaiting for the State Department's final approval.
The waiting game is taking an emotional toll on many of the immigrants — and their loved ones — whose visas are now up in the air.
Hoffman, the U.S. veteran awaiting his wife's visa to be approved, is worried about his own mental health. He told NPR his doctors have increased his psychiatric medicines.
"I was OK before all this started happening," he said.
He works as an Uber driver, and with Trump's war in Iran, gas prices have skyrocketed, cutting into his income.
He's struggling to pay both his mortgage in the U.S., and rent in Argentina for his family.
"We're living on a dream and a prayer right now," Hoffman said.
NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

title: Republicans are spending millions and still may not win districts drawn to favor them
body:
North Carolina Republican congressional candidates state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom and Laurie Buckhout (right) are embraced by President Trump during an election rally on Oct. 20, 2026, in Greenville, N.C. Buckhout is running in North Carolina's 1st District, which was redrawn to heavily favor Republicans and is now a toss-up. Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images hide caption
📲 Get the latest on the midterms & more in the NPR App
Starting last year, President Trump and his political team put pressure on Republican-led states to redraw congressional district lines to favor Republicans. It was supposed to build a firewall for Republicans hoping to avoid the historical pattern of heavy midterm losses for the president's party.
"It just has not turned out that way," said Nathan Gonzales, editor of Inside Elections.
Instead, Republicans are spending millions of dollars on House seats that were supposed to deliver easy wins and may end up losing them anyway.
Among those districts is North Carolina's 1st Congressional District, which the state legislature aggressively redrew late last year to try to make it a reliably Republican district. Under the new lines, Trump would have won the district by more than 11 percentage points in 2024. Now it is widely considered a toss up.
Trump recently headlined a rally in eastern North Carolina where former Republican Party chairman turned U.S. Senate candidate Michael Whatley got most of the attention.
It was cold and getting late when Trump finally got around to mentioning two congressional candidates sitting in the VIP section.
"Come up. The two of you, we have to get them in," Trump said of Laurie Buckhout, the Republican nominee in NC-01 and Jennifer Balkcom, the Republican running to represent NC-11 on the opposite side of the state. "We have to vote for them. These are two special people. Come on up."
On stage, Buckhout, a retired Army colonel, who ran and lost in the district two years ago, leaned into the partisan advantage Republicans should have in the district, saying it's "simple math."
"There are more of us," said Buckhout. "All you've got to do is get out the vote. God bless you, Mr. President."
But concern about turnout is exactly why Trump was in the state, begging voters to cast their ballots as if he were on it. Trump told the rally crowd that House Speaker Mike Johnson had asked him to give an extra boost to Buckhout and Balkcom, describing the situation as "tough."
"He said 'if you could, give them a special call out tonight, because they're going to have close races'," Trump said.
Buckhout and her team didn't respond to requests to participate in this story. But, if this redraw was meant to notch an easy Republican win, it hasn't worked out. This is now one of the most expensive House races in the country, with more than $42 million spent on advertising between Sept. 1 and Election Day, according to an NPR analysis of AdImpact data.
A volunteer snaps a photo of Democratic Rep. Don Davis with Onslow County Board of Commissioner candidates Rebecca Cooper and Michel Leandre Jr. outside an early voting location in Swansboro, N.C. Onslow is one of six counties added to North Carolina's 1st District in the latest redraw of congressional district lines. hide caption
One recent morning, Democratic Rep. Don Davis, was greeting voters at an early voting location in Swansboro, at the far southeastern tip of the district, an area he hasn't represented before.
As Davis introduced himself to a voter walking out of the polling place, the man told him he wasn't in his district.
"Oh, I'm sorry," Davis said, laughing and noting this has been happening to him a lot lately.
"This is my third run on a third new map," said Davis.
Davis has been a top target for Republicans in multiple rounds of redistricting. This time his home county was drawn out of the district and he got all or part of six new counties. He says issues in eastern North Carolina, though, are universal.
"You hear so much about affordability, inflation and costs but I believe this is becoming for many about survivability," said Davis, referencing farmers, truckers and fishermen hit by high fuel prices. "Just how they're able to make it and survive during these tough times."
Davis is a happy warrior, even joking about his predicament with a volunteer handing out flyers in front of the polling place.
"I just don't know how many other ways you could redraw it now, other than maybe, you know if you just start annexing Virginia or something or maybe taking it into the Atlantic Ocean or something," he said adding with a laugh, "I'll just swim and talk to the fish, you know."
Republicans and Democrats alike acknowledge Davis is a formidable campaigner, making this race more competitive than it should be just based on the way the lines were drawn.
"I think they believed that they had beaten Don Davis with the redistricting pen," said Morgan Jackson, a prominent North Carolina political consultant, who is running Democrat Roy Cooper's U.S. Senate campaign. "As it turns out, Don Davis has always been a tough out. He's a local politician who runs really strong."
Incumbent Democrats in several redrawn districts around the country decided to stay in and fight and now look well positioned to win, said Inside Election's Gonzales.
"Republicans gained an advantage in 15 congressional districts nationwide but what we are seeing this close to Election Day is that some of those that were supposed to be easy victories are not turning out that way and the party is having to pour in millions of dollars to win districts that were supposed to be easy victories," said Gonzales.
A Republican strategist involved with midterm races, but who wasn't authorized to speak publicly, pushed back on the idea that the redistricting push has been a bust, saying "redistricting creates new battlefields, it doesn't create outcomes." That's a lot less confidence than Republicans were projecting about these districts just a few months ago.
Two Florida congressional districts redrawn to boot Democratic incumbents are nearing a combined $90 million in ad spending. In Texas, districts drawn to have a 10-point Trump advantage have shifted toward Democrats and a previously safe Republican district that had some Democratic voters added to it in the redrawn maps now appears to be at risk as well.
"I think at the end of the day, this will go down as a dummymander rather than a gerrymander," said Jackson.

title: How AI is transforming hurricane forecasts
body:
A satellite image provided by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) shows Hurricane Isaias approaching the Gulf Coast of Alabama and Florida on Friday, Oct. 9 2026. NOAA/NOAA hide caption
Hurricane forecasters are increasingly using artificial intelligence to make predictions — and they say the technology is rapidly transforming the field.
When the first hurricane of the Atlantic season formed this month, an AI model beat out traditional models at predicting where it would go.
In early October, Hurricane Isaias made landfall near Destin, Fla., as a Category 2 storm. Conventional forecasting models initially predicted it would head further west, toward southeastern Louisiana.
But Google DeepMind's artificial intelligence model called it right out of the gate: the hurricane was going to hit the western Florida Panhandle.
"Google DeepMind, in particular, has really proven itself the last few years as the gold standard model," says Michael Lowry, a longtime meteorologist and hurricane expert in Miami, who has previously advised both the Federal Emergency Management Agency and the National Hurricane Center (NHC).
"That model has been, by far and away, the best performing computer model that we've ever seen. Period."
The National Hurricane Center first started incorporating the Google DeepMind model into its official forecasts last year.
By the end of the 2025 Atlantic hurricane season, it was already one of the best at predicting a storm's path and strength, says Brian McNoldy, a hurricane researcher for the University of Miami.
Usually, new models take years to refine after first being introduced.
"It's something we're not used to – to have a model, the new kid on the block, very quickly becoming the best model out there," McNoldy says. "This pretty much came out of the gate in first place, and that's a pretty impressive feat."
Traditional physics-based hurricane models use real-time atmospheric data, like temperature, humidity, pressure and wind shear, as measured by satellites and aircraft. Then they use complicated equations to predict what path a storm might travel and how strong it could get.
An AI model operates very differently: it relies more on history. It identifies patterns by analyzing thousands of past storms along with atmospheric data.
"The AI models don't really know anything about the atmosphere other than the current picture," Lowry says. "Beyond that, it's not leaning on the governing equations of the atmosphere, the physics, to make predictions."
Most of the people designing and developing these models aren't even meteorologists, Lowry notes: "They're software engineers, and they're developing neural networks."
A "neural network" is a set of computer algorithms modeled on the human brain and trained to find patterns in massive amounts of data.
As a result, the models can seem like a "black box," Lowry says: "We don't know why they might get a forecast right. We also don't know why they might get a forecast wrong."
It can be unsettling for meteorologists to depend on a system they don't totally understand – especially during storms when millions of people might be relying on their forecasts.
"It makes us a little uncomfortable, because we like to know why you're getting the right answer," McNoldy says. "And I feel like we don't – or at least I don't know why."
Not all AI models have performed well, though. There are lots of unproven weather forecasting AI models out there, Lowry says.
The two that have so far proven to be the most accurate, despite some pitfalls, are the models developed by Google DeepMind and by the U.K.-based European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF).
People retrieve belongings from a collapsed boat house in the aftermath of Hurricane Isaias in Destin, Fla., Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. An AI model from Google Deepmind beat out traditional physics-based models at predicting the path of the storm, though it didn't do as well in forecasting the storm's strength. Gerald Herbert/AP hide caption
Forecasters at the National Hurricane Center use several proven models – both AI and traditional – when putting together their official forecasts.
"Every storm has different forecast challenges," says NHC Director Michael Brennan. "That's why we take that consensus approach and use that blend of the best models."
And it's still humans who have to interpret the results of those models before deciding what to tell the public.
The NHC provides updates every six hours during active hurricanes. The models by themselves can sometimes show drastic changes from one update to the next. Forecasters have to translate those shifting predictions into clear guidance that people can act on.
"That's one thing that the human forecaster provides a lot of, is continuity," Brennan says. "We're using our expertise and our understanding to translate that hurricane forecast into the hazard space, and that's what people really need to pay attention to."
The Google DeepMind model still needs some work, Brennan says. While it topped other models in tracking the path of Isaias, it didn't do as well as the NHC's blended forecast in determining the intensity, or strength, of the storm.
Brennan's team gives regular feedback to Google DeepMind to help improve the model. Google didn't respond to questions from NPR for this story.
The "future of forecasting has always been changing," Brennan says. "It's never just one thing that's driving those improvements."
It wasn't that long ago when forecasters couldn't predict how strong a storm would be even within a couple of days, he notes. That changed, because of advances in prediction models and better data collected by satellites and planes.
"Errors are about half of what they were, say, at the time of [Hurricane] Katrina, in terms of intensity forecasting," Brennan says.
The exciting thing about AI, says meteorologist Michael Lowry, is how quickly it's improving. AI updates take only months or even weeks, unlike traditional models, which are updated annually at best.
"They are making advancements in skill and hurricane predictions over the course of a year that would have taken us 10 years, a decade or more, to make," Lowry says.
But even with AI coming in fast and strong, Lowry says he's not worried about artificial intelligence replacing people.
"For me, I don't feel some sort of existential crisis with AI," Lowry says. "If anything, I think it is a boon for our business."
