title: Loggers say Roadless Rule repeal won't solve their biggest challenges
body:
Logs from a salvage timber sale after a recent wildfire in the Willamette National Forest in Oregon. Kirk Siegler hide caption
EUGENE, Ore. - President Trump is widely expected to soon open up some 44 million acres of the country's last pristine national forests in a move he says will bring timber jobs back to struggling small towns and help prevent wildfires in overgrown lands.
Trump signaled the move with executive actions last year aimed at dramatically boosting timber sales on U.S. Forest Service land and reversing the agency's 25-year-old Roadless Rule, which blocked most new logging on undeveloped national forestlands.
Today with the formal repeal of the Roadless Rule rule expected early next year, the picture on the ground in timber country looks messier. Those who make a living in the forests say the problems are much bigger than access to more trees.
"I'm not saying these EOs [Executive Orders] are useless, they set the tone," says Sean Smith, CEO of the family owned Starfire Lumber in Cottage Grove, Ore.
Smith, standing in a bustling lumber yard with the sawmill cranking behind four story high stacks of freshly cut timber, says the industry has more pressing challenges now, starting with the record high price of diesel fuel. Economists largely blame that on Trump's war with Iran. And then there's inflation, which is driving up the costs of just about everything.
"Steel, you know, we have to buy sawblades, we have to buy ball bearings," Smith says. "We have to buy a million different parts to keep this mouse trap going."
So repealing the Roadless Rule - which has largely banned new road building and logging projects on some 44 million acres of pristine national forests since 2001 - is lower on the priority list.
Sean Smith, owner of Starfire Lumber in Cottage Grove, Ore. says opening up local roadless forests to forest health projects could create a more reliable local supply for mills. Kirk Siegler hide caption
Smith, a burly man with a dry sense of humor and a neatly trimmed salt and pepper beard, does support the reversal saying it will eventually give industry a more reliable local timber supply. He says a lot of the nearby Willamette National Forest, roaded or not, is dangerously overgrown. That built-up fuel makes these forests more prone to catastrophic wildfires.
"This is not a 'gee I sure want more cheap timber volume,' you know, this is not me promoting an agenda," Smith says. "This is a guy who lives here and is tired of seeing these beautiful places burn up."
Trump says a boom is coming but the industry is a fraction of what it was
The administration alongside the timber industry and some local officials are pushing for the repeal, saying it will give the Forest Service more flexibility to carry out wildfire prevention, including tree thinning, on land that's largely functioned as wilderness since 2001.
But under recent Republican and Democratic administrations, the Forest Service has struggled to get those projects going on forests that already have roads. Lawsuits and red tape are an ongoing challenge, as is finding enough workers.
"Right now, there's not a ton of people that want to wake up at 2 a.m. and drive a log truck for the same price that you could go work at McDonald's for," says Jeff Brink, a second generation logger near Eugene, Ore.
Brink says the industry is a fraction of what it was when his dad and uncles started Brink Land Development in 1981. The company is getting by ok, for now he says , due to a steady stream of forest restoration projects on private land as well as some recent salvage logging timber sales from nearby wildfire burn scars.
But for many smaller, less established loggers already struggling, Brink says, labor shortages and high diesel prices could be the tipping point.
"For an industry already operating on low margins, this is a tough one," Brink says.
Due to tightening environmental laws and other market forces including cheaper Canadian lumber imports, timber sales on U.S. federal land dropped by close to 90% since the 1990s. Brink says today the infrastructure just isn't there for the forest work that needs to be done, let alone a promised timber boom.
"Rural Oregon is struggling and all the mills that aren't along the I-5 corridor or near urban centers that can source wood are closing," he says.
Since the 1990s, an estimated 400 mills across the broader Northwest have closed, amounting to the loss of about 35,000 jobs. Seven mills have closed in Oregon since 2024 alone.
Industry experts project that overturning the Roadless Rule could lead to a five to ten percent boost in federal timber sales. That's hardly enough to boost much enthusiasm on the ground.
"We're in an industry that for decades has been in a state of contraction," Brink says.
Several national environmental groups have also already signaled they plan to sue once the administration formally repeals the rule, which is expected to happen by early next year.
Some fear a revival of the bitter Timber Wars
Timothy Ingalsbee turns his hybrid station wagon onto Forest Service Road 2408, near the scene of an infamous year-long tree sit and blockade that he helped lead against a Forest Service old growth timber sale in the nineties.
"The industry [back then] was headed for a crash, they had exhausted the supply," Ingalsbee says, as he stops the car and gets out at a vista.
Today, his hair cropped shorter and greying, Ingalbee notes that many of those towering, old growth trees, their bark cloaked in moss, have burned in recent wildfires. Ingalsbee, a retired Forest Service firefighter, today runs a national firefighter safety and advocacy group.
"The claim that they're going to do all this new road building and logging in roadless areas on behalf of wildland firefighters, and make it more efficient for them, is just a big lie," Ingalsbee says. "Not in our name you don't."
Retired U.S. Forest Forest Service firefighter Timothy Ingalsbee stands by a road in the Willamette National Forest, which was once the epicenter of the so-called Timber Wars. Kirk Siegler hide caption
Ingalsbee fears that punching even more roads into these forests will lead to more human-caused wildfires, which have been rising steadily for decades. But he doesn't think any of this is really about wildfire prevention or creating more logging jobs.
"What's driving a lot of Trump's executive orders for public lands management is not real economic drivers. I don't hear industry clambering for this," he says. "It's more ideology."
For Ingalsbee, the U.S. government is just racing to open up as much of the West as possible so industry can squeeze out maximum profits on timber, oil and coal.
Everyone is tired of policies 'whipsawing' from one president to the next
One thing that almost everyone on the ground in the Northwest agrees on is that Congress has largely failed to act on either protecting or opening up federal forest lands to more development.
When President Clinton signed the Roadless Rule by executive order at the end of his second term, Republicans controlled both the Senate and the U.S. House where appetite for passing more wilderness legislation was slim. The rule was the culmination of a sweeping inventory of land conducted by the Forest Service in which the agency had marked certain forests as prime acreage for wilderness protection.
Congress never codified it, and since then, the administrative rule has become an environmental flashpoint in a polarized country.
Back at Starfire Lumber, CEO Sean Smith is tired of federal forest and timber policy whipsawing from one presidential administration to the next.
"Sometimes the cynical side of me says, 'hey, what could be better than a do-nothing Congress at least they're not screwing anything up," Smith says, with a sardonic chuckle. "But that's no way to run a country long term."
Not to mention, he adds, it makes for a hard environment to keep a business going in.

title: JUST IN: Nigeria’s Ebola index patient evacuated from Abuja
body:
Nigeria’s Ebola index patient has been evacuated to Switzerland, the Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Muhammad Pate, has confirmed.
Mr Pate said the patient, whose evacuation was approved by him, departed Abuja early Monday alongside her spouse, who has remained asymptomatic.
In a post on his official X account on Monday, Mr Pate said the patient’s condition had improved significantly but warned that she could still be infectious, despite the improvement in her clinical condition and laboratory test results.
“The index patient was clinically much improved, stable, conscious, communicating, and her clinical laboratory test results were closing towards baseline,” he said.
Mr Pate added that the evacuation was conducted under strict public health protocols to minimise the risk of further transmission.
The confirmation follows an earlier report by ARISE News that the patient, a woman who is the wife of a Swiss diplomat in Nigeria, was evacuated through the private jet wing of the Nnamdi Azikiwe International Airport in Abuja.
ARISE News reported that its sources had indicated that the evacuation would take place by 6 a.m. on Monday, with a medical evacuation aircraft already at the airport.
The news channel said its crew later observed a convoy of ambulances and diplomatic vehicles arriving from Abuja city centre and entering the airport’s private jet section.
Mr Pate said the patient’s improved condition did not mean she was no longer infectious, stressing that strict protocols remained necessary throughout the evacuation.
He commended the clinical staff who provided care for the patient and the public health personnel who coordinated the transfer, saying the evacuation was carried out in line with appropriate public health measures.
Mr Pate said the government would provide further updates later on Monday after the patient and her spouse arrived safely at their destination.
He added that public health measures were continuing to contain the imported infection and urged Nigerians to remain vigilant and rely on credible sources of information.
The evacuation comes six days after Nigeria confirmed its first Ebola case in more than a decade, involving a 42-year-old Ugandan-born woman who lives in Abuja and returned from Uganda on 3 October.
She developed symptoms on 6 October and initially sought treatment at a private hospital, believing she had malaria, before being admitted to another facility.
PREMIUM TIMES reported on Sunday that the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) had identified 53 contacts linked to the patient, up from the 44 initially announced.
The contacts include healthcare workers, household members, domestic staff, her husband and people who attended to her at a clinic before she was admitted to another facility. None had tested positive or developed symptoms as of the briefing.
The NCDC says identified contacts are being monitored for 21 days after their last possible exposure, while surveillance, laboratory testing and infection prevention measures continue to prevent further transmission.

title: $110 oil price: Windfall or warning?, By Posi Olatubosun
body:
Ultimately, Nigerians will likely gauge this oil boom not by Brent crude prices, but by the results it delivers: reduced debt, stronger reserves, improved infrastructure, and meaningful support for vulnerable households. Oil windfalls are temporary, but the decisions made during them have lasting consequences. If Nigeria saves prudently and invests productively, oil prices of $110 per barrel could strengthen the foundations of economic recovery.
When oil prices rise sharply, Nigeria’s treasury benefits. Will Nigerians also benefit? On 16 October, Brent crude exceeded $110 per barrel, reaching its highest level since May, as conflicts involving Iran and the war between Russia and Ukraine continued to threaten global supply. For an economy that still derives most of its foreign exchange from crude oil, this surge appears to represent positive news. The 2026 budget was based on an oil price of approximately $65 per barrel, meaning that each barrel sold today generates substantially more revenue than anticipated. However, history counsels caution. Nigeria has experienced oil booms before, but too often they have ended with limited savings, increased debt, and little improvement in household welfare. The central question is not how much Nigeria earns from oil at $110 per barrel, but how it uses the proceeds.
The potential gains are substantial. Nigeria’s crude oil and condensate production averaged approximately 1.68 million barrels per day in August, according to the upstream regulator, while NNPC Limited reported a September production of approximately 1.82 million barrels per day. With prices more than $40 above the budget benchmark, the additional earnings could amount to billions of dollars over a period of several months. Increased oil revenues can strengthen foreign exchange reserves, support the naira, boost federation revenues distributed to state and local governments, and reduce the budget deficit. Reserves stood at about $55 billion in early October, reflecting this stronger external position in part. Precision is essential, however. Higher oil prices do not automatically translate into a proportionate increase in government revenue. Output has generally remained below the 1.84 million barrels per day assumed in the budget. Production costs, joint-venture obligations, and the volume of crude retained for domestic refining all reduce the amount credited to the Federation Account. Consequently, a windfall measured at the oil terminal may diminish considerably before it reaches the treasury. This underscores the importance of transparent accounting.
The first concern is transparency. The Excess Crude Account was established to save oil revenues exceeding the budget benchmark. However, reports in recent months indicate that its most recent disclosed balance was only about $535,823, with little evidence that it has benefited from the recent price surge. Opposition figures, including former Vice President Atiku Abubakar, have called for a full accounting of excess crude earnings. The government, meanwhile, has defended its borrowing as necessary to finance the deficit and infrastructure. Regardless of one’s political perspective, the public deserves clear figures: the amount of additional revenue generated by oil this year, how those funds have been allocated, and how much has been saved. The second concern is the paradox of borrowing during a boom. The Federal Government raised ₦7.15 trillion through FGN bonds between January and September, more than double the same period last year. It also spent ₦5.28 trillion on domestic debt service in the first half of 2026. Heavy borrowing, while oil prices are high, runs counter to sound public finance. Good years should be used to reduce expensive debt and build buffers, so that borrowing can rise when prices fall. A government that borrows during both booms and busts leaves itself no room for manoeuvre when the cycle turns.
…the boom may be short-lived. Much of the current price increase reflects geopolitical tensions, rather than sustained demand. Analysts expect prices to moderate if supply routes reopen and conflicts ease. Budgeting as though oil were to remain at $110 per barrel indefinitely would repeat a familiar mistake. Commitments based on a temporary windfall — such as recurrent spending, new salary obligations, or politically motivated projects — could become financial burdens once prices fall.
The third concern is the impact on households. Higher crude oil prices increase the cost of petrol and diesel, driving up transport fares and food prices. Pump prices in parts of Abuja have recently been reported at more than ₦1,400 per litre. Although inflation eased to 14.63 per cent in September, food inflation remains close to 20 per cent. If oil prices remain elevated, progress in reducing inflation could stall. This illustrates the dual impact of an oil boom in Nigeria: government revenues rise, while households face higher costs at the pump and in the marketplace. The fourth concern is that the boom may be short-lived. Much of the current price increase reflects geopolitical tensions, rather than sustained demand. Analysts expect prices to moderate if supply routes reopen and conflicts ease. Budgeting as though oil were to remain at $110 per barrel indefinitely would repeat a familiar mistake. Commitments based on a temporary windfall — such as recurrent spending, new salary obligations, or politically motivated projects — could become financial burdens once prices fall.
What would constitute the prudent management of windfall revenues? First, Nigeria should adopt a clear, rules-based framework under which revenues exceeding the benchmark are automatically saved, with disclosures published monthly. The Excess Crude Account, the Sovereign Investment Authority, or a dedicated stabilisation fund could serve this purpose, provided that the governing rules are codified in law and observed by all tiers of government. Second, the windfall could retire or refinance the most expensive debt. Reducing interest costs yields permanent savings, unlike a one-off spending spree. Given the scale of current debt service, even modest repayments would ease future budgets.
…the windfall could strengthen, rather than weaken, the drive to increase output and diversify. The benefits of high prices are limited when production falls short of its target. Security in the Niger Delta, investment in upstream production, and a predictable regulatory environment will determine whether Nigeria fully capitalises on future price movements.
Third, the government could direct any windfall expenditure toward investments that generate lasting returns, such as power, transport, and agriculture, rather than recurrent commitments. These investments enhance productivity in the non-oil economy, which ultimately provides the strongest protection against oil-price volatility. Fourth, the government could directly support vulnerable households. Targeted cash transfers funded by oil revenues would protect the poorest families from rising fuel and food costs far more efficiently than broad-based subsidies. They may also show citizens that the windfall delivers tangible benefits. Fifth, the windfall could strengthen, rather than weaken, the drive to increase output and diversify. The benefits of high prices are limited when production falls short of its target. Security in the Niger Delta, investment in upstream production, and a predictable regulatory environment will determine whether Nigeria fully capitalises on future price movements.
Ultimately, Nigerians will likely gauge this oil boom not by Brent crude prices, but by the results it delivers: reduced debt, stronger reserves, improved infrastructure, and meaningful support for vulnerable households. Oil windfalls are temporary, but the decisions made during them have lasting consequences. If Nigeria saves prudently and invests productively, oil prices of $110 per barrel could strengthen the foundations of economic recovery. If it spends as though the boom will continue indefinitely, it risks creating another missed opportunity. Policymakers must therefore convert this temporary windfall into lasting economic and financial resilience.
Posi Olatubosun is a UK-based academic faculty member in accounting and finance.

title: Two teenagers arrested in Tbilisi over alleged plot to attack school: what we know
body: School attack plot in Georgia Two 14-year-olds have been arrested in Tbilisi on suspicion of planning an attack on a school and acts of violence against pupils. They attend different schools and communicated with each other through social media. According to the prosecutor’s office, the teenagers had already chosen a specific school and planned their actions. Sixteen neo-Nazi group members arrested in Georgia 13 supporters of neo-Nazi groups and fascist ideology have been arrested in Georgia Opinion: New law on offenders under 14 could violate children’s rights in Georgia One of the teenagers has already been remanded in custody. The court is due to hold a hearing on the second suspect today. What we know about the case The Georgian outlet Sando Tskaro was the first to report the teenagers’ arrests. According to its report, police detained 14-year-old S.T. on the afternoon of Thursday, 22 October. The following day, 23 October, police arrested the second teenager at his home. The first suspect exercised his right to remain silent, while the second denies the charges against him. Police searched both teenagers’ homes. They seized a number of items, including a starter pistol, ammunition, pepper spray, gloves, a helmet and a knife. The father of the first suspect, S.T., told Sando Tskaro that he did not know who the teenager was with whom his son had allegedly planned to commit the crime. According to the father, the teenagers communicated through video calls on Telegram and TikTok. He said they had discussed the 2011 terrorist attacks in Oslo. They had also talked about films based on real events that depicted acts of violence. The prosecutor’s office has largely confirmed this account. It issued an official statement only after the information had already appeared in the media. According to the statement , the teenagers met in April and May 2026. They chose a specific school in Tbilisi, studied its layout and began preparing an attack. The prosecutor’s office says the teenagers planned to place a dummy explosive device outside the school. This would have allowed them to enter the building undetected, cause a disturbance and use weapons to injure people inside. “They acquired various items and created all the necessary conditions to commit the crime. However, they failed to carry out their plan because law enforcement officers uncovered their activities,” the prosecutor’s office said. Defence lawyer’s position Gia Darchia, the lawyer representing one of the teenagers, told Radio Liberty that the prosecution had no evidence in the case. According to Darchia, the case file contains only two days’ worth of messages from October, none of which mentions organising anything. Juvenile crime in Georgia: Why is it so high — and what can be done about it? Statistics point to a growing trend in juvenile crime, with the number of offences doubling over four years. According to the defence, the items seized from the suspects’ homes as evidence were intended for personal use. They included souvenirs given to them by their parents and ordinary household objects. The lawyers argue that any claims that the teenagers were “preparing to commit a crime” are therefore entirely “unserious”. “These people did not know each other. They had never even seen each other and had made no attempt to meet. What is more, they had never been to the school they allegedly planned to attack.” The lawyer says his client would not even recognise the second suspect if someone showed him to him. He notes that his client had never seen a photograph of the other teenager, who used an avatar on social media. He also stresses that the teenagers never communicated via video calls. The defence lawyer says the investigation began after the second suspect published a social media post calling for violence. However, the case file contains neither a screenshot nor any other visual evidence that the post existed. The lawyer argues that neither the investigative materials nor interviews with the suspects indicate any links between the teenagers and radical groups. Nor had anyone observed any suspicious behaviour on their part. “They had no intention of blowing anything up or harming anyone. There is no basis for talking about any kind of organised activity,” he says. The lawyer representing the second suspect has declined to comment to the media at this stage. Authorities have opened a criminal case under Article 225, parts 1 and 2, of the Criminal Code. The article covers organising group actions involving violence, looting, damage to or destruction of other people’s property, and the use of weapons. It also covers preparing to take part in such actions. The article provides for a prison sentence of six to nine years. School attack plot in Georgia

title: Magnitude 5.2 quake jolts parts of Afghanistan, Pakistan
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 26 (MNA) – A magnitude 5.2 earthquake struck parts of Afghanistan and Pakistan late Sunday, with tremors felt in several provinces of both neighboring countries, local media reported.
The quake shook Afghanistan's capital Kabul, Nangarhar and several neighboring provinces, according to Afghan broadcaster TOLOnews.
There were no immediate reports of casualties or damage in Afghanistan, the broadcaster said.
The European-Mediterranean Seismological Centre (EMSC) recorded the earthquake at magnitude 5.2, Anadolu Agency (AA) reported.
Pakistani broadcaster Geo News reported that the tremor was felt in parts of northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province and the northern Gilgit-Baltistan region.

title: Alpha Dhabi commits $1bn for global AI investments
body: Alpha Dhabi Holding , a subsidiary of the Abu Dhabi-listed International Holding Company, has signed an agreement to commit $1 billion for investments in artificial intelligence companies around the globe. Investment Holding Company is to invest through the Alpha Wave Global-managed fund Alpha Wave III, which also seeks to target high-growth companies, it said in a statement on Monday. Alpha Dhabi will deploy the committed capital over time, in line with “capital calls and the fund’s investment programme”, the company said in a filing to the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange, where its shares trade. Returns from the Alpha Wave III fund will be dictated by the performance and valuation of the underlying investments, with value expected to be realised through distributions and exits over the life of the fund. The investment commitment is in line with the company’s growth strategy and “broadens Alpha Dhabi’s access to artificial intelligence and innovation-led opportunities”, said Hamad Al Ameri, managing director and group chief executive of Alpha Dhabi. “This investment supports our portfolio diversification objectives and our focus on long-term value creation.” Building on commitment The latest commitment builds on Alpha Dhabi’s 2022 investment of Dh9.2 billion ($2.5 billion) in Alpha Wave Ventures II. The fund, launched by Chimera Capital and Alpha Wave, received a capital contribution of Dh2.6 billion and undrawn capital commitment of Dh6.6 billion to be drawn down over time for investments in growth-stage companies globally, the company said at the time . Through the venture fund, Alpha Dhabi has gained indirect exposure to companies including SpaceX, OpenAI and Anthropic. Alpha Dhabi intends to fund the investment in Alpha Wave III from the recycling of its cash distributions from Alpha Wave Ventures II and existing resources. “The financial impact will be recognised over time, reflecting the timing of capital deployment and the performance,” Alpha Dhabi said on Monday. Established in 2013, Alpha Dhabi manages a portfolio of more than 250 public and private investments, spanning 45 countries. It invests in companies in high-growth sectors, including AI and technology, real estate, industry, construction, health care, energy and hospitality. In August, Alpha Dhabi doubled its shareholding and capital commitment in its private credit joint venture with the emirate’s sovereign wealth fund, Mubadala Investment Company. Under the revised partnership agreement, the company boosted its capital commitment in Micad Credit JV to $1 billion. It also raised shareholding from 20 per cent to 40 per cent in Micad, which manages about $1.7 billion in assets across 45 portfolio companies, Alpha Dhabi said at the time. In May, Abu Dhabi's Ta'ziz signed a deal with Alpha Dhabi, targeting $10 billion in capital investment in its new industrial chemicals ecosystem in the emirate. The two companies said at the time that they were conducting a joint feasibility and market study, and the move remained subject to final investment decisions and regulatory approvals.

title: SBU agents detained for plotting drone attack on Moscow’s missile defense facility
body:
MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. The Federal Security Service (FSB) has detained two individuals from the South Caucasus who acted on instructions from Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) to carry out an FPV-drone attack on a key component of Moscow’s missile defense system and an electric power facility.
"The Federal Security Service has thwarted the subversive and terrorist activities of two individuals from the Transcaucasus region, born in 1991 and 1998, who were acting as agents of the Security Service of Ukraine and were involved in preparing a terrorist act," the FSB’s Public Relations Center (PRC) said.
According to the FSB, the suspects were tasked with assembling strike-capable unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) retrieved from hidden caches, transporting them to a launch site in the Moscow Region, and preparing them for launch.
"The drones were to be operated remotely from Ukrainian territory. FSB officers apprehended the individuals while they were preparing an attack on an electric power facility and a key component of Moscow’s missile defense system," the agency said.
The FSB reported that one of the detainees had been recruited by an SBU officer and traveled to Russia in exchange for a promised monetary reward to carry out the planned attack. He subsequently enlisted an acquaintance from his inner circle to assist him.
FPV drones and components intended for the manufacture of improvised explosive devices were recovered from caches in the Smolensk and Kaluga regions, the FSB said.
The FSB’s Investigative Department has opened a criminal case against the detainees under Part 2 of Article 205.4 of the Russian Criminal Code, which concerns participation in a terrorist organization. A court has ordered both suspects to be held in custody.
A comprehensive set of investigative and operational measures is underway to establish the full circumstances of the alleged activities and identify any possible accomplices, the FSB added.
The agency also warned that Ukrainian intelligence services were seeking to recruit civilians for illicit activities intended to harm Russia. It emphasized that anyone assisting what it described as the adversary would be identified and held accountable, according to the FSB’s Public Relations Center.

title: Indian Air Force Pilots Fly Su-30SM Fighter for the First Time in a Russian Exercise
body:
Russian Aerospace Forces and Indian Air Force (IAF) crews conducted joint flights involving Russia’s Su-30SM multirole fighter during the Indra 2026 military exercise, according to Russia’s Defense Ministry.
The drills focused on engaging small, low-flying targets, countering aircraft carrying short- and medium-range air-launched weapons, and practicing maneuvering air combat at medium and low altitudes.
Both aircraft are twin-engine, multirole fighters derived from the Su-27 family, featuring thrust-vectoring engines and highly maneuverable airframes. However, they differ in avionics, communications and weapons integration.
India’s Su-30MKI combines Russian systems with technologies from international suppliers and supports the BrahMos-A air-launched cruise missile and indigenous Astra air-to-air missile. Russia’s Su-30SM primarily uses Russian avionics and weapons, including compatibility with R-73 and R-77 air-to-air missiles.
Russia’s upgraded Su-30SM2 features improved engines and avionics. India, meanwhile, is pursuing the proposed Super Sukhoi modernization program for its Su-30MKI fleet, with Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) expected to play a key role.
Flying the Su-30SM could give Indian pilots first-hand experience of the aircraft’s handling, cockpit systems and operational procedures. The exercise may also offer useful comparative insights for India’s fighter modernization efforts, including “Super Sukhoi” by Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL).

title: Republic of Kazakhstan: From Declaration of State Sovereignty to Middle-Power Status in 36 Years
body: The Astana Times provides news and information from Kazakhstan and around the world. On Oct. 25, Kazakhstan celebrates Republic Day, a national holiday of particular historical significance for the formation of modern Kazakh statehood. On this day in 1990, the Declaration of State Sovereignty of the Kazakh Soviet Socialist Republic was adopted, marking a major political and legal milestone on the path to independence. Thirty-six years later, the principles set out in the Declaration – sovereignty, territorial integrity, autonomy and responsibility for the country’s own future – continue to shape Kazakhstan’s strategic development. Photo credit: shutterstock. For Kazakhstan, the date is not only an opportunity to look back at the origins of modern statehood, but also to reflect on the journey so far, assess the results achieved and identify priorities for further development. At a time of profound change in international relations, accelerating technological advances and growing interdependence among states, a country’s ability to set its own national priorities, modernise its economy consistently and strengthen the confidence of international partners takes on particular importance. Historical choices and the formation of statehood Adopted on Oct.25, 1990, the Declaration of State Sovereignty was one of the key documents that established the political and legal foundations of Kazakhstan’s future independence. It enshrined the principles of autonomy for the republican authorities, territorial integrity, citizenship, economic independence and the right to conduct independent international relations. The document thus marked a transition to a new understanding of the state’s responsibility to its people and laid the groundwork for the subsequent formation of the independent Kazakhstan. The proclamation of state independence on Dec.16, 1991 was a natural continuation of this historical process. The country faced enormous tasks: establishing independent state institutions, creating a national legal system, transitioning to a market economy, building foreign-policy ties and integrating into the international community. These processes unfolded in difficult economic and geopolitical conditions, requiring both strategic vision and the ability to make complex practical decisions. In the first years of independence, Kazakhstan established the fundamental principles of its statehood: preserving territorial integrity, strengthening interethnic harmony, developing national culture, maintaining domestic stability and pursuing an independent foreign policy. The multinational character of society became not an obstacle but an important factor in shaping a model of statehood in which civic identity is combined with respect for cultural and linguistic diversity. Building its own system of international relations was of vital importance. Kazakhstan established diplomatic ties with countries around the world, joined international organisations and treaties, and created a legal framework for trade, economic and humanitarian cooperation. Membership in the United Nations since 1992 confirmed the country’s standing as a full-fledged member of the international community. From the outset, independence was therefore regarded not merely as a political and legal status, but as a practical opportunity to determine the course of national development independently, protect citizens’ interests and build relations with other states on the basis of mutual respect and equality. Restoring and strengthening statehood required considerable effort. Yet it was during this period that the foundations were laid for Kazakhstan’s modern institutional system, its international standing and its long-term development strategy. Kazakhstan in a changing international order Since the early years of independence, Kazakhstan has pursued a foreign policy grounded in the protection of national interests, the development of good-neighbourly relations, pragmatism and cooperation with diverse centres of global economic and political influence. The country’s geographic position and international economic ties make a broad range of partnerships and the ability to navigate complex global interdependencies an objective necessity. In this context, a multi-vector foreign policy means seeking constructive relations with states and international organisations on the basis of sovereign equality, respect for territorial integrity, non-interference in internal affairs and the peaceful settlement of disputes. Its practical value lies in expanding diplomatic room for manoeuvre, economic cooperation and the protection of national interests. As geopolitical tensions intensify, preserving international law and the effectiveness of multilateral institutions becomes especially important. For states with an interest in stability, predictability and free trade, compliance with international norms is an essential precondition for long-term development. Kazakhstan consistently supports dialogue and multilateral cooperation within the United Nations. The country’s priorities include international security, sustainable development, nuclear non-proliferation, confidence-building and resolving regional issues through negotiations. These priorities are reflected in the Concept of the Foreign Policy of the Republic of Kazakhstan for 2020–2030. Nuclear disarmament occupies a special place in Kazakhstan’s international profile. The decision to close the Semipalatinsk Nuclear Test Site in 1991 and the subsequent renunciation of the inherited nuclear arsenal were important milestones in the country’s history and in international security policy. This experience remains a significant part of Kazakhstan’s contribution to global efforts to prevent the proliferation of nuclear weapons and strengthen international trust. The regional dimension of foreign policy is also strategically important. Central Asia’s resilience depends on the development of trade ties, the rational use of water resources, transport connectivity, energy cooperation and joint efforts to address environmental challenges. None of these issues can be effectively resolved by countries acting alone. Closer cooperation among the countries of Central Asia expands the region’s ability to pursue independent economic development, enhance its international competitiveness and respond to shared challenges in a coordinated manner. Kazakhstan regards regional stability and development as important conditions for its own long-term security and prosperity. At the same time, the country is interested in deepening engagement with the European Union and its member states. European partners are of considerable interest in industry, energy, transport, education, science, digital technologies and environmental modernisation. For Kazakhstan, such cooperation offers a way to expand export opportunities, attract investment and gain access to advanced technological solutions. Ultimately, a country’s international role is determined not only by its economic resources or geographic position, but also by its ability to turn these advantages into practical results, sustain dialogue and consistently honour its commitments. Economic transformation: from adaptation to diversification Since independence, Kazakhstan’s economy has undergone profound structural change. The country has established its own financial system, national currency, institutions for regulating economic activity and mechanisms for attracting foreign investment. The development of natural resources, industry and infrastructure, together with the expansion of trade ties, has enabled Kazakhstan to strengthen its position in the regional and global economy. Natural resources remain an important part of the country’s economic potential. Kazakhstan has substantial reserves of hydrocarbons, uranium, non-ferrous and rare metals, as well as significant agricultural capacity. The country’s resource base could underpin new production chains, provided that processing and technological capabilities are developed. According to the World Bank, Kazakhstan has more than 5,000 unexplored deposits of rare and rare-earth metals, with an estimated potential value exceeding $46 trillion. However, the long-term resilience of the economy depends not only on using these advantages effectively, but also on broadening the production base, raising labour productivity, developing competitive processing industries and creating new sources of growth. That is why economic diversification, the development of non-commodity exports and investment in high-value-added sectors are of strategic importance. The aim is a gradual shift from a model in which extractive industries play a substantial role towards a more sophisticated economic structure built on technology, skilled workers, efficient infrastructure and entrepreneurial initiative. Kazakhstan’s economic performance in recent years reflects both growing business activity and the ongoing challenge of diversification. As part of a new investment cycle and its economic development framework, Kazakhstan plans to attract an additional $150 billion in foreign investment by 2029. The highest growth rates were recorded in transportation and storage, construction, trade, industry, and information and communications. During the first nine months of 2026, the short-term economic indicator rose by 4.8 percent year on year. This performance points to broader activity across a range of sectors, although its long-term sustainability will depend on productivity gains and the development of non-commodity production. In August 2026, S&P Global Ratings raised the country’s sovereign rating to BBB with a stable outlook; Moody’s maintains its rating at Baa1 with a stable outlook. These assessments describe the government’s creditworthiness, but do not in themselves replace an analysis of investment quality, productivity or the sustainability of growth. Foreign trade and transport connectivity add to this picture. According to the Bureau of National Statistics, Kazakhstan’s total trade with all foreign partners amounted to $143.9 billion in 2025. The country’s geographic position creates opportunities to develop transit between Asia and Europe, but realising them depends on infrastructure capacity, logistics efficiency and the predictability of freight movements. International indicators related to innovation, education and digital skills also show changes. In the WIPO Global Innovation Index 2026, Kazakhstan ranked 73rd; the organisation noted the country’s most significant rise in the Central and Southern Asia region. These indicators reflect an expansion of economic activity beyond the traditional commodity sector. At the same time, the sustainability of this growth will depend on the country’s ability to improve investment efficiency, develop domestic competition, strengthen the business environment and enable small and medium-sized enterprises to play a broader role in creating added value. It is important to move from an approach to investment policy focused primarily on volume to a more selective model centred on project quality, technological content, export potential and long-term benefits for the national economy. Investment in raw-material processing, engineering, the agro-industrial sector, pharmaceuticals, digital solutions and logistics can support economic growth while strengthening resilience to external volatility. The development of entrepreneurship remains equally important. Small and medium-sized enterprises create jobs, make the economy more flexible and provide a basis for the diffusion of innovation. Their further development requires access to finance, predictable regulation, effective protection of property rights and a level playing field for competition. Ultimately, economic modernisation should be assessed not only by macroeconomic indicators. Its most important test is whether it gives citizens broader opportunities for employment, professional fulfilment and a better quality of life. Transit potential and a new economic geography Kazakhstan’s position between Europe and Asia has historically shaped its role in regional exchange. Today, this advantage is gaining further importance as international logistics chains are reconfigured, e-commerce expands and businesses seek alternative routes for transporting goods. Kazakhstan is developing transport infrastructure, rail and road corridors, logistics hubs and multimodal solutions. The Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, known as the Middle Corridor, plays an important role in this system, linking China and Central Asia with the Caucasus and European markets via the Caspian and Black Seas. The development of such routes matters for more than transit revenues. It helps expand trade opportunities, improve connectivity between regions, attract logistics operators and create new avenues for industrial cooperation. The competitiveness of transport corridors, however, is determined by more than geography alone: it requires harmonised customs procedures, predictable delivery times, efficient port infrastructure and digital data exchange among all parties involved in freight transport. In this respect, cooperation with European partners offers Kazakhstan additional opportunities. The European market is of interest not only as an export destination, but also as a source of technology, engineering solutions, investment expertise and modern standards for infrastructure management. At the same time, Kazakhstan needs to develop its own logistics and production base so that it serves not only as a transit territory but also as a place where high-value-added goods and services are created. It is the combination of transport connectivity, industrial development and technological renewal that can turn geographic position into a lasting competitive advantage. Digital transformation and artificial intelligence Digitalisation is becoming one of the most significant drivers of contemporary development. It is changing how governments and citizens interact, how businesses operate, and how education, healthcare and international trade are organised. For Kazakhstan, the development of digital technologies offers an opportunity to accelerate economic modernisation, improve public services and broaden access to knowledge and innovation. A key condition for digital transformation is the creation of a comprehensive ecosystem that brings together government agencies, universities, research centres, entrepreneurs and international technology partners. Sustainable results depend not only on introducing new software solutions, but also on developing skills, ensuring access to digital infrastructure, protecting data and building trust in technology. Artificial intelligence is attracting particular attention. Its use offers prospects for improving industrial efficiency, refining transport planning, analysing agricultural data, advancing personalised medicine and automating administrative processes. At the same time, wider use of AI calls for a responsible approach to safety, algorithmic transparency, personal data protection and workforce training. In the Government AI Readiness Index 2025, which assesses the readiness of public institutions to use artificial intelligence, Kazakhstan ranked 60th among 195 countries. These results show progress, but further improvement will require sustained investment in science, universities, workforce development and the adoption of technology across the economy. In the UN E-Government Development Index (eGov), Kazakhstan rose from 29th to 24th place globally, entering the top 25 digital governments. Human capital: the foundation of long-term progress Neither natural resources, geographic position nor technological infrastructure alone can guarantee sustainable development. Ultimately, the decisive factors are people’s knowledge, skills, health and initiative. Kazakhstan’s cultural diversity is also a significant asset. The Kazakh language and national traditions are an essential part of the country’s historical heritage, while multilingualism and openness to international engagement broaden opportunities for citizens in education, science, diplomacy and business. Preserving historical memory, developing culture and supporting creative initiatives are not secondary objectives; they are part of long-term social development. They strengthen ties between generations, help shape civic identity and enable Kazakhstan to present itself to international audiences through its history, art, literature and traditions. In 2026, Kazakhstan entered a new stage of constitutional development: the Constitution adopted at the national referendum on March 15 came into force on July 1. Official materials on the new Basic Law emphasise the importance of sovereignty and independence, human rights and freedoms, the supremacy of the Constitution, national unity, knowledge, innovation and human-capital development. Kazakhstan and Slovenia: 34 years of diplomatic relations Cooperation with Slovenia—a country with which Kazakhstan shares more than three decades of diplomatic relations, mutual respect and a common interest in practical partnership—holds a special place in Kazakhstan’s European foreign policy. Diplomatic relations between the Republic of Kazakhstan and the Republic of Slovenia were established on Oct. 20, 1992. Over the past 34 years, bilateral engagement has gradually expanded to include political dialogue, trade, investment, industrial cooperation, culture, education and scientific ties. An important milestone in the development of bilateral relations was the official visit of Slovenian President Nataša Pirc Musar to Kazakhstan in March 2025. The agreements reached gave fresh impetus to discussions on the prospects for economic cooperation and the practical implementation of joint initiatives. In 2024, Kazakhstan opened an Embassy in Slovenia, creating additional institutional capacity to develop bilateral ties. Economic cooperation between the two countries has considerable potential. Kazakhstan is interested in European technology, investment and production expertise, while Slovenian companies have experience in pharmaceuticals, medical technology, industrial equipment, digital solutions and other high-value-added sectors. Promising areas of cooperation include pharmaceuticals and biotechnology, digitalisation, artificial intelligence, transport and logistics, energy, industrial cooperation and infrastructure development. Practical issues include making use of the Port of Koper in Slovenia to expand Kazakhstan’s transport and logistics links with European markets. Trade turnover between Kazakhstan and Slovenia amounted to 193.5 million euros (US$217 million) in 2025, an increase of 20.6 percent compared with 2024. Trade turnover in 2024 totalled 160.4 million euros (US$180 million), while from January to August 2026 it amounted to 132.2 million euros (US$148 million). Further deepening of cooperation will involve not only increasing trade volumes, but also expanding joint projects, production links, technology exchange and contacts between business communities. Intergovernmental mechanisms, direct company-to-company contacts, cooperation among research institutions and the development of educational programmes can all play an important role in this process. Humanitarian ties remain equally important. Exchanges between universities, cooperation among researchers, cultural events and tourism contacts help people in both countries learn more about each other’s history, traditions and contemporary achievements. These ties provide a strong public foundation for a long-term partnership. The 34th anniversary of diplomatic relations is an opportune moment not only to take stock, but also to identify new practical priorities. Kazakhstan and Slovenia have the potential to expand cooperation further, drawing on the complementary nature of their economies, their shared interest in innovation and their commitment to strengthening links between Central Europe and Central Asia. The 36th anniversary of the adoption of the Declaration of State Sovereignty takes us back to the origins of modern Kazakhstan and reminds us that statehood is not only a historical legacy, but also an enduring responsibility for the country’s future. Over the past decades, Kazakhstan has established its own state institutions, strengthened international ties, developed its economy and broadened its participation in regional and global affairs. At the same time, further progress requires sustained efforts to diversify the economy, improve the quality of public governance, develop human capital, modernise technology and strengthen infrastructure resilience. Relations with Slovenia form part of Kazakhstan’s broader strategy to strengthen partnerships with European countries. Joint projects in industry, pharmaceuticals, logistics, science and digital technologies can contribute not only to the growth of bilateral trade, but also to new links between the economies of Central Asia and the European Union. Kazakhstan is entering the next stage of its history, drawing on its accumulated experience, economic potential and human capital. The country’s ability to meet the challenges of the 21st century and create new opportunities for future generations will depend on how successfully it combines these resources with strong institutions, innovation and international partnership. The full article was originally published on the IFIMES website. The International Institute for Middle East and Balkan Studies (IFIMES), based in Ljubljana, Slovenia, has held a special consultative status with the United Nations Economic and Social Council ECOSOC/UN in New York since 2018. The institute is publisher of the international scientific journal European Perspectives. The post Republic of Kazakhstan: From Declaration of State Sovereignty to Middle-Power Status in 36 Years appeared first on The Astana Times .

title: Sweden contracts Saildrone to operate four uncrewed vessels for Baltic Sea surveillance
body: The Swedish Defence Materiel Administration, FMV, signed the framework agreement on behalf of the Swedish Armed Forces through Nordic Defence Cooperation, or NORDEFCO. The vessels have supported Swedish naval surveillance since October 2026, and the agreement allows additional craft to be included. “This is fundamentally not about four unmanned vessels, but about access to sustained intelligence collection at sea,” said Johan Wahren, project manager at FMV. “In other words, we are purchasing a persistent maritime surveillance service, and Saildrone provides the vessels that supply the Navy with data.” The Swedish Navy sets mission requirements and receives information around the clock, while Saildrone deploys, maintains and operates the vessels. The arrangement provides sustained coverage without requiring Sweden to deploy additional crewed ships. Cameras, radars and other sensors detect nearby vessels and support checks on their identities and positions. The information can be compared with Automatic Identification System transmissions to identify ships broadcasting inaccurate details or locations. The 10-metre Voyagers rely mainly on wind propulsion, with solar panels supplying electricity to onboard electronics. They also carry a small engine and fuel tank and operate autonomously within assigned missions under continuous supervision by Saildrone personnel. “This mission reflects Sweden’s commitment to securing the Baltic Sea and highlights Saildrone’s growing operational presence across Northern Europe,” said Robert Kleist, Saildrone’s European managing director. The company described Sweden’s mission as its first national deployment under the NORDEFCO framework. “Sweden is investing in year-round maritime awareness as an operational capability. The NORDEFCO framework gives Nordic nations a common mechanism for accessing that capability while allowing each country to define and operate its own mission.” The vessels also contribute to NATO Allied Command Transformation’s Task Force X Baltic initiative, which aims to accelerate the development of uncrewed maritime surveillance. That initiative began under Baltic Sentry to improve monitoring and protection of critical undersea infrastructure following cable breaks in 2024 and 2025. The four Voyagers are registered in Denmark and operate under the Danish flag, providing a flag-state framework for international operations. Saildrone said further national deployments under NORDEFCO would follow, while its European operation plans to register additional vessels in the coming weeks.

title: Two killed, 17 injured in Ukrainian drone and missile strikes on Russia’s Voronezh, regional governor says
body: Update: Voronezh Governor Alexander Gusev said two people were killed and 17 others, including a child, were injured in the attack on Voronezh, according to preliminary data. Ukrainian forces struck Voronezh with missiles and drones overnight on October 26. According to the independent Telegram channel Astra, drones hit several apartment buildings and the 25-story Galereya Chizhova business center. Eyewitness video shows damaged buildings and cars burning in parking lots nearby. Residents of Voronezh told the outlet that air raid sirens did not go off in the city. Gusev said 117 drones were shot down over the region, including more than 70 over Voronezh itself. The press service of Russian Railways, Russia’s state rail operator, said a railcar on the Anapa–Moscow train was damaged in a Ukrainian drone attack at the Somovo station in the Voronezh region. Five people were injured, according to preliminary data. The Ukrainian military last struck Voronezh on October 23, when drones hit the Baltimor military airfield. title: NUJ Sokoto Correspondent Chapel Mourns Olugbemi
body: Onuminya Innocent in Sokoto The Nigeria Union of Journalists (NUJ), Correspondents’ Chapel, Sokoto State chapter, has been thrown into mourning following the death of its member, Mr. Adeniyi Olugbemi. Olugbemi, a veteran journalist and prolific writer, died last Saturday, leaving his colleagues, friends and the entire media community in Sokoto State in deep shock and sorrow. Reacting to the sad news, the Chairman of the Chapel, Mr. Ankeli Emmanuel, described Olugbemi as a hard-working and easy-going fellow, who was deeply committed to the ethics and practice of journalism. Ankeli stated that Olugbemi has left a vacuum that will not be easy to fill, stressing that the Chapel has lost a gem whose presence, experience and counsel will be sorely missed. He further described the late journalist as a prolific writer, whose pen gave voice to the voiceless and whose reports shaped public discourse in every state where he practised. Also reacting, the Secretary of the Chapel, Musa Ubandawaki, said Olugbemi was a dedicated colleague whose humility, diligence and passion for the job endeared him to many within and outside the profession. Late Adeniyi Olugbemi hailed from Yelwa in Ogun State, and built a rich and remarkable career that spanned several leading media organisations across Nigeria. He was a former correspondent of the Tribune Newspaper in Yola, Adamawa State, before he later joined The Sun Newspaper and then the Taraba State Newspaper, where he continued to distinguish himself. He also joined The Punch Newspaper, where he rose to become the Bureau Chief in Sokoto, and also had a stint with Leadership Newspaper, where his analytical depth and fearless reporting stood him out. Before his death, Olugbemi founded his own publication, The Guild Magazine, through which he continued to mentor young journalists and promote responsible journalism in Sokoto and beyond. The Correspondents’ Chapel has condoled with his family, friends,s and associates, praying to God to grant them the fortitude to bear the irreparable loss, as colleagues pray that his soul rests in peace.

title: Two dead, 17 injured: aftermath of Ukrainian attack on Russia’s central Voronezh Region
body:
VORONEZH, October 26. /TASS/. Two civilians were killed and 17 others, including a child, were injured in a Ukrainian attack on the Voronezh Region in central Russia, Governor Alexander Gusev reported.
According to him, many of the victims were on a train traveling through the left-bank suburbs of Voronezh when drone debris fell on it.
TASS has compiled the key information on the attack’s aftermath.
- On-duty air defenses shot down 113 Ukrainian drones over the Voronezh Region in central Russia overnight, with 70 of them directly over Voronezh, Governor Alexander Gusev reported on his Max channel.
- Two people were killed and 17 others, including a child, were injured as a result of the Ukrainian attack, the regional head emphasized.
- He specified that the deceased were two men born in 1960 and 1973.
- According to Gusev, many of the injured, including two with serious injuries, were on a train traveling through the left-bank suburbs of Voronezh when drone debris fell on it.
- At least five passengers on the Anapa-Moscow train were injured as a result of the drone attack in the Voronezh Region, Russian Railways reported.
- They are receiving the necessary medical assistance, the company added.
- According to Gusev, the Ukrainian attack caused fires at several industrial facilities, an office building in the city center, an apartment building, two suburban settlements, a school stadium, and a parking garage.
- Damage to building facades and windows has been reported in nearly all districts of the city.
- Due to the drone attack in the Voronezh Region on the Tresvyatskaya-Somovo-Otroshka-Voronezh section, train service has been temporarily suspended, Russian Railways said.
- Repair crews are working to restore service.
- Russian Railways has warned of possible delays for southbound passenger trains and commuter trains.
- Eighteen passenger trains are delayed, Russian Railways specified.
- The company added that train crew members are providing comprehensive assistance and support to passengers.
- Russian Railways is taking all necessary measures to bring trains back on schedule.
- The Voronezh Regional Prosecutor’s Office will monitor compliance with the rights of the victims and ensure they receive assistance following the Ukrainian attack.
- The Moscow Interregional Transport Prosecutor’s Office is conducting oversight activities in connection with damage to railway infrastructure in the Voronezh Region.
- The Transport Prosecutor’s Office is monitoring compliance with the rights of rail passengers.
- The Southern Transport Prosecutor’s Office has taken steps to ensure the rights of passengers on delayed trains on the Tresvyatskaya-Somovo-Otroshka-Voronezh route are upheld following damage to the railroad contact line caused by a drone attack, the press service said on its Telegram channel.
- Transport prosecutors are monitoring compliance with passengers’ rights.
- The Russian Investigative Committee has opened a criminal case over the terrorist attack under Article 205 of the Russian Criminal Code, Spokeswoman Svetlana Petrenko said.

title: Spurned by Trump, these outgoing Republicans aren’t helping their potential successors
body: Republicans spurned by President Donald Trump aren't interested in rescuing their would-be replacements. Instead, a growing number of retiring or ousted GOP incumbents from Nevada to North Carolina are sitting those races out, and in some cases, openly bucking their own party. Outgoing Sen. John Cornyn has raised money for various Republican Senate candidates — just not for Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who ousted him in the primary with support from Trump. He’s been vocal for months about what he sees as Paxton’s vulnerabilities and how Democrats could flip Texas blue for the first time in decades. North Carolina Sen. Thom Tillis — who has frequently criticized some of Trump’s Cabinet and broken with the White House on policy — has played little role in the campaign of former RNC Chair Michael Whatley, Trump’s hand-picked Senate candidate. The distance between the two Republicans is particularly notable as Whatley struggles to close the gap against Democrat Roy Cooper. Rep. Mark Amodei has repeatedly criticized, and now openly rejected voting for , the GOP nominee to replace him, David Flippo. “The bedwetting from outgoing moderate Republicans will define their legacy and only help socialists get elected,” said David McIntosh, president of the Trump-aligned Club for Growth, which has endorsed Flippo and Paxton. “People like John Cornyn and Mark Amodei need to get on board and support Republican nominees and stop posturing for an MSNOW contract.” But other Republicans defended their colleagues: “I never would question the loyalty to the party of Thom Tillis or John Cornyn. Both of them have contributed immensely to our party and our party's successes in the past and I suspect will be going forward,” said North Dakota GOP Sen. Kevin Cramer. “But I also don't begrudge them for their opinions and their right to be open about them.” These outgoing Republicans, several of whom were explicitly pushed out by Trump or persuaded to retire given his hold on the GOP, are using the midterms as a test: whether the party will demand loyalty to the president or can return to a pre-Trump era. “What [Trump’s] done is created a coalition that, in my opinion, will not stay with Republicans once we go back to traditional Republican platform priorities,” Tillis said in a recent interview with POLITICO . “A lot of the elements of the populism that Trump created to expand a base that made him successful running for president, I don't think that stays with the party long-term.” Some of those intraparty frustrations are starting to boil over, with Trump loyalist candidates and outgoing Republicans swiping at one another as Election Day barrels closer and the party’s overall fortunes look dire. The blame game is especially prominent in some of the Senate battlegrounds where Republicans have begun to quietly retreat in the final stretch of the midterms. Tillis never followed through on his offers to help Whatley by reaching out to holdout donors in the North Carolina Senate race, said one person familiar with the campaign who was granted anonymity to speak candidly about internal matters. "He was never part of our strategy because ... I mean, if he could have been helpful to us, then he could have ran," the person said, referring to Tillis' decision not to seek reelection last year. "The Tillis of the past year ain’t the same guy who worked overtime to help elect Republican majorities here in NC back in 2010." One person with knowledge of Tillis and North Carolina politics, also granted anonymity to speak candidly, countered that the outgoing GOP senator “doesn’t help sure winners or sure losers" and "Whatley has been a sure loser throughout 2026, running as Donald Trump’s ‘guy,’ and making zero effort to build his own brand." "All Whatley had to do was to keep this race competitive, but instead the party is facing a potential wipeout. This is an embarrassing effort by a former RNC chairman who only has himself and his consultants to blame for the completely avoidable beat down coming on Nov. 3," the person added. Spokespeople for Tillis did not respond to a request for comment. Whatley's campaign declined to comment. Natalie Baldassarre, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee, touted the president’s endorsement record in a statement. More pointedly, she said that “Republicans who chose not to help elect other Republicans may as well be helping Democrats.” The White House did not respond to a request for comment. While the dynamic is less pronounced on the House side — Reps. Don Bacon and Elise Stefanik have been helpful to the Republicans running to replace them — there’s a clear exception: Amodei. Flippo, who’s trying to replace him, has dealt with a host of scandals, from stolen valor accusations to carpetbagging to campaign finance issues , but Trump’s endorsement helped boost him through the Republican primary in June . Top Republican outside groups, including Club for Growth, have poured millions into his race in Nevada’s 2nd District to rescue a seat the president won by 14 points in 2024. Amodei said in an interview that whoever was advising Trump to jump in and endorse Flippo gave “awful advice.” "The only criteria shouldn't be, ‘Well, they're the Republican,’” said Amodei, who cast his ballot for a third-party candidate this week. “I mean, politics is a team sport. But when a member of the team turns out to be this way, clearly this is not a bright and shining moment for the vetting process." Asked about Club for Growth president McIntosh's criticism of moderate "bedwetting," Amodei scoffed: "At least this crowd is absolutely consistent. Forget fundamental factual and character messes that campaigns won't and can't respond to; and attempt to change the focus to party loyalty," the retiring representative said. "Let me know when Club For Growth does a statement on campaign finance compliance, stolen Valor, and individual background transparency.” Even as figures like Cornyn and Amodei catch the fury of more Trump-aligned Republican forces for not falling behind the party line, that doesn't mean they’re abandoning fellow Republicans overall. Cornyn has raised more than $1.1 million at events in Dallas and Houston last month for the campaigns of Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Jon Husted of Ohio and Dan Sullivan of Alaska — as well as for the National Republican Senatorial Committee and other Senate candidates: Iowa Rep. Ashley Hinson, former Michigan Rep. Mike Rogers and former New Hampshire Sen. John Sununu, according to a person familiar with the senator’s political operation who was granted anonymity to discuss private events. He still clearly and explicitly draws a line against helping Paxton, telling reporters earlier this year, “Everything I said about him in the primary is true.” A spokesperson for Paxton did not respond to a request for comment. In Georgia, popular GOP Gov. Brian Kemp has been all-in on the governor’s race for Republican Rick Jackson — but he’s been comparatively quieter when it comes to Rep. Mike Collins’ Senate campaign to oust Democrat Jon Ossoff. The governor had initially recruited, backed and supported a different candidate in the GOP primary, though he’s since helped the Collins campaign with a public endorsement and by headlining a major fundraiser in Atlanta and others. Still, some Collins allies want the governor to be more involved. “Brian Kemp is someone who needs to be on the trail and someone who needs to help if Republicans are going to win,” said one GOP strategist working on races in Georgia who supports Collins and was granted anonymity to discuss internal dynamics. “But he did create some of this mess with the primary he ran against Mike who we all knew would be the nominee.” Meyer Sigfried, a Collins spokesperson, in a statement dismissed any suggestion that Kemp isn’t fully supporting Collins: “He’s been on the trail rallying Georgians to get out and vote early for Mike and Republicans up and down the ballot, and his help behind the scenes has been just as important.” A representative for Kemp referred POLITICO to Collins’ statement of support. Across the map, other frustrated Republicans have more directly pointed the finger at Trump for his interference, lambasting the president’s tendency to prop up candidates whom they deem too weak for the role. In South Carolina, Rep. Ralph Norman said this week he has refused to campaign with Sen. Darline Graham, who defeated him in the primary with Trump’s help. Graham has been under scrutiny for her lack of experience in elected office. Republicans still expect her to win in deep-red South Carolina, but they’ve also made late investments to shore up her campaign as Democrat Annie Andrews dominates in fundraising. Norman blamed the president , saying, "What he did to South Carolina … it's just not right,” but added he will still vote for Graham. T.W. Arrighi, a spokesperson for Graham, thanked the representative for his support in a statement, before hammering other Republicans — like Norman’s son, Warren Norman — who will not be voting for the GOP nominee: “It is unconscionable for anyone who claims to be a conservative in South Carolina to not vote straight ticket Republican and therefore endorse a Chuck Schumer-led Senate.” In many cases, GOP lawmakers are defending their disgruntled colleagues who have decided not to help Trump-picked candidates. "Folks have to follow their conscience. If a guy 'smells bad' then I wouldn’t,” said Bacon, who is supporting Brinker Harding, an Omaha city councilmember, in the race to replace him in his blue-leaning Nebraska district. "I like Brinker. He’s a good person."A “I believe we all ought to do all we can to help the good guys win the election,” Cramer added. “But I also understand people that ... feel aggrieved and want to maybe not be as enthusiastic about that as I am.” Mia McCarthy, Meredith Lee Hill and Aaron Pellish contributed to this report.

title: Opposition Alliance Launches Protest Campaign With Tbilisi Rally Amid Party Ban Proceedings
body: An opposition-led protest march, “Georgia without Ivanishvili. Georgia deserves better,” took place in Tbilisi on October 25, launching a broader protest campaign to culminate in a larger demonstration on November 28 amid the ruling Georgian Dream party’s efforts to ban opposition parties through the Constitutional Court. The demonstration, falling on the second anniversary of the disputed 2024 parliamentary elections, was organized by the Opposition Alliance, formed by nine political parties in March. The leaders invited protesters to join the campaign, which is set to lead to another rally on November 28, also the second anniversary of non-stop protests that erupted after the Georgian Dream’s announcement of suspending EU integration efforts. The demonstrators set off from Tbilisi State University’s first building on Tbilisi’s Chavchavadze Avenue and marched down to Rustaveli Metro Station, where the politicians addressed the rally. 15/10/2026 – Backgrounder: Constitutional Court Starts Hearing Opposition Party Ban Case Among the speakers was Levan Tsutskiridze, leader of Freedom Square, a party not yet targeted in GD’s current opposition ban lawsuit, saying: “I would like to urge you to stand by the political parties because without the strengthening of the political parties it will be impossible to achieve the change we all want.” In her speech, Tamar Chergoleishvili, leader of the Federalist Party that is included in the lawsuit, said: “Ivanishvili admits his crisis of legitimacy by banning the alternative. He admits that he no longer trusts the Georgian people, that he is afraid of the free choice of the Georgian people, and rightly so.” Coalition for Change leader Nika Gvaramia called the planned November 28 demonstration a “significant peak day”, adding: “We will fight every small battle, and we will win them all. In the courtroom, where this unequal battle resumes tomorrow, as well as on the streets and in the media, wherever we are granted access and wherever we happen to be, we must win everything, everywhere.” Georgian Dream initially filed the constitutional lawsuit in October 2025, seeking to outlaw the United National Movement (UNM), Lelo/Strong Georgia, and Ahali/Coalition for Change. The lawsuit was subsequently expanded in April 2026 to include the Federalists and again in September to add For Georgia, the only opposition party still represented in Parliament. Each expansion required Georgian Dream to resubmit the lawsuit, resetting the court’s nine-month deadline to issue a ruling. The Constitutional Court concluded the third day of hearings on October 23, rejecting every motion presented by opposition parties, including Coalition for Change, Lelo, and Gakharia’s for Georgia, with hearings expected to resume on October 26.
