Application state is a separate choice. By default, dump-warm-image resets application-class static state so initialization can happen again. With :reset-classes nil, it preserves the state left by the warmups. An application designed to reuse that state can begin with much of its initialization already complete.
That is how the Spring Boot snapshot works.
The benchmark application uses auto-configuration, configuration properties bound into a record, dependency injection, and an auto-configured Jackson mapper. A CommandLineRunner produces JSON and reads a value back. Ordinary startup also prints Spring’s banner and logs through Logback.
Its snapshot entry point keeps the initialized context:
public class Snapshot { static ConfigurableApplicationContext ctx; public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (ctx == null) { ctx = SpringApplication.run(BootApp.class, args); } else { for (CommandLineRunner runner : ctx.getBeansOfType(CommandLineRunner.class).values()) { runner.run(args); } } } } With the Spring imports supplied, this is the benchmark’s entry point. The first call starts Spring. Later calls reuse the context and execute its runners.
After loading OpenLDK into SBCL and setting CLASSPATH to the application classes and each required JAR, the image can be built with:
(openldk::dump-warm-image "boot-snapshot" "demo.boot.Snapshot" :classpath (uiop:getenv "CLASSPATH") :warmups (list nil nil) :reset-classes nil) The first warmup initializes Spring; the second exercises the reuse path. Saving the image preserves that initialized object graph.
This is similar in spirit to CRaC (Coordinated Restore at Checkpoint): initialize the application once, save its state, and reuse that work on subsequent launches. CRaC restores a checkpointed JVM process. OpenLDK uses SBCL’s image-saving machinery and calls main again with the Spring context already present. It does not implement the CRaC API or preserve running threads, so thread pools and other process-local resources need attention when designing an application for this approach.
Here are the results from my recent run:
Host: Intel(R) Core(TM) Ultra 7 255H, 16 CPUs JDK: openjdk version “25.0.4.1” 2026-08-18 GraalVM: native-image 25.0.4.1.1 2026-08-18 OpenLDK: 39f33c0 Load average before: 3.75 5.29 3.83 Twenty timed runs per variant Variant Median Min Max Peak RSS HotSpot, fat jar 2138.3 ms 2078.9 ms 2219.0 ms 266 MB HotSpot, extracted jar 1791.3 ms 1755.0 ms 1880.1 ms 225 MB HotSpot + Spring AOT 1481.4 ms 1420.5 ms 1575.8 ms 194 MB HotSpot + JDK AOT cache 758.8 ms 713.4 ms 828.8 ms 181 MB HotSpot + Spring AOT + AOT cache 595.1 ms 568.5 ms 625.6 ms 157 MB GraalVM native image 53.5 ms 50.9 ms 63.1 ms 41 MB OpenLDK warm image 1261.7 ms 1237.8 ms 1283.2 ms 450 MB OpenLDK snapshot image 83.9 ms 77.5 ms 88.6 ms 175 MB These timings cover process launch through exit for the small command-line application; peak RSS is measured separately. The benchmark script checks that the application output matches across variants. This measures startup and a short task, not steady-state throughput or web-server readiness.
GraalVM is faster and smaller here: 53.5 ms and 41 MB, against OpenLDK’s 83.9 ms and 175 MB. GraalVM still runs Spring initialization at launch; OpenLDK reuses the saved context.
Standard GraalVM Native Image makes a closed-world assumption: all classes must be known at build time, with dynamic accesses covered by analysis or metadata. OpenLDK keeps its class loader and JIT compiler, so new classes and previously unused methods can still compile after launch. Those paths pay their compilation cost when first used.
Saved images also need their classpath files and JDK available at runtime. The image documentation covers deployment constraints.
OpenLDK still has compatibility gaps, including unimplemented bytecode verification. Development targets SBCL on Linux.
To try the polyglot examples, follow the build requirements, then run these commands from the OpenLDK checkout:
ocicl install make sbcl-polyglot ./sbcl-polyglot --load examples/one-form.lisp Seven languages later: LXI (sixty-one).

title: Saudi Defence Minister leads Makkah pact delegation to Tehran in major diplomatic push
body: Saudi Arabia 's Minister of Defence Prince Khalid bin Salman made a surprise visit to Tehran on Monday in a major push for de-escalation in the Middle East amid intensifying Houthi attacks on Saudi cities and fears of a renewed full-scale war between Iran and the US. Pakistan 's army chief of staff, Field Marshal Asim Munir, and Ibrahim Kalin, the director of Turkey's intelligence service, were also attending the meetings in the Iranian capital, said Rayed Krimly, Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy in the Saudi Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Saudi Foreign Affairs Ministry said that Prince Khalid's visit came as part of the Makkah Agreement states' efforts to "de-escalate between the parties to the current crisis, encourage dialogue and diplomatic solutions" as well as to support mediation efforts by Qatar and Pakistan. The Makkah Agreement is a collective defence alliance signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan in August. It has been submitted to Turkey's parliament for ratification this week and is based on the principle that an attack on one member is considered an attack on all. The talks mark the first time that senior officials from the Makkah Agreement countries have engaged in direct talks with Iran since the pact was signed and Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis began their escalation against Saudi Arabia in the same month. More diplomatic efforts were under way on Monday. Qatar's Prime Minister and Foreign Minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman, spoke by phone with Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan and Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty. They discussed ways to "de-escalate tensions and promote regional stability and security", the Qatari Foreign Ministry said. Concern has grown about the possibility of a return to war between the US and Iran, with both sides issuing renewed threats. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Monday's meeting was a "key development in shaping regional diplomacy". He told local media that a "quadrilateral meeting" that includes Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian "serves as a practical step towards deliberation and co-operation on regional security mechanisms". Qatari media had reported that a delegation from the country was in Tehran on Sunday. US President Donald Trump last week said Washington may carry out another "little Epic Fury", using the military's term for the war on Iran. The timeline is unclear for when that may happen because Mr Trump said previously that he would not launch attacks before the US midterm elections on November 3. He also spoke of a "big beautiful agreement" as an alternative to renewed strikes. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi confirmed that indirect talks with the US were continuing through mediators Pakistan and Qatar. But he said Tehran was ready to resume fighting, while insisting that diplomacy was possible. "All regional factors pushed towards the visit to Tehran, but the most important was the renewed deadlock in the Yemeni war and its increasing danger", a source in Tehran said. "Riyadh knows that one of the keys to solving the Yemeni issue lies in Iran, especially as the Yemeni war has become deeply intertwined with the wider regional conflict." Prince Khalid last visited Tehran in April last year. "His presence means that he personally represents both the King and the Crown Prince in this move, with a clear mandate, and is leveraging the special relationship that links Tehran with Islamabad and Ankara to open channels for a settlement," added the source. Saudi Arabia has come under intensified Houthi attacks in recent weeks, including deadly strikes on airports that have disrupted air travel and prompted the cancellation or postponement of major international conferences, diplomatic summits and sporting events in the kingdom. The Houthis have also claimed attacks on Saudi energy and military targets. In September, sources in Tehran, Aden and Cairo spoke to The National about a plan by Iran to use the conflict in Yemen as a new pressure point in its war with the US . The latest Houthi escalation began in July after what the rebels described as Saudi aggression against Sanaa airport, shortly before a direct flight from Tehran landed in Yemen .

title: Why Are Laws Vital to Ukraine’s EU Integration Stuck in Parliament as the Country Loses Money?
body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky recently signed laws abolishing the VAT exemption for foreign parcels worth up to €150 ($168) and introduced taxation of income earned by users of digital platforms. All three documents returned to parliament with the president’s signature on Oct. 22 and all laws were adopted as part of the EU’s requirements. Their passage took substantial time due to being highly unpopular.
One such requirement was the taxation of parcels arriving from abroad. The problem is that such “parcels” often serve as a convenient way to ship large quantities of various goods from third countries, primarily China. Everything from drone components to cosmetics, clothing, children’s toys and auto parts was imported under the guise of parcels.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The law proved extremely unpopular , despite Ukrainians’ desire to join the EU. During wartime, as Ukrainians face enormous expenses on fuel, generators and any equipment that could help them cope with the war and Russian attacks, nobody wants to spend extra money. This is especially true in the case of taxes which, in the wake of recent corruption scandals, many people believe do not always go where they should.
This is only the beginning of a long and politically unpopular road for a government that is already struggling to secure public support and approval for its initiatives.
By the end of the year, the Verkhovna Rada must adopt around 32 more laws, while the government must meet more than 30 benchmarks. Key reforms being monitored by Ukraine’s partners are as follows:
1. Reform of the State Bureau of Investigation (DBR) and the Security Service of Ukraine SBU) – two key state agencies involved in law enforcement and anti-corruption efforts and subject to the influence of the central authorities.
Draft Law No. 13602 concerns changes to the DBR’s head, the introduction of a transparent competition to select its director, the vetting of DBR employees, and the removal of several provisions that allow the President’s Office to influence the appointment of the agency’s head.
As for the SBU, the European Commission demands that it be stripped of functions that do not properly belong to a security service, particularly investigative powers, and that its activities focus on counterintelligence, counterterrorism, cybersecurity and the protection of critical infrastructure.
2. Adoption of an anti-corruption strategy and reform of the High Anti-Corruption Court.
Draft Law No. 15230 is intended to close many loopholes that allow corruption suspects to manipulate proceedings before the High Anti-Corruption Court, including methods of deliberately delaying cases. The anti-corruption strategy, for example, envisages selecting the Prosecutor General through an open competition. At present, the president appoints the Prosecutor General.
3. Joining the Single Euro Payments Area (SEPA) – the EU’s integrated system for euro payments.
Draft Law No. 14327 explicitly provides for Ukraine’s accession to the single European payments area, which already includes 27 countries, including some that are not currently members of the Schengen Area.
The draft laws remain in parliamentary committees, and in some cases, one or two alternative versions have already been drafted alongside the original proposals.
European officials are losing patience .
For example, Ukraine reportedly risks losing a substantial amount of $29.5 billion in planned international aid financing if parliament misses deadlines for required legislation, according to Ukraine’s Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi.
The EU has moved to a new approach: no more advances. The law comes first, and the money follows. This applies to every required piece of legislation.
So, what is the problem if these reforms are intended to make Ukrainian state institutions more effective?
The reality is complicated so let’s examine the main reasons.
One reason is that some draft laws are still in a rough form and have not been adequately prepared. For example, the anti-corruption strategy was drafted by the National Agency on Corruption Prevention (NACP), and some members of parliament have openly said it needs further work.
Some draft laws have been prepared by the government and still need to be brought into compliance with legislative requirements.
The three bills mentioned above are among the main priorities. And even the approximately 35 laws required by the end of the year are merely a warm-up. According to estimates by lawyers and members of parliament, between 9,000 and 11,000 provisions must ultimately be brought into line with EU legislation.
That is a huge amount of work in an environment where parliament is characterized by dysfunction .
Strengthening anti-corruption efforts, eliminating procedural delays at the High Anti-Corruption Court, and joining the European payments system, are concerns for many members of parliament, influential financial and industrial groups, and their lobbyists.
Ukraine is a country with a transitional economy, moving from the Soviet command-and-administrative system to a market economy based on private ownership. Amid the chaos of this transition – accompanied by the deterioration of Soviet institutions and the weakness of the newly established state apparatus – large areas of economic activity were left without proper legal regulation, while others were subjected to excessive regulation. This has led to blatant abuses and chaos in the former case, and to the search for corrupt “loopholes” to resolve issues quickly in the latter.
Now, many people fear that past “sins,” income and payments could become a source of legal trouble.
The same problem arises in connection with the work of anti-corruption agencies. Ten years ago, converting commercial premises into an office or residential property without changing the designated use of the land or building was not a problem. Now it could be. Examples can be found everywhere, from villages to parliament itself.
Take lawmakers’ salaries, for example. Since Soviet times, these have been very low. In the USSR, members of parliament were largely nominal figures. The situation has remained much the same in independent Ukraine. No one has been eager to raise lawmakers’ salaries because doing so would be deeply unpopular, especially when pay does not increase significantly during wartime.
Yet lawmakers do not want to take responsibility for drafting laws worth billions for next to nothing. Alternatively, they may take on that responsibility but also expect “bonuses” for drafting such laws. These payments began to be made through political parties , in cash-filled envelopes.
Such practice constitutes a criminal offense, and the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) has drawn up dozens of cases against members of parliament involving precisely this practice .
Yet the problem remains unresolved. Raising lawmakers’ salaries is politically unprofitable because it is unpopular, while they are unwilling to vote for government-backed bills for $1,000 – especially when those bills could potentially make their own lives more difficult.
Reforming the DBR, the SBU and the Prosecutor General’s Office runs up against rivalry among various law enforcement agencies. Through 35 years of independence, an informal division of responsibilities and a system of “checks and balances” have developed among them.
Any changes are interpreted by each agency as an attempt to increase or expand the powers of its “competitors.”
Adding fuel to the fire is the fact that both the DBR and the SBU fall under the president’s sphere of influence and strengthen his power. The president personally appoints the heads of these agencies. Critics argue that the DBR is sometimes used as an instrument of political pressure against the authorities’ opponents, since its jurisdiction includes top officials, members of parliament and judges.
Would President Zelensky want to relinquish his influence over law enforcement agencies? That seems unlikely, as this is not merely about maintaining control over the situation – from surveillance of journalists , as happened with the SBU in 2023, to carrying out the president’s instructions, particularly those of his inner circle .
It is also a question of state stability. With NABU and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO) outside the president’s direct sphere of influence, many people both on Bankova Street and in the Cabinet of Ministers fear that any redistribution of powers among the agencies could trigger another political crisis.
One argument against these initiatives is Euroscepticism. Ukraine has long been “fed” promises of EU membership, with the prospect of accession repeatedly pushed further into the future. Meanwhile, some countries admitted to the EU between the late 1990s and the mid-2000s were in no better condition than Ukraine is today in terms of legislation and the effectiveness of their state institutions.
This fuels a sense among many Ukrainians that the EU is simply stringing Ukraine along with empty promises.
Kyiv Post once asked a member of the European Parliament, “When will Ukraine become an EU member?”
“Immediately after Turkey,” the lawmaker replied optimistically.
That was 20 years ago, and the situation has still not changed. As a result, many people from different social backgrounds believe that reshaping the country to satisfy the EU – which, in their view, Ukraine will not join anytime soon, if ever – may not be worth the effort.
Ukraine’s parliament will continue its work, yet – for now at least – not on the EU-needed Bills.

title: Ebenezer Adjetey Sowah appointed Genkas Energy MD
body: Energy expert and a member of the International Society of Petroleum Engineers, Ebenezer Adjetey Sowah, has been appointed Managing Director of Genkas Energy Ltd, effective September 30, 2026. His appointment brings on board his vast experience in petroleum distribution, commercial operations and business management to the leadership of the company, which has interests in oil and gas and renewable energy. His membership of the International Society of Petroleum Engineers reflects his professional affiliation with the wider petroleum engineering community and connection to developments and professional knowledge within the petroleum industry. Mr Adjetey Sowah had previously served as a Dealer Cluster Manager at Vivo Energy Ghana, where he gained experience in dealer network management, commercial performance and stakeholder relations. He studied Aircraft Load Controlling at Emirates Aviation College and also has expertise in business intelligence analysis and health, safety and environmental management. In his new role, Mr Sowah is expected to oversee the company’s day-to-day operations, including oil and gas importation and distribution, financial management, staff supervision and regulatory compliance. His experience across energy operations, business intelligence, commercial management, and safety-related disciplines provides a broad perspective on the challenges and opportunities facing modern energy businesses. His professional outlook emphasises safety, accountability, operational discipline and data-driven decision-making. Reacting to his appointment, Mr Adjetey Sowah said, “My focus is on promoting operational excellence, strengthening business relationships and identifying opportunities for sustainable growth. He added that effective leadership must be supported by accountability, continuous improvement and practical industry knowledge to achieve lasting business results. Mr Adjetey Sowah’s responsibilities will also include developing business opportunities, managing relationships with customers and suppliers, and reporting to the Board on operational and financial performance. His appointment includes translating the company’s business objectives into measurable results while ensuring sound management and compliance with applicable industry requirements. The appointment was confirmed by the Board of Directors, with Board Chairman George N. Owodo and Board Secretary Anette Adjavon signing the appointment letter on behalf of the company. Company’s profile Genkas Energy Ltd is a limited liability company operating in the oil and gas sector, with business interests in the trading of energy materials, energy resources, and renewable energy products and solutions. The company aims to serve the energy needs of businesses, industries, institutions, and other commercial clients through reliable sourcing, trading, and the development of strategic business relationships. Genkas Energy Ltd says it is committed to professionalism, integrity, innovation, and sustainable development, and seeks to identify opportunities across the conventional energy industry and the growing renewable energy market. The company seeks to build lasting partnerships, advance the energy sector, and become a reputable, trusted energy company recognised for excellence in energy trading, oil and gas, and renewable energy solutions across Ghana and international markets. Its mission is to provide reliable energy resources and trading solutions through professional service delivery, strategic partnerships, responsible business practices, and a commitment to sustainable energy development.

title: Lula da Silva elected President of Brazil for fourth time
body:
Ukrinform reports this, citing Politico . With more than 99% of the votes counted, Lula da Silva received 51.76%, while his rival, Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, won 48.24%.
Lula thus became the first candidate in the history of democratic Brazil to win a presidential runoff after losing the first round.
“People went to vote because we convinced them it was important to preserve democracy,” he said after his victory. “This country doesn’t accept being anybody’s colony,” he added.
The election took place amid allegations of U.S. interference, corruption scandals and deep political divisions.
Last year, U.S. President Donald Trump imposed tariffs on Brazil and sanctions on a Supreme Court justice who sentenced Jair Bolsonaro for attempting to stage a coup.
Lula will face a strong opposition in Congress, as Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party secured the largest congressional bloc in the first round.
As reported by Ukrinform, the Brazilian president’s campaign accused technology giant Meta of interfering in the election.

title: 2027: Fintiri announces Adamawa APC campaign council, names Marwa co-chair
body:
Governor Ahmadu Fintiri of Adamawa has announced the composition of the All Progressives Congress (APC) Campaign Council for the 2027 general elections in the state. ‎ ‎This is contained in a statement issued in Yola by the Governor’s Chief Press Secretary, Humwashi Wonosikou. ‎ The statement said the council will be chaired by Mr Fintiri, with a retired Brigadier General, Buba Marwa, as co-chairman. ‎ According to the statement, the Deputy Governor, Kaletapwa Farauta, will serve as Deputy Chairman I, while the APC governorship candidate, Ahmed Galadima, will serve as Deputy Chairman II. ‎ ‎“Mr Titus Solomon has been appointed Director General of the Campaign Council, while Amb. Peter Kevin will serve as Campaign Director.”
‎It said the council comprises party stalwarts, stakeholders, and youth and women leaders drawn from the state’s 21 local government areas. ‎ ‎The governor charged members of the council to work in unity and deliver victory for the APC at all levels in the forthcoming elections. ‎ ‎He said the council was designed to reflect the party’s commitment to inclusivity and grassroots mobilisation.

title: Prado SUVs: Social media agog over Dayo Israel’s gifts to APC youth leaders
body: By Efe Onodjae Social media has been awash with reactions following the display of brand-new Toyota Prado SUVs by the National Youth Leader of the All Progressives Congress (APC), Dayo Israel, for selected youth leaders of the party. Israel, in a post on X on Sunday, said the 2026 Prado SUVs were presented to support the beneficiaries’ election mobilisation activities ahead of the 2027 general elections. He also expressed appreciation to First Lady Oluremi Tinubu for her support for the party’s youth structure. However, the announcement, accompanied by a video showing seven vehicles, sparked criticism from Nigerians, with many questioning the timing of the gesture amid the economic hardship confronting citizens. Some users also questioned the source of funding for the vehicles, while others compared the expenditure with the challenges facing the country’s healthcare sector and security personnel. An X user, @HarmlessHQ, criticised the development, linking it to the economic difficulties facing Nigerians. “Yesterday in Kaduna, Tinubu was blaming the opposition for the hunger and hardship in the country. Today, Dayo Israel, APC youth leader is casually dashing out 2026 Prado SUV to his fellow youth leaders,” the user wrote. Similarly, @RealAdeshina questioned the source of the funds used to acquire the vehicles, raising concerns about the state of healthcare facilities in the country. “Most hospitals in Nigeria don’t have MRI machines, yet Dayo Israel, a national youth leader of the APC, can buy seven 2026 Prados for his friends? Where did he get the money?” the user queried. Another X user, @Unkleayo, expressed outrage over the reported cost of the vehicles, questioning the priorities behind the presentation. “This is what you bastards are doing with our commonwealth,” the user wrote, adding that the development raised questions about the country’s priorities. Also reacting, @thoughtsmini2 argued that the luxury vehicles could undermine calls for Nigerians to endure the economic reforms. “They will drive this to tell the youth to endure the pain of reforms,” the user wrote. Another user, @Adewolessamuel, criticised Israel and the First Lady, saying they were disconnected from the economic realities facing ordinary Nigerians. “Out of touch with reality, tone deaf to the cry of the masses. You and your mummy, that’s who you are,” the user wrote. Meanwhile, Professor Pat Utomi, a chieftain of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), criticised the display, contrasting the cost of the vehicles with the salaries of Nigerian soldiers. In a post on X, Utomi said: “Nigerian soldiers are being paid peanuts as salaries, yet an APC youth leader is flaunting SUVs worth billions of naira.” He also questioned whether the money spent on the vehicles could have been used to provide ambulances and other essential healthcare equipment. The Nigeria Democratic Congress also criticised the development, estimating that the seven vehicles were worth about N1.015 billion based on its assessment of their market prices. However, Israel’s post did not disclose the cost of the vehicles or the source of funding for their purchase. The post was later deleted after generating widespread reactions online. Meanwhile a netizens with the username @Hausa wrote “Dear Dayo Israel, We all love the president and want him to succeed, but sharing of these expensive exotic cars solely for campaigning is not only insensitive but very poorly timed. What makes a great leader is also the ability to read between the lines, understand the present situation, and know when to act. Do you know what just one of this cars will do for a whole community? Nigerian need grassroots and structural development not enriching few people loyal to the party.” The post Prado SUVs: Social media agog over Dayo Israel’s gifts to APC youth leaders appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Twellium wins Beverage Manufacturing Brand of the Decade Award
body: Twellium Industrial Company Limited has been named Ultimate Beverage Manufacturing Brand of the Decade at the sixth edition of the National Governance and Business Leadership Awards 2026, recognising the company’s manufacturing growth, product development and expanding regional presence. The recognition marks a significant milestone for the Ghanaian beverage manufacturer, which has built a diverse portfolio of locally produced drinks and food products since commencing operations in February 2014. In a related achievement, Verna Mineral Water received the Outstanding Environmental Sustainability Initiative of the Year award for its No Seal, Less Wasteprogramme, which seeks to reduce unnecessary plastic packaging. The two distinctions at the National Governance and Business Leadership Awards 2026 highlight Twellium’s progress in manufacturing while drawing attention to efforts to incorporate environmental considerations into its business operations. A Decade of Manufacturing Investment and Growth Founded in Ghana in 2013 by Hussein Kesserwani and Hassan Kesserwani, Twellium began production on February 4, 2014. The company has since expanded its production capabilities, introducing products across the beverage and food manufacturing sectors. Its portfolio includes Verna Mineral Water, Rush Energy Drink, Bigoo, Planet, American Cola and Bubble Up, which have contributed to its presence in Ghana’s competitive consumer goods market. The company subsequently diversified into the baking industry through McBerry biscuits, wafers, cookies and cakes. Rosa Premium Glass Water and the recently introduced Dairy One range further demonstrate its efforts to broaden its product offerings. These developments have been supported by investment in manufacturing infrastructure and production capacity, positioning Twellium as a notable participant in Ghana’s industrial and consumer goods sectors. In Ghana, the company operates production facilities in the Accra area and Kumasi. Its regional manufacturing presence also includes Bobo-Dioulasso in Burkina Faso and company-reported local production in Sindia, Senegal. This regional footprint reflects an approach that combines exports from Ghana with production closer to consumers in selected West African markets. The Ghana Export Promotion Authority lists Burkina Faso, Liberia, Mali and Côte d’Ivoire among Twellium’s export destinations, illustrating the company’s participation in regional trade. Verna’s No Seal, Less Waste Initiative Earns Sustainability Recognition While Twellium’s decade award celebrates its manufacturing development, Verna Mineral Water’s environmental sustainability distinction recognises a specific packaging initiative. Through its “No Seal, Less Waste” programme, Verna removes additional plastic seals from its bottles, reducing unnecessary packaging at source. The initiative reflects an approach to environmental responsibility that focuses on product design and packaging decisions rather than relying solely on waste management after products have been consumed. It also aligns with the broader objectives of Sustainable Development Goal 12, which promotes responsible consumption and production. The recognition places Verna’s packaging initiative within the growing conversation about how manufacturers can reduce material use and address the environmental impact of consumer products. Twellium’s investment in effluent treatment also forms part of its wider environmental management efforts, complementing the company’s manufacturing activities. Social Investment Extends Beyond Manufacturing Twellium’s corporate activities also include social interventions through the Twellium Foundation and Verna Changing Lives, initiatives associated with support for healthcare, education and livelihoods. Documented interventions include donations of incubators and phototherapy equipment to health facilities, assistance with medical treatment, community infrastructure support and contributions to Ghana’s national amputee football team. These programmes extend the company’s engagement beyond its commercial operations, connecting its business presence with selected community and social development needs. For manufacturers operating at scale, such initiatives also highlight the broader responsibilities associated with industrial expansion, including community engagement and support for essential services. Twellium Awards 2026 Add to Manufacturing Recognition The Ultimate Beverage Manufacturing Brand of the Decade award adds to Twellium’s industry recognition, following its designation as Most Innovative Company of the Decade at the 2026 Ghana Manufacturing Awards. Together, the honours recognise different aspects of the company’s development, from manufacturing and product innovation to efforts to address environmental sustainability through Verna Mineral Water. The awards come against the backdrop of Twellium’s expanding product portfolio, investment in production facilities and participation in regional markets. For Verna, the “No Seal, Less Waste” distinction brings additional attention to packaging reduction as a practical area where consumer brands can pursue environmental improvements. Twellium’s latest recognition therefore represents an important milestone in its manufacturing journey, while Verna’s sustainability award highlights the role that product and packaging decisions can play in shaping more responsible production practices.

title: BACCIMA seeks dredging of Badagry channel for enhanced trade
body: By Godwin Oritse The Badagry Chamber of Commerce, Industry, Mines and Agriculture (BACCIMA) has called for the immediate and sustained dredging of the Badagry Channel to boost maritime trade and strengthen economic ties among countries in the West African sub-region. Speaking to Vanguard on the sidelines of the recently concluded World Maritime Day celebration at the Lagos Continental Hotel, the immediate past president of BACCIMA, Yahaya Idris, said the Badagry Channel had become a vital trade route for traders along the West African coast, particularly those from Nigeria, Benin Republic and Togo. Idris added that many traders from the Benin Republic access Nigeria through the Badagry Lagoon for commercial and other economic activities. He, however, noted that marine wreckage along the route posed navigational challenges to vessels plying the channel, underscoring the need for regular dredging and the removal of wrecks to ensure safe and efficient navigation. He explained that the CMS waterfront and the Liverpool area beneath the Apapa Bridge had become major hubs for traders who travel to Nigeria to purchase goods and transport them through the Badagry waterways to neighbouring West African countries. Idris expressed optimism that dredging the channel would enable boats operating under the National Inland Waterways Authority (NIWA) to utilise the route for commercially viable operations, thereby boosting inland waterway transportation and regional trade. He said:” We want the Badagry Lagoon or channels dredged for increased economic activities because we have a lot of traders coming from Benin Republic to Nigeria through that lagoon. “If you go to Liverpool in Apapa under the bridge, the volume of trade going on there between Nigeria and people from neighbouring countries is unbelievable. So the need to dredge the stretch of the water cannot be overemphasized.” The post BACCIMA seeks dredging of Badagry channel for enhanced trade appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Women in Central Asia Have Rights on Paper, What Holds Them Back in Practice?
body: The Astana Times provides news and information from Kazakhstan and around the world. ASTANA – For women across Central Asia, equal rights enshrined in law do not necessarily translate into equal opportunities in everyday life, researchers said during a CAPS Unlock discussion examining barriers to women’s economic and professional advancement. Researchers and gender experts examined how deeply rooted expectations about marriage, motherhood and professional leadership continue to shape women’s choices, even as governments seek to increase their participation in economic life. The more difficult challenge, experts noted, is ensuring that women have the freedom and institutional support to use the opportunities already available to them. The discussion was held as part of the Central Asian Think Tanks Forum organized by Paperlab in partnership with CAPS Unlock. Photo credit: CAPS Unlock Independent researcher Dinara Nurusheva said that workplace policies intended to support parents can fall short when employers and managers continue to operate under traditional assumptions about caregiving. For her, the barriers women face in the workplace are also personal. After she married, prospective employers repeatedly asked when she planned to have children, even though she would not become a mother until eight years later. Her experience later informed research into the “motherhood penalty,” the economic and professional disadvantages women face after having children. Nurusheva also challenged the notion that women’s decisions to return to work, change professions or accept lower-paying jobs after maternity leave are entirely voluntary. “What is interesting is that we often frame this as an individual problem for women to solve. A woman has to decide who will look after her child, what to do with her career and how she will earn a living. But in reality, this is a structural problem,” said Nurusheva. Moderator Bota Ayazbayeva, Dinara Nurusheva and Elmira Abylbek. Photo credit: CAPS Unlock “We often talk about choice: a woman’s choice to return to work after maternity leave, to change careers or to take a job that pays significantly less than the one she had before,” she added. “We need to create conditions that allow women to make genuine choices.” The burden of unpaid domestic work compounds those constraints. Nurusheva said 95% of women in her research spend at least an hour a day on unpaid household labor, with some spending more than six hours. Limited access to public childcare for children younger than three further restricts women’s options for returning to work, she said. Nurusheva called for expanded early childhood care and dedicated leave for fathers, noting that men seeking to take on greater caregiving responsibilities also encounter resistance rooted in traditional gender roles. In Kazakhstan, for example, only 1% of men take parental leave. Uzbekistan’s case In Uzbekistan, similar tensions have emerged around efforts to encourage fathers to take a greater role in childcare. Kamola Alieva, an associate professor of constitutional law at Tashkent State University of Law, discussed proposed legislation providing five days of paid paternity leave in Uzbekistan. However, she questioned whether the measure alone could change social expectations that caring for newborns is principally a mother’s responsibility. “Family is a shared responsibility,” Alieva said. She said she had also contributed to developing a draft concept titled the Well-Being of the Uzbek Family, which envisions how family life could evolve over the next decade. Active fatherhood was a central element in the concept, Alieva added, with men sharing responsibility for raising children and caring for family members. The concept had yet to be formally approved, underscoring the gap between policy ambitions and implementation. “Whatever changes we introduce, whether in legislation or policy, everything ultimately comes down to implementation and perception. There is a strong resistance,” she said. Alieva also questioned whether programs designed to expand women’s opportunities adequately account for the different circumstances in which women live. Equal rights, she noted, do not necessarily guarantee equal opportunities for a woman from a low-income rural household and one from a more affluent urban family. “For me, equal opportunity means taking into account the needs of a particular group of people,” she said. Alieva urged policymakers to assess whether programs, including educational grants and scholarships, translate into meaningful employment opportunities rather than simply measuring how many women receive support. The barriers extend into politics. Alieva described qualitative research involving women lawmakers and local council members across five regions of Uzbekistan, who reported difficulties balancing unpaid domestic responsibilities with political duties, financial costs associated with public office and harassment. The findings also pointed to obstacles preventing women active in local politics from advancing to national leadership positions. Alieva said women currently account for 39% of parliamentary representation in Uzbekistan. Kamola Alieva. “Yet women hold only around 5% of positions in the executive branch, and at present, we have no female ministers. This means women are virtually absent from decision-making processes and have very limited access to positions where resources are allocated,” said Alieva. Overlooked economic contributions The debate over how to support women today also raised questions about how their economic contributions have been recognized in the past. Elmira Abylbek, head of Bishkek-based Esimde research platform, highlighted research into women who became traders and entrepreneurs during the economic turmoil of the 1990s, helping sustain their families while establishing commercial networks that extended beyond national borders. Abylbek said an earlier research project had collected more than 100 interviews, while a newer study had already exceeded its initial target of 25 interviews, reaching more than 35 and continuing to expand. The accounts, she said, reveal not only stories of economic survival but also women’s growing influence in public life. Some became involved in social movements that later helped lay the groundwork for political organizations. “At the very least, this should be included in history textbooks,” Abylbek said. She noted that women developed financial and business skills long before concepts such as financial literacy became widely discussed, building cross-border trading networks and passing their knowledge to younger generations. Some of today’s entrepreneurs are the daughters and granddaughters of women who pioneered those businesses in the 1990s. For Abylbek, documenting these experiences is also a way of challenging narratives that overlook women’s agency in shaping the region’s transformation after the collapse of the Soviet Union. “We need to look at different periods and also talk about those periods when women pulled society and the state through very difficult times,” she said. Abylbek also pointed to the importance of the language of assistance. Women, she noted, should be recognized as equal economic actors because portraying them primarily as vulnerable beneficiaries risks diminishing their agency. Growing conservative backlash The discussion also turned to what some researchers described as a growing conservative backlash against gender equality, particularly among younger generations. The discussion mentioned emerging research suggesting that young men in Kazakhstan and Tajikistan may be adopting more conservative attitudes toward gender roles, even as young women increasingly embrace more liberal views. Abylbek, however, warned that the shift extends beyond Central Asia. “We are seeing a conservative turn in politics, economics and practically every sphere,” she said, adding that similar patterns could be observed in the United States and the United Kingdom. She said that the trend was reflected not only in political discourse but also in perceptions of leadership and expectations about how men and women should behave. Alieva also pointed to growing tensions between younger generations over expectations of marriage and family life. “Young women don’t want to live like their mothers, while young men want to live like their fathers, enjoying the same privileges their fathers had,” Alieva said. According to her, these conflicting expectations are increasingly visible in public debates about gender roles, particularly on social media, where men who speak out in support of gender equality can face hostility. This, however, discourages influential male public figures from addressing discrimination and violence against women, leaving much of the advocacy to women themselves. She called for more men with substantial public audiences to challenge discriminatory attitudes and serve as role models for younger generations. The post Women in Central Asia Have Rights on Paper, What Holds Them Back in Practice? appeared first on The Astana Times .

title: Israel must listen to its friends, not dismiss their warnings - editorial
body: When one of Israel's most outspoken American supporters says two ministers are damaging the country's standing, the government should listen. Bill Ackman's Sunday warning about Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich deserves attention because it comes from someone who wants Israel to succeed, has defended it publicly, and has praised Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.The Jewish-American billionaire investor made clear in his post on X/Twitter that Israelis must decide who becomes their prime minister. But from his vantage point in America, the national security minister and finance minister, respectively, have caused Israel “enormous reputational damage,” their statements and actions presented internationally as expressing the will of all Israelis.A government without them, Ackman argued, would signal a new beginning, help restore credibility, improve relations with Democrats and Republicans, and increase the prospects of expanding the Abraham Accords, which normalized relations between Israel and several Arab states.His warning should not be dismissed as another intervention by someone hostile to the government. Ackman has praised Netanyahu's leadership since October 7 while identifying the two ministers as a serious liability. His criticism cannot credibly be reduced to opposition to Netanyahu or indifference to Israel's security.That makes it politically uncomfortable and valuable. It asks government supporters to consider whether loyalty to particular coalition partners serves the country they intend to defend.US Ambassador Mike Huckabee offers another example. A longstanding supporter of Israel appointed by President Donald Trump, Huckabee told The Jerusalem Post in September: “I wish that they understood the damage they're doing to the country they claim to love because it is not helpful.”He was referring to violence against Palestinians in the West Bank, which he warned was damaging Israel's reputation, including among Republicans. He also argued that condemning Palestinian violence while refusing to condemn Israeli violence would be hypocritical. His support for Israel did not prevent him from demanding accountability.There is a moral obligation here, before any question of reputation. Violence and humiliating treatment deserve scrutiny because of the harm they inflict, regardless of the headlines they generate. Israel should demand standards of its representatives that it can defend openly before its citizens and its allies.Recognizing that friendship doesn't require silence when Israelis harm Israel's interests.These interventions differ in scope. Huckabee's criticism of specific conduct is not an endorsement of Ackman's proposed coalition arrangement. What connects them is the recognition that friendship does not require silence when Israelis damage Israel's interests.Jerusalem should be capable of hearing that distinction. Criticism must be judged on its merits, whoever delivers it. But when people who regularly defend this country describe the difficulties created by its ministers, their warnings deserve attention. They understand Israel's arguments abroad because they have made those arguments themselves.Nor can every damaging image be explained away as hostile coverage. Ministers hold public authority. Their words carry weight because of their offices, and the government cannot expect foreign audiences to treat them as private citizens whenever their conduct becomes embarrassing.There are limits to Ackman's prescription. Removing two ministers would not automatically restore Israel's standing, resolve disagreements over the Palestinians, or secure additional normalization agreements.Those outcomes require policy, diplomacy, and decisions by other governments. Changing ministers alone would not substitute for responsible policy and leadership.The people entrusted with power nevertheless help define a government's priorities and credibility. A prime minister who promises responsible leadership abroad must exercise it within his cabinet.Coalition calculations cannot be the only measure of whether a partnership serves the national interest. That responsibility belongs to whoever forms the next government and chooses its senior ministers.The test for any coalition should be whether it can protect the country while governing responsibly at home and maintaining credibility abroad. That requires leaders willing to confront damaging conduct among their allies, rather than dismiss every warning as disloyalty or leave accountability to those watching Israel from overseas.Israel needs leadership that puts security, responsible government, and national cohesion first. Israelis alone will choose that leadership. They should do so with an honest accounting of the costs of political partnerships, including those identified by friends who remain committed to the country.Listening to those friends is an act of responsibility. Their support should give their warnings weight, not excuse ignoring them.

title: Lula da Silva wins 51.79% of vote after 100% of ballots counted — electoral court
body:
RIO DE JANEIRO, October 26. /TASS/. Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court, which performs the functions of the Central Election Commission, has completed the vote count for the second round of the presidential election. According to the final results, with 100% of ballots counted, incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has officially been reelected.
According to the election authority’s final statistics, Lula da Silva, the candidate of the left-wing Workers’ Party, won with 51.79% of the vote, receiving 64,256,232 votes. His rival, right-wing opposition Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, received 48.21%, with 59,826,041 people voting for him. The total number of valid votes was 124,082,273.
Lula da Silva is now the first politician in the present-day Brazilian history to win the presidential election after trailing in the first round of voting. The elected head of state will assume the office on January 1, 2027.
Earlier, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who represents the right-wing opposition and lost in the second round of the Brazilian presidential election, refused to recognize the election results and stated that they should be annulled.

title: Monet, Warhol and pioneering Emiratis to feature in Sotheby’s first Abu Dhabi fine art auction
body: Works by Claude Monet and Andy Warhol will go under the hammer alongside paintings by pioneering Emirati artists when Sotheby’s holds its first fine art auction in Abu Dhabi this December. Titled Breaking Ground, the December 10 sale will include Mohamed Ahmed Ibrahim, Hassan Sharif and Najat Makki. It is the main addition to the second edition of Collectors’ Week, expanding the programme beyond the luxury sales that launched the event last year. All six auctions will take place at the new Saadiyat Grove Experience Centre on Saadiyat Island. Watches, jewellery, handbags, cars and high-performance bicycles will go under the hammer on December 9, followed by fine art the next day. The sales will take place during a particularly busy season for Abu Dhabi’s art scene, following Christie’s first fine art auction in the city on November 1 and the inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi from November 19 to 22. Sotheby’s fine art sale will fall a day before Guggenheim Abu Dhabi opens on December 11. Alongside its luxury auctions, the inaugural Collector's Week included a fine art exhibition. “Whilst those works were there to be seen rather than sold, they were a real focal point – we had queues of people clamouring to see these iconic pieces in the flesh,” Katia Boueiz, head of Sotheby’s UAE and chairman, Middle East, tells The National . “Together with conversations that took place with everyone who walked through our doors on the ground, this set the tone for our planning for this next edition.” This year, visitors will be able to bid on works including Warhol’s Ads portfolio from 1985. Created two years before his death, it reflects his fascination with glamour, fashion, film and celebrity. The Monet work, Prunes et Abricots, was painted between 1882 and 1885 and commissioned by his art dealer, Paul Durand-Ruel, for his apartment drawing room in Paris. A drawing by Christo depicts the Abu Dhabi Mastaba , the proposed permanent artwork in the Liwa desert conceived by Christo and Jeanne-Claude. The project was designed as a monumental structure made from hundreds of thousands of oil barrels. The sale also brings together several generations of artists from the region. Alongside paintings by Ibrahim and Sharif, both pioneers of contemporary art in the UAE, Sotheby’s says it is working with artists and their estates to introduce Nujoom Al-Ghanem and Nasser Al-Yousif to auction for the first time. Boueiz says the title Breaking Ground emerged from the idea of artists who paved the way for subsequent generations. That approach also informed the focus on women artists, with works by Najat Makki, Huguette Caland, Inji Efflatoun, Fahrelnissa Zeid and Etel Adnan among those selected. Other artists represented include S H Raza, Fernando Botero and Paul Guiragossian. “We hope that by them sharing a space, an exhibition, and a global platform, collectors will be able to see new and unexpected synergies,” Boueiz says. “There will definitely be eyes on this sale from around the world, not just our clients based in the UAE, which makes it all the more important to curate a cohesive mix of art from the region and beyond. What I hope this auction will achieve is to introduce these artists to a much wider audience – whether it is the Emirati artists being introduced to international collectors, or vice versa.” While fine art expands the programme, the luxury auctions will return with about 50 watches from the single-owner Shapes of Cartier collection, including a rare Twin Strap dating from about 1970–1971. The car sale will feature several Ferraris, including a 2009 Scuderia Spider 16M and a 2004 360 Challenge Stradale, while jewellery highlights include a fancy brown-orange diamond weighing more than 40 carats. Public exhibitions, panel discussions and masterclasses will precede the auctions. Sotheby’s will release further details of the lots in November; exhibition dates and visiting hours were not included in the announcement. Boueiz expects the offering and format of Collectors’ Week to evolve in future editions. Alongside the auctions, she sees a role for Sotheby’s in helping prospective collectors develop their knowledge through talks and access to specialists. “The investment in world-class museums, cultural institutions and education is creating an environment where collecting can flourish, not only at an institutional level but increasingly within the private sector,” she says. “Ultimately, our ambition is not simply to ‘bring’ the international art market to Abu Dhabi, but to help connect and embed Abu Dhabi even more deeply within the international art market.”

title: Nigerian govt disburses N38.93 billion to 166 tertiary institutions
body:
The federal government has disbursed N38.93 billion to 166 public tertiary institutions nationwide to address infrastructure gaps and improve teaching and learning facilities.
This is contained in a statement issued by the Head of Media, Federal Ministry of Finance, Efe Ovuakporie, on Sunday in Abuja.
She said the disbursement was under the Needs Assessment Revitalisation Fund, covering 79 universities, 46 polytechnics and 41 colleges of education.
Ms Ovuakporie said universities would receive N28.5 billion, while polytechnics received N5.8 billion and colleges of education were allocated N4.7 billion.
She said the intervention was also aimed at supporting the implementation of agreed measures under the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between the Federal Government and the Academic Staff Union of Universities (ASUU).
Ms Ovuakporie said the funds were expected to enable beneficiary institutions to commence or continue approved projects addressing critical infrastructure and other identified institutional needs.
She said effective coordination among relevant agencies and beneficiary institutions was essential to ensuring that the funds translated into tangible improvements in educational infrastructure.
The Head of Media also advised members of the public seeking details of beneficiary institutions and their allocations to visit finance.gov .

title: Nigeria must manufacture meters locally, secure sustainable financing — Experts
body: By Esther Ihejirika Electricity sector experts have called for increased local meter manufacturing, sustainable financing and wider adoption of smart technology to accelerate meter deployment and close Nigeria’s metering gap. They made the call during a webinar on rapid meter rollout, stressing the need for a coordinated national metering plan to improve revenue collection, reduce estimated billing and curb electricity theft. Mr. Odion Omonfoman, host of the webinar, disclosed that the company had achieved “over 90 per cent metering coverage” and deployed more than 200,000 meters through the Meter Asset Provider (MAP) scheme and vendor-financing model. He said the company was targeting 100 per cent metering coverage by extending installations to all customers across its transformers and feeders. “Metering remains a strategic investment in revenue assurance. It enables customers to pay for the electricity they consume while reducing the dissatisfaction associated with estimated billing,” he said. Engr. Alegie Alfred, Head of Metering, Power Limited Electric Company (MPLEC), said Abia Power was tackling energy theft, meter bypass and vandalism through routine inspections, remote monitoring, consumption-pattern analysis, customer education and revenue-protection teams. Speaking on India’s experience, Ms. Ravleen Sethi, Director of Large Corporate Ratings, CareEdge, said government-backed programmes, private-sector investment and improved financing arrangements had accelerated smart-meter deployment in the country. She identified the Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS), introduced in 2021, as a major driver of investment and expansion in India’s metering manufacturing capacity. From the manufacturing perspective, Engr. Durosola Omogbenigun, President, Meter Manufacturers Association of Nigeria, called for a national metering plan involving the Federal and state governments, electricity distribution companies, investors, regulators and local manufacturers. The post Nigeria must manufacture meters locally, secure sustainable financing — Experts appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Babcock Australasia names new CEO
body: Babcock International Group has appointed Peter Behrendt as the new Chief Executive Officer (CEO) for Babcock Australia and New Zealand (Babcock). Behrendt will officially step into the role in early 2027, taking the reins from Leah Grantham who has been acting in the position since March. A Royal Australian Navy veteran, Behrendt joins Babcock with a strong track record of delivering results across complex and diverse organisations. He’s previously held senior management roles within multiple defence and security-focused companies, including Saab, BMT, Dataminr Inc, and most recently Serco. Babcock International, Chief Growth Officer Nick Hine, congratulated Behrendt on his appointment, saying: “Peter is a known leader who brings a wealth of experience to Babcock from across the defence sector. His vision and enthusiasm for the company and its growth are exciting, and I look forward to working with him as we drive forward into this new era in Australia and New Zealand.” Behrendt said he is honoured to be joining Babcock at such an important time for Australia and New Zealand. “Babcock has strong foundations and talented people, and I’m optimistic about what we can achieve together. There is much to do as our customers’ needs evolve, and meeting those needs will take sustained effort, close collaboration and a clear focus on delivery. I look forward to working with the team to build on its achievements and deliver the critical capabilities our customers rely on.” Hine thanked Acting CEO Leah Grantham for her dedication and support since assuming the position. “The dedication, professionalism and commitment Leah’s shown has been instrumental to the continued success of the business. Leah’s leadership has been crucial during this transitional period, and her contribution to enhancing Babcock’s performance and relationships has had a notable impact.” For Editorial Inquiries Contact: Editor Kym Bergmann at kym.bergmann@venturamedia.net For Advertising Inquiries Contact: Group Sales Director Simon Hadfield at simon.hadfield@venturamedia.net

title: NiMet forecasts Nigeria’s weather for next three days
body:
The Nigerian Meteorological Agency (NiMet) has forecast dust haze, sunshine and thunderstorms across Nigeria from Monday to Wednesday, warning residents about potential weather hazards.
In its weather outlook released on Sunday in Abuja, the agency predicted slight dust haze over Jigawa, Kano, Katsina, Kaduna, Zamfara, Kebbi and Sokoto states on Monday.
NiMet said sunny conditions were expected across the North-east throughout the forecast period.
For the North-central region, it forecast sunny skies with patches of clouds and possible thunderstorms accompanied by light rain over parts of Kogi, Kwara, Benue, the Federal Capital Territory and Nasarawa.
Across the South, cloudy skies with sunshine intervals were expected, alongside possible morning thunderstorms and light rain over coastal states.
The agency said scattered thunderstorms accompanied by light rain could occur later over parts of Abia, Imo, Anambra, Enugu, Ebonyi, Ogun, Ondo, Lagos, Oyo, Osun, Edo, Delta, Bayelsa, Rivers, Cross River and Akwa Ibom.
For Tuesday, NiMet predicted sunny and hazy conditions across the North, with isolated thunderstorms and light rain possible over southern Taraba throughout the forecast period.
It forecast sunny and hazy skies with patches of clouds across the North-central region, with possible morning thunderstorms over Benue.
The agency added that thunderstorms accompanied by light rain were expected across most parts of the region during the afternoon or evening.
Across the South, NiMet predicted cloudy skies with sunshine intervals and possible morning thunderstorms accompanied by light rain over parts of Anambra, Ebonyi, Abia, Cross River, Akwa Ibom, Rivers and Bayelsa.
It said thunderstorms accompanied by light rain were expected across most parts of the southern region later on Tuesday.
For Wednesday, the agency forecast sunny and hazy conditions across the northern region throughout the day.
It predicted sunny skies with patches of clouds across the North-central region, with isolated thunderstorms and light rain possible over parts of Kwara during the afternoon.
NiMet said cloudy skies with sunshine intervals were expected across the South during the morning, followed by thunderstorms accompanied by moderate rain later.
The agency advised residents to take precautions against suspended dust particles, particularly people with asthma and other respiratory conditions.
“People with asthmatic health conditions and other respiratory issues should be cautious of the present weather condition,” it said.
NiMet warned that strong winds could precede thunderstorms and urged residents to secure loose objects to prevent them from being blown away.
It also advised the public to disconnect electrical appliances from sockets and avoid standing under tall trees during storms to prevent injuries from falling branches.
The agency advised airline operators to obtain airport-specific weather reports and flight documentation from NiMet to support effective operational planning.
It urged residents to remain informed through regular weather updates on its website.

title: Dangote charts path to Africa’s industrial revolution, prioritises power, financing
body: Africa’s ambition to become global industrial powerhouse hinges on its ability to mobilize long-term financing, deliver reliable electricity and adopt policies that turn its vast natural resources into manufactured products, President/Chief Executive, Dangote Industries Limited, Aliko Dangote, has declared. Dangote, who has outlined a $50 billion investment programme for 2026 to 2030, said the continent must build stronger financial institutions capable of funding large-scale industrial projects, expand electricity infrastructure and establish policies that encourage domestic manufacturing, value addition and economic diversification. Speaking in London at the 2026 Financial Times Africa Summit during a conversation with David Pilling the Africa Editor for the newspaper, the industrialist maintained that Africa possessed the natural resources, population and investment opportunities required to become a global manufacturing powerhouse, but needed stronger institutions and infrastructure to translate those advantages into sustainable economic prosperity. Responding to a question on why Africa had produced relatively few industrial enterprises of global scale despite its enormous economic potential, Dangote stressed the need for deliberate policies and institutions capable of supporting long-term industrial investment. Dangote said: “I think the number one thing that the continent has to concentrate on doing is having very strong financial institutions, their own financial institutions, and also to have very strong agricultural policy, and also industrial policy”. He maintained that infrastructure development was equally important but singled out electricity as perhaps the most urgent requirement for unlocking Africa’s industrial potential, adding; “For Africa, what we need the most today is actually power”. Dangote explained that inadequate electricity supply continued to undermine Africa’s ability to process its mineral resources locally, forcing countries to export raw materials rather than capture the greater economic value associated with manufacturing and processing. He cited the mining industry as a particularly striking example, noting that companies frequently identified unreliable electricity supply as a major reason for their inability to establish processing facilities close to extraction sites. The industrialist also drew on his experience developing the Dangote Petroleum Refinery in Lagos to illustrate how Africa’s financing environment could frustrate even commercially promising projects. He disclosed that the Group had been compelled to finance the refinery against its own balance sheet rather than depend on conventional project financing, which he described as extremely difficult to secure for major African industrial investments. He explained that prolonged financing negotiations could undermine the viability of industrial projects by delaying execution, increasing costs and exposing investors to changing economic conditions. For the Dangote Group, the decision to proceed with the refinery without conventional project finance involved extraordinary financial risks, compounded by severe currency depreciation and the enormous cost of developing supporting infrastructure. Dangote said the exchange rate moved from approximately ₦136 to the dollar to as high as ₦1,800 during the refinery’s development, while about 90 per cent of the Group’s revenue was denominated in naira. Dangote said the Group’s proposed $50 billion investment programme was designed partly to encourage other Africans to recognise the opportunities available across the continent. ‘‘The legacy we are trying to set up is how do we industrialise our continent?” he said. title: Vučić concedes defeat in Parliamentary election
body:
Reuters reported this, according to Ukrinform.
“It is clear that we have lost these elections, the Student List has won,” Vučić said after the polls closed, adding that the students would have between 135 and 140 seats in the 250-seat parliament and that his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) would have 105, based on preliminary results.
The snap election, called by the head of state in September, was held after nearly two years of student protests against corruption. The protests were sparked by a 2024 tragedy in the city of Novi Sad, where 16 people were killed when a canopy at the railway station collapsed. According to Reuters, the students have gained broad support, emerging as the most serious challenge to Vučić since he first became prime minister in 2014 and later president in 2017.
On October 25, voters elected 250 members of the National Assembly. Vučić, who represents the Serbian Progressive Party, had planned to remain in power by becoming prime minister.
As reported, at the end of September, Aleksandar Vučić announced in an address to the nation that he had resigned as president in order to take part in the snap parliamentary election and run for prime minister.
Vučić became President of Serbia on May 31, 2017, and was re-elected in April 2022.

title: Iraq's biggest ever budget for 2027 built for boom times amid economic bust
body: Iraq is debating a draft federal budget for 2027 that would be the biggest in its history, but the plan is also the most detached from the country's financial reality. The bill, a copy of which was seen by The National , looks like a welfare-state budget drafted for a stable time, not an austerity plan for a government in the middle of its worst financial crisis in years. The total public expenditure is projected at about 217.2 trillion dinars ($143.6 billion). The draft expects only 174.2 trillion dinars in revenue – about 144 trillion dinars is to come from selling crude oil and 30.2 trillion dinars from non-oil sources – leaving a gap of about 43 trillion dinars. The draft says the deficit "is covered from the surplus realised from the increase in crude oil export prices or increased crude oil exports or internal and external borrowing and from carry-over funds". But that is an assumption disproved by Iraq's recent fiscal performance. Inside the spending, the welfare state dominates. Salaries are about 64.7 trillion dinars and social welfare is around 33 trillion dinars. Grants, subsidies and interests are about 17 trillion dinars, while debt service is also around 17 trillion dinars. Iraq’s finances have collapsed since the Iran war began in late February and led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Iraq earns more than 90 per cent of its budget in dollars from oil exports, almost all of which must pass through the waterway – about a third of the world’s seaborne oil crosses the strait. Exports fell from 3.36 million barrels per day in February to 131,000 bpd in April. The result was the sharp drop in monthly oil revenue that previously hovered at about $7 billion. Finance Ministry execution data as of end of August showed revenue of only about 45.3 trillion dinars against spending of 78.9 trillion dinars. To close the gap, Iraq has mainly relied on foreign reserves that have fallen from about $109 billion to $80.6 billion, Iraqi Central Bank data shows. External help The scale of the shock forced Baghdad to seek external help for the first time since the 2016 Stand-By Arrangement with the International Monetary Fund. Iraqi officials approached the IMF and formally requested a financing programme, managing director Kristalina Georgieva said at the Annual Meetings in Bangkok this month. "We will get to Iraq both money and policy support," she said, adding that the IMF intended to support Iraq "very firmly" with a requested loan programme. “We have made significant progress towards the programme. We have still a bit more work to do together and I’m confident we will be successful." The IMF projected Iraq's economy would contract by 16 per cent in 2026, with a current account deficit of 10.8 per cent of GDP this year. Against that backdrop, the budget could be built around an oil price assumption of $58 per barrel and exports of around four million bpd, including from the Kurdistan region, a government official told The National . There are tentative signs of recovery. Iraqi oil exports have rebounded to about 3.4 million bpd so far in October. Despite higher export volumes, the State Organisation for Marketing of Oil (Somo) has faced pricing pressure and heavy discounts – sometimes $25 to $30 per barrel – owing to maritime risk premiums. The government expects further improvement in the coming weeks. However, with at least a two-month lag between export and revenue receipt, the full benefit will not be felt until later this year. While awaiting support from the IMF, the government borrowed internally to cover payroll and moved to devalue the dinar to inflate dinar-denominated oil revenue. 'Ignores reality' “The state is in severe financial distress and, instead of tightening, the government is expanding expenses,” Baghdad economist Nabil Al Marsoomi told The National . "We were surprised by a large, highly stretched expansionary budget, and it seems that the Ministry of Finance and Planning are very relaxed. The salary item is very large, along with social welfare and debt service, and the deficit gap is very large." Mr Al Marsoomi said the budget may take Iraq into "another tunnel because until today the picture is not clear, especially in the Strait of Hormuz", describing the draft as a political document rather than an economic one. "It is a budget that reflects the behaviour of the rentier state, a populist budget that tries to please people as much as possible. It does not care about economic efficiency, but rather cares about the desires and needs of people and electoral votes," he said. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi led a budget meeting on Saturday and issued a directive that 500,000 contract and daily-wage workers be made permanent, plus 120,000 new contract posts, in next year's budget. He explained that the government would work to “secure the necessary allocations to implement the decision”, according to a statement. Kurdistan commitments The draft also keeps Kurdistan region 's share at 12.7 per cent of actual total spending, after excluding sovereign expenditures despite calls from the region to increase it. It obliges the Kurdistan Regional Government to market no less than 400,000 bpd through Somo in co-ordination with the federal Oil Ministry. “If exports via Turkey’s Ceyhan or any other outlet is not possible, the KRG must deliver the quantities to the federal ministry for domestic use as needed," it said. It also obliges the KRG to hand over non-oil revenue to the federal treasury for audit by federal and regional audit boards, to hand over surplus gas to the federal government or have its value deducted from its share, and not to agree on contracts with foreign or local companies on oil and gas except through the federal oil ministry. On Sunday, Kurdistan's Prime Minister Masrour Barzani told local media that "no final agreement has been reached yet with Baghdad and talks are continuing to defend Kurdistan people's rights and to secure its financial allocations”. The Finance Ministry will only release monthly entitlements after compliance, with submission of monthly balances – a condition for continued financing, the draft said. The draft budget still needs to be approved by the Cabinet before the final endorsement by parliament.

title: Domestic crude supply to refineries declines 6.3% to 15.97mb —NMDPRA
body: By Obas Esiedesa Domestic crude oil supply to Nigerian refineries declined by 6.3 per cent to 15.97 million barrels in September 2026 from 17.05 million barrels in August. This comes as petrol supply from domestic refineries and imports fell sharply during the month. The September 2026 Midstream and Downstream Report released by the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority (NMDPRA) on Thursday shows that the decline in crude supply coincided with a 23.4 per cent drop in average daily petrol supply to 38.7 million litres from 50.5 million litres in August. The report attributed the fall in petrol receipts to lower domestic supply and reduced imports as approved import permit volumes were being exhausted. Between January and September 2026, refineries received a combined 156.51 million barrels of crude oil, comprising 125.85 million barrels of domestic crude and 30.66 million barrels of imported crude. Domestic production accounted for 80.4 per cent of total intake, while imported cargoes contributed 19.6 per cent. The report further showed that Dangote Refinery’s utilisation stood at 105.98 per cent in September, implying crude processing of approximately 689,000 barrels per day against average crude receipts of 618,000 barrels per day. The difference of about 71,000 barrels per day was drawn from refinery inventory, indicating that the refinery processed more crude than it received during the month. Despite the September decline, domestic refineries remained the larger source of petrol supply, accounting for approximately 73.6 per cent of total receipts during the month, compared with 26.4 per cent from imports. The September total was also below the 13-month average of 49.7 million litres per day recorded between September 2025 and September 2026. Over the 13-month period, domestic refineries supplied an average of 30.4 million litres per day, accounting for 61.2 per cent of total supply, while imports contributed 19.3 million litres per day, or 38.8 per cent. The NMDPRA said September petrol receipts declined as domestic supply fell 21 per cent below August levels, while imports dropped by 30 per cent amid the exhaustion of approved import permit volumes. The post Domestic crude supply to refineries declines 6.3% to 15.97mb —NMDPRA appeared first on Vanguard News .
