The exhibition features international initiatives to combat domestic violence, including stories from Australia, New Zealand, Italy, Chile, Finland and other countries.
Top stories in Azerbaijan, Armenia, and Georgia from 19-23 October, 2026

title: President Lula da Silva of Brazil elected for fourth term
body:
Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silv a has been re-elected for a fourth term, defeating Flávio Bolsonaro in a neck-and-neck election conducted on Sunday.
Mr Lula won the election with 51.75 per cent of the vote, while Mr Bolsonaro received slightly fewer votes, accounting for 48.25 per cent of the total, according to the state’s Superior Electoral Court.
This is the fourth win for the left-wing politician who served two terms as president from January 2003 to December 2010, and again from January 2023. He won despite losing to Bolsonaro in the first round of voting in early October.
PREMIUM TIMES reported that the first round of voting ended in a runoff as Mr Bolsonaro, despite having the most votes, failed to reach 50 per cent.
Mr Bolsonaro is a far-right senator and the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year prison sentence for masterminding a failed coup after losing the 2022 election.
This loss is particularly significant for Mr Bolsonaro, as it is the first time a candidate who won the first round of voting has lost in the second since the country’s return to democracy in 1988.
It also bucks a wider regional trend in which citizens have consistently voted for right-wing candidates. Right-wing leaders in the region have won seven straight elections within the last 18 months.
These right-wing candidates are allied with US President Donald Trump, raising concerns about his influence in Latin America.
Mr Trump quietly backed the campaign to put Mr Bolsonaro in power as he seeks to strengthen US influence in the region. His administration’s national security strategy outlined that the US wanted to “restore American preeminence in the Western Hemisphere.”
The Bolsonaros in power would have made this a reality. It would have been the biggest win so far for the ascendant right-wing movement marching across Latin America.
The politician’s campaign had capitalised on public dissatisfaction with the economy. It focused on the cost-of-living crisis, growing insecurity, and personal debt. Although Brazil has recorded declining poverty and unemployment, household incomes have failed to keep pace with rising living costs.
Mr Lula’s victory now leaves Mexico and Brazil, Latin America’s two most populous nations, with left-wing leaders.
Speaking in São Paulo after the result was announced, vice president Geraldo Alckmin said Mr Lula has “for the second time, saved Brazilian democracy.”
The president described the election as a victory over negativity and lies.
In his victory speech, Mr Lula said Brazil will “not accept being in anyone’s backyard.”
“People voted because we could convince them that the vote was important for the sovereignty of our country,” he noted.
Mr Bolsonaro, who was expecting to give a victory speech in Brasília after winning the first round, has rejected the result.
He called Mr Lula’s win “impossible” and “inexplicable.”
He also demanded that the result be annulled.

title: Jordan Arrests Suspects Over Deadly Attack on Greek Orthodox Church
body: Jordanian security forces have arrested three suspects over a deadly attack on a Greek Orthodox church in the southern village of Hamoud that killed nine people and injured 25 others, Jordanian state television reported. Security and specialist investigation teams detained the three suspects during a joint operation in the early hours of the morning, according to a statement published on X by the state broadcaster. “Following a joint security operation, teams specialising in investigations and interventions detained the three terrorists responsible for the heinous terrorist attack,” the statement said. The three suspects sustained injuries during the operation, which followed Friday’s attack on the church in Hamoud, southern Jordan. The attack left nine people dead and 25 others injured. title: Who is Giovanni ‘Banoy’ Lopez, the new DPWH secretary?
body: MANILA, Philippines – President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. appointed Transportation Secretary Giovanni “Banoy” Lopez as chief of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), replacing Secretary Vince Dizon. Dizon, meanwhile, returns to lead the Department of Transportation. A certified public accountant and lawyer, Lopez will be tasked to institutionalize reforms in the DPWH, which has been marred by corruption issues, said acting Presidential Communications Secretary Lino Cayetano. Lopez has been serving DOTr for nearly a decade. Based on available public information, he served as assistant secretary for procurement and project implementation and director for legal services in the DOTr in 2017. He was then appointed as DOTr undersecretary for finance and chief of staff in 2021. In the same year, he became executive director (officer-in-charge) of the Toll Regulatory Board. In 2022, Lopez became executive director of the Land Transportation Office. From February to August 2025, he was senior undersecretary for administration, finance, and procurement of DOTr. Marcos appointed Lopez as DOTr secretary in September 2025, after the post was vacated by Dizon. Lopez hails from Tuguegarao, Cagayan. He finished high school at the University of Saint Louis Tuguegarao in 1996. Lopez earned his accountancy degree as cum laude at St. Paul University Philippines. He studied law at San Beda University. – Rappler.com

title: Libya summons US envoy to protest Trump’s remarks
body: Libya’s foreign ministry summoned the US chargé d’affaires on ​Sunday to protest against rally statements by ‌President Donald Trump, which it described as “offensive”, after he called the North African nation “terror-infested”. The ministry said it rejected any ​statements that “undermine the dignity of its people ​or diminish their standing” At Saturday’s rally in ⁠Perry, Georgia, Trump said, “(US Senator) Jon Ossoff ​personally sponsored a bill to bring armies of ​migrants from terror-infested countries like Libya, Yemen, Haiti, Somalia. Remember what I called them? Shithouse countries,” in a reference ​to remarks made during his first term The ​US was committed to ties with Libya, Trump said on Truth ‌Social ⁠on Sunday night, calling its people “proud, resilient, hospitable, and deserving of peace and prosperity” “We respect the Libyan people and the sacrifices that brave Libyans ​made fighting ​ISIS, the ⁠common enemy of both our peoples, but Libya cannot remain a corridor ​for illegal migration, and this must ​end ⁠now,” he wrote Libya’s rival administrations in the east and west denounced Trump’s remarks, rejecting attempts to ⁠draw ​Libya into what they called “electoral ​debates”

title: VIDEO: 2 ships collide at Germany’s Bremerhaven port

title: South Korea, US launch joint air force drills dubbed Freedom Flag
body:
SEOUL, October 26. /TASS/. Air forces of South Korea and the United States kicked off their combined air drills, The Freedom Flag, the Yonhap news agency reported on Monday.
"The Freedom Flag exercise began Monday for a two-week run at Kunsan Air Base in Gunsan, about 180 kilometers [some 111.8 miles] southwest of Seoul, involving the allies' key aerial assets, including the South Korean Air Force's F-15K, KF-16 and F-35A fighter jets," the agency reported.
According to Yonhap, "the KC-330 transport aircraft and E-737 Peace Eye early warning and control aircraft will also be deployed for the exercise. The U.S. Air Force's F-16 Fighting Falcon jet, RC-135 reconnaissance plane and its Navy's MH-60S Seahawk helicopter, as well as the F-35B stealth fighter jet and the MQ-9 Reaper unmanned surveillance aircraft of the U.S. Marines Corps will also participate in the drills."
The semiannual Freedom Flag drills were launched in 2024, and this year they are taking place between October 26 and November 6 at Kunsan Air Base.

title: Jordan arrests three over church attack that killed nine
body: Jordanian troops have arrested three men on suspicion of carrying out an attack that killed nine people at ⁠a church in ​Karak governorate. The three, all Jordanians from the same family, were captured after a gunfight near the site of the killing, following a three-day manhunt, authorities said on Monday. Gunmen killed nine Christians and wounded 34 in the attack on Friday, during a funeral service at the Saint George Orthodox Church. The church is ⁠in the village of Hamoud, about 80 kilometres south of Amman. Major Gen Obaidallah Maaytah, head of the Public Security Directorate, told reporters that two of the three were brothers, with the third man married to a sister of theirs. It was the largest attack against Jordan's Christian minority in the kingdom since the 1950s. Christians number about 250,000 out of Jordan's population of 11 million. The nine killed were all men, and mostly belonged to the Halasah clan, one of the most prominent families in Jordan. Maj Gen Obaidallah said the three assailants hailed from an area near Hmoud, and named them as Hazzaa and Meshaal Mohammad, and Ahmad Sami. Their family name was not released. Gen Obaidallah called the three terrorists and takfiriyin, meaning that they believe that they have the right to consider others apostates. King Abdullah said on X that they had been chased to their “hiding holes” and that no one with an ideology that “discriminates between one Jordanian and another” will remain at large. Interior Minister Mazen Al Faraya said troops surrounded a building near Hamoud where the three men barricaded themselves inside. “The terrorists resisted fiercely,” Mr Al Faraya said, adding that they sustained “heavy wounds.” It was too early to determine whether the they had links to groups in or outside ​Jordan, Mr Al Faraya said. No group has claimed responsibility. Mr Al Faraya said that the “extremism file” will not be over with the arrests. Jordan, he said, needs to mount a “societal stand”, or “we will see ourselves in front of this typhoon again”. On Saturday, hundreds of Jordanians from across the kingdom attended a funeral service for eight of the nine Christians killed in the attack. The service was also held at Saint George's. The assault occurred at about 2pm Jordan time on Friday during a funeral for a woman in the church. Two witnesses told The National that three men, two of them brandishing weapons, got out of a pickup truck and walked into the main gate of the church. They stared firing at mourners in the courtyard of the church, who happened to be all men. Women and children were mostly inside the church. Those inside the church closed the doors as gunfire rang out. The assailants tried to break one of the doors but failed. However, they fired through the windows as people inside the church ducked. “The coffin was hit with two bullets, but those inside the church were mostly spared the carnage,” one of the witnesses said. Authorities have largely maintained stability in Jordan since driving out the Palestinian Liberation Organisation from the country in a 1970 civil war. However, the economy has been stagnant for the past 15 years and the official unemployment rate is 16 per cent.

title: We do not support our own, but we watch horrible Hollywood movies – Yvonne Okoro
body: Ghanaian actor and film producer Yvonne Okoro has bemoaned the lack of support for local films. Speaking to Kwame Dadzie on Joy FM’s Showbiz A-Z , Yvonne said that while Ghanaian film producers were doing their best to survive, local audiences often looked for faults in their work rather than supporting their productions. According to her, Ghanaians would watch and enjoy poor-quality films from other countries but criticise similar productions made by their compatriots. “We do not support our own. Everything Ghanaian, we see it as sub-standard. And when you say this, people get offended by it, but it’s the truth,” she said. “Like, you do a movie, and people are like, will the movie be nice? You are watching horrible movies. I am sorry, some Hollywood movies are horrible. You watch it and clap. “You are watching some of the YouTube videos from my people in Nigeria, and you think it’s fantastic. But then let it be a Ghanaian who does a horrible movie, and they will say we don’t know how to do good movies. “It’s horrible. And when we do good movies, they will go like, ‘I didn’t know this was there oo.’ I have been marketing for how long now; you didn’t know this was there. They just won’t come and watch it,” she added. Yvonne made the remarks during a discussion on the current state of Ghana’s film industry and what could be done to improve it. Yvonne has built a career spanning acting and film production, featuring in several Ghanaian and Ghanaian-Nigerian productions. Her acting credits include Beyonce: The President’s Daughter, The Return of Beyonce, Single Six, Contract, Potomanto, Rebecca, Ghana Must Go, Like Cotton Twines and Fix Us. She has also appeared in the Adams Apples film series, which explores the lives and relationships of a group of friends. As a producer, Yvonne has worked on films including Contract and Ghana Must Go , demonstrating her involvement in both the creative and production sides of the industry. She recently starred in Agency for the Dead , a new film by Ghanaian filmmaker Shirley Frimpong-Manso, hitting Silverbird Cinemas on 30th October 2026.

title: Ghana loses GH¢209.7m to cyber incidents in nine months – CSA
body: Ghana recorded an estimated GH¢209.7 million in losses from reported cybersecurity incidents between January and September 2026, the Director-General of the Cyber Security Authority (CSA), Dr Divine Selasi Agbeti, has disclosed. The Authority recorded 4,938 incidents during the period. This compares with 4,604 incidents and reported losses of more than GH¢22.5 million in 2025. Speaking at the fifth annual Cyber Secure Volta Regional Conference in Ho, Dr Agbeti described the figures as worrying. He urged individuals, businesses and public institutions to strengthen their cybersecurity practices. He cautioned that the reported cases did not capture the full scale of the problem. Some victims, he said, remained reluctant to report incidents because of embarrassment, fear of ridicule and other concerns. Dr Agbeti encouraged victims of online fraud, blackmail, cyberbullying and extortion to report their experiences to the appropriate authorities. He explained that reporting would support investigations and help prevent further victimisation. He said human error and social engineering accounted for a significant proportion of incidents, making public education and responsible online behaviour essential. The CSA plans to establish an office in the Volta Region before the end of 2026 to support law enforcement and strengthen the local response to cybercrime. Dr Agbeti said the government and the Authority were committed to preventing Ghana from becoming a haven for cybercriminals. He noted that arrests and prosecutions had been pursued since 2025, including operations in the Volta Region. He urged residents to report suspected criminal activity and cautioned against allowing their communities to become hiding places for cybercriminals. Landlords were advised to make reasonable enquiries before renting out their properties. Members of the public can also report suspected cybercrime through the CSA’s short code, 292 , which he said operates around the clock. Turning to digital financial services, Dr Agbeti warned mobile money, internet banking and digital wallet users to be wary of suspicious investment offers and promises of unrealistic returns. He also cautioned against transferring money to unfamiliar accounts and urged users to verify payment requests before authorising transactions. He said protecting passwords and other sensitive information remained essential to reducing exposure to online fraud.

title: At least 40 civilians killed in terrorists’ attack in Nigeria
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 26 (MNA) – At least 40 civilians were killed in a terror attack in Nigeria’s southeastern Taraba State.
At least 40 civilians were killed in a terror attack in Nigeria’s southeastern Taraba State, the Premium Times newspaper reported, citing human rights activists. A group of gunmen invaded the village of Binnari from the neighboring Plateau State. They burned the peasants' crops, destroyed their homes, looted shops, and indiscriminately killed civilians. According to eyewitnesses, the final death toll may be higher, as many residents are still missing. Search and rescue operations are continuing. MNA

title: Omitted candidates: PDP, ADC, NDC, LP meet INEC’s condition
body: •INEC to clarify omitted candidate’s status this week By Henry Umoru, John Alechenu, Luminous Jannamike & Emma Una ABUJA – The Peoples Democratic Party, PDP, has met the Independent National Electoral Commission’s, INEC, October 24 deadline for correcting the names of candidates omitted from its published list, the party’s National Organising Secretary, Captain Umar Bature, retd, has said. Read Also: Soldiers earn peanuts, APC youth leader flaunts billion-naira SUVs — Utomi The party’s governorship candidates in Ogun(Oladipupo Adebutu), and Gombe(Prof Isa Pantanmi) and seven House of Assembly candidates were omitted in the list published by the electoral umpire, recently. Apart from the PDP, other opposition parties such as the Social Democratic Party, SDP; Nigeria democratic Congress, NDC; African Democratic Congress, ADC; and Action Democratic Party, ADP; and Labour Party, LP, were also affected. The INEC gave the affected parties October 24 as deadline to correct the omissions. The affected candidates include governorship hopefuls in Gombe and Ogun states, as well as about six or seven House of Assembly candidates, whose names were missing from the list released by the electoral commission. Bature confirmed the development, yesterday, in a response to Vanguard, saying the PDP completed the corrections within the stipulated period. “Yes, we met the deadline since,” he said. NDC, ADP meet INEC deadline on omitted candidates Also, the National Leadership of the NDC said it met the INEC’s deadline for correcting the names of candidates omitted from the published list. When Vanguard sought to know if the party has met the deadline, the NDC National Publicity Secretary, Osa Director simply said, “ Yes, we did.” Similarly, the National leadership of the ADP said it met the deadline. Speaking with Vanguard yesterday, the National Chairman of the ADP, Engr. Yabagi Yusuf Sani,said, “we did. Thanks a lot.” LP in good standing with INEC — Asogwa in like manner, the National Publicity Secretary of the LP, Ken Asogwa, said the party is in good standing with the INEC on correction of names and replacement of candidates. His words: “The Labour Party is in good standing with INEC, including on matters relating to the correction of names and replacement of candidates,” adding that the party is confident and looks forward to a successful outing for all its candidates in the forthcoming general elections. INEC’s clarification awaited The electoral umpire has not released additional information on the status of the omitted candidates especially those NDC’s John Upan and Ambassador Nkoyo Toyo of ADC in Cross River State Ambassador Toyo told Vanguard that she had done all that was needed to be done before the deadline expired but INEC is yet to bring out the result. “They gave us the deadline of October 24 which was Saturday and I had done all that they asked for but they have not brought out any information. Let’s wait for them” Contacted, the Head, INEC Voter Education in Cross River , Mr Osaro Aisen, said: “The whole thing is handled from Abuja and it is a legal matter. Let’s see what will come forth tomorrow (Monday). “I cannot give you a categorical answer now till tomorrow.” Vanguard News The post Omitted candidates: PDP, ADC, NDC, LP meet INEC’s condition appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Serbia’s former President Aleksandar Vučić concedes defeat in parliamentary election to student-led opposition
body: Former Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić conceded defeat in the October 25 snap parliamentary election. “We don’t have the final results yet. Based on a stratified sample, it’s clear that we lost this election. The student-blockader list won: they’ll have 135 to 140 seats, and we’ll have around 105,” Vučić said at the Serbian Progressive Party’s headquarters. He said no other parties or lists had won seats in parliament. Later, however, he said some national minority lists might have won seats after all. After Vučić conceded defeat, songs, car horns, and whistles began echoing through streets across Serbia as residents stepped onto their balconies to celebrate the “Student List” victory, the newspaper Danas reported . Serbia held a snap parliamentary election on October 25. Former President Aleksandar Vučić, who resigned in late September, had planned to become prime minister if he won. His main rival was the “Student List — Students Win” movement, which was formally established just over a month ago but grew out of protests that began in Serbia in 2024. title: ‘We are not bandits’ – Herdsmen; want 30% of agric budget, 417 grazing reserves
body: By Omeiza Ajayi, ABUJA Pastoralist groups have rejected the profiling of Fulani pastoralists as bandits and called on President Bola Tinubu to immediately declare a national dialogue on farmer-herder conflicts, following what they say are the killings of hundreds of pastoralists in recent months. At a news conference on Sunday in Abuja, President of Kautal Pulaaku Fulbe Association of Nigeria, Dr. Huseini Buzaye, who signed an address on behalf of the Confederation of Pastoralist Non-Governmental Organisations CONPA, said the groups represent “millions of Nigerian pastoralists from all 36 states and FCT”, under over 30 associations. General Secretary of the association, Abdullahi Ardo, who read the prepared speech on behalf of the president, said; “For too long, the word ‘Fulani Pastoralist’ has been profiled and criminalized as synonymous with banditry, kidnapping and terrorism”. The groups said the stereotyping “has given impetus to jungle justice, extrajudicial killings, and hate speech against innocent pastoralists, including women and children who have no connection to crime.” “Criminals are criminals and have no tribe,” the statement said, urging security agencies and the media to “stop ethnic profiling but arrest and prosecute criminals as individuals, not as an ethnic group”, they added. On the killings, the coalition said in the last few months, hundreds of innocent pastoralists have been killed in coordinated attacks in Plateau, Niger, Sokoto, Kebbi, Zamfara and other parts of the country. It said women, children and the elderly were among the dead, thousands of cattle were rustled or killed, and entire Rugas were burnt down. “These killings are not reported. There is no national outrage. There is no compensation. There is no justice,” it said. The groups demanded an independent investigation into the killings. They also asked the Federal Government to direct the National Emergency Management Agency NEMA and the National Commission for Refugees, Migrants and Internally Displaced Persons NCFRMI to provide relief materials to displaced pastoralists “as it does for other communities”. They also asked security agencies to protect pastoralists “as Nigerian citizens under Section 14 and Section 33 of the 1999 Constitution.” The coalition commended Tinubu for creating the Federal Ministry of Livestock Development, calling it “a historic decision that gave us hope after 60 years of agitation.” But it said the ministry “remains largely unfunded and without a clear operational framework” years after its creation. It appealed for the ministry “to be seen active at the community level”, and asked the President and the National Assembly to allocate at least 30 per cent of the agricultural budget to it, to “immediately gazette and protect the 417 grazing reserves”, and to start pilot ranches and fodder production in the six geo-political zones. “Livestock is a 30 trillion economy. It cannot be treated with levity,” the statement said. Citing what it described as more than 20,000 deaths from the farmer-herder conflict in 10 years, the coalition said: “Nigeria cannot achieve peace by military means alone.” It called on the President to make “a Presidential Declaration of National Dialogue and Reconciliation on Farmer-Herder and Pastoralist Conflicts”. It said the dialogue should include Miyetti Allah groups, traditional rulers, the Christian Association of Nigeria CAN, Jama’atu Nasril Islam JNI, security agencies and state governments, with a mandate of “Truth, Justice, Forgiveness, Compensation, and a Roadmap for Peaceful Co-existence.” The groups also listed responsibilities for pastoralist communities, urging leaders, households and young people to respect farmers’ rights and lawful property, take “reasonable measures to prevent livestock from entering cultivated farmland”, and cooperate with lawful security investigations. They urged them to report cattle rustling and kidnapping, and to reject violence, banditry and retaliatory violence. The coalition said it intends to carry out mass awareness and sensitisation across the six geo-political zones, with a framework already worked out. “We are Nigerians. We are pastoralists. We are not bandits. We love this country. Our cattle feed this nation,” the statement said. It called on federal and state governments, traditional institutions, farmers’ associations, security agencies and development partners to work together, advocating “justice without discrimination, security without exclusion, development without marginalization, and peaceful coexistence based on mutual respect and the rule of law.” END The post ‘We are not bandits’ – Herdsmen; want 30% of agric budget, 417 grazing reserves appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Accept results, close ranks – Asiedu Nketiah urges NDC aspirants
body: The National Chairman of the National Democratic Congress (NDC), Johnson Asiedu Nketiah, has urged aspirants in the party’s constituency executive elections to accept the results and unite after the contest. Speaking at the Ketu North Constituency Delegates Conference at Weta in the Volta Region on Sunday, October 25, he said rebuilding unity after the elections was more important than individual victories. “What matters is not who wins, but how that person wins and how we are able to put the party together after the election,” he said. Mr Asiedu Nketiah explained that he had deliberately stayed away from constituency elections across the country to avoid influencing delegates or appearing to favour particular candidates. He said neutrality was essential to his role as National Chairman, allowing him to reconcile members after the polls, regardless of the outcome. “Everybody in the NDC is my friend and family member. If I select some of you and call you my friends, it means the others are my enemies, but I believe all of you are my friends,” he said. He urged unsuccessful aspirants not to interpret defeat as rejection by the party. Only one person could occupy a position at a time, he noted, adding that other opportunities to serve could arise. Mr Asiedu Nketiah encouraged delegates to let the best candidates emerge and urged aspirants to accept the outcome in good faith. He expressed confidence that the elections would strengthen the NDC if members remained committed and worked together after the results were declared.

title: Incumbent President of Brazil Lula da Silva wins presidency
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 26 (MNA) – Incumbent President of Brazil Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won in the second round of presidential elections and was re-elected as the president of the country for the fourth term.
Incumbent President of Brazil Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won in the second round of presidential elections and was re-elected as the president of the country for the fourth term, the Brazilian Superior Electoral Court (TSE) reported. According to the TSE, after 97.69% of the ballots in the runoff election were counted, Lula da Silva secured 51.74% of the votes, while his opponent, a right-wing opposition candidate Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, was backed by 48.26% of the votes. Lula da Silva is now the first politician in the present-day Brazilian history to win the presidential election after trailing in the first round of voting. The elected head of state will assume the office on January 1, 2027. The voter turnout in the second round was reported at 80.79%, with 127,807,732 citizens participating in the voting. The rate of abstainers was reported at 19.21%, which corresponds to 30,081,854 voters. The share of blank ballots was at 1.12% (1,426,055 votes), while the share of invalid ballots was amounted to 2.12% (2,713,225 votes).

title: Bitter Jest in Anticipation of a Post-Islamic Republic World
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 26 (MNA) – As long as there is a God to be God and a world to be the world, foolish people will remain foolish.
"As long as there is a God to be God and a world to be the world, foolish people will remain foolish."
This is not a quote from a famous figure. Rather, it was something a friend’s father said to us during the Iran-Iraq war, while on leave behind the front lines, in a discussion about Saddam. We, the sons of his friends, found it so striking that for a long time, we used to jokingly write it in beautiful Persian calligraphy and mount it on a wooden plaque in our bunkers before returning to the front.
Years after the war, when I had written an open letter to Trump warning him against going to war with Iran, Noam Chomsky gave me a fascinating response. He essentially said that while my letter was excellent, the problem was that Trump was too foolish to understand such advice. I later realized that Professor Chomsky’s brief observation was, in essence, a different translation of what my friend’s father had said during the war:
As long as there is a God to be God and a world to be the world, foolish people will remain foolish."
"The response I received from Chomsky eight years ago regarding my open letter is now echoed in today’s reality: the two characters from Pinocchio—the cunning Fox (Netanyahu) and the irrational Donkey (Trump)—are once again attempting to provoke an attack on Iran.
Richard Nixon once wrote in his book, War and Peace and Beyond [Note: referring to his concept of ‘Victory without War’], that one should always present the enemy with a dilemma where both choices lead to defeat. The current global narrative regarding this illegal aggression by these two narcissists against Iran follows this pattern. One of those paths, the results of which are already visible on the horizon, is the total collapse of American military prestige—a result I hold no concern for.
Instead, I wish to address a question that might sound strange coming from an Iranian: What will be the definitive and catastrophic consequences of the fall of the Islamic Republic for the world and the West?
Because the list is extensive, I will outline only the primary points:
1-The Emotional Domestic Opposition: Most domestic opponents of the Islamic Republic lack a true understanding of their country’s lack of independence following a collapse. They will soon realize how Trump has seized control of the nation’s wealth; all national revenues will, much like in occupied Iraq, be diverted to American banks. Their cries for ‘freedom’ will be nothing more than a deception, and within a year, they will likely join the supporters of the old regime.
2-The Myth of the Absolute Victim: A new confirmation of the long-standing narrative will emerge—the idea of Iranians as the ‘absolute victim’ against an ‘absolute tyrant’ West (paralleling the stories of Imam Hussein and Yazid, or the 1953 coup against Mossadegh). New revolutionary leaders, far more violent than the current establishment, will seek vengeance across the globe. Even the taboo of seeking nuclear weapons will be cast aside, as the West has effectively proven to them that tolerance toward Western predators leads only to ruin. In short: be as narcissistic as they are.
3-Guerrilla Warfare: In the first year following a collapse, Iranian guerrilla operations involving 35 million volunteers will begin. They will create scenes for the occupiers that will make the Iraqi insurgencies look like the mere lighting of a candle on a five-year-old’s birthday cake.
4-The Drowning Man’s Desperation: There is an Arabic proverb that says a drowning man will grasp at anything to save himself. To ensure the destruction of all infrastructure, Iran has prepared multi-hour plans targeting the aid-providing nations of the US and Israel.
The West, already struggling with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and Houthi missile strikes, will face a multi-y
Ahmadzadeh Haj Habib: ear crisis. How will they survive the aftermath of the destruction of Aramco, the desalination plants of Israel, and the subsea internet cables in the region?
5- The Strength of Solidarity: Every year, the Arbaeen pilgrimage in Iraq hosts nearly ten million Iranians and millions of Shia and Sunni from other nations—numbers far exceeding the non-political Hajj. The memory of the occupation of both Iran and Iraq will serve as a catalyst for unprecedented solidarity, driving these peoples to join forces and set this unjust world ablaze in response to the injustice dealt to them.
6- The Migrant Tide: A flood of millions of migrants from Iran, Iraq, and other Persian Gulf nations will pour into Western countries, whether intended or not, to trample upon their ‘green gardens.’"
7. Years ago, the Iranian negotiator Saeed Jalili privately told Catherine Ashton, the EU’s High Representative for Foreign Affairs, that if US and Western sanctions against Iran were to continue, Iran would only need to raise the price of gasoline in your countries by two dollars. Unlike our people, who have grown accustomed to sanctions and inflation, your people would rise in revolt—a phenomenon that has already begun to manifest in European nations. In the coming days of a new third conflict in the Persian Gulf region, the resulting chaos in the West will be so self-evident that any rational person would recognize its catastrophic security and economic consequences without further explanation.
8- The occupation of Iranian soil will sever any path of compassion or restraint for these foreign aggressors. Poor American and Western soldiers, along with their families, will pay the price for the enrichment of Western military cartels and the corrupt Trump family. It will be a war between men fighting for a land occupied under false pretenses, and American soldiers whose own people hate this conflict even more than they hated the Vietnam War.
In The Art of War, Sun Tzu says: ‘Never completely surround an enemy; always leave them a golden bridge to a retreat. If you do not, they will fight to the death.’
However, there is a point regarding the Shia people—unnoticed for thousands of years before Sun Tzu and entirely different from the rest of humanity—that is often overlooked: these Shia defenders, in the pursuit of saving their fortress or their country, do not even consider saving their own lives, nor do they hesitate to surrender them.
Eight years ago, when I wrote my advisory letter to Trump, I abstained from competing with the great inventors and grandmasters of world chess. Today, I have no hope that he will grasp the essence of that message: that whether he chooses attack or appeasement toward Iran, defeat is already a foregone conclusion. The only difference lies in the cost. He lacks the wisdom to create a ‘golden bridge’ for himself, because he fails to realize that he is currently the one under siege—and so is Iran.
The reason is quite simple. It is the very same sentiment shared by my friend’s father during the war and Professor Noam Chomsky, despite being thousands of miles apart:
As long as there is a God to be God and a world to be the world, foolish people will remain foolish."207:32

title: South Africa to allow fund managers 100% foreign assets under new framework
body: South African fund managers will be able to hold 100% of portfolios in foreign assets under ring-fenced mandates, regulators said on ​Friday, in a new framework that exempts qualifying vehicles from a ‌longstanding 45% offshore investment cap. The South African Reserve Bank, National Treasury and the Johannesburg Stock Exchange briefed investors on the draft Synthetic Financial Centre (SFC) framework, published on Wednesday, which would ​allow licensed asset managers, banks, insurers and private equity firms to manage ​global portfolios in any currency from a South African base. The ⁠45% limit would still apply when an institution commits capital to an SFC ​vehicle. But once the funds are inside a registered mandate, the manager could ​invest them entirely offshore. The originating institution would still count the investment towards its own prudential foreign limit. Stuart Theobald, executive chairperson of Krutham, a think tank, and convenor of Operation Phumelela, ​a private sector initiative led by the JSE to boost the competitiveness ​of South Africa’s financial sector, called the lifting of the cap “the most fundamental change” in the ‌framework. Close ⁠to 5 trillion rand ($301 billion) in South African portfolio assets are held offshore, much of it routed through overseas centres because local rules have made it difficult to manage fully global portfolios from Johannesburg. “The SFC really positions South Africa ​with a framework that ​makes it competitive,” ⁠JSE CEO Valdene Reddy said. The framework is part of a sweeping overhaul of South Africa’s decades-old exchange controls that the JSE ​estimates could attract 10 trillion rand in investment over time. Olano ​Makhubela, head ⁠of the SARB’s Financial Surveillance Department, said the 45% prudential limit would remain a “long-term feature” of South Africa’s capital-flow framework. Vukile Davidson, chief director of financial markets and ⁠stability at ​National Treasury, said a second phase could consider ​tax alignment and could allow foreign-currency listings on South African exchanges. The draft is open for ​public comment until November 30.

title: What Rubio really means when he talks about 'civilizational' renewal
body:
The Washington establishment is using new words to describe the old forms of interventionism
“The story of our civilization is the greatest story ever known to man.”
Secretary of State Marco Rubio delivered these triumphalist words earlier this month as he stood before the Acropolis in Athens, Greece. Rubio’s speech, which centered the need for Western civilizational rejuvenation, received laudatory marks among conservative circles. On a certain level, this is unsurprising. Civilizationism is indeed the cause du jour on the new right.
But on closer examination, one suspects that Rubio is not truly offering some radical new vision, but a lot of the same.
Take his bemoaning of the West for supposedly creating a vacuum in global leadership:
“Others were all too happy to fill the vacuum that we left – the vacuum left behind by our weakness. And as the West’s confidence faltered, its adversaries and its rivals only grew more assertive, building up their own wealth and their own power in our stead… Under President Trump, the United States has made its choice. We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power.”
Rubio goes on to juxtapose Western civilization with the “fanatics like the radical mullahs of Iran , whose cult of death hails child suicide bombers as national heroes, and portrays martyrdom as an end to itself.”
Clearly, Rubio recognizes that civilizational renewal resonates with national conservatives right now. But by so singularly focusing on power as the means to achieve such rejuvenation, he is in reality laying the rhetorical groundwork for sustaining American primacy. The portrait of Iran as irrationally barbaric also precludes any sort of diplomatic resolution to the war in Iran. Such a speech is thus no primer for American retrenchment; it is simply a rhetorical rebranding of the Bush-era Global War on Terror.
For decades, neoconservatism and liberal internationalism largely prevailed over the Washingtonian establishment. While the two respective ideologies may have somewhat diverged on their prescribed course of action, each operated from an underlying interventionist impulse, the use of American military might to socio-engineer change abroad.
Such an impulse thrust Democratic and Republican administrations alike to pursue grandiose nation-building projects without time-bound objectives. Unsurprisingly, they failed: the Iraq and Afghanistan debacles, Libya’s descent into sheer anarchy, arming the “moderate” Syrian opposition.
All this gives ample reason for introspection, not into the manner in which each project was conducted, but the underlying ideologies themselves. Sadly, however, such introspection is not really taking place. Instead, as Rubio vividly illustrated, the interventionist principle beckons onward, meeting the current moment by co-opting language more amenable to today’s populist-nationalist conservatives, but maintaining the baseline policy prescriptions of yesteryear’s Cold War hawks and neoconservatives.
Other Republicans have already seized on Rubio’s rhetorical sleight of hand to maintain their hawkish positions. Take Mississippi Sen. Roger Wicker’s recent statement justifying continued American support for Ukraine. Speaking to NATO’s resolute response to Russian aggression, Wicker concludes his statement by referencing Rubio’s speech:
“[Rubio] reminded us that the free world was born in that birthplace of democracy and that Europe and America are bound to one another still. He clarified our shared mission, saying, ‘We must strengthen an alliance capable of confronting threats of our age’ As I return from Europe, I could not agree more.”
As Luke Nicastro, senior editor at The American Conservative magazine, astutely points out , this is no more than conventional Atlanticist interventionism under the guise of civilizationism. Clearly, the grandiosity of Rubio’s speech does not lend itself to a reconsideration of America's place in an increasingly multipolar world. It is a recipe for American overextension and domination.
A similar dynamic is unfolding on the American left. Amid Israel’s appalling onslaught on Gaza, the spirit of solidarity and self-determination has understandably become the defining ethos of progressive foreign policy thinking. But, observing attempts to tie this sentiment to American foreign policy beyond Gaza, one cannot help but notice the mere rehashing of liberal internationalism, rather than a fresh new vision.
Take the words of Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), who calls for a Democratic foreign policy centered around human rights and self-determination, from Ukraine to Gaza and beyond. Such abstractions are grounds for American interventionism in perpetuity, untethered from concrete American interests. It is no break from the past, but simply the preservation of Wilsonian idealism that has dictated so much American foreign meddling.
Khanna follows from the speech by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) at the Munich Security Conference in February. She outlined a “ foreign policy for the working class ,” a policy that prioritizes the global working class over consolidated oligarchical capital. On the surface, such a vision appears to be charting a new path forward beyond conventional Democratic foreign-policy thinking. But when pressed at the conference on ongoing conflicts such as the war in Ukraine, AOC nonetheless retreated to conventional liberal internationalist bromides, decrying American retrenchment as a pathway to global authoritarianism.
Rather than embrace a foreign policy that genuinely recalibrates American strategic thinking, politicians on both the right and left remain wedded to interventionist impulses divorced from concrete realities.
Civilizationism is certainly an ideology in itself. But it need not fuel primacy. In fact, if Rubio really sought to view the world through a civilizationist lens, it would be prudent for him to acknowledge and understand other civilizations beyond the West.
This should begin with Persian civilization, one that of course predates the Islamic Republic by thousands of years. A true examination of its history would expose Trump’s threats to end it as grotesque. Such an empathic approach, however, might lead to a more restrained approach and god forbid, a diplomatic resolution to the war, which Rubio and the Trump administration seem disinclined to pursue with its adversaries.
The interventionist duopoly — including neoconservatives and internationalists — has insidiously continued for far too long, precisely because of each camp’s rhetorical flexibility to meet the current zeitgeist. If such machinations are not called out, American foreign policy will not evolve for the better, but remain entrenched in orthodox interventionist thinking to further destabilization and bloodshed.

title: Brett McGurk's account of Biden Gaza policy has a huge blind spot
body:
Brett McGurk's former colleagues challenge his book's central premise that pressuring Israel would have been counterproductive
In April 2024, an Israeli drone struck a humanitarian convoy in Gaza , killing seven aid workers with World Central Kitchen, the food relief organization founded by celebrity chef Jose Andres.
A phone call between Biden and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyau days later was perhaps the closest Washington and Israel came to a rupture during the president’s term, according to Brett McGurk, the coordinator for the Middle East and North Africa in the Biden National Security Council.
At the time, intelligence indicated that Iran was preparing to launch drones and missiles at Israel in retaliation for the bombing of an Iranian consulate in Damascus on the same day as the WCK strike. “If not for the pending attack from Iran, we may have taken irreversible measures against Israel at this juncture,” McGurk writes in his recent book “ Brink: Inside the Race to Free the October 7th Hostages ,” calling Biden as frustrated and angry as he’d ever seen him. But the president did not go further.
Though McGurk — one of a small group of key foreign-policy decision makers in the Biden White House — says he “wrestled” with whether cracking down on Israel was the right course of action at that time, his conclusion not to was firm.
Biden ultimately said that U.S. policy will be “determined by our assessment of Israel’s immediate action on … specific, concrete measurable steps to address civilian harm,” and days later he deployed the U.S. military to help defend Israel against the Iranian attack. “If there was a better way to end the crisis, whether at this moment or another, Biden would have taken it,” McGurk writes.
Threatening to cut off assistance and even “increasing public pressure” would have been detrimental, he insists. “It seemed to encourage those fighting against it,” He added that Tehran attacked Israel in part because it saw Washington under pressure to break with Tel Aviv.
Nearly two years after Biden shuffled out of office, McGurk is hard at work trying to paint the administration’s Gaza policy as the best response to a hopelessly complex crisis. The World Central Kitchen episode is one of many instances in which McGurk argues that public disagreements between Washington and Israel only served to strengthen their adversaries, undermining efforts to secure a ceasefire and the release of hostages held by Hamas. As a result, McGurk suggests Washington had few, if any, viable alternatives to the approach Biden and his team pursued.
While “Brink” also chronicles the regional conflicts that arose following Israel’s onslaught on Gaza, including in Iran and on the Red Sea, its central focus is McGurk’s painstaking efforts to negotiate the release of the hostages taken by Hamas on October 7. Throughout the book, he portrays any perceived daylight between the U.S. and Israel as counterproductive to his diplomatic endeavors, and places the responsibility for the prolonged conflict overwhelmingly on Hamas. But former Biden administration officials who served alongside McGurk challenge that framing, arguing that his account disregards both the potential benefits of pressuring Israel and the costs of Washington's reluctance to do so.
As one former Biden administration official said, pressure on Israel actually helped secure concessions from Hamas by giving Arab governments greater political latitude to press the militant group themselves.
"When the United States demonstrated that it was also willing to exert pressure on the party over which it had the most influence, Israel, then the Arab countries were actually able to really turn the screws," the official told RS, pointing to Egypt and Turkey's key roles in the negotiations during the Biden-Trump transition, and later in the implementation of the framework signed in October 2025.
And even when American pressure failed to advance the hostage negotiations, it could achieve other objectives. Speaking about that tense April 2024 phone call in which, according to McGurk, Biden threatened to cut off military aid, Ilan Goldenberg offered a different assessment of its consequences. Where McGurk laments the potential dangers of confronting Israel, Goldenberg, who served as a Middle East adviser to Vice President Kamala Harris, says “that is only if you view this purely as a hostage negotiation and you forget all about the Palestinian humans.”
Following this intervention, Israel agreed to the temporary reopening of the Erez Crossing, and April 2024 saw the most truckloads of humanitarian supplies enter the strip of any month between October 2023 and January 2025, according to United Nations data . This represented a “fundamental change,” according to Goldenberg, one that did not last long because Washington failed to keep up the pressure.
The narrow focus on the hostage negotiations runs throughout “Brink.” McGurk devotes considerable attention to the hostages and their families, whereas the suffering of Palestinians, while acknowledged, receives far less attention, with the devastation in Gaza —where roughly 46,000 people were killed by the time Biden left office in 2025, according to health officials in the strip — largely treated as a backdrop to his diplomatic efforts.
Whether greater American pressure could have helped bring about an earlier ceasefire — one that would have freed the hostages — remains a contentious question.
Examining Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar's conduct throughout the war, there was little evidence his willingness to reach a deal was meaningfully influenced by disagreements between Washington and Israel, said the former official who spoke with RS.
“He was singularly focused on maximizing the pain on Israel,” the official said, so it simply “doesn’t add up” that he would be responsive to outside events.
Another member of the Biden administration, speaking on condition of anonymity, argued that even if public pressure risked emboldening Hamas, Washington's reluctance to confront Netanyahu carried risks of its own, giving the Israeli prime minister latitude on how to conduct negotiations even as he seemed to want the war to continue. McGurk’s perspective instead emphasizes the times when Hamas is an intransigent negotiating partner while glossing over times when Netanyahu impedes talks.
That issue becomes particularly relevant in the author’s treatment of the failed efforts to secure a ceasefire in the summer of 2024.
In late May 2024, McGurk says, Netanyahu accepted a phased ceasefire and hostage release framework that Biden had endorsed. Hamas took more than a month to respond, a delay McGurk highlights as evidence of the group's unwillingness to compromise. “Hamas did not care at all about the plight of Gazans; it only cared about its own survival,” he wrote.
Phil Gordon, who served as Harris's national security adviser, challenged McGurk's account earlier this month, arguing Hamas's eventual response in early July represented a significant concession: the group had dropped its demand that Israel commit to a permanent ceasefire before any hostages were released.
“That felt to us like a significant step forward. Nobody was naive in thinking that this wouldn't be difficult,” Gordon recently told the Jerusalem Post.
In “Brink,” McGurk describes Hamas’s response as containing “about two dozen substantive amendments to a carefully negotiated text,” many of which were “unworkable.” The ceasefire plan was further derailed, he adds, because “new issues had also arisen.”
These “new issues” refer to Netanyahu's sudden insistence on maintaining an Israeli military presence along the recently-seized Philadelphi Corridor, on Gaza’s border with Egypt, and introducing a screening mechanism for Palestinians returning to northern Gaza. Other administration officials say these demands came during a July 4 phone call with Biden, and despite the U.S. president’s push to persuade Netanyahu to move forward with the agreement. That phone call is not specifically mentioned in “Brink.”
“In the book, Brett says the situation on the ground changed and therefore the Israelis had new requirements,” Goldenberg told RS. “That's a very coded way of saying when Biden got on the phone and said to take the deal, Bibi said no.” One Israeli former hostage negotiator has said that July 2024 represented a missed chance to secure the hostages’ release, because he “didn’t think the Philadelphi Corridor was so important that it was right to miss the window of opportunity because of it.”
The new Israeli conditions proved to not be immovable. In the eventual agreement, struck in January 2025, the IDF agreed to withdraw from the corridor, though Israel has refused to follow through on that part of the agreement.
McGurk disputes the analysis that Israeli concessions were ultimately what made the agreement possible. In a book talk at the Atlantic Council this month, he called that suggestion “totally not true” and maintained that Hamas had finally accepted terms it had rejected the previous summer, driven in part by Israel’s military victories and the death of Sinwar.
McGurk occasionally acknowledges Netanyahu was an obstacle to peace, describing the prime minister during closing stages of hostage negotiations as “the flip side of Hamas,” because he would delay potential agreements, believing that prolonging the war would strengthen his negotiating position. But this doesn’t seem to affect his thinking on whether it made sense to pressure the Israeli prime minister.
The final chapters of “Brink,” however, suggest that a change in the U.S. approach also played a decisive role in the January 2025 hostage deal. Steve Witkoff, the incoming Trump administration's Middle East envoy, joins McGurk in the final negotiations. With a deal nearly complete, Witkoff aggressively presses Netanyahu to increase the number of Palestinian prisoners who would be released in exchange for nine sick or injured civilian hostages, in the first part of a larger deal.
At one point, McGurk recounts his replacement as telling the head of Mossad “tell your prime minister this is over (...) or I’ll go out right now and say the Israelis don’t give two shits about their hostages.” Ultimately, the Israeli prime minister relented.

title: The DC-Silicon Valley anti-China coalition is falling apart
body:
The ad hoc group pushing confrontation with Beijing was never as formidable as it seemed
Arriving in the White House in 2021, President Joe Biden set about dismantling much of his predecessor’s foreign-policy agenda. But there was one clear area of continuity: China .
Here, Biden retained the first Trump administration’s confrontational approach, expanding the use of export controls on advanced technology and keeping China as the U.S. military’s pacing threat . In a time of deep political division, the newly formed China consensus appeared all-powerful. When the House voted in January 2023 to establish a select committee on “Strategic Competition between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party,” the tally was 365 to 65.
Once President Donald Trump returned to power, observers expected more of the same. But Trump has instead moved U.S. China policy in the opposite direction, seeking to de-escalate bilateral tension in favor of “ constructive strategic stability ” and revealing that the bipartisan consensus on the “China threat” may be more ephemeral than many assumed.
Indeed, there is good reason to believe the peak of anti-China sentiment in U.S. politics has passed.
China’s place as the primary U.S. strategic competitor has its roots back in the early 2000s, but the narrative really took hold during Trump’s first term, when it won support from five different groups.
The first group was Trump’s Rust Belt base, to whom he and others supplied a narrative that scapegoated China for the economic and social dislocation they had suffered. China was also blamed for deaths of despair, including overdoses caused by fentanyl, whose precursor chemicals often came from China.
This groundswell against globalization was seized upon by a second group, made up of critics of the conventional economic case for global free trade: Trump himself, Peter Navarro, and Robert Lighthizer. Beginning in 2018 , they imposed tariffs on some $360 billion of Chinese imports. The Biden administration maintained and entrenched this departure from free-trade globalism, announcing a “ worker-centered ” trade policy and reviving a U.S. industrial policy . Between them, the two administrations made bipartisan a shift away from the previous economic orthodoxy toward one focused on competitive trade with China.
The third group consisted of the foreign-policy establishment of liberal internationalists and conservative hawks. For this group, China filled a gap in U.S. foreign policy that had been empty since the end of the Cold War: the foreign adversary against which the U.S. could organize a global security bloc. In Trump’s first term, the role fell to the administration’s primacists and their allies – John Bolton, Matt Pottinger, and Mike Pompeo, who went to the Nixon Library in July 2020 to call for “ a new alliance of democracies .” Two years later, Biden’s National Security Strategy called China “the only competitor with both the intent to reshape the international order and, increasingly, the economic, diplomatic, military, and technological power to advance that objective.” Accordingly, Biden and his national security team set about trying to contain Chinese power.
The fourth group contributing to the anti-China consensus were the offensive realists, such as John Mearsheimer and Elbridge Colby . Although they explicitly positioned themselves against the China hawks on both sides of the aisle who viewed the adversary through more ideological framings, they converged on a preference for slowing China’s rise. This cohort came to fear that China’s growing military capabilities and ambitions posed a direct threat to U.S. interests in East Asia. In response, they urged the United States to double down on its military investments in Asia to preserve U.S. advantages where they still existed.
Silicon Valley was the fifth and final group. Though initially skeptical of national allegiances and defense contracts, America’s technologists came around in the late 2010s, when new business interests and renewed geopolitical competition changed their calculus. In November 2017 , Eric Schmidt, the former Google chief executive and a prominent Democratic donor, told an audience in Washington that China would catch up with the United States by 2020 and “dominate the industries of AI” by 2030.
Silicon Valley’s few Republicans fully embraced the geopolitical turn. Palmer Luckey founded Anduril in 2017 to build defense technology for the Pentagon. Peter Thiel and Alex Karp took Palantir public in 2020 with a filing that declared working with the Chinese Communist Party “ inconsistent with our culture and mission .” Before long, this position transformed from taboo to commonplace. By the 2024 presidential election, Silicon Valley had bet on a combination of Trumpian nationalism and anti-China alarmism. There were holdouts, Nvidia and Apple among them, but they were now fighting the discourse rather than shaping it.
For much of the last decade, alignment among these groups created a seemingly unshakeable anti-China consensus. Yet the common thread was always made up of separate strands, whose unwinding should come as no surprise. Each group had its own reason for diagnosing China as a menace and has now found its own reasons to move in the other direction.
For starters, although China still receives much of the blame for the economic dislocation of American workers, it was always only one villain in the story – and the most distant. Other competitors for the same slot have come to dominate domestic discussion: migrants, “woke” elites, and other assorted culture-war enemies have all been held responsible for the plight of America’s dispossessed, displacing China as a sole focus of concern.
The trade hawks have also had to temper their zeal. The second Trump administration came in boasting about tariffs, with real trade warriors in key positions: Navarro at the White House, Jamieson Greer at USTR, Howard Lutnick at Commerce. “Liberation Day,” on April 2, 2025 , was the big move. Within a week, the tariff on Chinese goods stood at 145%; but this effort hit a wall when China restricted its exports of rare earth metals. Since then, both sides have sought to de-escalate in the economic domain. The Trump administration still professes a desire for some rebalancing but has settled on a renewable trade truce as acceptable for now.
The liberal internationalists and neoconservatives continue to advocate a global containment strategy, but their influence is waning. While they still represent the largest cohort in Congress and occupy many think tank sinecures, they no longer dictate the terms of discussion. Their arguments have also started to fall flat abroad. “Allies and partners” who see relative U.S. decline are in no rush to back Washington and alienate Beijing, preferring instead to hedge.
The China threat remains central to the realist prioritizers, but they, too, have been forced to moderate their position. China’s military rise and the failed U.S. war with Iran have hastened the shift in the bilateral military balance while forcing a reevaluation of what the United States military can realistically achieve in Asia. Since the U.S. cannot afford a war with China in the medium term, realist prioritizers have started to shift the goal, from the pursuit of dominance to a “decent peace.”
Finally, the tech elite has softened somewhat on China. Jensen Huang and Nvidia were attacked in Congress, by both parties, for wanting to sell chips to China, but won the argument in the White House. The administration reversed its ban on the H20 chip in July 2025 and approved sales of the more powerful H200 in December, in exchange for a share of the revenue.
Meanwhile, the general public has decisively rejected the argument that an AI race with China requires all-out support for Silicon Valley. Polls show widespread support for AI regulation and broad opposition to the construction of data centers . American skepticism of Silicon Valley has so far eclipsed any anxiety over Chinese technological advancement.
Beyond the shifting perspectives of these five groups, the American public’s fatigue with confrontational foreign policy is also a factor. The public reaction to the war with Iran underscores the limited tolerance voters have for the disruption caused by unnecessary conflict.
None of these changes guarantees peaceful U.S.-China relations going forward. Despite recent leader-level summits filled with ceremony, the two sides continue to compete intensely in the security and economic domains. U.S.-China interactions will continue to be contentious for some time.
Still, the unraveling of the ad hoc coalition that created the apparent anti-China consensus makes any form of “new cold war” unlikely — and creates the potential for a real change in how the United States approaches China over the next decade.

title: Health hazzard: Fruit vendors use laundry detergents to sparkle produce for profit
body: By Elizabeth Adegbesan A disturbing new trend is fast gaining ground across major open-air food markets, sparking urgent public health warnings and triggering widespread panic among consumers. Read Also: Unhealthy profit: Fish vendors now using dye to fake freshness Economy&Lifestyle findings revealed that several local fruit vendors are systematically washing their produce with synthetic laundry detergents and liquid soaps. The dangerous practice is aimed at stripping away natural grime, pesticide residues, and blemishes, giving the fruits an unnaturally vibrant, polished sheen that irresistibly attracts unsuspecting buyers, while drastically cutting down on spoilage losses. From glossy, deep-green watermelons and bright yellow bananas to spotless apples, these chemically enhanced fruits have flooded urban centers. However, medical experts warn that this aesthetic transformation comes at a catastrophic cost to human health, turning nutritious snacks into toxic hazards. The glittering deception For many traders operating in highly competitive, low-margin environments, the pressure to move inventory before it rots is immense. Traditional washing with clean water often fails to remove stubborn mud or agricultural sprays, leaving produce looking dull. A vendor at a local market, speaking on the condition of anonymity, candidly explained the financial motivation behind the chemical cleansing. “Customers buy with their eyes first. If a watermelon looks dusty or faded, they will walk right past your stall to the next person. When we use a little detergent or liquid soap in the washing water, it cuts through the dirt instantl “It gives the fruits a beautiful, shiny coat that looks fresh from the farm. It helps us sell faster and reduces waste, which means more profit for us at the end of the day.” The practice is not limited to watermelons. Bananas, mangoes, and citrus fruits are also being subjected to these chemical baths. Because synthetic detergents contain powerful surfactants, they strip away the fruit’s natural protective waxy layer, replacing it with an artificial gloss that mimics premium, imported produce. On his part, Audu Musa, a fruit seller said: “The use of laundry detergent to wash fruit is to remove the dirt of mud from them and make them attractive to consumers. “But I don’t use detergents. I take my fruits to the market and shade them the way they were brought from the farm. My customers prefer them that way.” It was also discovered that when these fruits are washed with detergent, they are displayed like that without rinsing off the detergent water. This method makes the fruits appear glossy and attractive. While the vendors see an increase in patronage, food safety advocates and medical professionals are deeply alarmed. Unlike specialized, food-grade vegetable washes, household detergents are formulated with complex chemical compounds, including linear alkylbenzene sulfonate, optical brighteners, artificial fragrances, and bleaching agents. These chemicals are designed for fabrics and surfaces, not human consumption. Dr. Amara Nwosu, a gastroenterologist at a public teaching hospital, warned that the immediate and long-term health consequences of ingesting these chemical residues are severe. “Ingesting even trace amounts of laundry detergent can cause acute gastrointestinal distress, including severe abdominal cramps, vomiting, and chronic diarrhea. What is more terrifying is the long-term impact. “Consistent exposure to these industrial surfactants can severely erode the mucosal lining of the gut, disrupt the gut microbiome, and potentially lead to chronic kidney damage or liver toxicity over time. “Fruits are supposed to heal the body, not poison it.” The porous nature of certain fruit skins means that the chemicals do not just stay on the surface; they can seep directly into the flesh. Consumers who fail to peel or thoroughly scrub their fruits are effectively consuming household cleaning agents with every bite. Outrage and fear in the markets As word of the practice spreads, consumer anxiety has reached an all-time high. Many shoppers report feeling betrayed by traders they have trusted for years. Halima Yunusa, a trader, expressed her shock and deep concern over the lack of food safety ethics. “It is completely heartbreaking to realize that the things we buy to keep our children healthy could actually make them sick. “I used to think a shiny apple or a perfectly clean mango was a sign of quality. Now, I am terrified to buy anything. “How can anyone prioritize a little extra profit over human life? The government needs to step in and police these markets immediately.” As authorities scramble to contain the situation, food safety experts are advising consumers to be wary of fruits that appear excessively glossy, artificially bright, or carry a faint, unnatural floral scent. For now, the golden rule for shoppers is shifting away from aesthetic perfection toward a cautious preference for the natural, unpolished look of safe food. title: Yemen says missile strikes hit Saudi mercenaries
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 26 (MNA) – Yemen's armed forces spokesman Yahya Saree announced two successful ballistic missile operations against gatherings of Saudi-backed mercenaries in Aden and Lahj provinces, inflicting dozens of casualties.
Yemen's armed forces spokesman Yahya Saree announced two successful ballistic missile operations against gatherings of Saudi-affiliated mercenaries in Aden and Lahj provinces.
Gatherings of Saudi mercenary forces and their weapons depots in the Salah al-Din area of Aden province were targeted with a ballistic missile, Saree said.
The al-Waht area in Lahj province was also heavily struck with a ballistic missile, leaving dozens killed and wounded.
The strikes destroyed large numbers of tanks and military vehicles as well as weapons depots managed under a Saudi officer named Badr al-Harbi.

title: Lufthansa and SWISS delay Dubai return due to ‘volatility’ around Middle East
body: Lufthansa Group carriers Lufthansa, SWISS and Eurowings have delayed their planned return to Dubai after deciding that the situation in the Middle East remains too unsettled. On October 23, 2026, the Lufthansa, SWISS and Eurowings jointly confirmed that they would postpone their planned resumption of flights to Dubai until November 25, 2026. Previously, Lufthansa and SWISS were scheduled to restart their service on October 25, 2026, and Eurowings on November 1, 2026. The airlines said the decision was made “in light of the current situation and outlook in the Middle East”. Neither of the airlines have flown to Dubai since March 2026. SWISS Lufthansa said that passengers affected by the postponing will be contacted directly by their respective airlines and will be offered flexible rebooking options or a full refund. For their 2026/2027 winter schedule, Lufthansa has planned up to five weekly flights to Dubai from both Frankfurt Airport (FRA) and Munich Airport (MUC). SWISS plans to operate daily flights to Dubai from Zurich (ZRH) as does Eurowings from Berlin (BER). Austrian Airlines is scheduled to operate five weekly flights from Vienna (VIE), starting December 12, 2026. Eurowings will not operate the planned flights from Cologne/Bonn and Stuttgart to Dubai during the 2026/2027 winter schedule. At peak operation, Lufthansa Group airlines will offer up to 28 weekly flights to and from Dubai. “The Lufthansa Group continuously monitors and evaluates the situation in the Middle East and is in close contact with the relevant authorities,” the company said. “The safety of passengers and crew is always the top priority for the Lufthansa Group. Due to the continued volatility of the situation in the region, short-notice adjustments to individual routes may be necessary.” RELATED Riyadh Air moves operations away from Saudi capital to Al Qassim Airport The post Lufthansa and SWISS delay Dubai return due to ‘volatility’ around Middle East appeared first on AeroTime .
