title: The world's diesel crisis has no quick fix but there is a way out
body: The problem is well-known – the world is desperate for diesel. Two major wars have disrupted the delivery of this indispensable industrial fuel. But as presidents beg and bargain, is there really any solution? At the start of the year, it was already clear that diesel could be a problem . The world seemed to have ample crude oil, but the capacity of refineries – which convert crude into diesel, petrol, jet fuel and all the other vital petroleum products – was relatively limited. Numerous refineries have closed down recently – about 30-32 out of nearly 100 operating in Europe since 2009, and six out of eight in Australia this century. Contrary to propaganda, this is not because of “net-zero” carbon policies – it is mostly because they had high energy costs, faced declining domestic markets, and were simply outcompeted by large, ultra-modern new refineries in the Middle East , Nigeria, China and India. Nevertheless, the loss of this capacity left a hole. The war in the Gulf has seized on that pre-existing weakness. Over the past few years, the Gulf countries have built or upgraded several massive, modern refining complexes – at Yanbu, Rabigh and Jazan on the Saudi Red Sea coast, Duqm in south-eastern Oman , Ruwais in Abu Dhabi , Bapco in Bahrain , and Al Zour in Kuwait . Most of these have focused on producing diesel and jet fuel that meet the EU’s strict quality standards. Refining bottleneck Iran and its allies in Yemen and Iraq have attacked these refineries with drones and missiles, with disruption continuing. For instance, while Bapco is now back to about three-quarters of full operations, Jazan remains shuttered. Even more importantly, the refineries cannot export freely because of the continuing strikes in the Strait of Hormuz . The loss of medium-gravity Middle Eastern crude, with a high diesel yield, has affected refineries elsewhere. US output has increased, but its light crude is more suited for petrol and petrochemical feedstocks. While the US escorts and the shuttle schemes have restored Gulf crude flows nearly to prewar levels, refined oil is harder to protect — it is more flammable and comes in smaller parcels. Bigger, better and more sustainable ways to float petroleum products out of the war-zone are badly needed. Nevertheless, French President Emmanuel Macron , facing domestic unrest, visited all of the Gulf countries bar Oman, last week, securing commitments from the UAE , Saudi Arabia and Bahrain to supply more diesel. Refineries elsewhere have been running flat-out for months. They will either have to go into maintenance or risk unplanned breakdowns. India has increased diesel exports, running at nearly 750,000 barrels per day this month, the highest since the war began. But it will probably not be able to go much higher. Lorries carrying goods out of the Gulf to avoid the Strait of Hormuz are a source of unexpected diesel demand. Put these factors together, and average US diesel prices have risen to $6.18 per gallon, from $3.48 at the beginning of this year. In the UAE, diesel cost Dh2.55 per litre in January and Dh4.80 per litre this month. Russian diesel But Washington’s ire has fallen less on Tehran than on Kyiv. Ukraine has indeed mounted an ever-more-effective, long-range assault against Russian refineries. Russia used to export about 1 million barrels per day of the fuel. This has fallen almost to zero; it has turned to its ally Belarus to send it diesel. Now the White House has proudly proclaimed a suspension of sanctions to allow the US to import 2.25 million barrels of Russian diesel , with further volumes to follow from next month. On November 7, the first vessel, carrying a measly 300,000 barrels, less than a tenth of what the US consumes every day, should arrive in New York. In return, the US has put pressure on Ukraine to cease its attacks. But after a brief pause from October 10, Kyiv has since hit the St Petersburg refinery. Officials from Russia’s largest oil company, Rosneft, were quoted by Bloomberg as privately admitting it was unsustainable to keep repairing the damaged plants. If anything, President Vladimir Putin’s eagerness to reach a deal on diesel shows how much the Ukrainian attacks are hurting. That may encourage the Ukrainians to redouble their efforts. Unless Russia does indeed get its refineries running again, this is not new diesel – it is simply supplies that would otherwise have gone to someone else. It represents only about 7 per cent of the global deficit. Can China help? So if Russia isn’t the answer, what is? Maybe China could help? It has the only major refining complex that is both unaffected by war and running below capacity. But after US President Donald Trump met China's President Xi Jinping on September 24, and asked for more diesel, Beijing responded by actually banning fuel exports. On Thursday, Mr Trump invoked the Defence Production Act, allowing public money and expedited approvals to support refining and pipeline projects. But these will be too late or too small to make much difference. US refining margins are wildly profitable now – any company that can make more or switch output to diesel is already doing so. To a limited extent, refineries can shift between products. But making flights or petrol more costly to relieve some stress on diesel would not help the economy, US politics or European politics. A mooted US diesel export ban seems off the table for now, after European nations agreed to release some strategic stocks. These are again too small to change the game, and burning them now risks deepening a winter crunch. Home heating oil, chemically very similar to diesel, is still used in significant quantities in Germany, France and parts of the US. Promising solutions So if more supply isn’t on the table, what about demand? Here, the solutions are more promising, although it would have been better to start eight months ago. China has in recent years greatly strengthened its energy resilience by building fully electrified high-speed rail. During the crisis, this has allowed it to cut back on flights, saving jet fuel – another close relative of diesel. China has steadily switched its city buses and lorries to natural gas , and then to battery power. Swapping heavy diesel vehicles for electric vehicles could be done quite quickly in other countries. Unlike in other regions, diesel cars are popular in Europe – offering huge savings if replaced with battery-electric or hybrid models. Emergency programmes of insulation and solar heating could reduce the need for heating oil. Diesel for temporary or distributed generators — for example, those at mines, construction sites, telecom towers and off‑grid tourist areas — can be replaced with solar panels and battery packs. Such generators are a mainstay of electricity supply across much of Africa and several Middle Eastern countries, but are costly, noisy and polluting. These are not instant solutions, but they do not take three or four years, as new refineries or pipelines do. If the US goes back to full-scale war against Iran , diesel will again be in the front line. Instead of scratching around for small supply-side solutions, the strategic choice is to save on consumption, whenever and wherever possible.

title: ‘I visit Ozzy’s grave every day’ – Sharon Osbourne
body: It’s been 15 months since Ozzy Osbourne died at the age of 76, at his home in Buckinghamshire. Although he had suffered from health problems for years, including Parkinson’s disease and a fractured vertebra, his death was a shock. Less than three weeks earlier, he performed on stage in Birmingham for a triumphant farewell concert. After the show, he was on a high. “He was just so, so happy,” his wife Sharon recalls. “He was online, going through the reviews and saying, ‘There’s something terribly wrong’, and I’m like, ‘Why?’ “He goes, ‘I didn’t get slagged by anybody. Why are people being nice to me?’ “And I’m like, ‘Because they like you’.” On the morning he died, Ozzy woke up early and went downstairs for his usual morning workout. Shortly afterwards, he had a heart attack. An air ambulance was called, and paramedics tried to save him. But it was too late. “I was asleep,” says Sharon. “We’d spoken in the night. Ozzy had woken in the night, and he asked me to kiss him twice, and I did. “And then he said, ‘Hold me, hold me tight,’ and I did. “And then the next thing I know, it’s early in the morning, and someone comes rushing into the room saying, ‘Come down now’. “I ran down, and that was it.” Sharon and Ozzy Osbourne, pictured in 2017 after renewing their wedding vows The grief, she says, will never leave. “You’ve lost the love of your life, so you don’t just wake up and go, ‘I’m fine now. I’m cured’. “You never get over it. But you learn to live with it, and that’s what I’m trying to do. So you either sit in a room and don’t come out, or you accept it, befriend it, and that’s it.” The affection among Ozzy’s fans was apparent before the singer’s funeral. Thousands of people lined the streets of Birmingham, laying floral tributes and singing Black Sabbath songs as Ozzy’s body was transported through his home city in a hearse topped by a purple floral tribute in the shape of a cross. Sharon says he would have been mystified by the outpouring of love. “He’d have been like, ‘What’s the matter with you guys? Go home!'” she says. But for the family, the public response was a huge source of comfort. Daughter Kelly said last year: “I never could have imagined it to be as helpful as it has been to know that we’re not alone in our grief and our sadness, and that the rest of the world loved him as much as we did.” Sharon says the fans’ cards and messages were all collected, sorted and photographed; while the flowers were composted for the family garden, where Ozzy is buried. “There was no way I could put Ozzy in a public graveyard,” she says. “I’ve seen what happens to other people in the public eye. There’s no peace because people want to come and they want to pay their respects. That’s an ongoing thing, and I wanted Ozzy to rest and just be.” Does she visit him often? “Of course, every day. I can see him from my window.” She still talks to him regularly, she says. Asked what she discusses, she puts a finger to her lips and gives a gentle “shh”. Ozzy’s family – including children Jack and Kelly – stopped to read the tributes during his funeral procession last July Ozzy and Sharon’s relationship spanned more than 50 years. They met in 1970 and married in 1982. Their time together could be turbulent – he was arrested for attempting to murder her in 1989 (she dropped the charges), and they split briefly in 2016 amid rumours of infidelity – but the couple maintained that they were soulmates. “It was an unusual relationship because we had such highs and such terrible lows,” she admits. But at the end of his life, “he knew” how much he was loved. You can see proof of that love – from his family, his fans and his bandmates – in a new documentary about his final gig at Birmingham’s Villa Park last year, when he reunited with heavy rock legends Black Sabbath. Titled Back To The Beginning, it features more than 25 songs from that star-studded concert, including Ozzy’s solo set and Sabbath’s full performance. In backstage footage, fellow A-list performers discuss the star’s influence in awestruck tones. “If there was no Sabbath, there’s no Metallica,” says the band’s frontman James Hetfield. “It’s as simple as that.” Yungblud, whose version of Changes was one of the concert’s emotional high points, says that, as a kid who didn’t fit in, Ozzy changed his life. “The fact he was celebrated for his madness and his individuality gave me hope.” Sharon says the concert was Ozzy’s final wish: the one thing that would make him happy after years of deteriorating health. But it almost never happened. Six months before the show, Ozzy fell and fractured his vertebrae. In recovery, he caught pneumonia three times. After surgery on his back, he caught sepsis and nearly died. Two weeks before the show, doctors urged him to call it off. “They came to see us at the house and they said, ‘You can’t do this. We’re advising you not to do this. Your heart’s too weak’,” Sharon recalls. But the singer was determined to see it through. In the film, it’s hard to believe he’s so ill. Although he performs seated on a throne, his eyes are full of life and his voice is powerful. As he looks out at the crowd, he seems elated. Backstage, Sharon admits, “the whole family was terrified”. But something changed when Ozzy entered the stadium. “He was sat in his dressing room, watching everybody on a screen performing, and he was like, ‘I just can’t believe they’re all here’. “It’s amazing what support and love and determination can do for you, because [before the show] he was somebody that couldn’t breathe. He had a lung condition. He had a heart condition. He had terrible, terrible agony from his spine. He had blood clots and he had Parkinson’s. “Some days just to even talk was an effort, let alone sing. And I don’t know how he did it, but he did it. “And you saw it in his eyes, in his face. It just made him feel like he was alive again.” Ozzy is survived by Sharon, their three children (left-right: Kelly, Aimee and Jack) and three children from his previous marriage The effect was so galvanising that, when he came off stage, Ozzy declared he wanted to go on tour. “He was raring to go,” Sharon laughs. “He was like, ‘I can do this, and the fans don’t mind if I’m sat down’.” It’s an incredible and rare thing, I suggest, to be able to grant your partner their last wish. Ozzy may have suffered immense pain in his final years, but he was able to say goodbye in style. “To quote one of his songs, he was flying high again,” Sharon says. “He was just floating for those last 17 days. It was great. It was joyous.”

title: Bolsonaro refuses to concede, says he will seek annulment of Brazil vote
body: Brazilian right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has followed his imprisoned father's lead by refusing to concede defeat to leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who won a historic fourth term in Sunday's presidential election.Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, called into question a late-Sunday decision by a Lula-appointed Supreme Court justice that extended voting by two hours over alleged voter transport irregularities. He said he would ask for the result to be annulled."It is impossible to recognize the election results, given the circumstances under which things unfolded," Bolsonaro told journalists.Yet the scale of the loss, with Bolsonaro trailing Lula by over 4 million votes, makes it unlikely his efforts to annul the vote will succeed, analysts said. His petition is also undermined by the fact that his campaign also sought a voting extension due to heavy rains in the conservative-leaning south.Still, Bolsonaro's refusal to concede could spark a wave of protests in a country where faith in the electoral system, and in judicial independence, has been strained in recent years, observers say.Jair Bolsonaro plunged Brazil into a deep democratic crisis after the election in 2022, when his supporters stormed government buildings in protest against the result. He later received a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup.Lula defies expectationsLula's victory defied polls, precedent and global anti-incumbent sentiment to put the brakes on a wave of right-wing election victories across Latin America. The result will disappoint the administration of US President Donald Trump, whose State Department led a campaign to return the Bolsonaro family to power.Financial markets also expressed initial concerns at the shock result. A Tokyo-listed exchange-traded fund tracking Brazil's Bovespa index 1325.T dived nearly 15% in Asian trading on news of Lula's victory, while analysts expected the Brazilian real to fall against the US dollar.Lula had trailed Bolsonaro in the first round, but managed to convince voters to come out for him in the runoff.Speaking at a hotel in São Paulo late on Sunday, he took a conciliatory tone."I won't speak of national unity, because that doesn't always fit the reality of this country. No one is obliged to like the elected president, but he was put in place to govern for everyone," Lula said.'Countless' challengesDuring the campaign, Lula pointed to his track record of cutting poverty and inequality while also highlighting record-low unemployment, illiteracy, and deforestation, but his fourth term may prove challenging.He will have to work alongside a Congress packed full of Bolsonaro allies after a surge of right-wing voting recast Brazil's legislature in favor of the president's enemies.“The challenges are countless,” said Carlos Melo, a political science professor at Insper in São Paulo.

title: US proud of what it accuses Iran of: Baghaei
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 26 (MNA) – Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said the US secretary of state accuses Iran of piracy while the US president openly boasts of it.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei responded to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio's accusation that Iran attacked ships like Caribbean pirates. In a post on X, Baghaei wrote that Marco Rubio, accusing Iran of attacking ships، said: “We haven’t seen anything like this since World War II and the pirates of the Caribbean.” He added that U.S. President, on 1 May 2026, boasting about seizing commercial ships and confiscating oil cargoes: “we’re like PIRATES. We’re sort of like PIRATES.” "Perhaps the president won’t be too pleased to learn that his secretary of state has so quickly forgotten his own proud claim of being like pirates," Baghaei concluded.

title: IPoB alleges secret transfer of 68 detainees
body: By Steve Oko UMUAHIA—The Indigenous People of Biafra, IPoB, has alleged that 68 detained Biafrans were secretly transferred from Wawa Barracks to correctional facilities in Kuje, Keffi and Suleja, accusing the Federal Government of using the justice system to prolong the detention of its members. The group also alleged that the Court of Appeal had yet to list an appeal challenging the conviction of its leader, Mazi Nnamdi Kanu, despite the compilation and transmission of the record of appeal. IPOB made the allegations in its weekly address issued on Sunday by the Head of its Directorate of State, DOS, Mazi Chris Nwaogu. Nwaogu said the group’s legal team had identified the 68 detainees and was working to secure their release. He urged supporters to sustain legal efforts on behalf of those in custody. He further alleged that a separate fundamental rights suit concerning Kanu’s detention had suffered a setback after the presiding judge reportedly announced that the court file was missing. According to him, the suit concerns Kanu’s detention for 14 months following his discharge by the Court of Appeal on October 13, 2022. The IPOB spokesman also challenged the legal basis of Kanu’s conviction by Justice Omotosho on November 20, 2025, alleging that the judgment relied on a repealed law. He cited Section 36(12) of the Constitution, which provides that a person cannot be convicted of a criminal offence unless the offence and its penalty are prescribed in written law. Meanwhile, IPOB disowned an audio message circulating online that purportedly announced the return of an enforced Monday sit-at-home across the South-East. Nwaọgụ said neither the DOS nor the High Command of the Eastern Security Network, ESN, had authorised the action, warning against attempts to enforce an unauthorised shutdown. He urged residents to disregard the message and avoid actions capable of provoking violence or disrupting economic activities in the region. The group also announced what it described as a phased political disengagement, directing its supporters to boycott activities associated with the All Progressives Congress, APC, ahead of the 2027 general elections. It urged supporters to stay away from APC rallies, stop carrying the party’s flags and refrain from defending APC governors, while maintaining its position on boycotting the 2027 elections. Nwaọgụ said the proposed boycott was a response to what the group described as injustice, unlawful detention and persecution of its members. He, however, cautioned supporters against violence and warned politicians against hijacking the planned boycott for their own interests. IPOB reiterated its demand for Kanu’s immediate and unconditional release, urging the judiciary to list the appeal for hearing and determine the legal issues surrounding his conviction. title: Kojo Kwarteng: From journalism and corporate communications to law
body: On Friday, October 9, 2026, Emmanuel Kojo Kwarteng became a lawyer, adding the legal profession to a diverse career spanning journalism, marketing, corporate communications, public relations, banking, authorship, alternative dispute resolution (ADR) and community service. His story shows the power of continuous learning. He has never regarded education as an end, but as a tool for professional excellence, personal transformation and service to society. From Dunkwa-on-Offin/Tarkwa to Professional Excellence Kwarteng began at Boa-Amponsem Primary School in Dunkwa-on-Offin and Tarkwa Senior High School, where he served as Library Prefect, an early sign of his interest in knowledge, leadership, and service. He studied at the Ghana Institute of Journalism and the University of Ghana Business School, earned a Bachelor of Science in Administration, and later an MBA in Marketing from Central University. He then earned an LLB and LLM from Mountcrest University, Ghana and the University of Essex in the United Kingdom, and studied at the Kellogg School of Management, Northwestern University, Evanston, Illinois, USA. He has also undertaken executive master’s-level studies in Labour and Industrial Relations Law and Practice and ADR. This breadth lets him see organisations through the connected lenses of business, law, communication, marketing and dispute resolution. A Journalist Who Understands the Power of Information As an award-winning journalist at Ghana News Agency and Daily Graphic, Kwarteng covered public affairs, politics, business and society, gaining an appreciation of credible information and the media’s role in holding institutions accountable. As a Presidential Reporter, he covered the Presidency and national affairs, gaining a front-row understanding of governance and public policy. He is also credited with founding the Federation of Environmental Journalists (FEJ) in Ghana in the mid-1990s, which launched the war against illegal mining, environmental destruction, and abuse of communities’ rights. Corporate Communications, Public Relations and Marketing A defining chapter was his time as Head of Corporate Affairs at GCB Bank Plc, where he worked at the intersection of corporate leadership, media relations, stakeholder engagement, and reputation management. In his philosophy, corporate communication goes beyond press releases. It means building trust between an organisation and its stakeholders, managing reputation, communicating in a crisis, and ensuring employees, customers, regulators, shareholders, the media, and the public understand decisions. He is regarded as one of the best in his generation, and during GCB’s 2017 integration of UT/Capital Bank and the 2023 Domestic Debt Exchange Programme (DDEP), he was a household name in financial services. His marketing training complements this, shaping his view that an organisation must not only provide value, but also communicate and protect it. Why the Law Is a Natural Progression His entry into law is a natural extension of his career, not a departure. His interest in ADR fits this background. Disputes are inevitable, and what matters is whether they become destructive or are managed constructively. ADR offers solutions without prolonged litigation, reflecting his commitment to dialogue, negotiation and peaceful resolution. Author and Thinker Kwarteng has written two books. Leading an Extraordinary Life explores personal development and the belief that people can improve themselves through discipline, knowledge and purposeful action. Oil Cocoa Mines is a novel that shows his creative side. He has also written and reviewed many articles on business, leadership, communications, law and society. Environmentalism, CSR and Philanthropy He is committed to environmental advocacy, corporate social responsibility and philanthropy, believing organisations and professionals have responsibilities beyond profit and personal advancement. He has developed policy documents for national and international institutions and NGOs. For him, success carries a responsibility to contribute to society. A Man of Faith and Service A committed Christian, Kwarteng worships at Assemblies of God Church, Christ Worship Centre, Sowutuom, Accra, where he serves as a deacon and chairs the Education and Welfare Committees. This reflects leadership as service without seeking the spotlight, and a belief that spiritual development and human wellbeing complement each other. A Multidisciplinary Professional What stands out is not the number of qualifications but how they intersect across law, business, journalism, communications, marketing, banking, labour relations, ADR, social responsibility, environmental advocacy, authorship and Christian service. In a complex world, professionals who connect disciplines are increasingly valuable. A corporate crisis can be a legal, financial, communication, reputational and human resource problem at once, and his career has prepared him to see those connections. Another Chapter Begins October 9, 2026, marks not the end of his journey but the start of another chapter. From TARSCO to the legal profession, his path demonstrates lifelong learning and shows that career development need not be linear. The common thread is not a job title but the continuous pursuit of knowledge and the desire to use it meaningfully. The greater achievement lies in bringing his qualifications together to solve problems, mentor others, strengthen organisations and serve society.

title: FG: Era of Holding Nigeria’s Oil, Gas Assets as Souvenirs Over
body: *Drill-or-drop policy: Operators returning assets voluntarily, says Lokpobiri *Explains how exit of EPC firms pushed up project costs *Kachikwu: How govt interference delayed decisions as NNPC GMD *Ekpo: Nigeria’s 215TCF gas reserves must lead to higher domestic supply *NEITI: NUPRC has brought greater openness to oil bid rounds Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja The federal government has declared an end to the era of oil companies holding petroleum assets without developing them, insisting that operators must either invest in production or relinquish their licences under the drill-or-drop provisions of the Petroleum Industry Act (PIA). Minister of State for Petroleum Resources (Oil), Senator Heineken Lokpobiri, said the policy has empowered the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission (NUPRC) to recover undeveloped assets and make them available to investors willing and able to develop them. Also, a former Minister of State for Petroleum Resources, and Group Managing Director of the Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation (NNPC), Prof. Ibe Kachikwu, has recalled how government interference and cumbersome approval processes delayed decisions and constrained investment during his tenure at the national oil company. In the same vein, Minister of State for Petroleum Resources (Gas), Ekperikpe Ekpo, said Nigeria must translate its 215 Trillion Cubic Feet (TCF) of proven gas reserves into higher domestic supply, stronger infrastructure and industrial growth over the next five years. Similarly, the Olu of Warri, Ogiame Atuwatse III, has maintained that the PIA has brought greater calm and responsibility to oil-producing communities by giving them a clearer stake in petroleum operations through Host Communities Development Trusts (HCDTs). They all spoke in a series of interviews published in ‘Upstream Gaze’, a special edition of a quarterly magazine by the NUPRC to mark its fifth anniversary. Lokpobiri said the policy had helped make petroleum assets available for fresh investment, with 50 assets recently offered for bidding and another licensing round in the offing. The drill-or-drop policy, provided for under the PIA requires oil and gas companies to develop their licensed petroleum assets within the stipulated period or risk losing them to the government. The policy empowers the regulator to revoke or recover licences for undeveloped assets and make them available to investors willing and capable of putting them into production. Essentially, it is designed to discourage speculative ownership and the hoarding of oil blocks which has been the norm, accelerate exploration and development, attract fresh investment, increase crude oil and gas production, and help Nigeria achieve its production targets. Lokpobiri said: “The drill-or-drop provision is one of the most consequential provisions of the PIA. It has kept operators on their toes. If you do not develop your assets within the provisions of the law, the NUPRC has the authority to recover those assets and make them available to investors that are willing and able to develop them. “The era of holding assets as souvenirs or symbols of wealth is gone: you either drill or drop. Some operators are now willing to relinquish assets voluntarily because that may be preferable to regulatory recovery. Others are reassessing their portfolios and recognising that certain assets no longer fit their development plans.” He also attributed the increase in active drilling rigs to reforms and improved regulatory activity, saying the number had risen from between 10 and 14 in 2023 to more than 60 currently. However, the minister said the departure of major Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) contractors, deep-offshore contractors and other service providers had contributed to higher project costs in Nigeria, following prolonged uncertainty before the passage of the PIA. According to him, inadequate project activity had made it difficult for contractors to sustain their operations, prompting some to leave the country and reducing competition in critical areas of the industry. “The cost of our projects became higher than in some other jurisdictions because there was limited competition and insufficient project activity. Contractors can only survive where there are projects to execute. If the project pipeline dries up, they will leave,” he said. “Many contractors therefore left the country, leaving only one or two providers in some areas and contributing to prohibitive costs. That was a major challenge, but we are now working to bring them back.” Lokpobiri said the government was engaging contractors in Europe and America to encourage their return, while pursuing fiscal, operational and regulatory reforms to improve Nigeria’s competitiveness. He added that a recent presidential executive order was expected to help unlock almost $50 billion in deep-offshore investments, while the re-entry of shut-in wells following recent divestments was contributing to production growth. He cited developments following Seplat Energy’s acquisition of ExxonMobil’s assets and Renaissance Africa Energy’s acquisition of Shell’s onshore assets as examples of efforts to revive previously inactive wells. Looking ahead, Lokpobiri said Nigeria could significantly increase crude oil production over the next five years if investment commitments and development programmes materialised, projecting a potential output range of 3 million to 5 million barrels per day. Kachikwu: Govt Interference Hobbled My Work as Minister Also, former Group Managing Director of the NNPC and former Minister of State for Petroleum Resources, Prof. Kachikwu, has recalled how government interference and cumbersome approval processes delayed decisions and constrained investment during his tenure at the national oil company. Kachikwu said the petroleum industry had suffered from excessive government control, which restricted managerial independence and made it difficult to implement decisions quickly, even when the commercial case for action was clear. “The oil sector could be very frustrating because there was a great deal of government interference. In my case, I had the rare privilege of serving as both GMD of NNPC and Minister of State. Dealing with the investment process at NNPC was difficult because you could hardly do anything without government approval. “The lack of independence constrained decision-making. The oil sector was run almost like a conventional government agency, which limited creativity. One of the things I tried to do when I came in was to bring more of a private-sector orientation into NNPC and the Ministry. It took quite a while for the system to adjust to new ways of doing things,” he explained. He said the absence of clearly defined institutional powers under the old Petroleum Act meant investment decisions often depended on the initiative of individual officeholders, while the PIA had introduced greater clarity on responsibilities and institutional independence. However, Kachikwu expressed concern that significant government control remained and that the new law had yet to deliver the scale of investment anticipated. He noted that much of the investment recorded since the PIA’s passage involved domestic acquisitions, mergers and takeovers of existing assets, rather than the development of major new production platforms and floating production facilities at the expected pace. Kachikwu also argued that Nigeria needed to raise its production ambitions beyond the federal government’s 3 million barrels per day target, saying the country had the potential to produce 4 million barrels daily by 2030. “I think Nigeria could do four million barrels per day by 2030; targeting three million barrels may be underestimating our potential. We have to recognise that oil will not simply remain in the ground waiting for us indefinitely,” he said. “The world is changing. Electric vehicles are expanding, solar power is growing, alternative energy systems are developing and new producing countries are entering the market. The world will not wait while we increase production gradually. We need a significant volumetric shift and we should sit down and ask what would it take to reach four million barrels per day,” he added. He said Nigeria needed to identify the investments, projects, infrastructure and timelines required to achieve the higher target, warning that the country was competing with emerging oil producers, including Guyana and Namibia, for international capital. Predictable fiscal terms, transparency, competitive project economics and timely government decisions, he stressed, were essential to attracting the investments required to increase production. Ekpo: Enormous Gas Resources Must Benefit Nigerians In the gas sector, the Minister of State for Petroleum Resources (Gas), Ekpo, said Nigeria must translate its 215 trillion cubic feet of proven gas reserves into higher domestic supply, stronger infrastructure and industrial growth over the next five years. He reiterated that the country was targeting gas production of 10 billion standard cubic feet per day by 2027 and 12 billion standard cubic feet daily by 2030, but achieving the goals would require faster development of non-associated gas resources and sustained investment in processing and pipeline infrastructure. “Over the next five years, Nigeria must convert its 215 trillion cubic feet of proven gas reserves into increased production, stronger infrastructure and sustainable industrial growth. Success must ultimately translate into reliable gas supply for power generation, fertiliser production, petrochemicals, manufacturing, Liquefied Petroleum Gas and Compressed Natural Gas, alongside sustained regional gas supply projects and Liquefied Natural Gas exports,” he said. On the Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) initiative, introduced to provide a cheaper transport alternative following the removal of the petrol subsidy, Ekpo said the planned national network of refuelling stations was being expanded from 500 to 1,000. He repeated that more than $2 billion had been catalysed in the CNG ecosystem since 2023, supporting 120,000 vehicle conversions, more than 400 certified conversion centres and over 90 operational refuelling stations. He said the priority was to extend access beyond major cities and ensure that the lower cost of CNG translated into reduced transport expenses for Nigerians. NEITI: NUPRC Has Improved Licensing Processes Speaking on transparency in the upstream sector, the Executive Secretary of the Nigeria Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (NEITI), Musa Adar, commended the NUPRC for improving licensing procedures, disclosure and regulatory oversight since its establishment under the PIA. Adar, who chaired the House Committee on Petroleum Resources (Upstream) in the Ninth National Assembly, said the law had created a clearer institutional and regulatory framework after years of concerns over transparency, accountability and disclosure. “The NUPRC, as one of the institutions established under the Act, has helped to improve the licensing process, strengthen disclosure and provide more structured oversight of upstream operations. These are commendable developments,” he said. On the 2025 licensing round monitored by NEITI, Adar said the organisation was awaiting its final report and would not pre-empt its conclusions, although preliminary feedback from field officers had not identified any material misalignment in the process. He called for further improvements in disclosure, accountability and regulatory responsiveness, noting that investors valued regulators that were firm, fair, transparent and predictable. Adar also argued that Nigeria’s ambitions should extend beyond crude oil production to greater domestic refining and petrochemical processing to retain more value within the economy and reduce exposure to imported refined products. Olu of Warri: Indigenes Now Have Clearer Stake in Oil Sector For his part, the Olu of Warri, Ogiame Atuwatse III, said the PIA had brought greater calm and responsibility to oil-producing communities by giving them a clearer stake in petroleum operations through Host Communities Development Trusts (HCDTs). He said the framework had improved communities’ understanding of their entitlements and created incentives to protect petroleum infrastructure, although official data would be needed to establish the extent of any reduction in sabotage. The PIA requires oil companies to contribute 3 per cent of their actual operating expenditure for the preceding financial year to the applicable HCDT. “As someone who is on the ground, I would say that it has brought a sense of calm. There is also a clearer sense of direction and consideration. Before the PIA, these obligations were not set out in law in the same way. Today, the framework is captured in black and white and stakeholders have greater clarity about what is expected. “When people know that a defined percentage is available, there can be better planning and consideration of development priorities. That goes a long way towards giving communities a sense of ownership and belonging,” he posited.

title: Mourinho's Real Madrid stun Barcelona to blow La Liga title race wide open
body: Jose Mourinho hailed Real Madrid's 2-1 victory over Barcelona as a “great victory” but warned his players not to get carried away after Kylian Mbappe's late winner reignited the La Liga title race. Mbappe struck in the 87th minute to settle a thrilling Clasico at Camp Nou, cutting Barcelona's lead at the top of the table to three points and giving Madrid a statement victory against their title rivals. But Mourinho was already looking beyond Sunday's celebrations, insisting Real Madrid must use the result as a springboard for a sustained title challenge. “Real Madrid doesn’t play to win at Camp Nou,” he said. “Real Madrid plays to win championships. We have to keep going.” Mbappe's first goal four minutes before half-time was a fortuitous one. Barca defender Gerard Martin's attempted clearance flew in off the French striker past Joan Garcia. Ballon d'Or contender Lamine Yamal hit an effort into the side netting while Mbappe, another with aspirations of being named the world's best at Monday's ceremony in London, had earlier hit the post. A Barcelona equaliser arrived 16 minutes into the second half as captain Raphinha collected Pedri's pass and shot through the legs of Jude Bellingham into the far corner. The game looked to be heading for a draw before substitute Eduardo Camavinga broke forward and squared the ball for Mbappe to finish into an unguarded net three minutes from time. “It was a great match, high-level, which surely the world of football lovers stopped to watch and were not disappointed,” Mourinho said. “The boys played an extraordinary game, very organised, very focused, and with a lot of courage to play out from the back against an opponent that presses a lot.” “For me, this is a great victory for the boys against a great opponent.” It maintained Mourinho's excellent record in Clasico matches. The Portuguese has become just the third Real boss to go six Clasicos in a row without defeat - 13 years since he last led Los Blancos in this fixture. It was also just a second victory in eight games against Barcelona for Real, with the return of Mourinho to the fixture haunting the reigning champions. A Real defeat would have allowed Barcelona to establish a commanding nine-point advantage, but the result has transformed the top of La Liga, bringing Mourinho's side to within three points of their rivals. “This match was one where we could leave trailing by three, six, or nine points,” Mourinho said. “If you fall behind by nine, psychologically, it’s heavy.” “Being three points behind is different, and the way we won is also important.” Barcelona boss Hansi Flick said he didn't want to give excuses for the defeat but admitted his team paid the price for a punishing schedule. "We missed the freshness," he said. "It's not easy for our players. We have to recover well, train well and we have to respond from this defeat. "In big games, small things are important and they decide the games and today, it wasn't on our side."

title: Saudi-led attacks on Yemen reach 3,179: Saree
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 26 (MNA) – Yemen has been targeted by 3,179 air and missile attacks from the Saudi-led aggressor coalition since the escalation began, including 56 in the past 24 hours, armed forces spokesman Yahya Saree said.
Saree said the Saudi air force carried out 56 air and missile attacks on Yemen in the past 24 hours.
The attacks targeted civilian sites in the provinces of Hajjah, Lahj, Amran, Saada, Al-Jawf, Taiz and Ibb, he said.
The air raids were carried out by F-15 and Typhoon fighter jets that took off from Khamis Mushait and Taif air bases, while missile attacks were launched from the Najran area, according to Saree.
He said the total number of attacks by the aggressor Saudi-led coalition since the escalation began has reached 3,179, including air and missile strikes.

title: Four Seasons Kuda Huraa, Maldives review: A Maldives classic that still delivers
body: Four Seasons Resort Maldives at Kuda Huraa has been welcoming guests for nearly three decades. For an older, smaller property amid a sea of newer, sprawling five-star resorts, I wasn’t sure what to expect, but Kuda Huraa more than holds its own and the fabulous experience more than outweighs the hotel’s compact size. For my first visit to the Maldives , it was the perfect entryway, as I arrived by speedboat from Male's Velana International Airport, no seaplane necessary, and left with myriad memories, such as planting coral fragments on the ocean floor dedicated to my children and eating a whole fish while a baby shark cruised past in plain view of the table. The welcome A 25-minute speedboat transfer from Velana International Airport brings you to a small jetty on a coral island in North Male Atoll. The arrival is modest by Maldivian standards – there’s no seaplane moment, no sweeping reveal from above – and Kuda Huraa is the better for it. The island is compact, the resort’s 96 villas arranged in the style of a traditional Maldivian village, with thatched roofs and timber floors and the kind of scale that means the friendly staff remember your name quickly. The whole place has a rhythm that’s more village than resort. The room The Deluxe Beach Pavilion with Pool is perfect. It boasts 46 square metres of interior, with teak floors, wooden shutters and nautical inspiration. Outside, a private plunge pool leads to a swinging hammock and, beyond that, the shore, well screened by well-placed planting. You also have an outdoor shower set in a walled garden that, for me, is the highlight. The design draws on the island’s Maldivian village aesthetic throughout – lattice panels, natural timber, woven textures. It’s comfortable and cosy, nothing particularly showy, but still picturesque. The food Food is where Kuda Huraa truly distinguishes itself, and the kitchen does so across five restaurants and bars without the drop in quality you sometimes encounter when a resort tries to cover too many cuisines. The first dinner was at Reef Club, the resort’s beachside Italian restaurant, where I had grilled Maldivian local catch that tasted fresh and entirely of itself. Lunch the following day was a Hawaiian-style poke bowl with fresh tuna at Cafe Huraa, the all-day restaurant that overlooks the infinity pool and the ocean beyond. It was light and well-balanced – the kind of simple thing that’s easy to do badly and this kitchen does well. The meal I’ll be describing to people for a while came at Baraabaru, the resort’s Indian restaurant set over the lagoon and inspired by the architecture of Kerala. That evening it was running a special menu by Hari Nayak. I ordered the catch of the day with a Malvani fish preparation: mango coconut curry, served with roti. It arrived as a whole fish, head and body intact – no tableside carving, just an honest presentation that made it clear exactly what you were eating. The curry balanced sweetness and heat through several layers, a triumphant depth of flavour that can be difficult to achieve. At some point during the meal, a baby shark drifted past in the shallow water just beyond the restaurant. Idyllic. Hotel facilities The resort extends across two islands connected by traditional dhow. The main island has watersports and direct beach snorkelling; the water is shallow and clear, and the reef is worth exploring. I took a morning surf session – a first for me – and managed to stand up on the board by the end of the hour. The Marine Discovery Centre is the other stop worth making, as the team there rehabilitates turtles and runs the coral framing programme, through which guests attach live coral fragments to a metal frame placed on the ocean floor to grow and be monitored. Every six months, you receive an update on how it’s progressing. I dedicated mine to my children and dropped it into the sea, thinking about the time I bring them back to do their own. Spa and wellness The award-winning spa has recently been reimagined as Urja Naturopathy Island – urja meaning “vitality” in Sanskrit – and operates on a separate island reached by dhoni – the traditional Maldivian boat – a few minutes each way. The concept is grounded in naturopathic principles such as self-healing, root-cause care and therapies shaped around rest, cleansing, nourishment and reconnection. I had a consultation with Dr Shristi Paudel, a naturopathic physician, and left with a set of practical lifestyle adjustments to incorporate into my routine at home. The 60-minute massage that followed was excellent. When the weather is good, the short dhow crossing becomes a small ritual. When it isn’t, it’s a minor inconvenience, so book treatments around conditions if your schedule allows. Family-friendly factor The island's scale makes it genuinely well-suited to families. Children can roam freely without the distances of a larger resort, the beach water is calm and shallow, and the watersports and children's club give them enough to occupy the hours you'd like to spend by the pool. The coral framing activity works well for older children, too. Accessibility and sustainability Coral restoration is embedded into the guest experience here. Participating in the framing session and receiving continuing updates connects visitors to the reef in a way that outlasts the stay. For accessibility requirements, the resort should be contacted directly. Value for money Rates for a Deluxe Beach Pavilion with Pool start from US$1,255 (excluding taxes), although these vary depending on the season, villa type and package selected. Check-in time is 2pm and checkout is 12pm. Also note Kuda Huraa runs on something called ‘island time’, so it’s an hour behind Male. This review was conducted at the invitation of the hotel and reflects standards during this time

title: Winnipeg Jets’ winless skid hits 5 with another 1-goal loss in Heritage Classic
body:
A game on the outdoor rink couldn’t reverse the Winnipeg Jets’ fortunes.
The Jets lost their fifth straight game with a 2-1 defeat to the Montreal Canadiens in the Heritage Classic on Sunday at Princess Auto Stadium.
The Jets were almost shutout again in a Heritage Classic as it took them over 55 minutes to score a goal after being blanked by the Edmonton Oilers in the last outdoor game in Winnipeg in 2016.
After a scoreless first period, the Habs scored goals less than four minutes apart in the second period and held on for the victory.
“I thought we got better as the game went on,” said Jets head coach Scott Arniel. “I thought we started a little bit slow. Obviously the third period was our best period. Their goaltender was real good.
“Probably the biggest thing for me, we didn’t have enough traffic on (Jacob) Fowler. We didn’t make it a little bit more difficult for him to kinda find pucks and that’s just something that we got to make sure that we do a better job at.”
The Jets outshot the Canadiens in all three periods, but Fowler made 33 stops as the 21-year-old became the youngest goalie in NHL history to start an outdoor game.
The Jets now have five straight one-goal losses.
“We look at that game and there’s areas we got to clean up,” said Jets captain Adam Lowry. “I think in that stretch, there’s been a couple games where we haven’t liked but then it’s been one thing, whether it’s the penalty kill or a couple of D-zone faceoffs that has been the difference. They’ve been tight one-goal games and it’s about finding a way to be on the right side of that.”
Isak Rosen scored the lone marker for the Jets while Lane Hutson and Kaiden Guhle had the goals for Montreal.
Elias Salomonsson had over 17 minutes of ice time in his season debut after starting the campaign on the injured list following off-season shoulder surgery. And Dawson Mercer made his Jets’ debut after being acquired on Friday in the Connor Hellebuyck trade. He started on their third line but also spent some time on their second line in the final period.
“Pretty cool experience,” Mercer said. “Definitely worse situation to be thrown into, but honestly a pretty special one that’ll I definitely cherish. Obviously, the outcome is not what we wanted but overall, nice to get going with the guys right away and then build on it from here.”
Winnipeg has scored just six goals over their last four games with their power play now 0-for-12 during that stretch.
The Jets top line had eight of their first 10 shots on net.
“We need other people stepping up,” Arniel said. “It makes it hard if all the heat’s on Schife’s (Mark Scheifele) line to try to do that. That’s part of that mindset of our players that, like I just talked about, you got to get to the net. You got to go get greasy goals, some that bounce off your skate or your foot or your back, whatever it is.”
The Jets outshot them 34-21 as Stuart Skinner made 19 stops in the loss.
With the Hellebuyck trade and the Heritage Classic now behind them, the Jets will be looking for a fresh start when they host the Florida Panthers on Tuesday.

title: Banks’ credit to manufacturers falls 26.8% to N5.19trn
body: *… as credit guarantees unlock N47bn *MAN seeks stronger guarantee coverage, N1trn stabilisation fund *Nigeria needs $35bn yearly to industrialise —BoI *Guarantees critical to boosting access to finance — CPPE *FG advocates coordinated financing framework By Yinka Kolawole Loans extended by Nigerian banks to the manufacturing sector fell by 26.8 per cent year-on-year to N5.19 trillion in the first half of 2026 (H1’26), from N7.09 trillion in the corresponding period of last year (H1’25). Read Also: Stock market extend losses, 55 stocks depreciate; 20 record capital gains This comes as manufacturers grappled with persistent financing constraints and rising operating costs. The decline also comes amid concerns over the availability of affordable, long-term funding for industrial production, with the Manufacturers Association of Nigeria (MAN) calling for stronger credit guarantees and the full operationalisation of a N1 trillion Manufacturing Stabilisation Fund. Data from the Central Bank of Nigeria’s (CBN) Q2 2026 Statistical Bulletin also indicated a sustained decline as the outstanding bank credit to manufacturers declined by about 21 per cent between January and June 2026, from N6.57 trillion to N5.19 trillion. The 2026 monthly figures showed that credit fell from N6.57 trillion in January to N6.37 trillion in February, N5.77 trillion in March and N5.32 trillion in April. It declined further to N5.02 trillion in May before a slight recovery to N5.19 trillion in June. Despite the slight month-on-month recovery, the June figure remained substantially below the level recorded in the previous year. The contraction highlights the financing challenges confronting manufacturers amid high production costs, expensive electricity, logistics bottlenecks and exchange-rate pressures. However, the decline in outstanding credit does not, on its own, establish whether it resulted from reduced new lending, loan repayments or other changes in banks’ credit portfolios. Credit guarantees unlock N47bn Meanwhile, the National Credit Guarantee Company (NCGC) said it has unlocked N46.95 billion in loans for 67,512 borrowers across the country, renewing calls for credit guarantees to be expanded to improve access to finance for manufacturers and small businesses. Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer of NCGC, Dr Bonaventure Okhaimo, said the credit was unlocked using N21.59 billion in guarantees to share lending risks with financial institutions. Nigeria needs $35bn yearly to industrialise — BoI The development comes as the Bank of Industry (BoI) estimates that Nigeria requires more than $35 billion annually to finance industrialisation and raise manufacturing’s contribution to Gross Domestic Product (GDP) to 25 per cent. Highlighting the scale of the funding challenge, Managing Director of the Bank of Industry, BoI, Dr Olasupo Olusi, said no single development finance institution could close the gap. He stated: “It is a huge gap. BoI cannot do it alone from its balancesheet,\.” Olusi noted that the funding constraint was reflected in the bank’s 2025 pipeline, where loan applications reached N1.754 trillion against available funding of N645 billion, leaving a shortfall of about 63 per cent. He said the bank’s mobilisation of more than 2 billion euros through global syndication in 2024, which he described as the largest of such transaction by an African development finance institution, underscored the scale of capital required to support industrial expansion in the country. Unlocked credit commendable, but insufficient — MAN Reacting to the NCGC intervention, Director-General of the Manufacturers Association of Nigeria (MAN), Segun Ajayi-Kadir, described the credit guarantee model as an example of the risk-sharing mechanism manufacturers had consistently advocated. He said the amount was commendable but remained small relative to the estimated $35 billion annual industrial financing requirement. He stated: “Nigerian manufacturers are not unbankable, they are simply un-de-risked. “With MPR at 26.5 percent and CRR at 45 percent, banks would rather lend to oil and gas and government securities than to a factory in Kano or Port Harcourt or Lagos that is daily contending with power outage, logistics cost and high cost of forex. So we truly have a credit squeeze, not just high cost. “Now, this is where credit guarantees matter. A guarantee does not give money, but it gives confidence. Let us look at a situation where NCGC guarantees 60 percent of a facility. ‘’It tells the bank that if this manufacturer struggles because diesel jumps or production is disrupted one way or the other, someone will stand in the gap. That is how N21.59 billion could catalyse N46.95 billion – a multiplier of more than twofold. ‘’For our SMEs who form 70 percent of our membership and lack the 150 percent collateral banks demand, that is the difference between struggling and expansion, between 90-day overdraft and 5-year term loan to buy machinery to retool. “But let us be clear on scale. Nigeria needs $35 billion yearly to industrialise. That N46.95 billion was unlocked is commendable, within the context of the situation we are in. ‘’However, it is less than $30 million. It is a drop in that $35 billion ocean. So if we are to make any meaningful impact, we need to scale this model massively.” Ajayi-Kadir said MAN was seeking stronger guarantees and a dedicated financing facility to address the funding gap confronting manufacturers. “That is why MAN is asking for the full operationalisation of the N1 trillion Manufacturing Stabilisation Fund, to be domiciled with BoI, and for NCGC to be capitalised to provide 70 percent coverage for manufacturing at single-digit pricing. “Without that scale and without forcing transmission of MPR cuts to lending rates, guarantees will remain pilots. With scale, they can restore the N1.92 trillion we lost and finally align monetary policy with industrial reality.” Guarantees critical to boosting access to finance —CPPE Also commenting, Chief Executive Officer of the Centre for the Promotion of Private Enterprise (CPPE), Dr Muda Yusuf, described credit guarantees as critical to improving access to finance for manufacturing, agriculture and small and medium enterprises (SMEs). He said banks often perceived businesses in these sectors as high-risk borrowers, making guarantees necessary to reduce lending risks and expand credit allocation. His words: “Credit guarantee is very critical in enabling access to credit in the Nigerian economy. And one of the reasons the Nigerian banking system has been very reluctant in lending to some sectors is because of the risk of default in some of these sectors, particularly in the real sectors of the economy. And those businesses that are in the SME space. ‘’They are perceived as very risky. So in order to correct this or mitigate this challenge, credit guarantees have become extremely very important. “They have a very critical role to play in facilitating credits to the manufacturing sector to the agricultural sector and to small and middle enterprises. These sectors are perceived as very risky. “In order to facilitate credit to those sectors, we need this eh, ready guarantee uh skin. So it needs to be further strengthened. The capitalisation needs to be much more robust than what it is because you are talking of sectors that contribute over fifty percent of our GDP. And if you look at the credit allocation to these sectors, they are very, very low, compared to the potential they have in terms of contribution to economic growth and more particularly contribution to employment generation and contribution to food security and economic inclusion. “So, from a social and economic perspective, these sectors are very critical. But because of the risk inherent in investing in them, the banks have been, generally, very reluctant. So the credit guarantee scheme has a major role to play in mitigating the risk of lending to this sector. So the government needs to do a lot more to support this agency so that it can give a lot more support to this very critical sector.” FG seeks coordinated financing framework Meanwhile, Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, has called for a coordinated financing framework involving government, regulators, development finance institutions and commercial capital providers. Speaking at a Ministerial Roundtable of the Industrial Revolution Work Group (IRWG), Oyedele said Nigeria must move beyond conventional bank lending by mobilising public balance sheets, blended finance, institutional capital, pension and insurance assets, as well as the capital market. According to him, the proposed National Industrial Finance Compact should ultimately be measured by whether manufacturers can access financing and deploy it to expand installed capacity, create jobs and increase export earnings. Oyedele also stressed that fiscal, monetary and industrial policies were interconnected, warning that an incentive, guarantee scheme or development fund that manufacturers could not effectively access was the same as having no policy. On his part, Minister of State for Industry, Senator John Enoh, said Nigeria’s financing architecture remained poorly suited to manufacturing because industrial investments required longer repayment periods than conventional short-term bank lending could provide. According to him, the challenge was not simply the availability of money but its cost, tenor and structure. “Our manufacturers do not lack ambition, they don’t lack orders, they don’t lack markets. What they continuously lack is the right kind of money,” Enoh said. He argued that investments in machinery, factories and production capacity required affordable, long-term financing, noting that businesses pursuing projects with gestation periods of 10 to 15 years could not reasonably be expected to repay loans within three or six months. “The issue is not that there is no money. It is the price of the money, the term of the money and the capital architecture into the factories,” he said. Enoh warned that the mismatch between financing structures and industrial investment needs could make trading more attractive than manufacturing, with implications for Nigeria’s industrialisation drive. He said the ultimate objective was to align capital with production. “Nigeria has entrepreneurs. Our job is to align capital with production, so we make more at home, employ more at home, and compete,” he said.
