title: Presidential candidate Bolsonaro urges to annul Brazilian elections’ results
body:
RIO DE JANEIRO, October 26. /TASS/. Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who represents the right-wing opposition and lost in the second round of the Brazilian presidential election, refused to recognize the election results and stated that they should be annulled.
"What happened today was unacceptable. For the first time in history, the rules of the electoral process are being altered with a stroke of a pen," the politician said, commenting on the judicial authorities’ decision to extend the voting period by two hours.
"The [results of the] elections must be annulled. It is impossible to recognize such a result," he stressed.
The Brazilian Superior Electoral Court (TSE) reported earlier in the day that incumbent President of Brazil Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won in the second round of presidential elections and was re-elected as the president of the country for the fourth term.
According to the TSE, after 97.69% of the ballots in the runoff election were counted, Lula da Silva secured 51.74% of the votes, while Bolsonaro was backed by 48.26% of the votes.
Lula da Silva is now the first politician in the present-day Brazilian history to win the presidential election after trailing in the first round of voting. The elected head of state will assume the office on January 1, 2027.
The voter turnout in the second round was reported at 80.79%, with 127,807,732 citizens participating in the voting. The rate of abstainers was reported at 19.21%, which corresponds to 30,081,854 voters. The share of blank ballots was at 1.12% (1,426,055 votes), while the share of invalid ballots amounted to 2.12% (2,713,225 votes).

title: First time voters could determine as many as 12 Knesset seats with high turnout
body: On Oct. 27, Yael Chernyvsky, 18, from Ramat Hasharon in central Israel, plans to cast her ballot for the first time. “I'm voting so we can change the future of this country,” the teen told Jewish Telegraphic Agency earlier this month. She was entering a Tel Aviv auditorium where some of Israel's top politicians were about to address more than 1,000 first-time voters, including many in pre-military programs.Chernyvsky, who is studying in an army preparation program in the Negev, blames the current right-wing government led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for the country's problems.So she said she will vote for one of the opposition parties in the “change bloc,” which seeks to oust Netanyahu, who has been in office since 2009 except for a brief period in 2021-2022.Chernyvsky had not decided which party she will vote for, but she said it will “probably” be either the Democrats led by Yair Golan or Yashar led by Gadi Eisenkot.“We've basically had the same government for 20 years, and I genuinely think it's corrupt. Why has this war been going on for three years? Why did it take two years to return the hostages? Why does the government give so much money to haredi Jews who don't work and don't serve in the army?”   Chernyvsky is one of the estimated 640,000 Israelis aged 18 to 22 eligible to vote in Tuesday's election, according to the Israel Democracy Institute (IDI). Comprising nearly 10% of the electorate, their votes could determine as many as 12 seats in the 120-member Knesset.  High voter turnout expected“Israel is a young country with a high birth rate,” said Tammy Hoffman, head of the education policy program at the IDI, which co-sponsored the young voter event with the Yigal Allon Center. “If their turnout is high, as our research suggests, first-time voters will make a difference.”   In May, Hoffman and her colleagues surveyed potential young first-time Jewish and Arab voters about their attitudes and political engagement. Across Israel's population groups, 80% to 95% said they would “definitely” or be likely to vote. Secular Jewish youth expressed the highest level of certainty regarding participation, while 87% of Arabs said they intend to vote.   It's a higher percentage than in the US, where the youth turnout in the 2024 presidential election was only 47%, according to the Center for Information and Research on Civic Learning and Engagement. More than four-fifths of respondents to the IDI survey described the opportunity to vote as either “fairly meaningful” or “very meaningful,” with particularly strong responses among traditional and religious Jewish youth.A separate poll of 18-year-old to 22-year-old potential first-time voters for the Ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth news outlets also revealed high motivation: 67% of respondents said they were certain they would vote, while another 19% thought they would. National security, cost of living highest prioritiesIn both polls, national security and the cost of living were top priorities for both Jews and Arabs. Hoffman wasn't surprised."For the past several years, they've lived in an unstable environment during their adolescence. They were in junior high during COVID, they witnessed the judicial reform protests, and of course Oct. 7. They are worried about their future.” While the Hamas attack affected every Israeli, the fact that so many first-time voters are either serving in the Israel Defense Forces or will do so in the near future could influence how they vote. Jewish Israeli voters of all ages have moved rightward politically over the past couple of decades, Hoffman noted.“But military service doesn't necessarily lead you to a nationalist stance,” Hoffman emphasized. “It can do the opposite: It can bring up questions about the war and its goals.”Arab Israelis, meanwhile, haven't shifted rightward, but they are more eager to vote in this election than previous elections, reflecting their growing engagement in Israeli society, Hoffman said.     In a Sept. 23 N12 poll, 74% of young people described their political views as right-wing or center-right, while 23% identified as left-wing or center-left. If the election were held at the time the poll was taken, 16% of respondents would vote for Eisenkot's Yashar party and 14% would vote for Netanyahu's Likud party.Despite the assumption that the majority of Jewish youth will vote for right-wing and far-right parties, Hoffman said, mock elections at high schools around the country show a different picture.She said the majority of students voted for Eisenkot's Yashar party and Beyachad, led by former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid from the opposition Change bloc, and “some for Netanyahu's [right-wing] Likud, but not a lot for [Itamar] Ben-Gvir,” who heads a far-right party.  Omer Gross from Jerusalem, who graduated from high school in June and is now in an army-prep program in the Golan, plans to vote for the Religious Zionist party led by far-right politicians Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and Moshe Feiglin.   “I don't really agree with what Smotrich has been doing in Gaza,” he said, referring to Smotrich's objective to reestablish the uprooted Jewish settlements in Gaza and incentivize Palestinian emigration from the strip, “but I support what he does in the territories” – the West Bank. “We need a strong, secure Israel.”  Tomer Shiloh from Herziliyah, who attends the same Golan Heights program as his friend Omer, has different plans. “I'm voting for the 'Change' bloc, for Gadi Eisenkot or Naftali Bennett,” the 18-year-old said. If it were up to Shiloh, the next government would require Haredi, or ultra-Orthodox, young men to serve in the IDF, as he will do next year. He wants the next government to lower Israel's high cost of living. “I want the people who run this country to have good values and to do what's best for the country and not for themselves,” the teen said.  Sgt. M is a 22-year-old office worker doing his first stint of reserve duty following the conclusion of his mandatory army service. He says ensuring that all Israelis serve the country either in the IDF or through National Service is at the top of his election priority list. But he will be voting for the left-of-center Democrats party mostly for economic reasons. “Did you know that most university students have to work while they study to pay for tuition, books, food and housing?” the reservist, who requested anonymity due to IDF regulations, said as he traveled home by train from his army base. “I wanted to start studying right after finishing the army, but between the cost and reserve duty, that's impossible,” he said.    Speaking from his home in the northern Israeli city of Shef-Amra, Khalel Alaa Sabeh, 18, said he plans to vote for an Arab party that will prioritize addressing resource gaps in the Arab community.   “I want to see more money allocated to the Arab community,” he said, noting that historically, Arab municipalities have received less government funding than Jewish municipalities. “But most of all, I want our families to be safe. There's a lot of crime in the Arab sector and the Netanyahu government isn't doing enough to stop it.” Sabeh, who plans to start university next year, said he is urging his friends to show up to vote on Oct. 27. “I want to see change in this country, and if Netanyahu wins we'll have four more bad years.” Yet whatever the outcome on Election Day, he said, “I won't leave the country. This is my land, this is my home.”

title: Kimi Antonelli wins US Grand Prix to move within touching distance of F1 title
body: Italian wunderkind Kimi Antonelli took another step towards winning his first Formula One drivers' championship by claiming his ​ninth ​race of the ​year on Sunday at the United States Grand ⁠Prix in Austin, Texas. Antonelli , 20, capitalised on pole ⁠position and sailed to victory ​at the Circuit of the Americas, beating Ferrari's Charles Leclerc by a comfortable 13.078 ⁠seconds. Despite taking the chequered flag, Antonelli doesn't have the championship wrapped up quite yet, but his lead over Mercedes teammate George Russell expanded to 123 points with five races to go. The Briton ⁠must win the next race in Mexico City to remain in contention for ​the ⁠championship; otherwise, it will ‌go to Antonelli, who has dominated this year's championship in only his second F1 ​campaign. "I'm aware [securing the championship] is close, but the mindset doesn't change," Antonelli said post-race. "I want to finish the season on a high, to go into 2027 with high hopes." Antonelli and Mercedes' strategy paid off. While others pitted twice during the 56-lap race, Antonelli held on until Lap 25 to pit and didn't enter the pit lane again. "It was a perfect way to end the weekend; it was an incredible team effort, especially from strategy to believe in me and go for one stop," Antonelli said. "Let's keep pushing" 👊 Kimi Antonelli secures his ninth Grand Prix win! 🏆 #F1 #USGP @MercedesAMGF1 pic.twitter.com/rRiqa82A6k — Formula 1 (@F1) October 25, 2026 Antonelli won five grands prix in a row earlier this season, one of which was the Miami Grand Prix. He's now 2-for-2 in ​the United States this season, with the Las Vegas ‌Grand Prix still to come ⁠in November. "I know we're very close, but, yeah, we try to finish on a high and hopefully we can clinch it very soon,” Antonelli said. “I’m very excited. I would love to clinch the title in style with a great result. “I’m just going to try to enjoy every moment because they’re moments that will always be remembered.” A team effort in Austin... 🤝 And Kimi is eager to look ahead to Mexico, hoping to clinch the Title in style 😮‍💨 #F1 #USGP pic.twitter.com/ovFefVhcVI — Formula 1 (@F1) October 26, 2026 Max Verstappen, the four-time F1 ​champion for Red Bull , rounded out the podium 17.485 seconds behind ​Antonelli. After ‌rattling off every championship from 2021-24, Verstappen has been mathematically eliminated from this year's chase and ⁠will go two years without a world title. "Our overall pace was ⁠not good enough, and the tyres we had available were not the right ones," Verstappen said. "We still managed to get on the podium, maybe a bit lucky with the [Virtual Safety Car] at the end." A Virtual Safety Car was deployed after ​Valtteri Bottas' Cadillac stopped on the track in Lap 52. It lasted until the penultimate lap, by which time no one could catch up to Antonelli. Mercedes grew their lead in the constructors' standings to 133 points over Ferrari – 607 to Ferrari's 474.

title: Nigeria’s Index Ebola Case Set for Medical Evacuation Abroad Today, Two Contacts Test Negative
body: Quarantined persons may get N100,000 weekly upkeep Ebola, brain drain top agenda as doctors in W/Africa meet in Abuja Emmanuel Addeh and Onyebuchi Ezigbo in Abuja Nigeria’s index case of the Ebola virus disease is expected to be evacuated abroad for further medical treatment early Monday (today), a source familiar with the development told THISDAY last night. The source said arrangements had been made to fly the 42-year-old woman out of the country by 6am, adding that a medical evacuation aircraft was already at the airport awaiting her arrival. The fresh development came as the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) said two suspected Ebola cases from the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) and Rivers State have tested negative, while 53 primary contacts of the confirmed index case have been identified and are being monitored. The agency also said that based on complaints by the contacts in quarantine, the federal government was considering the payment of N100,000 per week. However, NCDC said that the welfare arrangement was in the interim, as states were expected to take over maintenance of the contacts cases in their domain subsequently. “The medivac plane is already at the airport waiting to evacuate her,” the source said, adding that the federal government was expected to announce the development after the patient had departed Nigeria. The proposed evacuation is coming amid heightened surveillance and contact-tracing efforts by Nigerian health authorities to prevent further transmission of the disease. Earlier, the Director General of the NCDC, Dr. Jide Idris, spoke at a press briefing in Abuja to provide an update on Nigeria’s Ebola disease response. Idris said the search for other secondary contacts was ongoing, assuring Nigerians that the federal government through Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, NCDC, FCT health authorities and partners was fully committed to containing the outbreak. “As previously announced, Nigeria has confirmed one case of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus. The patient is currently receiving medical care under isolation, with infection prevention and control measures in place. Clinical teams continue to monitor and manage patient’s condition,” he said. According to him, the 53 primary contacts comprise 44 personnel from the hospital where the index case is receiving treatment, while nine additional contacts from the index, three from Julius Berger office where she visited before coming down with symptoms, and three health workers who attended to index case. He said samples collected from the husband of the index case tested negative, adding that two suspected cases in FCT and Rivers also tested negative, but will have more follow up. Responding to a question about the true identity of the index case, the DG said she is from Uganda and married to a Swiss national, and the government is carrying out further investigations to establish her exact travel details. He said Nigerian officials will meet with Ugandan officials online to exchange information. Idris explained that the case was detected through event-based surveillance after vigilant healthcare workers recognised clinical features that raised concern. He said the response was being implemented through a structured Incident Management System coordinated by the Emergency Operations Centre under the leadership of the Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Prof. Ali Pate, and Presidential Task Force on EVD. Idris listed critical components as identifying and monitoring contacts for 21 days, ensuring safe clinical care, strengthening infection prevention and control across facilities, boosting surveillance and laboratory capacity, and community engagement. The DG said the centre is being assisted by the Department of State Services (DSS) in tracking contacts, has expanded case definition for community surveillance, and is boosting genomic capabilities of 12 laboratories to test for Ebola. He said the government has designated the University of Abuja Teaching Hospital as a special isolation centre and has fumigated premises of the index case. On the welfare of contacts, Idris said the federal government was considering the payment of N100,000 per week for feeding and upkeep of each quarantined contact, while states are expected to take responsibility for contacts in their domain. He appealed to Nigerians to cooperate with contact tracing teams, provide accurate information and adhere to public health advisories. “An identified contact does not mean you have Ebola. It means public health teams need to assess and monitor your health,” he said, urging hand hygiene, avoiding contact with blood or body fluids of suspected cases and prompt reporting. Idris commended healthcare workers whose vigilance led to detection and called on all public and private facilities to strengthen screening, triage and availability of personal protective equipment. He recalled leading Lagos State response in 2014 as Commissioner for Health, saying experience taught lessons on leadership, coordination and public trust which are being deployed. He warned against misinformation and stigmatisation, urging reliance on verified information from NCDC and Federal Ministry of Health. “The government has worked hard to strengthen the surveillance system and boost capacities of disease testing laboratories. Success depends on the whole of society,” he said, noting that the patient is improving. Meanwhile, to find solutions to major healthcare challenges facing West Africa, issues such as brain drain, infrastructure deficit and Ebola threat will be among key issues for deliberation as West African College of Physicians (WACP) marks 50 years anniversary with a summit in Abuja beginning on Monday. The body had earlier visited President Bola Tinubu at State House Presidential Villa in Abuja where the president urged them to help find solutions to some of the daunting healthcare challenges facing the region. Speaking at a press conference on Saturday, President of WACP, Dr. Mamadou Mourtalla, said the College will appraise developments in the health sector as it relates to new scientific discoveries, manpower training, infrastructure and infectious disease control. “We’ll be discussing various perspectives, how to deal with the pandemic, an epidemic coming up in Africa which puts a lot of stress on our health system. We have over 70 scientific papers based on this theme. At the end, we usually issue a communique,” Mourtalla said. He said implementation of resolutions is key, adding that the President of ECOWAS Commission, Director General of West African Health Organisation and President Tinubu who promised to send the Minister of Health will be present to make recommendations to leaders. Assistant Secretary General of WACP, Dr. Habibu Galadanci, said the conference has scheduled deliberations on several key areas including brain drain, infrastructure deficit, rise in non-communicable diseases like kidney disease, hypertension, and infectious disease epidemics including current spread of Ebola. “The scientific content will touch on several aspects of medicine, including disease conditions, health policies and contemporary medical issues,” he said. On brain drain, he said the conference has a whole session that will look at push and pull dynamics. “There are pull dynamics, push dynamics, and we are going to look at that and find solutions. When we saw President Tinubu, that was one main thing he charged us with, that we should discuss Japa syndrome and find solutions,” Galadanci said. He said the conference will also look at use of artificial intelligence in medicine and ethical concerns in managing patients, maternal and reproductive health, access to safe healthcare for women and children, mental health priorities and development of balanced scorecards for improving performance of public sector hospitals. Galadanci said the conference will be a landmark event that offers opportunity for stakeholders to pause and look at where College has come from in 50 years, achievements and pending issues. “We still have a lot of problems, but we have come a long way, at least we can train our doctors. We have specialists, so many doctors that they poach them from outside because of how good we are,” he said. Other areas include kidney disease epidemic, dementia which is creeping into society as population ages, and mental health often stigmatised and downplayed. As part of its corporate social responsibility, members of College organised a medical outreach programme in Waru community, a suburb in Federal Capital Territory (FCT) Abuja on Saturday, attracting a large crowd of men, women and children who benefited from free healthcare services. The week-long summit in Abuja is expected to bring over 1,300 experts from across West Africa to propose solutions for the next 50 years.

title: FirstHoldCo Reports N911bn Profit Before Tax in 9 Months 2026; Reinforcing Profitability and Resilience
body: First HoldCo Plc’s 9 months 2026 performance marks an important transition: the Group is moving from balance sheet repair toward a more resilient, capital-supported growth phase. The headline is compelling — profit before tax rose 60.8% year on year to N911.2 billion, while profit after tax advanced 65.1% to N744.5 billion; importantly, the quality of this growth is also improving. First, earnings have broadened year on year and beyond the traditional interest income. Second, operating discipline has improved efficiency. Third, stronger capital and better asset-quality indicators are increasing the Group’s capacity to absorb risk and pursue selective growth. These factors support a more durable earnings profile and a stronger long-term shareholder proposition. Profitability continues to strengthen Gross earnings increased 8.8% to N2.87 trillion, but profitability expanded faster: profit before tax reached N911.2 billion and profit after tax reached N744.5 billion. Post-tax return on average equity improved to 27.7% from 24.7% in the previous year, while return on average assets rose to 3.3% from 2.6% in 9M 2025 showing that balance sheet growth is generating stronger returns. This growth was supported by a more diversified revenue mix. Non-interest income surged 143.5% to N722.9 billion, supported by a 48.1% increase in net fee and commission income to N316.4 billion. Transaction-led revenues, including electronic banking, funds transfers and credit-related services and other non-interest income contributions are giving the Group more diversified avenues for earnings growth. Operating leverage is becoming visible Operating income rose 10.3% even as operating expenses declined 8.1% to N866.6 billion. The resulting cost-to-income ratio of 43.7%, down from 52.4%, is a strong indicator of improving operating leverage and cost discipline particularly in a 15.39% inflationary environment. The result suggests that management is not relying on balance-sheet expansion alone; it is extracting more value from the franchise while containing the cost base. Core margins present a compelling earnings-upside opportunity. Although net interest income moderated by 16.0% to N1.26 trillion and net interest margin adjusted to 8.7% from 11.3% amid softer asset yields, the improvement in cost of funds to 4.5% from 4.9% demonstrates effective funding discipline and provides a strong foundation for margin recovery. Enhanced risk-adjusted pricing and a more efficient funding mix offer credible levers for margin expansion and sustainable returns, while maintaining rigorous credit standards and asset quality. A balance sheet with greater strategic capacity The balance sheet provides greater capacity for disciplined growth. Total assets increased 18.1% from year-end 2025 to N32.20 trillion, while customer deposits grew 21.3% to N22.91 trillion. Group equity rose 17.0% to N3.86 trillion. In contrast, net customer loans expanded by a deliberate and measured 4.8% to N9.39 trillion. This combination of strong funding growth, firmer equity and selective lending reflects disciplined capital deployment rather than indiscriminate risk-taking. FirstBank’s capital adequacy ratio improved to 18.6% at September 2026 from 16.7% at half-year. The stronger capital buffer increases resilience supports regulatory confidence and provides greater flexibility to finance attractive opportunities. Importantly, capital is strengthening while profitability is accelerating, improving the Group’s capacity to compound value internally. Asset-quality repair is gaining traction Asset-quality repair is also advancing. The Group’s non-performing loan ratio declined to 10.4% from 13.9% at H1 2026 while NPL coverage, including regulatory reserves, increased to 98.8%. Impairment charges declined 28.3% to N207.1 billion and recoveries reached N94.3 billion. These figures show broad-based progress: stronger coverage, reduced impairment charges and meaningful recoveries to date. Although the NPL ratio remains above management’s desired level, the downward trajectory improves protection and loss-absorption capacity. To further strengthen asset quality by year-end, management could combine targeted restructuring of viable exposures, negotiated settlements and intensified recoveries with ongoing legal actions. These asset-quality measures are supported by more than N850 billion already held in regulatory risk reserves, providing a substantial prudential buffer against identified credit risks. Accordingly, subject to applicable accounting and regulatory treatment, additional impairment charges recognised in the books would be broadly capital-neutral, enabling management to accelerate the resolution or write-off of fully provided loans with limited recovery prospects without materially weakening regulatory capital, while recovery efforts continue. These measures should further reduce the NPL ratio, reinforce coverage and underscore the strength of the balance sheet. Diversification strengthens the earnings growth outlook Commercial Banking remains the Group’s principal earnings subsidiary, generating gross earnings of N2.70 trillion and profit before tax of N784.7 billion. Its scale, deposit franchise and broad customer relationships underpin recurring revenue. Alongside this core franchise, Investment Banking and Asset Management is becoming more significant. The segment generated gross earnings of N120.1 billion, up 85.5%, and profit before tax of N85.7 billion, up 133.6%. This high-growth, capital-light platform broadens the Group’s exposure to advisory, asset management, trusteeship, brokerage and securities activities, reducing reliance on traditional banking spreads. Why the investment case is strengthening FirstHoldCo’s investment case is increasingly persuasive because improvement is visible across several reinforcing dimensions: faster earnings growth, better operating efficiency, expanding transaction-led revenues, stronger capital, disciplined loan growth and an improving asset quality position. These are not isolated gains; they describe a franchise becoming more resilient and better positioned to convert scale into sustainable returns. The Group is well positioned to unlock the next phase of value creation by building on its current momentum. Continued progress toward a single-digit NPL ratio, sustained coverage, recovery in net interest margin, disciplined deployment of deposits, and greater fee income contribution provide clear pathways to stronger, more resilient earnings. Consistent execution should improve earnings quality and deepen market confidence. Enhanced dividend policy reinforces the shareholder-value proposition The market is already recognising this stronger proposition: as of 23 October 2026, FirstHoldCo’s 200.84% year-to-date share-price gain had delivered the highest total shareholder return in 2026 among its banking peers, signaling strong investor confidence in the Group’s earnings momentum and outlook. Reinforcing these market gains, FirstHoldCo earlier this year reaffirmed its commitment to shareholder returns through an enhanced dividend policy. Under the policy, the Board approved a minimum annual distribution of 60% of profit after tax, commencing with the 2027 accounts. The policy gives shareholders a clearer route to participate in earnings growth and signals confidence in the Group’s profitability, capital and cash-generation. The timing is strategically important. Beginning with the 2027 accounts allows FirstHoldCo to consolidate capital strength, further improve asset-quality and fund disciplined growth before the higher payout takes effect. Subject to distributable reserves, regulatory approvals and prevailing financial conditions, the policy offers a credible path to stronger shareholder returns. Outlook: Disciplined growth with meaningful optionality FirstHoldCo enters the final quarter of 2026 with a stronger balance sheet, improving credit metrics and enhanced operating leverage. Its N22.91 trillion deposit base provides substantial funding capacity, while the improved capital position creates room for selective expansion. Targeted investment in technology, innovation and customer experience can deepen transaction volumes and strengthen the durability of non-interest revenue. The investment story therefore extends beyond stronger earnings. Capital strength, franchise depth, cost discipline and diversified capabilities make performance more sustainable. Margin pressure and the remaining NPL stock still require attention, but each also presents a defined opportunity for improvement. Overall, the 9Months 2026 results show a Group regaining strategic flexibility and converting reform into measurable progress. Continued improvement in asset quality, margin recovery and disciplined capital allocation provide a credible path to resilient earnings and durable long-term value

title: Gazans want Netanyahu gone but expect no 'new beginning' from Knesset vote
body: Gazans are watching the final days of Israel's election campaign with a mixture of anger, exhaustion and deep scepticism, hoping Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will lose power but doubting a new leader would bring meaningful change. Defeat for Mr Netanyahu would offer a measure of emotional relief after years of bombing and destruction ordered by the Israeli Prime Minister. Yet the prospect of a new government elicits little optimism among Palestinians who have lost their homes, families and jobs and believe Gaza 's plight extends far deeper. Their concerns are more immediate: finding permanent shelter, securing food and water, restoring schools and hospitals, and rebuilding the economy, the collapse of which has left civilians dependent on humanitarian aid. “It makes no difference to us in Gaza who wins or loses the Israeli elections,” said Munir Isleem, 35, whose home in Gaza city's Shujaiya neighbourhood was destroyed in the war. “What matters to us is escaping this life of tents and humiliation, and putting an end to the hunger and poverty that the war has forced upon us,” he told The National . Mr Isleem, who has spent the past two years moving between displacement camps with his family, still hopes Mr Netanyahu will lose. “The war Netanyahu launched against us didn’t just take away our homes. It robbed us of our happiness, our dearest friends and the people closest to us,” he said. Before the war, Mr Isleem worked as a skilled machine operator at a plastic factory, earning about $1,000 a month – enough to provide for his family. Now, unemployed and displaced, he relies on aid to survive. The war “transformed us from productive people who worked and earned a living into unemployed people waiting for food from charity kitchens, humanitarian aid and our turn in the water queues”, he said. Political reality Mr Netanyahu faces a tough fight for re-election, with an array of challengers led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, and amid division within his governing coalition. While his handling of wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, and the October 7 Hamas attacks in 2023, has been criticised by rivals, few of them support Palestinian statehood or favour a radically different approach in military matters. Palestinian political analyst Mustafa Ibrahim said the election should not be seen as a referendum on Palestinian rights or Gaza’s future. “I don’t believe the situation will change significantly whether Netanyahu wins or loses, because Israeli policy towards Gaza has reminded largely consistent under successive governments throughout history,” he said. He added that the positions taken by Mr Netanyahu and Mr Eisenkot amounted to different ways of achieving Israeli security objectives, rather than any fundamental difference in policy towards Palestinians. “Ultimately the political approach and objectives remain the same, regardless of the individuals of governments in power,” he said. Like Mr Isleem, he said Palestinians in Gaza still want Mr Netanyahu to lose because they hold him primarily responsible for what they see as the genocide against them. However, this does not necessarily translate into support for other candidates. Years of disappointment For Ahmed Sammour, 61, a former Arabic teacher from Gaza city’s Sheikh Radwan neighbourhood, scepticism about Israeli elections has been shaped by decades of experience. Mr Sammour has lived under more than 10 Israeli governments and remembers periods of conflict and negotiations. But none of them offered lasting security or freedom to Gaza. “All of them have followed the same approach towards us as Palestinians,” he said. He recalled the Oslo Accords , signed by Israeli leader Yitzhak Rabin in the 1990s, as a moment when negotiations appeared to offer a different path. But Mr Rabin was assassinated in 1995 by an Israeli extremist opposed to the peace process, and the optimism of that period failed to last. Today, Mr Sammour lives with his family in a camp near his destroyed home. He holds Mr Netanyahu responsible for the devastation. Even if someone with better polices towards Gaza wins and begins rebuilding the territory, it will still take years Amal Al Hinnawi “The collapse of Netanyahu’s government and his defeat in the elections would certainly not represent a new beginning or a source of hope for us,” he said. “But at least we would be rid of a leader whom we hold responsible for killing children and innocent civilians.” Mr Sammour said Mr Netanyahu's government had inflicted destruction on a scale unlike anything he witnessed under previous Israeli administrations. Even so, he is reluctant to place his hopes in a successor. “Whoever comes after him will not necessary be any better,” he said. Amal Al Hinnawi, 25, a teacher at a tent school in northern Gaza, believes the scale of the destruction has made the results of Israel’s election secondary to the enormous task of rebuilding. Ms Al Hinnawi sees the consequences of the war for the education system, where makeshift classrooms have replaced conventional school buildings and children struggle to continue learning amid displacement and instability. “Israeli elections no longer matter much to us in Gaza because it will take decades for our lives to return to what they were before the war,” she said. “Even if someone with better polices towards Gaza wins and begins rebuilding the territory, it will still take years because the scale of destruction across every sector is beyond description.”

title: Northern Region NDC urges unity after internal polls, eyes 2028 victory
body: The Northern Regional Secretariat of the National Democratic Congress (NDC) has urged newly elected officers and unsuccessful candidates to close ranks after the party’s branch and constituency elections across the region. In a statement signed by Regional Secretary King Salam, the Secretariat congratulated the elected officers and urged them to lead with humility, fairness and a commitment to unity. “Your election is a clear expression of the confidence party members have placed in you. We urge you to lead with humility and fairness, and to serve as a unifying force for every member in your area,” the statement said. The Secretariat also commended unsuccessful candidates, saying their participation had contributed to the party’s democratic tradition. “The outcome of an election does not diminish your worth or your place in the NDC family,” it said. “The party still needs your experience, energy and commitment, and we count on you to remain active in its work.” The statement thanked delegates, supporters and party members for their peaceful participation, describing it as a demonstration of discipline and commitment to internal democracy. It urged members to put electoral differences behind them and focus on strengthening the party. “Competition was for a season; collaboration must now define our path forward. We call on all winners and losers, together with their supporters, to close ranks and build stronger bonds of unity,” the statement said. “There are no factions in the NDC. There is only one family with one goal.” The Secretariat said the priority was to consolidate the party’s gains, strengthen its structures and work towards victory in the 2028 general elections.

title: Vucic Concedes Defeat as Student List Wins Serbia Vote
body: Aleksandar Vucic acknowledged his party’s loss in Sunday’s early parliamentary elections, with the Student List emerging as the winner according to initial estimates. Vucic Concedes Defeat as Student List Wins Serbia Vote “It is clear that we lost these elections. The Student List won,” Vucic said. He projected the Student List would take 135–140 seats, enough for a majority, while his party would secure around 105. Final results are still pending. The vote followed nearly two years of student protests against corruption, triggered by the 2024 Novi Sad station collapse that killed 16. Vucic had resigned as president in September to seek the premiership, but the projected Student List majority blocks that plan. Presidential elections must be held by the end of December; Vucic cannot run for a third term. title: Investors Rush for Dangote Refinery Shares as Offer Closes on 27 October
body: Peter Uzoho Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals has reported a sharp increase in investor subscriptions as its landmark Initial Public Offering (IPO) enters its final days, with retail and institutional investors accelerating participation ahead of the closing date of October 27. The company confirmed, in a statement yesterday, that the IPO will close on Tuesday, October 27, as scheduled. The company said, “This is the final deadline, and no further extension will be granted. Investors wishing to participate must complete their subscriptions before the offer closes.” The surge in demand follows the refinery’s recently released nine-month financial results, which showed exceptional growth in revenue, profitability, and cash generation, reinforcing investor confidence in the company’s long-term prospects. Dangote Refinery reported revenue of $22.5 billion and net profit of $4.73 billion for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, representing a significant turnaround from a loss recorded in the corresponding period of 2025. Revenue increased by 144 per cent year-on-year, while Earnings, Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortisation (EBITDA) rose to $5.5 billion, reflecting higher refining throughput, improved operational reliability and stronger refining margins. The company also strengthened its balance sheet, moving from a net debt position to a net cash position during the period. It said the strong financial performance, combined with the refinery’s strategic importance to Africa’s energy security and industrial development, has continued to attract broad-based interest from individual investors, pension funds, institutional investors, asset managers, professionals, business owners and members of the African diaspora. The statement said, “The level of investor interest we are seeing reflects growing confidence in our business and in the strong financial results we have delivered. “Investors are recognising both the quality of our earnings and the long-term value creation opportunity represented by the refinery.” According to the refinery, the IPO has become more than a capital-raising exercise, evolving into an opportunity for Africans and international investors to participate directly in the ownership of one of the continent’s most significant industrial enterprises. It stated that subscriptions had been received from across Nigeria, other African countries and international markets, underscoring the refinery’s growing reputation as a world-class industrial asset. The company stated, “Investors recognise that this refinery is not merely an energy asset. It is a platform for industrial growth, foreign-exchange generation, regional trade, energy security and economic development across Africa. “The strong response to the offer reflects confidence in the future of African industry and in our ability to continue generating sustainable returns for shareholders.” The company also reiterated its commitment to broad-based ownership, emphasising that the IPO has been structured to ensure that ordinary investors can participate alongside institutional investors in the refinery’s future growth. It advised prospective investors who had not yet completed their subscriptions to do so immediately through their stockbrokers and approved distribution channels before the deadline. It stated, “This is the final opportunity for investors to participate in this historic offer. “We encourage all interested investors to complete their applications before the subscription window closes on 27 October.” Dangote refinery expressed appreciation to regulators, issuing houses, stockbrokers, financial institutions, fintech partners, investor associations, market operators, and the investing public for their support throughout the offer period. The company added that the strong demand recorded so far demonstrated growing investor confidence in African-owned industrial enterprises and highlighted the increasing capacity of African capital markets to support large-scale transformational investments. The statement said, “History is being made. The remarkable investor response is a powerful vote of confidence in Africa’s future, in African enterprise, and in the long-term value that world-class industrial projects can create when opened to public ownership. We remain committed to delivering sustained growth and enduring value for all shareholders.”

title: Iran to hold security talks with Saudi, Pakistan, Turkiye
body:
Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan will hold talks on regional security with Iranian officials on Monday in Tehran, Iranian and Saudi authorities said. The meeting follows eight months of war in the Middle East and recent US and Israeli threats of renewed attacks against Iran. "As agreed, Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief General Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin will participate in this meeting," said Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council. In an interview with state television, Kani said the meeting will also include Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei. Saudi Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy Dr Rayed Krimly confirmed that the kingdom's defence minister was heading a delegation to Tehran on Monday. "The visit comes as part of the continued efforts by the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement countries for de-escalation between parties involved in the ongoing crisis," Krimly said in a post on X. It is aimed at "promoting dialogue and diplomatic solutions, in support of the mediation efforts carried out by the State of Qatar and the Islamic Republic of Pakistan", he added. War has engulfed the Middle East since late February when the United States and Israel launched a wave of surprise attacks on Iran, just as Washington and Tehran were in the middle of negotiations on Iran's nuclear programme. An April ceasefire brought an end to the initial phase of intense bombardment but the two sides have continued to vie for control of the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to travel. Iran claims control over the strait and regularly targets vessels that attempt to cross without its authorisation, while the United States has imposed a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports. Diplomatic efforts to resolve the crisis remain stalled, especially since the collapse of a June deal which laid out a pathway to a permanent settlement. The war has since spread across the region to include fighting between Saudi Arabia and Ansar Allah in Yemen.

title: Lula Stages Historic Comeback to Beat Flávio Bolsonaro in Brazil’s Presidential Poll
body: Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the Brazilian president, has staged a dramatic election fightback, defeating his far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, to claim a historic fourth term in power. With nearly 99 per cent of votes counted this morning, the 80-year-old leftist received 51.75 per cent of the vote to his 45-year-old rival’s 48.25 per cent. Lula narrowly lost the first round of the election to Bolsonaro in early October, casting his political future into doubt and plunging progressive Brazilians into three weeks of despair. Never, since the return of democracy in the 1980s, has the first round runner-up won the second vote, the Guardian UK reported. But Lula did precisely that on Sunday, prompting joyous scenes on the streets of São Paulo, where he had been following the count, and at the hotel where he was watching the count. As the result was confirmed, Reginaldo Lopes, a key Lula ally, told the Guardian: “I feel incredible … This is Brazil telling the world that the extreme right is fascist, that the extreme right is against black people, is against the poor, against the state, against gay people … We are going to reorganise the democratic forces (in this country).” The incumbent, who had lost by 2.2 million votes three weeks ago, has now won by 4.3 million. The 81-year-old leftist appears to have made up much of the difference through what his allies had identified as his main opportunity: persuading his voters to turn out. After a record abstention rate of 21.08 per cent in the first round, which disproportionately affected Lula voters because they tend to live farther from polling stations, the rate fell to 19.21 per cent. For Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, the victory represents a sensational final chapter in a storied political career that began when he emerged as a union leader in São Paulo’s industrial suburbs in the late 1970s, the Guardian UK report added. After entering politics, the former factory worker who was born in rural poverty made three unsuccessful presidential bids, in 1989, 1994 and 1998, before finally becoming Brazil’s first elected working-class president in 2002. Lula stepped down after the maximum two consecutive terms allowed by the constitution but returned to power after winning the 2022 election against Bolsonaro’s father, then the incumbent president Jair Bolsonaro, who was subsequently jailed for plotting a coup. Lula’s win is bad news for Bolsonaro who is serving a 27-year sentence for that botched power grab and was hoping to be freed and given a role in government had his son prevailed. It is also a blow for Donald Trump, the Bolsonaro clan’s most important international ally. The US president had been hoping Bolsonaro would become the latest in a series of pro-Trump leaders to take power in Latin America, including Abelardo de la Espriella in Colombia, Daniel Noboa in Ecuador, José Antonio Kast in Chile and Javier Milei in Argentina. Confirmation of Lula’s victory was greeted with anger and bewilderment in Brasília, where Bolsonaro is living under house arrest and where his son watched the count. Lula’s victory came after his supporters staged two massive shows of support on Saturday, with more than a million people flocking to Rio’s Copacabana beach and an even larger number marching on Paulista Avenue at the heart of São Paulo.

title: Kane primed to beat Yamal, Mbappe to Ballon d’Or glory
body: England captain Harry Kane is the favourite to win a wide open race to be crowned Ballon d’Or winner at a glitzy London ceremony on Monday, with Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappe also in the running to be named the world’s best footballer. Read Also: 2026 Ballon d’or ceremony: date, time and how to watch The 70th edition of the award, established by the magazine France Football, will be hosted in England for the first time in recognition of the first winner Stanley Matthews and fittingly could have a first English winner for 25 years. Bayern Munich striker Kane struck a remarkable 73 goals in 65 games for club and country last season, leading the German giants to a league and cup double and England to the semi-finals of the World Cup. “I’d love to be able to achieve something like that. I would be a massive milestone in my career,” said the 33-year-old. But semi-final exits in both the Champions League and World Cup for Kane means the outcome is far from certain. “I think my wife would prefer to know and my family … it’s very stressful for everyone,” he added. “I can see why they don’t tell people. They want everyone to go, all the big names, and there will be more people watching it if they don’t know.” ‘I deserve it’ Yamal finished second to Paris Saint-Germain’s Ousmane Dembele last year and the 19-year-old Barcelona superstar seems destined to be a Ballon d’Or winner one day. However, after a hamstring injury ended his club season early, he was far from the shining light of Spain’s World Cup triumph that was built on being the best collective unit. Yamal was pipped to both the player and young player of the tournament by his Barcelona team-mates Rodri and Pau Cubarsi. That has not diminished his bullish confidence ahead of the ceremony. “For me, Mbappe and me, we’re the two best players in the world,” Yamal said last month. “I honestly think that, as the best in the world, maybe there are two of us, and this year I would deserve it because of what I’ve won.” Mbappe, by contrast, boasts plenty of personal milestones without medals for either Real Madrid or France. The 27-year-old was top goalscorer in La Liga, the Champions League and the World Cup without winning any of those trophies. His 10 World Cup goals made him the top goalscorer in the competition’s history on 22. “Being the all-time top scorer in World Cup history, overtaking all the great legends in the history of the sport in the most important tournament there is, is something that really stands out,” said Mbappe. “Who am I voting for? Myself.” One football journalist from each of the 100 top nations in FIFA’s rankings is invited to cast votes for their top 10 players from a 30-man shortlist, allocating a maximum of 15 points down to one based on their ranking. The Ballon d’Or goes to the player who accrued the most points. Although the award carries no cash prize, it can generate huge bonuses from clubs and commercial partners as well as increasing a player’s overall marketing value. Alexia Putellas is the frontrunner to win the women’s award for the third time with Aitana Bonmati’s three-year reign to come to an end after an injury-hit year. Putellas, winner in 2021 and 2022, was part of the Barcelona side that regained the Champions League last season before moving to London City Lionesses. Her former club team-mate, Poland’s Ewa Pajor is the main challenger to Putellas after she netted 11 Champions League goals in Barca’s latest triumph. title: Writing about pratt parsing so I remember it
body:
update: this post seemed to have been posted on a few link aggregator sites, spawned some discussion, and got bookmarked by people. that’s scary! that’s more attention than I anticipated for this post, especially since I wrote it mainly for myself to come back to as a reference without too much expectation on making it in a “teaching” style. as such, I put on my Due Diligence Hat and overhauled this post to make it more pleasant to read. the high-level outline of it is still the same, and it’s not some complete university-level polished writing, but the details are a bit smoother to follow now & I relate it more to pratt’s original paper. if you’re interested in the more unfiltered brain dump post, it’s available on the wayback machine or my website repository .
I got bored and decided to start making a C compiler. of course, one of the requirements of this is parsing C expressions 1 . my only experiences with “serious” parsing before this included:
I heard about this cool thing called “pratt parsing” before, but I never looked into it, so I wanted to try it out for this.
you won’t find much information about pratt parsing in a conventional learning path of computer science. the dragon book , for all it talks about parsing, doesn’t mention it. as far as I’m aware, most programming language courses will probably teach either LR or recursive descent depending on how academic it is. pratt parsing specifically appears to be relegated mostly to compiler development and PLT circles. the most mainstream description I know of it is in crafting interpreters , though wikipedia also mentions it with links to other posts.
I used the crafting interpreters text to get my bearings, but I also wanted to practice reading formal papers more, so I looked up Pratt’s original paper text and tried to exclusively use it as much as possible for implementing it. it did take a bit more time than I’d have liked to wrap my mind around the inner workings of the algorithm and convincing myself that it just works , but it did end up just clicking all at once.
interestingly, it clicked not when internalizing vaughan pratt’s own words, but rather when I noticed how pratt parsing related to the shunting yard algorithm. after that, I was able to understand the angle that vaughan pratt approached the algorithm, and now I see how wonderfully elegant it is :). this post will be organized in a similar manner: relating the shunting yard algorithm to pratt parsing, then seeing how pratt approached it and how it can be very cleanly implemented for really any kind of parsing.
the shunting yard algorithm , when boiled to its primitive form, is quite simple conceptually. there are two kinds of tokens: operators and literals. operators have “binding powers” associated with them—higher binding power means it gets evaluated “before” other operators. you have an input stream, output stream, and a stack for operators.
then, for every token in the input stream:

the primitive version of the algorithm has the following properties:
the first two problems are relatively easy to solve without much modification. split left and right binding powers for the first one, and attach some special handling of parentheses for the second. however, the third issue is slightly more difficult, along with a few other extensions that pose their own problems . it’s also pretty annoying to handle errors for shunting yard, as all stack unwinding is explicit and a lot of context gets lost from it. it’s a good start, and is certainly fine for many real-world things, but I wouldn’t quite consider it robust. so how does it generalize to pratt parsing?
the first insight to understanding pratt parsing is forming a different classification of tokens. instead of “literals” and “operators” from before, there are:
with this, one immediate observation is that any possible expression must begin with a nud . you can’t begin an expression with a token that expects something to its left, as there is no left!
next, the stack. handling operator precedence requires a stack of some kind. in shunting yard, it was explicit. for pratt parsing, the stack is implicit in nature; it’s the call stack!
this sounds handwave-y, but more specifically, moving back to the land of simple arithmetic: every time a number (nud) is consumed, some infix operator (led) or the end of the expression must follow. these infix operators expect an expression of their own on the right side of them. for those operators, we just call the “parse an expression” function again! that recursive call is equivalent to pushing to the stack in the shunting yard algorithm. we provide the recursive call with the binding power of the operator. once the call returns, that’s equivalent to “popping” said operator off the stack in shunting yard. the stack still exists; it’s just implicit now.
putting all this together, if we were to semantically, one-to-one, translate the shunting yard code from before to a pratt-style parser, we would get:

these combined allow for simple & straightforward extensibility. before extending it, a few more observations:
so, refactoring with those in mind, and adding parentheses, we get:
from here, it’s pretty simple to see what can be done to change extend functionality. you get arbitrary pre-operator and post-operator code paths for every single “nud” or “led” possible. you have some arbitrary check for determining if one operator dominates another. you don’t even need to use “binding powers” ! it’s the same power of recursive descent, but both easier to hack on and doesn’t nest nearly as much! how wonderful!
most implementations provide a bit more unified abstraction, where tokens are organized into “rules” and looked up to get its nud function, led function, and various binding powers or properties all at once. this is described in crafting interpreters and an example in my snippets repo . my example is for the same arithmetic grammar with the inclusion of a factorial operator ( ! ).
hope this helps anyone else. happy parsing :)

title: Pipeline Security Claims Raise Bigger Questions
body: Tracing the Reform Dividend from Fiscal Savings to Public Spending, Social Protection and Measurable Results There is a legitimate national conversation to be had about the cost, structure, transparency and effectiveness of Nigeria’s pipeline surveillance architecture. There is also a legitimate argument about whether communities in the Niger Delta should derive greater economic value from the protection of the natural resources extracted from their environment. When that conversation is reduced to ethnic insinuations, unverified figures and an apparent attempt to justify one contractor by attacking another, the country risks losing sight of the bigger issue: energy security is a national security matter, not a tribal entitlement. That is where Asari Dokubo appears to have missed the point. In a video circulating this week, the Niger Delta activist questioned why Government Ekpemupolo, popularly known as Tompolo, has faced criticism over pipeline surveillance while, according to him, the Olu of Warri, Ogiame Atuwatse III, and Dr. Osahon Okunbo were receiving as much as N2.7 trillion annually for protecting pipelines. Dokubo initially referred to the amount as monthly before correcting himself to annual. Importantly, however, no documentary evidence was presented in the video to substantiate the N2.7 trillion figure, and reports carrying the allegation have expressly treated it as unverified. That distinction is not cosmetic. It is fundamental. A claim of N2.7 trillion annually for pipeline surveillance is so extraordinary, that it demands concrete documentary evidence. Contracts, procurement records, payment schedules, scope of work, contracting entities and government approvals would have to be placed before the public. Without such evidence, the figure remains an allegation – Not a fact. That is perhaps the first thing Dokubo missed. The mathematics of the allegation in public domain – Therein is another problem where Dokubo’s allegation appears to collapse different entities, individuals and contractual relationships into one giant financial arrangement. Osahon Okunbo is associated with Pipeline Infrastructure Nigeria Limited (PINL), where he has served in senior executive capacity. The Olu of Warri has also been publicly associated with PINL’s leadership structure. The relationship between a monarch, a company and a pipeline surveillance contract cannot simply be translated into a claim that the monarch personally receives the entire value of a corporate contract. Indeed, this is not a new controversy. In 2022, reporting on the pipeline surveillance arrangement specifically recorded a denial that the Olu of Warri personally owned PINL, while identifying PINL alongside Tantita Security Services Nigeria Limited and Maton Engineering Nigeria Limited among companies awarded pipeline surveillance contracts. More recent reporting identifies Osahon Okunbo as a key executive of PINL, with the company operating on critical pipeline infrastructure. The distinction matters because corporate contract value is not automatically personal income. What Dokubo Gets Right To be fair, there is a legitimate question beneath Dokubo’s provocative presentation. If several companies are receiving public money to protect critical national infrastructure, Nigerians are entitled to know how much each contractor receives, what kilometres of infrastructure each is responsible for, what performance indicators apply and what results have been achieved. That is a serious governance question – So too is Dokubo’s broader argument that the Niger Delta should benefit economically from the protection and development of its natural resources. That argument should lead to a conversation about transparent procurement, community participation, local employment, measurable security outcomes and accountability – Not ethnic arithmetic(s). Pipeline security cannot become a competition over whether an Ijaw, Itsekiri, Bini or any other Nigerian is entitled to a particular contract. Nigeria’s oil infrastructure belongs to Nigeria. The responsibility to protect it is therefore national priority – This is where Osahon Okunbo becomes relevant. Perhaps the greatest irony in Dokubo’s intervention is that he appears to have overlooked what the emerging pipeline-security model represented by PINL is actually trying to do. Okunbo has publicly argued that sustainable infrastructure security cannot depend on force alone. At the World Economic Forum in Davos, he emphasised inclusion, community engagement and indigenous partnerships as critical to securing energy infrastructure. He has also spoken about the importance of patient capital and community buy-in to Nigeria’s energy future. In a public account of PINL’s operations, Okunbo described an approach built around traditional institutions, youths, local leadership, surveillance technology and continuous stakeholder engagement. That is a materially different proposition from simply putting men on boats and around pipelines. Modern energy security involves intelligence, technology, community relations, rapid response, environmental protection, infrastructure maintenance and the creation of incentives for communities to protect – Not destroy the assets around them. Indeed, host-community groups have publicly credited PINL’s engagement model with improved pipeline security and community relations, although such claims should themselves be assessed against independently verifiable production and security data. The Tompolo question is legitimate to an extent, but the comparison is wrong. Tantita’s role in pipeline surveillance is itself an important part of Nigeria’s evolving security architecture. Reports have put the company’s annual contract value at about N48 billion, following a federal government award reported in 2023. The appropriate question, therefore, is not whether Tompolo deserves a contract, while somebody else does not. The appropriate question is whether every contractor is delivering value commensurate with public expenditure. That standard should apply equally to Tantita, PINL and every other contractor. If Dokubo believes the Federal Government is paying too much for pipeline security, let the contracts be published. If he believes one company is receiving preferential treatment, let procurement records establish it. If he believes Niger Delta communities are being short-changed, let the data demonstrate it. If he believes there is corruption, the appropriate institutions can investigate, but once the argument moves from evidence to ethnicity, the substance begins to disappear. Energy security is bigger than Dokubo’s quarrel, as Nigeria has spent decades paying the price for oil theft, pipeline vandalism, illegal refining and production disruptions. Every barrel prevented from reaching the market affects government revenue, foreign exchange, investment confidence and the capacity of the country to finance development. Pipeline security is therefore not merely about who gets a contract. It is about whether Nigeria can secure the infrastructure through which its economic lifeblood flows. That is the point Asari Dokubo appears to have missed. His intervention could have opened a valuable national debate about procurement transparency and the economics of Niger Delta security. Instead, by advancing an extraordinary N2.7 trillion allegation without documentary proof and framing the matter partly through ethnic identity, he risks turning a serious national-security conversation into another quarrel over who owns the Niger Delta. Nigeria needs more accountability, not more suspicion; more evidence, not more allegations; more collaboration, not more ethnic polarisation. The pipelines do not know the ethnicity of the men protecting them. In a nutshell, the Nigerian economy does not either need such distraction(s) – What matters is whether the infrastructure is secure, whether oil production is protected, whether communities benefit, whether public money is properly spent and whether every contractor, regardless of name or origin, can account for the value delivered. That is the conversation worth having and that is precisely why energy security should never be twisted on its head. •Ayoola Ajanaku is a Communications and Advocacy Specialist based in Lagos, Nigeria

title: Trump: Libya Must End Illegal Migration Corridor Amid Turkey EEZ Dispute
body: President Trump said Libya “cannot remain a corridor for illegal migration, and this must end now.” He praised Libyans as a counterterrorism partner, citing their joint defeat of ISIS and honoring “sacrifices that brave Libyans made.” Trump said the U.S. backs unifying Libya and its institutions and supports a path to national elections. He noted Libyans have been “victims of terrorism and foreign meddling for years” and urged them to “unite, take back their sovereignty.” The remarks come amid ongoing disputes over Libya’s illegal EEZ agreement with Turkey, which ignores neighboring states’ maritime rights and has been rejected by Greece, Egypt, and others.
