title: U/W Regional Chief Imam’s education fund supports 61 students with GH¢138,536
body: The Upper West Regional Chief Imam Educational Endowment Fund has disbursed GH¢138,536 to support 61 academically promising but financially disadvantaged students pursuing tertiary education nationwide. The support covers the 2026/27 academic year. The number of beneficiaries has risen from 44 in the previous academic year to 61, an increase of 38.64%. The Secretary to the Fund, Dr Saeed Moomin, announced the disbursement at a press conference at the forecourt of the Regional Chief Imam’s residence in Wa. He said the Chief Imam’s office continued to receive numerous requests for educational assistance, reflecting the financial difficulties facing families in the region. Established in October 2022, the fund selects beneficiaries through academic assessments, interviews to establish financial need and home verification visits. For some beneficiaries, the assistance has made the difference between continuing their education and putting it on hold. Ibrahim Salim, a Level 400 Political Science student at UBIDS, said financial difficulties had nearly forced him to defer his programme. “Due to this wonderful programme, wonderful foundation, I am able, let me say, in a few months to come, I will be calling myself a graduate,” he said. Amatus Ahmed, a Diploma in Business Studies student at UBIDS, said the initiative offered an important lifeline to young people from rural communities who struggle to secure financial assistance. Ayisha Yahaya, a Level 300 Basic Education student at Nusrat Jahan Ahmadiyya College of Education, also expressed gratitude for the continued support that had helped her progress through her studies. Stakeholders at the event urged beneficiaries to make good use of the assistance and contribute to the fund when they were able to do so. Former Wa Municipal Chief Executive, Tahiru Issahaku Moomin, called for unity in tackling poverty, describing it as a “common enemy” holding back the region’s development. “We have a bridge to cross, and that bridge… is the bridge to cross to success and prosperity,” he said. The Headmaster of Wa Senior High School, Adams Iddrisu Thirdman, cautioned students against diverting the money to other purposes. He encouraged them to excel academically and help sustain the initiative for future beneficiaries. The President of the Upper West Bar Association, Siddique Obeidu, commended the fund for investing in the region’s human capital. He said expanding educational opportunities for vulnerable young people could help reduce their risk of turning to armed robbery or drug abuse. Mr Obeidu added that the fund provided a dependable platform for citizens to support education and contribute to the region’s development.

title: [Newspoint] Duterte’s Frankenstein monster
body: Lest we lose perspective in our preoccupation with Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial , she is the anointed political heir of the man who brought untold horrors upon us when he was president — her own father. And as though in too much hurry to prove herself deserving of the anointment, and with a sense of impunity that runs in the family, she got herself impeached even before she could go halfway through her term as vice president, the very first national office she has held. And impeachment being a dicey thing, wait till she is acquitted, thus retained in office and re-certified eligible to go for the heights of notoriety achieved by her father — or higher. Her prosecutors appear confident, however, that she will be stopped. They have decided to pursue only one of the articles of impeachment and drop the other three. They made that decision after their final witness, a financial forensicist, had lent a strong close to their case on that one article — unexplained wealth. If they get her on that, she is removed automatically as vice president and barred from holding public office ever again. But then again, in a court where senators, instead of professional judges, sit, politics is always a factor, making acquittal a realistic prospect regardless of the quality of the evidence. And how is this for political weight? Sara Duterte is polling the best numbers for the presidential vote in 2028. I confess I don’t quite get it myself, knowing that we need only look back on her father’s time to see what we’re in for if she does win. Rodrigo Duterte ’s presidency (2016-2022) was notorious across the board, but, for our purpose here — a quick, immediately relevant review of his treasonous , murderous , and corrupt regime — I have selected only a few cases, although cases sharply emblematic by themselves. Our first case is his war on drugs, which took tens of thousands of lives by extrajudicial means and for which he was flown to The Hague, the Netherlands, to face trial before the International Criminal Court for “crimes against humanity.” That war was generally explained away as Duterte’s own sick “final solution,” but it is turning out to be sicker than that. Duterte may have had Hitler’s deeply unprincipled conviction, but, apparently, he was all business too. Old and mostly hearsay allegations that his war was actually a coverup for his family’s own connection to the drug trade are gaining credence. Bank accounts held jointly by Rodrigo and Sara and submitted in evidence at the impeachment hearings have revealed payments from a drug-trafficking suspect . The second case tends to show another unholy connection. Congressional and judicial investigations into the biggest corruption conspiracy in our history have also led to the Dutertes. The conspiracy involves over a trillion pesos in taxpayer money budgeted for flood control. Most of that money has been traced to the accounts of public officials as kickbacks and to those of private contractors as fees collected doing nothing or, at best, for doing token work. The investigations have shown that the most audacious among the contractors — the couple Curlee and Sarah Descaya — had their start in Davao City, the Dutertes’ dynastic preserve, and that they also began to flourish there. The investigations have further shown that Rodrigo Duterte’s son Paolo received a generous PhP51-billion outlay for flood control for his district as its representative in Congress. Both the rise of the Descayas and the rain of fortune on Paolo Duterte came during his father’s presidency. So well-oiled was the conspiracy that it went on for three more years after Duterte had ended his term. However, once exposed, under the succeeding government, the two cases began to be addressed with tighter administrative and systemic controls and more aggressive judicial prosecution. But one problem remains intractable and self-compounding, and that problem happens to be the Frankenstein monster Duterte created for us. Upon taking office, Rodrigo Duterte pivoted away from our traditional democratic partners and aligned his presidency to the dictatorial regimes of China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin. Soon enough, Duterte practically ceded our West Philippine Sea to China. It was a pact between betrayers: it came around the time that our claim to sovereignty over that sea was affirmed by the Permanent Court of Arbitration in a process to which China, the rival claimant, had itself agreed. Duterte not only gave the Chinese control over traffic on that strategic waterway and access to its marine resources and minerals, but also facilitated the pursuit of their colonialist ends. Now, a decade later, they have established an effective full run over those waters, using a dedicated force of ships and planes to keep out our own navy and coast guard, our own marine researchers, and our own fisherfolk who had made their living there all their lives until Duterte made his treasonous deal. And if you now ask his anointed, Sara, about it, she would tell you, with the arrogant confidence that only a well-funded and well-protected collaborationist can exude, that it is us who are the “troublemaker[s]” in the West Philippine Sea — us Filipinos, us the rightful sovereign! Stand her against the wall? We can’t even put her on the stand! – Rappler.com

title: Adnoc’s Dh60 billion push can boost UAE manufacturing
body: The success of the UAE’s industrial strategy will ultimately be realised by the factories it builds, the high-skilled jobs it creates and the high-quality products it makes within the country. Seen in this light, the second iteration of the Make it with Adnoc Forum was yet another opportunity to connect government support with what local manufacturers actually need. Held in Abu Dhabi on Sunday, the forum brought together industry insiders, investors, partners and officials from the Ministry of Industry and Advanced Technology to find ways to scale domestic manufacturing. Manufacturing is playing an important role in the UAE’s efforts to diversify its economy and increase self-sufficiency in an increasingly unstable world. In 2021, the ministry launched Operation 300bn with the objective of raising the industrial sector’s contribution to the national gross domestic product from Dh133 billion to Dh300 billion by 2031. Reaching this target requires building and sustaining an ecosystem in which local businesses can grow and compete. There are several initiatives in place to achieve this – including, but not limited to, the National In-Country Value Programme, or ICV, designed to localise supply chains and push the government’s Emiratisation drive, and Factory Forward UAE, aimed at bringing all the country’s industrial technology transformation programmes on one platform. However, the success of these initiatives will depend on whether businesses, particularly small and medium enterprises , are able to access funding, more contracts and modern technology. New technology, in particular, is vital to building a strong industrial sector. While government support will help manufacturers increase production, policymakers know that the focus also needs to be on equipping factories with the latest technologies and ensuring continued improvement – both of which are required to produce better goods. The challenges of the past few years, from Covid-19 to the Iran war, further illustrate how crucial home-grown industries are. The Make it with Adnoc Forum and events like it serve to reduce the UAE’s dependence on foreign suppliers. Adnoc is already playing an important role in this regard by buying more products from UAE manufacturers and encouraging investment in local production. Since launching its ICV programme in 2018, it has channelled more than Dh307 billion back into the national economy. It has signed about Dh80 billion worth of offtake agreements directed at local manufacturing. And in the first edition of the forum, held in May, it announced Dh200 billion in planned project awards for the 2026-2028 period. On Sunday, the company unveiled more than Dh60 billion in local manufacturing opportunities until 2030. It also announced substantive changes in its procurement, supplier registration and ICV policies to make it easier for manufacturers, suppliers and investors to compete for its business. “We are inviting companies to build capabilities in the UAE that will serve our industry and country for years to come,” said Dr Sultan Al Jaber, Adnoc’s managing director and group chief executive, and Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology. These are promising developments – also because they are geared towards ensuring that locally made products meet international standards for quality and pricing, thereby helping manufacturers compete in overseas markets too. Of course, the proof of the pudding is in the eating. The next iteration of the Make it in the Emirates event – a platform created by the ministry for local and international companies to build and grow their manufacturing businesses in the country – will be held in May next year. It will again offer a clear opportunity to measure progress in investment, business partnerships, factory expansion and job creation. Over the longer term, it is sustained delivery on these fronts that will determine whether the UAE’s industrial strategy strengthens its economic foundations.

title: WGES 2026: How the UAE is driving discussions around green economy
body: Yousif Al Lootah has been embedded in the UAE’s green economy since 2010, long before it was a global conversation. The chief executive and founder of Lootah Biofuels, the UAE’s – and possibly the region’s – first biofuel company, was aged 19 when he started out. His brother, who owned a diesel-guzzling Hummer, was not convinced by the idea of putting used cooking oil into his car, but Mr Al Lootah persisted. “Now he loves it. They all love it,” he tells The National . Mr Al Lootah was one of the speakers on Thursday at the 12 th World Green Economy Summit, taking place at the Dubai World Trade Centre. He was one among dozens of policymakers, multilateral lenders, debt market analysts, fund managers and entrepreneurs, all of whom were there to talk about where the green economy is actually headed – and how the UAE, which has hosted WGES since its founding, has built a model that other markets are starting to study. "We get all this knowledge, we cook it in a cocktail, and we make our own decision and system for our country,” said Mr Al Lootah, adding that he’s proud that the UAE has achieved so much in this sector in such little time. ‘Exciting’ opportunities The Emirates has got a “very important” role to play in the world’s green economy, said Jonathan Maxwell, founder and group chief executive of Sustainable Development Capital LLP, who was an attendee at the summit’s first edition. “In my personal experience, Dubai is probably the best place in the world to convene people [because of] the facilities and the capability here, the focus, the sense of authenticity you get,” he said. “The future world green economy stage – Dubai has an absolutely firm place on that.” Mr Maxwell said he was “excited” about the opportunities presented throughout the summit. “We’re having some extremely constructive conversations about opportunities – talking about agency to actually do something together, which I’m excited about.” A summit like this is about developing a narrative, he added. “That’s what’s needed to penetrate government and private sector – use cases, success cases, rationale, bringing different experience together so that people can actually get around a table and come away with new ideas.” A decarbonising economy This should bring people comfort, said Syed Adeel Abbas, regional climate lead for the World Bank. “The green economy is a trend that’s not going to be halted anytime soon, regardless of what happens to the rest of the world,” he said. “The global economy is decarbonising. Products and services around the world are going to be more and more green and sustainable, and socially responsible, so if you’re a company or a layman or a government, you need to understand that that’s the trend that we need to follow. And if we do not follow that trend, we will stay behind.” The UAE is ahead in this regard, particularly in terms of competitive advantages, he added. "The UAE has sufficient capital to decarbonise its own industry and to achieve net zero targets committed at COP 28," he said. "It has the right frameworks for investments as well.” Meanwhile, green hydrogen is a credible export industry in the making and the EU’s carbon border adjustment mechanism, which will apply a carbon cost to imported goods, creates a direct near-term incentive for UAE industry to move faster than competitors. "The UAE has huge aluminium exports," he said, "and if they are produced in a less carbon emission intensity than other countries, the UAE will have a significant competitive advantage in terms of exports." His broader argument – and the message he wanted policymakers at WGES to take away – was that financing should follow this kind of competitive logic. Green bonds, blue bonds and sustainability-linked instruments are useful instruments, but "financing is not the solution and shouldn't be the starting point", he said. "It should be reliable, predictable policies that fall behind the targets and commitments that governments have made." Green financing in action Green financing is a “bigger story”, said Bashar Al Natoor, managing director and global head of Islamic Finance at Fitch Ratings. Outstanding green sukuk and bonds from the GCC have reached $73 billion. In the first nine months of 2026, GCC ESG issuance represented around 40 per cent of all US dollar ESG issuance from emerging markets, excluding China. The World Bank's IFC catalysed $112 billion in private sector investment in financial year 2026 alone. Last week, First Abu Dhabi Bank issued a digital green sukuk. Qatar has begun issuing in local currency and Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund placed a 100-year green bond. "The momentum has been there over the years, where we're seeing more and more coming,” said Mr Al Natoor. “Governments have their agendas. Banks are playing their roles. So, it’s a multi-dimensional story – and each one of them deserves to be told separately,” he added. Who pays for what should not be the focus, however, said Mr Maxwell. “The question shouldn’t be: should we pay for this? The question should be: how much better can we do with the same resources or less? How can we do the same or more work with less? And that will drive competitiveness," he said. His three-word summary of what a green investment case should look like is: cheaper, cleaner, faster. In that order, because cost is the most reliable metric and revenue matters. “If we can be more efficient – and that is the lens that I look at the world through – a green economy, a sustainable economy, where sustainability is consistent and synonymous, even with resource efficiency – then that’s better for the economy.” At the end of the day, everyone is on the same “big mission to save the environment”, said Mr Lootah. “With our young generation, who we’re going to give this world to, with the AI and robotics, and all these new technologies, it’s going to enhance the transition to a sustainable lifestyle. It’s happening.”

title: HSBC confident about Gulf property sector exposure despite war volatility
body: British lender HSBC is not worried about its exposure to the slowing property sector or the health of its corporate loan book in the Gulf region despite the war-driven economic contraction this year, its group chief executive has said. The provisions, just shy of $400 million for potential loan losses, taken so far by Europe’s second-largest lender for its Middle East exposure, are “benign”, and the bank is ready for challenges if they arise, Georges Elhedery told The National in an interview before the bank’s third-quarter earnings. “Of course, the short answer is I'm not worried. But, as you would expect, we keep monitoring the situation very closely,” Mr Elhedery said on the sidelines of HSBC’s 10th annual Future Forum in Dubai last week. “You may have idiosyncratic challenges that may appear. You can't rule them out but some of them likely will be in the normal course of business, and not necessarily related to the [geopolitical] situation”, he said. The US-Iran war, now in its eighth month, severely disrupted economic momentum in the early days of the conflict as Tehran launched waves of drone and missile attacks on civilian and energy infrastructure of its Arab neighbours. Retail, aviation, hospitality and tourism as well as real estate were among the worst-hit sectors in the region. Fighting has decreased since early April, but a US naval blockade on Iranian ports remains in place. Tehran's restrictions on merchant ships and tankers in the Strait of Hormuz continue, amid frequent retaliatory exchanges and maritime skirmishes with Washington's troops. Efforts by Qatar, Pakistan and other mediators to broker a peace settlement between the warring parties have so far failed. Last week, the International Monetary Fund said Gulf economies on aggregate are set to contract 4.8 per cent this year as the Iran war disrupts energy exports and weighs on non-oil activity. The multilateral lender, however, expects a 9.1 per cent rebound in 2027 . The latest forecast marks a sharp divergence of 6.8 percentage points from the 2 per cent expansion it projected in April, according to the IMF’s Regional Economic Outlook . Regional economies expanded by 4.5 per cent last year, driven by property, construction and tourism sector-fuelled gains in the non-oil economy. HSBC, which is among the major providers of corporate, project and home financing in the Middle East, faced loan losses, increased provisions, asset write-downs, sliding profits last year due to its exposure to Asian property markets, primarily in Hong Kong and mainland China. In the Gulf region, however, the “good responsiveness” of sovereigns and the financial policymakers helped mitigate risks. “Fiscal support where it was needed” also allowed resumption of economic activity after severe disruption in March, and with the rebound already underway “there is therefore no cause to worry”, Mr Elhedery said. Strong bounce back Despite the economic contraction this year, HSBC is optimistic about the short to medium-term outlook for the region, as there is a clear push by the Gulf sovereigns to offset the impact of the war on their economies and build “resilience at pace”. “It knows how to respond to the challenges quickly and has the agility to adjust,” Mr Elhedery said. Like any other problem the region has faced, including the lockdowns during the Covid-19 pandemic, policymakers will effectively deal with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, “which may, by the way, become redundant over the next five years”, he said. Continued investments in “all the resilience and redundancies being built to create a more sustainable and robust business model” will ultimately make the narrow waterway, through which a fifth of global oil and gas passed before the war, less important, he added. The last decade, Mr Elhedery added, has shown that “you can be very efficient operationally, but exogenous events, can knock you off course”, and these events can “take away 100 per cent of your earnings”. “This Middle East conflict is emphasising the importance of spending money on operational resilience,” he said. “I think the Middle East has done a lot of that already, but clearly there is much more going on now because of this conflict.” The financial strength and the economic vision of the leadership, as well as its “will to rebound” is what makes HSBC believe the rebound can be fast, and “we want to lean in to support it, and our clients”, he said. Changing risk profile The US-Iran war, which began on February 28, has turned into a multi-front conflict, with the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen launching missile and drone strikes on Saudi Arabia’s energy and aviation infrastructure on a daily basis. The kingdom, Opec’s largest oil exporter, is also facing a naval blockade and maritime embargo aimed at Saudi and international shipping through the Bab Al Mandeb strait and the Red Sea. But even with the Houthi dimension adding another layer of uncertainty to the region’s risk profile, Mr Elhedery said HSBC remained optimistic about growth prospects. “It's actually never been, frankly, a singular risk and, of course from time to time, items [events] pop up to top the agenda,” he said. “One has to keep in mind that the geoeconomic considerations have always been quite complex. Some of them ebb and flow, but that complexity has always been there, and our mission is to help clients navigate this complexity, but not stereotype it.” Impact on business Although HSBC has taken first-half provisions of about $400 million against possible loan losses, the “majority of these provisions are modelled on economic outlook and growth outlook”. “So, de facto, we have seen very little, literally insignificant impact on our business directly related to the conflict, and our focus has been on operational continuity and serving our clients throughout, and we haven't skipped a beat doing that,” the chief executive said. "If you look at the entire year, actually our businesses have been resilient, both on the revenue and profitability front, the impact has been very low, single-digit per cent, on the overall business." He added that although equity capital market activity throughout the region slowed this year, there are signs of revival and "we are in the market now with the first IPO since the events [of March]". "The indications are very good, the appetite is strong," he said. HSBC is among local and global banks working on the Dubai Investments' bid to sell a 20 per cent stake in its subsidiary DIP Holding in the first initial public offering in the UAE this year. "Of course, in a period like this, you would see less public activity and more private activity, so what used to be debt capital markets sometimes may become private placements," he said. "What used to be ECM sometimes becoming more M&A, but that is a normal reaction to these events." Infrastructure boom The next phase of growth will be driven by the infrastructure boom. The broader Middle East, North Africa and Turkey region already has close to $900 billion in infrastructure financing requirements. HSBC estimates that the project finance pipeline in the UAE alone is more than $190 billion, about 22 per cent of the Menat total. The HSBC-commissioned analysis of MEED data released last week has identified an $872-billion pipeline of individual project packages within a wider $1.4 trillion pipeline of planned and unawarded infrastructure projects. The value of planned but unawarded infrastructure projects and programmes increased by 54 per cent between January 2023 and January 2026, from $792 billion to $1.22 trillion, data showed. The sheer size of the infrastructure financing basket opens up new avenues of business for financial institutions that have been waiting for the better part of this year for the lull in the regional capital markets to end. "We, as a bank, are a financing bank, an infrastructure bank, an underwriting bank and a structuring bank. We have a whole skill set to support how these projects are designed … and financed," Mr Elhedery said. "The pie is huge as there is massive appetite [from project owners for funding] and there will be more appetite [in the future]. There is a substantial opportunity to be involved, and we're extremely pleased." Sharia fund controversy HSBC in recent weeks has faced investor criticism over some of the investments its Islamic Global Equity Index Fund has made, and Mr Elhedery said the bank is trying to address those concerns as best and as quickly as possible. The $9-billion fund, which tracks an index, is the top Sharia-compliant fund in the UK. The investment vehicle has bought shares in companies linked to the US and Israeli defence companies including US tech giant Palantir, prompting several investors to raise concerns with HSBC. "We take client and investor concerns very seriously," Mr Elhedery said. The bank, he said, had already set up a working group, which includes index providers and independent Sharia experts who have begun the review. HSBC is moving at pace and aims to resolve the matter swiftly, which could mean a revision of some of the filters used. "I don't want to preempt the outcomes, but … but we intend to reach a satisfactory conclusion."

title: For many Israeli voters, concerns over Israel's public image take a back seat in election
body: Over the past few months, Israeli media has been full of reports of Israeli holidaymakers in Europe, Asia and the Americas being harassed or physically attacked after being identified as Israeli.In July, a group of Israeli tourists visiting Montenegro was reportedly confronted by a man and a woman, apparently locals, who asked, “Taking a break from genocide?” and told them to stay in Israel. In Greece, an Israeli woman said a restaurant refused to serve her after she told an employee she was from Israel. In Thailand, a mother and daughter were allegedly beaten after they told a man they were from Israel, according to the mother's account.. And in the US, an Israeli couple checking into a hotel in California were asked if they were “baby killers.”These reports come as Israel's image around the world has fallen to historic lows. A Pew poll conducted between February and May this year found that across 36 countries, a median of 67% of adults held an unfavorable view of Israel.On the diplomatic front, hostility is also growing. Israel's ongoing military action in Gaza has been termed “disproportionate” by a growing number of world leaders, and unchecked violence by Israeli settlers in the West Bank – as well as Israeli government policy there – has prompted some countries, including some considered allies, to pull back or even impose sanctions.Growing foreign hostility not among primary concerns for Israeli votersDespite this hostility, the issue of Israel's diplomacy, its image worldwide and who is to blame for its deterioration is barely factoring into the fast-approaching election on Oct. 27.Yaakov Katz, a senior fellow at the Jewish People Policy Institute, told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency that there have been complaints about Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his government not being effective at explaining Israel's policies or actions to international audiences. Nevertheless, most Israelis see this as a problem beyond their control, he added.“There is the argument that Netanyahu makes, which is that no matter what we do, the whole world's against us, and no matter what we say, it's antisemitism,” said Katz, co-author of “While Israel Slept: How Hamas Surprised the Most Powerful Military in the Middle East.” “People accept that argument, and to a large extent, they don't push back on it. Why? Because part of it is true, right?”Katz pointed out that many Israelis believe the sharp rise in antisemitism worldwide would keep happening regardless of what Israel does.“In other words, Israelis believe that even if the number killed in Gaza was not 70,000 but 10,000, you still would have genocide claims; it makes no difference,” he said, adding that the average Israeli does not fully understand that declining support, particularly in the US, could eventually have “existential consequences for the country.”“Most people here don't think that far ahead,” Katz said. Instead, they take comfort in news such as President Donald Trump's endorsement of Netanyahu, he added.Ofir Dayan, a senior fellow at the Institute for National Security Studies at Tel Aviv University, said, however, that Israelis are painfully aware of what is happening abroad and are concerned about it. But she said there are other, more pressing issues in a country that has been grappling with more than three years of war.“When people talk about the elections and what the Netanyahu government did right or wrong, they definitely look at this issue, and it is something they care about,” Dayan said. However, she continued, most are unlikely to vote for a party or a candidate based on their position on this issue because it is just not a priority.“Israeli voters are very much one-issue voters, and the issue in this election is security,” Dayan said. “We're not remote enough from Oct. 7 for people to completely shift their vote and vote based on this idea.”In addition to security and the questions surrounding the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led terror attack, Peter Lerner, the former Israel Defense Forces spokesman for the international press, told JTA that the “issue of Israel's international standing is secondary to two things: Netanyahu or not Netanyahu, and the left vs. the right.”“Obviously, each one of those comes with its own package of Oct. 7-related issues and the question of who is most suited to deal with the threats that are around us,” he said, adding, “you just don't see very many talking about it and when they do talk about it, it is secondary to everything else.”Most parties have not suggested public diplomacy plansOf the dozen or so parties expected to win seats in Israel's parliament, the Knesset, only a few have referred to Israel's negative global image or suggested ways to improve public diplomacy.The B'Yachad Party, headed by former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, is one of those discussing it as part of a plan to repair ties between Israel and world Jewry. Under this plan, the party hopes to elevate the importance of Diaspora Jewry, allowing a non-voting observer in Israel's parliament, the Knesset, to focus on such issues.Amcha Yisrael, a new right-wing party led by former IDF Brig. Gen. Ofer Winter, has two candidates on its list who are prominent public diplomacy activists – Yoseph Haddad and Fleur Hassan-Nahoum. Haddad has said multiple times that he would like to be Israel's next minister for public diplomacy.Journalist Eylon Levy, a former spokesman for the Israeli government, told JTA's “Waiting for 61” podcast that public diplomacy, or hasbara as Israelis refer to it, “is not a goal in itself” for most of the candidates.He said the discussion was more about “who can manage relations with the world so that we can achieve our national interests.” Within that framework, Levy pointed out, there is a range of opinions. On the far right, the approach of the Otzma Yehudit Party, led by Minister of National Security Itamar Ben-Gvir, is to make Israel look tough and “screw the woolly-hearted soft liberals if they don't like it.”On the left, “the position may be equally detached from reality,” Levy said.“There is a belief on the left that if Israel starts behaving like a normal country and doesn't have ministers who say aggressive nonsense, then Israel's relations will snap back to normal,” he said. “I think there may be a denial there of how much public opinion has shifted against Israel and how much the expectations of policymakers have shifted as well.”While Levy said he did not believe there would be a massive change in perceptions if a new government were elected on Oct. 27, he did believe it would be given a grace period, at least by Israel's less-than-friendly allies.“The question is whether an alternative government would suddenly magically boost Israel's international standing; I don't think it will,” he said. “But I do think a more moderate government will buy Israel some goodwill, definitely among those who say, in theory, we support Israel.”

title: Police begin probe as officer kills colleague, self in Kogi
body: The Kogi State Police Command has launched an investigation into a shooting incident at ASCO Camp, Ajaokuta, which claimed the lives of two police officers on Friday, October 23. The Commissioner of Police, Naziru Bello Kankarofi, disclosed this in a statement issued on Sunday by the command’s spokesperson, ASP Saliu Oyiza Afusat. The officers were identified as Corporal Amos Yusuf and Corporal Grace Onimisi, both serving at the Ajaokuta Divisional Police Headquarters. According to the statement, the incident occurred around 9pm at the officers’ residential quarters in Ajaokuta. Preliminary findings indicated that Yusuf, who had resumed night duty, left his duty post with his service AK-47 rifle and went to the residence of Onimisi. He allegedly opened fire on her, inflicting gunshot wounds on her leg, shoulder and abdomen, before shooting himself with the same rifle. The police said the incident was reported at 11.04pm, prompting the Divisional Police Officer (DPO) in Ajaokuta to lead a team of officers to the scene. “Both officers were taken to separate medical facilities, where they were confirmed dead by medical personnel. Their remains have been deposited at the mortuary of ASCO Hospital. “An AK-47 rifle and four expended cartridges were recovered at the scene as exhibits,” the statement said. The command added that the case had been transferred to the State Criminal Investigation Department (SCID) for a thorough investigation. It said the circumstances surrounding the incident and the motive remained under investigation. “The circumstances and motive remain subjects of investigation, and the command will not speculate on matters yet to be established,” the spokesperson said. The Commissioner of Police assured the public that the command would provide verified updates as the investigation progressed.

title: Greece and Saudi Arabia Call for Secure Shipping Routes
body: Greece and Saudi Arabia have called for the protection of international shipping routes and uninterrupted energy supplies, warning that attacks on critical infrastructure threaten global markets and supply stability. The warning came as Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis met Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Riyadh on Sunday, with the two countries also pledging to accelerate energy projects, expand investment and strengthen defence cooperation as they mark 100 years of diplomatic relations. During the visit, the two countries issued a joint statement stressing the importance of protecting international shipping routes and ensuring the uninterrupted flow of energy supplies. Both sides expressed concern over attacks on energy infrastructure and the potential consequences for global supplies and market stability. Greece also praised Saudi Arabia’s efforts to stabilise international oil markets and maintain energy exports through alternative routes, including the Kingdom’s East-West Pipeline. The discussions come as maritime security and reliable energy supplies remain critical issues for international trade and the wider economy. Greece and Saudi Arabia Advance Electricity Link Energy cooperation featured prominently in the discussions, with both governments committing to accelerate work on the proposed Saudi-Greek electricity interconnection. The project aims to facilitate electricity exchanges between Saudi Arabia and Greece, improve power grid reliability and strengthen connections between the Middle East and European energy markets. The two countries also agreed to explore opportunities for exporting clean hydrogen from Saudi Arabia to Greece and other European Union markets. Further cooperation is planned across conventional and renewable energy, petrochemicals and related infrastructure, creating opportunities for investment and closer integration between the two economies. For Greece, the proposed electricity link could strengthen its role as a connection point between European energy markets and the wider Middle East. For Saudi Arabia, expanded energy partnerships offer additional routes into European markets as the Kingdom pursues broader economic diversification. Trade and Investment Ties Expand The two governments also highlighted growing commercial relations, with bilateral trade reaching approximately $1.7 billion in 2025. Both sides called for stronger investment cooperation in infrastructure, construction, energy, logistics and technology. Saudi Arabia encouraged Greek companies to establish regional headquarters in the Kingdom and pursue opportunities associated with major developments, including Riyadh Expo 2030 and the 2034 FIFA World Cup. Greece invited Saudi investors to explore opportunities in transport, energy, logistics, digital infrastructure and advanced technologies, highlighting the country’s position as a gateway to European markets. The discussions build on the strategic partnership council established following Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s visit to Greece in July 2022. The council held its first meeting during Mitsotakis’ visit to Saudi Arabia in January 2025. Submarine Cable Project Strengthens Digital Connectivity Digital infrastructure was another priority, with both countries welcoming progress on the EMC submarine cable project. The project is designed to strengthen digital connectivity between East and West, supporting international data transmission and communications infrastructure. The two governments pledged to coordinate efforts to complete the project according to the agreed timetable. The initiative forms part of broader efforts to strengthen economic links through technology, communications and infrastructure investment. Both sides also identified artificial intelligence and space technology as areas for future cooperation. Defence and Security Cooperation Greece and Saudi Arabia agreed to strengthen cooperation in defence and security, including efforts to combat crime, terrorism and terrorist financing. The two sides also supported greater exchanges of expertise and training, alongside closer cooperation on cybersecurity and information sharing. The commitments add a security dimension to a relationship increasingly focused on strategic infrastructure, energy and trade. Both countries also reaffirmed their commitment to the principles of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change and the Paris Agreement, while supporting cooperation on the circular carbon economy. Further areas identified for collaboration include healthcare, education, culture, tourism and sport. A Century of Diplomatic Relations Mitsotakis’ visit marks a significant milestone in relations between Greece and Saudi Arabia, which are celebrating a century of diplomatic ties. The discussions in Riyadh reflect efforts by both governments to translate their longstanding relationship into deeper economic, energy and security cooperation. With international shipping routes, energy infrastructure and digital connectivity high on the agenda, the partnership is expanding beyond traditional trade into areas with wider regional significance. The next phase will depend on the implementation of the proposed electricity interconnection, progress on the submarine cable and new investment commitments between the two countries. title: Zelensky: Bipartisan support for Ukraine in U.S. grows stronger
body:
Volodymyr Zelensky said this in an interview with TSN.Tyzhden , according to Ukrinform.
"Bipartisan support [for Ukraine] is now stronger than it has been in the past year and a half. Because everyone has realized—both from what is happening and from my conversations with them, both public and private—that this is unfair. Unjust actions have been taken against Ukraine that have nothing to do with finances or politics, but are related exclusively to people’s lives and Ukraine’s ability to defend itself. All these issues, from intelligence to Starlink, are about the ability to defend ourselves. Everyone has felt this. And we have strong support among both Democrats and Republicans . I am grateful to them for that,” the President said.
As reported by Ukrinform , Republicans in the U.S. House of Representatives are threatening to block a $350 billion package of additional defense spending for the Pentagon unless the Trump administration toughens its policy toward Russia.

title: Adongo defends GoldBod law’s passage despite opposition concerns, leaves door open to review
body: Parliament’s Finance Committee Chairman, Isaac Adongo, has defended the passage of the law establishing GoldBod despite opposition concerns about some provisions. He says the law can be reviewed if lapses emerge. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express Business Edition, he said opposition members did not reject the bill in principle. Their reservations concerned specific provisions. “The passage of the bill that led to the establishment of the gold board, for instance, from a political perspective, our colleagues do not disagree in principle, but their side of the divide was not comfortable with certain provisions,” he stated. He argued that Parliament needed to pass the law to allow the institution to begin its work. “Nevertheless, we needed to get that act out of the way, and you have seen the monumental impact of the gold board, so we needed to first get a handle on it.” Mr Adongo left the possibility of changes open. He acknowledged that implementation could expose weaknesses requiring parliamentary attention. “Of course, over time, there will be some lapses that can be identified, and a review is possible at any point in time.” He said he expected opposition members to support a review if the executive returned to Parliament seeking changes to clauses it believed could have been handled differently. He defended his position during a discussion about whether he could challenge government proposals, including those brought by Finance Minister Dr Ato Forson. Mr Adongo said the committee’s work involved scrutiny across party lines. He argued that its chairman could not impose decisions on members. “The reason is that almost every bill that has come to us has been scrutinised on a bipartisan basis.” He cited former Finance Minister and Ranking Member Dr Amin Adam, Deputy Ranking Member Dr Stephen Amoah, and Dr Gideon Boako as part of that scrutiny. Mr Adongo maintained that committee members had largely agreed on proposals brought before them. He said differences allowed both sides to express their views. For GoldBod, he said the passage was necessary despite the reservations, noting that any subsequent review would give Parliament another opportunity to examine provisions found wanting.

title: Dizon returns to DOTr, Lopez takes over DPWH in Marcos Cabinet reshuffle
body: MANILA, Philippines – Vince Dizon is leaving the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) a little over a year after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. tapped him to lead the agency and address corruption concerns. He is returning to the Department of Transportation (DOTr), which he previously headed. DOTr Secretary Giovanni “Banoy” Lopez, meanwhile, will take over the DPWH. Lopez was appointed as DOTr chief after the post was vacated by Dizon in September 2025. “We are shifting gears to accelerate reform. Secretary Dizon goes to DOTr to fix the daily commute. Secretary Lopez goes to DPWH to make sure the reforms there last. Lahat ng ito, para bumilis at gumaan ang serbisyo ng gobyerno para sa ating mga kababayan ,” Marcos said, as relayed by Presidential Communications Secretary Lino Cayetano in a press briefing on Monday, October 26. (All of this is to make government services faster and more accessible for our fellow Filipinos.) Cayetano said Dizon is returning to the DOTr with the President’s “full confidence” and a mandate to make daily commutes easier, shorten queues at the Land Transportation Office (LTO), and get rid of fixers. At the DPWH, Cayetano said, Dizon had opened thousands of projects to public scrutiny, pushed for the completion of long-unfinished projects, and begun reforms aimed at addressing corruption. Meanwhile, Cayetano said Lopez, a lawyer and certified public accountant, will be tasked with institutionalizing these reforms by establishing rules, processes, and systems designed to ensure they endure. In September, Dizon’s appointment was questioned by Senator Imee Marcos, as his appointment has yet to be confirmed by the Commission on Appointments. Dizon has been candid that he wanted to vacate his post as DPWH secretary. Must Read Is Vince Dizon still in — or out — as DPWH chief? – Rappler.com

title: Protests in Europe stem from instability on energy markets — Iranian top diplomat
body:
MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. Geopolitical tensions and disruptions in energy supplies have impacted the entire world and, among other things, resulted in protests across European countries and surging fuel prices, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi was quoted as saying in an article published by Russia’s Vedomosti daily.
"Any disruption and confrontation entail consequences that go far beyond our region and affect energy security, market stability and the economic interests of producers and consumers around the world," he stated.
"Take a look at the ongoing protests across Europe and the rapid rise in inflation and fuel prices in Europe and America," Araghchi noted.
The military actions on behalf of the United States and Israel against Iran and the ongoing military threats have led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and the disruption of global natural gas supplies, especially in Asia, the Iranian top diplomat stressed. He also pointed to a hike in gas prices in Europe and the low level of annual gas reserves required ahead of the coming winter.
Aragchi called on fuel producers to resort to stronger dialogue, diversify supply routes, protect vital infrastructure and create practical mechanisms in order to reduce the impact of geopolitical shocks on global energy markets.
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28. In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding providing for an immediate cessation of hostilities on all fronts, including in Lebanon. However, in the early morning hours of July 8, the US resumed large-scale strikes against Iran, accusing it of violating the terms of the agreements reached on the Strait of Hormuz.
Nearly 25% of global oil trade and about 20% of the liquefied natural gas trade are transported through the strait. The US administration then effectively indicated that it would stop using large-scale military force against Iran and instead seek to economically strangle the country through sanctions.

title: SERAP takes FG to ECOWAS Court over alleged N78.8bn cash transfer scandal
body: The Socio-Economic Rights and Accountability Project (SERAP) has filed a lawsuit against the Federal Government over “the alleged diversion, irregular expenditure and failure to account for over N78.8 billion in public funds involving the Ministry of Humanitarian Affairs and Poverty Reduction, the National Cash Transfer Office (NCTO) and the National Social Safety Nets Coordinating Office (NASSCO).” The allegations are documented in the Auditor-General of the Federation’s 2024 Annual Report, published on 7 August 2026. According to the Auditor-General, the findings cover various periods between January 2023 and 31 December 2024, according to a statement by SERAP on Sunday. In the suit number ECW/CCJ/APP/42/26 filed last week at the ECOWAS Community Court of Justice, Abuja, SERAP is seeking: “a declaration that the failure of the Nigerian government to account for over N78.8 billion in public funds allocated for federal cash-transfer and social-protection programmes is unlawful and a violation of Nigeria’s international human rights obligations.” SERAP is seeking a declaration that “the government’s failure to ensure the lawful administration of public funds allocated for cash-transfer programmes intended to benefit vulnerable households undermines the enjoyment of the rights protected under the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights.” SERAP, in the suit filed by its lawyers, Kolawole Oluwadare and Kehinde Oyewumi, is also seeking “an order of perpetual injunction restraining the government from administering or disbursing cash-transfer and social-protection funds without adequate financial accountability, beneficiary verification, auditing and oversight mechanisms consistent with Nigeria’s international human rights obligations.” In the suit, SERAP is arguing that “the government has violated, and continues to violate, the rights to social security and an adequate standard of living, including food, clothing and housing, by failing to properly administer social-protection funds and ensure access to benefits intended to meet basic needs.” SERAP is also arguing that “the failure to account for substantial public funds allocated for social protection, and to investigate and remedy deficiencies, undermines the socio-economic rights of millions of affected Nigerians.” According to SERAP, “The funds were intended to benefit over 3.2 million households across 35 states, whose access to financial assistance has been affected by the allegations made by the Auditor-General.”

title: ‘Replace complexity with compassion’ – Cardinal Turkson urges students
body: The Chancellor of the Catholic University of Ghana, Cardinal Peter Appiah Turkson, has urged students to embrace compassion and collective responsibility as they prepare for a world shaped by conflict, technological disruption and uncertainty. He said university education must go beyond academic achievement to instil ethical values and prepare graduates to contribute meaningfully to society. Cardinal Turkson was speaking at the university’s 25th Congregation and 38th Matriculation Ceremony at Fiapre, near Sunyani, on Saturday, October 24, 2026. The university admitted about 1,810 students and graduated 2,806, comprising 668 postgraduate and 2,138 undergraduate students. It also celebrated its first PhD graduate, Dr Godfred Etse Klugah. Drawing on the concept of a volatile, uncertain, complex and ambiguous world, commonly described as VUCA, Cardinal Turkson proposed a more human response to its challenges. He encouraged students to replace volatility with vulnerability, uncertainty with unlearning, complexity with compassion, and ambiguity with answerability. “The religious twist gives an ethical content to everything that seeks to transform the volatility, the uncertainty, the complexity and the ambiguity into something more human and more ethical,” he said. He explained that recognising vulnerability should encourage people to seek and offer support rather than face life’s challenges alone. “We are vulnerable, and because we’re vulnerable, we need to support each other with the common wisdom that we develop and acquire here,” he told the gathering. Cardinal Turkson also urged students to remain open to learning by letting go of prejudices and habits that could hinder their development. “To progress and to move on in life, we need to unlearn a lot of things. We need to let go of a lot of traits that we’ve come here with, and we need to forget and abandon lifestyles and prejudices with which we’ve come here,” he said. He said compassion should guide academic and social relationships, fostering collaboration and mutual support. Turning to artificial intelligence and emerging technologies, he cautioned against reducing human beings to figures and numbers at the expense of their inherent dignity. He cited conflicts in Ukraine, Gaza and Sudan, alongside rapid technological and economic changes, as examples of the difficult environment young people must navigate. On answerability, Cardinal Turkson said students must be willing to account for their choices. “In providing answers for everything that we do, we show responsibility, we show maturity,” he said. He described university education as building on lessons and values acquired at home, in school and across society. Like a manual for a new product, education should guide people in navigating life. He congratulated the graduates and encouraged newly admitted students to make the most of their university experience. The Bono Regional Minister, Joseph Addae Akwaboa, called on the university to strengthen practical learning, digital skills and industry partnerships to prepare students for the changing job market. He said education and youth empowerment remained central to Ghana’s long-term development. “The No Fee Stress Initiative is an important intervention aimed at easing the financial burden on eligible first-year students in public tertiary institutions,” he stated. Mr Akwaboa also urged the university to use research and innovation to address youth unemployment, agricultural productivity, sanitation and public health challenges. He assured the institution of the Bono Regional Coordinating Council’s commitment to partnerships that support regional development.

title: Foreign participation in capital market strengthens considerably in half-year 2026
body: Foreign investor participation in the capital markets strengthened considerably in the first half of 2026, according to the September 2026 Monetary Policy Report. This supported a decline in the risk of capital flight. The improvement was on the back of the issuance of the new bonds amidst improved macroeconomic conditions and financial market prospects. According to the report, improved macroeconomic conditions, declining sovereign risk perceptions, and continued exchange rate stability contributed to maintaining investor confidence and reducing the risk of sudden capital outflows. Overall, foreign investor participation is expected to remain robust if current macroeconomic stability is sustained. Sovereign Risk Spreads Meanwhile, Ghana’s sovereign risk spreads have been relatively stable since the last Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting and compared favourably with peer economies in the sub-Saharan Africa region. The stability reflects improved investor sentiment, and this is expected to have a positive knock-on effect on the country’s risk ratings while supporting inflows of portfolio investment and foreign direct investment.
