title: Market Capitalisation Down N210bn WoW on Profit-taking in Aradel, Others
body: Kayode Tokede The Nigerian stock market closed last week on a negative note, as sustained profit taking in Aradel Holdings, others dragged the market capitalisation low by N210bn. As the market capitalisation fell by N206 billion week-on-week (W-o-W) to N160.52 trillion, the Nigerian Exchange Limited All-Share Index (NGX ASI) dropped by 0.97 per cent W-o-W to close at 247,222.27 basis points. Consequently, the market’s year-to-date (YTD) return moderated to 58.87 per cent. Investor sentiment remained weak, as market breadth closed negative, with 20 gainers against 55 decliners, reflecting the dominance of declining stocks. ABC Transport Plc led the gainers, appreciating by 20.7 per cent to close at N7.30 per share. AVA Capital Partners Limited followed with a 17.7 per cent gain to close at N7.30 per share, while Caverton Offshore Support Group Plc rose by 17.1 per cent to close at N4.80 per share. On the losing side, Omatek Ventures Plc recorded the steepest decline, shedding 12.5 per cent to close at N1.40 per share. University Press Plc followed with a 12.1 per cent loss to close at N4.35 per share, while Regency Alliance Insurance Plc depreciated by 11.3 per cent to close at 71 kobo per share. Overall, a total turnover of 2.024 billion shares worth N110.773 billion in 173,113 deals was traded last week by investors on the floor of the Exchange, in contrast to a total of 1.659 billion shares valued at N98.088 billion that exchanged hands previous week in 184,632 deals. The Financial Services Industry (measured by volume) led the activity chart with 1.111 billion shares valued at N53.908 billion traded in 81,787 deals, contributing 54.89 per cent and 48.66 per cent to the total equity turnover volume and value respectively. The Consumer Goods Industry followed with 394.039 million shares worth N9.811 billion in 17,912 deals, while the Agriculture Industry pulled a turnover of 147.170 million shares worth N2.821 billion in 7,462 deals. Trading in the top equities, Multitrex Integrated Foods, Zenith Bank, and Livestock Feeds accounted for 521.565 million shares worth N19.093 billion in 16,487 deals, contributing 25.76 per cent and 17.24 per cent to the total equity turnover volume and value respectively. However, the Nigerian stock market direction is likely to be shaped by corporate earnings expectations, valuation levels, dividend prospects and broader investor sentiment amid evolving macroeconomic conditions, analysts said. They note that while continued price adjustments could create opportunities for bargain-hunting in quality equities, the sustainability of any recovery will depend on improved investor confidence and a broader return of demand across key sectors. Going forward, Cowry Assets Management Limited said, market direction is likely to be shaped by corporate earnings expectations, valuation levels, dividend prospects and broader investor sentiment amid evolving macroeconomic conditions. The firm noted that the negative market breadth, with decliners significantly outnumbering gainers, points to persistent selling pressure and suggests that investors may maintain a cautious, selective approach, favouring fundamentally strong stocks with attractive valuations, sustainable earnings and consistent dividend potential. It added that “nevertheless, continued price adjustments could create opportunities for bargain-hunting in quality equities, potentially supporting a market rebound if buying interest strengthens. However, the sustainability of any recovery will depend on improved investor confidence and a broader return of demand across key sectors.” Cordros Securities Limited pointed out that this week, trading is expected to remain cautious as the first batch of earnings releases begins to hit the NGX, driving heightened stock-specific activity, saying that investor focus is likely to centre on earnings quality and forward guidance, prompting selective repositioning across counters.

title: Tornadoes stun Abia Warriors; Insurance halt Rivers United’s unbeaten run
body: The Nigeria Premier Football League (NPFL) Week 10 matches played on Sunday witnessed high drama as Niger Tornadoes produced a commanding away display to stun Abia Warriors 1-0, while Bendel Insurance brought Rivers United’s impressive unbeaten run to a screeching halt in Benin City. A 55th-minute long-range strike by widely travelled and experienced striker Wasiu Jimoh proved decisive, as Niger Tornadoes held onto their slim advantage to secure a historic 1-0 victory over Abia Warriors in Umuahia. Prior to their first away win of the campaign, Tornadoes had struggled on their travels—suffering narrow 1-0 defeats to Katsina United and Nasarawa United, alongside scoreless stalemates against teams like Ranchers Bees. At the Samuel Ogbemudia Stadium in Benin City, Bendel Insurance scored two second-half goals to end Rivers United’s unbeaten run. Wuchirwa Freeman and Jonathan James found the net in the 60th and 90th minutes, respectively, to deliver a crucial victory that lifted Insurance to sixth position on the table. Before Sunday’s clash, table-toppers Rivers United had gone nine matches without defeat. Despite the loss, the “Pride of Rivers” remain atop the log with 17 points. At the Sani Abacha Stadium, Barau FC surrendered a first-half lead to draw 1-1 with Kwara United. Former Plateau United striker Anthony Sunday fired Barau FC ahead in the 40th minute, but Goodluck Ogbolu equalised for the “Afonja Warriors” in the 63rd minute to ensure the points were shared. Elsewhere, a 69th-minute strike from Benjamin proved decisive as Kun Khalifat inflicted more misery on bottom-of-the-table side Inter Lagos. Nasarawa United continued their strong form by edging Enyimba 1-0 in Lafia, courtesy of John Joshua’s 23rd-minute winner. Meanwhile, the South-West derby between Ikorodu City and Shooting Stars (3SC) ended in an entertaining 2-2 draw at the Mobolaji Johnson Arena in Lagos. In a highly tactical encounter where neither side could break the deadlock, visiting Kano Pillars forced Warri Wolves to a goalless draw in Oghara to maintain their steady climb up the table. In the round’s opening fixture on Saturday, Katsina United pulled off a stunning late comeback to draw 2-2 with Plateau United at the Muhamadu Dikko Stadium Katsina.

title: NFF hails Alex Iwobi on another milestone
body: The Nigeria Football Federation has celebrated Super Eagles’ midfield ace Alexander Iwobi on his new milestone of becoming the joint-second most-capped African football player in the English Premiership, alongside Egyptian icon Mohamed Salah. Iwobi, who celebrated his 100th cap for Nigeria during this summer’s friendly match with Portugal at the Estádio Dr. Magalhães Pessoa in Leiria, has now featured in 328 matches in the English Premier League. Acting General Secretary of the NFF, Dr Emmanuel Ikpeme congratulated Iwobi on his latest accomplishment. “The NFF celebrates Alex Iwobi for this new achievement and we wish him even greater glory. We will be very happy to see him become the African with the most appearances in the Premier League in the near future.” The 30-year-old, who has won silver and two bronze medals with Nigeria at the Africa Cup of Nations, achieved the latest milestone when he featured for his English Premiership club Fulham in their 1-0 win over Coventry City on Saturday. The game was his 328th appearance in the EPL, taking him joint-second with Salah, and 25 games more to match the all-time record holder, Ivorian Kolo Toure. Ivorian legend Toure played a total of 353 matches in the EPL – widely regarded as the biggest and most glamorous football league in the world.

title: Nigeria ready for Commonwealth Kabaddi Championship debut
body: Nigeria is set to participate in the 2026 Commonwealth Kabaddi Championship scheduled to hold in India next week, the country’s kabaddi leader, Daniel Damola, has confirmed. Damola disclosed this during a visit to Cross River State Governor Bassey Otu in Calabar at the weekend, where he highlighted the importance of the competition to the development of the sport in Nigeria. Kabaddi is a popular contact tean sport that originated in ancient India. It is played between two teams of seven players, where the main objective is for a single offensive player – called a “raider” – to run into the opposing team’s half of the court, tag out as many of their defenders as possible, and return to their own half, all without being tackled and within a single breath. He said participation would expose Nigerian athletes to international competition, improve their skills and encourage more young people to take up the sport. Damola commended Otu for supporting the introduction and development of kabaddi in Cross River State, describing him as the first Nigerian governor to endorse the sport. He said kabaddi, which is popular in several Asian countries, was gradually gaining ground in Africa. The technical head of the team, Collins Eko, also commended the governor’s interest in sports, expressing confidence that the athletes would represent Nigeria and Cross River State well at the championship. Otu pledged appropriate support for the Nigerian athletes ahead of the competition, reaffirming his administration’s commitment to sports development and youth empowerment.

title: Putin maintains permanent contact with new Cabinet members — Kremlin
body:
MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. Russian President Vladimir Putin currently has no plans on holding separate meetings with the new members of the government, Russian Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov told TASS.
"No meetings as of yet. Who’s new there? There’s no one new. Everyone there [in the Cabinet] is someone who is constantly in contact with Putin," Peskov noted.
"You well know that [Prime Minister Mikhail] Mishustin earlier said there is no time for adaptation. This is why, there is no need for such meetings in this case," he added.
The candidacies of four new deputy prime ministers and a minister were proposed by Mishustin, they were granted support by Putin and endorsed by deputies of the State Duma on October 21.
The government was bolstered by former First Deputy Head of the Ministry of Finance Irina Okladnikova as she assumed the post of deputy prime minister. Her former superior, Anton Siluanov, also assumed the seat of a deputy prime minister, remaining in charge of the Finance Ministry.
Andrey Nikitin was promoted to the post of a deputy prime minister from the post of the head of the Transportation Ministry, where he was succeeded by former head of the Federal Air Transport Agency (Rosaviatsia) Dmitry Yadrov, while Oleg Kozhemyako was promoted from the post of governor of the Primorye Region.

title: T20 World Cup: Nigeria beat Uganda, clinch sub-regional Africa qualifier ticket
body: Nigeria beat favourites Uganda in Abuja to win the T20 World Cup Sub-Regional Africa Qualifier and pick one of the two tickets to the next stage of the qualifier. This is Nigeria’s first victory over Uganda after 13 failed attempts. The tournament featured hosts Nigeria, Uganda, Zambia, Lesotho, Mozambique and The Gambia, who competed in a round-robin format at the twin cricket ovals in Abuja. The Nigerian side, known as the YellowGreens, finished the Sub Regional Qualifier C unbeaten, topping the table with a perfect 10 points, while Uganda secured second place with 8 points. Despite the loss, Uganda also booked their spot in the Africa Qualifier slated for October 2027. Speaking after the final match, the captain of the YellowGreens, Chima Akachukwu, said there were shivers at some points during the final match, saying, “When defending, there were shivers because at some point, the game was as if it was shifting, but I kept on talking to the boys.” “We keep fighting for every game, ball by ball until the last ball,” he said. Looking ahead to the African qualifier next year, Akachukwu said the team has a clear mindset. “The mindset is to keep winning every game that comes our way. So, we will keep training hard. The Nigerian Cricket Federation (NCF) has been doing so well. So, they will continue to do the good work,” he said. On his part, Stephen Mangongo, the high-performance manager for NCF and head coach of the senior men’s team, commended the players for their performance. “The boys have put in a lot of hard work behind the scenes. We’ve worked a lot on their fitness, mental toughness, and skills development. And without committed players, you don’t go anywhere,” he said. He also commended the Federation for providing funds for the team’s training programmes, saying the team got all the support needed to succeed. The NCF President, Dr Uyi Akpata, while commending the team for the feat, pledged the Federation’s continued support to take cricket to the next level in Nigeria.

title: U-17 WWC: Flamingos face Mexico as Africa’s last four battle for quarter-final tickets
body:
Nigeria will lead Africa’s challenge in the Round of 16 at the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup after qualifying alongside Ghana, hosts Morocco and Kenya.
The Flamingos finished second in Group B with six points, the highest tally among Africa’s five representatives, and will face Mexico after winning two of their three group matches.
Nigeria recovered from an opening 2-1 defeat to Poland with victories over Puerto Rico (2-0) and DPR Korea (3-1) to secure their place in the knockout stage.
Ghana also advanced automatically after finishing second in Group C with four points. Following a 3-0 defeat to Norway and a 3-3 draw with Brazil, the Black Maidens beat Canada 2-0 to set up a Round of 16 meeting with Argentina.
Hosts Morocco and Kenya qualified as two of the four best third-placed teams, finishing their respective groups with three points each.
Morocco opened with a 4-0 win over New Zealand but lost to Germany and Argentina. They will now face DPR Korea as they seek to extend their home campaign.
Kenya, meanwhile, recovered from losses to China and the United States with a 4-0 win over Samoa. The result secured their progression and a Round of 16 clash with Japan.
Zambia were the only African representatives eliminated at the group stage, finishing fourth in Group D without a point. They lost 5-0 to Japan, 3-2 to Venezuela and 1-0 to France.
Nigeria’s clash with Mexico on Thursday, 29 October, presents the Flamingos with an opportunity to build on their strong finish to the group stage. Ghana will look to carry their winning momentum into their encounter with Argentina.
Hosts Morocco face DPR Korea after conceding nine goals in their final two group matches, while Kenya must overcome Japan to keep their campaign alive.
With four African teams in the last 16, the continent has several chances to advance. Consistency, defensive organisation, and clinical finishing will be crucial as they seek quarter-final spots.
Tunde Eludini is a graduate of the Obafemi Awolowo University Ile-Ife, Nigeria where he studied International Relations. He is a Senior Correspondent coordinating the sports section for PREMIUM TIMES. Twitter : @tundeyeludini

title: Tinubu: Lion at home, lamb abroad?
body: We should begin where we must. President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has his virtues. For one, he is not given to petty vindictiveness as former President Obasanjo too often was. Tinubu has not been involved in any open political fights with governors or lawmakers as Obasanjo did. Instead, he appears generally forgiving and conciliatory, having brought several of his fiercest political critics into his government. Also, unlike many of Nigeria’s previous leaders, Tinubu did not come to office by accident, nor was he enthroned by anyone. He arrived office by sheer personal grit, itself an unusual thing in Nigerian political leadership at that level. Now, the average Nigerian president is a very powerful person. How they wield that power, however, is the key difference between one president and another. Tinubu is no average Nigerian president. He sits above his party and the nation, in a way that no president has done since 1999. Nigerian ruling parties are characterised by internal dissent, fictionalism, and opposition, which serve as a check on a president’s power, often better than can be expected from the official opposition parties. There is no such thing under Tinubu. By removing Senator Abdullahi Adamu as Chairman of the APC within weeks of assuming office, Tinubu made that point clear early on. Now, a personal anthem, “On your mandate we shall stand”, rings out at the mention of his name among officials and party faithful because everyone gets the message. The President also has an iron grip on his cabinet, the national assembly, the governors, the security agencies, anti-corruption agencies, and as the rumours go, the courts, and perhaps INEC too. From 1960 to date, the National Assembly, particularly, has never been this plaint to a president, often passing executive bills in less than 48 hours, even before some members had a chance to read it. By removing officials without cause or notice, he has signalled that even the most favoured appointees can get the sack. He has induced the defection of all but one or two governors to his party, in name or at least in function. Criticism from the media, civil society, or labour has been blunted, if not outrightly buried, save for a few notable exceptions. All of this leaves no one in doubt that Tinubu is the lion in Nigeria’s political jungle. Yet, Tinubu’s power is not backed by authority in that specific Weberian sense. behind this image of an all-powerful president still lies something cosmetic. Obasanjo came to office with the charisma of a former head of state and national hero at multiple points in the country’s history. Buhari was the face of a political movement with more than 10 million loyal votes each election for nearly 20 years. Jonathan came to office by accident, but once there, he commanded the unflinching loyal of nearly as many Nigerians as Buhari. Tinubu has none of these. His personal anthem may ring out loud, but it rings hollow still because the President’s political coalition is held together not by popular admiration or ideological belief in his programme, but by the depth of his pocket or the fear of losing one’s job in a Nigeria that has grown much harsher economically for nearly all but those in government. Tinubu is quite possibly the most politically vulnerable president facing re-election since 1999. But the opposition lacks money, and the mass public lacks food. A clear majority of Nigerians may well not be happy with the current conditions in the country, but they lack the energy—or the hope—to put up a sustained fight. And then, there is the not-so-small matter of the incompetence of the government, although in a different sense than Nigerians are used to in their government. Few governments in Nigerian history have initiated as many far-reaching economic reforms from the start than the Tinubu administration: complete fuel subsidy removal, wholesale naira devaluation, free university tuition converted loans, high electricity tariffs, tax reforms, and so on. Yet, the government clearly appears to lack the capacity to make a genuine success out of its own reforms, and by the end of the first year, all the swagger Tinubu came into office with had gone. Far-reaching economic reforms generate costs and benefits, and thus, winners and losers. Who are the winners and losers of the fuel subsidy removal policy, for example? How can the policy be tweaked to spread the gains or mitigate the pains? How can we build a genuine political coalition strong enough to sustain the reforms beyond this administration? These are the questions that would engage a more competent reformer, and they would answer them with evidence-based policy adjustment, rather than a shouting match with catholic Bishops. Yet, beyond infographics that have little bearing on reality, you would struggle to find a serious policy paper or further policy actions produced by this government since 2023. But it is in foreign policy that the real character of the current government is laid bare. Tinubu maybe a lion at home, but he is lamb on the world stage. As Daily Trust reported two weeks ago, Nigeria has agreed to a U.S “America First Global Health Strategy” framework that effectively amounts to signing off our sovereignty for a transactional aid. Under this agreement, Nigeria would provide U.S companies with our health data on short notice. The companies manufacture drugs and vaccines they will resell back to us at huge profits, effectively turning Nigerian sickness into a cash cow for America. And all of these under a health minister who has talked the most about developing local manufacturing capacity in the healthcare sector. Mortgaging Nigerian sovereignty—for a pittance or for free—is the norm under this government. Virtually every single foreign policy action this government has taken since 2023 has been either on behalf of or to the benefit of foreign countries, principally France, Britain, the United States, Israel or Saudi Arabia. Nigeria itself gets almost nothing out of its foreign policy engagements. Under Tinubu, Nigeria has sparred with two neighbours on behalf of France; sold our tax administration to the same country without any receipts; accepted a controversial asylum-seeker deportation deal with Britain; joined a Red Sea Alliance with Saudi Arabia that has no discernible benefit for us; and watched almost helplessly as the United States promotes a narrative that directly threatens our fragile peace. A bolder government has several counter measures for each of these foreign policy engagements. France can train our tax officials, rather than hand over our entire system to them. A more strategic government should be capitalising on the current conflict in Europe and the Gulf to do deals that would pump out more of our oil and gas reserves. An Obasanjo, Yar’Adua would have more forcefully rejected the narrative of Christian genocide the U.S is self-servingly imposing on us to fleece our resources like rare minerals and colonial healthcare deals. A bolder and more sovereignty-inclined Tinubu would at least get the nation to convene an open hearing on this issue, at least to take matters into our own hands. For Tinubu’s foreign policy, however, the problem is not just the decisions or actions, but the approach and the attitude behind it. The government’s foreign policy actions are almost always conducted in complete secrecy. This means that the President may well be entangling Nigeria into unfavourable or unnecessary foreign arrangements that might be difficult for future leaders to repair. At a time when many countries on the continent are flexing self-determination muscles, the so-called Giant of Africa is crouched on the ground licking foreign what-not. Most disturbing of all, President Tinubu appears to believe that once an idea, policy, or agreement has the approving stamp of a western government or western aligned international institutions like the World Bank and IMF, then, such a policy or idea is automatically also good for Nigeria. Ours appears unable or unwilling to go against any foreign governments or institutions. This is perhaps the sole reason the government has stuck to a punitive fuel subsidy removal that no one in the administration can point to the gains with any confidence. The government may yet be returned this election. But some things cannot be left unsaid.

title: UK, Nigeria Collaborate on AI Governance, Digital Transformation
body: Emma Okonji The British High Commission in Nigeria has reaffirmed the UK’s commitment to supporting Nigeria’s digital transformation agenda following a successful suite of events and engagements during a recent visit by the British Standards Institution (BSI) to Nigeria. Central to the visit, was the successful delivery of an Executive Workshop on Artificial Intelligence Governance and Standards in partnership with the National Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics (NCAIR) under the UK Government’s Digital Access Programme. The four-day workshop brought together senior government leaders, regulators and technology practitioners to strengthen Nigeria’s capacity for responsible AI adoption, governance and oversight. It explored practical approaches to implementing internationally recognised standards for AI governance, risk management, assurance and accountability, while supporting Nigeria’s ambition to become a leading AI economy in Africa. Speaking at the event, First Secretary for Economic Partnerships and Digital at the British High Commission, Grace Bell, highlighted the strategic importance of standards in unlocking the benefits of emerging technologies. She said: “Artificial Intelligence presents enormous opportunities for economic growth, innovation and social development. However, realising these benefits requires the right governance frameworks, strong institutions and trusted standards that can underpin safe, secure and responsible adoption.” National Coordinator of the National Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics (NCAIR), Dr. Olubunmi Ajala, highlighted the importance of strengthening national capability for AI governance and thanked the UK government and BSI for their continued support. He said: “Together, we have moved beyond theoretical conversations about emerging technology to build genuine, sovereign institutional capacity.”

title: Cash Outside Banks Hit N4.92tn, Now 89% of Currency in Circulation
body: Nume Ekeghe Cash held outside Nigeria’s banking system stood at N4.92 trillion in September 2026, accounting for 89.23 per cent of the N5.52 trillion currency in circulation, the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) Money and Credit Statistics has revealed. Analysis of the data showed that despite the increase in cash outside banks over the past year, its share of currency in circulation declined slightly, while cash accounted for a smaller proportion of the country’s expanding money supply. A breakdown showed that currency outside banks rose by 10.26 per cent year-on-year from N4.47 trillion in September 2025 to N4.92 trillion in September 2026. On a month-on-month basis, it increased by one per cent from N4.87 trillion in August. However, the proportion of currency in circulation held outside banks fell to 89.23 per cent in September from 90.15 per cent in the corresponding period of the previous year. This suggests that although the amount of cash outside the banking system increased, its share of total currency in circulation moderated. Currency in circulation, which represents cash held both within and outside banks, rose to N5.52 trillion in September from N4.95 trillion a year earlier, an increase of 11.40 per cent. It also increased by 1.50 per cent from N5.44 trillion in August. A comparison with the beginning of the year showed a different trend. Currency outside banks declined from N5.25 trillion in January to N4.92 trillion in September, representing a contraction of 6.28 per cent. Currency in circulation also fell from N5.73 trillion to N5.52 trillion over the same period, a decline of 3.73 per cent. The figures indicate that the amount of cash outside banks remained substantial, even as the total value of currency in circulation stayed below its January level. Another notable development was the declining weight of physical cash relative to the broader money supply. Currency in circulation represented 3.76 per cent of broad money supply, measured by M3, in September 2026, compared with 4.21 per cent in September 2025. Broad money supply increased to N146.60 trillion in September from N117.78 trillion a year earlier, representing a rise of 24.47 per cent. The faster expansion of broad money relative to currency in circulation explains the decline in cash’s share of the monetary aggregate. On a month-on-month basis, currency in circulation accounted for 3.91 per cent of broad money supply in August, before declining to 3.76 per cent in September, as M3 increased from N139.09 trillion to N146.60 trillion.

title: Majiyagbe: AACN Unlocking Critical Factors in Financing Nigeria’s Growth Trajectory
body: The Association of Asset Custodians of Nigeria recently held its flagshipAnnual Nigerian Investors Day in London, attracting a global audience who had the opportunity of gaining critical insight into Nigeria’s economic reforms. Presidentof the association, Mr. Babatunde Majiyagbe, said the primary goal of the conference is making Nigeria one of the most compelling destinations for investment in Africa remains unshaken. Congratulations on your successful outing at this year’s investors’ conference organized by your group, the Association of Asset Custodians of Nigeria (AACN) in London, of which you are president. What would be your key takeouts from the event? Let me start by noting that since inception of the Annual Nigerian Investors Day by the Association of Asset Custodians of Nigeria 15 years ago, our cardinal objective has remained to promote portfolio investments in Nigeria by providing a platform through which investors can gain critical insight into the Nigerian economy, as well as an opportunity to engage with appropriate government officials. This year’s event met those fundamental objectives. We had in attendance almost 100 enthusiastic participants, including global custodians, fund managers, international brokers and dealers as well as domestic and foreign institutional investors. A major takeaway that undoubtedly galvanized participation was the presence of the Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Mr. Taiwo Oyedele. With his presence, attendees had the benefit of hearing directly, as the Honorable Minister provided details of ongoing economic reforms by the Federal Government, the expected outcome and possible future interventions and policies. Present also at the conference was the Executive Commissioner, Operations at the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) – Mr. Bola Ajomale, who represented both the commission and the Director General, Dr Emomotimi Agama. Other principal players in the Nigerian capital market, the Chief Executive Officer of the Nigerian Exchange Limited, Mr. Jude Chiemeka represented by Mr. Abimbola Babalola; Mr. Shehu Shantali, CEO, Central Securities Clearing Systems (CSCS) Plc, Mrs. Onome Komolafe also from CSCS, among others. We also had the leadership of the Angolan Stock Exchange; BODIVA (Bolsa de Dívida e Valores de Angola) as we look towards future collaborations between Nigeria and Angola. With the aforementioned heavyweights in attendance, practically every facet of the Nigerian economy and capital market in particular were meticulously dissected to the delight of the participants and global audience. Of course, the participants also had the opportunity to air their views and challenges. But, I can confidently declare that the principal purpose of the gathering was accomplished with resounding success. We remain grateful to the Global Custodian Banks who consistently engage us in looking for ways on how Nigeria will continue to attract capital in a more sustained manner. What factors underscored your choice of theme for the event, Nigeria’s Next Chapter: From Reforms to Returns? Our choice of theme was to highlight the primacy of the capital market as the foundation of capital formation from which economic development spins. So, it was imperative to examine various vital aspects of the Nigerian capital market in terms of the current standing, interventions, direction, among other policies. As you are aware, Nigeria remains a destination of interest as far as Africa and the emerging markets are concerned. The growing appetite that foreign portfolio investors have in the Nigerian capital market and economy in general makes it expedient to engage them diligently and provide information and data that would enhance their confidence in the economy. A key motivation for investment in any sector or economy is the hope of earning impressive returns. Nobody would dabble into a venture in an environment that is risk prone. So, a clear understanding of the environment where you want to invest your money or capital is very vital. That is why we were delighted by the remarkable participation of leaders of the capital market at the conference, not just by showing their physical presence but also by providing crucial answers to very salient issues and reforms. As you know, foreign investors are crucial to the Nigerian economy. They contribute immensely toward improving liquidity in the capital and money markets. Also, they are a major supplier of foreign exchange which helps to ensure the stability of the local currency, the naira. As asset custodians, we see ourselves as ambassadors of Nigeria and share in the responsibility of protecting the interests of these investors in the market.The expectations of such investors include effective regulations and development of market infrastructures that result in better asset protection, automation and straight through processes. We occupy a unique position in the investment ecosystem. We see capital before it arrives, while it is invested, and when it leaves. Few participants are therefore better positioned to gauge investor sentiment and confidence. What we are seeing today is not a retreat from Nigeria, but a desire for greater policy predictability and sustained reform momentum. Thankfully, our very resourceful speakers and panelists did justice to the theme during the event. Indeed, officials of the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Nigerian Exchange Limited spoke glowingly about the readiness of the Nigerian capital market to continue to unlock transformative opportunities for individual and institutional investors. Does the reality support such propositions? Every leading capital market continuously evolves, and Nigeria is no exception. Even in the most developed economies, regulation and market enhancement remain ongoing priorities. In course of the presentations and fireside chats, the speakers made it abundantly clear that the primary objective of the Nigerian capital market remains to create a well-functioning financial system that enables the economy to exploit its growth potential. This in turn would benefit those investing in the economy. The process is an ongoing one and will always vary depending on developments in the wider macroeconomic environment. As a player in the industry, I am conscious of concerted efforts being made to create an ideal setting for capital formation. I commend the regulators such as the Central Bank of Nigeria and the Securities & Exchange Commission for their untiring efforts. Of course, investors understand that the quality of leadership of the capital market has an impact on direction of growth and development of any capital market. Nonetheless, performance could be impacted by the happenings in the macroeconomic environment. You announced the association’s determination to strengthen the annual forum as a must-attend event for showcasing Nigeria’s economic credentials and crystallizing its economic development . What are we expecting in the next edition bearing in mind that a general election is scheduled to hold early next year? Usually, at the end of each conference, we devote time to reflect on what transpired. The goal is to enable us re-examine issues and developments identified at each conference and put those into context when determining the direction of the next edition. So, regarding the next edition, we shall articulate the highlights of this year’s event and previous editions before determining next year’s focus. The Honourable Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy graciously suggested that our next discussion should focus on reinvestment as the natural progression from reforms to returns. The conversation should increasingly move beyond whether reforms are taking place to whether those reforms are improving Nigeria’s competitiveness relative to alternative investment destinations. Capital has choices. Our objective should be to make Nigeria one of the most compelling destinations for investment on the continent. This review process is embedded in our association’s workflow and helps ensure that no critical issue is overlooked. We remain confident that the association will continue to provide a valuable platform for investor engagement irrespective of the electoral cycle. AACN clocks 17 years this year. What milestones will you be celebrating and what are your plans for the future? I would rather describe our journey so far as interesting and fulfilling. At the onset, there were just a few members and that naturally constrained our influence and visibility. Also, quite a large number of operators in the capital market did not understand the role of a custodian. But today everything has changed, the awareness level and market landscape have grown considerably. Our membership has also increased significantly. Local and foreign clients now engageour services and we facilitate a significant proportion of investment transactions in the market. Also, through our market advocacy initiatives, we have contributed to the development of the Nigerian capital market in general. In the past, we had collaborated with the Central Bank of Nigeria in developing the guidelines for custody of money market and other fixed income instruments; and the electronic certificate of capital importation (e-CCI). We have also worked with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on securities lending and borrowing; the mandatory appointment of custodians to registered Collective Investment Schemes as well as privately managed products. The list is almost endless. Going forward, we will continue to contribute our quota towards advancement of our industry. We shall continue to engage regulators, financial market infrastructures and market operators for the benefit of investors and the country as a whole. Additionally, we intend to continue to enlighten the market of our role so that a significant portion of investors begin to use and benefit from our services. Yes, there is a huge retail market that remains untapped. With deft interventions, we will remain relevant in the economic scheme of things. How would you assess the current state of the Nigerian custody industry considering its role as enabler of investment decisions? Remember that i nvestor confidence remains the most pivotal element in capital market vibrancy ! One maxim that readily comes to my mind each time a question like this arises is: The financial market which encompasses equities, fixed income, money market, and commodities will inevitably experience shocks whenever something disrupts the macroeconomic environment. But it would always rebound. The logic behind this conviction is that the marketplace never closes completely because there will always be someone willing to stake his money even after a crisis or any other adversity. Confidence in the capital market is derived from the existence of an attractive operating environment characterized by safety, stability and certainty. Government, regulators, market infrastructures and industry participants all play important roles in sustaining such an environment. Capital ultimately chases trust. Nigeria’s greatest opportunity is not only to improve returns but to continually strengthen trust in its institutions, policies and markets. As confidence grows, investment will naturally follow. The custody market in Nigeria is in a stable state and optimism steadily increasing. From its humble beginnings over 30 years ago, it has evolved into a major subsector in the capital market, attracting commensurate expertise associated with its role. Today, our industry is linked to the worldwide network of asset protection and investment. From the perspective of an expert and banker, what is your reading of the current Nigerian economic landscape? Yes, it is good to seek foreign investment. But have we looked at the policy situation in the country? Nigeria’s economy is at a pivotal point in its development journey. The reform agenda being implemented by government demonstrates a willingness to address structural issues that have constrained growth for many years. From foreign exchange reforms to fiscal measures and efforts to strengthen market institutions, the direction of travel is clearly towards building a more competitive and sustainable economy. For investors, policy matters just as much as opportunity. While Nigeria offers compelling investment opportunities, investors also look for policy consistency, regulatory certainty and macroeconomic stability. Encouragingly, recent reforms have signalled a commitment to improving these fundamentals. It is important to note that foreign investment and domestic investment are mutually reinforcing. International investors gain confidence when they see local businesses continuing to invest, expand and create jobs. Therefore, alongside attracting foreign capital, continued support for domestic enterprise remains critical. While foreign capital remains important, some resilient economies are built on strong domestic pools of long-term capital. Pension assets, insurance funds, mutual funds and retail investment participation will continue to play a critical role in financing Nigeria’s growth story. My assessment is one of cautious optimism. The reforms underway are laying foundations for long-term growth, and if pursued consistently, they will further strengthen Nigeria’s position as one of Africa’s most attractive investment destinations. It is also important to recognize that foreign investment and domestic investment are closely linked. A foreign investor often takes comfort when local investors are expanding, reinvesting, and demonstrating confidence in the economy. Therefore, alongside attracting international capital, there should be continued emphasis on creating conditions that enable Nigerian businesses to thrive, expand, and create jobs. Overall, my reading of the Nigerian economy is cautiously optimistic. The policy direction signals a commitment to long-term economic sustainability and growth. The key priority going forward is maintaining consistency, allowing reforms sufficient time to deliver results, and ensuring that the policy framework remains stable, transparent, and supportive of both local and international investors. If these elements are sustained, Nigeria is well-positioned to unlock its considerable economic potential and strengthen its attractiveness as an investment destination. You have been a major player in the Nigeria capital market for quite a while. What is the difference in the capital market today compared to when you entered the market three decades ago? Like I indicated previously, market development is a continuum that takes into account the evolution of society and happenings in the macroeconomic environment. As human needs evolve with time, there is also the attendant necessity to adjust to satisfy those needs. Two key drivers of change in the capital market are technology and trends. The capital market was once a place where a few presumably discerning individuals would approach their stockbrokers or the stock exchange to buy shares of a few well-known companies. They earn a well-cherished dividend. Even the traditional structure of banks was one in which the individual walks into the banking hall to deposit or withdraw money. It was like a cashier’s world. But not anymore! What we are witnessing today is the result of advancements in new technology. It has unleashed a wide gamut of processes, products, services, disruptions and more. It has opened participation in the market to practically everyone and democratized trading processes with the participation of retail investors in the capital market. Look at core banking; the traditional structure of banks was no longer adequate in delivering personalized services instantly, especially in far-flung rural communities. You no longer have to establish branches everywhere with every customer visiting to make transactions. Fintechs have taken over such functions by using technology to deliver financial services to almost all classes of customers with speed and efficiency. This is disruptive innovation in the digital age. Several tech startups have grown to become global brands and making invaluable contributions to economic growth. Ultimately, I believe that competition would inherently engender technological innovation that would determine the success or failure of any business or sector. In addition, effective regulation is imperative to ensure adherence to ethical conduct and stability within the financial ecosystem. Nigeria’s story is often told through the lens of its challenges. Investors, however, must also consider its fundamentals: a large and entrepreneurial population, deepening financial markets, growing institutional capital, abundant resources and a demonstrated willingness to undertake difficult reforms. Our responsibility as market participants is to convert these fundamentals into sustained investment outcomes. I believe Nigeria’s next chapter can be one of inclusive growth, deeper capital formation and greater prosperity.

title: Turkish Flag Joke Sparks Online Meme War with China
body: A viral meme featuring a cat and a SpongeBob SquarePants character has sparked an online battle between Chinese and Turkish users on X, drawing in participants from Japan, Taiwan and other countries. The feud began on October 19 with a joke about Turkey’s national flag and quickly escalated into an exchange of memes, historical claims and nationalist arguments. Thousands of social media users have joined the debate, with some dubbing it the “First Twitter War” — a tongue-in-cheek reference to an international conflict fought entirely through online posts.Chinese and Indian users have also found common ground amid the online exchanges. How the China-Turkey meme war began The controversy gained traction on October 19, when Turkish X account ArdaaZz (@BarkinResmii), which had around 85 followers at the time, posted a meme featuring a cat wearing a straw hat and a thin moustache.A Chinese X user responded with an image comparing Turkey’s national flag to Patrick Star, the pink starfish from SpongeBob SquarePants .The image showed Patrick descending by parachute beside the Turkish flag, jokingly suggesting that the cartoon character had inspired its crescent-and-star design.The comparison quickly drew reactions from Turkish users, who responded with memes of their own. Why the Great Wall of China entered the feud Turkish users escalated the exchange with memes claiming that ancient Chinese dynasties built the Great Wall of China to defend themselves against Turkic warriors.Chinese users countered by highlighting the geographical distance between modern-day Turkey and the Great Wall.The argument also drew on historical references. Successive Chinese dynasties built and expanded defensive walls over centuries to protect their territories against northern groups, including the Xiongnu and later nomadic forces.However, the claim that the entire Great Wall was built specifically to repel modern-day Turks oversimplifies a complex history spanning many centuries. Japan and Taiwan join the online battle The meme war soon moved beyond national flags and historical disputes. Participants began comparing economic conditions, cultural achievements and even IMDb ratings, while Japanese and Taiwanese users joined the increasingly international exchange.Some accounts also created fictional alliance maps, portraying countries as rival teams in an imaginary online conflict.The so-called “First Twitter War” remains an online feud between individual users rather than a conflict between governments. Nevertheless, the exchange has blended humour with nationalist arguments, turning a joke about Patrick Star into a viral contest involving history, geography and national identity. title: Despite fresh Houthi attacks, Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh airport resumes flights
body: Flights resumed at Riyadh’s international airport on Sunday following a series of deadly attacks on the facility that saw it closed for two weeks, even as Yemen’s Houthis targeted the country with strikes. King Khalid International Airport’s website showed several domestic and international flights scheduled on Sunday, including arrivals to the kingdom from Dubai, Paris and Cairo. The renewed operations at the airport came as explosions rattled Riyadh early Sunday, after a text message was sent to residents warning of a hostile threat targeting the city. The airport closure was a major blow for Saudi Arabia, with the kingdom’s flagship investment conference postponed until 2027 as residents scrambled to find alternatives to enter and exit the country. The prestigious motor sport race, the Dakar Rally, also added its name to a long list of events to be cancelled, postponed or relocated amid the fallout from the war. Saudi officials did not provide additional information when asked by AFP about the scope of the renewed operations at the airport. But the tracking website Flightradar24 showed a small number of flights had departed, though the vast majority were cancelled. The Houthis have carried out waves of strikes on the airport, including an attack this month that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree earlier warned that Riyadh airport was still “unsafe” and a “military target”. “The Yemeni Armed Forces warn all international, regional and local airlines – as well as staff and travellers – against using King Khalid Airport in Riyadh, as it is unsafe and serves as a military target for our forces,” he said. “The Saudi regime shall bear the consequences of any operations at the airport.” ‘Everything is shaking’ Later on Sunday, Saree said Saudi Arabia had struck Yemen dozens of times over the previous 24 hours. “During the past 24 hours, Saudi warplanes launched 56 airstrikes and missiles targeting civilian objects in the governorates of Hajjah, Lahj, Amran, Saada, Al-Jawf, Taiz and Ibb using F-15 and “Typhoon” planes that took off from the bases of Khamis Mushait and Taif, and missiles from Najran,” he said on X. As operations at the airport restarted, Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis arrived in Riyadh and met with Saudi de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. During the meeting, Mitsotakis “responded favourably to the kingdom’s request to keep the Patriot system in Saudi Arabia, given the current challenging circumstances”, his office said. Greece has deployed a battery to operate the US-made Patriot air defence system in Yanbu, a major oil export hub on the Red Sea coast. The SPA news agency added that the two leaders “underscored the critical importance of safeguarding the security and integrity of international maritime corridors and ensuring the safe and continuous flow of energy supplies to global markets”. Earlier, the Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said it intercepted at least 10 ballistic missiles. The fighting erupted after a years-long truce between the Houthis and Yemen’s Riyadh-backed government fell apart. “The bombardment has been very heavy since this morning – may God keep us safe. Everything is shaking because of the explosions,” one resident in Khamis Mushait told AFP on Sunday on condition of anonymity. The kingdom’s civil defence agency later said two people were injured in the south by falling debris, also reporting damage to several buildings and vehicles. Images released by the official Saudi Press Agency showed a building with part of its upper facade destroyed, exposing metal rods. Another image captured large windows shattered, with shards of glass strewn across the pavement and part of the road. Attack warning AFP journalists in Riyadh heard three explosions in the early hours of Sunday, with residents receiving alert messages for a “hostile aerial threat” and urging them to stay in a safe place. The warning came as the Saudi-led coalition said it had downed a ballistic missile launched by the group towards the capital, as well as two drones in the Riyadh area. “Air defences intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward Riyadh,” the coalition posted on X. Later Sunday morning, the coalition said its forces intercepted a cruise missile fired by the Houthis at the kingdom’s southern city of Khamis Mushait. Attacks appeared to target areas across the south, with warnings also issued for Abha city along with areas in Taif, Namas and Jazan. The attacks came after the Houthis said they targeted three Saudi airports, including one in Riyadh, energy installations, a pipeline and an air base within 24 hours.

title: Nigeria-Cyprus bilateral relations enter new era as Amb. Ufochukwu presents credentials
body: Diplomatic and economic ties between Nigeria and Cyprus reached a significant milestone on Friday as Her Excellency Nkechi Linda Ufochukwu, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of Nigeria to Israel with concurrent accreditation to Cyprus, officially presented her Letters of Credence to Cypriot President Nikos Christodoulides at the Presidential Palace in Nicosia. Ambassador Ufochukwu pledged to aggressively deepen bilateral cooperation and expand trade, educational, and political channels between Abuja and Nicosia during her tenure. Welcoming the new envoy, President Christodoulides praised Nigeria’s pivotal role in driving regional integration, economic growth, and stability across West Africa. He reaffirmed Cyprus’s commitment to forging an ambitious partnership with Africa’s largest economy, targeting key sectors including trade, investment, higher education, and political dialogue. “Cyprus and Nigeria share ties of friendship born out of shared historical experiences, common principles, and enduring links between our peoples,” President Christodoulides stated, emphasising his government’s readiness to address shared global challenges bilaterally and multilaterally. The renewed alliance is expected to unlock commercial pathways for Nigerian businesses, expand opportunities for students and professionals, and catalyse incoming Cypriot investment. Following the ceremony, Ambassador Ufochukwu is slated to begin high-level engagements with Cypriot policymakers, business leaders, and the Nigerian diaspora to translate this diplomatic momentum into tangible economic outcomes.

title: Gabon restores social media after eight-month ban
body: Gabon restored access to social media on Saturday, its media regulator said, after an eight-month suspension that sparked widespread criticism. The High Communication Authority (HAC) pulled the plug on social networks, including Facebook and TikTok, on February 17, blaming content posted online for stoking conflict and division in society. The crackdown came as Gabonese President Brice Oligui Nguema faced a wave of social unrest less than a year after his election. “The HAC has decided to lift the suspension of social media platforms,” spokesman Jean-Claude Franck Mendome said in a statement read on television. Facebook and TikTok, the most-used platforms in the central African nation, as well as YouTube and Instagram, were shut down, while WhatsApp was on and off. Some people still managed to access social networks via a VPN, with provider Proton reporting a 60,000-per cent increase in downloads of its VPN tool the day after the ban came into force. The HAC said the suspension aimed to “allow the government to adapt its legal framework to better regulate social media”. The government now requires social media users to provide formal identification, effectively ending online anonymity. The HAC said it was working with Meta – which owns Facebook and Instagram – as well as TikTok and YouTube to “improve content moderation” on those platforms. Gabon’s opposition had slammed the social media ban as an abuse of power. Former prime minister Alain-Claude Bilie-By-Nze, who has been in prison since April over alleged abuse of trust and fraud dating back to 2008, was one of the policy’s most vocal critics. Critics have cited the social media ban and Bilie-By-Nze’s arrest as examples of a repressive climate in Gabon, shattering hopes that President Nguema’s rise to power would lead to democratic change. The 2023 coup that brought the military general into office ended 55 years of rule by the Bongo family, sparking scenes of jubilation, and he was elected president in April last year. (AFP)

title: Recapitalisation: Mutual Benefits Strengthens Position as Protection Partner for Nigerians
body: Ebere Nwoji With huge success recorded in the recent recapitalisation exercise in the insurance industry, Mutual Benefits Assurance said it has been well positioned for sustainable growth while strengthening its role as a trusted protection partner to Nigerians. Commenting on the development, Managing Director/CEO of Mutual Benefit, Femi Asenuga said: “For over three decades, Nigerians have entrusted Mutual Benefits with what matters most to them. This includes their families, businesses, assets and financial futures. That trust is both our greatest privilege and our greatest responsibility. Our recapitalisation strengthens the foundation from which we can serve our customers better, innovate more meaningfully and build sustainably for the future.” According to him, for Mutual Benefits, the significance of recapitalisation goes beyond meeting a regulatory requirement. It provides a stronger platform to deepen investment in products, technology, customer experience and service capabilities, while responding to the evolving financial protection needs of Nigerians. He said the company’s portfolio spanned to Non-Life and Life Assurance solutions covering key areas including Motor, Home, Marine, Fire & Special Perils, Travel and Group Life Insurance, among others, as well as a suite of solutions supporting children’s education, retirement, savings and investment. “As customers increasingly expect greater convenience and accessibility, Mutual Benefits is also accelerating its digital transformation, strengthening its online platforms and customer journeys to make insurance easier to access and interact with. The company is equally placing renewed emphasis on customer experience, with a focus on improving engagement and service delivery across the customer journey,” Asenuga stated. He further stated that the ambition of Mutual Benefit was not simply to grow bigger, but to become better for the customers. He added, “Every investment we make in technology, people, products and service must ultimately translate into greater convenience, stronger value and greater confidence for the people and businesses we serve.”

title: Okupe: Soulsight Framework ‘ll Help to Turn Brands into Engines of Business Growth
body: The Chief Executive of Soulsight Africa and innovator of the Brand-Led Business Growth framework, Joko Okupe, in this conversation with Ayodeji Ake, explains why organisations must move beyond conventional branding and turn their brands into engines of business growth by aligning strategy, leadership, people and customer experience with brand for improved business performance and sustainable growth Soulsight Africa recently unveiled its Brand-Led Business Growth (BLBG) framework. What informed its development, and why do you believe organisations need a different approach to building brands and achieving growth? Having been involved in branding and communications for over 20 years, we have observed a fundamental challenge in many businesses and this is the gap between what organisations promise through their brands and what they are equipped to deliver. This gap erodes brand strength, which in turn impairs growth. First, many organisations treat branding as a communications function rather than an integral part of business strategy. An organisation may have an attractive identity, a compelling brand story and strong visibility, but if its people, processes, products and operating systems are not aligned with its brand promise, the business may struggle to deliver the value customers expect, which depletes customer trust and confidence in the brand. Many businesses, who have built strong brands through substantial investment in branding, marketing, advertising, public relations, brand visibility and a whole gamut of other initiatives, still struggle to leverage the strength of their brandto build better businesses for greater growth. At Soulsight Africa, we believe that brand and business should be inseparable activities. The brand must inform the organisation’s strategic priorities and the capabilities required to deliver value consistently. All of these put together, birthed the BLBG Framework, which is a structured approach to aligning business strategy, business operations, leadership, organisational culture, customer experience with the brand, using the brand as an engine to drive business growth. Our objective is to help organisations move beyond visibility and ask a more fundamental question: are we creating and delivering the value our brand promises, and is that value supporting our business objectives? Many organisations already have branding strategies, business plans and marketing departments. What distinguishes the BLBG framework from conventional approaches, and what is the brand–business growth Gap it seeks to address? The distinction lies in the relationship between these activities. Conventional branding often concentrates on positioning, identity, reputation and communication, while business strategy focuses on growth, resources, operations and performance. Both are important, but they can become disconnected when the brand promise is not reflected in how the business actually operates. We describe the resulting disconnect as the Brand–BusinessGap. It is the gap between what a brand promises, what the business delivers, what customers experience and what the market ultimately rewards. Consider a company that promises exceptional customer service but has inefficient processes, poorly coordinated service channels or employees who lack the authority and resources to resolve customer problems. Its communications may create expectations that the business cannot consistently deliver. Similarly, a company may position itself as innovative without investing in the product development capabilities, technology or organisational culture needed to support innovation. BLBG encourages management to examine these inconsistencies and address their underlying causes. Rather than automatically responding to weak commercial performance with more advertising, leaders should investigate whether the challenge concerns the value proposition, product relevance, operational efficiency, employee capabilities or customer experience. The framework therefore, positions the brand as a strategic business asset, capable of improving the business and not simply a marketing tool. It helps organisations keep the promise made to the market by ensuring that internal capacity is built to deliver that promise. From your explanation, this framework follows six stages: Discover, Define, Design, Align, Activate and Grow. How do these stages work together to help an organisation move from strategy to measurable business outcomes? The six stages provide a holistic, structured pathway from understanding the business challenge to implementing initiatives designed to support growth. Discover involves examining the organisation, its market, customers and the opportunities or challenges affecting performance. It establishes the basis for understanding where the business stands and what may be preventing it from achieving its objectives. Define clarifies the business opportunity, positioning, value proposition and brand promise. The organisation must understand the value it intends to create, the customers it seeks to serve and how it intends to distinguish itself in the market. Design focuses on developing the brand, customer experience initiatives and organisational capabilities required to translate the value proposition into practical action. Align is particularly important because it connects leadership, people, culture, processes and systems with the organisation’s strategic priorities. A business may have an excellent strategy, but without the appropriate organisational capabilities, execution becomes difficult. Activate focuses on implementing the agreed strategy and initiatives, while Grow concentrates on advancing the organisation’s growth objectives. The stages are interconnected. Discover and Define establish the strategic foundation; Design and Align prepare the organisation to deliver; Activate translates the strategy into action; and Grow focuses attention on the organisation’s growth objectives. The framework is not intended to replace financial planning, operational management or other established business disciplines. Rather, it provides an overarching approach for connecting them to the organisation’s promise and the outcomes it seeks to achieve. What practical benefits can business leaders expect from the BLBG framework to improve performance? The first benefit is strategic clarity. Organisations need to understand the value they want to create, the customers they want to serve and the capabilities required to compete effectively. A clearly defined value proposition can help management make more focused decisions about products, investments and priorities. The second benefit is organisational alignment. BLBG encourages leadership, marketing, operations, human resources, technology and customer service to work towards a common strategic direction, pointed by the brand promise. When these functions reinforce the same value proposition, the organisation can reduce inconsistencies between itspromises and actual delivery. The third is improved customer experience. Customers encounter a brand through its products, services, employees, systems and processes. When these elements are aligned, the business is better positioned to deliver consistently, strengthen customer confidence and build lasting relationships. The fourth is better-informed resource allocation. Management can examine whether its investments in brand building are supported by the operational capabilities needed to generate value. It can also identify where improvements in processes, products, technology or employee development or re-orientation may be necessary. Finally, the framework encourages organisations to connect brand strategy with measurable business objectives, which may include customer acquisition and retention, higher conversion rates, customer satisfaction, market penetration, revenue growth etc. These benefits are not automatic. Commercial outcomes depend on the relevance of the organisation’s offering, market conditions, leadership commitment and the quality of implementation. BLBG provides a structured approach to improving alignment and decision-making, but the organisation must still execute effectively and measure its results. One of the framework’s central arguments is that brand-led growth cannot be left to the marketing department. What does this mean for leadership, organisational culture and employee performance? It means creating a consciousness that involvement and commitment of the entire organisation is required to fulfil the brand promise. Marketing may communicate that a company is reliable, innovative or customer-focused, but operations, employees, technology and management decisions determine whether customers experience those attributes. Leadership therefore, has to make the brand promise relevant to how the organisation is structures, enabled and managed. Strategic priorities, resource allocation, performance expectations and organisational culture should reinforce the value the business intends to deliver. Human resources, for example, has a role in developing the employee capabilities and behaviours needed to fulfil that promise. Operations must provide effective processes, while technology should enable the organisation to deliver value more efficiently. Employees need to understand how their work contributes to the customer experience and the wider business objectives. This is why the Align stage matters. It encourages organisations to examine whether their people, culture, processes and systems support the promise. For a business that competes on service quality, it is not enough to communicate a commitment to excellent service. Employees must have the orientation, training, tools and authority to deliver the excellence promised. For an organisation that promises innovation, its culture and investment priorities must support the development and implementation of new ideas. The CEO and Board must ensure that these elements reinforce one another. Brand-BLBG, is therefore a leadership and management responsibility, not simply a marketing initiative. How can organisations translate the framework into measurable performance, particularly when business leaders are under pressure to justify investments and demonstrate returns? Measurement must begin with the organisation’s strategic objectives. There is no single indicator that applies to every business, because different organisations face different challenges and pursue different growth priorities. A company seeking to improve customer retention, for example, must track repeat purchase patterns, customer churn and satisfaction levels. An organisation pursuing market expansion should monitor customer acquisition, product adoption, market penetration and revenue performance levels. A business seeking to improve operational delivery may examine service turnaround times, error rates, customer complaints or process efficiency. The important point is to connect these measures to the changes the organisation is implementing. Management should establish a baseline, define the outcomes it wants to achieve, assign responsibilities and review progress constantly. Businesses must also distinguish between activity and results. The number of campaigns executed, advertisements placed or people reached does not, by itself, demonstrate that the organisation has improved its commercial performance. BLBG encourages leadership to examine whether brand-related initiatives contribute to the broader objectives of the business. This requires collaboration between marketing, finance, operations, customer service and other functions so that brand strategy is evaluated alongside the indicators that matter to the organisation. The framework does not eliminate the need for financial analysis, market research or operational performance management. It actually accentuates their importance. It encourages organisations to connect these disciplines to a coherent strategic direction and assess whether the value promised to customers is being delivered effectively. Looking ahead, why should future-facing organisations embrace BLBG and what is your message to business leaders seeking sustainable growth in an increasingly competitive environment? Future-facing organisations must continually reassess their value propositions, capabilities and relationships with the markets they serve. Customer expectations change, competitors introduce new offerings, and technological developments can alter how value is created and delivered. Organisations cannot assume that yesterday’s positioning or operating model will remain sufficient for tomorrow’s challenges. BLBG encourages leaders to examine whether their brand promise remains relevant and whether the organisation has the capabilities to deliver it. This is particularly important when entering new markets, introducing products, repositioning an established business or responding to changing customer expectations. The framework also has broader implications for institutional effectiveness. While commercial businesses may measure success through revenue, profitability, market share and customer retention, public institutions must focus on public value, service quality, accessibility and the achievement of policy objectives. The principles of alignment and delivery can inform both contexts, although the measures and implementation must reflect their different mandates. Ultimately, our focus at Soulsight Africa is to advance a more integrated understanding and execution of brand strategy and business performance. The brand defines the value an organisation promises; its strategy establishes how it intends to create that value; and its people, processes and systems determine its ability to deliver. Our message to business leaders is straightforward: do not separate the promise your brand makes from the performance your organisation must deliver. Sustainable growth requires more than visibility. It requires a relevant value proposition, organisational alignment, disciplined execution and the ability to demonstrate results. That is the thinking behind BLBG. Our mantra is stronger brands. Better business. Greater growth.

title: 2023 Lagos defeat wake-up call – Obanikoro
body: The Lagos State chapter of the All Progressives Congress (APC) says it has set a target of nearly three million votes for President Bola Tinubu and the party’s 2027 governorship candidate, Dr Kadri Obafemi Hamzat, vowing that it would not allow a repeat of its defeat in the state during the 2023 presidential election. Director-General of the PBAT-KOH Campaign Council, Senator Musiliu Obanikoro, disclosed this on Sunday at a press conference in Ikeja, Lagos, where he also announced plans for the unveiling of Hamzat’s governorship manifesto ahead of the 2027 election. Obanikoro said the party had learnt important lessons from the 2023 election, when the Labour Party presidential candidate, Peter Obi, defeated Tinubu in Lagos, securing 582,454 votes against the APC candidate’s 572,606 votes. Describing the outcome as a wake-up call, the former minister said the APC had since taken steps to strengthen its membership base and improve its mobilisation ahead of the next general election. “You know what it means to wake up a hungry tiger? It’s bad news. That’s exactly what the opposition have done. They have woken up a hungry tiger, and it is going to roar.” He said the APC had registered about one million members in Lagos, adding that the party expected a substantial proportion of them to turn out and vote during the election. Explaining how the party arrived at its projected votes, Obanikoro said: “So, in a worst-case scenario, let’s say 70 or 80 per cent of our members come out, which they will do. That is already 800,000 votes. “Let’s assume they will bring a minimum of one voter. That is 1.6 million votes. No matter how much some of these opposition members hate us, there are APC lovers in this state of ours who, come rain or shine, will come out and vote for us. “Modestly, we are looking at almost three million votes.” Obanikoro said the campaign council would intensify grassroots mobilisation across the state to achieve the target. The campaign council also announced that the APC would unveil Hamzat’s manifesto on Friday, October 30. Obanikoro explained that the document would focus on sustaining development while addressing challenges facing residents across the state. “Our campaign is anchored on two principles: continued shared progress and inclusivity,” he said. He added that the campaign believed Lagos residents should have a voice in shaping the state’s future, irrespective of their backgrounds. “Continuity is not about doing things the same way simply because they have been done before. It is about protecting what works, correcting what needs improvement and building on existing progress,” he said. “Lagos cannot afford to lose valuable experience or abandon the foundations on which its considerable development has been built. We must move forward with clear plans and practical solutions.”

title: Korea reaffirms strategic partnership with Nigeria
body: The Republic of Korea has reaffirmed its commitment to driving sustainable development, technological innovation, and youth empowerment in Nigeria as an equal partner. Speaking at Korea’s National Day reception on October 23, 2026, in Abuja, Korean Ambassador to Nigeria H.E. Jeong Yoan highlighted Korea’s historic transformation from a war-torn nation in 1953 to a global economic power. He emphasised that mutual support and international solidarity were central to Korea’s survival and remain key to its foreign policy. “We do not come with all the answers. We come as friends and partners, ready to share, learn, and grow together,” Ambassador Jeong stated, identifying Nigeria’s vibrant youth population as its greatest asset. Underlining this developmental synergy, the Ambassador pointed to key collaborative milestones, including the recently ground-broken Abuja Centre for Entrepreneurship—a joint project by KOICA, SMEDAN, and UNDP designed to nurture local start-ups. Additionally, he said Korea’s Smart School initiative alongside UBEC has reached over 8,000 Nigerian children and trained 300 educators, while KOICA-FAO partnerships continue to pioneer green agricultural jobs. He said major Korean conglomerates including Daewoo E&C, LG, Samsung, Hyundai, and Solpia also continue to deepen their footprint in Nigeria’s energy, manufacturing, and digital technology sectors. Reflecting on the cultural bridge uniting both nations—from K-pop and Korean dramas to Afrobeats and Nollywood—Ambassador Jeong called for global unity, grounding the bilateral relationship in shared human values: “One Heaven. One Earth. One Humanity.”

title: Mixed reactions trail Emir of Katsina’s address to Tinubu’s campaign council
body: The Emir of Katsina, Dr. Abdulmumini Kabir Usman’s address to President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s Presidential Campaign Council during its recent visit to the Katsina Emirate has sparked mixed reactions among residents and political observers. While some have described the monarch’s remarks as a courageous act of patriotism and a demonstration of responsible leadership, others believe he crossed the boundaries of his traditional institution by publicly addressing prominent political figures on sensitive political issues. The reactions gathered momentum days after an audio recording of the visit went viral on social media. In the recording, the Emir was heard urging political leaders to prioritise citizens’ welfare, promote peaceful coexistence, and address the challenges facing Nigerians. The remarks attracted attention because they appeared to depart from the usual formalities associated with such visits, with the monarch delivering a blunt message about the responsibilities of political leaders to the people they seek to govern. The Emir, who received the delegation led by Governor Dikko Umaru Radda and the Director-General of the campaign council, Senator Abdul’aziz Abubakar Yari, stressed that politics should not be reduced to hostility, confrontation, or personal attacks. He urged members of Tinubu’s 2027 campaign council to place the interests of citizens above political ambitions, warning that leaders would ultimately be held accountable for how they discharged their responsibilities. In the audio, the Emir told Yari that political leaders must support the people if they expected divine assistance in their own endeavors. “DG, you are on board now, and as a community leader, I must say the truth whenever I open my mouth.
