You have to assist the people for God to assist you, whoever you are. We should know that God will surely ask us someday,” he said. The monarch also called for unity among political leaders in the North-West, questioning the region’s response to persistent insecurity and the difficulties faced by farmers. “We should unite ourselves, especially the North-West. North-West, where are we? Different forums here and there, and yet we are denied the opportunity to go to our farms, and we keep quiet. No, we have to talk,” he said. During the visit, Yari said the delegation was at the palace to pay homage to the Emir and seek the support of the Katsina Emirate and the people of the state for Tinubu’s re-election bid. Katsina-based political analyst, Dr. Bashir Ibrahim Kurfi, described the Emir’s address as an expression of responsible and responsive leadership, saying it reflected what many Nigerians expected from traditional rulers. Kurfi said the monarch had identified fundamental issues requiring urgent attention, particularly insecurity, economic hardship, and the need to improve citizens’ living conditions. He noted that while many residents welcomed the address as a timely reminder that public welfare should remain the priority of elected officials, others interpreted it as a significant intervention in the political conversations surrounding the 2027 general elections. According to him, the Emir’s emphasis on the welfare of ordinary Nigerians reflected the concerns of people struggling with the rising cost of living and insecurity. He added that political leaders should devote more attention to delivering on their promises than engaging in struggles for political power. However, a politician, Ibrahim Ahmad KK, said he did not consider the substance of the Emir’s remarks wrong but disagreed with the manner and timing of their delivery. KK argued that publicly addressing prominent political figures in such a manner was inappropriate, adding that the Emir could have convened a private meeting to raise the same concerns. “He has the power to call for a meeting secretly and address all the valid issues he raised that day, but addressing top public figures publicly like that is wrong, and this is my personal belief,” he said. He added that the incident could reignite discussions about the relationship between traditional rulers and politicians, particularly the limits of public criticism by traditional institutions. In contrast, Malam Abubakar Ahmed, spokesperson for Senator Ahmad Babba Kaita, the African Democratic Congress (ADC) governorship candidate in Katsina State, said the Emir’s remarks accurately reflected the realities facing the region. He said the monarch’s position aligned with the ADC’s advocacy for people-centred governance across the North-West. “ADC is going to run a people-centred government, and that is why all the ADC candidates in the North-West have agreed to run a consecutive government approach to issues simultaneously in order to be able to tackle those pressing issues affecting the people of the region,” he said. Despite the differing interpretations of the Emir’s address, the debate has drawn attention to the expectations of citizens regarding leadership, accountability, and the role of traditional institutions in public affairs. For supporters of the monarch’s intervention, his message was a necessary reminder that the welfare and security of the people should take precedence over political interests. For his critics, the controversy centres on how such concerns should be communicated to political leaders.

title: Spotify uploads lyrics for Dolly Parton’s Welsh version of Jolene in Irish
body: Spotify mistakenly uploaded the lyrics to Dolly Parton’s Welsh version of her hit Jolene in Irish. The song was recorded before her death on 25 August and is a collaboration with Welsh singer-songwriter Bronwen Lewis and Parton’s niece, Jada Star. The version has parts sung in English and Welsh, but the lyrics on the digital audio streaming service Spotify showed the language as Irish. Spotify removed the Irish lyrics after the BBC approached it for comment. The BBC asked Spotify when it uploaded the single and lyrics, when it noticed the error, and when it would be replaced, but it did not respond. The lyrics on Spotify have been removed since the BBC approached the service for comment The single came out on 9 October , and is the second posthumous release from Parton – who was of Welsh descent. The legendary country artist won 10 Grammy Awards, sold more than 100 million records worldwide, and wrote more than 3,000 songs over a seven-decade career. Jolene was released in 1973 and is about the fear she might lose her husband, Carl Dean, to a red-headed bank clerk who had flirted with him early on in their marriage . It was was nominated for a Grammy in 1974, gave Parton her second number one single on the Billboard Hot Country Singles chart and her first foray into the main Hot 100 chart (60). It has since earned more than one billion streams on Spotify, and many famous singers have covered Jolene. Lewis and Star recorded their parts in the UK, while Parton recorded her parts in her studio in Nashville The Welsh version came about after Lewis, from Neath, translated the country classic and posted it on social media. Then Star, Parton’s niece, reached out and suggested recording Jolene in Welsh with Lewis – and Parton joined too. In 2008, during a concert at the Cardiff International Arena, Parton reportedly revealed her Welsh ancestry to fans in the crowd. The star revealed that one side of the family, from Parton’s mother, Avie Lee Owens, was initially believed to be from Conwy. Following the singer’s death, research by staff at Conwy Council’s archives suggested Parton’s ancestors were from Machynlleth, in Powys, not Conwy as previously thought.

title: Zenith General Insurance Donates Learning Items to Supports Students
body: Ebere Nwoji Zenith General Insurance Limited, has donated school bags, exercise books and mathematical sets to students in six selected schools in Lagos State. In doing this, the company said it was combining educational support with a message urging young people to embrace preparation, perseverance and purpose as pathways to success. The company said the initiative, implemented under its Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) programme, sought to ease the financial burden on parents, improve students’ access to essential learning materials and promote inclusive education, particularly among children in public schools. Speaking during the presentation, the General Manager, Zenith General Insurance Limited, Mrs. Dolapo Olatayo Talabi, challenged students to recognise their present academic experiences as the foundation for future achievements. She engaged students at Alimosho Junior Grammar School, in an interactive session around the theme, “Prepared for Success,” encouraging them to develop habits that would position them to take advantage of opportunities. She described the classroom, textbooks, assignments and everyday choices students make as essential parts of their preparation for the future. Explaining the rationale behind the donation, Head of Corporate Communications at Zenith General Insurance Limited, Hashim Okunbor, said the company regarded children as the foundation of the nation’s future and considered investment in education essential to sustainable community development.

title: ADC, APM knock APC flag-off campaign
body: Opposition political parties, the African Democratic Congress (ADC) and the Allied Peoples Movement (APM), have accused the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) of “staging a disappointing Northwest flag-off,” saying Nigerians will reject Tinubu in 2027. However, the Publicity Secretary of the APC, Felix Morka, said the comments by the two political parties did not deserve any response from him. “Nigerians watch the flag off and know what happened,” he simply said. The ADC Presidential Campaign Council described the APC rally in Kaduna as a “monumental disappointment,” accusing the ruling party of relying on rented crowds, empty seats, and recycled promises. Director of Media and Publicity of the ADC-PCC, Kola Ologbondiyan, said an event intended to demonstrate the APC’s political strength across the Northwest had instead exposed what he described as the “party’s declining public acceptance.” Ologbondiyan alleged that the APC mobilised people from the seven states of the Northwest and beyond, with payments reportedly ranging from N50,000 to N100,000 per person, yet the stadium, with a capacity of 5,000, remained sparsely occupied. “For a rally billed as the Northwest zonal flag-off, what we witnessed was a shameful spectacle. Despite the alleged mobilisation of crowds from across the zone and beyond, the stadium remained scantily filled, with empty seats everywhere,” he said. The ADC-PCC Director also criticised President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s reported commissioning of road projects at the event, describing the exercise as troubling and questioning the administration’s claims of performance. In the same vein, the APM and the Makinde-Daura Presidential Campaign Organisation (MDPCO) said President Tinubu’s flag-off in Kaduna is another carnival of deceit, “recycled lies, and brazen political fraud.” Richard Ihediwa, Director of Strategic Communications of the Makinde/Daura campaign, said the campaign was a desperate attempt to “sell repackaged failed promises and fresh illusions to the North, a region battered by insecurity, crushed by hardship, and betrayed by President Tinubu’s government, which is now on its fours begging for re-election.” The campaign said as usual, “President Tinubu chorused ‘prosperity, continuity and progress,’ yet offered the North and Nigerians no convincing reasons they should endure more of the hardship his administration has presided over since May 2023.” The MDPCO also condemned the attempt by the president to blame the “opposition for the pervasive hunger and poverty in the land. What a bold evasion of responsibility from a failed President who plunged Nigeria into an unprecedented economic crisis, such that she now competes alongside Afghanistan in the axis of failed nations.” It added, “President Tinubu also promised young Nigerians ‘a better tomorrow.’ The same youths whom his incompetent management of the economy threw into joblessness, desperation, and disillusionment. Some of them who made bold to protest against hunger in August 2024, including minors, were hauled from the streets of Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Gombe, among other states, to Abuja, cramped into detention, and charged with treason. “The Kaduna comedy of absurdities came to a peak when a Commander-in-Chief who claimed to have dealt with insecurity in the North could not visit a claimed project site, but resorted to commissioning an inherited, partially constructed 88 km stretch of the Abuja-Kaduna Highway inside the stadium holding the rally. It is either the President was afraid of insecurity or fears the boiling volcano of popular anger against his failed government. “At this point, nobody is still in doubt that the APC presidential campaign is headed for the rocks and nothing can save it. The decision to flood Kaduna with security forces during the flag-off is a telling response to the growing rejection by the people. A government confident of its popularity does not need to turn a campaign rally into a security operation.”

title: Outrage as APC youth leader shares new Prado SUVs to mobilisers, then deletes post
body:
Many Nigerians have criticised the National Youth Leader of the All Progressives Congress (APC), Dayo Israel, after he shared a video showing seven new Toyota Land Cruiser Prado SUVs presented to selected party youth leaders, before deleting the post about three hours later.
Mr Israel posted the video on his X account on Sunday , saying the vehicles were intended to support the mobilisation activities of the beneficiaries ahead of the 2027 general elections.
“Today, I presented brand new 2026 Prado to my committed selected youth leaders to aid their election mobilisation activities,” he wrote.
He also expressed gratitude to First Lady Oluremi Tinubu for her “continuous support to the party structure” under his leadership.
“The party is supreme and that supremacy will show in our action in this election period – we will deliver polling unit by polling unit,” he added.
The post triggered angry reactions from Nigerians, many of whom questioned the reported cost of the vehicles and the decision to deploy such resources for political mobilisation amid the economic hardship in the country.
One X user, @iamchibuzoree, questioned the contrast between the vehicles and the financial difficulties facing public institutions and ordinary Nigerians.
The user cited the inability of the government to meet some demands of health workers and provide adequate support for citizens struggling with high living costs.
“A government that told us there is NO MONEY to pay striking doctors. NO MONEY to pay nurses, lab scientists, medical personnel who are saving lives with empty stomachs,” the user wrote.
“SUDDENLY found money to buy a CONVOY of brand new 2026 Toyota Land Cruiser Prado SUVs?”
The user estimated that the seven vehicles could cost more than ₦1 billion and argued that the money could instead support healthcare, food assistance and student loans.
Another user, @ogundamisi, said the video illustrated what he described as a growing disconnect between political leaders and Nigerians facing economic hardship.
“For context, @dayoisrael is the youth leader of Nigeria’s ruling APC, the same party whose president, Tinubu, is asking Nigerians to endure more suffering,” the user wrote.
The user also criticised the display of expensive vehicles while many Nigerians struggle to meet their basic needs.
Similarly, @ayshaHamman questioned the opportunity cost of the vehicles, asking how many primary healthcare centres could be established with the money spent on the seven vehicles.
The user’s question drew attention to the potential alternative uses of the money, although the actual purchase price of the vehicles and the source of funding were not disclosed in Mr Israel’s post.
Another user, @ukocarter, criticised the development against the backdrop of the economic difficulties facing Nigerians, while @harmlessHQ drew a comparison between the vehicle presentation and President Bola Tinubu’s remarks on the country’s economic challenges.
“Yesterday in Kaduna, Tinubu was blaming the opposition for the hunger and hardship in the country. Today, Dayo Israel, APC youth leader is casually dashing out 2026 Prado SUV to his fellow youth leaders,” @harmlessHQ wrote.
Mr Israel deleted the post about three hours after publishing it, following the criticism on X.
However, the deletion did not end the controversy, as screenshots and recordings of the video continued to circulate on the platform.
Mr Israel did not provide a public explanation for deleting the post as of the time of this report.
It was also unclear who paid for the vehicles, their exact purchase price and whether they were acquired with party funds, privately donated or provided through another arrangement.

title: W’African Insurance, Technology Conference Holds in November
body: The 2026 edition of the insurance meeting with technology providers tagged Insurance Meets IMT 5.0, will hold Novermber 2026. The IMT, is Annual West Africa’s leading insurance and tech conference organised by marketing and corporate communication expert, Odion Aleobua. According to the organiser, at this year’s edition, Andela and Flutterwave Co-Founder, Iyin Aboyeji has been slated to deliver the keynote address. He will speak on Capital, Code and the Race to Nigeria’s First Insurance Unicorn.” The organisers said Aboyeji would examine how a better-capitalised industry, paired with scalable technology, could place insurance on the platforms Nigerians already use, and what it would take for a homegrown insurer to reach that milestone. According to the organisers, Aboyeji was selected for his vantage point as both founder and investor, having helped creation of two of the continent’s first technology unicorns, and through Future Africa he continued to back founders solving hard problems across Africa.

title: Omosehin Tasks Insurers to Contribute Towards Bridging Infrastructural Deficit
body: Ebere Nwoji The Commissioner for Insurance, Mr Olusegun Ayo Omosehin, has urged insurance managers to contribute their quota towards bridging infrastructural deficit in Nigeria through sustainable risk management and local capital participation. Omosehin said insurers could do this through pool funds,infrastructure bonds and tailored risk guarantees which would position them as enablers of national development. Omosehin spoke at the 2026 National Insurance Brokers’ Conference and Exhibition in Abuja. While pledging NAICOM’s commitment to creating an enabling environment that encourages product innovation, capital growth, and market expansion, Omosehin said he expected NCRIB and its members to lead from the front by building strategic alliances across the banking, energy, manufacturing, and public infrastructure sectors. “I urge us all to view this conference as an opportunity to move beyond discussions and develop practical recommendations that will strengthen the brokerage profession, advance the implementation of NIIRA 2025 and position insurance as a more effective instrument for infrastructure financing and national development. “Let us work together to build an industry that commands public trust, delivers value to policyholders and contributes meaningfully to Nigeria’s economic aspirations”, he stated. At this year’s conference which has the theme “Insurance: Infrastructure Financing & National Development Agenda” , Omosehin stated that as Nigeria advances toward sustainable economic renewal and a multi-trillion-dollar economy, the imperative for long-term domestic capital formation and robust risk management mechanisms had never been clearer. Informing the insurance brokers of their critical role in this regard, the insurance Commissioner said brokers occupy a central and indispensable position within the Nigerian insurance ecosystem. According to him, as trusted risk advisors, intermediaries, and advocates for policyholders, brokers generate a significant portion of the total premium volume in insurance market.

title: Fitch revises Access, Zenith, UBA, GT, 5 others outlook to positive
body: Fitch Ratings has revised the Outlooks of nine Nigerian banks and two bank holding companies to Positive from Stable. Their Long-Term Issuer Default Ratings (IDRs) have been affirmed at ‘B’. The affected issuers are Access Bank Plc, Zenith Bank Plc, First HoldCo Plc (FHC), First Bank of Nigeria Ltd (FBN), United Bank for Africa Plc (UBA), Guaranty Trust Holding Company Plc (GTCO), Guaranty Trust Bank Limited (GTB), Fidelity Bank PLC, First City Monument Bank Limited (FCMB), Wema Bank PLC and Bank of Industry Limited (BOI). According to the UK-based firm, the Outlook revisions to Positive follow a similar action on Nigeria’s ‘B’ Long-Term IDRs on 9 October 2026 that reflects ongoing reform of the policy framework and Fitch’s increased confidence that momentum will not be disrupted by upcoming elections. The revision of the Outlooks on the Long-Term IDRs of Access Bank, Zenith Bank, FHC, FBN, UBA, GTCO, GTB, Fidelity Bank, FCMB and Wema Bank reflects Fitch’s view that the sovereign’s credit profile and Nigeria’s operating environment may become less of a constraint on the issuers’ standalone creditworthiness. The revision of the Outlook on the Long-Term IDRs of FHC and FBN is supported by the issuers having restored compliance with the total capital adequacy ratio (CAR) requirement. BOI’s Outlook revision reflects our view that the government’s ability to provide support to the policy bank may improve. The National Ratings of all the issuers and the Government Support Ratings (GSRs) of the eight commercial banks and two bank holding companies are unaffected.

title: Ex-PDP spokesman, Ikem joins APC
body: Former Cross River State Chairman of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), Venatius Ikem, has defected to the All Progressives Congress (APC). Ikem, who was PDP national publicity secretary, announced his decision at a defection rally in Obudu Local Government Area, said he was impressed by the reception he received from APC leaders and members since leaving the opposition party. Ikem said political disagreements should not be allowed to damage relationships among family members, friends and community leaders. “APC and PDP and all other political parties are not bad parties. It is we, the people, who are bad. Do not fight your brother over politics,” he said. The former PDP chairman resigned from the party about two weeks ago, citing internal divisions, lack of clear direction and leadership incoherence. He also questioned the rationale behind the party’s Rainbow Coalition. Ikem thanked Otu, the governor’s Chief of Staff, Dr Emmanuel Ironbar, and other APC leaders for facilitating his return to the ruling party. He said the defection offered an opportunity to rebuild political relationships and promote development in Obudu. An APC stakeholder from Ogoja, Ntufam Emmanuel Monjok, described Ikem’s defection as a setback for the PDP in the northern senatorial district, while another stakeholder, Ekpenyong Ekpenyong, from Calabar South, said the move could reduce political tensions in the area. However, the PDP has said Ikem’s resignation would not affect its stability or electoral prospects.

title: Stakeholders Saeek Expanded Financial Inclusion
body: Kemi Olaitan in Ibadan Government, financial services and technology stakeholders have examined ways to expand financial inclusion and improve access to digital financial services for underserved communities in Nigeria. The discussion took place in Ibadan, Oyo State, at TechConnect 6.0, an industry engagement organised by digital payments company, Interswitch to discuss the development of financial infrastructure and the growth of Nigeria’s digital economy. The event with the theme, “Built for What’s Next: Designing Adaptive Financial Infrastructure for a Dynamic Market,” brought together participants from the public and private sectors to examine how technology, shared infrastructure and collaboration could support businesses and widen economic participation. The Managing Director of Ilorin Innovation Hub, Temi Kolawole, while delivering the keynote remarks, highlighted the need for infrastructure and solutions that support innovation, business expansion and sustainable economic development. His address focused on the role of technology and collaboration in helping businesses respond to changing market conditions and take advantage of emerging opportunities. The Vice President, Business Innovation and Growth at Interswitch, Tyoyila Aga, on his part, said businesses need more than new technologies to respond effectively to changing customer expectations and market demands. The conversations also underscored the role of sustained collaboration in translating technological innovation into practical solutions that address real business and societal needs.

title: Stanbic IBTC Pension Managers Supports PenCom
body: Ebere Nwoji Stanbic IBTC Pension Managers, has thrown it’s support behind the National Pension Commission (PenCom) as it hosts the inaugural National Pension Week from Monday, 26 to Friday, 30 October 2026. The Pension week which has the theme “Building a Ssecured Future together’, aims to deepen public understanding of pensions, promote financial inclusion, encourage retirement planning and strengthen confidence in Nigeria’s pension system. According to the National Pension Commission, ( PenCom) , the organiser, the five-day initiative will engage different segments of society through youth engagement; SME engagement and fair; Retiree fair; National Pension Summit and media briefing; creating opportunities for conversations around pension inclusion, retirement security and the future of Nigeria’s pension industry. Speaking on the initiative, Chief Executive Officer of Stanbic IBTC Pension Managers, Olumide Oyetan, said: “We commend PenCom on the introduction of National Pension Week and its commitment to deepening pension awareness and inclusion across Nigeria. We believe that when people plan confidently for the future, they are better positioned to pursue opportunities, navigate life’s transitions and achieve meaningful growth.” He said building that future begins with understanding the importance of pensions, planning early and taking deliberate action.

title: Maccido’s Enduring Legacy of Peace, 20 Years After
body: By Senator Iroegbu Some deaths are mourned and gradually consigned to history. Others leave a void that time cannot completely fill, not merely because of the circumstances surrounding them, but because of the extraordinary lives they brought to an end. Twenty years after the tragic ADC Airlines Flight 053 crash of October 29, 2006, the death of His Eminence, Alhaji Muhammadu Maccido, the 19th Sultan of Sokoto and President-General of the Nigerian Supreme Council for Islamic Affairs (NSCIA), remains a profound loss to Nigeria. The ill-fated aircraft crashed shortly after departing Abuja for Sokoto, claiming 96 lives, including the Sultan, his son, Senator Badamasi Maccido, his grandson, and several other distinguished Nigerians. The Sultan had travelled to Abuja to participate in a Presidential Forum on Education. Tragically, a journey undertaken in the service of national development became his last. Yet, two decades later, what remains remarkable is not merely the magnitude of that tragedy, but the enduring relevance of the man whose life it prematurely ended. I had the privilege, as a young journalist, of documenting Sultan Maccido’s life and legacy. One particularly memorable experience was my exclusive interview with former President Shehu Shagari, at his residence in Sokoto in October 2008, two years after the tragedy. Shagari’s testimony was especially profound. He had taught Maccido at Sokoto Middle School in the 1940s, maintained a longstanding relationship with him, and subsequently appointed him Presidential Liaison Officer in Sokoto State during the Second Republic. He also lost his own son, Abdulrahman, in that unfortunate crash. A few people were therefore better positioned to speak about the Sultan’s character, leadership and humanity. What struck me most during our conversation was Shagari’s repeated emphasis on Maccido’s humility, patience, tolerance and willingness to consult others before taking decisions. “He hardly does anything without seeking or consulting those who know,” Shagari said, stressing: “He does not rush or dictate things.” According to him, those who misunderstood the Sultan’s disposition sometimes considered him too quiet or excessively peaceful. But Shagari offered a remarkable observation: “He acts more than he speaks.” That statement has remained with me over the years. It captures the essence of a leader, who understood that influence does not necessarily require intimidation; that wisdom often resides in restraint, and that genuine authority is earned through conduct rather than demanded through position. Born in 1926 in Dange, Sokoto, Muhammadu Maccido was a direct descendant of Sheikh Usman dan Fodio and the son of Sultan Abubakar III. Even his name carried a touching story of hope and survival, having been given following the loss of earlier children in the family. His education, administrative training and exposure to governance in Nigeria and abroad prepared him for decades of public service. He served in traditional administration and politics before eventually ascending the Sokoto throne in April 1996. His journey to the throne was not without challenges. Following his father’s death in 1988, his succession was set aside under the military administration. Rather than allow disappointment to consume him, he demonstrated the patience and restraint that would subsequently define his reign. For ten years, he presided over one of Africa’s most influential traditional institutions during a particularly delicate period in Nigeria’s political and religious history. The return to democratic rule, controversies surrounding the implementation of Sharia law, and recurring religious tensions in parts of Northern Nigeria demanded leadership that could reconcile competing interests without compromising deeply held convictions. Admirably, Maccido rose to that responsibility through dialogue, moderation and an unwavering commitment to peaceful coexistence. He understood that religious devotion should strengthen humanity rather than diminish it, and that the responsibility of spiritual leadership extended beyond one’s immediate religious constituency. Through it all, the Sultan spoke the language of moderation. He worked with Christian leaders to keep tempers from boiling over, knowing that religious conviction need not become hostility towards others. In 1998, he became the first Sultan of Sokoto to meet a Pope, when John Paul II visited Abuja. In 2003, parts of the North boycotted polio immunisation on the strength of baseless rumours, and he lent his authority to the vaccine. There is no doubt that his interventions in interfaith relations, public health campaigns against polio and HIV/AIDS, and educational development demonstrated his appreciation of traditional institutions as instruments of national progress. It was, therefore, fitting that former President Olusegun Obasanjo described him as a man who lived and died for peace. Beyond his public responsibilities, Maccido was remembered for his simplicity, generosity and accessibility. Those close to him recall a man of simple tastes. Accounts of his household feeding numerous people daily reflected a tradition of hospitality that placed communal welfare above personal accumulation. His household fed scores of people every evening, largely from grain sent as gifts. His life showed that leadership is measured by how authority is used in the service of the people, not by the distance between ruler and ruled. When he changed parties on the eve of the Second Republic, he took care to return the money he had received from the party he left. He respected people, in Shagari’s words, “whatever their profession”, and never let his position make him overbearing. If he had a fault, his old teacher said, it was being accommodating “sometimes to a fault”. But such qualities are particularly instructive today as Nigeria continues to grapple with terrorism, banditry, communal violence, religious intolerance, political polarisation and the growing weaponisation of misinformation and disinformation. So, 20 years after his demise, what does Sultan Maccido’s example mean for Nigeria today? We confront terrorism and communal violence, and banditry now stalks the very Sokoto countryside he loved. Religious intolerance persists, and disinformation spreads faster than ever. Our public life increasingly rewards loudness over wisdom and confrontation over consensus. Maccido proved that a leader could be influential without being intimidating, and courageous without being confrontational. He showed that one could be deeply religious without being intolerant. He knew that peace is more than the absence of conflict. It is the deliberate cultivation of justice, trust and mutual respect. Regrettably, even Sokoto and its surrounding communities, which once benefited from the Sultan’s stabilising influence, now confront security challenges that threaten livelihoods, social cohesion and peaceful coexistence. Therefore, at a time when public discourse increasingly rewards confrontation over consultation, noise over wisdom and political expediency over moral conviction, Sultan Maccido’s leadership offers a compelling alternative. He demonstrated that one could be influential without being overbearing, courageous without being confrontational, and deeply religious without becoming intolerant. His death also leaves an enduring lesson about institutional responsibility. The ADC tragedy reminds us that honouring departed leaders must extend beyond commemorative ceremonies to ensuring that preventable disasters do not recur. Aviation safety, regulatory accountability and the protection of human life must remain enduring national obligations. This, therefore, provides a second lesson, as it concerns how he died. For years, many of us lamented that Nigeria honours its dead without learning from their deaths. The Accident Investigation Bureau eventually published its findings: the crew took off into known adverse weather and failed to recover from wind shear. The Bureau called for better crew training and windshear alert systems at our airports, and reforms followed. Yet a report is only as good as the vigilance that follows it. We cannot honour our departed heroes through ceremonies alone while neglecting the lessons of how we lost them. Shagari’s own counsel was plain: we should not put all our eggs in one basket. Fortunately, His Eminence Sultan Muhammad Sa’ad Abubakar III, who succeeded him, has carried forward his legacy through interfaith dialogue and national unity efforts. The Sultan Muhammadu Maccido Foundation was established to preserve his ideals. That work matters. But the truest memorial is whether those of us who remain choose his way. That means listening, consulting and respecting the ordinary person. It means keeping faith with peace when division would be easier. For the Maccido family, this twentieth anniversary is undoubtedly a moment of profound remembrance, but also one of legitimate pride. Their beloved father, grandfather and patriarch bequeathed something far more enduring than titles, wealth or political influence: a good name, an honourable reputation and a lifetime of service to humanity. As I reflect on my encounter with President Shagari and the testimonies of those who knew the late Sultan intimately, one lesson remains unmistakable: history ultimately judges leaders not by the power they wielded, but by the lives they touched, the conflicts they prevented and the values they left behind. Twenty years after his passing, Sultan Muhammadu Maccido remains relevant because the virtues he embodied are precisely those Nigeria desperately needs today. He might have suddenly vacated his throne twenty years ago, but his place in the moral history of our nation remains permanently occupied. May Almighty Allah forgive his shortcomings, grant him Al-Jannatul Firdaus, comfort his family, and reward his contributions to Nigeria, Islam, peace, and humanity. Twenty years on, the Man of Peace is still teaching us. Ameen. *Senator Iroegbu is a journalist and a security and geopolitics analyst. He is Editor-in-Chief of Global Sentinel and Convener of the Geopolitics Series. senator.iroegbu@yahoo.co.uk

title: Why Oil Production, Asset Protection Matter to Nigeria’s 7% Economic Growth Target
body: Nigeria’s ambition to achieve seven per cent economic growth in 2026 will depend partly on its ability to increase crude oil production and protect the assets that sustain the industry. With crude oil exports accounting for a significant share of the country’s foreign exchange earnings, production losses arising from oil theft, pipeline vandalism and other disruptions could undermine efforts to boost revenue and expand the economy. As the government pursues its growth target amid domestic and external economic pressures, sustained oil production, effective asset protection and the role of Tantita Security Services Nigeria Limited in safeguarding oil infrastructure in the Niger Delta have become important considerations in the country’s economic outlook. Victoria Ojiako writes Nigeria’s ambitious seven per cent Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth forecast for this year will not be a tea party. The World Bank projects growth at 4.4 per cent, citing stronger resilience and better-than-expected economic performance. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) forecasts real GDP growth at 4.1 per cent;PwC Nigeria estimates economic expansion at 4.2 per cent, driven by improved crude oil production and key sector performance. The Federal Government is targeting around 4.68 per cent, while domestic groups like the Lagos Chamber of Commerce and Industry (LCCI) hold a more ambitious outlook of up to seven per cent. One thing is standing out in these projections. It is the role to be played by the oil sector, which continually holds the ace on the economic performance especially in revenue inflows. The growth projection will therefore be largely driven supported by several factors including higher crude oil production and stronger performance in dominant sectors. With crude oil export accounting for over 80 per cent on Nigeria’s FX earnings, the continuous flow of petrodollars will play a critical role in achieving the projected growth rate. Analysts said that sustaining investments and increasing exploration activities were critical to achieving the target and boosting the nation’s reserves. It is equally important to develop a comprehensive framework for increasing production, expanding reserves and enhancing the sector’s contribution to national economic development. Achieving these feats requires sustaining ongoing oil assets protection and security, infrastructure repairs as well as consistent industry reforms. The operations of Tantita Security Services Nigeria Ltd (TSSNL) in the Niger Delta region is also key. For many stakeholders, the Federal Government of Nigeria’s appointment of Tantita Security Services Nigeria Ltd (TSSNL) to protect oil assets and ensure peace and stability in the Niger Delta comes to play. President Bola Ahmed Tinubu had appointed Tantita Security Services Nigeria Limited (TSSNL) led by High Chief, Dr. Government Oweizide Ekpemupolo, alias Tompolo, to protect Nigeria’s oil assets in the Niger Delta region. The apointment was to enable TSSNL, through its security operations, support the national economy in getting the full benefits of oil resources. The TSSNL works in collaboration with other security outfits to achive its goals of securing oil assets and ensuring peace and stability in the Niger Delta region. Tantita’s operations had ensured the security of oil pipelines, ensuring the uninterrupted flow of petroleum resources, and ensuring that Nigeria migrated from a position of constant loss management to stability, planning, growth and development. The TSSNL operations have transformed the oil and gas landscape and allowed Nigeria to expand oil production quota and significantly cut rampant oil theft. Its track record in mitigating risks associated with oil pipelines has positioned it as a reliable partner in preserving Nigeria’s economic backbone. As stakeholders advocate for the continued collaboration with TSSNL, the imperative of securing oil infrastructure remains at the forefront of efforts to ensure the nation’s sustainable development. In the development process of any society, certain assets contribute to the advancement of society and its people. These assets ensure economic or monetary benefits for the people. These assets could be regarded as operating assets, non-operating assets or leased assets, among others. The impact of TSSNL’s operations was captured in a recent survey, with majority of the respondents attributing the de-escalation of security incidents in the Niger-Delta region to the pipeline surveillance operations executed by TSSNL. Tantita’s Milestone Achievements Tantita Security Services Nigeria Limited’s sustained efforts to protect oil pipelines and other critical infrastructure in the Niger Delta have contributed significantly to improved crude oil production, environmental safety and economic activities in the region, the company’s Media Consultant, Dr Paul Bebenimibo, has said. Bebenimibo, who is also Special Adviser to Tantita Chairman, Government Ekpemupolo, popularly known as Tompolo, made the disclosure while speaking on the sidelines of an award presented to Tantita by Blueprint Newspapers in recognition of the company’s contributions to pipeline security and national development. He said the award was further recognition that Tantita’s intervention in the Niger Delta was yielding tangible results, particularly in the fight against oil theft, pipeline vandalism and other illegal activities threatening Nigeria’s oil industry. According to him, since Tantita assumed a major role in pipeline surveillance and protection in 2022, the company has recorded significant progress in securing oil facilities across the Niger Delta. “Over the years, awards have been coming in, and that shows that Tantita is really doing the job very well,” Bebenimibo said. He noted that improved security around oil-producing communities had also created an environment conducive to the revival of legitimate economic activities, including fishing and farming. Bebenimibo said Tantita remained committed to supporting efforts to increase Nigeria’s crude oil production to 2.5 million barrels per day, stressing that effective protection of oil infrastructure was critical to achieving the target. He attributed part of the company’s success to the leadership and extensive knowledge of the Niger Delta terrain possessed by its chairman, Tompolo. According to him, Tompolo’s familiarity with the creeks and communities has enabled the company to develop strategies for effectively monitoring and securing oil infrastructure. Bebenimibo disclosed that Tantita had deployed modern technology, including drones, to monitor activities in the creeks and detect illegal operations. “We have acquired drones that are now picking up every illegal activity that is going on in the creek,” he said, adding that illegal operators were increasingly finding it difficult to evade the company’s surveillance efforts. Beyond pipeline surveillance, Bebenimibo said Tantita had placed significant emphasis on youth empowerment as part of its strategy to tackle insecurity and discourage young people from engaging in oil theft, bunkering and other criminal activities. He disclosed that more than 60,000 youths were currently employed by the company and paid monthly. He further said Tantita had introduced skills acquisition programmes and supported young people, women and other members of host communities through grants and other forms of economic empowerment. “Tantita is not just employing the youths. It is also giving them skills and promoting their businesses in the area by giving grants to youths, women and men,” he said. According to him, the combination of employment, skills development and community support had contributed to reducing criminal activities in parts of the Niger Delta. Bebenimibo also highlighted the growing relationship between Tantita and the media, describing journalists as important partners in communicating the company’s activities and promoting transparency around its operations. He disclosed that Tantita had built a correspondents’ secretariat in Delta State and was planning to extend similar structures to other states in the Niger Delta, as well as establish a facility for journalists at the national level. He said the initiative was part of the company’s commitment to strengthening its relationship with the media and ensuring that its activities and contributions to national development were properly communicated to Nigerians. Bebenimibo maintained that Tantita’s approach to security was not limited to enforcement, but also involved creating legitimate economic opportunities for youths and supporting host communities. He expressed confidence that sustained collaboration among security agencies, oil companies, host communities, the media and private security contractors would further strengthen the protection of Nigeria’s oil infrastructure and contribute to increased national revenue. Examining Nigeria’s H1 and H2 2026 Economic Outlook and reform journey, PwC Partner, Chief Economist and Lead Strategy & West Africa, Olusegun Zaccheaus; Partner, Clients & Market Leader, West Market, Pedro Omontuemhen and Director, Akolawole Odunlami agreed that macroeconomic conditions have continued to improve, supported by greater foreign-exchange stability, moderating inflation, stronger external reserves, higher revenue mobilisation and increased capital inflows. Insight from their “Unlocking Nigeria’s reform dividend From macroeconomic stabilisation to inclusive growth” revealed that the next step is to translate these gains into stronger household incomes, higher productivity, more jobs, and broader-based economic growth. “Nigeria entered the second half of 2026 from a stronger macroeconomic position. Real GDP grew by 3.89 per cent year-on-year in Q1 2026, supported by ICT, Finance & Insurance, Construction and Agriculture. Headline inflation moderated to 15.91 per cent in June, while the naira remained broadly stable at N1,379.68/US$. Gross foreign reserves rose by 38.3 per cent per cent year-on-year to US$51.46 billion in June, providing a stronger external buffer and supporting confidence in the foreign-exchange market,” they said. On the other hand, household affordability remains under pressure, private-sector financing conditions are still tight, and growth remains concentrated in a relatively narrow group of sectors. External risks have also increased, particularly through geopolitical tensions, energy-market volatility and weaker global growth. These factors will influence how quickly Nigeria can move from macroeconomic stabilisation to more inclusive and sustainable growth. Economic Outlook for H2 2026 Nigeria’s economic outlook remains positive, although the second half of the year will continue to be shaped by domestic and external risks. Inflation is expected to moderate, although food-price pressures, other supply-side shocks and pre-election spending could create upside risks. The naira is expected to remain broadly stable, supported by improved external buffers and foreign-exchange market reforms, but it remains exposed to shifts in oil prices, capital flows and domestic FX demand. Monetary policy is expected to remain relatively tight, with room for gradual rate reductions if the decline in inflation is sustained. Fiscal pressures may also persist as continued spending needs, the budget deficit, and government financing requirements place demands on available resources. The central task for Nigeria in H2 2026 is therefore not simply to preserve macroeconomic stability. It is to make that stability work more effectively for households and businesses. Progress will depend on lowering essential costs, expanding access to finance, improving infrastructure and productivity, and converting stronger investor interest into productive investment and jobs. Successfully navigating this next phase would require sustaining the operations of Tantita in oil assets protection. The move is expected to allow Nigeria to move beyond stabilisation and begin unlocking the broader reform dividend through stronger incomes, improved welfare and more inclusive economic growth. Improving domestic energy supply and distribution will help ease cost pressures on households and businesses. In April 2026, energy prices rose significantly y/y, led by diesel (+43.67 per cent) and kerosene (+34.12 per cent), followed by PMS (+23.69 per cent) and LPG (+10.43 per cent). Higher diesel and PMS prices raise transport, logistics and business operating costs, while increases in kerosene and LPG place more direct pressure on household energy spending. Expanding domestic refined-product supply and reducing distribution bottlenecks will help moderate energy costs, while sustained FX stability will limit imported cost pressures. Positive Outlook for Oil Production The Petroleum and Natural Gas Senior Staff Association of Nigeria (PENGASSAN) has promised to work closely with the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission (NUPRC) to unlock three million barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil by 2030. The new President of PENGASSAN, Comrade Bosun Olabiyi-Agoro, disclosed this while on a visit to the NUPRC corporate headquarters. In a statement signed by the Head, Media and Corporate Communications, NUPRC, Eniola Akinkuotu, also noted that the PENGASSAN President said inasmuch as the union is open to negotiations, issues bordering on the rights of workers to freely associate and join the union are non-negotiable. He added that issues surrounding contract staffing will be one of the key issues his administration will address.

title: 'MAGA conservatives' dream candidate': Trump administration eyes Orban as next UN chief - report
body: US President Donald Trump is pushing former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orban as a candidate for UN secretary-general, according to a report citing sources from three countries.US officials reportedly approached Orban with the proposal and encouraged him to enter the race. Although he expressed interest, he has not yet made a final decision on whether to run.According to the report, Washington believes, based on previous discussions, that Russia and China would also back Orban, potentially making him a joint candidate supported by all three powers.Officials from the US and another country said that when Washington, Moscow, and Beijing agree on an outcome at the Security Council, they can generally secure it.A US State Department official acknowledged that the proposal initially seemed far-fetched but maintained that Orban could garner substantial support on the council.The official estimated that eight of the Security Council's 15 members would "easily" back his candidacy, with the possibility of securing as many as 10 votes.However, the report did not cite any public commitments from countries to support Orban.A key question is how the UK and France, both permanent Security Council members with veto power, would respond.The report suggested that the two countries might refrain from blocking a candidate backed by a majority of the council and the other three permanent members. However, neither London nor Paris was cited as having taken an official position.From 'someone like Orban' to direct outreachAccording to the report, Orban's name repeatedly surfaced during discussions among US officials about their preferred candidate for the next UN secretary-general.American officials reportedly said they were looking for "someone like Orban," a suggestion their Chinese and Russian counterparts agreed with. Washington subsequently began considering whether to approach Orban directly.US officials then contacted Orban to gauge his interest in the position. According to the report, he was receptive to the proposal but expressed reservations related to his identity as a nationalist politician.Orban was also reportedly reluctant to announce his candidacy unless he was confident he could win. He declined to comment on the report.A State Department official described Orban as the "dream candidate for MAGA conservatives," citing his opposition to large-scale immigration, liberal nongovernmental organizations, and established centers of power within Hungary's judiciary and media.During his time in office, Orban repeatedly clashed with the European Union while cultivating closer ties with China.Trump endorsed Orban during Hungary's April elections, while Vice President JD Vance also took part in campaigning on his behalf.According to another source familiar with the initiative, Trump and Vance are expected to back Orban in the race for UN secretary-general if he decides to run.The source said any potential announcement would be delayed until after the US midterm elections.Orban's potential candidacy could spark controversyAn official from another country said the current field of candidates consists largely of figures with backgrounds in international bureaucracy or behind-the-scenes diplomacy.Orban, by contrast, would bring the approach of a political leader accustomed to exercising power, the official said.The US official echoed that assessment, arguing that Orban has the right ideological outlook, knows how to navigate opposition, and would not be intimidated by the UN establishment.However, the report also raised concerns that Orban's appointment could turn the UN secretary-general into a defender of Russian President Vladimir Putin and other authoritarian leaders.His ties to Moscow and Beijing, along with controversies surrounding his policies in Hungary, are expected to come under scrutiny if he enters the race.Emirati diplomat Lana Nusseibeh gains momentum in UN leadership raceAmong the other candidates is Emirati diplomat Lana Nusseibeh, who entered the race last week and whose candidacy is reportedly gaining momentum.Nusseibeh is expected to answer questions on Tuesday, ahead of another Security Council "straw poll" scheduled for Wednesday, which will also gauge support for her candidacy.The informal vote is intended to assess support for the various candidates as Security Council members work toward reaching a consensus on a nominee.It remains unclear whether Orban's name will be included in Wednesday's vote, and additional candidates could still enter the race.The term of current UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres ends on December 31.For now, efforts to advance Orban's candidacy remain based on discussions and assessments provided by sources cited in the report. There has been no official announcement of his candidacy or public confirmation that the three powers would support him.

title: Tricky art of campaign rallies
body: The most visible element of the Nigerian political season is the rally, and until last Saturday when the ruling APC launched its presidential campaign with a rally in Kaduna, most Nigerians thought the campaigns had not started. A political rally is a tedious undertaking. It involves securing a venue, usually a stadium or a large open space; adorning it with flags and banners, getting security agencies to sweep it for explosives and then guard its surroundings; decorating adjoining city streets with banners, deploying thugs to guard the banners lest rival gangs tear them up, move thousands, or even tens of thousands, of party “supporters” to fill the venue, wave flags and shout party and candidate slogans, then bring in dancing and singing troupes to add colour to the occasion. Lastly, eloquent party leaders and the main candidates must get their thoughts together and say something meaningful at the rally. How difficult is it to organize a rally? Not very, according to what an experienced politician once told me. We had just attended the launch of a governor’s reelection campaign rally, and I found myself departing from the venue in the State Assembly Majority Leader’s car. I complimented him on the success of the rally, but he said, “It is not difficult at all. All you have to do is to deploy hired buses at town motor parks, say whoever enters a bus, it will take him to the rally venue and back, that food will be served in the bus and everyone will get 5,000 naira, then inside the bus you distribute posters and banners to them. Once you arrive at the venue, they will jump out and shout themselves hoarse. So it is not really difficult, once you have money.” How much money? Ahead of APC’s Kaduna rally last Saturday, a “memo” by Kaduna State Governor Uba Sani, supposedly sent to APC campaign director general Abdulazeez Yari, went viral on social media, saying N2.3 trillion had been released for the event. It turned out to be an artfully placed hoax. Kaduna State government said its combined three years’ budgets did not amount to that much, so there was no way it could spend such money on a single rally. There is however no way to know how much was actually spent, to prepare the venue, arrange food, accommodation and security, mobilise and move the huge crowds that attended the rally. Certainly the expenses were “decentralized” [to borrow a phrase from Prof M. J. Kuna], since every state contingent must had been financed by its own governor and party leaders. How much political impact does a rally make? The most obvious one is to impress town folks and, through TV images and social media, other Nigerians as well, that the party is popular. But not always; local folks have a good idea how the crowd was mobilised, how much was given to each rally attendee and the singers, and whether or not they actually support that candidate or they were just guns for hire, because they will return home and tell stories to their friends and relatives. A rally is also meant to intimidate opponents; although they know that it is not an accurate measure of political popularity, they feel challenged to mount a similar spectacle lest people get the impression that their own party is not popular. In mounting dazzling campaign rallies, ruling parties, especially, seem oblivious to the danger that they may instead convey to the public an impression of opulence and waste. A convoy of one hundred or more vehicles, mostly jeeps, luxurious Coaster buses and limousines, with security vehicles endlessly blaring sirens, could give down-and-out townsfolk the impression of elite opulence, instead of an impressive political outing. They may think of fuel price of N1,400 per litre and wonder how much fuel those vehicles needed to get there. The rally may be the most conspicuous element of a Nigerian political campaign, but it is not the only one. Ahead of APC’s Kaduna rally, its VIP campaign team visited important clerics and traditional rulers. It is an old tradition, with some changes; back in the Second Republic, three of the five presidential candidates [except Malam Aminu Kano and Chief Obafemi Awolowo] made the palaces of traditional rulers the first stop when they visited every town. Locally it is symbolic, because by visiting the royal father, the politician is seen to “respect” the community. Yet, traditional rulers are supposed to be strictly non-partisan, to receive every candidate who visits them, but to refrain from endorsing any candidate. It is a tricky business, because traditional rulers often fear incumbents or they feel obliged to support those who appointed them. Besides, some candidates also splash money around the palaces they visit, making courtiers to shout their praises. On the flip side, how much “truth” should a traditional ruler tell a visiting candidate, without being seen to humiliate him? A viral social media post recently showed a prominent Northern emir telling a visiting campaign team that they only come looking for support every four years while local folks are in IDP camps or are held hostage in bandit camps. It was unusual; a Northern emir’s normal script during such a visit is to pray for peace in the country and pray for the visitor’s safety and good health. The “truth,” such as it were, can be told by taking the visitor into the palace’s inner recesses, out of reporters’ earshot. Campaign teams have also been seen visiting prominent clerics. Clerics, too, are supposed to be non-partisan, since their congregations are often a political mixed-bag. In reality, many of them stray out of line. In 2003, LP presidential candidate Peter Obi got a lot of bashing for a leaked “Yes Daddy” phone call to the leader of a mega church. On the Muslim side, the most controversial cleric has been the Jos-based sect leader who has been intently campaigning for the “Muslim/Muslim” ticket, even though it has receded to the background in most Nigerians’ political reckoning. After four years, the Christian community probably saw no harm in the ticket beyond the symbolic, while the Muslim community laughed that it brought no special advantages. Perhaps, a future Christian/Christian ticket would elicit no special controversy. This year, several groups have jumped into the fray to compliment the efforts of political parties. They include Arewa 4 Asiwaju, led by former Kano State governor Malam Ibrahim Shekarau and made up of a dozen other former governors and ministers; City Boys Movement, apparently promoted by the president’s son Seyi Tinubu; PBAT Door to Door Movement, supported by First Lady Remi Tinubu; Tinubu and Mbah Move [ATM], promoted by Minister of Science and Innovation Dr. Kingsley Udeh, as well as the opposition Tinubu Must Go [TMG] movement, quite prominent on social media and in some states. Nigerian youths eagerly welcome the onset of political campaigns and rallies. Youths are the ones with the numbers to fill stadiums and city squares; they are the ones with the time, the energy and the dare devilry to jump, sing, dance, cling to the sides of speeding vehicles, race across cities on motorcycles, shout themselves hoarse at rallies, guard posters and billboards, if necessary clash with and chase away thugs deployed by opponents. All because they can do with some naira notes dished out by rally organisers, in these hard times. Chinua Achebe said proverbs are the palm oil with which words are eaten. Money is the grease with which the political machine is oiled. In 2023, when Central Bank threw a spanner in the works by changing the currency ahead of an election, a prominent North Eastern state governor running for reelection told me that he had to suspend his campaign tours for a week because he had no cash. Campaign vehicles were already lined up and ready to go, when his party chairman came and asked the governor if he had cash. He had none, but suggested they could send out money by transfer. The chairman said, “Your Excellency, let us suspend the rally. Dancers, singers and thugs cannot be paid by transfer. Most of them have no bank accounts.” Where in all these is the place of records of achievement and promises for the next governance period? Surely, incumbents reel out projects that they say they did in the last four years. At APC’s Kaduna rally for instance, Works Minister Dave Umahi reeled out the length of roads he said the Tinubu Administration built. Since roads are the most tangible of government projects, road users all over the country were either nodding in agreement or shaking their heads in disbelief. As for promises, APC and Tinubu Administration were completely upstaged last month by ADC presidential candidate Atiku Abubakar’s promise to restore fuel subsidy if elected. Removal of fuel subsidy is the Administration’s single most unpopular deed, and most citizens blame it for the current socio-economic hardship in the land. Atiku’s promise to restore it was a master stroke. Never mind if the promise will be hard to keep; most folks are just happy with it. The challenge facing all the major candidates, as the campaign season finally picks up, is to sit down with teams of clever intellectuals, grassroots politicians and publicists, and work out mouth-watering campaign promises that immediately capture the public’s imagination. Trouble however is, a lot of water having already gushed under the Nigerian political bridge, we are able, given a candidate’s previous record, to determine if indeed he is capable of or can be relied upon to fulfill a mouth-watering campaign promise.

title: El Clásico: Kylian Mbappe scores twice to end Laliga leaders’ winning start
body: Kylian Mbappe scored twice, including an 87th-minute winner, to earn victory for Real Madrid against Barcelona in El Clasico. Barcelona were aiming to set an outright record for the most consecutive victories at the start of a Spanish top-flight season. However, Hansi Flick’s side were unable to surpass the mark of nine straight wins set by the Real Madrid team of 1968-69. Mbappe’s first goal four minutes before half-time was a fortuitous one; home defender Gerard Martin’s attempted clearance of Yan Diomande’s low cross flew in off the France striker past Joan Garcia. Both teams had created chances beforehand but the game really opened up in the period between Mbappe’s opener and the interval, with Mbappe hitting the post and Barcelona teenager Lamine Yamal side-footing wide from close range at the other end. A Barcelona equaliser arrived 16 minutes into the second half as captain Raphinha collected Pedri’s pass and shot through the legs of Jude Bellingham into the far corner. Martin almost made amends for his part in Real’s goal shortly afterwards but his header was superbly clawed away one-handed by Andriy Lunin – who was starting in place of first-choice goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois with the Belgium international ruled out because of illness. When it seemed as though the points would be shared, some brilliant skill by Bellingham started a move on halfway, substitute Eduardo Camavinga broke forward and squared the ball for Mbappe to finish into an unguarded net. Visiting manager Jose Mourinho celebrated with a small knee slide by the dugout and a fist pump. League leaders Barcelona have a two-point lead over second-placed Atletico Madrid after 10 matches, with Real one point further back in third spot.

title: Firms Promote EU Market Entry Pathways for Nigerian Entrepreneurs
body: Oluchi Chibuzor As Nigerian professionals increasingly seek global prospects, immigration experts have highlighted structured entrepreneurial pathways to some European countries as a viable alternative to traditional relocation routes. This, they said, is because some countries prioritise innovative startup ideas backed by governmental authorities such as ENISA in Spain and the Ministry of Economy in France. Both bodies, the experts added, ensures that applicants can find appropriate co-founders to gain necessary permits to do business thereby contributing to their local economy rather than just being a migrant. Speaking during an engagement with the business community in Lagos, the CEO O&J Capital, Mr. Johnson Anorh, said Nigerians entrepreneurs must begin to think of doing business in the European market legally, noting that it is needed to contribute to their nation’s economy. According to him, “Expanding abroad often presents hurdles, particularly regarding trust, guarantees, and navigating bureaucratic language barriers. Firms like O&J Capital, iworld and Mirsatori, work closely with Nigerian clients to bridge these gaps by pairing vetted entrepreneurs with comprehensive legal and corporate support structures.” Commenting, The Head of Migration Department, Mirsatori, Maksin Mayer Nikitin, explained that the collaboration is designed to connect Nigerian entrepreneurs with European markets through startup-based programmes, tailored business proposals and professional immigration support. “The partnership is to guide Nigerian business owners through the legal and regulatory requirements for establishing operations in Spain and France respectively. Startup creation could provide an alternative pathway for qualified entrepreneurs in Agriculture, IT, construction and logistics seeking to establish a business presence in these two countries,” he said.

title: SAHCO Affirms Importance of Collaboration in Growth of Air Cargo
body: Chinedu Eze The Chairman of Skyway Aviation Handling Company (SAHCO) PLC, Dr Taiwo Afolabi has emphasized the critical need for robust stakeholder collaboration, mutual trust, and shared responsibility to drive the growth, efficiency, and global competitiveness of Nigeria’s aviation cargo industry. He spoke at SAHCO Plc Cargo Stakeholders Forum held in Ikeja, Lagos recently. Afolabi, who was represented by the Managing Director of the Skyway Aviation Handling Company (SAHCO) PLC, Mrs. Adenike Aboderin highlighted that the air cargo sector plays a vital role in facilitating international trade, connecting markets, and supporting broader economic development. He affirmed that SAHCO’s success is inextricably linked to the cooperation of every stakeholder within the value chain, from airlines and freight forwarders to regulatory agencies, cargo agents, importers, exporters, and other service providers. To meet the evolving demands of the global economy, Afolabi shared that SAHCO has continuously invested in cutting-edge technology, modern equipment, and infrastructure. He explained that the recent enhancement of its equipment includes the introduction of a new dual-view X-ray machine for advanced cargo screening, an exclusive Trace Detection (ETB) machine for identifying potential exclusive traces, a 16-ton forklift to handle heavy and oversized consignments, and specialized cold-chain handling capabilities designed for temperature-sensitive cargo like pharmaceuticals and perishables. Afolabi said “The air cargo sector plays a vital role in facilitating international trade, connecting markets, supporting businesses, and contributing to economic development. In today’s interconnected global economy, the speed, reliability, security, and efficiency of cargo operations are critical to the competitiveness of businesses and the growth of our nation.”

title: Removing Next.js Got My Blog to 100 on Every Lighthouse Category
body:
My blog just scored a perfect 100 on every Lighthouse category. I love blogging. I wanted to build a blog that’s light, fast, free of clutter, able to run multiple blogs, and fully accessible on top of that. And finally, at long last, I’ve more or less pulled it off. It was quite a tedious process. Ugh… and I even had to remove Next.js, the framework I’d been using most. It was far, far more painful than I expected. I’d like to share the journey of improving performance while building this blog.
When you think of blogs, a few names come to mind. Medium, Blogger, Ghost… But none of them satisfied me. Medium and Blogger are bloated with features, and their actual performance wasn’t satisfying either.
Hmm…… And there was another problem: it’s a hassle to work directly with the markup and raw code we all love (Markdown, HTML, CSS).
For the record, all performance measurements were taken with pagespeed.web.dev .
Of course, there are plenty of alternatives: WordPress, Ghost, Hugo. I didn’t like WordPress’s plugin hell. Ghost has to be self-hosted (there’s ghost.org too, but it’s way too expensive…), and every version upgrade broke something in the editor, so keeping it up to date was a chore. Hugo is the best of the bunch, but in the end, setting it up is still a hassle. Looking back, I guess what I really wanted was SaaS.
The one I liked most was Bear Blog. Great performance. I love its product philosophy, too. But its extreme minimalism was a downside for me. The editor UX didn’t work for me, either.
If it at least let me add AdSense and attach images for free, I probably would’ve just used Bear Blog.
As fast as Bear Blog, but with a bit more functionality and better usability. That’s the blog I wanted to build. Oh, and if you’re curious, you can check it out at bloffy.co .
Anyway. Enough about me. Let me share how I actually improved the performance.
It goes without saying that caching is essential. Get caching right and performance improves dramatically. And Next.js makes caching really convenient. There’s ISR , and it also extends fetch with a next option for caching . Handy. Using these well alone gets you a long way on performance.
Unfortunately, though, our site can be reached from anywhere in the world. Why is that unfortunate? Within the same region, caching makes things fast, but visitors from other regions still end up eating the network latency.
Yes. That’s why we use a CDN. And if you deploy a Next.js app to Vercel, you get a CDN out of the box. I don’t dislike Vercel; it’s incredibly convenient. But the Pro plan is pricey right from the start, there’s the serverless cold start problem, and the dependency on the Vercel ecosystem isn’t something you can ignore either.
So why not use a different CDN service? Cloudflare, for example. I honestly think Cloudflare is a genuinely nice company. You can run large-scale infrastructure and most apps on it for free. But then I figured I didn’t really need Next.js’s caching anymore. Having to invalidate two caches every time I publish a post makes things a pain to manage.
In short, for a static website, I figured a CDN alone is enough. And that’s reason number one why I didn’t need Next.js.
Images these days run over 10MB. Serve those on the web as-is and your performance will go completely off the rails.
Optimizing images is quite a hassle. You have to resize per device, compress, and then handle the CDN on top of that. On a previous project, I had a serverless function (AWS Lambda) compress and resize images whenever one landed in storage (S3), and I put CloudFront in front as the CDN. It was a pretty reasonable setup for tailoring things exactly the way I wanted. But it’s also a setup that needs a fair amount of upkeep.
So this time I went with Cloudflare’s Image Transformations . Even on the free tier you get 5,000 images, so I use it without a second thought.
At this point I sound like a Cloudflare sales rep. I’m just an ordinary solo developer.
Pretty high scores. But this isn’t enough. We want 100. A clean, no-asterisks 100. So I dug into what the problem was.
It said a substantial amount of legacy JavaScript was found, and it wasn’t code I wrote. It came from the framework runtime that Next.js ships in its bundle.
But this page is a static page with zero interaction. Every page is pre-rendered with ISR, and I thought I’d followed the Next.js guidelines well. So as an experiment, I ripped out every client component the app had, left only server components, and measured again. The score didn’t budge.
At first I suspected hydration , but once I dug in, the problem wasn’t hydration alone. The cause was the client runtime that Next.js always ships, even for static pages. Even with only server components, the runtime chunks, hydration, and the RSC payload for the router all stay. That’s because next/link and next/image are themselves client components ( 'use client' ), so having just those two is enough to pull in the runtime and trigger hydration.
So what if I strip out next/link and next/image too? The App Router’s own runtime, the router and error boundaries, still remains. There’s no official way to get it down to zero; the only option was a hack: stripping the scripts out of the rendered HTML. That’s when it hit me: “If I’m going to do that, why am I even using Next.js?”
You can see that the bulk of the JavaScript is code that isn’t needed. Unused code alone comes to 230,460 bytes. That’s not good. Most static websites don’t need JavaScript at all. Unused JavaScript is needed even less.
This is where I really agonized. Is dropping Next.js for the sake of 100 points the right call? I’d spent a lot of time building the public-facing web app.
In the end, for the quality of the blog (even if it’s just 5 points), I decided to rip Next.js out entirely. My judgment was that I wouldn’t need Next.js’s excess features in the long run either. I considered going fully vanilla, but I didn’t want to give up the productivity and infrastructure benefits of a framework. I needed to find the right one.
I chose Hono . I liked its technical philosophy. “Fast and simple” was exactly the solution I needed most, and JSX support was a bonus. The migration cost didn’t look too big, either.
Tada. And just like that, 100 across the board. Go ahead and run the very page you’re reading right now through pagespeed.web.dev .
There’s no JavaScript, and unused code dropped sharply to 407 bytes. As a bonus, build time went down by about 40% too.
Oh, why is SEO at 69? That site was built for testing, and it deliberately blocks search indexing. That’s why it’s 69.
By the way, if you score 100 on everything in DevTools, Lighthouse actually sets off fireworks for you. 🎉🎉
The long task that runs before anything is rendered on screen took 309.3ms on Next.js, and when I built the same page with Hono, it took 68.01ms. That’s roughly a 78% improvement.
Is a JS payload, hydration included, really doing a static site any good? I don’t think so. It leaves behind unnecessary JavaScript, so in most cases I think it’s simply not needed.
That said, for an interaction-heavy app, I think Next.js can be a great framework. In fact, the management app for this very blog is built with Next.js!
P.S. This blog runs on Bloffy, the blogging platform I’m building. If you want a blog that scores like this without the setup, you can try it at bloffy.co .

title: Digital Asset Markets with Nicky Okoye
body: Digital Assets and Enterprise Development Nation-building primarily focuses on job creation, rising living standards for citizens, and economic prosperity for the nation-state. In this respect, all nation-building efforts, at the national and sub-national levels, must consider how digital asset markets stimulate enterprise development and entrepreneurship. Nothing will affect entrepreneurship and enterprise development more than the expansion of digital assets and the ability of digital asset classes to move frictionlessly across global blockchain rails. Enterprise Development Strategy and Digital Assets Enterprise Developmentand Digital Assets are inseparable. As the World continues to evolve in the Digital Asset Markets space, some of the most important applications of the digital asset revolution will be felt by enterprises seeking to access or raise capital from global sources, using previously unavailable strategies which have now become very strategic, including several digital asset classes, decentralised capital and decentralised financial ecosystems. Collectively, these strategies are changing the game for enterprise fundraising in the 21 st century. Large and small enterprises seeking to innovate and respond to local and global market opportunities can use strategies outlined in my upcoming “Digital Asset Markets Strategy guide” to deliver value-innovation development processes. For intentional enterprises and entrepreneurs, this approach will be customised and tailored to each industrial segment, depending on the industry’s peculiarities, reach, capital requirements, and the talent of the professionals operating within it. Tokenisation strategies to raise capital are already becoming common worldwide. This can be achieved through real-world asset digital tokens or utility tokens, which are designed to enhance community participation and reward systems. Using digital assets to fund municipal projects, set up new decentralised enterprises, build infrastructure etc., are all options that are now available Where will the new capital come from to grow the digital asset market ecosystem? I would like to use this illustration to make my point. On 1 September 1972, in what was considered the “Match of the Century,” chess grandmaster Bobby Fischer defeated Russian grandmaster Boris Spassky during the World Chess Championship in Reykjavik, Iceland. This history-making feat was the first time since the inception of the global chess tournament, which began in 1866, that an American won the Championship, and the first time in 22 years that a non-Russian was crowned the King of Chess. For the leadership of Nation States, Financial Institutions, Global Capital Markets, Global Enterprises as well as Entrepreneurs, the next twenty-five years will redefine and will determine, the geo-political zones, nation states, the families, communities and individuals, that will benefit from the newly created wealth that is projected from the monumental growth of global GDP as it grows to heights of over $200 trillion, by 2050. This monumental economic growth is projected to add $100 trillion in new economic value in just under 25 years.
