Positioning and winning key niche markets, including the Digital Asset Markets, as a major part of the Next One Hundred Trillion Dollars GDP growth that is projected, in my opinion, is going to be as exciting for nation-states, capital market operators, enterprises and entrepreneurs as winning the “Match of the Century” Championship was for the citizens of the United States of America in 1972. We at the Global Investment Advisory Community (GIAC) are committed not only to making this process of participating in the digital asset markets exciting but also profitable. The Next One Hundred Trillion Dollars (N1HTD) Nothing holds more promise and excitement for nation-states, sub-national regions, communities, enterprises, and individuals actively engaged in enterprise and commercial activity than this projected growth forecast for the global economy, which is expected to expand to over two hundred trillion by 2050, adding an unprecedented additional over One Hundred Trillion dollars between now and then. This means that in less than twenty-five years, the global economy’s GDP will more than double. Enterprise Development and the next one hundred trillion dollars We in the GIA community expect policymakers and legislators to design strategic, job-creating government policies and growth-enabling legislation to position their people for this monumental shift in global economic fortunes. In our Digital Asset Markets Strategy, we have extracted proprietary analysis which guides leaders on the way forward. Our Next One Hundred Trillion Dollars analysis and strategic information provide wealth-creation-driven policies that reposition and stimulate 21st-century job creation through enterprise development at the nation-state level, as well as for geopolitical regions, municipalities, and enterprises, particularly those exclusively participating in our N1HTD Mastermind community. The most strategic use of our N1HTD analysis will be to design and develop 21st-century wealth maps that reflect the direction and growth of global GDP within the N1HTD context. In my “Digital Asset Markets Strategy” guide, members of our global investment advisory community will find analysis of global economic disruptive indicators as they relate to N1HTD’s projected growth. I also include my opinion on industry expansions and trends in enhanced economic value, as defined by industrial segments, geography, geopolitics, and even access to technological advancements. Population migration trends and resultant consumer behaviour. Guide to t he Next One Hundred Trillion Dollars The Next one hundred trillion dollars in global GDP growth will be impacted by the following drivers: Digital Asset Markets Strategy. Artificial Intelligence, Artificial General Intelligence, Artificial Superintelligence and machine learning with specific industry impact and analysis. Technological advancements in industrial applications, as they relate to specific industries. Industrial ecosystems and global value chains, with specific engagements for African suppliers. Global supply chains as they relate to the World’s most critical industries. Geopolitical touchpoints, including economic disruptions and transformations with strategic impact from specific innovations. Global populations, changing consumer behaviour and the direction of economic demand trends. 21st-century indicators and the impact of BIG DATA analysis in strategic industries. Value Chain Intelligence and Enterprise Excellence, projections and trends. The Geopolitics of the Next One Hundred Trillion Dollars A strategic look at China China currently accounts for over 30% of global manufacturing output, whereas the USA accounts for just under 16%. China’s high-speed rail infrastructure shows it has installed and operates over 40,000 km of high-speed rail, accounting for over 70% of global high-speed rail infrastructure. The United States has just about 753km, which is less than 2% of China’s installed capacity. In the electric vehicle arena, China has overtaken the United States, with over 60% of global Electric Vehicle (EV) production compared to the United States, which has 10-15% of global capacity. In 21st-century telecommunications, built on 5G networks, China has over 2.9 million 5G base stations, representing over 60% of global output. The United States has about five hundred thousand (500k) 5G base stations, less than 20% of China’s capacity. In the value chain required for processing rare earth metals, which are essential for modern electronics, quantum computers and Artificial Intelligence, China has nearly cornered the global market. Currently, China accounts for 90% of global rare earth metal processing capacity, while the United States has less than 5%. In industrial robot use and installation, China again accounts for 51% of installed capacity. In this case, annual industrial robot installations include not only Chinese-designed and built robots but also those fully installed in Chinese factories. The rest of the world, including the USA and Europe, shares the remaining 49% of industrial robot installation capacity. And it’s going to get worse for the West and better for China, depending on how you look at it. According to an OECD report, by 2030, 37% of all science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) graduates worldwide will be Chinese. This compares with projections of just 4.2% for the USA, 1.2% for Germany, 1.2% for the UK, and 0.8% for France. India is projected to follow China closely with 26.7% of STEM scientists. In 2011, China produced and used more cement than the United States used in the entire 20 th century. In 2011, a Chinese firm built a 30-story skyscraper in just15 days. In 2014, a different Chinese firm topped that by building a 57-story skyscraper in 19 days. China built the equivalent of Europe’s entire housing block in just 15 years. In 2024, a Chinese construction company built an entire highway with Artificial intelligence robots, with no human engineers. China has the first all-AI hospitals, which can perform diagnosis-to-treatment with no human doctors involved. In the Maritime industry, China currently has 129 times the shipbuilding capacity of the United States. In other words, competition with China in shipbuilding is nonexistent. As the global economy races to $200 trillion in GDP by 2050, China’s economy is projected to grow to over $60 trillion in GDP, ahead of every other country in the entire World. India, also in Asia, is projected to grow to over $51 trillion in GDP within the same timeframe. This means China and India combined will represent over half of global GDP by 2050. This is fascinating and significant, and it shows why we must continue to study and monitor the Next One Hundred Trillion Dollars (N1HTD), in the interest of those coming after us. Global Investment Advisor’s opinion It is important to understand what nation-states and sub-nationals need to do to ensure their regions remain competitive, even in the face of a rising China. Simply outsourcing everything to China will ensure that your people will lose in the long run. Leaders must look at the guides I have provided as key areas of impact for the next one hundred trillion dollars in global GDP and find ways their regions or nations can compete. As far as we in Africa and the Caribbean are concerned, the most important factor to hold on to will be a grand, large, and coordinated effort to educate the next generation of our people in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM), and not much anything else. The arts and entertainment will always be important; however, when it comes to the matter of life and death of Nation-states over the next fifty years, those that will win and those that will dominate will be those Nations whose Leaders decided in 2026/2027 to drive an elaborate education policy in STEM for their young people. There is no other way. The global digital asset market ecosystems and transformational artificial intelligence systems will both ride on the backs of the World’s STEM-educated experts. Indeed……Great Things are Happening. Nicky Okoye Global Investment Advisor Founder, Global Investment Advisory Community (GIAC)

title: Vicky Safra and Maria Angelicoussis Among the World’s 500 Richest People
body: Two of the richest Greek women in the world now sit among the 500 wealthiest people on the planet. Banking heiress Vicky Safra and shipping chief Maria Angelicoussis together hold an estimated fortune of almost US$40 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, as Fortune Greece reported on 23 October. Where the richest Greek women rank Fortune Greece, citing the index as published on 23 October 2026, places Vicky Safra and her family 95th in the world, with an estimated US$26 billion. Maria Angelicoussis follows in 248th place, with US$13.4 billion. Together, their fortunes total about US$39.4 billion. However, the two figures are not directly comparable. Bloomberg counts Safra’s wealth together with that of her children, while it values Angelicoussis’s fortune mainly through her shipping fleet. Moreover, the index updates every day as markets and asset values move. Bloomberg’s own pages showed Angelicoussis at 249th on 22 October and 250th on 23 October, still with US$13.4 billion. Elon Musk, meanwhile, tops the ranking with an estimated US$904 billion. Vicky Safra: a banking dynasty Vicky Safra, 74, was born in Greece in 1952. According to Forbes, she holds both Greek and Brazilian citizenship and lives mostly in Switzerland. She and her four children inherited their fortune from her late husband, banker Joseph Safra, who died in December 2020. Today, the family controls the J. Safra Group, which Bloomberg says has more than US$590 billion of assets under management across more than 30 countries. The group’s flagship, São Paulo-based Banco Safra, held about US$57.7 billion in assets as of December 2025. In addition, the family owns Swiss private bank J. Safra Sarasin, created after Joseph Safra bought Bank Sarasin in 2012, as well as Safra National Bank of New York. Its property holdings include London’s Gherkin office tower. Forbes reports that her eldest son, Jacob, runs J. Safra Sarasin and the New York bank, while David manages Banco Safra in Brazil. Maria Angelicoussis: Greece’s biggest shipowner Maria Angelicoussis, 44, is chief executive of the Athens-based Angelicoussis Group, which Bloomberg describes as the biggest Greek shipowner. Her grandfather, Antonis, founded the business in 1947, and she took the helm after her father, John, died in 2021, Forbes reports. Interestingly, she trained as a doctor. Forbes says she earned a medical degree from Cambridge University and worked as a junior doctor in Britain’s National Health Service for two years, before joining the family firm in 2008. The group operates through three units: Maran Gas Maritime for liquefied natural gas (LNG) carriers, Maran Tankers Management for oil tankers, and Anangel Maritime Services for dry bulk. Its fleet numbers about 160 vessels. Because the company is privately held and does not publish financial results, Bloomberg bases its estimate on the fleet. It values the active ships at US$18.2 billion gross, using September 2026 valuations, without counting the value of charter contracts. The family controls the group through Angelicoussis Shipping Group, a Cayman Islands holding company. Notably, her fortune has grown by about US$4 billion, or more than 40%, so far this year, according to the index. Different methods, different numbers Rich lists do not always agree, even on the richest Greek women. Forbes’s real-time tracker, for instance, valued Angelicoussis at US$7.5 billion on 25 October, compared with Bloomberg’s US$13.4 billion. On the same day, Forbes put Safra and her family at US$26 billion, broadly in line with Bloomberg. title: T-bills auction: Government exceeds target by 12%; 91-day and 182-day yields decline
body: Demand for treasury bills increased as the government exceeded its target by about 12%. This is coming after the government announced it would raise GHȼ15.3 billion in the final quarter of 2026. The government received total bids of GH¢4.26 billion from the investors, but accepted GH¢3.9 billion. A little over GH¢2.8 billion of the bids were tendered for the 91-day bill, representing 67% of the total bids. The uptake was, however, GH¢2.5 billion. The 182-day bill received bids of about GH¢533.28 million. About GH¢ 420 million was accepted. For the 364-day bill, about GH¢873 million of the bids were tendered. A little above GH¢420 million of the bids were accepted. Meanwhile, interest rates went down on the shorter end of the yield curve, but rose on the longer end of the yield curve. The yield on the 91-day bill declined by a basis point to 4.61%. Again, the 182-day bill also fell to 6.27% from the previous week’s 6.31%. However, the yield on the 364-day bill increased by 4.0 basis points to 9.75%. title: Gold Board concerns did not justify holding up law – Adongo
body: Parliament’s Finance Committee Chairman, Isaac Adongo, has defended the passage of the law establishing the Gold Board, saying concerns about some provisions did not warrant delaying it. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express Business Edition, he said the minority supported the bill in principle. Its reservations concerned specific provisions. “The passage of the bill that led to the establishment of the gold board, for instance, from a political perspective, our colleagues do not disagree in principle, but their side of the divide were not comfortable with certain provisions.” Mr Adongo argued that Parliament needed to allow the institution to begin its work. He pointed to what he described as its impact as justification for that decision. “Nevertheless, we needed to get that act out of the way, and you have seen the monumental impact of the gold board, so we needed to first get a handle on it.” He said passing the law did not close the door to changes. Any weaknesses identified during implementation could be addressed through a review. “Of course, over time, there will be some lapses that can be identified, and a review is possible at any point in time.” Mr Adongo also expressed confidence that minority members would support amendments if the executive returned to Parliament with proposals to revise certain clauses. His defence came amid questions about whether he could challenge government proposals despite his party being in power. He said the committee’s decisions went beyond the chairman and reflected scrutiny from both sides. “The reason is that almost every bill that has come to us has been scrutinised on a bipartisan basis.” He cited the presence of ranking member and former Finance Minister Dr Amin Adam, deputy ranking member Dr Stephen Amoah, and Dr Gideon Boako. Mr Adongo maintained that disagreements did not necessarily signal opposition to an entire proposal. They also allowed members to put their concerns on record. “Those disagreements are basically giving an opportunity to members on both sides to air their views about what ought to be done, but largely we agree on most of the things.”

title: Lydia Panagiotidou Becomes First Greek Girl to Win Tennis Europe Junior Masters
body: Greek tennis prodigy Lydia Panagiotidou has dedicated her historic Tennis Europe Junior Masters title in Monte Carlo to her coach and her parents. The 16-year-old won the Girls’ 16 & Under crown on Saturday, 24 October, becoming the first Greek girl ever to lift the trophy, as Tennis24 reported. A heartfelt dedication In an emotional message on Instagram, Panagiotidou thanked the people who stand beside her. “This win is dedicated to my coach Marios Michailidis and to my parents Maria and Savvas. Thank you so much for your support and for everything you do,” she wrote. Michailidis is head coach at the Thessaloniki Tennis Club (OA Thessalonikis), where Panagiotidou trains, according to Tennis24. How Lydia Panagiotidou won in Monte Carlo The Junior Masters is the season-ending event of the Tennis Europe Junior Tour. Each year, it brings the continent’s top eight boys and girls in the 14 & Under and 16 & Under categories to the Monte-Carlo Country Club. This year’s event ran from 21 to 24 October. Panagiotidou arrived as top seed. Moreover, she and Serbia’s Zana Peric had finished the season level at the top of the Race to Monte-Carlo, with 1,110 points each, so the final also decided the year-end No. 1 spot. The clay courts of the Monte-Carlo Country Club, venue of the Tennis Europe Junior Masters (file photo). Photo: Domaina / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0 First, she topped Group A without dropping a set. She beat Austria’s Leonie Schauer 6-2, 6-3, then Cyprus’s Danai Margariti 6-1, 6-1, and finally Georgia’s Ana Chachkhunashvili 6-0, 6-1. In the final, she then defeated Peric 6-3, 6-2 in about 80 minutes. Remarkably, it was the pair’s first meeting. According to Gazzetta, she broke twice in the opening set and then broke again in the second and eighth games of the second set. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Lydia Panagiotidou (@lydia_panagiotidou) Overall, she won four matches in straight sets and dropped just 13 games all week. Tennis Europe also noted that she won 76% of her first-serve points, the best average among all 32 players, and spent only four hours and 10 minutes on court. Year-end No. 1 and a growing list of titles As a result, Lydia Panagiotidou finishes 2026 alone as Europe’s No. 1 in the Girls’ 16 & Under category. The Monte Carlo crown is her fourth Tennis Europe title of the season, according to the governing body. Earlier this year, she won Category 3 events in Thessaloniki and Larissa. Notably, she also claimed the Super Category under-16 tournament at Rome’s Foro Italico, held alongside the ATP and WTA Internazionali d’Italia. She now joins a list of former Junior Masters champions that includes Rafael Nadal, Kim Clijsters, Alexander Zverev and Belinda Bencic. Back-to-back Greek success Meanwhile, the title keeps a Junior Masters trophy in Greek hands for a second straight year, after Rafael Pagonis won the Boys’ 14 & Under event in 2025. Hellenic Tennis Federation coach Apostolos Triantafyllidis accompanied Panagiotidou in Monte Carlo, the federation said. The next step With her Tennis Europe under-16 career now complete, Panagiotidou turns her focus to the ITF Junior Tour, Tennis24 reports. According to Sport FM, she already sits inside the top 180 of the ITF world junior rankings, and her next goals include climbing further and earning places in junior Grand Slam draws such as Roland Garros and Wimbledon. title: Incumbent President of Brazil Lula da Silva wins presidential election
body:
RIO DE JANEIRO, October 26. /TASS/. Incumbent President of Brazil Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won in the second round of presidential elections and was re-elected as the president of the country for the fourth term, the Brazilian Superior Electoral Court (TSE) reported.
According to the TSE, after 97.69% of the ballots in the runoff election were counted, Lula da Silva secured 51.74% of the votes, while his opponent, a right-wing opposition candidate Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, was backed by 48.26% of the votes.
Lula da Silva is now the first politician in the present-day Brazilian history to win the presidential election after trailing in the first round of voting. The elected head of state will assume the office on January 1, 2027.
The voter turnout in the second round was reported at 80.79%, with 127,807,732 citizens participating in the voting. The rate of abstainers was reported at 19.21%, which corresponds to 30,081,854 voters. The share of blank ballots was at 1.12% (1,426,055 votes), while the share of invalid ballots was amounted to 2.12% (2,713,225 votes).

title: Greece Targets Golden Visa Abuse Over Hidden Rebates
body: Greece is warning golden visa investors that residence permits could be revoked over hidden property rebates and prohibited short-term rental arrangements, as authorities step up enforcement of the country’s investment migration programme. Migration and Asylum Minister Thanos Plevris issued the warning at the Prodexpo 2026 real estate conference in Athens on October 15, signalling a tougher approach as housing affordability remains a major political issue. Plevris said authorities would target property transactions that appear to meet the minimum investment threshold on paper but effectively fall below it through undisclosed rebates or side agreements. He also warned that investors who use prohibited subleasing arrangements to operate short-term rentals risk losing their residence permits. “The golden visa will be taken away,” the minister said, referring to investors who breach the restrictions on short-term letting. The remarks signal a shift in Greece’s approach to one of Europe’s most popular residency-by-investment programmes, with greater emphasis on compliance, housing policy and the actual terms of property transactions. Hidden Rebates Under Government Scrutiny Under Greece’s golden visa rules, investors must meet the applicable minimum property investment threshold and provide evidence that the required payment has been completed through traceable financial channels. However, some property offers have reportedly used arrangements designed to make investments appear eligible when the effective purchase cost is lower than the legal minimum. Plevris cited an example involving a property advertised at the €250,000 threshold, with an arrangement that effectively returns approximately €100,000 to the buyer through a leasing agreement. The minister made clear that authorities would scrutinise the substance of such transactions rather than relying solely on the price stated in the purchase documents. The issue is particularly relevant to properties marketed under Greece’s remaining €250,000 golden visa investment categories. However, the legal position requires an important distinction. While Greece’s legislation establishes payment requirements and penalties for certain violations, the precise legal basis for revoking a residence permit solely because of a post-sale rebate may be contested. Investors facing such allegations could challenge revocation decisions if they believe the authorities lack a sufficient statutory basis. Short-Term Rentals Carry Clearer Penalties The government has also reiterated its opposition to golden visa properties being used for prohibited short-term accommodation arrangements. Article 100 of Greece’s Migration Code prohibits properties acquired under the applicable golden visa rules from being used for short-term rentals or subletting within the sharing economy. Violations can result in the revocation or non-renewal of an investor’s residence permit, alongside a €50,000 fine for the property’s owner or holder. Ministerial Circular 1/2026, issued in April 2026, defines short-term letting as a lease or sublease lasting fewer than 60 days that provides accommodation without additional services, regardless of whether the property is advertised through an online platform. The restrictions do not apply universally to every golden visa property. Certain properties acquired under the rules in force before the 2024 reforms, as well as those covered by transitional provisions, may be exempt. The acquisition date and the rules applicable to each property are therefore important when determining whether a rental arrangement is permitted. Greece Raises Golden Visa Investment Thresholds Greece has significantly tightened the financial requirements for its golden visa programme since 2023. Under the revised framework introduced in 2024, the minimum investment increased to €800,000 in high-demand areas, including Attica, Thessaloniki, Mykonos, Santorini and islands with populations exceeding 3,100. The minimum is €400,000 in other eligible areas. Both routes generally require investment in a single property measuring at least 120 square metres. The €250,000 threshold remains available for specific categories, including the conversion of qualifying commercial properties into residential use and the restoration of listed buildings, subject to the relevant conditions. Plevris said the programme was originally intended to support construction and economic activity during a difficult period. However, he argued that Greece’s housing pressures have changed the government’s priorities. The government wants to attract investors who bring unused buildings back into residential use, either for personal occupation or long-term rental, while encouraging investment outside central Athens. Applications Fall as Enforcement Tightens The higher investment thresholds have already affected demand. New golden visa applications fell by 39% during the first seven months of 2026, reaching 3,086, according to figures cited in the report. At the same time, faster processing has helped reduce the application backlog, with active investor residence permits reaching 34,278 by the end of July. Chinese nationals account for just over half of active permits, followed by investors from Turkey, Israel and the United Kingdom. The programme remains politically contentious. PASOK, Greece’s main opposition party, has proposed ending the real estate investment route and extending the short-term rental prohibition to existing permit holders when their residence permits come up for renewal. The governing New Democracy party has rejected the proposal. Within the property sector, stricter enforcement has attracted support from lawyers who argue that tackling questionable arrangements would help preserve the programme’s credibility. Others maintain that the golden visa scheme is not the primary cause of Greece’s housing shortage and question whether abolishing it would significantly increase the supply of available homes. What Golden Visa Investors Need to Know The minister’s warning places greater pressure on investors, property developers and agents to ensure their transactions comply with the rules. Prospective buyers should verify the applicable investment threshold and ensure that the full qualifying amount is paid through traceable channels. Side agreements, guaranteed returns and arrangements that effectively reduce the purchase price warrant particular scrutiny. Existing investors should also establish whether their properties fall under the short-term rental restrictions, taking into account when the property was acquired and which legal provisions apply. Where rental income is involved, long-term leasing may offer a more appropriate option for investors seeking to remain within the programme’s requirements. Investors considering properties advertised below the standard investment threshold should seek independent legal advice before signing contracts or transferring funds. Greece Signals a New Era for Golden Visa Compliance Greece’s latest warning highlights a broader shift in investment migration policy, as governments seek to balance foreign capital with housing affordability and regulatory oversight. For international investors and family offices, the implications extend beyond the headline investment amount. Transaction structures, payment records and the intended use of a property can all affect compliance. For developers and real estate agents, arrangements designed to make properties appear eligible for residency benefits may carry growing legal and reputational risks. The scale of the impact will depend on how consistently the government enforces the rules, whether further legislation clarifies the treatment of hidden rebates and how courts respond to disputed revocation decisions. Greece’s message is clear: golden visa eligibility will increasingly depend not only on what property contracts say, but also on the financial arrangements behind them and how the properties are used. title: IDF veteran completes Hawaii Ironman race three years after losing leg in Gaza combat
body: Three years after being injured and losing his right leg while in Gaza, IDF veteran Boris Baruch Shtonda completed the Ironman World Championship in Hawaii on October 10.Shtonda competed in the long-distance triathlon consisting of a 3.8-kilometer swim, a 180-kilometer bike ride, and a full marathon  in a division for athletes with disabilities while wearing a custom-fitted specialized running prosthetic. Shtonda lost his right leg while serving in the IDF's Duvdevan as a reservist after Hamas's October 7 massacre. A month after being deployed, he was severely wounded by an explosive device in the northern Gaza city of Beit Hanoun.He underwent multiple surgeries before his leg was amputated above the knee and made athletic challenges a central goal for his recovery.Since starting his recovery, Shtonda climbed Mount Kilimanjaro twice, swam across the Sea of Galilee, and finished a half Ironman race in Spain before deciding to train for the Hawaii Ironman.Shtonda completed the race after a year and a half of training and support from Friends of the Israel Defense Forces (FIDF).Shtonda dedicates Ironman achievement to wounded soldiers in rehabilitationShtonda dedicated his race to wounded soldiers and others undergoing rehabilitation, encouraging them to draw on their inner strength, believe in themselves, and become their own heroes.“I want to share a message with all wounded soldiers and anyone going through a rehabilitation process: you are your own compass,” Shtonda said. “Sometimes, we have to be our own heroes and pull ourselves out of the predicaments we find ourselves in. Keep the faith, and always–always–believe in yourselves.”Shtonda also received support from FIDF supporter Mike Hochstein of Dallas, who was moved by his aspirations, determination, and mental resilience after meeting him during a visit to Israel.“I first met Boris during an FIDF bike ride through Israel last year, and from that first meeting, Boris's determination and spirit made a lasting impression,” Hochstein said. “His dedication, perseverance, and commitment to pushing his limits are truly inspiring. I'm so proud to support Boris on this extraordinary journey.”FIDF helps wounded IDF soldiers rebuild their lives through sports and rehabilitationFIDF's support for Shtonda is part of the organization's broader efforts to assist wounded IDF soldiers and their families through rehabilitation programs, sports, and adventure activities designed to build physical and mental resilience. These initiatives aim to help wounded veterans regain their independence, return to everyday life, and pursue new goals beyond their initial medical treatment.“Boris's achievement reflects the determination wounded soldiers bring to the long process of rehabilitation,” said FIDF CEO Maj. Gen. (Res.) Nadav Padan. “Recovery does not end when medical treatment is over. It takes continued support, opportunities to rebuild strength and confidence, and the chance to set new goals. Through the commitment of FIDF supporters in the United States, we help wounded soldiers and their families navigate that process and continue moving forward.”Shtonda's journey highlights the inner strength and resilience of wounded IDF soldiers, demonstrating how rehabilitation extends beyond medical treatment and how sports, personal determination, and community support can help wounded soldiers regain confidence, overcome challenges, and rebuild their lives after injury.

title: ‘Consummate actor has left the stage’ – Kanayo, others mourn Francis Duru
body: Nollywood actors have mourned the death of their colleague, Francis Duru, describing him as a talented performer whose contributions to the film industry will be remembered. Duru died on Friday at the age of 57 after a brief illness. His death comes two years after he lost his 15-year-old son, Ifeanyi, leaving fans and colleagues in the film industry in mourning. Actor Kanayo O. Kanayo, in a tribute on his Instagram page, described Duru as a complete actor and one of Nigeria’s most versatile and prolific performers. “A consummate actor has left the stage. One of Nigeria’s most flexible, prolific performers. Rest in peace, my brother,” Kanayo wrote. Actress Kate Henshaw also mourned Duru, reflecting on life’s brevity and praying for his soul’s repose. “Like a flame gone out, so are our lives when it all ends,” she wrote, praying for God to grant him eternal rest and comfort his family. Actress Mercy Johnson-Okojie said she was too overwhelmed by the loss to find words. “Too tired and speechless about this loss,” she wrote. Actress Stephanie Linus described Duru’s death as tragic and heartbreaking, praying for strength for his family. “Such a tragic and heartbreaking loss. May God grant his family the strength and fortitude to bear this loss. May his soul rest in peace. RIP Francis Duru,” she wrote. Duru became popular for his role as Ahanna in Amaka Igwe’s classic film Rattlesnake and built a career spanning more than three decades in Nollywood. His family announced his death in a statement on his official Instagram page in the early hours of October 23, 2026.

title: Lula, Brazil’s iconic working-class president, wins historic 4th term in dramatic comeback
body: SAO PAULO, Brazil – Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won an unprecedented fourth term on Sunday, October 25, the country’s electoral court said, in a shock result that defied polls, precedent and global anti-incumbent sentiment to put the brakes on a wave of right-wing election victories across Latin America. Lula, an icon of the global left and the most dominant force in Brazilian politics this century, defeated Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. The senator had finished first in the election’s first round and hoped to revive his father’s far-right movement. At times, Lula’s reelection looked like a long shot, as voters soured on him and his Workers’ Party after years of corruption scandals and rising prices, while sweeping societal changes left the former metalworker and union leader looking out of touch with an increasingly app-based economy and its growing ranks of informal workers. Lula’s victory marks another comeback in a career full of them. The 80-year-old was jailed from 2018 to 2019 on corruption charges that were later overturned, paving the way for him to beat Jair Bolsonaro in the 2022 election. “He is a statesman, a giant,” leftist federal lawmaker Erika Hilton, who was with Lula in Sao Paulo during the vote count, told Reuters. Unlikely path to victory Pollsters said better-than-expected turnout had powered Lula to victory. Leonardo Barreto, the co-founder of consultancy Think Policy, said voters had chosen Lula’s familiar embrace over Bolsonaro’s novelty. “People today are choosing between change, with some apprehension, and a known path, which guarantees certain rights,” he said. During the campaign, Lula pointed to a track record of falling poverty and inequality, while unemployment, illiteracy and deforestation hit record lows during his third term. He warned Bolsonaro would cut welfare spending, backslide on social advances and hand over Brazil’s sovereignty to US President Donald Trump, whose State Department led a campaign to get the Bolsonaros back to power. Lula’s win deprives Trump of a major addition to what has been a growing bloc of friendly right-wing Latin American governments that have embraced Washington’s agenda on security and migration. Celso Amorim, a former Lula foreign minister, told Reuters the leftist “would be very important for establishing a point of balance in Latin America. Lula is that balance.” Comeback king Lula becomes the first candidate since Brazil’s return to democracy in the 1980s to be elected after finishing second in the first round. Lula, who was president between 2003 and 2011, campaigned on a potent mix of pragmatism and populism that has shaped his career in national politics for half a century, rolling out a slew of reforms aimed at improving the lives of workers and poor Brazilians. These gained steam with late-campaign pledges that ranged from free nationwide weekend public transport, which has to be formally submitted to Congress, to a 15% increase in his trademark welfare program that is already being implemented. Lula also championed a constitutional amendment that became Brazil’s biggest labor reform in decades, which passed with wide support in Congress. Challenging legislative reality Still, Lula’s fourth term could be his most difficult yet, after Brazil elected its most conservative Congress since returning to democracy in the 1980s. Combined, Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party (PL) and allied parties could control over 280 seats in the lower house and up to 50 seats in the Senate, enough for comfortable majorities in both chambers. “He is likely to be a lame duck from the start,” said Oliver Stuenkel, a professor of international relations at the Getulio Vargas Foundation in São Paulo. The incoming legislature will likely deepen recent trends of presidents ceding power to Congress, Stuenkel said, predicting Lula will face waning influence over Supreme Court nominations, unwieldy party coalitions, and even the threat of impeachment. Economic headwinds Lula faces an economy that his government forecasts will grow a meager 2.3% next year, adding to fiscal concerns tied to high interest rates and public debt that has risen past 82% of GDP, the highest since the pandemic. The president’s critics blame spending, though interest costs have driven most of the increase in debt. Goldman Sachs said it expects Lula to make modest progress at most to contain spending in a fourth term, as he stays committed to a state-led growth model. Surging household debt also concerns economists. Trying to address the issue, Lula rolled out a provisional ban on online betting and unveiled a new debt relief program during the campaign. The incoming right-wing Congress will try to pass structural reforms that favor businesses, experts say, prompting spending cuts that could fuel social upheaval. – Rappler.com

title: Brazil’s Lula clinches victory over Flavio Bolsonaro to win fourth term
body: Brazil’s leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva pulled off a dramatic comeback on Sunday as he clinched election victory against right-wing senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who trounced him in the first round. The leftist icon, who turns 81 on Tuesday, defied all projections to win an unprecedented fourth term at the helm of Latin America’s largest country. According to official results, he won 51.75 percentof the votes to 48.25 percent for Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro, who had entered election day confident with his lead in the polls. With Lula’s victory, Brazil staved off a conservative wave that has seen numerous countries — such as Argentina, Chile, Colombia, and Peru — all shift right, backed by US President Donald Trump. After a campaign marred by scandal and mud-slinging, Sunday’s vote plunged into chaos after a last-minute Supreme Court ruling extending voting by two hours, at the request of Lula who said buses had been pulled from circulation in various cities, barring citizens from voting. Supporters of Brazil’s President and Workers’ Party (PT) re-election candidate Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva react to the presidential runoff election results in the state of Sao Paulo, Brazil, on October 25, 2026. Lula da Silva pulled off a dramatic comeback on October 25, 2026, as he clinched election victory against right-wing senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who trounced him in the first round. (Photo by NELSON ALMEIDA / AFP) Flavio Bolsonaro also requested an extension in some parts of the country due to heavy rains, but his camp lashed out at the country-wide extension. “Either we win. Or we win. Consider yourself warned,” pro-Bolsonaro lawmaker Nikolas Ferreira wrote on X as the votes streamed in. The bitter campaign laid bare the deep divisions in the country of over 200 million people. “It’s a disgrace. We’ve never had anything like this in Brazil, and now they’ve come up with the idea of extending the election period by two hours,” said Aurelio Junior, 45, a dentist in Brasilia. Jacqueline Maria Lima de Franca, 34, a business owner in Rio de Janeiro backing Lula said it was “more than fair…everyone should have the right to vote, and that was being neglected.” – Lula rises from the ashes, again – Lula, a defining figure in Brazilian politics over four decades, was blindsided after his first-round defeat to Bolsonaro. The left swung into action with massive rallies declaring “Never Again Bolsonaro,” where protesters recalled the former president’s chaotic handling of the Covid pandemic, devastation of the Amazon rainforest and cuts to public programs. Lula also revamped his social media strategy, taking video selfies and even bought his first cellphone, while supporters carried out a feverish campaign to change the minds of family, friends and neighbors, and encourage them to vote after high levels of abstention. His re-election marks another remarkable comeback for the man who grew up dirt poor in the northeast in a family of illiterate farmers. Lula, revered for social welfare programs that lifted millions out of poverty, made a dramatic return to office in 2022 elections after a corruption scandal saw him jailed for over 18 months. The charges, annulled on procedural grounds, have continued to haunt him. In his third term he has overseen a drop in inflation and unemployment, and lifted millions out of hunger, but voters complain about the cost of living and a sense of insecurity. Lula’s social policies became a point of tension as he expanded welfare programs during the campaign. “Brazil needs more time with Lula, primarily because the country is on the verge of falling into the clutches of fascism,” Maria Fernanda Elisbao, a 21-year-old editorial assistant, told AFP. – A tricky term ahead – Lula heads into a fourth term with a country divided, with almost half of the nation voting against him and desperate for change. “We’re in a deep hole, things are dire. People can barely afford to eat — buying meat is out of the question,” said Tereza Cristina Ramos, a 68-year-old retiree, who voted in Rio de Janeiro. Already one of the world’s oldest leaders, Lula will be 85 by the end of his new term in 2030. He will thus have spent 16 years in power, following his first stint as president from 2003 to 2010. Lula is also facing a hostile Congress dominated by the right. His options are also constrained by the economic outlook, with growth expected to slow. He has also come under renewed pressure to confront rampant insecurity in a country plagued by criminal factions that sow terror in working-class neighborhoods. The president’s campaign leaned heavily on the theme of sovereignty in the face of commercial and diplomatic pressure from Trump’s United States. Voters must “choose a country where the flag is respected,” he said, his raspy voice more hoarse than ever after a tireless campaign. He accused his rival of wanting to “govern with the American flag.” The post Brazil’s Lula clinches victory over Flavio Bolsonaro to win fourth term appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Trump critic Lula wins reelection in Brazil, securing fourth presidential term
body:
Flavio Bolsonaro is refusing to concede defeat to incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who bested him by nearly 4.4 million votes, following a chaotic delay in poll closing times ordered by a Supreme Court justice
RIO DE JANEIRO -- Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a vocal critic of U.S. President Donald Trump, was reelected Sunday in a result that provides relief to critics of widening U.S. influence in Latin America .
With 100% of the vote counted, Brazil’s electoral court announced that the soon to be 81-year-old Lula had a lead of nearly 4.4 million votes over opponent Flávio Bolsonaro, giving him 51.8% of the total vote. Bolsonaro quickly refused to concede defeat and asked for the election results to be annulled after an evening of chaos at some polling places that followed a last-minute decision to extend voting by two hours.
Bolsonaro is the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, whom Lula defeated to take the presidency in 2022.
Lula's triumph bucks a regional trend of victories for right-of-center presidential candidates allied with Trump. It also means Latin America’s largest economy, with a GDP of $2.6 trillion per year, will likely continue defying Trump’s demands, despite the pressure of increased tariffs .
A video published by Lula’s campaign shows the veteran leader celebrating with First Lady Rosângela da Silva and allies after his runoff victory was confirmed by Brazil’s electoral court. Wearing star-shaped red glasses, he kissed his wife.
Speaking to his supporters, thousands of whom gathered on Sao Paulo's main artery and in Rio de Janeiro's Cinelandia Square, Lula expressed his gratitude to the Brazilian people, and pledged to respect all Brazilians, regardless of gender or religion. He also attacked Bolsonaro.
“This was a defeat for denialism and lies. I must confess that every time I attended a debate, I felt embarrassed,” he said.
He also doubled down on his commitment to Brazil’s sovereignty.
“Either the homeland remains free, or we die for Brazil,” he said. “This country will not accept being anyone’s backyard.”
In Rio de Janeiro, cars beeped their horns and a woman dressed in red — the color of Lula supporters — shouted “You lost! Cry harder!” to four men in yellow and green sipping beers, Bolsonaro's signature colors. A huge roar echoed in the street as the result was confirmed.
Rodrigo Valentim, a 51-year-old businessman and supporter of Bolsonaro, said that another Lula government would harm the economy. He pointed to financial markets’ positive reaction to the result of the first round, when Bolsonaro bested Lula.
“I don’t understand how people can vote for Lula,” he said. “The country is collapsing.”
Lula is set to begin his fourth non-consecutive term as president on Jan. 5, 2027.
The electoral court's announcement ended an evening of confusion at polling places after Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin ruled three minutes before the scheduled end of voting to keep polls open for two more hours, following requests by both candidates. Lula’s request came after issues with buses that provide transportation to polls in Sao Paulo and Salvador, two cities that tend to favor the incumbent. Bolsonaro’s request was due to heavy rains in Brazil’s south, where he is favored.
The decision delayed tallying the votes by two hours. It was unclear how many polling stations stayed open after the scheduled closing time. Polling stations in Brasilia and Rio de Janeiro closed shortly after the original 5 p.m. deadline, reporters for The Associated Press observed.
Bolsonaro, whose father is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting a coup after he lost the 2022 presidential election to Lula, pointed out that Zanin is Lula’s former lawyer and criticized him for “changing the rules of the game in the middle of the game.”
“It's impossible to recognize the results of the election in the context of these things that happened,” he said.
It's not clear if Bolsonaro’s complaint could meet the legal threshold to annul the results. Bolsonaro also has the right to request a recount if he has evidence of fraud, but that might not change the results.
The president of the electoral court, Kassio Nunes Marques, who was appointed to the Supreme Court by former President Bolsonaro, said that the extension of voting hours did not impact results.
Joao Pedro Padua, a law professor at the Fluminense Federal University, said that Bolsonaro can file a lawsuit directly with the country’s electoral authorities or the Supreme Court, asking for the elections to be declared null and void.
“But there isn’t much legal basis for that,” Padua said. “The extension of voting hours is unusual, but for it to invalidate the elections, the candidate would have to prove that it affected voters’ ability to freely express their will. There doesn’t seem to have been any such impact.”
Bolsonaro bested Lula by more than 2.2 million votes in the first round of the election earlier this month. Sunday night's victory by Lula marked the first time since Brazil’s military dictatorship ended in 1985 that the second-highest vote-getter in the first-round elections won the presidency.
Lula faced a tough reelection battle because of concerns about the cost of living and security. Bolsonaro made a tough-on-crime approach the cornerstone of his campaign and pledged to bring down food costs while Lula, trying to lure undecided voters, has invested in costly incentives .
Both have been hit by corruption suspicions involving family members and allies, with Bolsonaro implicated in a sprawling scandal rocking Brazil. Lula previously spent more than a year in prison on corruption convictions that were eventually annulled .
This will likely be the last victory of the veteran leader’s political career. Lula began his political career in the 1970s as a union leader. He then helped found the Workers’ Party, which he represented as a presidential candidate three times until he finally won it in 2002. He was reelected four years later and was succeeded by one of his cabinet ministers, Dilma Rousseff, in 2010. She was reelected in 2014 but impeached two years later.
Lula tried to run for president again in 2018 but was jailed in March after being convicted. He was released from prison after 580 days and saw Brazil’s Supreme Court annul his sentence after police found messages that showed the judge who convicted him was biased. He quickly became one of Jair Bolsonaro’s biggest critics and narrowly beat him in 2022.
Since he lost the first round, Lula reorganized his campaign, appealed to young voters, put millions of Brazilians on the streets to defend democratic values and his legacy, raised fears of another Bolsonaro administration and boosted several government initiatives.
He joins Trump and Nicaragua’s President Daniel Ortega — all aged 80 — as one of the oldest presidents in the Americas.
Savarese reported from Sao Paulo. Brigida reported from Brasilia.
Follow AP’s coverage of Latin America and the Caribbean at https://apnews.com/hub/latin-america

title: Brazil's left-wing President Lula elected for fourth term
body:
Supporters of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva cheer as the results of Brazil's presidential runoff election are announced in São Paulo on Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. Natacha Pisarenko/AP hide caption
BRASILIA, Brazil — In a stunning political comeback, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has been elected president of Brazil, according to official results from Sunday's runoff election, with more than 96% of the votes counted.
Lula secured more than 51% of the vote, defeating Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, who received more than 48%.
The result marks a historic moment in Brazil's democratic era. Since democracy was restored in 1989, no candidate who failed to win the first round of voting has gone on to win the presidency in the second round.
The victory also adds another chapter to Lula's long political career, securing him a fourth, nonconsecutive presidential term. Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, will be among the oldest sitting leaders in the Americas, alongside President Trump and Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega, both 80.
In a speech to ecstatic supporters in São Paulo, Lula said the election was a "defeat of denialism. A defeat of lies."
"I want to thank the Brazilian people for this generosity they have shown me for so long, to thank the youth who took to the streets to defend democracy, and the elders who went to vote," Lula told the crowd.
President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva addresses supporters after winning a fourth term in the presidential runoff in , Brazil, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. Andre Penner/AP hide caption
Lula's victory bucks a broader rightward shift across Latin America in recent years. In a pointed message to Trump, Lula declared that Brazil would not accept being "anyone's backyard."
Election day unfolded chaotically. Around midday, Lula's campaign requested an extension of voting hours, arguing that some local governments had reduced bus services, making it harder for voters to reach polling stations. Bolsonaro also sought an extension, citing heavy rain in some states.
Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin extended voting by two hours, to 7 p.m., but some polling stations had already deactivated their electronic voting machines and could not resume voting.
Speaking briefly to journalists outside his home in Brasilia, Bolsonaro called the result "inexplicable" and said he would seek to annul the vote. "I will not give up on my Brazil, and I hope you won't give up either," he said.
Bolsonaro, 45, had campaigned on closer ties with President Trump and pledged to pardon his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for plotting a coup to overturn his 2022 election defeat to Lula.
Opposition presidential candidate Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro speaks after the presidential runoff in , Brazil, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. Eraldo Peres/AP hide caption
Brazilians showed little enthusiasm for street campaigning in the early months. But Bolsonaro's first-round finish on Oct. 4 energized the contest, and in recent days supporters of both candidates have filled rallies and flooded social media in an effort to sway voters.
In the end, Lula's message of continuity and a focus on social spending prevailed.
"I think people woke up about the risk of a Bolsonaro government after the first round, and the mobilization made a difference," said Alessandra Miguel, a 35-year-old spa worker who voted for Lula in Rocinha, a favela in Rio de Janeiro.
Lula rose to national prominence as the leader of a metalworkers' union that organized strikes that helped bring down Brazil's dictatorship in the 1980s. Unions and progressive Catholic activists joined forces at the time to form the Workers' Party, which Lula has now represented in seven presidential elections.
During Lula's first two terms in office, from 2003 to 2010, Brazil's economy boomed, and millions of Brazilians rose out of poverty. But many voters turned their backs on the party when Lula and other leaders became embroiled in corruption scandals in the 2010s. Lula himself was jailed, though his convictions were later overturned on procedural grounds.
On foreign policy, Lula has worked to boost the political influence of countries in the Global South as a founding member of the BRICS group, a grouping of major emerging economies that includes Brazil, China, Russia, India and South Africa. He has argued that Brazil should maintain friendly relations with all major world powers, though his ties with China and Russia have sometimes led him to clash with Washington.
Supporters of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva celebrate after he wins a fourth term in the presidential runoff in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. Silvia Izquierdo/AP hide caption
Lula's approval rating rose after he stood up to Trump, but his disapproval rating remained higher than his approval rating at the start of the election season. Brazil's economic growth has been slower than during Lula's first two terms, and many Brazilians felt he had not done enough to address crime and public security.
During the campaign, Lula sought to address those concerns by proposing a ban on sports betting, announcing a debt renegotiation program and backing tougher penalties for minors who commit crimes.
He will govern a sharply divided country. Brazilian political scientist Jairo Nicolau, who studies presidential elections, said one of the most striking features of this year's contest was the rigidity of Brazilians' political allegiances.
Unlike in past years, Nicolau said, "people's identity of belonging to a tribe became more important than how they view different policy options."

title: Two rescued after Nairobi building collapse, with five still missing
body: Two people have been pulled alive from the rubble of a building that collapsed in Kenya’s capital, Nairobi, as a search continues for five still missing. Dramatic footage shows the bottom floor of the block, thought to have been 16 or 18 storeys, giving way before the rest of the building crumples, sending a plume of dust into the surrounding streets on Friday. Dozens of builders were working on the upper floors when it collapsed, but they emerged largely unscathed. Those missing were believed to have been in shops at the building’s base. The incident has raised fresh concerns about construction standards and regulations in Kenya. Police said on Saturday that they had launched a manhunt for the building’s owner and the contractor responsible for the site. The block collapsed on Friday afternoon while under construction, with footage showing scaffolding still wrapped around the outside of the building. Officials said 11 shops had already opened on the bottom floors. Interior ministry official Kipchumba Murkomen said 66 of the 67 construction workers in the building at the time had escaped unharmed, while the other had suffered non-life-threatening injuries. He had said on Friday that seven people had been reported missing and rescue teams had made contact with some of those trapped beneath the rubble. Police said the two survivors rescued on Saturday have been taken to hospital. Images from the scene in Nairobi’s Eastleigh area show the building’s concrete floors piled on top of one another, as rescue workers saw through metal to reach those believed to be trapped underneath. Footage taken from nearby shows moments before (left) and moments after (right) the building collapsed Questions have emerged about why the building suddenly collapsed and whether it met planning regulations. Kenya’s National Construction Authority said in a statement that it had identified the company behind the development, as well as the architect and structural engineer, but did not say whether it had inspected the site before Friday. The National Police Service said it had launched an investigation to establish the cause of the collapse and determine whether anyone was criminally liable. It warned that anyone found responsible for negligence or violating building regulations would “face the full force of the law”. Nairobi Governor Sakaja Johnson told local media that the building’s owners lacked the required paperwork to occupy it. He urged the national government to give local authorities greater powers to penalise “developers who disregard approved building plans and safety standards”. Building collapses are not uncommon in Nairobi, with poor construction or improper planning often cited as contributing factors.

title: Kharkiv establishes first anti-drone corridor
body:
This was reported by a Ukrinform correspondent.
The work was recently completed. The corridor is seven meters high. As Oleh Syniehubov, head of the Kharkiv Regional State Administration, confirmed to journalists, there are plans to cover other sections as well. The current priority is the section of the ring road from the “Losk” car market to the Oleksiyivka residential area. This is approximately 14 km. The corridor will be constructed using funds from the regional budget.
“This is what will happen in the near future. This is what we see as critically necessary to do. We will allocate about 10 million hryvnias for this,” said Syniehubov.
As reported by Ukrinform, on the morning of May 21, Russian troops used an FPV drone to attack a truck traveling on the Kharkiv Ring Road, killing the 40-year-old driver. Following this, a section of the ring road (the M-03 highway between km 491 and km 501, from Feldman Ecopark to the Lyptsivske Intersection) was closed to traffic.
In July, the installation of anti-drone nets was completed on this section , but the road remained closed to traffic.

title: Research project to deliver certified laser repairs for military aircraft components
body: An industry-led research collaboration is set to transform how Australia maintains its most critical defence aircraft — shifting from costly and long lead-time component replacement to certified, high-performance laser repair. Supported by the Additive Manufacturing Cooperative Research Centre (AMCRC), the two-year collaboration brings together Rosebank Engineering, RMIT Centre for Additive Manufacturing and Swinburne University of Technology to develop a certifiable Laser Direct Energy Deposition (L-DED) repair process for high-value aerospace alloys used broadly across modern military aircraft. The research focuses on precipitation-hardening materials widely used in defence aviation, including Inconel, Titanium, and 15-5PH stainless steel, with the goal of demonstrating the repair of an advanced military aircraft component in line with Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) and NASA-STD-6030 requirements. At the core of the project is an innovative laser rescanning technique designed to control microstructure during the repair process itself. By tailoring heat input locally, the team aims to achieve the required material property performance without post-process heat treatment — a major barrier to qualifying additive repairs in aerospace. Rosebank Engineering will lead process development and validation, integrating its unique Adaptive Monitoring and Control of Laser Additive Deposition (AMCLAD) system to ensure consistent and repeatable repair outcomes. Jarrod Watts, Senior Manager Engineering and Projects, at Rosebank Engineering said the project is a substantial step toward achieving certified laser repairs of high-value high-strength steel components. “These types of high-value components are currently sourced – in the sustainment environment – from complex international supply chains with long lead-times. We know laser offers the opportunity to repair in-country with significant cost and lead-time reductions. This project tackles that challenge directly”, Watts said. “Through the use of our AMCLAD capability, and in-process refinement of the microstructure, we can deliver material performance that meets aerospace requirements without risking distortion or damage of the original component. Developing the ability to reliably repair critical components in-country mitigates supply chain risks, reduces cost of ownership for our customers and enhances operational readiness.” Researchers at RMIT Centre for Additive Manufacturing and Swinburne University of Technology will generate the technical evidence supporting qualification, including tensile strength, fatigue life, residual stress, corrosion and wear performance, forming a comprehensive Material Property Suite aligned with NASA standards. Professor Milan Brandt of RMIT Centre for Additive Manufacturing, overseeing the laser process optimisation, said the project pushes additive process control into new territory. “Laser rescanning allows us to refine microstructures in ways conventional heat treatment cannot achieve in repair scenarios. By controlling phase transformations during deposition, we can unlock performance levels that meet aerospace standards,” Professor Brandt said. Swinburne University of Technology will undertake detailed material characterisation and mechanical testing as part of the project. Professor Suresh Palanisamy of Swinburne University of Technology underlines the importance of rigorous validation to industry adoption. “Certification is evidence-driven. Our role is to produce the data that proves the process is robust, repeatable and capable of meeting aerospace requirements. That depth of validation is what enables industry confidence”, Professor Palanisamy said. The project will also explore repair pathways for in-demand F/A-18 engine components, providing a near-term commercial opportunity that equally supports broader adoption across a broad family of aircraft. Simon Marriott, Managing Director of AMCRC, said the project reflects the CRC’s industry-first focus. “Australia has strong additive manufacturing research capability. AMCRC exists to translate that strength into commercial and defence outcomes”, Marriott said. “This project exemplifies that mission — industry-led, defence-relevant, and built around certification from day one. By enabling certified local repair, we strengthen sovereign manufacturing capability and deliver long-term economic and strategic benefit.” For Editorial Inquiries Contact: Editor Kym Bergmann at kym.bergmann@venturamedia.net For Advertising Inquiries Contact: Group Sales Director Simon Hadfield at simon.hadfield@venturamedia.net

title: Justice, fairness, peace and Nigeria’s 2027 election
body: By ANTHONY OGBEIFUN As Nigeria approaches the 2027 general election, the country stands again at a familiar crossroads: the choice between narrow, sectional calculation and the broader national demand for justice, fairness and peace. Elections are not merely contests for power. In a plural society such as Nigeria, they are also referendums on whether citizens believe the state belongs to all of them. Few Nigerian voices expressed this truth more memorably than the late elder statesman and Dan Masanin Kano, Alhaji Yusuf Maitama Sule. In May 2015, Sule led a delegation of the Northern Leaders Forum to congratulate then President-elect Muhammadu Buhari. His counsel on that occasion remains strikingly relevant today. Sule told Buhari: “With justice, you can rule Nigeria well. Justice is the key.” It was a simple statement, but one carrying the weight of Nigeria’s history. The country’s recurrent crises—ethnic suspicion, religious tension, electoral violence, insecurity, economic exclusion and the erosion of public trust—are not disconnected accidents. They are symptoms of a deeper disorder: the feeling among many citizens that fairness is selective, opportunity is unequal and power is used to reward loyalty rather than serve the common good. Sule understood this. “Behind every crisis anywhere in the world is injustice,” he said. And the antidote, he insisted, is “justice.” That insight should guide every political party, candidate, campaign organisation and voter ahead of 2027. A nation cannot be held together by slogans alone. Neither can it be governed successfully by force, intimidation or the temporary advantage of incumbency. Sule warned: “The world itself can never be governed by force, never by fear, even never by power. In the end, what governs is the mind. What conquers is the spirit and the weapons of governing the mind and conquering the spirit are justice and fair play.” Nigeria’s 2027 election will therefore test not only the popularity of candidates, but the moral seriousness of the political class. Justice, in the sense Sule meant it, is broader than court judgments or legal technicalities. It includes fair representation, equitable distribution of public resources, respect for the rule of law, protection of minorities, credible elections and equal treatment before public institutions. It means that a farmer in Zamfara, a trader in Onitsha, a teacher in Lagos, a fisherman in Bayelsa and a herder in Sokoto should all be able to expect the state to protect their lives, respect their rights and respond to their needs without discrimination. Sule put it plainly: “If you do justice to all and sundry — and I say all and sundry — because Allah says, ‘If you are going to judge between two people, do justice irrespective of the tribe, religion or even political inclination; justice must be done to whosoever deserves it.’” That standard is demanding. It rejects the politics of “our turn” when it becomes a cover for exclusion. It also rejects the politics of revenge, where one group’s victory is treated as another group’s defeat. Nigeria needs leaders who can rise above such thinking. The late Dan Masanin Kano was equally clear that justice must not be selective. “I am not asking you — and I know you will not — to discriminate against any part of Nigeria,” he told Buhari. “But I am asking you to do justice to all parts of Nigeria.” For political parties preparing for 2027, fairness must begin before the first ballot is cast. It must be visible in candidate selection, zoning arrangements, internal party democracy, campaign financing and the treatment of aspirants. When parties manipulate primaries, impose candidates, marginalise women and young people, or allow money to determine nomination, they weaken the legitimacy of the eventual winner. A flawed process produces a fragile mandate. And a fragile mandate makes governing harder, especially in a country where citizens are already sceptical of political promises. Fairness also requires issue-based campaigns. Nigeria’s problems are real: insecurity, unemployment, inflation, poor infrastructure, weak public services, climate pressure on agriculture and widespread poverty. These challenges do not respect ethnicity or religion. Candidates should therefore be judged on their plans to secure communities, create jobs, reform institutions, expand opportunities and restore public confidence. A campaign built on fear, sectional resentment or religious division may win attention, but it cannot build a nation. Sule’s warning remains urgent: force, fear and power cannot govern the mind or conquer the spirit. Only justice and fair play can. Sule linked justice directly to peace and development. “Justice will bring about peace,” he said. “Peace and stability are the pre-requisites of development.” No society develops sustainably in an atmosphere of fear. Investors hesitate where contracts are uncertain and violence is common. Farmers abandon land where insecurity prevails. Young people lose hope where merit is ignored and corruption rewards the connected. Communities retreat into distrust when they believe the state protects some citizens more than others. Peace is not merely the absence of gunfire. It is the presence of confidence: confidence that elections will count, that courts will be impartial, that public offices will serve the public, and that no region, faith or class will be permanently shut out of opportunity. The 2027 election offers Nigeria a chance to rebuild that confidence. But it will require more than campaign rhetoric. It will require electoral institutions that are visibly independent, security agencies that act professionally, political actors who accept results peacefully, and citizens who refuse to be used as instruments of violence. Nigeria does not lack talent, resources or ideas. What it often lacks is the disciplined commitment to justice that turns diversity into strength rather than division. Maitama Sule’s message was not addressed to one president alone. It was addressed to every Nigerian leader, in every generation, and to every citizen who hopes for a better country. As 2027 approaches, voters should ask hard questions: Which candidate will uphold the rule of law even when it is inconvenient? Which party will distribute opportunity fairly? Which leader will govern for all Nigerians, not merely for those who funded a campaign or share a regional identity? The answer should not be based on sentiment, ethnicity or fear. It should be based on justice. Sule’s counsel remains a compass: “With justice, you can rule Nigeria well. Justice is the key.” If Nigeria’s political class embraces that key, the 2027 election can become more than another contest for office. It can become a renewal of the national promise—a step towards a country at peace with itself, fair to all its people, and capable at last of fulfilling its vast potential. •Ogbeifun wrote in from Lagos. The post Justice, fairness, peace and Nigeria’s 2027 election appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Making gas operations safer
body: Nigeria’s ambition to expand the use of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) must be matched by a serious commitment to safety. The Nigerian Association of Liquefied Petroleum Gas Marketers (NALPGAM), at its recent webinar on operational excellence and compliance, warned that rising consumption alone cannot guarantee a sustainable industry. Every facility must be safe, every operator competent, every process compliant and every customer protected. The warning is timely. LPG offers households and businesses a cleaner alternative to firewood, charcoal and other polluting fuels, but it is highly flammable. Leaking gas, overfilled cylinders, defective valves, poorly maintained equipment and unsafe storage can turn premises into disaster scenes. Illegal decanting and unauthorised propane blending compound these risks, endangering workers, consumers and neighbouring communities. Such practices must not be treated as commercial shortcuts. NALPGAM’s proposed Standard of Operational Excellence, built around safe facilities, trained personnel, compliant processes and consumer protection, deserves support. But a declaration is not enforcement. The association must translate its aspiration into measurable obligations for members, while the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority (NMDPRA) must sustain inspections, investigate violations and apply sanctions. Operators should maintain equipment, verify cylinder integrity, provide fire and gas-detection systems, and report incidents promptly. Regulators should publish inspection and enforcement data so the public can judge progress. Technology can strengthen this effort. Smart filling systems, calibrated load cells, flow meters, automated tank gauges and vehicle tracking can improve measurement, trace product movements and expose losses or suspicious transactions. Digital tools, however, are no substitute for trained staff, independent checks and functioning emergency procedures. Small operators may need affordable training, technical guidance and finance for compliant upgrades; such assistance must never become an excuse to relax minimum safety standards. Safety also has an economic dimension. Accidents destroy lives, property, investment and public confidence. Consumers who fear explosions or suspect short-changing may avoid cooking gas, frustrating efforts to broaden its use. Reliable cylinder traceability, approved exchange arrangements, accurate measurement and clear consumer information can build trust. Government should involve marketers in LPG penetration and cylinder recirculation programmes, while improving supply and distribution infrastructure to make fuel more accessible and affordable. The stakes extend beyond individual kitchens. Wider adoption of LPG can reduce household exposure to smoke from solid fuels and ease pressure on forests. A safer, better-regulated market can also attract investment, support certified local cylinder manufacturing, create jobs and deepen Nigeria’s energy economy. The national target of five million tonnes of annual LPG consumption by 2030 will mean little if expansion outpaces safety capacity. Government, regulators and marketers must turn promises into deadlines, audits, transparent reporting and consequences for negligence. Safety must govern every delivery, filling and transaction. Only then can Nigerians embrace gas with confidence, the environment benefit, and the industry become a pillar of economic diversification.
