title: When a police officer is caught at crime scene
body: By Owolola Adebola The sight of a police officer at a crime scene should ordinarily inspire confidence, reassurance and hope. It should signal the arrival of law, the protection of innocent citizens and the beginning of justice for victims. But what happens when the very officer expected to prevent a crime is caught participating in it? What happens when the uniform that should represent honour becomes a disguise for criminality? At that moment, the incident transcends the conduct of an individual officer. It becomes a test of the integrity of the police institution, the effectiveness of internal supervision and the willingness of the state to hold its own agents accountable. A police officer caught at a crime scene under suspicious circumstances presents a troubling contradiction. The law enforcement agent who should be chasing criminals may suddenly find himself on the other side of the law. The individual entrusted with protecting lives and property may become a threat to the very people whose safety he has sworn to defend. Such an incident demands serious investigation, not institutional excuses. Of course, insanity creeps in when the uniform becomes a shield for criminality because the police uniform carries authority. It commands attention, opens doors and gives its wearer powers that ordinary citizens do not possess. These privileges are granted for public service, not personal enrichment, intimidation or criminal enterprise. Unfortunately, when an officer abuses that authority, the consequences can be devastating. A police officer involved in robbery, kidnapping, extortion, unlawful possession of weapons or the protection of criminal gangs does more than violate the law. He exploits public confidence and undermines the institution he represents. The situation becomes even more disturbing when an officer is found at a scene where criminal activities are taking place and credible evidence suggests that he may be involved. Rather than automatically treating the officer as guilty, the authorities must establish what brought him there, what role he played and whether his presence was lawful. An officer could be at a crime scene to prevent an offence, rescue a victim, investigate an incident or arrest suspects. But where evidence points to complicity, the uniform must offer no protection from investigation. The badge is not a licence to commit crime. It is a badge of honour and not a badge of horror. The uniform is not immunity from prosecution. And membership of the police force must never become a passport to escape justice. Public cooperation is indispensable to effective policing. Citizens provide information, identify suspects, report suspicious activities and assist investigations because they expect the police to act in their interest. But when officers themselves become suspects in criminal investigations, that confidence suffers. A trader who sees a police officer allegedly collaborating with armed robbers may hesitate before reporting the next suspicious movement. A family whose relative has been victimised by an officer may lose faith in the complaint process. A community that repeatedly encounters alleged police misconduct may begin to regard law enforcement as a source of danger rather than protection. This erosion of trust gives criminals additional room to operate. Witnesses become reluctant to speak, victims withdraw complaints and valuable intelligence disappears into a climate of suspicion. The damage is not limited to the immediate victims. Honest police officers also pay the price. Their sacrifices, courage and commitment can be overshadowed by the misconduct of colleagues who betray the institution. It is therefore in the interest of the police themselves to confront criminality within their ranks decisively. Protecting a compromised officer does not protect the institution; it places the reputation of the entire force at risk. In a way, investigation must replace cover-up. Whenever a police officer is apprehended at a crime scene under circumstances suggesting criminal involvement, the first responsibility of the authorities is to establish the facts. The scene must be secured. Weapons, documents, surveillance footage and other relevant evidence must be preserved. Witnesses should be interviewed without intimidation, and the officer’s movements and communications should be examined where legally authorised. Where there is credible evidence of wrongdoing, the officer should be subjected to the same lawful investigative process applicable to other suspects. Rank, seniority, political connections and years of service must not determine whether an investigation proceeds. At the same time, fairness requires that allegations be distinguished from proven facts. Being present at a crime scene does not, by itself, establish guilt. The officer must have an opportunity to respond to the allegations, and the investigation must respect due process. This balance is essential. Accountability without fairness can become persecution, while fairness without accountability can become an excuse for impunity. The Nigeria Police Force must demonstrate that its disciplinary procedures are effective and that credible allegations of criminal conduct receive prompt, impartial attention. Where the evidence establishes criminal responsibility, administrative discipline alone may be insufficient; criminal prosecution should follow where warranted. A transfer to another command, quiet retirement or internal reprimand must not become a convenient substitute for justice in a serious criminal case. Come to Think of It: The Responsibility of Police Leadership Police leadership has a duty to ensure that officers understand the limits of their authority and the consequences of abusing it. Recruitment, training, supervision and disciplinary systems must reinforce the principle that integrity is as important as operational competence. Commanders must also be prepared to investigate officers under their supervision without fear or favour. Where a superior officer obstructs an investigation, destroys evidence or shields a colleague from accountability, that conduct must itself attract scrutiny. Independent oversight, accessible complaint channels and protection for whistle-blowers can help citizens report misconduct without fear of retaliation. Regular audits of police operations, transparent reporting of disciplinary outcomes and effective collaboration with relevant oversight bodies can further strengthen accountability. In addition, technology also has a role to play. Properly managed body cameras, vehicle tracking systems, digital duty records and evidence-management procedures can help establish where officers were deployed and what occurred during an operation. Such tools must be governed by clear rules to protect privacy, preserve evidence and prevent manipulation. The objective is not to portray every police officer as a potential criminal. It is to build a system in which honest officers are protected, misconduct is detected and those who abuse their authority cannot easily escape scrutiny. Justice Must Be Seen to Be Done When a police officer is caught at a crime scene and credible evidence indicates possible criminal involvement, the public deserves more than official silence. It deserves a credible investigation and, where necessary, prosecution. The authorities must communicate verified developments responsibly without compromising investigations or prejudicing a fair trial. If the officer is cleared, that outcome should also be acknowledged. Justice must not be manipulated to satisfy public anger, political interests or institutional embarrassment. Ultimately, the true strength of a police force is not measured by the number of arrests it makes, the weapons it recovers or the criminals it parades before television cameras. Its strength is measured by its willingness to obey the law it enforces. A police officer who catches a criminal deserves commendation. An officer who becomes involved in crime must face the consequences established by law. There should be no confusion between the two. Nigeria cannot build a society governed by law if those entrusted with enforcing that law are permitted to stand above it. The police uniform must remain a symbol of service, discipline and courage—not a hiding place for criminal conduct. When an officer is caught at a crime scene, the decisive question is not whether the institution can protect its reputation by remaining silent. It is whether the institution possesses the courage to protect that reputation by telling the truth, investigating the evidence and allowing justice to take its course. The uniform may command respect, but only integrity can sustain it. And when the hand entrusted with enforcing the law is suspected of breaking it, the law must be allowed to do its work without fear, favour or compromise. •Adebola, the State Publicity Secretary of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Ondo State Chapter, wrote in from Akure. title: Gabon says access to social media restored after eight-month ban
body: Gabon says it has lifted a social media ban imposed eight months ago, a move that drew widespread criticism at the time. The High Communication Authority (HAC) announced the U-turn on Saturday in a televised statement. The BBC has approached the country’s media regulator for comment. The HAC introduced the ban on 17 February, saying online content was fuelling conflict and deepening divisions in the country. The move came as a shock to the central African nation of about 2.5 million people, where social media platforms such as Facebook, TikTok, YouTube and Instagram have been particularly popular with younger people who use it for business as well as pleasure. Many turned to VPNs to keep accessing social media sites after the ban. The ban came at a time when Gabonese President Brice Oligui Nguema was facing a wave of social unrest less than a year after his election. Teachers and civil servants had staged strikes over what they said were low pay and poor working conditions. The opposition said the suspension was an abuse of power. Nguema won last year’s elections with more than 90% of the vote, two years after his coup ended more than five decades of Bongo family rule. At the time, he pledged to reform Gabon, a small, oil- and timber-rich country, where digital blackouts were used by the previous governments to control information.

title: “AI Skills” are worthless in 2026
body:
When I was first learning the C programming language, in my early 20s, it was common knowledge that of the two ways to increment a variable, i++ was slower than ++i . The post-increment function returned the original value of i , which meant stashing a copy of that value before performing the increment. Pre-increment avoided this wasteful operation.
And by âcommon knowledgeâ I really mean folklore, because I turned 20 in 1995 and even by then, the most basic of optimising compilers knew to check if you ever used the return value of i++ , and if not, skip the operation to save it.
Scratch an old programmer and you'll probably find a dozen or so ingrained habits that, in an era where CPUs are doing branch prediction and code reordering, are just as likely to make their program slower.
It makes sense to believe that all the tricks we come up with with to make models behave better, the ways of working with models that get us to a useful result faster, if they work, are going to be folded back into the product, packaged, and become the default experience a few months later. And yet, in five years, Iâm sure there will be old heads doggedly adding âyou are an experienced software developer, make no mistakesâ to their custom instructions.
I'm not saying it's worthless to keep up with the state of the art. You still need to be able do your job today, to the best of your ability. But a skill that can be picked up in a few weeks, and will be obsolete in a few months, has no value outside the moment.
Eighteen months ago, I was sitting in a crowded room watching a CEO enthusiastically declare that it was time to get on the AI train, because if you didn't get on it right now you'd be left behind. Maybe I'm getting old, but in a world where Google, Facebook, the iPod, iPhone and iPad, and so many other examples have shown that getting it right is more valuable than getting in first, I feel content to just keep pace with the pack, ready to pull Steven Bradbury if and when the time comes.

title: We never left Egypt, only prodigals need to return home, by Owei Lakemfa
body: President Bola Ahmed Tinubu told Nigerians on October 19, 2026, that they will not return to Egypt. He seems unaware that Egypt is our ancestral home and that we never left and will never leave. This Niger Area is the land of milk and honey we inherited from our fathers and mothers. We were never slaves in this land, will fight any attempt to enslave us; therefore, we never had any reason to flee. We never had any reason to part ways with the sea or for the sea to part ways for us. We never needed to wander in any desert for forty years or more, seeking pathways to freedom or prosperity. This has never been, and will never be, our portion in life. Ancient Egypt is the origin of modern civilisation. It civilised the Greeks and Romans, who were its pupils before they passed that civilisation to the rest of Europe. The peoples who make up Nigeria were self-sufficient, with viable city-states and empires, and well-schooled in their non-Western education. One of the natural endowments of this beautiful country is oil. We began producing it in commercial quantities from 1956–57. We were self-sufficient in it, including local refining, with the country running four refineries. As then Head of State Yakubu Gowon said in 1973: “Money is not Nigeria’s problem, but how to spend it.” What has happened to Nigeria is not that oil has stopped flowing. It is not that the technology to refine sufficient petroleum products for local consumption and export has been lost. Rather, the tragedy we face is that we have had a mainly prodigal leadership since military rule began sixty years ago. So, in our Egypt, we have sufficient oil reserves that will last at least the next sixty years. There was no fuel subsidy because we did not need to subsidise what we have. It is like asking a rich farmer with fertile soil and bursting barns of yam to subsidise the pounded yam his family will have for supper. What has happened is that a prodigal political class took over, deliberately ran down the refineries, refused to build new ones and, most criminally, insisted on denominating fuel in inflated dollar accounting. Their paper accounting is based on our country having no drop of oil, which we all know is false, and having to import finished products which are bought by dubious officials from their chosen partners, pay freight, insurance, port fees, demurrage and storage fees. These products are then handed over to a cartel which transports them through deliberately neglected or abandoned roads and sells them to hapless Nigerians at rates imposed by the cartel. In this dubious process is built what is touted as subsidy. Since the Babangida regime, this dubious subsidy mirage has been factored into our petroleum products. When the latest subsidy removal was touted on May 29, 2023, Nigerians were told the proceeds would be used for development. But what we have experienced is greater misery, multiplication of the hungry, dilapidating infrastructure, a rising number of out-of-school children, lack of mass housing, virtually abandoned basic healthcare and insecurity. Whenever we ask the administration what has been done with the so-called subsidy savings, it points at increasing the revenue allocation to states and local governments. It is aware that most leaders of these tiers are like cats being told to watch over fried fish. Deceptively, it does not point at itself as being the largest recipient of these extra funds, which remain unaccounted for. When President Tinubu announced that his administration had removed fuel subsidy, the price of a litre of PMS was increased from about N197 to an average N500. Today, it is thrice that price, and the government blames this insanity on the war in Iran. In this, the Tinubu government is behaving like the dirty widow with head lice creeping all over her hair who blames this on mourning her husband by not allowing a drop of water to touch her head since his demise. If the Nigerian government blames the war in Iran for the outrageous price of PMS in the country, why is Iran, which has suffered the catastrophe of having its leadership wiped out, children buried under the rubble of their classrooms, infrastructure and oil facilities bombed and punishing sanctions imposed by the United States, not been similarly affected? Honourable Victor Afam Oghene, Member, Federal House of Representatives, Ogbaru Constituency of Anambra State, debunked, with verifiable statistics, these childish fairy tales of the Tinubu government. He gave comparative statistics of PMS prices in four oil-producing countries: Iran, which has been at war for years; Libya, which has suffered state collapse since 2011 and had at least three factional governments in Tobruk, Tripoli and Benghazi; Saudi Arabia, which is engaged in war with neighbouring Yemen; and Nigeria, which is not at war. In his statistics, which the increasingly intolerant Tinubu government and its army of internet propagandists have not been able to fault, Honourable Oghene revealed that a litre of PMS in Iran is N38, Libya, N32, Saudi Arabia, N832, and Nigeria, at least N1,300. In contrast, the National Minimum Wage in Iran is N165,000, Libya is N210,000, Saudi Arabia, N1.4 million, and N70,000 in Nigeria! Oghene then analysed these basic statistics in value terms. He showed that the minimum wage in Iran can purchase 4,242 litres of PMS, Libya, 6,562 litres, Saudi Arabia, 1,700, and only 46 litres in Nigeria! Tragically, despite such sound analysis and the situation in the country, the Tinubu administration appears increasingly irritated, deaf to the cries of Nigerians and incapable of basic thinking. For instance, rather than examine the arguments of various patriots and pro-people activists on the issue of fuel subsidy and the calamitous effects on the populace, it is threatening Nigerians with dire consequences. In its unfathomable scare-mongering, the administration’s Minister of Finance, Taiwo Oyedele, threatened that even an inkling of the administration rethinking the subsidy issue would trigger capital flight. This, he claimed, would lead to the naira, which has already been devalued over fifty per cent by Tinubu, suffering a further sixty per cent devaluation. Oyedele told Nigerians this fable, not based on any analysis, but beliefs. He also claimed that this would raise the price of petrol to at least N2,000 per litre. Even as a product of Yale University and London School of Economics, and an advertised policy expert, the Honourable Minister could not provide the cost component of this his projected N2,000-per-litre PMS. We Nigerians never left our Egypt, so there is no issue of a return. It is the prodigals of the political class that need to return home, ask for forgiveness and stop suffocating the country. The post We never left Egypt, only prodigals need to return home, by Owei Lakemfa appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Death toll in Nigeria village raided by gunmen rises to 48, police say
body: The death toll from Friday’s attack on a remote village in the north-eastern Nigerian state of Taraba has risen to at least 48, police have told the BBC. The police had initially reported 10 deaths after unidentified gunmen on motorcycles raided the village of Binnari, looting shops and setting houses ablaze. More bodies were discovered on Sunday, according to state police spokesperson Victor Mshelizah, who said some of the victims had drowned while trying to escape the attackers, while others were killed in nearby bushes. Meanwhile, Amnesty International’s director for Nigeria said his organisation had confirmed 52 deaths, citing sources on the ground and members of the local community. The attack happened just after midday Muslim prayers, and the rampage went on for up to four hours. State police had initially recovered 10 bodies with gunshot wounds after officers responded to a distress call. The attackers had fled by the time officers arrived, but they continued to patrol the area to restore calm, Taraba’s police told the BBC on Saturday. “We were able to disperse the unknown gunmen, though there were no casualties on their side or ours because the terrain is difficult and they’re used to the terrain,” Assistant Superintendent of Police Victor Mshelizah said. Community leader Malam Abubakar Saifullahi told news agency AFP that the attackers had arrived on about 50 motorcycles, two men apiece. “They looted shops and took cash, foodstuffs and other provisions,” he said. “They also took motorcycles abandoned by people fleeing the attack.” Isiyaku Musa, who survived the attack, told AFP: “People were running in different directions to escape the attack. Nobody knew where it was safe to go.” Amnesty’s Nigeria director Isa Sanusi has called for an impartial investigation into the killings, accusing the authorities of leaving rural communities “at the mercy of gunmen that are repeatedly committing atrocities with impunity”. Parts of north-eastern Nigeria have been affected by years of violence involving jihadist groups and armed gangs, which raid communities, abduct residents and demand ransoms. Similar armed groups operate in the country’s north-west and central regions. The latest attack comes as Nigeria prepares for elections next year, with insecurity expected to feature prominently in political debates. Survivors who spoke to AFP said they had counted at least 20 dead. “People were running in different directions to escape the attack,” Binnari resident Isiyaku Musa said. “Nobody knew where it was safe to go.” Another survivor, Sa’idu Nuhu, said that some people were still missing. Amnesty’s Nigeria director, Isa Sanusi, told BBC News on Saturday that the NGO had spoken to some of the bereaved families who said up to 50 people had died. “The initial funeral had 37 people,” he said. Sanusi called for an impartial investigation into the killings, accusing the authorities of leaving rural communities “at the mercy of gunmen that are repeatedly commit atrocities with impunity”.

title: Houston’s message to Africa: Innovation must deliver more barrels, lower costs and better returns
body: By Kunle Odusola-Stevenson The future of Africa’s oil and gas industry will not be determined by the resources beneath its soil alone, but by how effectively it deploys technology, attracts investment and translates policy into commercial results. This was a central takeaway from the Society of Petroleum Engineers’ (SPE) Annual Technical Conference and Exhibition (ATCE) 2026, held in Houston, Texas, from October 21 to 23. Under the theme, “Exploring New Horizons with Innovative Solutions,” the conference brought together energy professionals to examine the technologies, engineering practices and operational strategies shaping the industry’s future. For Nigeria, where increasing production, developing natural gas resources and strengthening indigenous operators remain national priorities, the message was clear: innovation must translate into measurable business performance. The global energy industry is under pressure to deliver reliable supplies, improve capital efficiency and reduce environmental impacts. For Africa, these demands coincide with a pressing need to expand electricity access, industrialise economies and create productive employment. The challenge is not simply to defend the relevance of hydrocarbons, but to demonstrate that African energy resources can be developed competitively, responsibly and profitably. The lessons from Houston offer a practical starting point. Artificial intelligence, advanced reservoir analytics, predictive maintenance, drilling automation and digital production monitoring are creating opportunities to improve oil recovery, reduce equipment failures, shorten operational delays and strengthen investment decisions. Their significance lies not in technological novelty, but in their potential to improve the economics of producing assets. Consider Nigeria’s mature oilfields, many of which face declining production, ageing infrastructure, rising water cuts and expensive maintenance requirements. Better integration of geological data, well-performance records and production information can help operators identify underperforming wells, prioritise interventions and determine where additional investment is most likely to recover lost production. Predictive maintenance can similarly help operators identify early warning signs in pumps, compressors and other critical equipment before failures cause costly shutdowns. Improved drilling analytics can support better well planning, reduce non-productive time and strengthen operational safety. Meanwhile, methane monitoring and flare-management technologies can help operators identify emissions sources, reduce avoidable losses and improve environmental performance. These are practical applications for Nigeria’s oil and gas industry, not automatic outcomes of technology adoption. Results depend on reliable data, competent personnel, appropriate infrastructure and disciplined implementation. Every investment should therefore be assessed against measurable indicators, including incremental production, reduced downtime, lower operating costs, improved recovery and emissions reduction. This approach is particularly important as Nigeria’s upstream industry undergoes structural change. The transfer of selected onshore and shallow-water assets from international oil companies to indigenous operators has created opportunities for domestic companies to expand their participation and retain more value within the economy. Yet a change of ownership does not automatically produce higher output, stronger profitability or sustainable operations. Indigenous operators must combine ownership with the technical and financial capacity to manage complex reservoirs, rehabilitate infrastructure, improve recovery and meet environmental obligations. Access to technology, long-term financing, specialised engineering expertise and dependable evacuation systems will be critical to their success. Nigeria’s ambition to achieve three million barrels of crude oil production per day by 2030 must therefore be treated as an execution challenge rather than a statement of intent. New developments, improved recovery from existing fields, reduced production losses, reliable evacuation and sustained investment must work together to deliver the desired outcome. The leadership transition within the SPE Nigeria Council, from Engr. Francis Nwaochei to Engr. Etta Agbor, also presents an opportunity to strengthen the connection between global technical knowledge and local operating realities. Professional institutions such as SPE can support this process through applied research, technical training, industry collaboration and the development of Nigerian engineering talent capable of evaluating and deploying advanced technologies. However, technology alone cannot overcome an uncertain investment environment. Regulatory predictability remains fundamental. The Petroleum Industry Act provides an important statutory framework, but investors also require transparent fiscal arrangements, timely approvals, consistent regulatory decisions and clarity over contractual obligations. Effective regulation should protect public interests while enabling commercially viable projects to proceed without avoidable administrative delays. Security and infrastructure are equally important. Production cannot generate its full economic value if crude oil and gas cannot reach markets reliably. Pipeline disruptions, theft, infrastructure failures and insecurity increase operating costs, undermine revenues and weaken investor confidence. Government institutions, regulators, operators, security agencies and host communities must work together to protect infrastructure and strengthen the reliability of Nigeria’s energy supply chain. Environmental performance is also becoming integral to commercial competitiveness. Methane detection, flare reduction, emissions monitoring and environmental remediation increasingly influence investor assessments and access to international financing. Operators must incorporate these responsibilities into field-development plans and operating budgets rather than treating them as separate sustainability commitments. Beyond upstream production, Africa’s energy investment proposition extends across the value chain. Gas processing, pipelines, gas-to-power, domestic LNG and LPG distribution can support industrial growth where viable markets and bankable offtake arrangements exist. Refining and petrochemical development can create additional value through domestic processing, fertiliser production, manufacturing and associated logistics. Each opportunity, however, requires commercially realistic assumptions, dependable infrastructure and appropriate risk allocation. For international investors, the question is no longer simply whether Africa possesses substantial hydrocarbon resources. It is whether specific projects can offer credible returns, transparent governance, manageable risks and reliable access to markets. African governments and operators must make that case through predictable policies, technical competence and consistent delivery. Industry platforms such as the Nigeria International Energy Summit can help connect technology providers, indigenous operators, regulators, policymakers and international financiers. Their value should ultimately be measured by what follows the discussions: capital mobilised, partnerships established, technology deployed, infrastructure completed and production improved. The message from Houston to Abuja is unmistakable. Africa’s energy future will not be secured by resource abundance alone. It will depend on the disciplined convergence of engineering excellence, investment, reliable infrastructure, environmental responsibility and decisive policy execution. Nigeria has the resources and entrepreneurial potential to compete more effectively in the global energy economy. The task is to create the conditions that allow those advantages to translate into sustained production, industrial growth and shared prosperity. Africa must move beyond selling the promise of its resources to demonstrating the strength of its energy business case. Innovation must deliver more barrels, lower costs and better returns. That is how global technology can become local capability, investment can become productive capacity, and energy can become a foundation for lasting economic transformation. Odusola-Stevenson is CEO of The Legend & Legacy Company Ltd. title: Russia’s Alexander Nikishin signs $3 mln one-year contract with NHL Carolina Hurricanes
body:
WASHINGTON, October 26. /TASS/. Russia’s Stanley Cup winner Alexander Nikishin has inked a one-year contract with the US-based NHL club Carolina Hurricanes, the club’s press office announced in a statement.
The contract with the 25-year-old Russian defenseman was signed for one season and stipulates a salary of $3 million.
"We’re glad that Alexander is returning to our group," the statement quotes Carolina Hurricanes General Manager Eric Tulsky as saying.
"This has been a long process, but we look forward to him re-entering our locker room ready to contribute with the Hurricanes, as he did during a Stanley Cup championship season last year," he added.
According to the club’s provided data, "The 25-year-old was named to the NHL’s All-Rookie Team in 2025-26, after ranking second among NHL rookie defensemen in goals (11) and points (33) and tied for second in assists (22)."
"[Nikishin] appeared in 17 playoff games for the Hurricanes in 2026, earning one assist and helping Carolina capture the Stanley Cup," the statement added.

title: Tinubu: Lion at home, lamb abroad? By Suleiman A. Suleiman
body: We should begin where we must. President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has his virtues. For one, he is not given to petty vindictiveness as former President Obasanjo too often was. Tinubu has not been involved in any open political fights with governors or lawmakers as Obasanjo did. Instead, he appears generally forgiving and conciliatory, having brought several of his fiercest political critics into his government. Also, unlike many of Nigeria’s previous leaders, Tinubu did not come to office by accident, nor was he enthroned by anyone. He arrived in office by sheer personal grit, itself an unusual thing in Nigerian political leadership at that level. Now, the average Nigerian president is a very powerful person. How they wield that power, however, is the key difference between one president and another. Tinubu is no average Nigerian president. He sits above his party and the nation, in a way that no president has done since 1999. Nigerian ruling parties are characterised by internal dissent, factionalism, and opposition, which serve as a check on a president’s power, often better than can be expected from the official opposition parties. There is no such thing under Tinubu. By removing Senator Abdullahi Adamu as Chairman of the APC within weeks of assuming office, Tinubu made that point clear early on. Now, a personal anthem, “On your mandate we shall stand”, rings out at the mention of his name among officials and party faithful because everyone gets the message. The President also has an iron grip on his cabinet, the National Assembly, the governors, the security agencies, anti-corruption agencies, and, as the rumours go, the courts, and perhaps INEC too. From 1960 to date, the National Assembly, particularly, has never been this pliant to a president, often passing executive bills in less than 48 hours, even before some members had a chance to read them. By removing officials without cause or notice, he has signalled that even the most favoured appointees can get the sack. He has induced the defection of all but one or two governors to his party, in name or at least in function. Criticism from the media, civil society, or labour has been blunted, if not outright buried, save for a few notable exceptions. All of this leaves no one in doubt that Tinubu is the lion in Nigeria’s political jungle. Yet, Tinubu’s power is not backed by authority in that specific Weberian sense. Behind this image of an all-powerful president still lies something cosmetic. Obasanjo came to office with the charisma of a former head of state and national hero at multiple points in the country’s history. Buhari was the face of a political movement with more than 10 million loyal votes each election for nearly 20 years. Jonathan came to office by accident, but once there, he commanded the unflinching loyalty of nearly as many Nigerians as Buhari. Tinubu has none of these. His personal anthem may ring out loud, but it rings hollow still because the President’s political coalition is held together not by popular admiration or ideological belief in his programme, but by the depth of his pocket or the fear of losing one’s job in a Nigeria that has grown much harsher economically for nearly all but those in government. Tinubu is quite possibly the most politically vulnerable president facing re-election since 1999. But the opposition lacks money, and the mass public lacks food. A clear majority of Nigerians may well not be happy with the current conditions in the country, but they lack the energy—or the hope—to put up a sustained fight. And then there is the not-so-small matter of the incompetence of the government, although in a different sense than Nigerians are used to in their government. Few governments in Nigerian history have initiated as many far-reaching economic reforms from the start as the Tinubu administration: complete fuel subsidy removal, wholesale naira devaluation, free university tuition converted to loans, high electricity tariffs, tax reforms, and so on. Yet, the government clearly appears to lack the capacity to make a genuine success out of its own reforms, and by the end of the first year, all the swagger Tinubu came into office with had gone. Far-reaching economic reforms generate costs and benefits, and thus, winners and losers. Who are the winners and losers of the fuel subsidy removal policy, for example? How can the policy be tweaked to spread the gains or mitigate the pains? How can we build a genuine political coalition strong enough to sustain the reforms beyond this administration? These are the questions that would engage a more competent reformer, and they would answer them with evidence-based policy adjustment, rather than a shouting match with Catholic bishops. Yet, beyond infographics that have little bearing on reality, you would struggle to find a serious policy paper or further policy actions produced by this government since 2023. But it is in foreign policy that the real character of the current government is laid bare. Tinubu may be a lion at home, but he is a lamb on the world stage. As Daily Trust reported two weeks ago, Nigeria has agreed to a U.S. “America First Global Health Strategy” framework that effectively amounts to signing off our sovereignty for transactional aid. Under this agreement, Nigeria would provide U.S. companies with our health data on short notice. The companies manufacture drugs and vaccines they will resell back to us at huge profits, effectively turning Nigerian sickness into a cash cow for America. And all of this under a health minister who has talked the most about developing local manufacturing capacity in the healthcare sector. Mortgaging Nigerian sovereignty—for a pittance or for free—is the norm under this government. Virtually every single foreign policy action this government has taken since 2023 has been either on behalf of or to the benefit of foreign countries, principally France, Britain, the United States, Israel, or Saudi Arabia. Nigeria itself gets almost nothing out of its foreign policy engagements. Under Tinubu, Nigeria has sparred with two neighbours on behalf of France; sold our tax administration to the same country without any receipts; accepted a controversial asylum-seeker deportation deal with Britain; joined a Red Sea Alliance with Saudi Arabia that has no discernible benefit for us; and watched almost helplessly as the United States promotes a narrative that directly threatens our fragile peace. A bolder government has several countermeasures for each of these foreign policy engagements. France can train our tax officials, rather than hand over our entire system to them. A more strategic government should be capitalising on the current conflict in Europe and the Gulf to do deals that would pump out more of our oil and gas reserves. An Obasanjo or Yar’Adua would have more forcefully rejected the narrative of Christian genocide the U.S. is self-servingly imposing on us to fleece our resources like rare minerals and colonial healthcare deals. A bolder and more sovereignty-inclined Tinubu would at least get the nation to convene an open hearing on this issue, at least to take matters into our own hands. For Tinubu’s foreign policy, however, the problem is not just the decisions or actions, but the approach and the attitude behind it. The government’s foreign policy actions are almost always conducted in complete secrecy. This means that the President may well be entangling Nigeria in unfavourable or unnecessary foreign arrangements that might be difficult for future leaders to repair. At a time when many countries on the continent are flexing self-determination muscles, the so-called Giant of Africa is crouched on the ground licking foreign what-not. Most disturbing of all, President Tinubu appears to believe that once an idea, policy, or agreement has the approving stamp of a Western government or Western-aligned international institutions like the World Bank and IMF, then such a policy or idea is automatically good for Nigeria. Our government appears unable or unwilling to go against any foreign governments or institutions. This is perhaps the sole reason the government has stuck to a punitive fuel subsidy removal that no one in the administration can point to the gains of with any confidence. The government may yet be returned in this election. But some things cannot be left unsaid. The post Tinubu: Lion at home, lamb abroad? By Suleiman A. Suleiman appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Lula wins fourth term in Brazil but faces hostile Congress and divided country
body: Brazil’s veteran left-wing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has been re-elected after a bitter campaign, defeating his right-wing rival, Flávio Bolsonaro. It is Lula’s fourth win in a presidential election, having served two terms as president from January 2003 to December 2010, and again from January 2023. But the road to his win in Sunday’s run-off was not smooth. Bolsonaro beat Lula in the first round on 4 October, and many did not think he could turn the result around in just three weeks. He has also bucked a wider Latin American trend, where voters have punished incumbents and turned right. Across the region, larger countries such as Argentina, Chile and Colombia all now have conservative leaders at their helm. Lula greets supporters after casting his ballot on Sunday Lula’s campaign sprang back to life following his first-round defeat, driven by street demonstrations and a massive social media push. The former metalworker, who has dominated Brazil’s left since he first ran for president in 1989, nevertheless faces the most challenging political landscape since he first took office in 2003. His new term, set to begin on 5 January 2027, will start amid significant constraints at home and abroad, including animosity from US President Donald Trump. While Trump did not endorse Lula’s rival, Flávio Bolsonaro, directly, as he did with the right-wing candidates who went on to win presidential elections in Colombia and Honduras, there is little doubt his administration would have preferred a conservative at the helm of this country of 213 million people. The White House regards Latin America as an area of US influence, and the Trump administration is keen to have leaders in power who support its policies, including on defence, security, and trade. It is also keen to reduce China’s influence in the Western Hemisphere. Brazil, oil-rich and home to the world’s second-largest reserves of rare earth minerals, is the only major country in South America not governed by a right-wing leader, with Lula widely seen as China-friendly. Flávio Bolsonaro had promised to align Brazil more closely with Washington, while Lula warned the US not to interfere in the election and insisted Brazil would “never fit into anyone’s backyard”. But while the White House may be disappointed, environmentalists will welcome Lula’s victory, having feared that a Bolsonaro win would have given Brazil’s influential agribusiness and mining sectors more power. They pointed to record levels of deforestation and forest fires in the Amazon during his father Jair’s presidency, arguing that under the younger Bolsonaro’s laxer environmental policies, destruction could recur in this key ecosystem. An aerial view from a Greenpeace flyover shows a fire burning in the Amazon rainforest during the UN Climate Change Conference (COP30), held near Centro Novo in the state of Maranhao, Brazil, in 2025 While Lula’s supporters are ecstatic about his victory, the result shows that the country remains deeply divided, with more than 48% of voters choosing Bolsonaro. In addition to the challenge of uniting such a deeply polarised country, Lula will have to govern alongside the most right-wing Congress in Brazil’s democratic era. Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party (PL) was the party that made the biggest gains in the election. Yet Lula’s Workers’ Party organised huge rallies ahead of the run-off, showing the strong grassroots support it commands. Before the election, Lula had described the poll as “a parting of the waters for Brazil”. He promised to bridge the gap between Brazil’s opposing political poles with “a new way of governing”, adding in a WhatsApp livestream before the election that “this country will never be the same again”. While he offered little detail on what the new way of governing would entail, he insisted he would “remain firm in the fight for a more just country, with opportunities for all and policies directed at the needs of the population”. With a largely hostile Congress, this fight just may prove much harder for the veteran leader – who will be 85 by the end of his fourth term – than in his three previous terms in office.

title: Israel fuel prices could top NIS 9 per liter as tax cut expires after elections
body: Fuel prices in Israel are expected to rise sharply immediately after the elections, as a temporary NIS 1 per liter fuel tax reduction introduced by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich is set to expire on November 3.Combined with rising global oil prices amid expectations of renewed fighting involving Israel, the US and Iran, the expiration of the tax cut could push the price of 95-octane gasoline above NIS 9 per liter, up from its current price of NIS 7.77.Smotrich introduced the temporary reduction in the state's excise tax on gasoline last month to prevent fuel prices from soaring ahead of the elections.The original order, signed a month earlier, reduced the tax by half a shekel per liter. However, rising oil prices prompted Smotrich to double the reduction.Under normal circumstances, taxes account for more than 60% of the price of gasoline in Israel, generating approximately NIS 20 billion in annual state revenue.According to the Finance Ministry's Budget Department, the tax cuts introduced over the past two months are expected to reduce state revenue by approximately NIS 467 million, at a time when the ongoing war has driven defense spending to record levels.Election outcome could determine fate of fuel tax relief as fuel prices could top NIS 8Following the elections, Smotrich will have to decide whether to extend the tax reduction. However, if it becomes clear the current government will not remain in office, he could let fuel prices surge, leaving the next government to deal with the economic consequences.Regardless of whether the tax cut is extended, the first fuel price increase is expected as early as Saturday night.Expectations of a third round of fighting involving Israel, Iran and the US have already pushed oil prices up by approximately 10% compared with late September, when the Energy Ministry's Fuel Administration set gasoline prices for October.As a result, even if the tax reduction remains in effect, gasoline prices are currently expected to rise by approximately 30 agorot per liter, bringing the price to just over NIS 8.The final price will be determined toward the end of the week, based on oil prices in the Mediterranean basin at that time. However, the new price could remain in effect for only a few days.

title: Duchess Magazine Leadership Summit Makes UK Debut
body: The Duchess International Magazine Leadership Summit 2026 marked a significant milestone in the publication’s international growth on October 14 to 16, by bringing together academics, public officials, entrepreneurs, professionals and community leaders into Brighton, United Kingdom for a brainstorming session. Organised by Duchess International Magazine, a publication of Custodian Global Consult Ltd, in collaboration with the University of Brighton, the three-day summit combined leadership dialogue, cultural engagement, professional networking and recognition of outstanding contributions to society. Convened by Duchess Abolaji Odunuga, the event was held under the theme, “Honouring Our Communities: The Audacity to Lead, Redefining Power, Purpose and Legacy.” The programme opened on October 14 with a Meet and Greet at the DoubleTree by Hilton Hotel, Brighton. Ms Yemisi Jenkins MBE led the welcome, creating an opportunity for delegates to introduce themselves, establish professional connections and engage with fellow participants ahead of the main summit. The gathering set a collaborative tone for the programme, bringing together individuals from diverse backgrounds united by an interest in leadership, service and community development. On October 15, delegates took part in a cultural sightseeing programme, visiting the Royal Pavilion and SEA LIFE Brighton. Beyond the opportunity to experience some of Brighton’s prominent attractions, the excursion gave participants time to strengthen relationships in an informal setting. It complemented the summit’s emphasis on cross-cultural engagement, professional interaction and the value of building connections beyond the conference room. The main summit took place at the University of Brighton on October 16, providing a platform for discussions on leadership, personal development, communication, accountability and community impact. Anchored by Dr. Dayo Olomu, the event featured contributions from Professor Abubakar Sulaiman, Karen Dobres, Tony Kalume, Valdirene Ruston, Hon. Sa’adatu Mohammed, Praise Agomounso, Dr Jess Moriarty, Dr. Yetunde Adeshile, Dr. Kemi Ogunyemi and Funke Nnenanya Michaels. Their presentations explored different dimensions of leadership, challenging participants to consider how individual responsibility, purposeful influence and collaboration can help address societal needs and create lasting value. The programme concluded with the Duchess International Magazine Leadership Awards Night, anchored by Dr Femi Aratokun Ale and Tokunbo Olunloyo. The ceremony recognised individuals whose contributions span governance, public service, women’s advancement, healthcare and community development. Recipients included Hon. Daniel Amos, Professor Abubakar Sulaiman, Dr Yetunde Adeshile, Dr Kemi Ogunyemi and Hon. Joyce Viyanto Antonza Ibrahim. The University of Brighton was also honoured, further highlighting the importance of institutional engagement in advancing leadership conversations and collaborative initiatives. A key development from the summit was the call for the initiative to continue beyond its 2026 edition. Dr. Lara Perry, Interim Dean of the School of Humanities and Social Science at the University of Brighton, called for continuity, underscoring the value of sustaining a platform that brings together academics, professionals, public officials and community leaders to exchange ideas and explore opportunities for collaboration. The call added weight to discussions about the summit’s future and the potential to build on the relationships established in Brighton. The collaboration between Duchess International Magazine and the University of Brighton provided an important foundation for the summit, connecting the publication’s leadership platform with an academic institution and creating space for dialogue across professional and cultural boundaries. For Duchess International Magazine, the initiative reflects its broader commitment to celebrating leadership while encouraging conversations about social responsibility, community development and the constructive use of influence. With the 2027 edition planned for October, attention is turning to how the summit can build on the momentum generated in Brighton. The next edition presents an opportunity to deepen existing relationships, widen participation and strengthen collaboration among leaders and institutions. As Duchess International Magazine looks ahead, the 2026 summit stands as an important step in the platform’s international development, with the call for continuity adding impetus to its ambition to sustain leadership dialogue beyond a single events

title: Lagos 2027: APC Banks on Continuity as Hamzat Unveils Manifesto October 30
body: Wale Igbintade The All Progressives Congress (APC) in Lagos State has pledged to sustain the development policies of successive administrations while addressing persistent challenges in housing, transportation, security, healthcare and infrastructure under its 2027 governorship candidate, Dr. Kadri Obafemi Hamzat. The party said Hamzat would build on the foundations laid by President Bola Tinubu, former governors Babatunde Fashola and Akinwunmi Ambode, and the incumbent governor, Babajide Sanwo-Olu, while correcting existing shortcomings and responding to the demands of Lagos’ growing population. The Director-General of the PBAT-KOH Campaign Council, Senator Musiliu Obanikoro, disclosed this yesterday at a press conference in Lagos, where he announced that the APC would unveil Hamzat’s governorship manifesto on Friday, October 30, ahead of the 2027 election. According to him, the manifesto launch, scheduled for the Wole Soyinka Centre for Culture and Creative Arts, formerly known as the National Arts Theatre, Iganmu, Lagos, would provide an opportunity for Hamzat to outline his vision, policy priorities and plans for the state’s continued development. Obanikoro said the campaign was anchored on two principles: continued shared progress and inclusivity, emphasising the need to consolidate existing achievements while ensuring that no segment of the population was excluded from the state’s development agenda. “Continuity is not about doing things the same way simply because they have been done before. It is about protecting what works, correcting what needs improvement and building on existing progress,” he said. He argued that Lagos could not afford to abandon the foundations upon which its development had been built, adding that the state required experienced leadership, careful planning and practical solutions to meet the demands of its expanding population. Obanikoro said Hamzat’s combination of private-sector experience and years in public service equipped him with an understanding of business, governance and public-service delivery. He said Hamzat obtained a PhD in Systems Process Engineering from Cranfield University, England, at the age of 28, and subsequently worked with international financial institutions, including Merrill Lynch, Morgan Stanley and Citibank, in the United States before entering public service. He added that Hamzat’s experience as a commissioner under successive administrations and his current position as deputy governor had given him valuable insight into the state’s administrative and developmental priorities. “His experience in the private sector, where he gained knowledge of business and management, goes well with his years in public service as a three-time commissioner and deputy governor of Lagos State,” Obanikoro said. The campaign director-general cited the Blue and Red rail lines, completed roads and bridges, improvements in schools and hospitals, housing projects, and support for businesses and young people as examples of development initiatives pursued under the Sanwo-Olu administration. He said Hamzat would draw on his experience in government to consolidate these initiatives, address outstanding challenges and deepen development across the state. However, Obanikoro acknowledged that Lagos continued to face significant pressures arising from its estimated population of about 25 million, limited landmass and cosmopolitan character. He identified transportation, human capital development, housing, infrastructure, security, healthcare and environmental management as areas requiring sustained attention. He said these challenges demanded leadership capable of building on existing achievements while responding to residents’ changing needs. On inclusivity, Obanikoro said the campaign was committed to ensuring that governance served residents regardless of religion, ethnicity, gender, social status or place of origin. He added that while Lagos belonged to everyone who called the state home, the interests and heritage of its indigenous population must also be recognised and preserved. “Every resident and taxpayer have a stake in its future, and every community deserves to be heard. Our differences should not divide us. They should strengthen our resolve to work together for the common good,” he said. Obanikoro disclosed that Hamzat and members of the campaign organisation had consulted religious leaders, traditional rulers, market women, traders, young people, professionals, artisans, community leaders and other stakeholders across the state. He said the consultations were intended to ensure that residents’ concerns informed the candidate’s priorities and that his proposed development agenda reflected the realities of different communities. “We believe that leadership must listen before it acts. We want the concerns of ordinary Lagosians to inform our priorities. We want a development agenda that reflects the realities of our people,” he said. The campaign director-general also announced that the manifesto would be made available for download after its presentation, enabling members of the public to examine the proposals and submit feedback through designated party channels. He said the campaign welcomed constructive comments and suggestions from residents, adding that the document should reflect the needs of the people it was intended to serve. He urged party members, stakeholders and members of the public to engage with the campaign’s proposals, reiterating its commitment to shared progress, inclusivity and continued development in Lagos.

title: Archaeologists Uncover Bronze Age Defences at Ancient Cyprus Site
body: By Bill Giannopoulos Archaeologists have identified the first Late Bronze Age fortification system at Palaepaphos, an ancient city in southwestern Cyprus, uncovering new evidence of how the settlement defended itself thousands of years ago. Archaeological remains of a Late Bronze Age defensive tower and rampart uncovered at Marchello in Palaepaphos, Cyprus. The discovery was announced by the Department of Antiquities following excavations conducted in August and September 2026 at the Marchello site, near the modern village of Kouklia. The excavation was led by a team from the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens (NKUA), which has been investigating the site since 2021 to establish the chronology and development of its defensive structures. Evidence dates fortifications to the Late Bronze Age Marchello lies less than one kilometre northeast of the sanctuary of Aphrodite at Palaepaphos, one of ancient Cyprus’ important religious centres. General plan of the excavated remains at Marchello, including the rampart and monumental gate across Plots 96 and 110. Credit: NKUA Earlier excavations by British, German and Swiss teams, as well as researchers from the University of Cyprus, had uncovered a long defensive wall and a monumental gate. However, the date of their construction and the relationship between the structures remained uncertain. The latest excavation has provided clearer evidence for the age of the fortifications. Beside a newly exposed section of the defensive wall, archaeologists uncovered an undisturbed archaeological layer containing pottery from the Late Cypriot IIC to IIIA periods, near the end of the Late Bronze Age. A layer of marl, a clay-rich soil, was found above the archaeological deposit and directly beside the wall’s stone foundations. Researchers believe builders prepared the marl at the site and spread it over the stone base to create a level foundation for the mudbrick wall above. Its position alongside the pottery and foundations helps date the earliest phase of the rampart to this period. Tower reveals successive phases of construction The excavation also clarified how a defensive tower developed as part of the fortification system. Builders initially incorporated a rectangular bastion into the rampart during the Late Cypriot IIIA period. A three-sided extension was later added to its front, creating a nearly square structure measuring approximately 7.4 by 7.3 metres. The tower’s thick walls enclosed a central room of around nine square metres. Its design suggests the structure may have had additional floors, although only the foundations survive and its original height remains unknown. The tower was subsequently reinforced with an additional wall measuring approximately 2.7 metres thick along its northwestern side. Researchers believe this strengthening work probably also took place during the Late Cypriot IIIA period. The successive construction phases indicate that the inhabitants of Palaepaphos repeatedly invested in strengthening their defences during the Late Bronze Age. Fortifications were reinforced centuries later The defensive complex continued to be modified long after the Bronze Age. During the fourth century BC, in the Late Cypro-Classical period, another reinforcing wall was added along the tower’s northeastern and southeastern sides. Pottery recovered from the foundation trench helped researchers date this later construction phase. The rampart was also widened at a subsequent stage, possibly during the same period. However, important questions remain about the history of the site. The excavation team has not yet identified construction phases from the Cypro-Geometric or Cypro-Archaic periods within the area investigated. It is therefore still unclear whether the fortifications remained in continuous use between the Late Bronze Age and their later reinforcement. Further archaeological work and analysis of the recovered material are expected to help establish how the complex evolved and what role it played in the history of Palaepaphos. At the conclusion of the 2026 excavation season, the team covered the exposed architectural remains with protective ground-cover fabric to safeguard them. The findings add to the archaeological record of ancient Cyprus, offering new evidence of the construction techniques, defensive planning and long-term development of one of the island’s historically significant settlements. Source: Department of Antiquities, Deputy Ministry of Culture, Republic of Cyprus. title: Defence Spending: Challenges for the Budget and Beyond
body:
Mounting pressure: John Healey, the chancellor, must decide whether to commit to reaching 3% by 2030. Image: Wikimedia Commons, contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0
Funding further increases in defence spending would require hard choices â cutting spending elsewhere, raising taxes or borrowing more â both at this Budget and in the years ahead.
In June this year, John Healey resigned as Defence Secretary over the governmentâs refusal to increase defence spending further, arguing that 'a headmark date for 3% of GDP on defence in 2030 is what Britain must set'. Now, as Chancellor, he must decide whether to commit to reaching 3% by 2030 â meaning increasing defence spending faster than current plans â and, if so, where any additional money is to come from.
Defence spending has increased substantially in recent years. Existing plans imply that NATO-qualifying spending (a broad measure including most Ministry of Defence spending, along with military pensions and some spending on intelligence agencies) will reach 2.7% of GDP by 2027â28, up from 2.1% in 2023â24. But there is clear pressure for the UK to go further and faster. The government has committed to spend 3% of GDP on defence at some point in the next parliament, and 3.5% by 2035 alongside NATO Allies. (NATO Allies also committed to spend an extra 1.5% of GDP on wider 'resilience and security' by 2035, but the government has suggested this would be met within pre-existing spending plans, so here we focus on 'core' defence spending.)
While the UK has increased spending considerably, some other NATO countries have moved further and faster. Poland spent a similar share of GDP on defence to the UK four years ago, but by 2025 had increased defence spending to 4.3% of GDP . Germany is also planning to increase defence spending faster than the UK, and overtook the UK as having the second -largest defence budget in NATO in 2024.
Further increases could be expensive. Even before any new commitments, the government still needs to find an average of Â£1.2 billion per year to fully fund top-ups announced alongside the Defence Investment Plan in June. Reaching 3% of GDP on defence by 2030â31 would require around Â£11 billion of additional spending in that year, relative to keeping defence spending at 2.7% of GDP. Going further to 3.5% would require an even larger, and more sustained, increase.
The central question â at both this Budget and next year's Spending Review â is how the government will reconcile its defence ambitions with an already-challenging fiscal outlook, a commitment to reduce the size of the deficit and substantial pressures to increase spending on other public services. The government could fund higher defence spending through cutting spending elsewhere, increasing taxes or raising borrowing. But all three look challenging.
Note: Defence spending here refers to NATO-qualifying defence spending. Scenario shows a linear path of defence spending to 3% ofÂ GDP by 2030â31 and to 3.5% ofÂ GDP by 2035â36.Â
Source: Figure 6.9 from Boileau, Harvey-Rich and Snape 2026 ( https://ifs.org.uk/publications/public-service-spending-plans-and-pressures )
One option is to squeeze spending on other public services â such as schools, prisons or transport. This is how the government already plans to fund much of the increase in spending it announced as part of the Defence Investment Plan. But this could be challenging: growth in public service spending is set to slow in coming years, and services face a range of other pressures, including from higher inflation.
Consider next year's Spending Review: even with defence spending flat at 2.7% of GDP, if the government decided to grow health spending in line with plans at the last Spending Review, this would imply small real-terms cuts to the combined budgets of all other departments between 2027â28 and 2030â31. Increasing defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030â31 without topping up overall spending would deepen these cuts.
Alternatively, the government could cut spending on areas outside departmental budgets â for example, spending on working-age benefits or the state pension â to top up defence budgets. This would also involve difficult choices, and have consequences for households receiving those benefits.
Another option is to pay for higher defence spending with tax rises. For a sense of scale, funding an increase to 3% of GDP by 2030â31 would require additional revenue equivalent to around a 1p increase to all rates of income tax, or a 1p increase to the standard rate of VAT. Here, though, the government is politically constrained by the tax commitments in its manifesto, and taxes are already set to reach historically high levels.
The final option is borrowing. Borrowing for a permanent increase in defence spending is unlikely to be sustainable, and would be hard to justify on the grounds that defence spending will boost long-term economic growth. There could be a case for using increased borrowing in the short term as a means of delivering immediate increases in spending while more gradually increasing taxes or cutting spending elsewhere. But this would need to be weighed against the costs of additional borrowing â UK debt and borrowing costs are already very high, and debt interest now accounts for Â£1 in every Â£13 the government spends. Some other countries, including Poland and Germany, are relying partly on higher borrowing to increase defence spending, but both start from a stronger fiscal position than the UK.
Much of the recent debate has focused on defence spending targets, in part because of the importance of international agreements. But the primary goal is an increase in defence capabilities, and the link between increased spending and the resulting capabilities is not automatic.
Get a weekly round-up of the latest commentary and research straight into your inbox.
One important consideration is the timing of spending increases. Even if defence spending reaches 3.5% of GDP by 2035, different paths to that commitment could have different consequences. 'Backloaded' increases â with slower growth now and faster growth in the early 2030s â would mean that the government spends less cumulatively to reach the target. But given the importance of investment in equipment, which takes time to procure and builds up over many years, this would leave defence capabilities lower in 2035 than if spending had been increased in a smoother way. Backloaded growth could also mean capabilities will be lower in the years before 2035, and could open questions in early years over how credible the commitment to 3.5% is.
Decisions on where money is spent also matter. In recent years, a growing share of spending has gone on investment in major equipment, rather than spending on personnel and other day-to-day costs. How this balance changes will also determine the sorts of capabilities increased by higher spending.
The government is also banking on substantial efficiencies to deliver existing plans. The Defence Investment Plan set out efficiencies of around Â£1.8 billion per year over the next four years, around 70% of which it classes as 'low maturity', suggesting substantial uncertainty around their delivery. In principle, making defence spending more productive â so that more can be delivered within the same budgets â is very attractive. But if these efficiencies are not achieved, the government will need to choose between topping up spending further or allowing capabilities to grow more slowly than planned.
The Chancellor does not need to resolve all these challenges at the Budget. Indeed, John Healey has said that it will be at next year's Spending Review that he will set out âa clear pathâ to the NATO commitment in 2035 and a target date for 3%. But at the Budget, he needs to set out plans for total spending on public services over the next five years.
These totals do not need to be allocated to departments until next year, but they should be ones he would be willing to live within. The government's plans to reduce borrowing and meet its fiscal rules will be predicated on the spending totals he sets out; if these totals are ones he has no intention of delivering and intends to top up at a later date, his fiscal plans will not be credible. Of course, he could fund higher defence spending within existing budgets, or choose to scale back ambitions for defence, but should make these choices â and their consequences â clear.
Much recent discussion has focused on the short-term challenges of increasing defence spending â how the Defence Investment Plan is funded, what this means for the Budget, when the UK will get defence spending to 3% of GDP. But we should not lose sight of the bigger picture. Beyond this Budget, higher defence spending will continue to reshape the British state.
For decades, falling defence spending as a share of GDP allowed governments to spend more on health and benefits without a correspondingly large increase in the size of the state â the so-called peace dividend. The government can no longer rely on this. Meeting the NATO commitment to spend 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035 will mean increasing defence spending while also facing pressure to increase spending elsewhere, including on health and social care.
The challenges of funding higher defence spending are therefore not isolated to this Budget, or next year's Spending Review, but will shape the UKâs public finances for years to come.
