title: THE COURAGE TO UNLEARN
body: The courage to unlearn gives an organisation a future, contends LINUS OKORIE There is a stage in leadership when experience stops being an advantage and quietly becomes a liability. It happens when a leader becomes so confident in what has worked that they stop questioning whether it still will. The strategy that built the company becomes untouchable. The product that created the brand becomes sacred. The management style that produced results becomes the default. The assumptions that once gave the organization an advantage become so familiar that nobody thinks to challenge them. This is one of the most dangerous transitions in leadership. Because the world can change while the leader is still using yesterday’s map. One of the most instructive examples came from Intel. In its early years, Intel built much of its reputation and commercial strength around memory chips. The company had developed deep technical expertise in the business, and memory was central to its identity. Then the competitive landscape changed. Japanese semiconductor manufacturers began producing memory chips at increasingly competitive prices, putting enormous pressure on American companies. Intel’s leadership initially tried to fight its way back into profitability. But the numbers kept telling a different story. The question eventually became bigger than how to improve the memory-chip business. It became: Should Intel remain the company it had become, or become the company the future required? Andy Grove and Gordon Moore faced a decision that demanded something more difficult than innovation. They had to let go. Intel moved away from memory and increasingly committed itself to microprocessors. That decision helped transform the company and positioned it at the center of the personal-computing revolution. What makes the story remarkable is that Intel did not simply learn something new. It had to unlearn something that had made it successful. That is a fundamentally different leadership challenge. Learning asks: “What do we need to know?” Unlearning asks: “What do we believe that is no longer true?” The second question is harder because beliefs become attached to people. They become attached to careers, investments, reputations and identities. An executive who spent years building a particular strategy may find it difficult to accept that the strategy has run its course. A founder may struggle to replace a management structure that worked beautifully when the company was small. A senior leader may continue using a leadership style that delivered results in one generation but frustrates another. A company may continue investing in a product because it once defined the organization, even as customers have moved on. This is why success can be dangerous. Failure forces questions. Success often postpones them. When the numbers are good, there is little incentive to ask whether the underlying assumptions are becoming obsolete. But markets do not freeze because an organization is performing well. Technology changes. Customers change. Competitors change. Employees change. The basis of competition changes. The executive’s responsibility is therefore not simply to protect today’s success. It is to recognize when the foundations of that success are beginning to shift. Consider Nokia. There was a time when Nokia’s name was almost synonymous with mobile phones. It had enormous market presence, a powerful brand and considerable engineering capability. But the mobile-phone industry was transformed by the rise of smartphones. The competition was no longer primarily about making a reliable handset. The value proposition had changed. Software, ecosystems, applications, user experience and developer communities became increasingly important. The lesson is not that Nokia lacked intelligent people. It is that intelligence inside an organization is not enough if the organization is interpreting a new world through an old model. The question for leaders is not only, “How good are we?” It is also, “Are we still solving the problem that customers now care about?” This distinction matters in every industry. A bank can have an excellent branch network while customers increasingly prefer digital services. A media company can produce quality content while audiences change how they consume it. A school can have a respected history while the skills required by the next generation of students evolve. A manufacturing company can operate an efficient production system while new technology changes the economics of its industry. The old model may not have been wrong. It may simply have reached its expiration date. That is why leaders must learn to separate principles from methods . The principle may remain. The method may need to change. A commitment to excellent customer service does not require keeping the same customer-service model forever. A commitment to quality does not mean refusing new technology. A company’s mission can remain stable while its strategy changes dramatically. This is where strategic maturity begins. Great leaders are not loyal to methods. They are loyal to purpose. This also requires leaders to become comfortable with being wrong. Not every old decision was a mistake simply because circumstances changed. A strategy can be completely rational when it is chosen and completely unsuitable several years later. The mistake is not changing it. The mistake is allowing pride to turn history into policy. This is particularly relevant for executives who have been successful for a long time. Experience creates pattern recognition, but it can also create blind spots. A leader begins to think: “We have tried that before.” “Our customers don’t want that.” “That is not how our industry works.” “We have always done it this way.” Sometimes these statements are wisdom. Sometimes they are warnings. The difference is whether the leader is using experience to understand the present or using the past to avoid confronting it. One practical discipline is to periodically ask questions that challenge the organization’s most comfortable assumptions. What would we stop doing if we were starting today? Which of our products exists mainly because we are emotionally attached to it? What are customers doing differently that we have not yet responded to? Which competitors are solving tomorrow’s problem better than we are? What part of our business model would be hardest for us to abandon? And perhaps the most uncomfortable: If we were not already successful, would we choose this strategy today? These questions create something every organization needs: the capacity for renewal. They also require leaders to create room for disagreement. If everyone around the executive has learned that challenging the established view is dangerous, the organization will become increasingly certain at precisely the moment it should be questioning itself. Leaders should therefore listen to people who see the organization differently. Younger employees often experience changes in technology and consumer behavior differently from senior executives. Customers can see problems that internal teams have become accustomed to. Competitors can expose weaknesses that insiders have learned to rationalize. Dissent is not always disloyalty. Sometimes it is an organization’s early-warning system. And there is another difficult reality. Unlearning often involves loss. It may require abandoning investments. Changing structures. Retraining employees. Admitting that a previous strategy no longer works. Giving up authority. Walking away from something that still feels familiar. That is why unlearning is not primarily an intellectual exercise. It is an act of leadership courage. The leader must be willing to say: “This worked. It mattered. We built something valuable with it. But the future requires something different.” That statement does not diminish the past. It protects the future. The most resilient organizations are not those that change everything constantly. They are those that know what must never change and what must. They preserve their purpose while questioning their assumptions. They protect their values while reinventing their methods. They honor their history without becoming prisoners of it. This is perhaps one of the most important responsibilities of an executive: to prevent yesterday’s success from becoming tomorrow’s limitation. Because organizations rarely collapse simply because they cannot learn. Sometimes they collapse because they cannot let go of what they have already learned. The future will continually challenge leaders to reconsider what they think they know. The question is whether we will have the humility to listen. Whether we will have the discipline to examine our assumptions. And whether we will have the courage to release what once worked before it becomes the thing holding us back. The courage to learn gives an organization knowledge. The courage to unlearn gives it a future. Okorie MFR is a leadership development expert spanning 30 years in the research, teaching and coaching of leadership in Africa and across the world. He is the CEO of the GOTNI Leadership Centre. www.gotni.africa

title: DOES NIGERIA HAVE 103 MILLION VOTERS?
body: CHIDI ANSELM ODINKALU argues that the INEC electoral register is suspect Ahead of Nigeria’s general elections in January and February 2027, Africa Confidential warns that “turnout in the elections is likely to be even lower than the average 26.7% four years ago. Nigerian voters are among the least enthusiastic in the world…. Out of more than 93.4 million registered voters, 24.9 million total votes were cast. This represented an 8.03-point decline from the 2019 elections and was the lowest voter turnout since Nigeria’s return to civilian rule in 1999.” Complaints about “voter apathy” are the staple of Nigeria’s electoral commentariat. The numbers and patterns seem to bear this out . In 1999, turnout was 52.3%. Officially, it grew to 69% in 2003; and has fallen since then to 57.5% in 2007; 53.7% in 2011; 43.7% in 2015; and 34.8% in 2019, before cratering to 26.7% in 2023. These claims require us to accord credibility to the underlying numbers from the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC). That begins with belief in the baseline of INEC’s electoral register against which turnout is judged. If that register is flawed, then all calculations hinged on it also suffer. Yet, the foundational affliction underlying of Nigeria’s elections is not in INEC’s numbers. Rather, it is an absence of credible demographic management system against which to verify INEC’s claims. The National Population Commission (NPoPC) claims 53% of births in the country are registered and only 10% of deaths are. The implications of this for the credibility of the electoral register should worry everyone. To be sure, electoral rolls are ambulatory. People are not static: we move; relocate, and die too. This is why a demographic management system is essential. In Nigeria, this does not exist. A register of voters does not automatically change because a person whose name is on it has died. But a person should also not be on the register one decade after their death. In Nigeria, there is no way of stopping this. These define the many curiosities about Nigeria’s voting numbers. First, they bear no rational relationship to wider demographic trends. Nigeria’s pattern of supposedly precipitous collapse in voter turnout, for instance, is inversely proportional to both baseline population and civic gripe. In 1999, Nigeria’s population was estimated to be 115,766,000. Nigeria’s current population is estimated at 244 million . That means the country has more than doubled its population since 1999 by 128,234,000 or 110.77%. Over the same period, the voting roll has grown by 81.4%, even as life expectancy in the intervening quarter century has increased by about nine years. If life expectancy is growing with the population and crude death rates falling, then the rate of growth in the voting population should ordinarily outstrip the underlying population growth rate. In 20 years from 1999 to 2023, Nigeria’s population rose by about 87% but the register of voters grew by 36,530,063 or 63.05%. The mis-match between the two trendlines is significant. In 1999, Nigeria had 57.94 million registered voters. This rose by 2.88 million or 4.97% to 60.82 million in 2003 and then by a mere three-quarters of a million or 1.23% to 61.57 million in 2007. By 2011, the number of registered voters climbed by over 12 million (20.5%) to 73.53 million, representing an average yearly growth rate of nearly 5.12%, where previously it had grown by 1.24 % in 1999-2003 and 0.3% between 2003-2007. By 2015, the population of registered voters fell to 68.83 million, a deficit of 4.7 million voters or 6.39%, representing an annualized rate of reversal of 1.6%. Yet, over the same period, Nigeria, a country with a median age of just under 18 years, had grown in population from an estimated 162.9 million to 181.2 million, an increase of 15.174 million or 11.23%, representing an annual growth rate of 2.8%. The patterns from these numbers do not lend themselves to easy explanations. It is possible to speculate about what may explain this significant delta in growth between the general population and register of voters. Rational factors such as migration; agency dysfunctions in INEC; civic inertia or disaffection; or high transaction costs may be relevant. But there remain worrying patterns that are not easily accounted for even by all these. As the Justice Uwais presidential committee on electoral reform pointed out in its 2008 report, much of what passed for electoral numbers in Nigeria before 2011 was voodoo. Just to illustrate this point, the INEC does not have a breakdown of official results for the 2007 presidential elections yet there are turnout figures for that election. This leads to a second issue: Nigeria’s register of voters has always had invalid voters. The current register of voters in Nigeria dates back to November 2010 when the Attahiru Jega-led INEC set about establishing a credible register of voters for the country. The Commission had limited time to authenticate the raw data before the 2011 general election. When the Automatic Fingerprint Identification System (AFIS) finished its work on the 2011 register nearly four years later, INEC invalidated 4.7 million entries, which reduced the number of registered voters from 73.53 in 2011 to 68.83 in 2015 but not before these invalid 4.7 million were eligible to vote in 2011. Third, the biggest problem may be dead voters. That’s an oxymoron because the dead should not vote. In 2022, INEC explained that it could not expunge the dead from the register because “the country does not have reliable data of births and deaths and the commission cannot engage in arbitrary removal of the names of individuals it suspects are deceased.” This has not changed. It means we have no way of knowing how many ghosts there are among the 103.4 million on INEC’s current register. By failing to display the register as required by law , the Commission does not even care to disabuse suspicions that its register may be bloated. Its response to non-compliance is institutional insouciance. Nigeria’s register of voters is the classic Hotel California : it is “programmed to receive” and, for anyone with their name on it, “you can check out any time you like but you can never leave.” The implications of this for electoral integrity are staggering. An illustrative exercise may help. Nigerian law allows adults alone to vote. The World Bank estimates the country’s crude mortality rate at 11.64 per 1000 . Applied to a baseline from 2011, that is about 34,748,845 dead in 15 years. But not all these will be adults. Mortality rate for under-5s is 117 per 1000 live births. That’s 700,000 to 855,000 under-five child deaths yearly . To 2025, that could be about 12 million dead under-fives since 2011. The country also reported an estimated median of 111,425 deaths among 5–14-year-olds from 1990 to 2016 . Applied again to a 2011 baseline, that’s another 1,671,375. In total, there could be up to 13.67 million infants, children, and adolescent deaths since 2011. Adjusting the crude death rates for mortality among infants, children, and adolescents, there could be about 18-20 million people liable to be lanced from the electoral register since 2011. Applying the same methodology to a baseline of the 2023 register, that could be up to five million dead people alone on the register since the last election. In its latest announcement, however, INEC said it captured a total of 10,772,421 new voters . It has not accounted for deaths or natural attrition. Separately, at the end of 2025, the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre, (IDMC) reported that Nigeria had at least 3.7 million in internal displacement . The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees adds up to 478,000 Nigerian refugees outside the country. Admittedly not all of these are adults of voting age. Almost assuredly, INEC’s 103.4 million voters is corpulent. When you look at the numbers on INEC’s register and account for the fact that the baseline data goes back to 2011, there is a reasonable likelihood that up to about 25% on it could be dead or dud. That should put all the talk about voter apathy in perspective. But this story has a uniquely Nigerian sting: our diaspora on earth may not have a vote, but we may have a diaspora in Heaven with a veto. A lawyer and a teacher, Odinkalu can be reached at chidi.odinkalu@tufts.edu

title: Trump invokes 9/11 in urging Michigan voters to oppose Muslim Senate candidate El-Sayed
body: President Donald Trump at a Sunday campaign rally ratcheted up his push to link US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed to Muslim extremists, comparing him to the 9/11 attackers while saying Democrats would let violent anti-American terrorists into the United States."I'm here to keep a jihadist, Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator," Trump told a receptive audience in Port Huron, Michigan.If he wins, El-Sayed would be the first Muslim elected to the US Senate. Trump has sought to paint him as an anti-American Muslim radical, and on Sunday he took the rhetoric to a new level, likening El-Sayed to the attackers who took over United Flight 93 during the September 11, 2001 attacks.Michigan has one of the nation's most competitive US Senate contests going into the November 3 midterm elections, with former US Representative Mike Rogers, a Republican, and El-Sayed vying for an open seat that will help to decide control of the chamber.The president on Sunday compared voting against El-Sayed to the actions of Michigan native Todd Beamer and others who fought back against the Flight 93 hijackers."Twenty-five years later, Michigan needs to stand up and fight, just like Todd did, to stop a jihadist from walking into the Capitol," Trump said.If El-Sayed wins, "he would be the only senator that will have to go through a metal detector before he's allowed to go in the Senate," Trump said.El-Sayed says questioning his loyalty is 'shameful' El-Sayed has dismissed the accusations against him and, in a recent advertisement, defended his religion, saying, "Faith is a thing there's just too little of in Washington."Rogers has alleged without evidence that El-Sayed has ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, one of the Arab world's oldest and most influential Islamist groups.El-Sayed has denied affiliation with the group, saying it is "shameful" for Rogers to question his allegiance to the United States.Rogers said in an interview on NBC's "Meet the Press" on Sunday, before the Port Huron rally, that El-Sayed had not sufficiently responded to questions about the allegations."He's a Democrat Socialist of America-aligned candidate who has these pretty radical support groups that don't like America," he said.Trump's speech in eastern Michigan on Sunday came a day after former President Barack Obama campaigned for Democrats in the state, underscoring its importance in next week's elections.At Saturday's rally in Detroit, Obama framed the attacks by El-Sayed's opponents as an attempt to make him look "less patriotic and less American than they are."The former president compared them to his experience as the target of false claims that he was born in Kenya."We have seen this movie before," Obama said. "I starred in it ... This stuff didn't work on me. Not in Michigan. It's not going to work on Abdul."Manufacturing investmentsPort Huron is part of an area of Michigan that Trump won in the 2024 presidential election with more than 66% of the vote.One issue in focus during the campaign in the state has been the US-Canada tariff standoff, which has affected the Detroit-based US auto industry and prompted Rogers to distance himself from the president's policy.Rogers on Sunday hailed Trump's tariffs for securing manufacturing investments for Michigan by Chevrolet and Detroit Diesel, but said "the automobile portion of these Canadian tariffs worries me a little bit.""There's some good and there's some things we have to work on," he told "Meet the Press."In a Fox News interview ahead of Sunday's rally, Trump praised Rogers as someone who shares Michigan voters' beliefs."He's going to be an amazing senator," Trump told the "Sunday Briefing" program. "Solid as a rock. Apple pie."Democrats need to gain just a handful of seats each in the US Senate and House of Representatives to overturn Republicans' narrow 53-47 and 218-214 majorities.

title: Thales boosts Australia’s defence capabilities with new sonar facility in Western Sydney
body: A new sonar manufacturing facility within Thales Australia’s Western Sydney advanced manufacturing complex, opened this week by the Minister for Defence Industry Pat Conroy, will become a hub for the design, manufacture, integration and sustainment of advanced undersea acoustic systems. Thales Australia and Australia jointly invested in the multimillion-dollar facility at Rydalmere which has been built within the wider Thales Australia Acoustics Centre of Excellence and will be a critical piece of the sovereign supply chain for the Thales towed array system onboard the Hunter Class Frigates. The hall is 100 metres long and is designed to facilitate the end-to-end manufacture of towed array sonar systems that act as the ‘ears’ of submarines, surface ships and autonomous maritime systems. For more than three decades, the Rydalmere facility has supported the Royal Australian Navy with world-class sonar technologies that enhance anti-submarine warfare (ASW), maritime surveillance and undersea domain awareness, including on the Collins Class submarine. The new facility boosts this Australian-made deterrence by ensuring end-to-end sovereign manufacturing capability and capacity for next-generation towed array sonar systems that support submarines and surface combatants, and thin-line towed arrays for uncrewed maritime systems serving both Australian and export markets. It also enables the local sustainment of acoustic systems, maximising deployment times for Australian intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) activities and reducing the need for lengthy offshore maintenance periods. In particular, the towed array facility will deliver: Hunter Class Frigate Program Towed Array Sonars enabling long-range submarine detection and tracking while enhancing fleet survivability and maritime domain awareness. Collins Class Submarine Sonar System, built upon more than 35 years of collaboration between Thales Australia, the Royal Australian Navy and Australian defence science organisations. BlueSentry®, a Next-Generation Autonomous Surveillance Capability which combines advanced thin-line fibre-optic towed array sonar technology with uncrewed maritime platforms. The facility is expected to create dozens of direct engineering and advanced manufacturing jobs in Western Sydney over coming years, as well as roles for our supply chain partners, contributing to national security and the protection of Australian fleets and defence personnel. Pat Conroy, Minister for Defence Industry, said: “Through this new co-invested manufacturing facility, Australia is strengthening national security, creating high-value jobs and establishing a sovereign centre of excellence for advanced acoustic systems that will support both Australian Defence and export opportunities for decades to come.” Jeff Connolly, CEO, Thales Australia and New Zealand, said: “The capabilities developed and manufactured at Rydalmere demonstrate Australia’s ability to deliver sovereign undersea warfare technology, including from the Collins Class submarine fleet of today to the Hunter Class frigates and autonomous BlueSentry® surveillance systems of the future. Thales Australia researches, designs and delivers high-quality sensors that return best-quality data, allowing for quicker and better decisions that relate to national security. These capabilities will be made and sustained here at home, to secure our nation.” For Editorial Inquiries Contact: Editor Kym Bergmann at kym.bergmann@venturamedia.net For Advertising Inquiries Contact: Group Sales Director Simon Hadfield at simon.hadfield@venturamedia.net

title: Saudis say Riyadh airport partly reopens despite renewed Houthi threats
body: Saudi Arabia said its main airport resumed operations at two terminals on Sunday, October 25, even as Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis vowed to keep striking the facility, which they called a “military target.” King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh had halted operations on October 10 following an attack claimed by the Houthis that killed 13 people, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade. Saudi Arabia said it intercepted another wave of missiles and drones on Sunday as fighting with the militant group continued unabated. The Houthis said they had launched attacks on the air hub among other sites in the kingdom, including in Khamis Mushait and Jazan. It was not immediately clear if those were the strikes the kingdom said it had blocked. The conflict has become an increasingly destabilizing element in the US-Israeli offensive against Iran , turning US ally Saudi Arabia into a pressure point in the wider war. Flight tracking data shows little traffic After Saudi authorities announced the partial resumption of operations at the airport, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree vowed the facility would “never be safe” and urged airlines, airport staff and travelers not to use it. Late on Saturday, October 24, the airport said Terminal 1 would be designated for domestic flights and Terminal 2 for international flights operated by national carriers starting Sunday. Despite the announcement, flight tracking data from Flightradar24 showed little traffic at the airport on Sunday. The Saudi-led coalition said earlier this month that the Houthis had carried out 20 attacks on the airport between October 1 and 11. Missile and drone attacks continue Saudi civil defense said on Sunday that shrapnel from the interception of two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis over Khamis Mushait and Ahad Rafidah injured two people and damaged residential buildings and vehicles. Civil defense authorities earlier issued emergency alerts for Riyadh and the cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran on Sunday, before saying minutes later that the danger had passed. The coalition said two drones and a ballistic missile were launched toward Riyadh, and a cruise missile toward the southern city of Khamis Mushait. It later said it intercepted 10 ballistic missiles fired toward southern Saudi Arabia. The Houthis said they attacked the airport and Saudi oil facilities on Saturday. Saudi authorities did not comment directly on the Houthi statements. Saudi Arabia has stepped up its strikes against the Houthis after the group seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month, closing in on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait – a global maritime chokepoint and shipping route for Gulf oil producers on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula from the Strait of Hormuz. The renewed fighting in Yemen has shattered a UN-brokered truce that had largely held since 2022. Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen’s civil war in 2015 at the head of a coalition supporting the internationally recognized government, after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa a year earlier. – Rappler.com

title: Next parliamentary elections in Slovakia to be held on September 25, 2027 — radio
body:
PRAGUE, October 25. /TASS/. The next regular parliamentary elections in Slovakia will be held on September 25, 2027, Slovak Radio said, citing parliament speaker Richard Rasi.

title: Greece Sends Ohi Day Message to Greeks Abroad
body: By Bill Giannopoulos Greece has delivered a message to the Greek diaspora ahead of Ohi Day on October 28, honouring the courage of those who resisted Fascist Italy’s ultimatum in 1940 and highlighting the responsibility of future generations to preserve the nation’s history and identity. Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Ioannis M. Loverdos issued the message to Greeks living abroad, reflecting on the significance of the historic refusal that brought Greece into the Second World War. On October 28, 1940, Greece rejected an ultimatum from Italian dictator Benito Mussolini demanding the country accept conditions that would undermine its sovereignty. The response, remembered as Ohi , meaning “No” in Greek, became a defining moment in modern Greek history and a lasting symbol of resistance, freedom and national dignity. Ohi Day’s message reaches Greeks worldwide Loverdos said the significance of Ohi Day extended well beyond Greece’s borders, inspiring Greek communities across the world. He highlighted the contribution of Greeks living in the United States, Australia, Egypt, South Africa and other countries who supported the homeland during the war. Some sent financial assistance, others volunteered, while some returned or offered their services to the country of their parents and ancestors. The message also honoured the women who transported supplies to Greek soldiers under difficult wartime conditions and the families who endured the anxiety, separation and loss brought by the conflict. The sacrifices of Greek soldiers in the Pindus Mountains became part of the nation’s collective memory, while the poetry of Odysseas Elytis helped capture the determination and suffering of the Greek people. Preserving Hellenism across generations In his message, Loverdos stressed that the Greek diaspora played a vital role in keeping the nation’s identity alive far from its geographical borders. “Homeland is not only a geographical place. It is memory, language, family and national responsibility,” he said. He pointed to Greek families, community organisations, schools and churches as essential to preserving the language, history, culture and shared memory of Hellenism. Passing this heritage to younger generations, he said, was a responsibility that required children to understand not only what happened in 1940, but why the events continue to matter. The message also connected Ohi Day’s historical legacy with contemporary challenges, including armed conflicts and economic and energy crises. Loverdos said freedom, dignity and faith in shared values could not be taken for granted, calling for responsibility and unity in confronting the challenges of the modern world. “Long live October 28” The Deputy Minister concluded by honouring those who fought and sacrificed their lives for Greece’s freedom, urging Greeks abroad to pass the memory and meaning of Ohi Day on to their children. He called on the diaspora to keep the anniversary’s message alive as a responsibility to future generations. “Long live October 28! Long live Greece!” he declared. For Greek communities around the world, Ohi Day remains an occasion to honour the sacrifices of the past while strengthening the cultural ties that connect the diaspora with Greece. Source: Embassy of Greece in Australia, message from Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Ioannis M. Loverdos. title: GSAT-7C satellite to strengthen Indian Air Force communications
body: India’s $270 million GSAT-7C satellite contract with NewSpace India Ltd marks a strategic step toward resilient, sovereign air combat communications, connecting frontline aircraft with critical intelligence beyond conventional radio range. As India expands its military satellite investments, the dedicated Air Force platform will help bridge the gap between space-based surveillance and operational decision-making, while strengthening secure communications in contested environments, says GlobalData , an intelligence and productivity platform. GSAT-7C is expected to launch in mid-2028 and replace GSAT-7A, which was launched in December 2018 with an eight-year design life and is shared by the Indian Air Force (IAF) and the Indian Army. The Navy has already replaced its own satellite: GSAT-7R, a 4,410kg multi-band platform with a 15-year design life, launched in November 2025 to succeed GSAT-7, which has been in orbit since 2013. GlobalData’s report, “ Global Military Satellite Market Forecast 2026-2036 ,” projects that India will spend approximately $9.6 billion on military-satellite procurement between 2026 and 2036. Of this amount, approximately $1.3 billion will be allocated to communications satellites, accounting for approximately 13.5% of total expenditure.Top of FormBottom of Form Vinayak Kamath, Aerospace and Defense Analyst at GlobalData, comments: “India is directing a substantial share of its military space budget toward space-based surveillance, including programs such as the 52-satellite Space Based Surveillance-III constellation. Surveillance satellites are effective only when their data reaches pilots and air defense crews in time to act. Standard line-of-sight radios can lose connectivity when aircraft fly at low altitudes, operate deep beyond the border, or fly behind mountain ranges. GSAT-7C is intended to address this gap by providing a secure, encrypted link between sensors and frontline combat units through Indian satellites, ground stations, and radios.” This communications link would build on India’s existing networked air-defense architecture. According to the Ministry of Defence’s Annual Report 2025-26, the Integrated Air Command and Control System (IACCS) centrally coordinated India’s air defense during Operation Sindoor. GSAT-7C expands that coverage directly into the cockpit, bringing the Indian Air Force’s diverse fleet of Russian, French, and domestic fighters onto a single sovereign datalink run through indigenous software-defined radios. This would enable faster data sharing and strengthen command resilience in contested operational environments. Kamath concludes: “India’s two-front challenge now extends into orbit, underscored by reports of Chinese operational support to Pakistan during Operation Sindoor and Beijing’s expanding counterspace and jamming capabilities. Dedicating GSAT-7C to the Air Force alongside the Navy’s GSAT-7R disperses communications capacity across distinct platforms, making military networks harder to disrupt than a single shared system. While two satellites represent an initial step toward survivability rather than complete protection, this architecture begins building the operational redundancy India requires to ensure no single orbital disruption can sever critical air combat links.” For Editorial Inquiries Contact: Editor Kym Bergmann at kym.bergmann@venturamedia.net For Advertising Inquiries Contact: Group Sales Director Simon Hadfield at simon.hadfield@venturamedia.net

title: Unemployed man jailed 10 years for attempted robbery
body: An unemployed man who attacked a mobile money vendor with a machete in an attempt to rob him of GH¢40,000 has been sentenced to 10 years’ imprisonment. Kwame Agyapong, alias Michael Osei, was sentenced by an Adenta Circuit Court to 10 years’ imprisonment for attempted robbery and two years for causing harm. The sentences are to run concurrently. The court, presided over by Mrs Angela Attachie, convicted Agyapong after a full trial, during which he had pleaded not guilty. It also ordered that the court deduct the time he spent in custody from his sentence. The court held that the prosecution had proved its case beyond reasonable doubt through witness testimony and other evidence. Chief Inspector Eric Abban, prosecuting, said the complainant, Christian Owusu, was a mobile money vendor residing at Adenta Accountancy, while Agyapong lived at Ashaley Botwe Highways. He said that on June 5, 2025, at about 2030 hours, Owusu was returning home from work when Agyapong attacked him from behind with a machete near Adenta Accountancy. Agyapong demanded the money Owusu was carrying, leading to a struggle during which he inflicted machete wounds on the complainant’s legs, head, hand and face. The prosecution said Owusu wrested the machete from Agyapong, who abandoned his bicycle and fled. The police were informed of the incident. Investigations revealed that Agyapong visited a bicycle repair shop and a barbering shop on the day of the incident, leaving the bicycle and machete there. On June 26, 2025, he was spotted at a barber shop and fled when he saw Owusu. He was later spotted at Madina, arrested and handed over to the Police.

title: Melania Trump comments on possible visit to Ukraine
body:
That is according to the New York Post , Ukrinform reports.
"We will see," Melania Trump said on Saturday, October 24, in response to a question about whether she would make a personal visit to Ukraine.
U.S. President Donald Trump commented on the possibility, saying, "It could happen."
The presidential couple spoke to reporters in Palm Beach after casting their ballots in early voting for the midterm election.
The first lady, for the first time, addressed the cease-fire she said she brokered between Russia and Ukraine for the city of Oleshky, which is facing starvation.
Melania Trump said that, as part of her efforts, she had communicated with both Russian ruler Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
"We talked. We signed the agreement," the first lady said.
President Trump, who has been trying to negotiate a long-term cease-fire between the two nations, said his wife is doing better than his professional envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
"She does better than our professionals," he said as the first lady smiled.
And he did not rule out sending her in to join the negotiations.
"I think she's doing better than the professionals right now," he said. "She got a ceasefire. This has to do with children and people, elderly people."
The article notes that she received international acclaim for her work but questions arose on Saturday about the role Pope Leo played after it was revealed he also called Zelensky and Putin to urge a ceasefire. His calls were a few days before the first lady announced the deal was secured. The pontiff contacted Putin on October 16 and then spoke to Zelensky three days later.
"It is great to have Pope's support, and they are starting a ceasefire on October 27, and I hope everything goes as it's planned," the first lady said.
Democrats accused Melania Trump of stealing the pope's credit but both Russia and Ukraine confirmed her role in brokering the deal. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov praised the first lady's involvement in securing the cease-fire, as did Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets.
As Ukrinform reported, U.S. First Lady Melania Trump said she had secured a local ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine covering only the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in the Kherson region.
The General Staff of the Ukrainian Armed Forces reported that Ukraine would introduce a ceasefire in a designated area starting on the night of October 27 to facilitate a humanitarian operation in temporarily occupied Oleshky.
Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets held an online meeting with Russian human rights ombudswoman Yana Lantratova, during which they discussed previously agreed details of the humanitarian mission in Oleshky.

title: CUGS project reaches final milestone for unmanned ground capabilities
body: The Combat Unmanned Ground System (CUGS) project has successfully reached its final major milestone, demonstrating the progress achieved in the development of next -generation uncrewed technologies for ground operations. Funded by the European Defence Agenc y (EDA) and coordinated by Leonardo, CUGS is the EDA’s largest research and technology initiative in this sector, aimed at developing and validating new uncrewed technologies for land operations. During the project’s final demonstration, several remotely operated systems developed by the partner countries were tested in simulated operational scenarios. The tests demonstrated their full interoperability and highlighted the potential of European cooperation in developing technologies based on a common open architecture. The three simulated scenarios brought together the Lince VTLM-2 with Hitrole (IDV and Leonardo, Italy), Themis (Milrem, Estonia) with Hornet (Arquus, France), ZSMU 1276 (Zakłady Mechaniczne Tarnów, Poland), Wiesel (Rheinmetall, Germany), Scout Vehicle (WAT and PIAP research institutions, Poland), Patria AMV (Patria, Finland), Scout UAV (Thales, France), and loitering munitions systems (MBDA) in a complex operational environment, with the Command Post located several kilometres away f rom the operational area. Each system was deployed at a dif ferent location, and all were tasked with reaching and identifying a number of simulated potential threats. The combat functional modules developed as part of the project and integrated onboard the uncrewed vehicles provided autonomous navigation—including situational awareness through the use of onboard sensors—as well as Communication-Command-Control and Cooperation capabilities and effector management capabilities. The land and aerial systems were therefore able to autonomously move, detect, track, classify, and engage targets, supported by Artificial Intelligence and under the continuous supervision of human operators (human-in-the-loop), who could take control of the platforms involved at any time. title: Bayern beat Freiburg as fans unveil Kompany banner
body: Bayern Munich won 3-1 at Freiburg to return to the top of the Bundesliga, as the German champions paid tribute to absent manager Vincent Kompany. The 40-year-old, who played for Manchester City for 11 years and then managed Burnley, was taken to hospital on Friday after he collapsed while watching Bayern’s second team train. Before Sunday’s match, Bayern fans unveiled a banner that translated as ‘Get well soon, Vincent – we are by your side’. Dayot Upamecano put Bayern ahead when he raced on to Michael Olise’s pass from the halfway line and finished superbly, before Serge Gnabry added a second just before half-time after good work from Nathaniel Brown. Freiburg pulled a goal back with eight minutes left through an own goal from Bayern’s Tom Bischof, but Olise sealed Bayern’s victory by adding a third in the fifth minute of stoppage time. Bayern have won the Bundesliga in the past two seasons and this victory takes them back above Borussia Dortmund on goal difference after Niko Kovac’s side had defeated Eintracht Frankfurt 1-0 on Saturday. On Sunday, Bayern assistant coach Aaron Danks gave an update on Kompany’s condition and said: “The feedback is really positive at the moment. He’s stable [in hospital], he’s doing well. He feels a little better every day. “They are continuing to conduct tests, but the signs are really positive.” On Saturday, Bayern director of sport Max Eberl said Kompany would not be on the touchline for the near future and added: “We need to firstly figure out what it is and then we’ll discuss calmly what the recovery time is to be. We won’t be talking about days, but weeks. We need to all be clear on that.” Eberl added that Bayern had considered asking to postpone the game at Freiburg, but believed the best tonic for Kompany would be to “play and be successful”. Bayern were captained by England striker Harry Kane, who on Monday might become the first English player since Michael Owen in 2001 to win the Ballon d’Or – awarded to the best player in world football over the past 12 months.

title: Northrup Grumman becomes 5th US Navy prime to adopt AML3D’s ARCEMY tech
body: AML3D announced a $2.2 million initial order for a large-scale ARCEMY X system from US Navy prime contractor Northrop Grumman Marine Systems. Northrop Grumman is a key supplier to the U.S. Navy, providing critical components for naval propulsion, power generation, and missile launch systems. The order includes a two-year maintenance and services package. AML3D is advantaged by its track record of supplying ARCEMY systems to solve US Navy supply chain constraints impacting submarine and naval shipbuilding programs. The ARCEMY X will be supplied from AML3D’s US technology center in Stow Ohio, and installed at Northrop Grumman’s manufacturing facility in Sunnyvale, California (“NGC-Sunnyvale”). The terms for the order include a 50% payment upon completion of the initial project milestone, with subsequent milestone payments through final installation, which is expected in the fourth quarter of the 2027 financial year. This initial order for NGC-Sunnyvale demonstrates AML3D’s continuing success converting the demand for ARCEMY systems to support the US Navy’s Marine Industrial Base (“MIB”) into orders. It is also a validation and expansion of AML3D’s strategy to drive US growth by becoming increasingly embedded in US Navy MIB supply chain. AML3D now has contracts in place covering 17 ARCEMY systems in the US, with major prime contractors including Newport News Shipbuilding, Austal USA, Cogitic and Laser Welding Solutions Rob Denney, Country Executive Australia, Northrop Grumman, said, “This contract is an important milestone for Northrop Grumman and for Australian industry. AML3D is the first Australian supplier we’ve engaged for submarine industrial base manufacturing. By joining our Australian supply chain, AML3D will play an important role across multiple programs, accelerating SIB manufacturing in the United States.” AML3D CEO Sean Ebert said: “Beginning work with Northrop Grumman is very exciting for AML3D and further validates ARCEMY as a technology solution for critical US Navy supply-chain requirements. The Board and management have worked closely and diligently to develop and implement AML3D’s US Scale-up growth strategy and supplying our technology to another major US prime contractor strongly endorses that strategy and our ability to convert demand into commercial orders.” For Editorial Inquiries Contact: Editor Kym Bergmann at kym.bergmann@venturamedia.net For Advertising Inquiries Contact: Group Sales Director Simon Hadfield at simon.hadfield@venturamedia.net

title: Chania Film Festival Showcases 400 Films from 53 Countries
body: The 14th Chania Film Festival has brought cinema, education and international cultural exchange to Crete, with approximately 400 films from 53 countries, more than 30 premieres and an extensive programme of workshops, exhibitions and special events running from 21 October to 1 November. The festival opened on Wednesday, 21 October, at the Chania Cultural Centre, combining international cultural exchange with tributes to Greek cinema and local artistic talent. Poland’s Ambassador to Greece, Wojciech Ponikiewski, attended the opening ceremony, which honoured the legacy of acclaimed Greek filmmaker Nikos Koundouros with a screening of his landmark film The Ogre of Athens ( O Drakos ), in the presence of his wife, Sotiria Batziri Koundourou. The festival also honoured two Chania-born artists, Marinella Vlachaki and Dimitris Kalogerakis, recognising their longstanding contributions to theatre and cinema and their influence on the region’s cultural life. Festival promotes cinema, education and cultural exchange Festival director Matthaios Frantzeskakis welcomed guests and described artistic passion as the driving force behind the event’s growth over the past 14 years. More than 300 filmmakers and film professionals are expected to attend this year’s festival, creating a meeting place for culture, education, dialogue and creative exchange, he said. Frantzeskakis also highlighted the festival’s year-round initiatives, which connect cinema with education, local communities, history and cultural heritage. Metropolitan Titos of Kydonia and Apokoronas spoke about cinema’s role in people’s intellectual and emotional development. He welcomed the participation of thousands of children, emphasising the importance of introducing young people to new images, films and creative experiences. Deputy Minister of Migration and Asylum Sevi Voloudaki, representing the government, said the festival demonstrated that regional Greece could lead cultural developments rather than simply follow them. “Chania is not only a place with a great history and significant cultural heritage. It is a place that produces ideas and creates contemporary culture,” she said. Chania MP Alexandros Markogiannakis, representing the President of the Hellenic Parliament, praised the organisers for building a successful cultural institution outside Athens. He attributed its longevity to the team’s dedication, support from local organisations and the festival’s strong connection with audiences. Poland’s Ambassador Ponikiewski expressed his pleasure at attending the event, particularly because the festival has dedicated a special programme to Polish filmmaker Andrzej Wajda. The tribute marks 100 years since Wajda’s birth and ten years since his death. The ambassador congratulated the organisers for recognising Wajda’s contribution to cinema and for the festival’s wider artistic, cultural and social impact. Crete Regional Deputy Governor for Chania Nikos Kalogeris highlighted the role of the Chania Cultural Centre, which has served as the festival’s permanent home throughout its history. Chania Mayor Panagiotis Simandirakis noted that the festival began during Greece’s economic crisis but has continued to grow, becoming an integral part of the city’s cultural identity. Platanias Mayor Giannis Malandrakis and Kissamos Deputy Mayor for Culture Giorgos Makrakis stressed the importance of the festival’s educational programmes for local schoolchildren. Representatives of the Chania Chamber of Commerce and Industry and the National Centre for Audiovisual Media and Communication (EKΚOMED) also highlighted the festival’s contribution to regional development, film education and the international promotion of Crete. The opening ceremony concluded with a screening of Koundouros’ acclaimed film The Ogre of Athens . Around 400 films from 53 countries This year’s programme features approximately 400 films spanning documentaries, animation, fiction, short films and classic feature films. Organisers have also scheduled more than 30 premieres and expect around 300 guests, including directors, actors, cinematographers and other film professionals. Approximately 8,500 children and educators have registered for the festival’s school activities. The programme extends beyond conventional screenings to include virtual reality, podcasts, workshops, masterclasses, live music, late-night screenings, performances, book presentations, exhibitions and discussions. Throughout the festival, Chania hosts activities designed to bring together filmmakers, audiences and communities of different ages and backgrounds. Screenings and events already held The festival’s programme began with a series of screenings and discussions during its opening days. On Thursday, 22 October, audiences watched Siamak Etemadi’s The Stuff We Are Made Of , followed by a discussion about disability, desire and cinema. The same evening, Giannis Soldatos’ documentary I Dreamt You Didn’t Die… explored the life and work of Nikos Koundouros, with friends and collaborators joining a discussion after the screening. Friday, 23 October, featured Marianna Economou’s Where Shadows Rest , followed by a discussion with the filmmaker. The programme also included a cycling-themed selection presented in collaboration with the Podilatreis group. On Saturday, 24 October, the festival screened Eva Libertad’s Sorda , winner of the 2026 LUX Audience Award, followed by a discussion titled When Art Gives a Voice: Life Experiences Through Cinema . The evening concluded with the scheduled midnight screening of Vilma: The Last Goodbye , directed by Kostas Bakirtzis and Kostis Stamoulis. On Sunday, 25 October, the festival presented student films and other productions, while journalist Alexandra Christakaki spoke with film critic Panagiotis Timogiannakis about his book OSCAR and with Giannis Kokkiasmenos, the only Greek actor in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey . Upcoming film highlights The festival’s remaining programme includes several notable screenings and special events. On Tuesday, 27 October, audiences can watch Vicky Anastasiadou’s Wheel to Live , which recently received an award at the 49th Drama International Short Film Festival. The programme also includes Stories of a Lie by Olia Verroiopoulou and a screening of Béla Tarr’s Damnation . Wednesday, 28 October, will feature the award-winning documentary NAZA by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, alongside a panorama of Cypriot films. The programme also includes Andrzej Wajda’s Afterimage , presented in collaboration with the Polish Embassy. On Thursday, 29 October, the Fournos bar in Halepa will host selected short films accompanied by live music from Melentini. The venue will welcome Melentini for a separate live musical performance on Friday, 30 October. Friday’s programme also includes the premiere of Nikos Kavoukidis’ Mikis, the Lambrakis Family and Peace . On Saturday, 31 October, audiences can watch Bugboy by Loukas Paliokrasas, which won an award at the 28th Thessaloniki Documentary Festival. The international programme also features Alexander Lind’s Trine on Fire and a retrospective of Canadian-based animation filmmaker Joe Chang’s work. Other Greek productions featured in the festival include Angelos Kovotsos’ When I Went to America and Dimitris Vernikos’ Manos Hadjidakis – The Mirror and the Knife: The Continuation . New virtual reality programme and inclusive activities For the first time, the festival has introduced a dedicated VR Screenings section, with support and collaboration from the Thessaloniki Film Festival and the Technical University of Crete. A podcast room operates daily throughout the event. The organisers have also arranged activities for older people and people with disabilities, including special film screenings, visits to care facilities and animation workshops. Children remain central to the festival’s educational mission. Activities include morning school screenings, visits to schools in rural areas, radio programmes, podcasts, mobile-phone filmmaking, digital shadow theatre, augmented reality, animation, character design through Manga Lab and cyanotype workshops. The programme also features 23 films created by students and educators during the 2025–2026 CineMathimata annual educational programme. The Stories to Be Heard initiative will present and award audiovisual projects from schools across Greece. The Hellenic Open University will screen student films from across the country in a three-part programme. The festival has also prepared workshops and masterclasses in collaboration with academic institutions, educational groups, networks, EKΚOMED and ASIFA Hellas. Tributes to international and Greek artists The festival’s special tributes recognise artists from Greece and abroad, including Joe Chang, through a retrospective titled Between the Lines: A Duet of Chinese Animation . Other tributes focus on comic-book creator and visual artist Giorgos Botsos, Hungarian composer, musician and actor Mihály Víg, and Polish filmmaker Andrzej Wajda. The programme also celebrates composer Manos Hadjidakis and his special relationship with Crete, alongside honorary events recognising acclaimed cinematographer Nikos Kavoukidis. The festival will host further discussions on cinema, disability and sexuality, children’s rights, mental health and media literacy. Psychiatrist Giorgos Nikolaidis, director of the Institute of Child Health, will discuss culture, schools and mental health, with cinema as a central theme. The programme will also explore how art can give people a voice through personal experiences. The festival will host the Festival Animation Network, with support from ANIMASYROS. As part of the IZIMATA exhibition by Georges Salameh and Stefania Orfanidou at the Monastery of Saint Francis, organisers will screen three of Salameh’s films, followed by a discussion between the filmmaker and Frantzeskakis. Book presentations, exhibitions and public discussions will take place at the Chania Cultural Centre, the Chania Chamber of Commerce and Industry, and the Venizelion Conservatory. Closing ceremony on 1 November The 14th Chania Film Festival and its educational programmes operate under the auspices and support of the Hellenic Parliament, with the auspices of the Ministries of Culture, Education, Religious Affairs and Sports, and Tourism. EKΚOMED serves as the festival’s strategic and financial supporter, while the Chania Chamber of Commerce and Industry also provides support. The Region of Crete, the municipalities of Chania, Platanias and Kissamos, and the Chania Cultural Centre jointly organise the event. The Cultural Society of Crete designs and implements the festival. The Botanical Park and Gardens of Crete serves as strategic sponsor. Telekom sponsors the festival, ERT supports the awards, Aegean Airlines sponsors air travel, ANEK Lines supports sea travel, and Let’s Drive provides local transport sponsorship. The festival will conclude on Sunday, 1 November, with a closing ceremony and the presentation of awards and commemorative certificates, beginning at 11:30 am. For the full programme and updated screening details, visit the official Chania Film Festival website . title: Isak finally living up to price tag as Liverpool patience rewarded
body: It’s been a long time coming, but Alexander Isak may finally be living up to his price tag. The Sweden striker arrived at Anfield amid huge fanfare in August 2025 when he signed from Newcastle for a British record £125m. But a slow start, followed by a broken leg in December, turned his first season at the Reds into a nightmare, scoring just four goals in 22 games. This season has been a different story. Isak’s goal against Brighton on Sunday helped Liverpool secure an impressive 2-0 win over the Premier League’s in-form side, taking his tally to six for the campaign. The 27-year-old is averaging almost a goal per game and has scored more than half of Liverpool ‘s Premier League goals this season. Like last weekend at Brentford , Isak didn’t necessarily set the game alight, but again it was another crucial goal from the Swede. His strike gave Liverpool breathing space against a Brighton team that had 64% possession and actually ended the game with a higher xG than Andoni Iraola’s side. In the end, Liverpool saw the game out and this was arguably their finest display in the league under Iraola, who secured his first league win at Anfield at the fourth time of asking . Only Erling Haaland (nine) has scored more Premier League goals this season than Isak and when Liverpool signed him from Newcastle these were the numbers they expected. During Isak’s struggles in an injury-plagued campaign in 2025-26, the belief inside the club was that this was a long-term signing and any judgement would be reserved for when he was fully fit. Judging by recent performances, that patience is proving to be warranted. “Today, the performance was really good against a really good team,” Isak said. “The first half is really what we want to be about – winning balls and the intensity.” The exciting thing for Iraola and Liverpool is that Isak is nowhere near his best yet, and that should be a cause of worry for the rest of the top flight. It is Arsenal next up in the league. “Alex [Isak] is threatening, especially if we can get him in those positions and we can provide him good crosses. In this case, it’s a matter of Bradley [Barcola] winning the duel and being faster than the opposition to get us in that. An impressive performance all-round For Iraola, this was a fourth win in a row since the loss to Manchester City at Anfield a fortnight ago. The fans who braved the conditions after Storm Boelo were treated to a display where Liverpool were aggressive from the outset and defended really well to keep a Brighton side that scored 15 league goals in their previous four games at bay. Bar an early chance for Yasin Ayari, which the Swede blazed over, Fabian Hurzeler’s side didn’t have any major chances of note. Ronald Araujo was again immense and the Liverpool backline kept their fourth clean sheet in eight league games this season. Interestingly, Liverpool ‘s possession of 35.6% was their second lowest on record (since 2003-04) in a Premier League home win. Iraola’s Bournemouth side certainly preferred to have less of the ball and this was a reminder that, with the quality at his disposal going forward, Liverpool are perhaps fine with teams coming to Anfield and having more of the ball, especially if it means the opposition aren’t set up in a low block . Both Florian Wirtz and Barcola were excellent and Cody Gakpo threatened all afternoon too, with Wirtz unlucky not to be credited for the goal when his strike took a deflection off Pascal Gross and gave Liverpool the lead. Slowly but surely, his confidence is increasing in a Liverpool shirt and it is clear to see the impact he has on a game. The German just needs the numbers to improve on his end and Liverpool will hope that he isn’t set for a spell on the sidelines after he was substituted in the second half. “Unfortunately, he had to leave the pitch with a small twist of the ankle,” said Iraola. “It doesn’t look very big but we are playing every three days so we need to see where he is.” As for Barcola, there is a style to his play that can energise a crowd and the way he won possession for Isak’s goal felt like it ticked off exactly what Iraola wanted with the high press and sheer desire to win the ball back. That left Isak to finish instinctively and Barcola imitated Isak’s celebration, just like they did last weekend in west London, as Liverpool moved up to fourth. Theirs is a combination that cost the Reds a total of £248m but if they can keep on combining and winning games, that will do just fine for Iraola and Liverpool .

title: F-Zero X on Nintendo 3DS
body:
How G-Diffuser, the PC port of the F-Zero X decompilation, got onto the Nintendo 3DS: one person directing, Claude agents writing all of the code, 11 weeks from first research to multiplayer.
Hardware: card-6 test logs, build ba0692e , 10-26 (1P vs CPU field, 3D on); how the numbers got there is on Road to 60 . Tokens and cost: session transcripts to 10-26, method on Cost .
The clips and photos below are from v0.9 (2026-09), before DASH replaced the debug console on the bottom screen.
Three console builds from one source tree:
Each installs from the HOME menu (.cia) or the Homebrew Launcher (.3dsx). No ROM or disk image ships: players extract their own.
Both consoles draw through the same native renderer by default. The New 3DS's first-phase render-thread path is still built in as an option; Frontier and Road to 60 cover it.
The first phase (08-11 → 09-03) ported the game to the New 3DS. The second (09-07 → 10-19, not originally planned) brought it to the Old 3DS through a native renderer and shipped v1.0.0. Then a week of v1.1.0 work.
See Agentic workflow for how the second phase was run and The road to 60, all over again for the Old 3DS campaign, card by card.

title: Airbus and Denel Sign Pact to Lift SAAF Helicopter Availability
body: South Africa’s helicopter fleet has spent years waiting for spare parts, funding, and workshop capacity. At the Africa Aerospace and Defence (AAD) 2026 exhibition in Pretoria, Airbus Helicopters and Denel Aerospace signed an agreement intended to shorten that wait. The two companies say the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) sets a long-term framework for industrial cooperation that should strengthen support to the South African Air Force’s (SAAF’s) helicopter fleet and raise its rotary-wing serviceability. According to a DefenceWeb’s post, the signing took place during AAD 2026 , held from 16 to 20 September at Air Force Base Waterkloof, and it matters because the SAAF’s flying hours have fallen well short of what the service plans each year. What the Two Companies Signed An MoU is a statement of intent and not a purchase contract, and the published account does not give a value, a schedule, or a list of work packages. Airbus says the agreement establishes a long-term framework to increase national air defence capabilities and to boost aviation industrial growth across Southern and East Africa. The practical aim is to combine what each company already does. Airbus Helicopters brings the manufacturer’s engineering knowledge and its global support network. Denel Aerospace brings local engineering, fabrication, and maintenance facilities, and long experience on SAAF aircraft. Airbus says the agreement intends to build on the companies’ existing capabilities and anchor a self-reliant domestic support ecosystem that can serve both South Africa and regional operators across Southern and East Africa. Arnaud Montalvo Chastellier, Head of Africa Middle-East Region at Airbus Helicopters, framed the agreement as a commitment to local industrial skills alongside mission-critical capability for the SAAF and the wider African market. He said the pairing of Airbus’s helicopter know-how with Denel’s local expertise would build an ecosystem that improves operational readiness. Chris Boshoff, Chief Executive Officer of Denel Aerospace, said the partnership will develop the “sovereign aviation capabilities” needed to sustain the SAAF’s current and future fleets, and that an extended industrial footprint across the country and the region would provide long-term self-reliance and operational resilience. A Shared Heritage in Metal The two companies are not strangers. Denel Aerospace is the design authority for the Oryx medium transport helicopter and the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) of the Rooivalk attack helicopter. Both types use dynamic components derived from the Airbus Puma and Super Puma, the rotors and gearboxes that carry the heaviest loads, and both are powered by Turbomeca Makila turboshaft engines, now part of Safran. That shared engineering base explains why the cooperation makes technical sense. Airbus and Denel also signed an MoU at AAD in 2016, covering a phased modernisation of the Rooivalk. That earlier agreement focused on improving the reliability of the Rooivalk Mk1 fleet and replacing obsolete items. The 2026 document is broader, since it covers the helicopter fleet’s support and a regional industrial footprint, and it does not name a single type. Denel says it is also cooperating with Airbus on maintenance, repair, and overhaul (MRO) and refurbishment of the H215 and H225 military helicopters for Africa . Both are Airbus’s Super Puma-family aircraft, and a number of African air forces fly them. The Serviceability Problem The SAAF’s difficulty is documented in its own accounts. In the Department of Defence’s annual report for 2025/26, the SAAF said it planned to fly 12,000 hours during the financial year, but flew 6,340.08. That is 52.8% of the target for the period from 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026. The hours break down into 5,085.51 Force Preparation hours, 610.47 Force Employment hours, and 644.10 flown for very important person (VVIP) transport. The report links the shortfall to budget constraints and says air defence capabilities remained under pressure. It attributes the unavailability of serviceable aircraft to delays in placing contracts, a lack of funding for maintenance and spare parts, long lead times for parts, inadequate stock levels, and obsolescence. The helicopter fleet has been among the hardest hit. A written parliamentary reply from the Minister of Defence in October 2023, showed that 15 of the SAAF’s 88 helicopters across five types were available to fly. Of 11 Rooivalks, three were serviceable with restrictions. Of 41 Oryx, five were serviceable. Those figures are three years old, and the picture has since improved in places, but they show the scale of the problem the partnership is meant to address. Part of the difficulty lies in how specialised the support is. Denel operates a Makila engine repair shop for the Oryx and Rooivalk that needs accreditation from Safran, and the Department of Defence has warned that the facility is at risk of losing that capability without enough work from the SAAF. Capability that goes unused tends to disappear. Signs of Recovery Boshoff told DefenceWeb earlier that Denel Aerospace is making progress across the business, rebuilding its engineering, fabrication, and maintenance capabilities and investing in technical skills development. He said that, working with the SAAF, Denel is putting more fixed- and rotary-wing aircraft into the air, while opening opportunities in Africa and elsewhere. There is evidence behind that. This year, Denel Aerospace has returned multiple Oryx and Rooivalk helicopters to service. At AAD in September, the SAAF flew a large number of aircraft, including several Hawk and Gripen jets alongside Oryx, Rooivalk, A109, and BK117 helicopters. The display was the sort of show that an air force chooses to put on when it has aircraft to show. Denel’s own position has also shifted. AAD 2026 was the first time the group exhibited with the Department of Defence as its shareholder, and Denel’s Group Chief Executive, Tsepo Monaheng, described it as part of a renewal of the company. Airbus’s Existing Footprint in Southern Africa Airbus is not new to South African military and security aviation. It has long supported the SAAF with maintenance contracts for the air force’s three C212 light transport aircraft. On the rotary-wing side, it has a long relationship with the South African Police Service (SAPS), which operates 16 AS350 (H125) helicopters, with more being acquired. Namibia and Botswana also fly Airbus helicopters for their police forces. The wider market is large. Airbus says there are more than 60 operators of its helicopters in Africa, flying more than 500 aircraft, of which 300 are in Southern Africa. Customers come from government and commercial sectors, and the helicopters are used for emergency medical services, law enforcement, anti-poaching, and inspection of critical infrastructure. A support network in South Africa that can service those aircraft is the commercial logic behind the regional language in the agreement. What Has to Follow the Signature The agreement will be judged on what comes after it. The first test is whether it turns into funded work orders, since the SAAF’s maintenance problems have been as much about contracts and money as about workshop capacity. An MoU does not place an order, and the annual report names late contract placement as a cause of unavailability. The second is skills and parts. Denel has said it is investing in technical skills, and the partnership could bring Airbus training and parts supply into the process. Whether spare parts arrive faster is the measure that matters to squadron commanders. The third is the regional promise. A service centre that supports Airbus helicopters across Southern and East Africa would need certifications, customers, and export approvals, and it would compete with established support networks in Europe and the Gulf. The fourth is the SAAF’s own budget. A better-supported fleet still needs flying hours funded, and a 52.8% flying-hour result reflects constraints that no industrial agreement can remove on its own. If those pieces fall into place, the Oryx and Rooivalk fleets could spend more of their lives in the air and less in the hangar, and South Africa could build a support industry that earns income from neighbours. If they do not, the MoU will join a list of agreements whose intentions were good.

title: Mbappe, Kane, Yamal Are Ballon d’Or Front Runners Today
body: Duro Ikhazuagbe France’s Kylian Mbappé, England’s Harry Kane and Lamine Yamal of Spain are amongst the men front runners for this year’s Ballon d’Or awards to be unveiled this evening in London. According to the organisers of the 70th edition of this prestigious football honour, the ceremony is scheduled to begin at 8pm UK time. The 2026 edition scheduled to hold at the London Palladium, is the first time ever that the Ballon d’Or will take place outside its traditional Paris venue. It was selected in honour of the inaugural 1956 winner, Sir Stanley Matthews. Expectedly, the awards ceremony has created abuzz in the British capital city, with most football fans looking in the direction of England/Bayern Munich’s forward, Harry Kane, to win his first Ballon d’Or. No British male footballer has won the award since 2001 when Michael Owen was the recipient of the exclusive top football honour. Spain’s Yamal on the other hand has done more than enough for both club and country to be considered for the title. This year, he led Spain to win the World Cup in North America after defeating Argentina in the final. Other top runners for the award include; defending champion Ousmane Dembélé of France/Paris Saint-Germain, and Norway/Manchester City striker Erling Haaland, amongst others. In the women’s categories, Barcelona midfielder Alexia Putellas is among the nominees seeking to add to her previous Ballon d’Or Féminin victories. The award will recognise the standout performer in women’s football over the relevant assessment period. In addition to the men’s and women’s Ballon d’Or, the ceremony will recognise achievements across several categories. These include the Kopa Trophy for young players, the Yashin Trophy for goalkeepers, the Johan Cruyff Trophy for coaches, the Gerd Müller Trophy for goalscorers and the Club of the Year awards. The ceremony will also feature the Sócrates Award, which recognises football-related solidarity initiatives and contributions to social causes.

title: Iheanacho, Dessers, Arokodare on Fire in European Leagues!
body: Kelechi Iheanacho has become unstoppable in the second tier Turkish Lig. Yesterday, he thumped in another goal to make it straight 16 goals in favour 12 matches for Bursaspor. ‘Senior Man’ Iheanacho scored Bursaspor third goal in the 50th minute at Keciorengucu. His team won 4-2 on the road to climb top of the Turkish second division with 28 points from 12 matches. Bursaspor are now pushing for a return to the Turkish Super Lig and the goals of Iheanacho will go a long way in determining just how far they go in their quest. His goals in Turkey will also boost his chances of being part of next month’s 2027 AFCON double-header against Tanzania. He has already scored on his international recall against Russia last month. Elsewhere, another Nigerian forward, Cyriel Dessers, is pushing for a Super Eagles recall after he scored for Panathinaikos for the fourth straight game. The experienced striker, who was forced out of the Super Eagles final squad to the 2025 AFCON by injury, was the match winner for Pana to win 1-0 at Volos in the Greek league. The Nigerian forward has thus followed up with his brace against Kairat in the UEFA Conference League. In the Dutch Eredivise, Super Eagles striker, Tolu Arokodare, was again the match winner for Ajax on Sunday evening. He scored in first half stoppage time for Ajax to win 2-1 at Sparta Rotterdam. It was his fifth league goal and his ninth in all competitions for the Dutch giants. His goals should stand him in good stead for his loan transfer to be made permanent at season’s end.
