title: Does Nigeria truly have over 103 million voters?, By Chidi Anselm Odinkalu
body:
Ahead of Nigeria’s general elections in January and February 2027, Africa Confidential warns that “turnout in the elections is likely to be even lower than the average 26.7% four years ago. Nigerian voters are among the least enthusiastic in the world…. Out of more than 93.4 million registered voters, 24.9 million total votes were cast. This represented an 8.03-point decline from the 2019 elections and was the lowest voter turnout since Nigeria’s return to civilian rule in 1999.”
Complaints about “voter apathy” are the staple of Nigeria’s electoral commentariat. The numbers and patterns seem to bear this out . In 1999, turnout was 52.3 per cent. Officially, it grew to 69 per cent in 2003; and has fallen since then to 57.5 per cent in 2007; 53.7 per cent in 2011; 43.7 per cent in 2015; and 34.8 per cent in 2019, before cratering to 26.7 per cent in 2023.
These claims require us to accord credibility to the underlying numbers from the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC). That begins with belief in the baseline of INEC’s electoral register against which turnout is judged. If that register is flawed, then all calculations hinged on it also suffer.
Yet, the foundational affliction underlying of Nigeria’s elections is not in INEC’s numbers. Rather, it is an absence of credible demographic management system against which to verify INEC’s claims.
The National Population Commission (NPoPC) claims 53 per cent of births in the country are registered and only 10 per cent of deaths are. The implications of this for the credibility of the electoral register should worry everyone.
To be sure, electoral rolls are ambulatory. People are not static: we move; relocate, and die too. This is why a demographic management system is essential. In Nigeria, this does not exist.
A register of voters does not automatically change because a person whose name is on it has died. But a person should also not be on the register one decade after their death. In Nigeria, there is no way of stopping this.
These define the many curiosities about Nigeria’s voting numbers. First, they bear no rational relationship to wider demographic trends. Nigeria’s pattern of supposedly precipitous collapse in voter turnout, for instance, is inversely proportional to both baseline population and civic gripe.
In 1999, Nigeria’s population was estimated to be 115,766,000. Nigeria’s current population is estimated at 244 million . That means the country has more than doubled its population since 1999 by 128,234,000 or 110.77 per cent.
Over the same period, the voting roll has grown by 81.4 per cent, even as life expectancy in the intervening quarter century has increased by about nine years. If life expectancy is growing with the population and crude death rates falling, then the rate of growth in the voting population should ordinarily outstrip the underlying population growth rate.
In 20 years from 1999 to 2023, Nigeria’s population rose by about 87 per cent but the register of voters grew by 36,530,063 or 63.05 per cent. The mis-match between the two trendlines is significant.
In 1999, Nigeria had 57.94 million registered voters. This rose by 2.88 million or 4.97 per cent to 60.82 million in 2003 and then by a mere three-quarters of a million or 1.23 per cent to 61.57 million in 2007. By 2011, the number of registered voters climbed by over 12 million (20.5 per cent) to 73.53 million, representing an average yearly growth rate of nearly 5.12 per cent, where previously it had grown by 1.24 per cent in 1999-2003 and 0.3 per cent between 2003 and 2007.
By 2015, the population of registered voters fell to 68.83 million, a deficit of 4.7 million voters or 6.39 per cent, representing an annualised rate of reversal of 1.6 per cent. Yet, over the same period, Nigeria, a country with a median age of just under 18 years, had grown in population from an estimated 162.9 million to 181.2 million, an increase of 15.174 million or 11.23 per cent, representing an annual growth rate of 2.8 per cent.
The patterns from these numbers do not lend themselves to easy explanations. It is possible to speculate about what may explain this significant delta in growth between the general population and register of voters. Rational factors such as migration; agency dysfunctions in INEC; civic inertia or disaffection; or high transaction costs may be relevant. But there remain worrying patterns that are not easily accounted for even by all these.
As the Justice Uwais presidential committee on electoral reform pointed out in its 2008 report, much of what passed for electoral numbers in Nigeria before 2011 was voodoo. Just to illustrate this point, the INEC does not have a breakdown of official results for the 2007 presidential elections yet there are turnout figures for that election.
This leads to a second issue: Nigeria’s register of voters has always had invalid voters. The current register of voters in Nigeria dates back to November 2010 when the Attahiru Jega-led INEC set about establishing a credible register of voters for the country. The Commission had limited time to authenticate the raw data before the 2011 general election.
When the Automatic Fingerprint Identification System (AFIS) finished its work on the 2011 register nearly four years later, INEC invalidated 4.7 million entries, which reduced the number of registered voters from 73.53 in 2011 to 68.83 in 2015 but not before these invalid 4.7 million were eligible to vote in 2011.
Third, the biggest problem may be dead voters. That’s an oxymoron because the dead should not vote. In 2022, INEC explained that it could not expunge the dead from the register because “the country does not have reliable data of births and deaths and the commission cannot engage in arbitrary removal of the names of individuals it suspects are deceased.”
This has not changed. It means we have no way of knowing how many ghosts there are among the 103.4 million on INEC’s current register. By failing to display the register as required by law , the Commission does not even care to disabuse suspicions that its register may be bloated. Its response to non-compliance is institutional insouciance.
Nigeria’s register of voters is the classic Hotel California : it is “programmed to receive” and, for anyone with their name on it, “you can check out any time you like but you can never leave.” The implications of this for electoral integrity are staggering.
An illustrative exercise may help. Nigerian law allows adults alone to vote. The World Bank estimates the country’s crude mortality rate at 11.64 per 1000 . Applied to a baseline from 2011, that is about 34,748,845 dead in 15 years.
But not all these will be adults. Mortality rate for under-5s is 117 per 1000 live births. That’s 700,000 to 855,000 under-five child deaths yearly . To 2025, that could be about 12 million dead under-fives since 2011.
The country also reported an estimated median of 111,425 deaths among 5–14-year-olds from 1990 to 2016 . Applied again to a 2011 baseline, that’s another 1,671,375. In total, there could be up to 13.67 million infants, children, and adolescent deaths since 2011.
Adjusting the crude death rates for mortality among infants, children, and adolescents, there could be about 18-20 million people liable to be lanced from the electoral register since 2011. Applying the same methodology to a baseline of the 2023 register, that could be up to five million dead people alone on the register since the last election.
In its latest announcement, however, INEC said it captured a total of 10,772,421 new voters . It has not accounted for deaths or natural attrition.
Separately, at the end of 2025, the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre, (IDMC) reported that Nigeria had at least 3.7 million in internal displacement . The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees adds up to 478,000 Nigerian refugees outside the country. Admittedly not all of these are adults of voting age.
Almost assuredly, INEC’s 103.4 million voters is corpulent. When you look at the numbers on INEC’s register and account for the fact that the baseline data goes back to 2011, there is a reasonable likelihood that up to about 25 per cent on it could be dead or dud. That should put all the talk about voter apathy in perspective. But this story has a uniquely Nigerian sting: our diaspora on earth may not have a vote, but we may have a diaspora in Heaven with a veto.
Chidi Anselm Odinkalu , a lawyer, teaches at the Fletcher School of Law and Diplomacy and can be reached through [email protected] .

title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1705: Starlink speed restored for Ukraine’s troops, Musk says SpaceX simply enforced its terms

The SpaceX owner, who had earlier said the US government decides such limits, wrote that his company had closed a gap he says Ukrainian troops used for drone strikes. This is the fancy new F-16 Ukraine could get. It’s not what its pilots need most. . Ukraine could buy newly built F-16 Block 70/72s from US firm Lockheed Martin. But that's not the greatest need. Ukraine now fights two enemies. One is America . In two weeks, Washington sanctioned the court prosecuting Putin, waived its own sanctions on Russia, and called him a humanitarian. Military Ukraine strikes Russian plant supplying batteries for ballistic missiles and glide bombs with Storm Shadow missiles, OSINT reports – another hit on Russia’s weapons supply chain . The plant is reportedly Russia’s only producer of batteries for glide bomb guidance modules and a key supplier of specialized power sources for missile systems used in attacks on Ukraine. Russian titanium plant in Urals reportedly hit by Ukrainian drones, 1,500 km from Ukraine . AVISMA, a major titanium producer in Russia’s Perm Krai, was reportedly hit by drones early on 25 October. The plant’s titanium alloys are used in military aircraft, engines, missiles, and space technology. Ukrainian drones reportedly strike major shopping mall in Russia’s Belgorod overnight . Ukrainian forces reportedly struck the MegaGRINN shopping complex in Belgorod overnight, when it was closed. Russian plant supplying components for Iskander missiles reportedly struck by Ukrainian Storm Shadow missiles . OSINT projects reported that a strike hit the Proton plant in Orel, a facility whose electronic components are used in several Russian weapons systems. Drone strike sinks cargo ship near Romania, killing Ukrainian sailor. Romanian President blames Russia . The Khoryv capsized about 13 nautical miles off Romania’s coast, with nine crew members rescued and three still missing. The incident adds to a wave of attacks threatening Black Sea shipping and Ukraine’s export routes. Denmark rushes 50,000 cannon rounds to Ukraine to help F-16s hunt Russia’s advanced jet drones . Ukrainian pilots are already using the 20-mm ammunition to intercept jet-powered attack drones, as Russia deploys faster targets that challenge Ukraine’s air defenses. Ukraine wants partners’ Patriot interceptors now. Europe can hand them over only with US approval, Ukraine’s president says . Ukraine is contracting about 1,000 Patriot missiles that will take years to arrive, so it wants partners’ stocks today. Intelligence and technology Musk warns military use of Starlink could spark space war. Kyiv’s ex-disinformation chief says he’s building alibi after Starshield scandal . The warning lands weeks after his company throttled the Starshield service Ukraine’s drones rely on. A modem from a Russian drone led reporters to its Chinese maker—which invoiced 500 for Russia’s drone plant . Posing as a Russian military supplier, journalists got a $2.87 million invoice, three bank accounts, and no pushback on military use. Russia may stage sabotage in Eastern Europe, but wants Kyiv blamed, Ukraine’s Intelligence warns . The agency says Moscow aims to weaken European support for Kyiv by making Russian attacks appear to be the work of Ukraine’s military. The money starts as bags of cash in a Moscow market and ends up clean in China, leaked files show . The firm, co-owned by the bank behind Russia’s defense industry, hides where the money starts before it reaches foreign banks. The Starlink hot potato: Musk points to Trump, Trump points to nobody, then credits Musk with the fix. The speed limit stays . Ukraine’s military Starlink terminals still lose connection above about 160 km/h, nine days after the limit took effect, and Kyiv has no official explanation of who imposed it. International 40,000 tons of Russian diesel are bound for New York—due four days after Americans vote . The tanker loaded at a Baltic port Ukrainian drones struck in March. Trump wants cheaper diesel before the midterms. Russia’s attacks on Black Sea shipping raise risk of global famine, German FM warns . As Russian strikes increasingly threaten civilian vessels and Ukrainian grain exports, Germany’s foreign minister warned that shipping disruptions could leave vulnerable countries without essential food and fertilizers. Austria expels Russian Embassy and OSCE diplomats over suspected spying. Vienna remains a Russian spy hub . Austrian security authorities raised suspicions of espionage involving four Russian diplomats, prompting Vienna to declare them persona non grata. Russian Geran drone crashes in Moldova near homes and energy facility: Chisinau expels Russian diplomat . President Maia Sandu condemned the latest incursion as Russia’s war on Ukraine increasingly threatens neighboring Moldova. Finland gives Ukraine 10 diesel locomotives that keep trains running when Russian strikes cut the power . The engines come free from Finland’s state railway, part of a visit that also brought winter energy money and new defense, housing, and satellite deals for Kyiv. 45 seconds of voting in the Lviv Oblast Council sparked a new dispute with Poland: Warsaw says Kyiv promised the UPA year decision will not take effect . Poland is Ukraine’s main hub for Western aid, and every new fight over the two nations’ WWII past erodes the trust that role rests on. Humanitarian and social impact Pope’s envoy becomes first foreign representative to gain access to Ukrainian POWs held by Russia since 2022 . Cardinal Matteo Zuppi, Pope Leo XIV’s special envoy, was allowed to physically visit Ukrainian prisoners of war held by Russia during his recent visit, Ukrainian ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said. Ceasefire planned for occupied Oleshky as residents face starvation and blocked escape routes, White House announces . A truce announced by Melania Trump is due to take effect October 29, opening the way for humanitarian supplies and evacuations if Russia and Ukraine implement the agreement. Ukraine frees 270 from Russian captivity in “historic” prisoner swap, including 5 Olenivka survivors and American teacher Stephen Hubbard . The latest exchange returned 261 military personnel and nine civilians. Some had been held since 2018, while many others were captured during the defense of Mariupol in 2022. Russia has kept the Red Cross away from Ukrainian POWs since 2024. Now about 1,500 captives it never confirmed as prisoners face prosecution . A captive soldier’s wife says that whenever families find a relative, Russia moves them to another prison and contact is lost again. Political and legal developments US midterms could restore Ukraine’s American aid and curb Trump’s Russia deals, if Democrats win Congress . Trump waives sanctions on Moscow that Congress wrote into law. Democrats could fight back after 3 November. Putin claims Russia is ready for new talks with Ukraine, calls occupied land historical Russia . He also cited unnamed genetic studies to claim Russians and Ukrainians are one people, a day after hosting a US envoy. Russia keeps hitting Ukraine’s arms plants. Now private developers can dig them space underground—and sell or rent it to them . The state budget has paid to keep war-damaged arms plants running. The new model brings private money into the digging. Read our previous daily review here .

title: Voting at Brazil’s runoff presidential election extended for two hours
body:
RIO DE JANEIRO, October 25. /TASS/. Voting in the runoff presidential election in Brazil has been extended for two more hours amid reports on serious logistics problems, the Brazilian Superior Electoral Court (TSE) decided after voting officially finished at 5:00 p.m. local time (8:00 p.m. GMT).
Earlier, the campaign headquarters of the country’s incumbent president, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, stated that voters in several cities were unable to reach polling places due to a lack of free public transportation. The situation was further exacerbated by weather conditions: heavy rains have been falling in southeastern Brazil since early morning, causing road flooding and traffic gridlock.
Voters are to choose between Lula da Silva and his rival, a right-wing opposition candidate Senator Flavio Bolsonaro. According to the results of the first round of voting on October 4, Bolsonaro took the lead with 47.03% of the vote, while Lula da Silva was second with 45.16%. The margin between the candidates was less than two percentage points.
The winner will take office on January 1, 2027.

title: Panagia Soumela Icon Arrives in Crete In Historic First Visit
body: Hundreds of faithful gathered in Rethymno, Crete, on Saturday evening to welcome the revered icon of Panagia Soumela and fragments of the holy relics of Saint Demetrios, as the city marked the feast of the Four Martyrs and the 160th anniversary of the Arkadi Holocaust. The Diocese of Rethymno and Avlopotamos announced the ceremony on Sunday, noting that the icon had travelled to the city for the first time from its pilgrimage site on Mount Vermio in northern Greece. Metropolitan Panteleimon of Veria, Naousa and Kampania brought the icon in response to a request from Metropolitan Prodromos of Rethymno and Avlopotamos. He travelled with Archimandrite Panteleimon Papaemmanouil, abbot of the pilgrimage site, Georgios Tanimanidis, president of the Panagia Soumela Association, and members of the institution’s board. Rethymno Mayor Giorgos Marinakis welcomed the delegation outside the town hall. A procession then accompanied the icon to the Church of the Four Martyrs, led by the municipal philharmonic band. Religious Ceremony Draws Church and State Representatives The church hosted a doxology service and a solemn episcopal vespers, presided over by Metropolitan Panteleimon and concelebrated by Metropolitan Ioakeim of Lambi, Sivritos and Sfakia and Metropolitan Prodromos of Rethymno and Avlopotamos. Deputy Prime Minister Kostis Hatzidakis represented the Greek government. Rethymno MP Giannis Kefalogiannis also attended, alongside representatives of local authorities, the Armed Forces, security services, Cretan and Pontian associations, and the Hellenic Red Cross. Brigadier Nikolaos Kostakis, commander of the 5th Airborne Brigade, represented the Chief of the Hellenic Army General Staff. Panagia Soumela Symbolises the Pontian Greek Heritage In his address, Metropolitan Panteleimon spoke about the meeting of Pontian and Cretan traditions through the icon’s presence in Rethymno. He highlighted Panagia Soumela’s importance to Pontian Greeks and its enduring association with displacement, exile and the uprooting of communities. He also recalled the icon’s transfer and eventual establishment on Mount Vermio, where the pilgrimage site continues to preserve its religious and cultural significance. Holy Relics Exchanged Between the Dioceses Following the vespers service, Metropolitan Prodromos presented Metropolitan Panteleimon with fragments of the relics of the Four Holy New Martyrs of Rethymno. The relics will be placed at the Monastery of Panagia Dovra in Veria. The ceremony concluded with an exchange of commemorative gifts between the two metropolitans. title: Incomar Unveils Drone, Munition and Avionics Suite at AAD 2026
body: First published on Unmanned Africa South African aerospace and defence company Incomar used the Africa Aerospace and Defence (AAD) exhibition at Air Force Base Waterkloof in September to debut a set of unmanned aircraft, avionics and ground control products. The portfolio covers radar-tracking validation, weapons testing, autonomous strike and counter-drone defence. DefenceWeb first reported the line-up. Three Unmanned Platforms The first is the IBIS aerial target drone, a reusable, high-performance aircraft built to mimic modern unmanned and attack aircraft threats. A Jet A1-fuelled micro turbine engine gives it high-speed, high-altitude flight for radar system evaluation, combat readiness testing and weapons system development. Target drones matter more as air defence spending rises, because crews and radars cannot be trained or validated without realistic things to shoot at. Egypt has been offered Russia’s Bizon short-range counter-drone system , and ASELSAN recently staged a live-fire Korkut 35 demonstration for 12 countries . Systems like these have to be tested against targets that behave like the threats they will face. IBIS also enters a field where South Africa already has domestic work under way. The South African National Defence Force relied for decades on the Denel LOCATS (Low Cost Aerial Target System). Denel Dynamics unveiled the high-speed Loki target demonstrator at AAD 2022 , and the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research is developing Project Swift, a low-cost electric vertical take-off and landing target drone . A turbine-powered, high-speed aircraft appears to sit nearer the Loki end of that spectrum than the low-cost Swift end, though Incomar has not said how IBIS is launched or recovered, or whether any customer has been named. The second platform is GANNET, a low-cost, autonomous one-way munition built for beyond-line-of-sight engagements. A one-way munition flies to its target and detonates, destroying itself, unlike a reusable drone that returns to land. GANNET is offered in long-range, medium-speed and high-speed variants and, according to Incomar, provides flexible precision effect against fixed targets and critical infrastructure. That target set is narrower than the moving vehicles Kalashnikov markets its KUB-10ME against, and it differs from the reusable approach Paramount took with its V-Raven ISR and light attack aircraft , which returns to land after each mission. Any export of a strike munition from South Africa would also fall under the country’s conventional arms control regime, a step Incomar did not discuss. The third is the SAHM/DRAGOFLY counter-UAS interceptor, a compact quadcopter designed to neutralise small, agile unmanned threats. Incomar says it combines rapid deployment, high manoeuvrability and autonomous flight for tactical counter-UAS operations. The material does not explain whether the two names refer to a product and its brand or to two versions, and it does not say how the interceptor defeats a target. Interceptor drones have become one of the fastest-growing counter-drone categories since the war in Ukraine and the 2026 Iran war, with Ukrainian designs drawing Western and Gulf demand and firms such as Airbus testing larger missile-armed interceptors. The gap for African users is the one this outlet has described in Kill the Drone and in its analysis of engaging Shahed-type drones : man-portable jammers cannot handle a coordinated drone attack, and a missile fired at a cheap drone loses the cost exchange. Avionics and Ground Control Incomar paired the aircraft with three supporting products. The Portable Ground Control System (PGCS) is a rugged, rifle case-sized control station with dual 21-inch sunlight-readable full high-definition displays, a high-performance computer and an integrated operator interface. It is self-contained and designed for rapid deployment in austere environments. The Peregrine Avionics Suite is a modular, military-qualified avionics system for small to medium unmanned aircraft and munitions. It is built around the Peregrine Flight Computer, with a family of modular peripherals around it: configurable air data sensing, Ethernet switching and platform-specific interfaces. Air data sensing supports the flight control and navigation loops, Ethernet switching distributes data on board, and the platform-specific interfaces connect to mission payloads, effectors and ground links. The aim, Incomar says, is a scalable architecture that integrators can tailor to different platforms without going back to the drawing board each time. Incomar positions Peregrine as a locally developed answer to growing local and international demand for military-qualified avionics. It argues that the small-to-medium drone and loitering munition segment is among the most contested in global defence, with operators wanting platforms that are cheaper, faster to field and easier to sustain than manned aviation, and that almost every such programme needs a trusted, qualified avionics stack that drops into different airframes with minimal re-engineering. The company describes the result as “a complete avionics solution ready for integration into any platform,” which reflects its turnkey approach to system integration. It did not say which qualification standards the suite has been tested against. The third product is IMPACT, a mission planning software suite that unifies unmanned aircraft and precision effectors under one operational interface and supports planning, coordination and execution across different systems. Taken together, IBIS, GANNET and SAHM, with PGCS, Peregrine and IMPACT, make up a single ecosystem covering a target, a strike weapon and an interceptor on one control and avionics stack. That avionics push fits a theme in this year’s South African unmanned announcements. ShadowfaxUAS said its SF45 redesign was driven by restrictions on Chinese components and by Western buyers’ demands for Chinese-free supply chains. Incomar did not frame Peregrine in those terms in the material reviewed, but a locally developed flight computer and sensor stack speaks to the same concern about reliance on foreign parts. A Flight-Test Company Moving Into Systems Incomar was founded in 2000 as a flight test and integration specialist and has grown into a full-spectrum aerospace engineering company , with in-house flight test aircraft, military-trained experimental test pilots and deep systems integration capability. Its quarter-century milestone coincides with what it describes as a renewed focus on autonomous systems, rapid deployment and multi-domain operational readiness. The company says it employs close to 600 people. It operates from two hangars at Wonderboom National Airport, three offices in Gauteng, Jaffie Aviation Training in Robertson and the Incomar Aeronautical Academy. Its fleet gives context to the new products. A Learjet 35A and a Cessna Grand Caravan serve as systems test beds, an Aermacchi AM-3C is used for weapons testing, and a Van’s RV-7A supports practical training on the company’s in-house professional flight test course. Owning test aircraft lets Incomar fly its own avionics and weapons integrations without hiring platforms, a practical advantage for a company selling qualified flight computers and strike munitions. Military Africa reported in 2023 that Incomar was part of the privately owned Arya Group and offered structural design, avionics enclosures, thermal management, printed circuit board development and firmware development, alongside mission computers, flight computers, stores management systems and ground control systems. The AAD 2026 portfolio extends those capabilities into complete aircraft. The Market Behind the Launch The timing reflects how the African drone market has changed. Military Africa’s Africa Drone Procurement Report 2026 records 234 procurement records across 34 African nations, covering an estimated 1,959 drones from at least 21 supplier countries between 1980 and 2026, and identifies indigenous manufacturing as an emerging strategic priority. South Africa already hosts the continent’s largest indigenous drone fleet, at 94 units. Other South African firms are also moving up the unmanned value chain. Paramount has unveiled V-Raven, and ShadowfaxUAS has launched its larger SF45, while Incomar is concentrating on targets, munitions, interceptors and the avionics that run them.

title: Mourinho keeps Clasico midas touch 13 years on as La Liga heats up
body: Jose Mourinho has done it again. The Real Madrid manager celebrated Kylian Mbappe’s late winner at Barcelona on Sunday with a trademark knee slide, maintaining his Midas touch over their bitter rivals. Mourinho has become just the third Real boss to go six El Clásicos in a row without defeat – 13 years after he last led Los Blancos in this fixture. Four wins and two draws in his past six matches in charge of Real Madrid against Barcelona put him up there with Miguel Munoz (1962 to 1965) and Vicente del Bosque (2001 to 2003) as Real managers who have gone six in a row without defeat against the old enemy. It was also just a second victory in eight games against Barcelona for Real, with the return of Mourinho to the fixture haunting the reigning champions And more importantly for Mourinho, Mbappe’s double in Real’s 2-1 win ended Barcelona’s nine-game unbeaten domestic run with a crucial Clasico victory at the Camp Nou. A Real defeat would have allowed Barcelona to establish a commanding nine-point advantage but the result has transformed the top of La Liga, bringing Mourinho’s side to within three points of their rivals. “In my view, Real Madrid do not play to win at the Camp Nou, Real Madrid play to win La Liga,” he said. “We could win with luck, but we won with calmness and with all merit,” he said. “It’s a very strong group. Everyone works very hard. Everyone was ready to win. “The credit goes to the players. When you win, the credit goes to the players. But when you lose, the blame falls on you. And that’s why we see coaches being sacked from their positions every week.” The Portuguese, who returned to Real 13 years after his first stint in charge this summer, has now won six and lost six El Clasicos. He said: “I’ve learned that I have an extraordinary group, with the quality and mindset to play. “In midfield, having a mix of talents gives us more than just having two players with similar characteristics. This mix of talents gives us balance when defending and quality when we go on the attack. “We’ve beaten several teams by four or more goals, but this is Barca, and the players put on a great performance. We need to continue like this and don’t go over the moon after this win.” Barcelona boss Hansi Flick said he didn’t want to give excuses for the defeat but admitted his team lacked fresh legs after a demanding few weeks. “We missed the freshness,” he said. “It’s not easy for our players. We have to recover well, train well and we have to respond from this defeat. “In big games, small things are important and they decide the games and today, it wasn’t on our side. “I can see that today we were not fresh and this is what we have to change.”

title: U.K. won’t join Canada-led defence bank, but pledges cooperation
body:
The British government has turned down Ottawa’s attempts to have it join the international Defence, Security and Resilience Bank, though London says it will work in lockstep with Canada to meet NATO spending targets.
The DSRB is meant to reduce borrowing costs for military spending by pooling credit strength among allies.
Canada has tried for months to convince the U.K. to join the project, but London has instead been pursuing its own program called the Multilateral Defence Mechanism.
Both countries agreed Sunday to craft a framework for cooperation between both banks, “having mutually concluded that it is best to develop two distinct but complementary institutions.”
The two will “work in close partnership” on investment opportunities and challenges, according to a joint media statement.
The DSRB will be based in Canada and has the support of countries such as Belgium, Turkey and Ukraine.

title: Reverse-Engineering Instruction Encodings (2001)
body:
Pp. 133–146 of the Proceedings Reverse-Engineering Instruction Encodings Wilson C. Hsieh University of Utah [email protected] Dawson R. Engler Stanford University [email protected] Godmar Back University of Utah [email protected] A short version of this paper that only described the D E R I V E solver appeared in the proceedings of the DYNAMO 2000 workshop [ 6 ] . Abstract Binary tools such as disassemblers, just-in-time compilers, and executable code rewriters need to have an explicit representation of how machine instructions are encoded. Unfortunately, writing encodings for an entire instruction set by hand is both tedious and error-prone. We describe D E R I V E , a tool that extracts bit-level instruction encoding information from assemblers. The user provides D E R I V E with assembly-level information about various instructions. D E R I V E automatically reverse-engineers the encodings for those instructions from an assembler by feeding it permutations of instructions and analyzing the resulting machine code. D E R I V E solves the entire MIPS, SPARC, Alpha, and PowerPC instruction sets, and almost all of the ARM and x86 instruction sets. Its output consists of C declarations that can be used by binary tools. To demonstrate the utility of D E R I V E , we have built a code emitter generator that takes D E R I V E ’s output and produces C macros for code emission, which we have then used to rewrite a Java JIT backend. 1 Introduction Binary tools such as assemblers, debuggers, disassemblers, dynamic code generation systems [ 3 , 8 , 10 , 15 , 18 ] , just-in-time compilers [ 4 , 7 , 12 ] , and executable code rewriters [ 14 , 21 , 24 ] need to contain a representation of how machine instructions are encoded. For example, a JIT needs to know that the x86 instruction addl %ecx, %ebx corresponds to the bits 0x01cb (formed by a bitwise OR of the addl opcode 0x01c0 with 0x8 for the %ecx argument and 0x3 for the %ebx argument). Unfortunately, specifying instruction encodings with current tools requires looking up and detailing the offsets, sizes, and values of many instruction fields. Unsurprisingly, this process is both error-prone and tedious, especially for CISC machines such as the x86. Currently, system builders must transcribe instruction encodings from an architecture reference manual. We have built a tool called D E R I V E that eliminates the need to specify many of the bit-level details of instruction layout. The user supplies D E R I V E with an assembly-level description of an instruction set: instruction names and operand types (registers, immediates, or labels). D E R I V E outputs a description of how each instruction is encoded, which is given in the form of C structure declarations. The user does not specify binary-level details such as operand widths, operand offsets, opcode values, and register value encodings. As a result, the potential for misspecification by the user is less than that with other tools. D E R I V E is based on a simple observation: virtually all architectures for which a programmer needs binary encodings will already have programs (assemblers) that contain this information. Therefore, we should be able to extract the information from the assembler, which is what D E R I V E does. At a high level, D E R I V E does so by feeding permutations of each instruction to the system’s assembler, and doing equation solving on the assembler’s output to determine how the instruction is encoded (its opcode and its operand encodings). The D E R I V E implementation solves the entire MIPS, SPARC, Alpha, and PowerPC instruction sets. It handles most of the ARM and x86 instruction sets: it does not yet handle some instructions, such as those with non-continuous fields. D E R I V E produces C data structure declarations that describe how an instruction set is encoded. It would not be difficult to produce declarations in other languages. These declarations can be used by tools that interpret or manipulate binaries. As an example, we have built a code emitter generator that takes the reverse-engineered declarations and generates C macros for fast code emission. To demonstrate the utility of these tools, we have rewritten Kaffe’s [ 25 ] JIT compiler to use these macros. Using our automatically generated code emitters reduced the size of the Kaffe backend description by 40%. On a side note, D E R I V E can be viewed as an assembler tester. Because of how it reverse-engineers instructions, it can quickly find differences between what an architecture manual says, and what an assembler actually implements. In Section 2 we discuss related work: Collberg’s compiler-reverse-engineering system and the New Jersey Machine-Code Toolkit. Section 3 describes our assumptions about instruction set encodings, and explains how D E R I V E works. Section 4 discusses the code emitter generator that we have built on top of D E R I V E . Section 5 summarizes our conclusions and describes our future work. Appendix A gives a complete input specification of the MIPS instruction set for D E R I V E . 2 Related Work The most important precedent to D E R I V E is Collberg’s work on reverse-engineering compilers [ 1 ] . Collberg’s system does a “reverse interpretation” to infer what assembly instructions should be used to implement a high-level language. It runs pieces of mutated assembly code to see how the semantics of the instructions changes. His work is aimed at building automatically retargeting compilers, where the descriptions of the semantics of assembly instructions are used to automatically retarget the BEG back-end generator [ 5 ] . D E R I V E is complementary to Collberg’s work. D E R I V E computes information that can be used to bypass the assembler, which is important for building JITs and binary manipulation tools. D E R I V E addresses a simpler problem domain than Collberg’s system, since it reverse-engineers a syntax transformation and not a semantic transformation. On the other hand, our problem domain is much more tractable: it takes on the order of minutes to hours for D E R I V E to reverse-engineer an instruction set’s encoding, whereas Collberg’s system takes days to reverse-engineer an instruction set’s semantics. The work whose goals most closely match D E R I V E is the New Jersey Machine-Code Toolkit (NJT) [ 20 ] . The NJT automatically generates routines to manipulate machine-code from user specifications written in a language called SLED. SLED specifications are exact descriptions of instruction layout, written at several levels of abstraction. At the lowest level of description, SLED “fields” are used to describe instruction bitfields. For example, the description of the SPARC instruction fields in SLED reads as follows [ 19 ] : inst 0:31 op 30:31 disp30 0:29 rd 25:29 op2 22:24 imm22 0:21 a 29:29 cond 25:28 disp22 0:21 op3 19:24 rs1 14:18 i 13:13 asi 5:12 rs2 0:4 simm13 0:12 opf 5:13 D E R I V E could be used to eliminate the field level of specification in NJT specifications. Users of D E R I V E need only worry about an interface that is at the level of assembly language (the level at which NJT’s “constructors” are written). Removing such extra levels of detail eliminates some potential sources of specification error. The authors of NJT use the assembler to do testing of specified encodings [ 9 ] , by choosing random values from within the space of encodings. We turn the process around and use the assembler to derive encodings. Because a user of NJT specifies the various classes of encodings, the NJT specification tester does not need to search as much of the encoding space as D E R I V E does. NJT supports several features that D E R I V E does not, such as support for relocation. For targets such as JITs, which are our primary interest, relocation is not an issue. As another example, NJT can handle synthetic assembly instructions cleanly. The current implementation of D E R I V E does not yet handle complex synthetic instructions well; however, we could easily layer a tool that described synthetic instructions on top of D E R I V E . 3 Implementation D E R I V E takes a high-level description of an instruction set and an assembler, and generates C header files that describe the instruction set. Figure 1 illustrates the tool chain for D E R I V E . idc is described in Section 3.1 ; the solver is described in Section 3.2 ; and the code emitter generator is described in Section 4 . Figure 1: An example tool chain that uses D E R I V E . We have built the tools that are in double boxes. D E R I V E extracts the encoding of each instruction by sampling a small number of possible input sets. We assume each instruction takes a fixed number of fields as operands. We assume that fields have three types: registers, immediates, and labels/jump targets. Registers are a (usually small) set of textual names; immediates are integer values that can range over a large set of possibilities (e.g., on the x86, some instruction take several 32-bit immediates); and labels are symbolic instruction addresses. These assumptions are sufficient to describe the instruction sets for which we have written specifications (which cover a wide range of modern ISAs). We make the following assumptions about instruction encodings: Assembly encodings are stateless transformations. That is, a particular instruction always has the same encoding. In addition, assembling two correct instructions together gives the same results as concatenating the results of assembling them separately. To satisfy this assumption, assemblers must be prevented from adding, removing, or reordering instructions; in general, the user must provide D E R I V E with the appropriate assembly directives. This assumption lets us batch together the assembly of many instructions into one file, which reduces solving time by a large constant. For example, on our machine (a dual-processor 600 MHz Pentium III), we can assemble 2000 instructions in just about twice as much time as we can assemble one instruction--process creation and file I/O dominate the cost of assembly. We assume that the validity and encoding of a value in a field does not depend on the value of any other field. We can thus compute a field’s encoding by enumerating every legal value for it while holding all other fields constant. This assumption allows us to solve for each field separately. Some instructions in certain instruction sets (such as the ARM) do not satisfy this assumption, in which case D E R I V E must do a more expensive search. The field for an n -bit immediate whose high bit is set is independent of the low bits of the immediate. That is, constants between 2 n - 1 and 2 n - 1 can all be encoded in the same instruction field. This assumption lets us solve for immediate fields more quickly; otherwise, our solver would have to enumerate all legal operand values. Immediates are encoded with “simple” transformations. “Simple” means that an immediate’s value can have leading or trailing zeros removed, constants subtracted from it, or leading one bits added (for sign extension). If D E R I V E detects a complex transformation that it cannot represent (such as the scale factor in x86 memory instructions, which is encoded as the logarithm of the scale factor), it immediately stops and tells the user, who can provide D E R I V E with the transformation explicitly. Our implementation currently makes the assumption that negative immediates are encoded using twos-complement; this assumption could be changed fairly easily. 3.1 Specifying Instructions The front end to D E R I V E , idc , translates assembly-level instruction set descriptions into the intermediate form that D E R I V E uses. idc is about 900 lines of lex and yacc code. Users describe instructions with a yacc-like description that contains a list of instructions to generate and a format description that describes the assembly syntax and the operand types. Note that the formats are grouped by assembly syntax, not by encoding class; we believe that the former is far more readable, as it expresses logical relationships rather than encoding relationships. The description of SPARC ALU instructions reads as follows. It states that there are register-register and register-immediate forms of all of the instructions listed. The placeholder &op& indicates where the instruction name appears. The operand specification says that the formatting substring ``r _ 1:iregs'' is replaced by members of the list of registers iregs . Several conventions apply: register field names begin with r , a jump target has the unique name &label& , and an immediate field is any other field. 3.2 The Solvers D E R I V E is composed of three solvers, each specialized to derive a specific operand type: the register solver solves for register fields/operands, the immediate solver solves for immediate fields, and the jump solver solves for jump target fields. Each solver uses the assembler to compute instruction encodings. D E R I V E emits code into an assembler file, runs the assembler, and finds the code in the resulting executable. D E R I V E tests for any difference in endianness between the target and the solving architectures, and appropriately swaps bytes in the object code before doing any solving. To demarcate the machine code in the executable, D E R I V E explicitly emits fenceposts around the code using assembler data directives. Our fenceposts are a randomly chosen sequence of bytes. It is unlikely that D E R I V E emits a sequence of instructions that match the fencepost, since it does not exhaustively search the set of instructions: we only search the entire space of values for register fields, and not for immediate and jump fields. Although we do not currently do so, a simple way to detect and avoid fencepost conflicts would be to solve each instruction twice with different fencepost values. D E R I V E represents instruction encodings as an opcode mask and an arbitrary number of operand fields. The opcode mask contains the bitmask of 1’s that must be set in an instruction to specify a given opcode. Register fields are specified as a sequence of masks, one for each legal register value; immediates and label fields are represented as a size, an offset, and a simple transform. and %g7 , %g6 , %g0; 0x8009 0xc006 and %g7 , %g6 , %g1; 0x8209 0xc006 and %g7 , %g6 , %g2; 0x8409 0xc006 and %g7 , %g6 , %g3; 0x8609 0xc006 and %g7 , %g6 , %g4; 0x8809 0xc006 and %g7 , %g6 , %g5; 0x8a09 0xc006 and %g7 , %g6 , %g6; 0x8c09 0xc006 and %g7 , %g6 , %g7; 0x8e09 0xc006 and %g7 , %g6 , %o0; 0x9009 0xc006 and %g7 , %g6 , %o1; 0x9209 0xc006 and %g7 , %g6 , %o2; 0x9409 0xc006 and %g7 , %g6 , %o3; 0x9609 0xc006 and %g7 , %g6 , %o4; 0x9809 0xc006 and %g7 , %g6 , %o5; 0x9a09 0xc006 and %g7 , %g6 , %o6; 0x9c09 0xc006 and %g7 , %g6 , %o7; 0x9e09 0xc006 and %g7 , %g6 , %l0; 0xa009 0xc006 ... Figure 2: The assembly that D E R I V E generates to solve for the last register field of the SPARC add instruction, and the resulting binary instructions that it analyzes. The solvers all work in the same basic manner. Each one locates a field and determines its size by emitting one instruction for each legal operand value of that field (while holding all other fields’ values fixed) and finding all bits that change in the binary encoding. Figure 2 illustrates this process for the last operand of the SPARC and instruction. Those bits that change belong to the field. Its offset is given by the lowest changing bit; its size by the difference between its lowest and highest bit. A specific operand’s value exactly equals the value of these bits when it is used. All other bits belong to other fields, or to the opcode mask. As each solver is run, the opcode mask is refined. That is, each solver “claims” bits for various fields. After all fields have been solved for, the opcode mask is set to the remaining unclaimed bits (i.e., those that are set to 1 in every emitted instruction). We make one general assembler-dependent assumption, which is that the assembler will produce errors “when expected.” For example, we assume that assemblers will return an error when illegal registers are used in an instruction, or when constants are too large. D E R I V E finds the sizes of immediate fields by testing larger and larger immediates, and it expects that the assembler will eventually return an error message. Unfortunately, assemblers do not always report errors when they should. Gas shows some unexpected behavior, in that it will accept some positive constants that are too large for signed fields (for example, for a 16-bit signed field it accepts constants between 32768 and 65535). In general, we try to remove such dependencies by checking the generated code: D E R I V E gets around this particular bug by making sure that each constant value examined actually results in a different instruction. 3.2.1 Register Solver The register solver is D E R I V E ’s most basic solver, and is called by the other solvers. It has two tasks. First, it computes an instruction’s opcode mask with respect to the register fields. The opcode mask consists of all of the bits that are not used by the register fields. Second, it finds both the location and size of each “register” operand field, along with the bitmask that must be set to specify a given operand value. A register operand is any operand for which the client enumerates the possible textual values. The register solver works in the following manner for a particular register field: Iterate over all legal registers in the field. For each register, create a copy of the instruction format string. Replace the operand with the register value, and all other operands with some legal values. Emit the instructions and read them back into a buffer inst . While iterating over each register value, incrementally reduce the opcode mask by ANDing it with each binary instruction: op_mask = ~0; foreach r in registers op_mask &= inst[r]; This process will leave the mask with 1’s in every bit that has a 1 set for all instruction instances. Examine the emitted instruction stream, and look for all bits that change between 0 and 1. Such bits belong to the current field, since all other operand values were fixed, and all values for the field were enumerated. To find these bits, bitwise AND each instruction with the complement of the opcode mask and logically summing the result: field = 0; foreach r in registers field |= (inst[r] & ~op_mask); At the end, the field mask has a 1 set for every bit in the field. The size of the field is bounded by the most and least significant bits set in this computed mask. The field’s offset is given by its least significant bit. To derive the 1’s that must be set to encode each register for the current field, iterate again over all legal registers, and bitwise AND each instruction with the computed field mask: foreach r in registers fmask[r] = inst[r] & field; We have implemented two main extensions to this simple scheme. First, on some architectures, a specific register value can change the actual instruction encoding. For example, on the x86, different instruction forms are used when the %eax register is used as an operand. The solver detects such discontinuities by checking that all instances of an instruction are of the same length. That is, when it emits the sequence of instructions (as shown in Figure 2 ), it checks that the number of instruction bytes emitted equals the number of instructions multiplied by the size of one instruction. If it does not, it solves for the register values independently, and emits multiple instruction specifications: each specification identifies which specific register values it corresponds to. Second, the solver allows users to supply register operand lists that contain illegal values, which it automatically culls. This syntax is useful for situations where instructions only accept subsets of possible register values. For example, the SPARC architecture supports floating-point instructions that take different combinations of registers, depending on whether the inputs and outputs are single-, double-, or quad-precision. Specifying exactly which operands are legal would increase the size of the SPARC specification by about 40%, and would also increase the probability of error. Instead, clients can state that every floating-point instruction takes any floating-point register as an operand: fregs = ( %f0, %f1, %f2, %f3, %f4, %f5, %f6, %f7, %f8, %f9, %f10, %f11, %f12, %f13, %f14, %f15, %f16, %f17, %f18, %f19, %f20, %f21, %f22, %f23, %f24, %f25, %f26, %f27, %f28, %f29, %f30, %f31 ); fadds, fsubs, fmuls, fdivs, faddd, fsubd, fmuld, fdivd, faddq, fsubq, fmulq, fdivq, fsmuld, fdmulq --> &op& r_1:fregs, r_2:fregs, r_3:fregs; D E R I V E automatically eliminates “bad” registers by first randomly selecting operand values until it finds a sequence that the assembler accepts. It then finds all legal values for a field by trying all of its values while holding the others operands fixed to legal values. 3.2.2 Immediate Solver The immediate solver computes the width and position of each immediate field, and also any transformation of the values in immediate fields. The immediate solver is called after the jump solver, if there are relative jump targets; it is used directly to solve for absolute jump targets (since those are just transformed immediate values). We explain it before the jump solver, because its behavior is closer to that of the register solver. The main difference between this solver and the register solver is that it is impractical to enumerate all legal values for an immediate operand: an n -bit immediate field would require 2 n permutations. Register fields tend to be small (on the order of 5 bits for modern architectures), whereas immediate fields can be substantially larger. As a result, we solve for each bit size of the immediate field, rather than each possible value. The solver first finds an immediate field’s size by iterating upwards from 1 bit, 2 bits, etc., until the assembler refuses to assemble the instruction. It then iterates down from the maximum number of bits (call it n ) and solves for each immediate size. The immediate solver works in the following manner for each bit size m : Choose a random m - 1 bit value and create two m -bit constants, v 0 and v 1, by setting v 0 to the value and v 1 to its complement. Then set the m th bit in both v 0 and v 1: x = (1 << (m - 1)); # randomize low m-1 bits v0 = random() % x; # v1 complements those bits v1 = ~v0 % x; # set mth bit in v0 and v1 v0 = v0 | x; v1 = v1 | x; By emitting instructions with these two constants, we force the low m - 1 bits of the immediate fields to have complementary bit values, while all other bits remain constant. Next, create two instructions, the first with the immediate operand replaced with v 0, the second with v 1. Use the the register solver to derive the register field encodings for these two similar-looking instructions. # copy instruction inst0 = inst1 = inst; # replace immediate operand with v0 rewrite(inst0.fmt, op.field_name, v0); # replace immediate operand with v1 rewrite(inst1.fmt, op.field_name, v1); # solve each copy register_solve(s0, inst0); register_solve(s1, inst1); The two specifications s0 and s1 should have the same register masks, and the same size in bytes. The only difference between the two should be the opcode masks computed by the register solver, which will differ by exactly the bits that differ in v0 and v1 . Find the immediate field by first XORing the two opcode masks. Since only the lower m - 1 bits of the field differ, this action sets 1’s exactly in the location of these bits and 0s everywhere else; we add the m th bit in explicitly (note that we assume that this bit is contiguous with the rest of the field). The least significant bit gives the field’s offset. Refine the opcode mask by removing all field bits from it. # set the low m-1 bits in field field_bits = s0.op_mask ^ s1.op_mask; # find least significant bit field_offset = lsb(field_bits); # add back mth field bit field_bits |= 1 << (m + field_offset - 1); # fix opcode mask s0.op_mask = s0.op_mask & ~field_bits; Check the value of the field against the value of the encoded field to see if any simple transformations are used. such as a shift to the right by a small constant. Check to see if a previous encoding matches this one. Since we work our way down from larger-valued immediates to smaller-valued immediates, we may have already discovered the encoding for the field. For example, a SPARC 13-bit signed immediate field encodes all signed values between 1 bit and 13 bits. In contrast, on the x86 4-byte memory displacements are encoded differently than 2-byte memory displacements. If we have already found an encoding, the current encoding is ignored; otherwise, it is added to the list of derived encodings. We must evaluate the encoding for each immediate size, because some instruction encodings on certain architectures (x86) vary with the size of the immediate provided. Our actual solver is more general than this sketch, and handles instructions with an arbitrary number of immediate operands. For instructions with more than one immediate operand, any variable-length immediate fields are not independent of each other--the length of one will affect the position of any others. Therefore, D E R I V E cannot solve for immediate fields separately. The current implementation has two limitations. First, it assumes that every immediate value that fits in a given field is legal: that is, there are no “holes” in the value space for an immediate field. This restriction is not a real problem. Second, it does not handle immediates that are encoded as multiple non-contiguous bit ranges. It should not be difficult to extend D E R I V E to handle such immediates. 3.2.3 Jump Solver The jump solver derives the encoding for relative jump target fields (labels). Jumps can be classified in two ways: (1) relative vs. absolute jumps and (2) jumps that take immediates vs. those that only take labels. The jump solver finds encodings for relative jumps that take labels as operands. Jumps that accept immediate operands are handled by invoking the immediate solver. Absolute jumps that only take labels do not seem to occur in practice. The difference between the jump solver and the immediate solver is that the jump solver must generates values (labels) differently. To set all bits in an n -bit immediate field, the immediate solver can emit the immediate directly; the jump solver may have to place a label about n instructions away. As a result, it would be impractical to solve for large offsets directly. We assume that backwards jumps are encoded using twos-complement, so that we can solve for the sizes of offsets. D E R I V E computes whether a jump is absolute or relative by emitting two consecutive jumps to the same target and comparing the emitted code values. Absolute jumps will have identical bits, since both instructions encode the same target address. Relative jumps will differ, since they are different distances from the target and thus will have different offset values. Given an instruction that is a relative jump, the solver must find the jump target field’s width and offset in the instruction, starting point (how many bytes a jump of 0 bytes actually jumps from the jump instruction), and minimum jump size. The target address of the jump is target = start + encoded field ï¿½ jump size . Find the minimum jump size by emitting jumps of 1, 2, . . . bytes until the jump field changes. Find the starting point for the jump (the placement of the label that results in an offset of 0). The starting point is found by searching for a label placement that results in an instruction i , where ORing against i is the identity function. In other words, emit jumps to different labels around the jump, and OR each of the jumps against the others to find one whose offset field must be all 0’s. Find the label’s offset in the instruction by emitting a forward jump just past the starting point for the jump. These two instructions will differ by a single bit, which is the lowest bit in the target field. Find the label’s size in the instruction by emitting a negative-offset label. Assuming that relative jumps are encoded using twos-complement (or even ones-complement), this label sets the high bit of the label. We assume that the label is contiguous in the instruction, and that it consists of the bits between the label’s high and low bits. Finally, determine how the jump distance is encoded by referencing labels at known offsets and comparing the field’s value to these locations. We check for the following transformations: subtraction by a constant, truncation of trailing zeros, or having leading bits truncated. For example, truncation of trailing zeros from a byte offset happens in SPARC jump instructions, since instructions are word-aligned. Like the other solvers, the jump solver assumes that label fields are contiguous. It would be challenging to deal with non-contiguous label fields, because of the need to generate labels at large distances from jumps. 3.3 User Extensions Violated Assumption Architecture Instruction Class Fields values ARM Register pre-/post-indexed addressing modes are independent Base and index registers must differ PowerPC Load multiple instructions Address register must not be a target PowerPC Update instructions Base register must not equal target register Simple transforms x86 Scale factor in memory addressing Scale is encoded as a log SPARC Sethi argument must have 10 low zero bits ARM Certain addressing modes expect offset ï¿½ 4 Table 1: Exceptions that we have found to our encoding model. D E R I V E ’s hooks let clients easily extend its model to handle these cases. For fields that depend on each other, users annotate dependent registers in their specification, and supply a function that takes a list of symbolic register names and returns TRUE iff they are a legal combination. Users add missing transformations by providing a function that takes an immediate and returns the transformed value, and annotating immediates that use this encoding in the specification. Some instruction sets (such as the ARM) do not satisfy all of the assumptions we have described. In addition, incorrect assemblers can provide bad information to D E R I V E . We give the user mechanisms to address these problems: the user can inform D E R I V E of complex immediate encodings, tell it when register field values may depend on each other, and provide explicit field widths when necessary. One use of D E R I V E -generated specifications is to generate code emitters from them. We have written an emitter generator that processes instruction specifications and generates C procedures or macros that can emit instructions into a code buffer. Figure 3 shows the structure declaration for D E R I V E ’s output. Figure 4 shows a sample specification that D E R I V E generates for the MIPS break instruction, which causes a breakpoint. Each instruction specification is transformed into a function or macro whose arguments are an index into the code buffer and the registers, immediates, or labels that are operands for that instruction. The choice of macros allows the compiler to propagate constants if parameters, such as register values, are known at compile-time. The following example shows the macro generated for the x86 addl instruction, and how it is used: #define E_addl_rr_1(_code, rf, rt) do { \ register unsigned short _0 = (0xc001\ | ((((rf)) << 11))\ | ((((rt)) << 8)));\ *(unsigned short*)((char *)_code) = _0;\ _code = (void *)((char *)_code + 2);\ } while(0) /* emit "addl %ecx, %ebx" in code_buffer */ E_addl_rr_1(code_buffer, REGecx, REGebx); With simple heuristics, we are able to generate code automatically that in most cases is as efficient and readable as the code a human would write. There are two challenges in generating efficient emitter code. First, we try to keep the number of arithmetic and bit shift operations on the instruction’s operands small. Second, we try to minimize the number of stores to the code buffer. For architectures with constant instruction lengths, such as all RISC architectures, our generated emitters incur one memory write per instruction generated. Operands to an instruction are not always known when the instruction is generated. Dynamic code generators, for example, do not know the value of a forward-referenced label. Such a label must be patched later by a simple linker, once the actual value of the operand becomes known. D E R I V E allows instruction operands to be marked so that they are not used in the emitter macro. Instead, the emitter generator generates an additional macro that can be called to fill in the operand. D E R I V E clients can build their own linkers on top of this mechanism. Our emitter generator can emit extra debugging information. First, our emitter generator is able to generate emitters that check the validity of their arguments. This feature is useful to catch bugs as early as possible during dynamic code generation. In addition, the generator can also produce emitters that print a textual description of each instruction generated during dynamic code generation. The emitters are also useful as a means of testing D E R I V E . For each instruction, we generate the emitter and a test program that invokes it with a given subset of parameters. The instruction encodings generated by the emitter function are then compared to the output generated by the target assembler. This procedure allows us to test D E R I V E without actually running code on the target platform. D E R I V E ’s emitter generator can cross-compile between architectures whose endiannesses match. To demonstrate that our tools work, we have retargeted Kaffe’s [ 25 ] x86 JIT backend to use automatically generated emitters from just a subset of the x86 ISA. We reduced the number of lines in the backend description from 2,084 to 1,267. We also discovered that the original coders missed shorter instruction encodings in one case. Retargeting the JIT took approximately one day, which indicates that the emitter functions generated by D E R I V E are usable in real applications. D E R I V E -generated emitters can be used in several other ways to support dynamic code generation. For example, they can be used to support back end construction for general-purpose dynamic code generation systems such as vcode [ 8 ] and ccg [ 17 ] . These systems provide assembly-like interfaces to C for dynamic code generation, and need encoding information to actually generate code. D E R I V E could also be used to compute templates for application-specific systems such as DPF [ 7 ] . Templates can be specified in terms of symbolic instruction sequences, fed to D E R I V E to get the corresponding binary encoders, and then reincorporated into the system. 5 Conclusions The D E R I V E system reverse-engineers instruction encodings from the system assembler. Users need only give assembly-level information about the instructions for which they want encodings, and not low-level information about bitfield layout. D E R I V E successfully reverse-engineers instruction encodings on the SPARC, MIPS, Alpha, ARM, PowerPC, and x86. In the last case, it handles variable-sized instructions, large instructions (16 bytes), multiple instruction encodings determined by operand size, and other CISC features. As a proof of its utility, we have built a code emitter generator on top of D E R I V E . We plan to extend D E R I V E ’s techniques to reverse-engineer object code file formats, including debugging and linkage information. Such information will enable us to build a set of reverse-engineered tools, including versions of ATOM [ 21 ] , dynamic linking libraries [ 11 ] , object-level sandboxers [ 23 ] , executable optimizers, and linkers. Builders of such tools are plagued by the need to repeatedly reimplement functionality contained in existing software. For some systems, it is too expensive to call existing programs: dynamic code generation systems cannot afford the time to call an assembler. In other cases, the software has an inappropriate form and must be rewritten from scratch. For example, one common “trick” that commercial companies use to discourage third-party vendors is to have proprietary symbol table layouts, which change on every software release [ 16 ] . The cost of manually reverse-engineering these formats has forced some implementors to avoid object-level modifications, in spite of the strong advantages for such an approach.
