title: Building Java ME Apps with Modern Tooling
body:
Java ME (Micro Edition, also referred to as J2ME) is a platform for running Java applications on small resource constrained devices, such as feature phones from before the iPhone era. It is largely considered a dead platform with the advent of smartphones, and modern feature phones such as KaiOS use web technologies instead for their apps.
However it is likely that you or someone you know have one of these old phones lying around, and you may be interested in how you can make Java apps that will run on it. This post goes through how to build a simple Java ME app solely with modern tooling in a modern environment, without needing anything from the old Sun Java ME SDKs.
The instructions in this blog post assume a Linux-y terminal environment, but you could also follow along with Git Bash or a similar environment on Windows.
Here is a simple Hello World MIDlet that we will use. It will show a simple form using the LCDUI API with the text âHello World!â:
We will compile this with javac , but we first need the stub JARs from MicroEmulator available in the lib directory. Extract cldcapi11.jar and midpapi20.jar and put them in a lib directory next to the src directory.
The cldcapi11.jar provides the CLDC 1.1 API and midpapi20.jar provides the MIDP 2.0 API . MIDP 2.0 is circa 2002, and is probably what you want to use for widest compatibility, while it has some important features that MIDP 1.0 lacks.
Then we can compile the Java source file with the following command:
(To compile multiple .java files in src , you would put $(find src -name "*.java") instead.)
MIDlets need some metadata in the META-INF manifest file to work. Most of the fields are self-explanatory:
For the MIDlet-1 field, the format is a comma-separated list of three values: The human-readable name of the MIDlet, the path to the icon inside of the JAR, and the fully qualified class name of the entrypoint class. Since the above Java code specifies no package, it will be in the default package at the root of the JAR.
Save this to resources/META-INF/MANIFEST.MF , creating a resources/ directory to house assets to put in the final JAR. Also put a 16x16 PNG icon in resources/icon.png . Then letâs package everything together into a JAR:
Now we have a JAR file build/input.jar â¦ But we need to preverify it before it can be run on a Java ME device.
Preverification is a process required for the KVM (the minimal Java virtual machine used in Java ME) to ensure that the bytecode is valid. Traditionally this would be done by a preverify tool from the original Java ME SDK, but ProGuard supports doing the same thing and is more modern.
You can also use ProGuard to shrink, optimise and obfuscate your code to reduce the footprint of the resulting JAR, which is especially important for Java ME apps where the JAR size limit can be very strict. But for this example we disable all of that for now and just specify -microedition to do the preverification.
Now you have a app.jar file that can actually be run on a Java ME device or in an emulator. You can use MicroEmulator to run it, or something with more features like FreeJ2ME-plus , currently the best J2ME emulator for desktop platforms.
Now that you have gotten it running in an emulator it would be nice to get it running on the real hardware. The feature phone I had lying around thatâs the most functional is the Sony Ericsson S312, a budget feature phone from 2009. It even has a camera!
Java feature phones tend to have connectivity and storage mediums that are generally considered obsolete nowadays. My Sony Ericsson S312 has a proprietary charger cable with no USB on either end - supposedly you can use a special USB transfer cable, but that was a separate accessory that doesnât seem worthwhile to obtain. In addition to this, the physical external memory storage is some strange card format that is distinct from any standard kind of SD card (M2 memory stick, not to be confused with the M.2 connector).
Bluetooth ended up being the easiest way to transfer files to and from the phone. After connecting the phone to my computer and installing bluez-obex for OBEX, used for transferring files over Bluetooth, I was able to explore the files on the phone like I had plugged it in via USB and then copy over the JAR file.
Itâs quite slow - very slow in fact, but a simple app should only be a few kilobytes in size. Once transferred over, I was able to go into the file manager on my phone, find the JAR and then install it. After some time, it showed up in the list of games.
After getting the Hello World working, I expanded upon it a bit to draw images to the screen. I used the same image that was used for the app icon, a raccoon pixel art. Then I made them bounce across the screen. Just something simple to get the satisfaction of seeing something moving on the screen.
This code and the final build.sh script to build a functioning JAR of it can be found on GitHub for reference. One thing you might need to customise is the path to where OpenJDK 8 is installed - I just hardcoded it to where I have it on my system at the top of the buildscript:
Iâd also like to end with a section of the limitations of the Java ME platform, of which there are many important ones to be aware of.
First of all, you will be writing Java 1.3 code. While the basic language features are the same, it is very limited compared to modern Java or even something like Java 8. In addition to this, the API that MIDP 2.0 provides is very limited compared to the Java SE API when it comes to classes in the standard library. A full reference of all the classes you have available is available in the old MIDP 2.0 API documentation .
Different phone manufacturers have different implementations of the Java ME platform, and some of them implement their own APIs on top of the standard ones. Developers back in the day would typically ship several different versions of their app for Nokia, Sony Ericsson and generic MIDP 2.0 baselines to make use of these additional features. While MIDP 2.0 is the common denominator, you may also find that there are some discrepancies between different phone manufacturers. A lot of work was made for Android to not make the same mistake, despite its own diverse ecosystem of devices.
As for the specs of the phones you are targetingâ¦ Well, they are very limited. One thing to note is that many older feature phones have no hardware accelerated FPU - while the float type is available in Java, it will be emulated in software and be very slow on devices without a FPU. Generally you would always want to use fixed point math when doing heavier calculations.
As the size of your app will also be constrained, general advise for size optimisation applies. You can use ProGuard to shrink your code, PNG optimisers to reduce the size of your assets, and try to minimise the amount of separate classes and image files you have to take the most advantage from the per-file compression of JAR files. Your Java code will likely end up looking the complete opposite of what is considered clean code by Java OOP standards, but thatâs okay.
You can discuss the blog post in this forum thread on the Voxelmanip Forums.
All blog posts are written by a human who would also appreciate a donation if you got some value out of this piece of writing.

title: Businessman in court over alleged World Cup visa fraud
body: A businessman has appeared before an Adenta Circuit Court for allegedly defrauding a colleague of US$3,000 and GH¢20,600. Kwaku Duah allegedly collected the money and other items from the complainant under the pretext of securing United States and Canadian visas for him to attend the 2026 FIFA World Cup. Charged with defrauding by false pretences, Duah pleaded not guilty. The court, presided over by Mrs Angela Attachie, admitted him to bail in the sum of GH¢60,000 with two sureties, one to be justified with landed property. It also ordered him to deposit his passport with the court registry. The court adjourned the case to February 17, 2027. Chief Inspector Maxwell Lanyo led the prosecution. The facts presented to the court were that the complainant, whose name was withheld, was a businessman residing at Adenta, while Duah lived at East Legon Hills. In March 2026, one John Teiko introduced Duah to the complainant as a friend who needed spare parts for his tipper truck. The complainant supplied the parts, and the complainant made payment. The prosecution said that after the transaction, Duah told the complainant that a top official of the National Sports Authority (NSA) had introduced his personal assistant, identified as Gyamfi, to help his clients secure US and Canadian visas to attend the 2026 FIFA World Cup. Duah allegedly told the complainant that each participant had to pay US$4,500, which he described as the NSA’s official fee. The complainant said he could raise only US$3,000, but Duah insisted that US$4,500 was required. Prosecution said Duah later proposed an alternative arrangement: the complainant would supply four brake drums and four 22.5R tyres for his tipper truck, valued at GH¢18,300, in addition to paying a visa fee of GH¢2,300. The complainant allegedly supplied the items and paid GH¢2,300 and US$3,000. The prosecution said the complainant became concerned when the visa interview was delayed and questioned Duah, who allegedly took offence and stopped answering his calls. The complainant subsequently reported the matter to the Adenta Police. Investigations allegedly established that Duah had made a false representation, as he did not know anyone at the NSA and no visa interview had been scheduled for the complainant. The court heard that Duah retrieved the complainant’s passport upon his arrest.

title: Ebola: Day pandemic killed an Aláàfin, By Festus Adedayo
body:
Our forefathers warned against this posture of dangerous complacency. In both the careless handling of firearms and the timid caressing of venomous reptiles, they frowned at such folly in two graphic proverbs, warning that: “A kì í fi ọwọ tẹtẹrẹ mú ìbọn; a kì í fi ọwọ rọrọ mú ejo” – you do not handle a gun carelessly, nor do you grasp a snake with soft, hesitant hands.
History provides a stern warning about what happens when public health complacency meets administrative lethargy. Between 1827 and 1831, in Ọyọ-Ilé, the majestic capital of the Old Oyo Empire, the people tried to ignore the subtle signs of danger. But as the Yoruba say, bullets eventually escaped, the gun boomed, and the snake’s bite led to documented catastrophe.
A strange, debilitating disease called Pẹhẹ had suddenly sprouted from nowhere. It was an infectious, highly contagious disease that waged a deadly, relentless war on the human respiratory system. Pẹhẹ ravaged the capital of the Empire, a tragic chapter meticulously recorded by the legendary historian Samuel Johnson on page 254 of his monumental work, History of the Yoruba .
Because it is only the beginning of a war that human beings can anticipate and never its ultimate ending, by 1831, Pẹhẹ had mutated from a localized health scare into an uncontrollable pestilence. In that fatal year, it breached the sacred palace walls and took away the highly revered supreme monarch of the Empire, Aláàfin Májòótú. When Májòótú succumbed to the breath-stealing plague, Aláàfin Amodo ascended a throne already sitting atop a crumbling nation.
The tragic death of Aláàfin Májòótú’s in the hands of an ordinary pandemic stands as an eternal reminder that not even the most sacred grove or exalted royal court is spared when pestilence wages war. Plagues are fiercely democratic; they respect neither crown nor stool.
This tragic historical truth brings to mind one of my favorite musical lines by Kelani Yesufu, the legendary Egba-born Yoruba Sakara music singer and social poet. It was in a masterwork track that the bard titled “Ikú ò Mo Olówó ”. It is a profound philosophical treatise asserting that death is no respecter of wealth, crown, or social status.
Yesufu composed the track as a grieving tribute to Shittu Shitta Alabi, his master lead drummer, who suddenly slumped and died on stage at Sokenu Village, Abeokuta, during a live performance in 1972. In a haunting symbol of lifelong devotion to craft, Alabi passed into eternity with his Sakara drum still clutched tightly in his lifeless hands.
Kelani Yesufu’s musical prowess and cultural prominence reached its zenith during the mid-to-late 20th century. Standing tall alongside contemporaries like S. Aka (Sanusi Ayinde Aka, Baba Wahidi, a.k.a. Omo Lawale), the legendary Sakara genre lord Yusuff Olatunji, Haruna Ishola, and Lefty Salami, Yesufu combined traditional Yoruba instrumentation, specifically the solemn, melancholic goje violin and rhythmic Sakara hand drums, to attack public decay and social vices.
Kelani became renowned as an against-the-grain musician due to his unorthodox, cutting poetry. He deployed his storytelling craft in fighting well-known social crusades, manifested in tracks like “ Emu Ògùrò” (where he mercilessly attacked reckless drunkenness) and “April Fool ,” another of his sharp, satirical social commentaries.
Yesufu was the courageous bard who first dared to break the ancient cultural taboo surrounding venereal diseases with his famous track “À tòsí” (Gonorrhea). Before Yesufu’s bold intervention, Yoruba society was conditioned to mask the disease under the deceptive, romanticised label À rùn Gbajúmò — an infection reserved for notables and men of means. In his track, Yesufu urged society to face hard epidemiological facts, dismantling the hypocritical contradictions inherent in romanticising a disgraceful affliction simply because it affected the elite.
While lamenting the death of his master drummer in a grief-encrusted voice, Kelani sermonized on the absolute inevitability and impartiality of death. The track eventually became a sacred document frequently cited by cultural historians, a poignant testament to the profound, lifelong spiritual bond developed between traditional Yoruba vocalists and their lead drummers. It was that exact same symbiotic bond that existed between Yusuff Olatunji and his lead drummer, Kasumu Ishola Sanni; between Haruna Ishola and Raufu Ojubanire; between Lefty Salami and Nosiru Akanmu; and between the fiery Ayinla Omowura and Adewole Alao, famously known as Onílù Olà , the drummer of fortune. Plagues, like death itself, sever these human bonds without mercy.
In Ọyọ-Ilé, Pẹhẹ claimed the lives of thousands of citizens in rapid succession. The pestilence was reported to be the devastating climax of a four-year cycle of recurrent epidemic outbreaks in the empire’s capital. It provoked a historic visit to Ọyọ-Ilé in 1827 by the famous Cornish explorer, Richard Lander. Lander had arrived in the Empire’s capital riding on the fame of his association with solving the mystery of the course and outlet of the River Niger, alongside the Scottish explorer Hugh Clapperton. After Clapperton and other members of the expedition succumbed to tropical illnesses, Lander was commissioned by the British government to return, sailing with his brother from Badagry to Bussa by canoe, where they were eventually captured and ransomed.
When Lander arrived at Ọyọ-Ilé, he recorded his astonishment at the crude yet organised quarantine structures implemented by the empire’s authorities. The traditional council had taken victims of Pẹhẹ to an isolation centre, established inside a dense forest roughly half a mile outside the city walls. In his journal, Lander observed that the sick were placed systematically “underneath the branches of trees…”
The strict customary law of the empire dictated that the next of kin of Pẹhẹ victims were solely responsible for bringing food and water to the perimeter of the forest isolation grounds.
However, this outbreak severely crippled the empire because it arrived alongside a devastating combination of external and internal crises. A brutal drought had covertly walked into Ọyọ-Ilé that same year. Consequently, the metropolis suffered the double agony of severe famine and political instability, which had commenced a decade earlier due to internal rivalries. The Pẹhẹ pandemic was like rubbing coarse salt into an open, bleeding wound. Historical descriptions of Pẹhẹ paint it as a highly contagious respiratory illness that caused swift, terrifying fatalities across all social strata. Aláàfin Májòótú and Ọyọ-Ilé’s ancient political structures were completely overwhelmed.
In his notes, Lander helped preserve the oral memory of this tragedy. He recorded that the combination of acute famine and political turmoil severely worsened the plight of those confined to the forest isolation center. Because the victims were largely drawn from poor backgrounds, many ended up dying of sheer starvation rather than the viral load of Pẹhẹ itself.
It was recorded that although Pẹhẹ directly killed thousands in 1831, Ọyọ-Ilé was already suffocating from the loss of more than 100,000 of its inhabitants to famine, civil strife, and disease combined. This massive health disaster shattered Old Oyo’s demographic foundation and completely paralysed its military leadership. It dramatically accelerated the empire’s fall to Fulani invasions and internal rebellions, culminating in the total evacuation and permanent abandonment of Ọyọ-Ilé as the capital between 1835 and 1836. Plagues do not merely kill bodies; if mishandled, they topple empires.
If pre-colonial Nigeria was naive in curtailing the spread of infectious pathogens, centuries later, it is outright criminal for modern authorities to follow suit. Long before modern medicine, diseases like chickenpox and smallpox attacked the rich and the poor with equal, indiscriminate fury.
In response to their inability to comprehend or halt the ravages of smallpox, the ancient Yoruba deified the disease out of sheer terror. Smallpox was elevated to the pantheon of sacred deities as Ṣọnpọnná. Because of the mysterious way it struck from nowhere, the deity was given fearful, exalted appellations. One was Olóde, “The Owner of the Outside” or “Lord of the Open Space,” referencing how the contagion traveled invisibly through open air and wind; Ọbalúayé “The King Who is Lord of the World”; and Babalúayé “The Father Who is the Lord of the Earth.”
Till this day in ancient Ilé-Ifẹ, the annual Ìtàpá festival is celebrated to memorialise those ancient pox outbreaks. When you observe the intricate lesions of white chalk painted across the bodies of Ọbàtálá priests during the sacred festival, you are looking at a living artistic ritual depicting the skin pustules suffered by their ancestors.
Ṣọnpọnná priests were both deeply revered and terrifyingly feared as specialist medical practitioners. They presided over the containment of pox outbreaks, performing ritual sacrifices, administering botanical variolation (inoculation), caring for the afflicted, and executing strict, solitary burials for those killed by the disease to prevent further contamination.
Until its global eradication in the 20th century, no disease struck deeper dread into the Yoruba psyche than smallpox, owing to its high transmission rate, swift lethality, and unpredictable seasonality. The disease routinely peaked between January and February, the dry, dusty harmattan months, proving itself to be an opportunistic killer that exploited seasonal vulnerability.
Similarly, cholera has been an explosive, killer epidemic in Nigeria’s history. It struck water supplies and wiped out entire communities overnight. But no historical outbreak matched the terrifying speed of the 1918 Influenza Pandemic.
Originating in March 1918 in Kansas, USA, and carried across oceans by returning World War I troops, the “Spanish Flu” quickly earned the grim distinction of killing more people than any other pandemic in human history. It became the first truly nationwide pandemic to sweep through Nigeria, imported directly by maritime passengers and crew arriving at coastal ports.
Lagos was the epicentre of the tragedy. Public historian Oludamola Adebowale notes that passengers who contracted the virus in Accra, Gold Coast (modern Ghana), boarded ships bound for Lagos and seeded the contagion upon arrival. The spread was so violent that within the first two months, maritime quarantines completely collapsed. Lagos lost 1.5 per cent of its entire population of 81,941 people in a matter of weeks. Out of a national population estimated at 18 million in 1918, over 500,000 Nigerians died within six months, with between 50 per cent and 80 per cent of the entire population contracting the virus.
From Lagos, the flu followed trade routes like wildfire. In 1918 October, Abeokuta was to get its first index patient. Ibadan got its on October 5, 1918 and gradually, Oyo, Ilorin, Minna, Bida, Jebba, Zaria, Kano, and Bauchi got theirs. Calabar and Onitsha got theirs on October 14, 1918 while it was spread farther by ships through Forcados port to Warri and Asaba, Port Harcourt and Bonny. Traveling through passengers on River Niger, the Spanish flu pandemic spread to Lokoja, Sokoto, Maiduguri, as well as to other parts of the Northern Nigeria, so much that, by December 1918, the whole of the country had completely bowed to the Spanish flu.
Traveling via passengers along the River Niger, the Spanish flu penetrated Lokoja, Sokoto, and Maiduguri. By December 1918, the entire geographic entity of Nigeria had completely bowed to the devastating flu. With this mountain of historical tragedy, and our recent, painful experience during COVID-19, Nigeria’s current dilly-dallying on the reported Abuja Ebola case is utterly incomprehensible.
Ebola is not an abstract threat. Since its discovery in September 1976 along the Ebola River in Yambuku, (in the Democratic Republic of Congo, then Zaire) where it claimed its first victim, a local school headmaster named Mabalo Lokela, the virus has exhibited one of the highest case-fatality rates known to science. Historically, regional outbreaks in the DRC have claimed 4,690 lives out of 9,742 confirmed cases, representing a terrifying crude case fatality rate (CFR) of roughly 48 per cent.
Nigeria should know better because we have faced this monster before. In 2014, Nigeria admirably fought and won a decisive war against Ebola. When Patrick Sawyer, an index patient from Liberia, arrived at First Consultants Medical Centre in Lagos, the nation stood on the precipice of unimaginable catastrophe. It took the extraordinary courage of Dr Stella Ameyo Adadevoh, the timeless amazon who sacrificed her life so millions might live, alongside her medical director, Dr Benjamin Ohiaeri, and their heroic team, to halt the chain of transmission.
In a modern parallel to the strict isolation protocols of Ọyọ-Ilé two centuries prior, Dr Adadevoh and Dr Ohiaeri stood firm against intense diplomatic pressure from Liberian officials who demanded that Sawyer be discharged to attend an international conference in Calabar. Instead, they held him in a makeshift containment unit, locked down their hospital, and immediately alerted health authorities. Dr Adadevoh paid the ultimate price, contracting the virus and passing away on 19 August, 2014, alongside noble colleagues. But her brave stand kept Nigeria’s total casualty count to just 20 cases and eight deaths — a miraculous feat praised globally.
Look at how other nations manage this threat today. Consider Rwanda. Despite its proximity to the DRC and despite the busy border city of Gisenyi, sitting directly adjacent to DRC’s Lake Kivu region, Rwanda has consistently maintained zero recorded Ebola cases during major regional surges. This is not by luck; it is by design. The Rwandan Ministry of Health and the Rwanda Biomedical Center maintain active, continuous border screening, rigorous contact tracing protocols, and specialised containment facilities in sites like Rusizi, Rubavu, and Kigali. They understand that public health requires constant vigilance, not reactive panic.
Meanwhile, in Nigeria, when reports of a new Ebola threat surfaced, the government reacted with its typical bureaucratic fanfare: on 9 June, a ₦10 billion emergency intervention fund was approved, and a Presidential Task Force on Ebola Virus Disease Preparedness was constituted under the chairmanship of the Chief of Staff to the President. Months later, as reports of new cases trickle into the Federal Capital Territory, Nigerians are rightly asking: Where is the readiness? What tangible containment infrastructure has been built? How has the ₦10 billion emergency allocation been utilised?
We cannot afford to treat a deadly pathogen with administrative levity or political rhetoric. As our ancestors warned us through the sacred memory of Aláàfin Májòótú, when a government fails to cut the sapling of an epidemic early, it will eventually grow into an uncontainable beast that demands the ultimate sacrifice from the nation. Nigeria must wake up, stop caressing the nozzle of the rifle, put down the head of the rattlesnake, and act before history repeats its grim legacy once more.
Festus Adedayo is an Ibadan-based journalist.

title: Grok releases the first seven minutes of its AI-generated ‘Odyssey’
body:
Three months after Elon Musk declared that Grok would release a full-length, “historically accurate” movie version of “The Odyssey,” Grok has published a whole seven minutes, which the company is now calling “Episode 1 of our Odyssey series.”
Musk had previously lashed out at Christopher Nolan’s version of “The Odyssey” because Nolan cast nonwhite and transgender actors. And Nolan is, in many ways, a perfect foil for Musk — while SpaceX and Tesla CEO hypes up data centers in space and posts an unending stream of AI-generated content, Nolan has described himself as “a techno-skeptic ” and said that before AI, he’d never seen a technology “so completely rejected by the public.”
And while Nolan’s version of “The Odyssey” certainly used plenty of visual effects, it’s primarily a feat of practical filmmaking , with a shoot spanning six countries and a cast and crew of thousands. After its release in July, the film became an extraordinary box office success , selling out Imax screenings for months and becoming the likely front-runner at the next Academy Awards .
As for the Grok version of “The Odyssey” (created in collaboration with Wonder Studios and director Dev Walker), well, you can watch for yourself.
Watch Episode 1 of our Odyssey series made with Grok Imagine. Let us know in the comments if you'd like a full breakdown of how it was done! Creative collaboration with @WonderStudiosX and director Dev Walker @glumlot_ pic.twitter.com/xpgpkqSCpq
I’ll admit it’s not as spectacularly ugly as I’d expected, and certainly more impressive than other videos that Musk has posted recently. If I didn’t know better, there were moments when I might have thought these were real actors sailing across a real sea. And while I can’t speak to Grok’s historical accuracy, it does seem that some fudging was necessary, since no one’s speaking in ancient Greek. But hey, all the characters come in a Musk-approved skin color, while the narrator uses a British accent that will sound familiar to anyone who’s played a fantasy video game or watched a generic Hollywood epic from the past 25 years.
What the footage really lacks is any sense of artistry, inspiration, or human interest. The backstory — delivered via the aforementioned voiceover — seems to go on forever, finally giving way to one bearded face after another, each shouting stilted lines that make Nolan’s questionable dialogue (“Our age of bronze is collapsing!”) sound like Shakespeare.
While a few individual shots might provide a reasonable simulacrum of reality, as a whole, the clip feels completely airless, offering viewers no sense of momentum, no reason to care about anyone or anything on-screen. And where I had no trouble paying attention for the nearly three hours of Nolan’s “Odyssey,” I was listlessly checking how much time I had left before the Grok version was even halfway through. If it was a video game cutscene, I would have hit the “skip” button.
It’s hard to imagine being interested in another seven minutes of this, much less a full movie’s worth.

title: Fire in residential building in Kharkiv kills one person and injures five others
body:
The State Emergency Service of Kharkiv region reported this on Telegram , according to Ukrinform.
It is noted that on October 25 at 6:06 p.m., the emergency number “101” received a report of a fire in a six-story residential building in the Industrial District of Kharkiv .
Upon the arrival of fire and rescue units, apartments on the 5th floor of the building were on fire, and the fire covered an area of 20 square meters.
Due to heavy smoke, firefighters had to rescue people from the smoke-filled stairwell. “In total, we managed to rescue eight residents of the building. The cause of the fire is under investigation,” the rescue workers said.
They added that 30 of their personnel and eight pieces of equipment from the State Emergency Service were working at the scene.
As previously reported, four people were injured in Kharkiv as a result of an enemy attack on a shopping center and a business, three of whom were rescue workers.

title: EDGE, Morocco signs drone weapons contract, production MoU
body: EDGE Group signed a contract to supply guided weapons to the Royal Moroccan Air Force on Friday, 9 October 2026, at the Marrakech Air Show. The company also signed a separate agreement to explore the local production of weapons in Morocco. The Abu Dhabi-based defence group concluded both agreements with Morocco’s Administration of National Defence (ADN), the body responsible for procurement for the Royal Armed Forces. The weapons contract covers two systems: the DESERT STING 16 (DS-16), a guided glide bomb, and the THUNDER P-31, a precision-guidance kit designed for the MK 81 general-purpose bomb. Both systems are manufactured by HALCON, an EDGE subsidiary. The agreement extends beyond a straightforward purchase. EDGE will also undertake integration work across Morocco’s fleet of unmanned combat aerial vehicles (UCAVs), including the aircraft modifications and software required to enable Moroccan drones to carry and deploy the munitions. Saif Al Dahbashi, EDGE’s President of Missiles & Weapons, said the contract reflects the air force’s requirements. Each system comes with “assured supply and long-term sustainment,” he said, describing the agreement as a foundation for “an enduring relationship” with Morocco. The two weapons serve distinct roles. The DS-16 weighs 23 kg, including a 12 kg warhead, and can strike targets up to 15 km away when released from an altitude of 30,000 feet. It is a complete glide weapon rather than an add-on kit. The THUNDER P-31 operates differently: it converts an existing MK 81 bomb into a precision weapon by adding a guidance kit. This extends its range to 10 km when launched from drones and up to 20 km from faster, higher-flying aircraft. Both systems rely on GNSS-assisted inertial navigation, which combines satellite positioning with onboard sensors, and can be equipped with an optional semi-active laser seeker for increased accuracy. The pairing provides Moroccan drones with two distinct strike profiles: a lighter glide weapon for shorter-range precision operations and a modified general-purpose bomb for longer-range stand-off engagements. EDGE has prior experience integrating the DS-16 onto unmanned platforms. In January 2024, the company announced a programme to integrate the weapon onto the Bayraktar TB2, a drone already operated by Morocco, with further aircraft integrations planned thereafter. The second agreement signed on Friday points in a different direction: manufacturing weapons in Morocco rather than importing them. The memorandum of understanding (MoU) tasks EDGE and the ADN with identifying opportunities for local production of small arms and aeronautical engines. This work would be conducted through partnerships with Moroccan companies rather than by EDGE alone. Two EDGE business units are likely to play a central role in this effort. CARACAL designs and manufactures high-performance small arms and small-calibre ammunition. POWERTECH develops aero engines and propulsion systems for unmanned platforms. Both are part of EDGE’s wider manufacturing network in the UAE, which the group has been extending to partner countries seeking to develop their own defence industries. Hamad Al Marar, EDGE’s Managing Director and CEO, presented the MoU as part of this broader approach. “Morocco is a key partner for EDGE in Africa, and this MoU puts our partnership-first approach into practice,” he said, describing a model based on “knowledge exchange, local production, and technology transfer.” He added that working with Moroccan companies on firearms and aero engines would help build “an industrial backbone” for the kingdom’s defence requirements. Friday’s signings took place during EDGE’s second appearance at the Marrakech Air Show, where the company also displayed surveillance, counter-drone, navigation-protection and loitering-munition products. EDGE first exhibited at the show in 2024. The contract is consistent with EDGE’s broader expansion across Africa . The company is currently delivering a €1 billion naval modernisation programme in Angola, which includes three Combattante corvettes and six naval unmanned helicopters. In 2025, it also signed a letter of intent with Angola’s interior ministry for a border-security programme. Further south, EDGE is reportedly in advanced discussions concerning a $300 million equipment deal with Nigeria , focused on the army’s ground forces and counter-terrorism units. Morocco’s fighter procurement has progressed unevenly in recent years. In 2022, the UAE offered Rabat its entire fleet of Mirage 2000 jets , but a planned transfer of 30 Mirage 2000-9 aircraft was postponed this year. The decision was linked to regional instability, which has prompted the UAE to retain more of its combat aircraft in service. Arming the drone fleet instead gives Morocco a faster route to precision-strike capability while the fighter transfer remains unresolved. For the Royal Moroccan Air Force, the agreement addresses a capability gap rather than establishing an entirely new capability. Morocco has operated armed drones for several years, but integrating a two-tier weapons set—a lighter glide bomb and a longer-range guided kit—broadens the range of targets its UCAVs can engage without requiring new airframes. The production MoU represents a longer-term commitment: if it leads to manufacturing agreements, it would mark a shift from purchasing finished weapons to producing components of Morocco’s own defence supply chain.

title: Election Day picks, programs, and discounts
body: If you want to make the most of your day off on Election Day on October 27 and catch a movie or head for the great outdoors, there are some deals to sweeten these options, and some special programming.One sweet deal comes from Cinema City, which is offering the chance to super-size some refreshments – including popcorn, Kinder Bueno snacks, Ben & Jerry's ice cream – as well as Crazy Jumper dolls sold in theaters, for a flat NIS 27 fee.Planet is offering tickets purchased at the theater for NIS 27, except for IMAX, 4DX, and ScreenX showings.The Jerusalem Cinematheque features the top three Israeli movies in its audience poll in honor of its 50th anniversary.These include a serious, animated documentary about the First Lebanon War from the point of view of IDF soldiers – Ari Folman's Waltz with Bashir; and two comedies about army life – Assi Dayan's Halfon Hill Doesn't Answer and Talya Lavie's Zero Motivation. Tickets are just NIS 15 and are free for Jerusalem Cinematheque members.Israel Nature and Parks Authority offers outdoor tours, activities For those who want to enjoy a day in some of the national parks, the Israel Nature and Parks Authority is offering guided tours, family activities, and evening attractions at parks and nature reserves around the country.At 15 sites, visitors can play “Mysteries in Time,” an interactive game that uses a WhatsApp bot to guide participants through riddles while introducing them to the sites' history.In the North, Kochav Hayarden National Park will offer bird migration tours, kite-making and flying workshops, and family activities. At Ein Afek Nature Reserve, visitors can explore the wetlands, join guided tours, and enjoy children's crafts and face painting. An on-site ballot box will let them vote for their favorite spot in the reserve.Beit She'an National Park's “She'an Nights” experience will illuminate the ancient city through audiovisual displays, with visits to the bathhouse, Temple of Dionysus, and Roman theater. Hamat Tiberias National Park will stay open late for evening bathing in its thermal pools, along with access to its ancient synagogue, an audiovisual presentation, and a reflexology path.Special tours at the Gamla Nature Reserve will focus on its vulture colony and conservation efforts, while Beit She'arim will offer tours of its burial caves, inscriptions, and reliefs.At Beit Guvrin, couples and families can order picnic packages in advance for collection at the visitor service center. Farther south, visitors can try the cliffside Masada Challenge route or attend the evening “Masada: From Sunset to Sunrise” multimedia show on the mountain's western side.The authority advises visitors to check weather and trail conditions, bring sufficient water, and follow marked routes. Details about activities, reservations, and any additional charges are available at www.parks.org.il.Also, ANU – Museum of the Jewish People will remain open on Election Day, offering permanent exhibits alongside interactive family activities like the Heroes gallery and the “Guardians of the Stories” quest.Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

title: Serbia's Vucic concedes defeat to student led movement in parliamentary election
body: Serbia's Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat to the student-led protest movement in parliamentary elections on Sunday."We still do not have final results, on the basis of a sample ... it is clear that we have lost these elections, the Student List has won, they will have between 135 and 140 seats and we will have 105, no one else has entered parliament," Vucic said.The snap elections, called by Vucic in September, came after almost two years of student-led demonstrations against perceived corruption and creeping authoritarianism triggered by the deaths of 16 people when a train station canopy collapsed in the city of Novi Sad in 2024.The students have since gained widespread support to become the greatest threat to Vucic since he first became prime minister in 2014 and then president in 2017.Serbia saw record-breaking voter turnoutLong lines snaked from polling stations in cities and towns across the country, and even Vucic waited for nearly two hours to vote. Pollsters and monitors CeSID and Ipsos put turnout at 67.6% by 7 p.m., the highest since the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1992.A student victory would is a profound political shift in the Balkan country of some 6 million people, reminiscent of the defeat of Hungary's Viktor Orban in April. It could also offer a blueprint for other student movements across Europe, which have taken to the streets in recent weeks to protest, in some cases violently, against poor education standards and a lack of prospects."(The turnout) did not surprise me because there was a large and strong mass that has formed throughout the past two years," said voter Katarina Petrovic.Opinion polls predict tight raceVucic has pledged higher pensions and public sector salaries, and investment in state healthcare. Internationally, he has sought closer ties with China, a major investor, and remained close to Russia, Serbia's traditional ally and principal supplier of natural gas. At the same time, he still says he wants to join the European Union, Serbia's largest trading partner, but the bloc has become increasingly frustrated with a lack of reform."I voted for our children, our young people...our children deserve peace and work, only Vucic can bring that," said Hatidza, a Roma woman.The students' domestic agenda aims to root out graft and improve schooling, but they have been quieter on their international ambitions. Their list of 250 largely unknown candidates includes university professors, actors and farmers, and is led by cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, although it is not clear who would be prime minister should they win."I hope that today will pass in a democratic atmosphere, in peace, and that we will legitimately elect a new government in Serbia," Srdanovic said after casting his vote in Novi Sad early in the morning.After casting his vote, Vucic said he would respect the result."If we lose we will acknowledge the will of the electorate, if we win no one will take it (from us)," he said.Opinion polls ahead of the vote had predicted a tight race to win the 250 seat parliament. The head of the Election Commission, Vladimir Dimitrijevic, said voting had passed without incident, but police cordoned off the road leading to the state commission building. Monitoring bodies CeSID and CRTA pointed to incidents related to the electoral roll and secrecy of voting.Student protests increase pressure on VucicThe student-led street protests sparked by the station disaster quickly became the biggest in a generation, calling for Vucic to step down. Rights groups and activists say repression has worsened in the period since."For decades the people have been waiting for this time, something to bring hope that we can live freely and by the rules of democracy," said actor Jelena Stupljanin, 48, at a Belgrade polling station.Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) have repeatedly denied accusations of repression, corruption and spying on their opponents. He says the students are funded by foreign agents in Croatia and Montenegro, a charge the students dismiss."This has been one of the most difficult but the most emotional campaigns," Vucic told his supporters on Thursday. "We stood against those who wanted to destroy Serbia."

title: Northern Ashanti Mines seeks injunction to block government takeover of $110m mine investment
body: Northern Ashanti Mines Limited Company has filed an injunction application seeking to stop a government takeover of its Konongo concession, warning that about $110 million in committed expenditure is at risk. The application, filed at the Commercial Division of the High Court in Accra, seeks to restrain the Minerals Commission and the Minister for Lands and Natural Resources from taking possession of the mine or reallocating it to third parties. The company wants the restrictions to remain in place until the court determines its challenge to the termination of its mining lease. The Attorney-General is also named as a respondent. In a supporting affidavit, Administrative Manager Jonathan Adongo alleges that Minerals Commission officials, accompanied by military personnel, visited the mine on October 22, 2026. He says they ordered the company, its staff and workers to vacate the mine, offices and residential accommodation by midday that day. The company argues that any takeover before the court determines the legality of the lease termination would threaten its investment, equipment and operations. “The threatened military takeover is imminent, and I humbly pray this Honourable Court to hear this application with urgency,” Mr Adongo states. According to the affidavit, Northern Ashanti Mines is wholly Ghanaian-owned and was formerly known as Owere Mines Limited. It is redeveloping the historic Konongo Gold Mine in the Ashanti Region. The company says it renewed its lease on February 2, 2023, for 13 years, covering about 125 square kilometres. It maintains that Parliament ratified the renewed lease, which runs until February 1, 2036. It says it has committed capital and incurred expenditure exceeding US$83.34 million on the concession. It also recently secured a facility of more than US$30 million to develop a gold processing plant, which it describes as more than 50% complete. The affidavit puts its committed expenditure at about US$110 million and says the company employs approximately 422 people directly and indirectly. The dispute follows a termination notice dated April 30, 2026, issued by the Minerals Commission on behalf of the minister. The notice, attached to the application, states: “Your company failed to remedy and/or refused to remedy the breaches which were served within the statutory and regulatory timeframe.” Northern Ashanti Mines disputes that position. It says no notice of any breach was served and that it was given no opportunity to remedy alleged breaches or explain why its mineral rights should not be cancelled. The company says it received no response to a letter from its lawyers dated May 4 and a petition dated May 20 seeking a review and reversal of the decision. Its injunction application also seeks to prevent security deployments intended to enforce the termination and to stop the granting or transfer of mineral rights over the concession. The company argues that a forcible takeover could endanger staff and surrounding communities, damage equipment and destroy exploration records and geological data. It is asking the court to preserve its possession of the concession pending the final determination of its judicial review application.

title: Nanbeige Releases Nanbeige4.3-33B, a 33B Open Agentic Coding Model
body:
Nanbeige LLM Lab has released Nanbeige4.3-33B on Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 license. Nanbeige4.3-33B is a 33B dense language model built for agentic coding and office-style ‘cowork’ tasks. The lab sits inside the recruitment platform BOSS Zhipin . It also published Nanbeige4.3-33B-Base for custom post-training. The model supports a 524,288-token context window. In the lab’s own table, it leads 17 of 20 benchmarks against 3 open models near 30B. TL;DR Size: 33B parameters, dense (no MoE), 524,288-token (512K) context, BF16 weights. Runs on: Multi-GPU servers. The card’s SGLang and vLLM recipes use 4-way tensor parallelism. BF16 weights need about 66 GB (our arithmetic). 1 community quantization is listed. Performance: Leads 17 of 20 rows in Nanbeige’s own comparison against Qwen3.8-27B, Muse-Glimmer-30B and Gemma4-31B. Best: 80.9 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, versus 73.0 for Qwen3.8-27B. Worst: 23.8 on Terminal-Bench 4.0 (its lowest score). It also trails Qwen3.8-27B on SWE-Bench Pro, 60.3 vs 61.7. What is Nanbeige4.3-33B? Nanbeige4.3-33B is the flagship ‘teacher’ model of the Nanbeige4.3 series. The lab’s stated strategy is to build a strong teacher first. It then plans to distill agentic skills into smaller models, starting with Nanbeige4.3-3B. How is Nanbeige4.3-33B built? The config.json declares a standard LlamaForCausalLM architecture. There is no expert routing, so all 33B parameters run on every token. 52 layers, hidden size 7,168 56 query heads and 8 key-value heads (grouped-query attention), head dimension 128 FFN intermediate size 22,016, vocabulary of 166,912 tokens RoPE theta of 120,000,000 and 524,288 max positions The chat template exposes 3 controls. enable_thinking toggles reasoning and is on by default. preserve_thinking keeps reasoning from earlier turns. Nanbeige recommends it for multi-turn tool use and code agents. Passing tools enables tool calling, and an XML call format is recommended. How does Nanbeige4.3-33B perform on benchmarks? Nanbeige compared the model with Qwen3.8-27B, Muse-Glimmer-30B and Gemma4-31B. Every model ran at its highest thinking effort, with shared hyperparameters and harnesses. All scores in this section are self-reported. Agentic coding : It scores 80.9 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, against 73.0 for Qwen3.8-27B. DeepSWE shows the widest gap: 65.5 versus 42.5. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, it scores 23.8 while Gemma4-31B scores 0.0. Agentic cowork : It posts 54.2 on Automation Bench versus 38.3, and 44.8 on JobBench versus 34.5. On YC-bench, simulated earnings reach $1,025,437 versus $641,290. Reasoning : It reports 95.2 on AIME 2026 and 84.0 on AA-LCR. It loses 3 of 20 rows. Qwen3.8-27B leads SWE-Bench Pro (61.7 vs 60.3) and GDPval (86.4 vs 84.8). Gemma4-31B leads GPQA Diamond in Nanbeige’s table, 91.3 vs 89.5. The Base model beats Gemma4-31B-Base on all 8 reported tasks. Examples include MMLU-Pro (66.9 vs 59.3) and GPQA (62.0 vs 41.5). Back

The model card provides Transformers, SGLang and vLLM recipes. Its server examples use 4-way tensor parallelism with Qwen3 reasoning and tool-call parsers. Recommended agent settings are temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95 and 65,536 max new tokens. Reasoning and chat use temperature 0.6 and 262,144 max new tokens.
