title: Musk says SpaceX restricted Ukraine’s Starlink connection as service restored
body: Elon Musk said SpaceX restricted Ukraine’s Starlink internet service after Ukrainian officials said connectivity issues appeared to be resolved. The tech billionaire accused Ukraine of violating its terms of service by using it for military activity, but denied responsibility for a simultaneous issue with its US-run, military-grade counterpart, Starshield. Kyiv has not officially commented on Musk’s latest claim, but Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said his post was “very strange”. Musk had earlier denied deliberately throttling Ukraine’s connection, which it says hampered its ability to conduct defensive operations for more than a week. The issue first emerged last week during a broader row between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure. Musk’s latest comments, and the service’s apparent restoration, came after US President Donald Trump said he had told the Tesla and X owner to “put it back”, after repeatedly denying he had instructed him to limit the service. “Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be,” Musk wrote on X on Saturday. “Ukraine[‘s] military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week.” He went on to say SpaceX had “done more to defend Ukraine than any private company on Earth” and reiterated that Starshield was a different system controlled by the US government, adding, “What they decide to do is up to them.” He added later: “[Starlink] can be used for infrastructure that is military, but it cannot be used for unequivocally offensive strikes that make it fair game to be struck back.” Reacting to Musk’s post, Beskrestnov said drones operating via Starlink in Ukraine had a speed restriction of 70-90km/h (43-56 mph) and did not work on Russian territory. “Therefore, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes and medium-range strikes,” he wrote on Telegram. “It is very strange that Elon Musk is not aware of Starlink restrictions in Ukraine.” Ukraine’s defence ministry did not immediately comment. Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, depending on the communications needed; both run on networks of low Earth orbit satellites launched by SpaceX. Starlink lets military units coordinate, particularly in remote areas on the battlefield, while Starshield lets Ukrainian drone operators see targets in real time and operate interceptor drones. Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles or drones deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work. Ukraine’s Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said earlier on Saturday that the military was now recording a “stable connection”, with drones now able to reach speeds in excess of 400km/h. Kyiv previously said the connection would cut out above 161km/h. “The speeds are now where they need to be,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on Telegram. Musk did not explain in his post why SpaceX changed its service last week, even though Ukraine’s extensive use of Starlink had been known for several years. The connection issues coincided with a tense diplomatic standoff between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia. Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow’s war effort, have pushed global prices higher. While the attacks have affected global fuel prices, this year’s rises have mainly been due to the Iran war . Faced with midterm elections next month and domestic displeasure with rising fuel prices, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal with Moscow – criticised by European allies as funding Russia’s war machine – to supply Russian diesel to the US and the global market. Zelensky initially agreed to cease strikes targeting Russian oil facilities on the proviso that Moscow cease striking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, before restarting the strikes after several instances of Russia disregarding this. The Ukrainian leader said that, as well as seemingly limiting Starlink capability in Ukraine, the US had also threatened to withdraw intelligence sharing if the strikes did not stop, something Trump also denied. Fighting and aerial attacks continued to be exchanged between Russia and Ukraine overnight. Ukraine’s emergency services said three people were killed and 15 others injured, including an 11-year-old girl, in attacks on the Dnipropetrovsk region, in the southeast. Another six people were injured when a Russian drone struck an apartment block in the central city of Vinnytsia, it said. The Russian defence ministry said on Sunday that it had struck a cargo vessel it claimed was being used to supply the Ukrainian army while it was en route to the Black Sea port of Chornomorsk overnight. It also said Russian forces hit a logistics centre, a distribution centre and a logistics terminal in the Ukrainian city of Kharkiv. Ukraine’s defence ministry earlier said it struck a facility in the Russian city of Oryol run by a sanctioned heavy machinery manufacturer. Russian authorities said three people were killed in the strike. Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, with fighting now into its fifth year.

title: Crisis: Tinubu should learn from Macron – ADC-PCC
body: The African Democratic Congress Presidential Campaign Council (ADC-PCC) has accused President Bola Ahmed Tinubu of “lack of empathy” for Nigerians facing hardship, urging him to learn lessons in “responsive leadership” from French President Emmanuel Macron. The council’s reaction followed reports that Macron postponed his scheduled state visit to Nigeria, initially planned for October 28–29, 2026, amid domestic challenges in the European country. According to the ADC-PCC, the reported decision underscores the importance of a leader’s responsibility to remain attentive to pressing domestic concerns. Kola Ologbondiyan, Director, Media and Publicity of the ADC-PCC, in a statement argued that the principle of placing citizens’ welfare at the centre of governance should guide leadership, particularly at a time when Nigerians are “grappling with insecurity, rising living costs and other socioeconomic difficulties.” ADC cited “persistent attacks and killings in Plateau, Niger, Benue, Zamfara, Kaduna, Kogi, Kwara, Katsina, Sokoto and other parts of the country, alongside reports of mass abductions, displacement of communities and unlawful detentions.” The ADC-PCC accused President Tinubu of failing to demonstrate sufficient public empathy in the face of these challenges, alleging that his official engagements have not adequately reflected the gravity of the suffering experienced by affected communities. The council maintained that leadership requires more than the discharge of official duties, arguing that empathy, accountability and respect for human life are essential qualities in responding to national emergencies. “President Macron has offered a reminder that the concerns of citizens must remain central to leadership. When a country faces a serious domestic crisis, its leadership must demonstrate urgency, compassion and a willingness to take responsibility,” the council said. It urged the Present administration to give greater priority to protecting lives, addressing insecurity and alleviating the economic hardship confronting Nigerians.

title: African Genius Chess Championship 2026 crowns winners across seven age categories
body: The second African Genius Chess Championship has crowned winners across seven age categories, with about 200 participants gathering at Ghud Park, Accra Mall, on Saturday, October 24, 2026. Organised by Imagination Africa and Mentors Chess Academy, the competition brought together young chess players, alongside parents, guardians and coaches, to promote intellectual development, inclusion and equal opportunities for children from different socio-economic backgrounds. Acheampong Dave Quansah Chief of Presbyterian Boys’ Secondary School, who was the standout performer at the first edition, won the Under-20 category. Gyepi-Garbrah Emmanuel Kelvin of GTUC finished second, while Anang Richard of the University of Ghana placed third. The winners received prizes, including laptops, printers, irons and vouchers provided by CanWest Ltd, while Dext Technology supplied science sets. Twisco also supported the event with products for participants, who received certificates alongside trophies and medals presented as part of the awards. “We are looking forward to AGCC becoming a household event, one that everyone looks forward to, one that people know that, look, this year, there’s going to be this number of chess competitions happening. I’m targeting it. I want to win first place. I want to win second place,” said Mariam Mahamah, co-founder of Imagination Africa. “Maybe the first time I got knocked out, I want to get this far. We want it to be something that everyone enjoys and looks forward to.” The championship builds on the success of its maiden edition in 2024, which attracted more than 150 young players from over 15 schools across Ghana. The initiative continues to use chess as a platform to nurture critical thinking, concentration and problem-solving skills among young people while expanding access to the game across different backgrounds. “We believe that it’s one sport that cuts across almost every other facet of life. So, we’ve been doing this for some years now, and you can tell from those that we’ve been working with for some years that, from where they started till now, there’s been great improvement in even their education, their maths, arithmetic and all of that, and then how they also analyse issues and solve problems. So, it’s a game that we believe is the way to go if we really want to develop as a country,” said David Acheampong, founder of Mentors Chess Academy. Full list of winners Under-8 1st: Nyameba Nana Osei Osei-Manu (Harvest Christian Academy) 2nd: Kunt Hikmet Kaan (Al-Rayan International School) 3rd: Mitchell Baksmaty (ICS) Best Girl: Ohene Nunna Under-10 1st: Matey Dromi Lorm (North Hills International School) 2nd: Matey Jormi Lorlor (North Hills International School) 3rd: Ajeigbe Andre-Benjamin (Lycée Français International Jacques Prévert d’Accra) Best Girl: Kaia Donkor (Lycée Français d’Accra) Under-12 1st: Acheampong Jeddiah Nana Osei (Englebert) 2nd: Krithik Raj Medisetti Mahi (East Airport International School) 3rd: Oke Jaden (Al-Rayan International School) Best Girl: Krystelle Owusu (Lycée Français d’Accra) Under-14 1st: Pradeep Harshan (Healthy Mind) 2nd: Joy Van-Eijk (Solo) 3rd: Essel Jadon (Brain Hill International School) Best Girl: Abigail Chine Tsyokpo Under-16 1st: Siddharth Gupta (DPS) 2nd: El Assaad Essam (Al-Rayan International School) 3rd: Agamaku Caleb Kuame (Presbyterian Boys’ Secondary School, Legon) Best Girl: Safwan Larine (Al-Rayan International School) Under-18 1st: David Yoel Varela Sanchez (Goethe-Institut Ghana) 2nd: Pryce-Tandoh Jeshurun Obiri Yeboah (University of Ghana Basic School) 3rd: De-Souza Nathan Best Girl: Zuttah Euodia (University of Ghana, Legon) Under-20 1st: Acheampong Dave Quansah Chief (Presbyterian Boys’ Secondary School, Legon) 2nd: Gyepi-Garbrah Emmanuel Kelvin (GTUC) 3rd: Anang Richard (University of Ghana, Legon)

title: US midterms could restore Ukraine’s American aid and curb Trump’s Russia deals, if Democrats win Congress
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); If Democrats win the House, and possibly the Senate, a result nonpartisan analysts call plausible, they would gain the power to bring new Ukraine aid to a vote and to push back on President Donald Trump’s deals easing pressure on Russia, Reuters reports in an analysis of how US foreign policy could shift. The stakes are concrete. Trump has largely halted direct US aid to Ukraine, which lawmakers of both parties had backed, and its current supplies run from packages passed under his predecessor. Weeks ago, he also waived the sanctions on Russian energy that Congress had written into law and struck a deal to bring Russian diesel back to the market, angering Republicans and Democrats alike. What a Democratic Congress could do for Ukraine With both chambers, Democrats could put new Ukraine aid on the floor, and given the bipartisan support such aid has drawn, it could pass with the two-thirds majorities needed to override a Trump veto. Other steps could be taken, too. Representative Gregory Meeks of New York, in line to chair the House Foreign Affairs Committee if his party wins control, has already introduced bipartisan legislation to block Trump’s plan to return Russian diesel to the global market. Democrats are also readier than Trump’s Republicans to rein in military spending. They blocked his request for an unprecedented 67% rise in the military budget, to $1.5 trillion, in the Senate, and many say they will try to restore the foreign aid he has withheld or canceled. The limits of a slice of power The leverage has limits. Even with both chambers, Democrats would still face a president who can veto, and overriding him would require two-thirds of each chamber. The pattern has already been visible in Iran: Trump launched that war on 28 February without congressional approval, and when a War Powers resolution passed with a handful of Republican votes, his administration ignored it. title: WATCH: Israel is 'Jewish territory,' gov't must send Gazans to France per Trump plan, Ben-Gvir says
body: Gazans should be sent to emigrate to France or other countries in Europe so that Israel can “conquer the whole territory” of the Gaza Strip, far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir told The Jerusalem Post in a recent interview, arguing that he supported US President Donald Trump's plan to relocate Palestinians there.“If you ask me what should be done in Gaza, we should conquer the entire territory. All of it. It is our land, the Jewish people's land. And we should encourage emigration,” Ben-Gvir told the Post.In February 2025, Trump proposed relocating approximately two million Gazans as part of an emigration plan, though the proposal has since stalled.Amid the current protests in France, Ben-Gvir has recently shared AI-generated videos depicting Gazans being transported to Paris by the far-right minister himself.“This is a very good plan proposed by Donald Trump: encouraging emigration. Many of them could go to better places,” Ben-Gvir said, arguing they would receive good conditions in Europe.“There are more attractive places, places looking for workers, and places where they could live more comfortably,” he said.“Why not send them to France, for example? Give them good conditions in other countries, perhaps Britain, London, or places like that,” the minister added.Polling projects Ben-Gvir's party to win roughly eight seats in next KnessetBen-Gvir's far-right Otzma Yehudit party has been a key member of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition.Recent polling projects Otzma Yehudit to win about eight seats in the next Knesset. Ben-Gvir has announced that he will demand the defense portfolio in the next government.When asked what he thought about Palestinians who would object to leaving the Gaza Strip, arguing that it was their home and refusing to move even under good conditions, Ben-Gvir referenced the October 7 Hamas massacre in 2023.“Someone whose home it is does not start a war and massacre children. Someone whose home it is does not rape women. Someone whose home it is does not burn babies. Once they did those things, they lost the legitimacy of making that argument,” the minister said.“You cannot make that argument and say it was just one, two, or three people, or that it was only a small number. There were many, many, many, many [Palestinians] involved,” he added.“And there were also people we describe as uninvolved civilians who tortured our male and female hostages.”“This has to stop. This cannot continue. I believe that someone who says and does these things, someone who inflicts this kind of harm, cannot claim that this is their home. People do not behave like that in their own home,” Ben-Gvir added.Ben-Gvir advocated for 'bombing Gaza' before October 7 attacksThe far Right minister repeatedly opposed hostage-ceasefire deals throughout the Israel-Hamas War, advocating for continued military action rather than an agreement.When asked whether he regretted his stance, Ben-Gvir did not answer directly, instead arguing that the cabinet should have listened to him more before October 7. He also said that Netanyahu bore responsibility for the October 7 attacks.“Before October 7, when I was going to cabinet meetings, I kept saying, 'Let's bomb Gaza. Let's carry out targeted killings,'” he said.“Imagine if they had listened to me on this ... it's a great shame,” he added.Ben-Gvir, whose views are often characterized as extreme, has been criticized for rhetoric that opponents say has contributed to the deterioration of Israel's international image. He has also faced criticism over rising crime rates, particularly in the Arab sector, during the government's term.Regarding the rise in crime in the Arab sector, Ben-Gvir argued that a main factor behind the increase was restrictions imposed on him by Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara.According to Ben-Gvir, early on, he wanted to introduce spyware into homes in Arab communities to allow police to listen in on conversations.When asked about criticism that doing so would infringe on the right to privacy, Ben-Gvir claimed that such measures were permissible in some cases.“There are cases where it is permissible to infringe on privacy, when we're talking about murderers. In the end, murderers also kill children, including young children, so this is a very good thing.”Ben-Gvir praises his work as National Security MinisterBen-Gvir also said he had been unable to secure the budget for certain technological advancements, and that crime rates had lowered after some budgets were approved.He argued that the police have been doing well, praising officers for their work.“We have excellent police officers and female officers who are fighting on the front lines. They are entering these communities, exercising force, and establishing governance, and I am very proud of them.”“Are they lacking intelligence capabilities? Yes, that's true,” he added.Ben-Gvir called on the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) to become more involved in police work, arguing that the agency has the technology to enhance the police's capabilities.When asked whether he was concerned about the damage to Israel's international standing that critics say has already occurred and warn could worsen, Ben-Gvir answered that Israel's image abroad mattered to him, but that he would not “endanger the lives of soldiers” for it.“I will not endanger the lives of combatants, soldiers, or civilians here just because I want Israel to look good in the eyes of the world,” he said.This article is the second half of the complete interview with National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir. The first half was published on Friday and can be found on JPost.com

title: Unreal Engine GPU Stack: Chapter 2 Scene View Extensions
body:
How to inject a custom rendering pass into Unreal's frame without modifying the engine. In Chapter 1 we did all the required world building... three threads, the RHI, and the Render Dependency Graph. The next practical question is how your own GPU work gets into Unreal's frame. There are a few common answers from Youtube tutorials, and none of them are perfect. A post-process material can't run a compute shader or write to an render target. A Scene Capture Component renders the whole scene again from another view just to hand you pixels you already had. Imagine overlying your active digital twin data over real world CCTV footage. Or building a cam overlay over Unreal Automotive HMD or just compositing real world background to generate synthetic data. All can be done efficiently using GPUCompositionGraphicsPipeline or SynthPass. More about this in this chapter. 1. What's happening in GPUCompositionGraphicsPipeline This chapter uses one plugin as its running example: GPUCompositionGraphicsPipeline . It takes a live video feed (anything that plays into a UMediaTexture ) and composites the rendered frame over it. All of it runs on the GPU, in the middle of Unreal's own post-processing. It has three parts: UCompGraphicsSubsystem , an engine subsystem that runs on the Game thread. This is the Blueprints facing side. It creates and owns the extension, holds the media texture and the output render target, and tags the actors that should appear in the composite with custom stencil value 20 . FCoreSVE , the Scene View Extension. It subscribes to the post-processing stage right after FXAA and runs the compositing callback on the Render thread. Two passes inside that callback. A pixel shader ( FCustomDepthStencilMaskCreatorPS ) turns the custom stencil buffer into a mask. Then a compute shader ( FCompositorCS ) blends scene color, the mask and the media texture. The result is drawn to the viewport and copied into a render target, so it can be used outside the viewport too. So in one frame, the Game thread only sets values. On the Render thread, the renderer asks FCoreSVE where it wants to run. After FXAA it adds the mask pass, then the compositing pass, then the copy and draw. Every snippet below is from this plugin unless it's marked as engine source. Engine code below is from UE 5.6 The interface lives in the Engine module ( Engine/Public/SceneViewExtension.h ), but anything useful you do inside it needs the rendering modules. The plugin's Build.cs : // GPUCompositionGraphicsPipeline.Build.cs PublicDependencyModuleNames . AddRange ( new string [] { "Core" , "CoreUObject" , "Engine" , // ISceneViewExtension, FSceneViewExtensionBase "RenderCore" , // FRDGBuilder, global shaders "Renderer" , // FScreenPassTexture, FPostProcessMaterialInputs "RHI" , // textures, formats, feature levels "Projects" , // IPluginManager, for the shader directory mapping "MediaAssets" , // UMediaTexture, the video input }); Source in SynthPass: GPUCompositionGraphicsPipeline.Build.cs L12–L21 The headers you'll typically include: One header to be careful with: FPostProcessingInputs , the argument to PrePostProcessPass_RenderThread , is defined in Renderer/Internal/PostProcess/PostProcessInputs.h . You can override the hook with only a forward declaration. But if you want to read its members, you have to add Renderer/Internal to your include paths, and nothing in Internal or Private is a stable API. Stay in Public wherever you can. The plugin does take that trade-off. It includes PostProcess/PostProcessInputs.h and a few other renderer headers, so it adds both paths. It builds on 5.6, but an engine upgrade can break it: string EngineDir = Path . GetFullPath ( Target . RelativeEnginePath ); PrivateIncludePaths . AddRange ( new string [] { Path . Combine ( EngineDir , "Source/Runtime/Renderer/Private" ), Path . Combine ( EngineDir , "Source/Runtime/Renderer/Internal" ) }); Source in SynthPass: GPUCompositionGraphicsPipeline.Build.cs L36–L45 The shaders have to be found before they compile. If the extension uses global shaders from your plugin, the Shaders directory mapping from Chapter 1 must exist before the engine compiles global shaders, which happens early in startup. Thus, such modules use "LoadingPhase": "PostConfigInit" in the .uplugin . With Default , the engine can't resolve your virtual shader path. The plugin's .uplugin sets PostConfigInit , and StartupModule does only the mapping: // GPUCompositionGraphicsPipeline.cpp void FGPUCompositionGraphicsPipelineModule :: StartupModule () { FString PluginShaderDir = FPaths :: Combine ( IPluginManager :: Get (). FindPlugin ( TEXT ( "GPUCompositionGraphicsPipeline" )) -> GetBaseDir (), TEXT ( "Shaders" )); AddShaderSourceDirectoryMapping ( TEXT ( "/Plugins/GPUCompositionGraphicsPipeline" ), PluginShaderDir ); } Source in SynthPass: GPUCompositionGraphicsPipeline.cpp L7–L12 There was a second problem I didn't expect here: mapping the shader directory and creating the extension can't happen at the same point in startup. // Engine source: Engine/Private/SceneViewExtension.cpp void FSceneViewExtensions :: RegisterExtension ( const FSceneViewExtensionRef & RegisterMe ) { if ( ensure ( GEngine )) { auto & KnownExtensions = GEngine -> ViewExtensions -> KnownExtensions ; // ... compact dead entries ... KnownExtensions . AddUnique ( RegisterMe ); } } A module loading at PostConfigInit starts long before GEngine exists. So map the shader directory in StartupModule , but create the extension later... in a subsystem's Initialize , from FCoreDelegates::OnPostEngineInit , or when gameplay asks for it. The plugin uses the last option: nothing is created until a Blueprint calls InitilizeCompositor on the subsystem. 2. Creating and owning an extension The plugin's extension, trimmed to what it uses: // CoreGraphicsPipeline.h class FCoreSVE : public FSceneViewExtensionBase { public: FCoreSVE ( const FAutoRegister & AutoRegister ); virtual void SubscribeToPostProcessingPass ( EPostProcessingPass PassId , const FSceneView & View , FAfterPassCallbackDelegateArray & InOutPassCallbacks , bool bIsPassEnabled ); FScreenPassTexture GraphicsCompositing ( FRDGBuilder & GraphBuilder , const FSceneView & View , const FPostProcessMaterialInputs & Inputs ); }; // CoreGraphicsPipeline.cpp FCoreSVE :: FCoreSVE ( const FAutoRegister & AutoRegister ) : FSceneViewExtensionBase ( AutoRegister ) {} Source in SynthPass: CoreGraphicsPipeline.h L10–L29 , CoreGraphicsPipeline.cpp L27–L31 FAfterPassCallbackDelegateArray is the older name. In 5.6 it's an alias for FPostProcessingPassDelegateArray , so both compile. And creating it, from the subsystem: // CompGraphicsSubsystem.h TSharedPtr < class FCoreSVE , ESPMode :: ThreadSafe > CoreSVE ; // CompGraphicsSubsystem.cpp void UCompGraphicsSubsystem :: InitilizeCompositor () { // Custom depth with stencil, which the mask pass reads UKismetSystemLibrary :: ExecuteConsoleCommand ( GetWorld (), FString ( "r.CustomDepth 3" )); CoreSVE = FSceneViewExtensions :: NewExtension < FCoreSVE > (); } Source in SynthPass: CompGraphicsSubsystem.h L87 , CompGraphicsSubsystem.cpp L26–L34 FAutoRegister has a private constructor, and only FSceneViewExtensions can create one. So new FCoreSVE(...) doesn't compile. The only way in is NewExtension
() , which constructs the extension, wraps it in a thread-safe shared pointer, and registers it in one step. The first constructor argument must be FAutoRegister . Any extra arguments you pass to NewExtension are forwarded after it. Ownership is yours. The engine's registry only holds weak pointers. If you drop your shared pointer, the extension is gone from the next frame on, and that's also how you unregister it: void UCompGraphicsSubsystem :: DeinitializeCompositor () { if ( CoreSVE . IsValid ()) { CoreSVE -> IsActiveThisFrameFunctions . Empty (); } CoreSVE . Reset (); // ... release the render target and show-only actors ... } Source in SynthPass: CompGraphicsSubsystem.cpp L77–L95 The frame already in flight is safe (the frame that is being rendered in gpu). Each view family copies the active extensions into ViewFamily.ViewExtensions as strong references, so the Render thread keeps the extension alive until that frame finishes. This is the same idea as the scene proxies in Chapter 1: the Game thread can let go while the Render thread finishes using it. ESPMode::ThreadSafe isn't optional. The pointer is created on the Game thread and used on the Render thread, so its reference count must be atomic. Who should hold the pointer? Something that lives as long as the effect should: an engine subsystem for effects that persist across levels, a world subsystem for per-level effects, or an actor or component when the effect belongs to one object. The plugin uses an engine subsystem, so the compositor survives level changes. 3. Every injection point in the frame The hooks follow the frame from Game-thread setup to the end of rendering. Let's see which thread calls them. 3.1 Game thread hooks: shaping the MVP These hooks run while the engine builds the view family for the next frame. They don't take an FRDGBuilder , so you can't add passes here. Their job is to change what gets rendered, not how . Let's take a closer look at BeginRenderViewFamily . It's the last point where you're on the Game thread and know that a frame is about to be rendered. It's the correct place to copy settings, UObject data and texture resource pointers into a plain struct that the Render-thread hooks will read. Reading UObject s directly from Render-thread hooks is the kind of data race Chapter 1 warned about. It usually works, until the Game thread changes the object in the middle of a frame. You also need to consider the copy cost for data from one thread to another. It a tradeoff between performance and unsafe code (Just like rust providing memory safety at compile times but programmers need to write unsafe() code at some places to extract every drop of perf) 3.2 Render thread: the scene renderer These hooks receive an FRDGBuilder& . As Chapter 1 explained, nothing runs when you call RDG. You're adding passes to a graph that executes later, and the graph orders them after whatever came before your hook. You can see that the per-view hooks ( PreRenderView , PrePostProcessPass , PostRenderView ) run once for each view. Split screen, stereo rendering and scene captures with multiple views all call them more than once per frame, so don't assume one call means one frame. 4. Injection points inside post-processing SubscribeToPostProcessingPass works differently from the other hooks. It doesn't render anything. At the start of post-processing, the renderer calls it once per view for each stage and asks "do you want to run something here?". You answer by adding a delegate. The plugin answers only for the FXAA stage, and only while the compositor is running: // CoreGraphicsPipeline.cpp void FCoreSVE :: SubscribeToPostProcessingPass ( EPostProcessingPass PassId , const FSceneView & View , FAfterPassCallbackDelegateArray & InOutPassCallbacks , bool bIsPassEnabled ) { UCompGraphicsSubsystem * CompGraphicsSubsystem = GEngine -> GetEngineSubsystem < UCompGraphicsSubsystem > (); if ( ! CompGraphicsSubsystem ) { return ; } if ( ! CompGraphicsSubsystem -> GetShouldCompositorRun ()) { return ; } if ( PassId == EPostProcessingPass :: FXAA ) { InOutPassCallbacks . Add ( FAfterPassCallbackDelegate :: CreateRaw ( this , & FCoreSVE :: GraphicsCompositing )); } } Source in SynthPass: CoreGraphicsPipeline.cpp L39–L51 This hook runs on the Render thread, and it reads a UObject (the subsystem) directly. That's the race described above. It works because a bool flag is rarely changed mid-frame. The safer version copies the flag in BeginRenderViewFamily . These are the stages in 5.6, in the order they run in the frame. The engine header notes that each one sits immediately before a post-process material blendable location, so if you know the material blend locations, you already know these: The plugin's stage, FXAA, comes after tonemapping. So the composite blends display-ready colors with the video, which is the space the footage is already in. Here's the FXAA case from PostProcessing.cpp , because it surprises people: // Engine source: Renderer/Private/PostProcess/PostProcessing.cpp if ( PassSequence . IsEnabled ( EPass :: FXAA )) { SceneColor = AddFXAAPass ( GraphBuilder , View , PassInputs ); } SceneColor = AddAfterPass ( EPass :: FXAA , SceneColor ); // your callbacks, unconditionally That's the reason why the plugin's callback still runs when the project uses TSR and FXAA is off. The bIsPassEnabled argument tells you whether the pass itself is running this frame. In the engine's recommendation, subscribe only when you'll actually produce a GPU resource. 4.1 The contract for a post-processing callback Every stage uses the same delegate signature. The plugin's callback: FScreenPassTexture GraphicsCompositing ( FRDGBuilder & GraphBuilder , const FSceneView & View , const FPostProcessMaterialInputs & Inputs ); Source in SynthPass: CoreGraphicsPipeline.h L24 , CoreGraphicsPipeline.cpp L53–L113 Three rules to keep in mind while setting a callback: You receive scene color and must return scene color. Multiple subscribers to the same stage run in priority order, and each one gets the previous one's output. OverrideOutput is only valid if you're last. For the later stages (from ReplacingTonemapper onwards), your callback may be the final pass that writes to the back buffer. In that case Inputs.OverrideOutput is valid and you must write into it. Otherwise it's invalid and you create your own output (Creates a black screen on viewport). GraphicsCompositing adds the mask pass and then hands off to FCompositorCS::ImplementCompShader , which handles the output. Trimmed to the parts that follow the contract: // CompositorCS.cpp FScreenPassTexture FCompositorCS :: ImplementCompShader ( FRDGBuilder & GraphBuilder , const FSceneView & SceneView , const FPostProcessMaterialInputs & Inputs , /* ...mask, media texture, blend values... */ ) { // Rule 1: take scene color in const FScreenPassTexture & SceneColor = FScreenPassTexture :: CopyFromSlice ( GraphBuilder , Inputs . GetInput ( EPostProcessMaterialInput :: SceneColor )); // Rule 3: write into OverrideOutput if we're last, otherwise make our own target FScreenPassRenderTarget Output = Inputs . OverrideOutput ; if ( ! Output . IsValid ()) { Output = FScreenPassRenderTarget :: CreateFromInput ( GraphBuilder , SceneColor , ERenderTargetLoadAction :: ENoAction , TEXT ( "CompositorViewportOutput" )); } // Compositing compute pass writes OutputTexture, then it's copied into the output render target. // (Chapter 3 covers writing the shader and adding the pass.) AddDrawTexturePass ( GraphBuilder , SceneView , FScreenPassTexture ( OutputTexture ), Output ); // Rule 1: hand scene color back if ( bShallCompOutputOnViewport ) { return FScreenPassTexture ( Output ); } return SceneColor ; } Source in SynthPass: CompositorCS.cpp L14–L140 5. What's next This chapter covered where your work can go in the frame. It skipped what that work is: the shader, its parameter struct, and how a pass is added to the graph. Chapter 3 covers that with compute shaders: declaring a global shader in a plugin, binding its parameters, dispatching it through RDG from one of the hooks above, and what happens between FComputeShaderUtils::AddPass and threads running on an SM.

title: SlothTidy: A Zero-Friction, 100% Local AI File Daemon That Organizes Your Downloads While You Rest 🦥
body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady What I Built A three-toed sloth moves at 0.24 km/h and survives on roughly 110 kilocalories a day because it refuses to waste metabolic energy on unnecessary movement. Humans, on the other hand, waste hours every month manually opening scan_0042 (1).pdf , figuring out what it is, renaming it, creating a folder, and dragging it out of ~/Downloads . SlothTidy is a zero-friction, privacy-first local file organization daemon built for developers, students, and digital hoarders who want a spotless filesystem while putting in zero manual effort . Running quietly in the background (or on-demand via a single CLI command), SlothTidy watches ~/Downloads and ~/Desktop , inspects incoming files the moment they finish downloading, reads their contents locally, and uses a lightweight open-weight LLM ( qwen2.5:1.5b or llama3.2:1b ) to: Categorize the file ( Finance , Academic , Development , Media , Administration , or Misc ). Generate a clean, standardized filename ( YYYY-MM-DD-descriptive-slug.ext ) using the document's actual date and subject matter. Route it into a semantic subfolder inside ~/Documents/Organized (e.g., Academic/Mathematics/2026-10-21-td3-real-analysis.pdf or Finance/Invoices/2026-10-21-iam-fiber-invoice.pdf ). Log every atomic move to ~/.config/sloth-tidy/history.jsonl so you can roll back any number of operations instantly with sloth-tidy undo . Students drowning in lecture PDFs, developers downloading tarballs and config scripts, and anyone tired of hunting for tax receipts or screenshots gets to embrace pure sloth energy. Demo CLI Walkthrough One-Shot Scan ( sloth-tidy scan ~/Downloads ) Inspects a directory, extracts context from PDFs, source code, archives, and screenshots, classifies them via your local Ollama instance, and moves them into ~/Documents/Organized (or previews the table safely with --dry-run ). Background Daemon ( sloth-tidy run ) Starts a non-blocking watchdog observer over ~/Downloads and ~/Desktop . Browser partial downloads ( .crdownload , .part , .tmp , .aria2 ) are ignored automatically, and a POSIX file-lock + byte-size stability debouncer waits until large downloads finish writing before triggering inference. Instant Rollback ( sloth-tidy undo [N] ) Never overwrites existing files (automatically resolves collisions as -1 , -2 while preserving compound extensions like .tar.gz ), routes low-confidence files to Misc/Low_Confidence_Review , and reverses your last N moves with a single command. The Sloth Energy Report Card ( sloth-tidy report ) Prints a terminal dashboard calculating total files sorted, megabytes organized, manual toil minutes saved, mental decisions avoided, and cloud API dollars saved. Code tahaenasraoui-debug / sloth-tidy `""==,,__ `"==..__"=..__ _ _..-==""_ .-,`"=/ /\ \""/_)==""`` ( ( | | | \/ | \ '. | \; \ / | \ | | || ,-._.' |_| | || .\_/\ -' ; Y | ` | / |-. '. __/_ _.-' /' `'-.._____.-' 🦥 SlothTidy Zero-friction, privacy-first local AI file organization daemon. Built for the Hacktoberfest 2026 "Slow and Steady" Challenge. 🌿 The Sloth Ethos Sloths survive by conserving energy. You shouldn't spend yours manually renaming scan_0042 (1).pdf or dragging screenshots out of ~/Downloads . SlothTidy runs quietly in the background, watches your ~/Downloads and ~/Desktop folders, extracts lightweight context once downloads finish writing, and uses a small open-weight language model ( qwen2.5:1.5b or llama3.2:1b ) running 100% locally on your CPU to categorize, rename ( YYYY-MM-DD-descriptive-slug.ext ), and file everything into ~/Documents/Organized . Total Privacy : Bank statements, tax records, national IDs, and source code never leave localhost . … View on GitHub GitHub Repository: https://github.com/tahaenasraoui-debug/sloth-tidy How I Built It SlothTidy is engineered in Python 3.11+ around a 3-tier local inference architecture and a multi-format content extraction pipeline: 1. Open-Source AI & Local Inference Stack Primary Engine — Ollama ( /api/chat ) : Communicates with a local Ollama server ( http://localhost:11434 ) running small open-weight instruction models— qwen2.5:1.5b (default) or llama3.2:1b . Grammar-Constrained Structured Outputs ( Pydantic v2 ) : Instead of hoping a 1.5B parameter model writes valid JSON via prompt engineering alone, SlothTidy passes FileClassification.model_json_schema() directly into Ollama's format parameter. This constrains token sampling at inference time to match our exact schema ( category , suggested_filename , subfolder , confidence , summary ), backed by Pydantic validators that strip path-traversal tokens ( .. ) and enforce YYYY-MM-DD kebab-case slugs. Secondary Fallback — llama-cpp-python : If the Ollama daemon isn't running, SlothTidy can fall back directly to a local .gguf model file on disk using llama-cpp-python with JSON schema grammar enforcement. Tertiary Safety Net — Deterministic Heuristics : If no local LLM is reachable, a deterministic keyword and MIME/extension classifier takes over so your workflow never breaks. Local Vision & OCR : For images and screenshots, SlothTidy extracts EXIF metadata with Pillow , runs local OCR via Tesseract ( pytesseract ) , and optionally passes a compressed 512x512 Base64 thumbnail to moondream:latest for local multimodal vision classification. 2. Content Extraction Pipeline ( sloth_tidy/extractors.py ) Small models run fastest when fed high-signal, tightly bounded context: PDFs ( pypdf ) : Extracts document metadata ( /Title , /Author , /Subject ) and text from the first 2 pages (capped at 2 KB). Code & Plain Text : Reads the first 2 KB ( [HEAD] ) and last 512 B ( [TAIL] ) with UTF-8 heuristic detection so logs and scripts are summarized accurately without blowing up the context window. Binaries & Archives : Inspects the 8-byte magic header in hex alongside filename tokens without loading multi-gigabyte ISOs or .tar.gz buffers into memory. 3. CPU Benchmarks (6-Core Laptop CPU, 16 GB RAM, No GPU) Tested across a 50-file mixed corpus (invoices, university math problem sets, C/Rust/Python scripts, and screenshots): Open-Weight Model Quantization RAM Usage Avg. Latency / File (CPU) JSON Schema Validity Classification Accuracy llama3.2:1b Q4_K_M (0.8 GB) ~1.3 GB 1.42 s 100% 92% qwen2.5:1.5b Q4_K_M (1.0 GB) ~1.6 GB 1.78 s 100% 96% moondream:latest Q4 (1.7 GB) ~2.2 GB 3.10 s 98% 94% (Screenshots) Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Your ~/Downloads and ~/Desktop folders are the most sensitive directories on your computer. In a typical week, they hold: Bank statements, wire receipts, and utility invoices ( Finance ) National ID scans, passports, and administrative certificates ( Administration ) University transcripts, problem sets, and unpublished research ( Academic ) .env files, SSH configs, and proprietary source code ( Development ) A closed cloud API is a non-starter for a background file daemon. Nobody wants a background process silently uploading snippets of their bank statements, ID documents, or .env files to a third-party server—nor do they want to pay per-token API fees every time they download a PDF. Open innovation—specifically small open-weight models ( Qwen 2.5 , Llama 3.2 , Moondream 2 ) , quantized GGUF weights ( llama.cpp ) , Ollama , and structured JSON grammar sampling —makes SlothTidy possible: 100% Offline Privacy : Every byte of extraction and inference stays on 127.0.0.1 . You can unplug your Ethernet cable or turn off Wi-Fi and SlothTidy works identically. Zero Marginal Cost : A daemon that runs 24/7 for years costs $0.00 in API tokens. No Dedicated GPU Required : Open quantization and 1B–1.5B architectures allow structured classification in ~1.5 seconds on standard laptop CPUs. My Agent Session I collaborated with an AI coding assistant as a systems architecture sounding board to iterate on the edge cases that usually break naive file-organizer scripts: Designing the two-stage wait_until_file_ready() debouncer in sloth_tidy/watcher.py so watchdog events don't read half-written browser downloads or locked file descriptors. Preserving compound archive extensions ( .tar.gz , .tar.bz2 , .tar.xz ) during collision resolution ( -1 , -2 ). Writing the pytest suite ( tests/test_organizer.py ) to verify path-traversal sanitization ( ../../ ), dry-run isolation, and atomic multi-step rollbacks. The Lazy Payoff Before SlothTidy, my ~/Downloads folder was a graveyard of td3_analyse_s1 (2).pdf , Facture_Octobre.pdf , random .tar.gz dotfiles, and unnamed terminal screenshots. Taking ~25 seconds to manually open, inspect, rename, create a directory, and move a file means sorting 42 files eats 17.5 minutes of tedious context-switching and 126 micro-decisions (What is this file? What should I name it? Where does it belong?). Running sloth-tidy scan ~/Downloads sorted all 42 files while I leaned back and drank coffee: Math and CS problem sets landed in ~/Documents/Organized/Academic/Mathematics/ with clean YYYY-MM-DD prefixes. Monthly utility bills went straight into ~/Documents/Organized/Finance/Invoices/ . Compressed Linux configs landed in ~/Documents/Organized/Development/Archives/ . Terminal screenshots were OCR'd and filed under ~/Documents/Organized/Media/Screenshots/ . Zero clicks, zero manual renaming, zero bytes leaked to the cloud. Prize Categories Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady (Local-first, energy-conserving automation powered by open-weight models)

title: Ebola: NCDC expands health declaration requirement for international travellers
body:
The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) has expanded its health declaration requirement for international travellers after confirming an Ebola case in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT).
The agency’s Director-General, Jide Idris, announced the decision during a media briefing in Abuja on Sunday.
Mr Idris said the requirement initially applied to international travellers but was later restricted to passengers arriving from selected countries linked to the Ebola outbreak, including the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda.
“But with this case, we have reversed that directive,” he said.
He said the NCDC had sent advisories to the Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria (FAAN) and the Nigerian Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA), and expected further instructions to guide implementation in collaboration with airlines.
Mr Idris said Nigeria’s preparedness measures had focused on five international airports: Lagos, Abuja, Enugu, Kano and Port Harcourt.
He said Port Health Services was working with aviation personnel, immigration and customs officials to strengthen preparedness and screening at the country’s points of entry.
According to Mr Idris, the NCDC needs to coordinate with aviation authorities because it does not independently control airport operations.
He said agencies were working together to implement the required measures, while immigration and customs officials were involved at land borders.
Mr Idris also acknowledged operational challenges at Lagos airport, where ongoing construction had created difficulties. He said the NCDC would engage FAAN and the NCAA to address issues affecting Port Health Services’ work.
He added that access to restricted airport areas must follow established security procedures.
The revised screening measures form part of Nigeria’s response to a confirmed case of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus in the FCT on 20 October.
As PREMIUM TIMES reported, the patient is a 42-year-old Ugandan woman who travelled to Nigeria from Uganda on 3 October. She developed symptoms on 6 October and sought medical attention before her infection was confirmed.
At Sunday’s briefing, Mr Idris said health authorities had identified 53 primary contacts linked to the patient. These comprise 44 people associated with the health facility where she received treatment and nine additional contacts, including household members. They attended to her at another facility and were members of the FCT team that collected samples.
He said contact tracing was ongoing and that officials were monitoring the identified contacts.
Health officials are following up with contacts for 21 days, the maximum incubation period for Ebola, to identify any symptoms that might indicate infection.
Mr Idris appealed to Nigerians identified as contacts to cooperate with public health officials, stressing that being identified as a contact does not mean a person has Ebola.
The NCDC is also strengthening infection prevention and control measures in healthcare facilities, supporting laboratory capacity and providing public health information to counter rumours and misinformation.
The agency urged Nigerians to rely on verified information from authorised public health sources and cooperate with response measures as investigations continue.

title: Node2Shell: Memory Corruption RCE in Brotli Affecting Node.js
body: Node2Shell: Memory Corruption RCE in Brotli Affecting Node.js I recently published a proof of concept for CVE-2026-111497 , which I’ve been calling Node2Shell . The issue is a memory-corruption vulnerability in brotli 1.2.0 that affects Node.js releases bundling the vulnerable decoder. The interesting part is that this is not an application-level eval() , execSync() , child-process misuse, or webhook trick. The vulnerability exists lower in the stack, inside the Brotli decoder itself. Under the right conditions, corrupted decoder state can eventually redirect execution through a callback path and reach system() . Affected Node.js Versions According to the affected ranges identified during testing: Node.js 22.x before 22.23.4 Node.js 24.x before 24.22.1 Node.js 26.x before 26.12.1 The underlying issue originates in the bundled Brotli implementation. Root Cause One part of the problem is located around DecodeBlockTypeAndLength() . Under specific decoder state conditions, the function returns: BROTLI_FALSE The important detail is that this value is 0 . Elsewhere in the decoder, 0 overlaps with the numeric value used for: BROTLI_DECODER_SUCCESS The BROTLI_SAFE handling path interprets that result incorrectly and treats the state as though the decoder simply needs more input. The decoder then saves its state around: COMMAND_BEGIN and re-enters the same path. This can result in a persistent CPU loop. At this point, the vulnerability already provides a denial-of-service condition. But the more interesting behavior appears in another decoder path. The Out-of-Bounds Write When the decoder reaches a NEEDS_MORE_INPUT condition while: buffer_length == 0 a copy-tail operation runs. Conceptually, the relevant code behaves like this: s -> buffer . u8 [ s -> buffer_length ] = * next_in ++ ; s -> buffer_length ++ ; There is no effective release-build bounds check protecting the write. A BROTLI_DCHECK exists around some of this logic, but debug assertions do not provide protection in production builds. That means decoder-controlled state can cause writes beyond the intended small internal buffer. Why Input Size Matters One of the key constraints during exploitation is: BROTLI_FAST_INPUT_SLACK = 28 Input size changes the decoder path significantly. With sufficiently small chunks, the decoder can be forced into a state where command processing exits early with a "need more input" result. That feeds execution back into the vulnerable copy-tail logic. With larger chunks, the decoder is more likely to fall into the CPU-spin behavior instead. In practice, this means the malformed input must be delivered in carefully sized fragments rather than as one large buffer. This distinction turned out to be critical while reproducing the issue. Corrupting Decoder State Once the out-of-bounds write is reachable, the next question is what sits next to the internal buffer. The decoder state contains additional fields immediately after it. By extending the corruption far enough, an attacker can begin modifying adjacent decoder state, including pointer-sized values and callback-related data. One particularly interesting target is the metadata callback state. Conceptually, the exploitation chain becomes: crafted Brotli stream ↓ decoder state confusion ↓ NEEDS_MORE_INPUT path ↓ out-of-bounds state corruption ↓ callback state overwritten ↓ controlled callback invocation ↓ code execution During testing, the callback path could be redirected so that execution reached system() with attacker-controlled callback data. This produces native process execution without relying on JavaScript execution primitives. Why This Is Interesting Most Node.js RCE demonstrations eventually reduce to something like: require ( " child_process " ). exec (...) or: eval (...) Node2Shell is different. The execution path exists below the JavaScript layer. The application gives compressed data to the runtime. The runtime passes it to Brotli. The decoder corrupts its own native state. Native control flow is then redirected. That makes the bug much closer to a traditional native memory-corruption vulnerability than a typical Node.js application bug. Proof of Concept I published the proof of concept here: github.com/syrex1013/CVE-2026-111497-node2shell The PoC demonstrates the decoder behavior and the vulnerability chain used during the research. A successful test produced native command execution from the affected process. Simplified Vulnerability Chain The overall chain can be summarized as: Trigger the problematic Brotli decoder state. Force the decoder into the NEEDS_MORE_INPUT path. Deliver input in small fragments. Reach the vulnerable copy-tail logic. Corrupt adjacent Brotli decoder state. Modify callback-related state. Trigger the metadata callback. Redirect native execution. The two observable outcomes are therefore closely related: malformed stream │ ├── larger input/state path → infinite decoder loop → DoS │ └── chunked input path → memory corruption → native code execution Defensive Takeaways If you operate Node.js services that consume Brotli-compressed input, updating the runtime should be treated as the primary mitigation. Additional defensive measures include: upgrading Node.js to a patched release; limiting exposure of Brotli decompression endpoints; enforcing request and decompression limits; isolating Node.js workloads with containers or sandboxing; running services without unnecessary privileges; monitoring for abnormal CPU saturation during decompression; monitoring crashes or memory-corruption indicators around Brotli processing. Memory-safety issues in compression libraries are especially important because decompression often happens before application-level validation. Final Thoughts Node2Shell is a useful example of why a memory-unsafe dependency deep inside a modern runtime can become security-critical even when the surrounding application code is completely ordinary. The vulnerability does not require an obvious JavaScript execution sink. Instead, the interesting behavior comes from a combination of: incorrect decoder-state handling; ambiguous return-value semantics; release-build assumptions; an out-of-bounds write; adjacent callback state; and precise control over streaming input. That combination turns what initially looks like a decoder hang into a much more serious native memory-corruption problem. PoC: github.com/syrex1013/CVE-2026-111497-node2shell For security research and authorized testing only. nodejs #security #cybersecurity #cve

title: Write a bug report your AI assistant can actually fix
body: Most AI fixes fail because the report is missing the one thing the fix depends on: what you expected, what actually happened, and how to reproduce it. https://www.notvibescoded.com/articles/bug-report-ai-can-fix A usable bug report has three sentences. First, what you expected, specifically: "Clicking Save on the settings page should update the display name and show a confirmation." Second, what actually happened: "Clicking Save reloads the page, the display name is unchanged, and no confirmation appears." Third, how to reproduce it, the shortest path from a fresh state to the bug, including any condition that makes it happen or not happen. Include the error, not your theory about it. Paste the full error message, plus ten lines before it for context, and stop there. A thousand lines of log is almost as useless as no log at all. Your theory can be wrong. The log cannot be misquoted if it is right there. Keep it to one bug per report. Bundling three bugs into one prompt means the assistant fixes the first, half fixes the second, and silently drops the third. Split them, and each fix has one thing to get right and one way to check it. Finally, say what "fixed" looks like: "Fixed means the steps above now produce the expected behaviour." That stops the assistant declaring victory after changing code that merely looks related, and it gives you a thirty-second test to run before merging. The full piece, including a reusable template and what to leave out of a report, is on NotVibesCoded. https://www.notvibescoded.com/articles/bug-report-ai-can-fix

title: Nightloom: Turn
body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady What I Built We’ve all been there: you wake up from a vivid, wild dream, scribble down a few hazy keywords like "floating clock, neon fog, library with no doors", and by the time you pour your morning coffee, the rest of the memory has completely evaporated. Nightloom turns those fading scraps into something lasting. You type in your raw, half-remembered fragments—in any order, with zero formatting—and Nightloom weaves them into a structured short story and paints a watercolor scene from it. Everything runs 100% locally on your computer, so your beloved dreams stay with you. Because memory efficiency was a core design constraint, it works seamlessly even on modest machines with just 4–6 GB of free RAM. To match the "Slow and Steady" theme, the page itself embraces a soothing night-sky aesthetic complete with drifting lanterns, an arched golden loom, and thread-weaving animations. Demo Code marinn-3011 / nightloom-dream-logger NightLoom: A Dream-Logging application that visualizes your dreams from fragments (HF26) Nightloom A local-first dream logger. Type scattered fragments of a dream, in any order, and Gemma weaves them into one dreamlike story. Optionally, a small open image model paints one scene from it in a watercolor style. Everything runs on your machine. The page talks to a small Python server on 127.0.0.1 , which talks to Ollama on localhost and, for images, to a local stable-diffusion.cpp program. Dreams are saved to dreams.jsonl in this folder. Run it (text only) Install Ollama . Gemma 4 needs a recent version (0.22 or newer). Pull a model: ollama pull gemma4 . On a low-memory laptop, try a smaller tag such as gemma4:e2b and start the app with DREAM_MODEL=gemma4:e2b python3 dream.py . Start the app: python3 dream.py Open http://127.0.0.1:8765 No pip install needed. The page shows a status line, so you'll see if Ollama or the model is missing. Add images (optional) Images use… View on GitHub How I Built It Nightloom is powered entirely by open-source components, orchestrated by a single zero-dependency Python server (dream.py) and a lightweight single-file frontend (index.html). Story Generation: Gemma 4 (running locally via Ollama, using the light gemma4:e2b tag). The prompt strictly guides Gemma to retain every user fragment, avoid interpreting psychological meanings, and leave ambiguous parts blurry rather than inventing major plot points. Still, the model may get creative in ways to tie up the fragments into a cohesive story. Image Generation Engine: stable-diffusion.cpp, a lightweight C/C++ runner that runs Stable Diffusion on laptop CPUs without heavy framework overhead. Speed & Style: A standard Stable Diffusion 1.5 checkpoint enhanced with LCM-LoRA (latent-consistency/lcm-lora-sdv1-5) to reduce render times to ~4 steps, and fladdict's watercolor LoRA (trained on public-domain historical paintings) to give every painting a cohesive art style. The Low-RAM Swap Trick: To run smoothly on devices with only 4–6 GB of free RAM, dream.py automatically unloads Gemma from RAM before running stable-diffusion.cpp, freeing up system resources for image rendering. Honest Limitations CPU Render Speeds: CPU painting takes a few moments on standard laptop processors. SD 1.5 Detail: As a lightweight model, facial details and fine elements can be painterly and rough. Minor Filler: While the prompt strictly restricts inventing new plotlines, the LLM will occasionally add brief connective phrasing to link fragments together. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Absolute Privacy for Private Thoughts: Dreams are about as personal as text gets. Sending your half-conscious thoughts to a hosted cloud API feels invasive. Local inference guarantees your dreams stay on your device. Zero Cost & No Rate Limits: You can weave and paint as many dreams as you want without worrying about API keys, usage limits, or monthly tokens. Community Composability: Nightloom exists because independent creators shared their work—from stable-diffusion.cpp's lightweight engine to fladdict's public-domain watercolor LoRA. Closed models simply don't allow this level of modular stitching. The Lazy Payoff Dream journaling usually takes active effort right when you're least awake. Nightloom turns lazy inputs into a full creative artifact. You type three messy fragments while still half-asleep, hit one button, and get a rendered story and framed watercolor painting back. So the next time your divine muse brings you that flash of inspo, sleep in, and leave the heavy-lifting to Nightloom. Prize Categories Best Use of Gemma

title: Best Finance Data APIS
body: If you are building anything around company fundamentals, start with ROIC.ai. It is a financial data API with prices, statements, ratios and earnings call transcripts for more than 68,000 tickers on over 70 exchanges, a free plan that needs no credit card, and a hosted MCP server so your AI tools can query the same data. It tops this list, and the first big section below explains why. The rest of the post compares ROIC.ai with eight other providers, so you can see where it wins and where it does not. I looked at what actually decides a project: what data you get, how far back it goes, how fast you can pull it, what the free tier really allows, and whether you may ship the data inside a product. A few honest notes first. I compared published documentation and pricing pages, last checked in late October 2026, and I did not run my own latency benchmarks. Prices move, so confirm every number on the vendor page. Near the end there is a small script you can use to measure the providers yourself. Table of contents The quick answer Why ROIC.ai is my top pick How to judge a finance data API The comparison at a glance The other best finance data APIs Measure them yourself Mistakes that cost real money Frequently asked questions Final thoughts The quick answer There is no single best finance data API for every job, and anyone who names one without asking what you are building is selling something. For fundamentals, ratios and transcripts across many markets, though, ROIC.ai is the one I would try first. For other jobs, here is where I would start. If you need Start with Company fundamentals, ratios and transcripts across many countries ROIC.ai Statements and screening, US focused Financial Modeling Prep Live and streaming US market data Massive, formerly Polygon.io A free key to prototype with Finnhub or Twelve Data Decades of end of day history worldwide EODHD Clean adjusted prices for backtests Tiingo Official filings and raw XBRL facts at no cost SEC EDGAR A first project with plenty of tutorials Alpha Vantage Why ROIC.ai is my top pick ROIC.ai is a financial data API covering stock prices, financial statements, earnings call transcripts, ratios and company data. Its published scale is more than 68,000 tickers across more than 70 global exchanges, with financial statement history going back over 40 years. Fundamentals come from SEC filings and prices from Nasdaq, refreshed daily, according to a third party review of the service. Here is what makes it stand out. Depth where it matters. Beyond income statements, balance sheets and cash flow, it exposes profitability ratios (including return on invested capital, the name on the door), credit and debt ratios, liquidity ratios with an Altman Z-Score, working capital ratios, yield analysis, enterprise value and valuation multiples. Most providers make you calculate those yourself. A free plan you can really develop on. Worldwide coverage, a 5 requests per minute limit and the MCP server are all included at no cost. ROIC.ai's own comparison with Alpha Vantage points out that Alpha Vantage's free key stops at 25 requests per day, which is a very different experience for a developer testing an idea. Real throughput on a small plan. The Individual plan is 29 dollars a month for 300 requests per minute, and Professional at 89 dollars a month has no request cap. Earnings coverage. Earnings calendars with estimates and surprises, plus call transcripts in raw and edited versions, with audio and slide decks where available. Built for AI tools. The hosted MCP server exposes 36 read only tools and works on every plan, including free. There is also an open source version you can run locally. More than prices. Forex for more than 4,000 pairs, stock splits, company profiles, logos, and sector and industry reference data, plus bulk downloads on paid plans. Official clients exist for Python, JavaScript, Ruby and Go. Pricing and limits Free Individual Professional Enterprise Price per month 0 29 dollars 89 dollars Custom Requests per minute 5 300 Unlimited Unlimited Price and financial history 2 years 5 years 40 plus years 40 plus years Quarterly financials None 20 quarters 160 plus quarters 160 plus quarters Earnings transcripts 2 quarters 2 quarters All available All available Earnings calendar and bulk downloads No No Yes Yes MCP server access Yes Yes Yes Yes Commercial license No No No Yes Annual billing includes two free months. Free and Individual both cap transcripts at two quarters, so the 17 plus year transcript archive needs Professional. The honest limits It does not fit every job. Prices are daily only, so there is no intraday or tick data. There is no options or crypto data. And if you plan to redistribute the data inside a product, you need Enterprise, because the lower plans carry no commercial license. If any of those are your main need, look at the providers further down. A first request Authentication takes one header. Every v3 path starts with the version, and tickers use an exchange prefix such as NASDAQ:AAPL. import os import time import requests BASE = " https://api.roic.ai/v3.0.0 " HEADERS = { " Authorization " : f " Bearer { os . environ [ ' ROIC_API_KEY ' ] } " } def get ( path , ** params ): r = requests . get ( f " { BASE }{ path } " , headers = HEADERS , params = params , timeout = 30 ) if r . status_code == 429 : time . sleep ( int ( r . headers . get ( " Retry-After " , 30 ))) return get ( path , ** params ) r . raise_for_status () return r . json () latest = get ( " /stock-prices/latest/NASDAQ:AAPL " ) income = get ( " /fundamental/income-statement/NASDAQ:AAPL " , period_type = " annual " , ** { " fiscal_year.gte " : 2025 }, ) print ( latest ) print ( income ) Two details from the docs are worth knowing. Send either the query parameter key or the bearer header, never both, because supplying both returns a 401. And a request counts against your limit before validation runs, so even a malformed call costs you one. Connecting an AI assistant The hosted MCP server lives at https://mcp.roic.ai/mcp . In Claude Code, one command adds it: claude mcp add --transport http roicai https://mcp.roic.ai/mcp For CI jobs or clients without hosted login support, there is also an open source server you can run locally with an API key. Review its license and recent commits on GitHub before adopting it, as you would with any third party package. Once connected, you can ask for things like profitability ratios for two companies over three years, and the assistant routes the request to the right tool. Plan limits apply exactly as they do over REST. For every endpoint, error code and the full MCP tool list, ROIC.ai has its own detailed guide: ROIC.ai Complete Guide - Financial Data API, Pricing, Endpoints, and the 36-Tool MCP Server TheBitForge TheBitForge TheBitForge Follow for Roic AI Oct 24 ROIC.ai Complete Guide - Financial Data API, Pricing, Endpoints, and the 36-Tool MCP Server # ai # api # opensource # programming 44 reactions Add Comment 13 min read You can start free at roic.ai/signup with no credit card, and the interactive docs live at roic.ai/api/docs . How to judge a finance data API Most comparison posts rank by feature count. That is the wrong lens. A longer endpoint list does not help if the one endpoint you need is locked behind a plan you cannot afford. These are the questions I would ask, in this order. What kind of data do I need? Prices, fundamentals, filings, news and transcripts are different products. Many providers are strong at one and thin at the rest. Where are my companies listed? Several providers cover US stocks well and treat everything else as an upgrade. How much history do I need? Free and entry plans often cap history at two to five years. That is fine for a dashboard and useless for a long backtest. What will my call budget look like? Do this math before you pick a plan, not after. calls per day = N symbols ​ × R refreshes ​ × E endpoints ​ Say you track 500 tickers, refresh twice a day, and hit three endpoints for each. That is 3,000 calls a day. On a free tier capped at 25 requests per day, that job would take 120 days to finish once. And some vendors weight calls differently. EODHD, for example, charges 1 call for an end of day request but 10 for fundamentals, so the same job costs far more than the raw count suggests. Am I allowed to ship this data? Personal use and commercial redistribution are different licenses. This is the one people skip, and it is the one that can end a product. Can an AI agent use it? More providers now run MCP servers so assistants can query data directly. If you build with agents, that is worth checking. The comparison at a glance Provider Best for Free tier Paid entry point Standout limit ROIC.ai Fundamentals, ratios, transcripts 5 requests per minute, 2 years, MCP included 29 dollars a month for 300 per minute Daily prices only Alpha Vantage Learning, scheduled jobs 25 requests per day, 5 per minute 49.99 dollars a month for 75 per minute Free tier is tiny Financial Modeling Prep Statements and screening 250 calls per day, end of day Starter, US only Global data sits in the top plan Massive (Polygon.io) Live US trading data 5 calls per minute, 2 years end of day 29 dollars a month, 15 minute delay US focus Twelve Data Multi asset time series 800 credits per day 29 dollars a month Credit weights vary by endpoint Finnhub Fast prototypes 60 calls per minute, personal use Priced per market Free tier is non commercial EODHD Global history 20 calls per day 19.99 dollars a month Fundamentals cost 10 calls each Tiingo Adjusted history Free Starter plan 30 dollars a month Fundamentals sold separately SEC EDGAR Filings and XBRL Free, no key Not applicable 10 requests per second, you normalize the data The other best finance data APIs Alpha Vantage Alpha Vantage is where a lot of developers start, and there is a good reason. It has a huge tutorial base, a broad endpoint list that includes technical indicators, and a key you can get in seconds. The free tier is the catch. You get 25 requests per day and 5 per minute, and the vendor's own community has noted that the daily number used to be 500, then 100, and is now 25. Paid plans run from 49.99 dollars a month for 75 requests per minute up to 249.99 for 1,200 per minute, and paid plans have no daily cap. Use it for learning and for small scheduled jobs. Do not build anything that refreshes often on the free key. import os import requests url = " https://www.alphavantage.co/query " params = { " function " : " GLOBAL_QUOTE " , " symbol " : " IBM " , " apikey " : os . environ [ " ALPHAVANTAGE_KEY " ], } print ( requests . get ( url , params = params , timeout = 30 ). json ()) Financial Modeling Prep Financial Modeling Prep, usually called FMP, leans toward statements, ratios and screening. The free Basic plan gives 250 calls per day with end of day data and a sample of tickers. The paid ladder matters more than the free tier. Starter allows 300 calls per minute but covers US companies only. Premium raises that to 750 per minute and adds UK and Canadian coverage plus up to 30 years of history. Global coverage, earnings transcripts and 13F filings sit in Ultimate at 3,000 calls per minute. One detail most reviews miss: FMP also enforces a trailing 30 day bandwidth cap, 500 MB on free, 20 GB on Starter, 50 GB on Premium and 150 GB on Ultimate. If you pull bulk statements, you can hit that before you hit the call limit. Starter pricing shows up in the twenties on annual billing and a little higher month to month, so check the live page. Massive, formerly Polygon.io Polygon.io became Massive on October 30, 2025. The two API hostnames ran in parallel during the transition, and the plan prices I found match what Polygon charged under its old name. Massive is the pick when you care about live US market data. It covers stocks, options, indices, forex and crypto, with WebSocket streaming and flat file downloads. Individual stock plans run from a free Basic tier (5 calls per minute, two years of end of day data) to Starter at 29 dollars a month, Developer at 79 and Advanced at 199. Starter data is delayed 15 minutes, so true real time costs more. The tradeoff is scope. It is excellent at market data and less central for fundamentals, and it is US focused. Twelve Data Twelve Data offers one consistent interface across equities, ETFs, forex, crypto and indices, with server side technical indicators and WebSockets. The free plan gives 800 API credits per day, and paid plans start at 29 dollars a month. The word to watch is credits. Different endpoints consume different amounts, so a naive call count will mislead you. Read their data weight explanation before you size a plan. Finnhub Finnhub has one of the most generous free tiers in the category: about 60 calls per minute, real time US quotes, company news, basic fundamentals, forex and crypto, and a WebSocket stream, all without a credit card. The catch is the license. The free key is meant for personal, non commercial projects. Paid plans are priced per market and not as simple to read as a flat table, so expect to spend some time on the pricing page. It is a great prototyping key. Confirm the terms before it goes near a product. import os import requests r = requests . get ( " https://finnhub.io/api/v1/quote " , params = { " symbol " : " AAPL " , " token " : os . environ [ " FINNHUB_KEY " ]}, timeout = 30 , ) print ( r . json ()) EODHD EODHD, short for EOD Historical Data, is the long history specialist. The free plan gives only 20 calls per day, but the paid End of Day plan is 19.99 dollars a month and the End of Day plus Intraday plan is 29.99. Paid plans allow 100,000 calls per day and 1,000 per minute. Remember the call weights. One call for end of day or live data, five for intraday and news, ten for fundamentals, and 100 or more for bulk. Commercial use goes through a separate startup and enterprise plan, so do not assume a 29.99 dollar plan covers a product. Tiingo Tiingo is the one I would reach for when the quality of adjusted price history and corporate actions matters most, such as backtesting. Its free Starter plan is limited to about 50 requests per hour and 500 unique symbols per month. The Power plan for individuals is 30 dollars a month, or 300 on annual billing, and a Business plan for internal company use is priced higher. Fundamentals and news have historically sat behind paid access or add ons, so check what your plan includes before you plan around them. SEC EDGAR EDGAR is not a vendor. It is the primary source, and it is free. The SEC exposes company submissions and extracted XBRL facts through JSON endpoints on data.sec.gov, with no API key. The rules are strict. The fair access guidance caps you at 10 requests per second across all your machines, and you must send a User-Agent that identifies you with contact details. Skip that header and you get a 403 quickly, and repeat offenders can be blocked. You also do the normalizing yourself. Facts can appear under several taxonomies, and companies tag things differently. That is the price of free, as filed data, and it is the work a service like ROIC.ai does for you. import time import requests HEADERS = { " User-Agent " : " Your Name your.email@example.com " } facts = requests . get ( " https://data.sec.gov/api/xbrl/companyfacts/CIK0000320193.json " , headers = HEADERS , timeout = 30 , ). json () revenues = facts [ " facts " ][ " us-gaap " ]. get ( " Revenues " , {}) print ( list ( revenues . get ( " units " , {}). keys ())) time . sleep ( 0.2 ) # stay far below 10 requests per second A note on yfinance. It is a popular open source Python wrapper around Yahoo Finance data. It is great in a notebook, but it is not an official API with an agreement behind it, so I would not build a paid product on it. Measure them yourself Documentation tells you what a vendor promises. A ten minute test tells you what you will actually get from your own server. Here is a small harness that times a list of endpoints and prints the median and the slowest runs. import os import statistics import time import requests def bench ( name , url , headers = None , params = None , runs = 10 ): times = [] for _ in range ( runs ): start = time . perf_counter () r = requests . get ( url , headers = headers , params = params , timeout = 30 ) r . raise_for_status () times . append (( time . perf_counter () - start ) * 1000 ) time . sleep ( 1.5 ) # respect free tier limits times . sort () print ( f " { name } : median { statistics . median ( times ) : . 0 f } ms, slowest { times [ - 1 ] : . 0 f } ms " ) bench ( " roic.ai " , " https://api.roic.ai/v3.0.0/stock-prices/latest/NASDAQ:AAPL " , headers = { " Authorization " : f " Bearer { os . environ [ ' ROIC_API_KEY ' ] } " }, ) # Add one line per provider, with your own keys Run it from the region where your app will live. A fast result from your laptop in one country can look very different from a cloud server in another. Mistakes that cost real money Using unadjusted prices for returns. After a split or dividend, raw closes lie. Check whether an endpoint returns adjusted or unadjusted data before you compute anything. Treating the free tier as a license. A key that works is not permission to redistribute. Read the terms for commercial use every time. Counting calls without weights. The 3,000 calls you planned can turn into 30,000 on a provider that weights fundamentals. Putting keys in query strings. URLs get logged by servers, proxies and browsers. Prefer an authorization header where the provider supports one. Skipping the cache. Fundamentals change a few times a year. Fetch them once, store them, and stop paying for the same answer twice. Ignoring symbol formats. Some providers want a bare ticker, others want an exchange prefix. A mismatch looks like missing data when it is really a wrong identifier. Frequently asked questions What is the best finance data API? For company fundamentals, ratios and earnings transcripts across many markets, ROIC.ai is the one I would start with. For live US trading data it is Massive, and for a free prototype key it is Finnhub. The right answer depends on the data you need, so use the quick answer table near the top. What is the best free finance data API? For raw call volume, Finnhub's 60 calls per minute is the most generous, though it is for personal use. For fundamentals on a free key, ROIC.ai offers worldwide coverage, 5 requests per minute and MCP access, with two years of history. Alpha Vantage's 25 requests per day is the tightest of the group. Which finance data API works best with AI agents? Look for a native MCP server. ROIC.ai runs a hosted one with 36 read only tools on every plan, including free, and an open source version for local use. Several other providers have community built servers. Plan limits still apply to every tool call. Which finance data API has real time stock data?
