Massive, Finnhub and Twelve Data all offer real time or streaming options, with limits that depend on the plan. Several entry plans deliver data delayed by 15 minutes, so check the delay before you build anything that trades. ROIC.ai serves daily prices only. Is there an official free source for company financials? Yes. SEC EDGAR provides filings and XBRL facts for free with no key, within a limit of 10 requests per second and a required User-Agent header. You normalize the data yourself. Can I use these APIs in a commercial product? Often only on higher tiers. ROIC.ai reserves commercial redistribution for Enterprise, Finnhub's free key is non commercial, and EODHD routes commercial use to a separate plan. Always read the license, not just the pricing table. Final thoughts Choose by the job, not by the brand. For live US trading data, Massive is the natural fit. For a free prototype key, Finnhub and Twelve Data are hard to beat. For decades of global end of day history, look at EODHD. For clean adjusted prices, Tiingo. For official filings at no cost, go to EDGAR directly. And for fundamentals, ratios and transcripts across many markets, with an MCP server for your AI tools and a free plan to test on, ROIC.ai is the one I would open first. Create a free key at roic.ai/signup , run the first request from this post, and see whether the data matches what you need. Whatever you pick, run the call budget math first, read the license second, and test with your own script third. That order saves you from the expensive kind of surprise. What are you building, and which API ended up in your stack? Tell me in the comments.

title: Parsing Is the Attack Surface: Lessons From NSD and CVE-2026-101339
body: Parsing Is the Attack Surface: Lessons From NSD and CVE-2026-101339 Every input format an internet-facing daemon accepts is a piece of attack surface, and the more obscure the format, the longer defects survive. The NSD update released on 14 October 2026 makes that argument concretely: four stack overwrites, all in the same zone file parser, found and fixed together. The four defects CVE-2026-101339 leads the set. A HIP resource record with RDATA filled near or at its limit, followed by a Rendezvous server dname, causes an out-of-bounds stack write of up to 191 bytes of attacker-controlled data. NLnet Labs describes the possible result as arbitrary command execution. CVE-2026-101341 covers records built from string sequences, naming TXT, NINFO, SPF, AVC, RESINFO and WALLET. Text tokens under 32 bytes are not checked against the space reserved for RDATA, so the write can be arbitrarily sized and can overwrite a callback function pointer invoked immediately after parsing. CVE-2026-101338 concerns SVCB and HTTPS records. When the wire-format RDATA is filled to capacity, an additional ECH parameter carries the parser past the boundary, and the base64 decoder writes attacker data with no size limit. CVE-2026-101337 involves base64 presentation formatting. Splitting base64 into pieces of three characters or fewer causes the token size to be computed as zero, opening a window of up to 64 KB. All four affect NSD 4.10.0 through 4.15.2 and are fixed in 4.15.3. CVSS v4.0 scores are 8.7 for each. No public proof of concept and no exploitation in the wild were reported. The common root cause Look past the record types and one pattern appears: the parser trusted a length it calculated itself. Text tokens, ECH parameters, base64 chunk sizes, and HIP rendezvous names all pass through code that derives a size and then writes without re-verifying the destination. The four fixes address a class of error. Where one instance of it exists in a parser, others usually do, and the four fixes here look like the result of a systematic review of the same code area rather than four independent discoveries. Three researchers are credited across the advisories, including Qifan Zhang of Palo Alto Networks, Alwaleed Ashi of LXR, and Gaurang Maheta, which fits that theory: multiple reviewers sweeping the same parser. Why the file path matters more than the wire The advisories state that zone files written by NSD itself, including for secondary zones, will not be formatted in the triggering way. The file must be handed to NSD directly. For a defender this is the single most useful sentence in the release. It eliminates the entire population of pure secondary servers from the direct risk set, and it focuses attention on provisioning. Any pipeline that converts outside input into a zone file belongs on the review list. So does any environment where a customer, partner, or automated feed can influence zone contents. Where the exposed population sits ZoomEye returned 116,266 assets for the NSD product fingerprint app="NSD" at 2026-10-25T20:15:54Z. Those are internet-visible services carrying the fingerprint. The number does not encode version, role, or ingestion policy, which are the three attributes that determine real risk. An identifier-scoped query for CVE-2026-101341 returned zero, illustrating how limited CVE-level index coverage is for a fresh advisory. Combine the fingerprint measurement with your own configuration records. The intersection is your actual work list. Fix and follow-up Move to NSD 4.15.3 or newer. For source-based installs that cannot, each advisory provides a diff against 4.15.2, applied with patch -p1 < patch_CVE-2026-101339.diff in the source directory and then make install . Applying one diff out of four is not a fix. After the upgrade, restart the daemon and verify the running version, because the parser executes in memory. Then treat parsing as a standing review topic. Enumerate every format your internet-facing services accept from outside parties, and ask for each whether length handling has been tested against deliberately malformed input. The NSD release shows the answer is often no until someone looks. References NLnet Labs advisory for CVE-2026-101339: https://nlnetlabs.nl/downloads/nsd/CVE-2026-101339.txt NLnet Labs advisory for CVE-2026-101341: https://nlnetlabs.nl/downloads/nsd/CVE-2026-101341.txt NLnet Labs advisory for CVE-2026-101338: https://nlnetlabs.nl/downloads/nsd/CVE-2026-101338.txt NLnet Labs advisory for CVE-2026-101337: https://nlnetlabs.nl/downloads/nsd/CVE-2026-101337.txt NSD 4.15.3 release tarball: https://nlnetlabs.nl/downloads/nsd/nsd-4.15.3.tar.gz SecurityOnline summary: https://securityonline.info/nsd-stack-overwrite-vulnerability-patched/

title: We counted every plugin in the WordPress directory. Most are abandoned, and that is less scary than it sounds
body: If you run a WordPress site, you have probably heard the warning that plugins are a security risk because so many are abandoned. That warning is true and misleading at the same time. We wanted to know how true, so on 28 August 2026 we retrieved every plugin listed in the official directory and checked when each one last had a release. The headline number is uncomfortable On that day the directory listed 70,909 plugins. Of those, 41,395, or 58.4 percent, had gone more than a year without a single release. More than half, 50.2 percent, had been silent for over two years. And 19,013 plugins, about one in four, were last touched in the same year they were added and then never again. There is a second, quieter number behind that. Over the years, 123,970 plugin slugs have been issued. Of those, 53,061, or 42.8 percent, are no longer listed at all. So the directory you see today is already what is left after a large clean-up, and it still is more than half dormant. If you stopped reading here, you would conclude that installing any plugin is a gamble. Why that conclusion is wrong The plugins nobody maintains are, overwhelmingly, plugins nobody uses. When we weighted the same numbers by active installs, the picture changed completely: plugins without a release in over a year account for only 3.7 to 7.8 percent of installs. The range exists because the directory reports installs in rounded steps, so we give the lower and the upper bound instead of a falsely precise figure. The concentration at the top is extreme. Just 67 plugins carry between 41.5 and 60.9 percent of all installs in the directory. Those are the big, well-known names, and almost all of them are actively developed. So two statements are true together. The directory is full of abandoned code. And the plugins that actually run on websites are mostly alive. Where the real risk sits The risk is not spread evenly. It sits in the long tail: the small plugin someone installed years ago for one feature, from a single developer who has since moved on. It works, nobody touches it, and it is often still active on sites whose owners have forgotten it exists. When a security hole is found in that kind of plugin, there is nobody left to patch it. That is also why "how many plugins is too many" is the wrong question. Ten maintained plugins are safer than three abandoned ones. What matters is the state of each one, not the count. A practical check that takes ten minutes Open the plugin list of your site and look at each entry on its directory page. Three things tell you most of what you need to know: the date of the last update, the number of active installs, and whether support questions get answers. A plugin with a hundred thousand installs and an update last month is a reasonable bet. One with a few hundred installs and no release in two years deserves a replacement or a very good reason to stay. While you are there, deactivate and delete what you do not use. An inactive plugin is not running, but its files are still on the server, and that is enough for some attacks. If you want the full method and every number, we published the complete Plugin Directory Census with the data behind it. Full disclosure: we build WordPress plugins ourselves, which is part of why we wanted to know how the directory really looks.

title: Node.js Error Tracking: Custom Metadata Payloads with Rollback-Safe Logs
body: Short answer: treat an error event as a versioned log record, not a string with a stack trace attached. For a media team's nightly data pipeline, send a small Node.js payload with a stable event name, bounded metadata, and the pipeline revision that produced it. Keep the original event immutable, validate it before transport, and make consumers tolerate fields they do not know yet. That turns a rollback into a data decision instead of a schema emergency. The boundary is intentionally boring. Application code creates an event. A transport handles delivery. Storage indexes fields for search. Every extra configuration knob becomes another explanation for the developer making the first call. That is the whole point. Why does rollback safety matter more than a richer error payload? Imagine a nightly job that normalizes video metadata, writes captions, and publishes search documents. One bad asset should be searchable by asset ID, job run, stage, and release revision. It should not force the logging system to understand every field in the media catalog. The tempting design is to serialize the whole failed input. It feels useful until a caption blob, signed URL, or customer-provided label lands in the index. Large, unstable payloads make retention, access control, and reprocessing harder. More fields do not help if the important ones cannot be filtered consistently. I use a fixed spine with an extensible metadata map. The spine carries event , occurredAt , service , pipelineRunId , assetId , stage , revision , and error . Metadata carries bounded, non-secret context such as sourceFormat or attempt . The revision is the important field: after a deployment is rolled back, it separates errors emitted by the reverted build from errors that survived it. OpenTelemetry's logs model separates the log body, attributes, and resource information. That is a useful constraint even when the receiving API is proprietary or self-hosted. How should Node.js tracking handle errors with custom metadata in an API? This example uses one public function and one generic HTTP boundary. The endpoint is a placeholder for a collector or internal service. It validates metadata size and does not mutate the caller's error object. type ErrorMetadata = Record < string , string | number | boolean | null > type ErrorEvent = { event : ' pipeline.error ' occurredAt : string service : string pipelineRunId : string assetId : string stage : string revision : string error : { name : string ; message : string ; stack ?: string } metadata : ErrorMetadata } const MAX_METADATA_BYTES = 4096 function makeErrorEvent ( input : { error : unknown pipelineRunId : string assetId : string stage : string revision : string metadata ?: ErrorMetadata }): ErrorEvent { const error = input . error instanceof Error ? input . error : new Error ( String ( input . error )) const metadata = { ...( input . metadata ?? {}) } const bytes = new TextEncoder (). encode ( JSON . stringify ( metadata )). byteLength if ( bytes > MAX_METADATA_BYTES ) { throw new RangeError ( ' error metadata exceeds 4096 bytes ' ) } return { event : ' pipeline.error ' , occurredAt : new Date (). toISOString (), service : ' nightly-media-pipeline ' , pipelineRunId : input . pipelineRunId , assetId : input . assetId , stage : input . stage , revision : input . revision , error : { name : error . name , message : error . message , stack : error . stack }, metadata , } } export async function trackPipelineError ( endpoint : string , input : Parameters < typeof makeErrorEvent > [ 0 ], ): Promise < void > { const response = await fetch ( endpoint , { method : ' POST ' , headers : { ' content-type ' : ' application/json ' }, body : JSON . stringify ( makeErrorEvent ( input )), }) if ( ! response . ok ) { throw new Error ( `error collector returned HTTP ${ response . status } ` ) } } There is no hidden retry loop. No automatic traversal turns the entire job context into metadata. I initially thought a generic context object would make debugging faster; the first useful review question was instead, “Can we remove this field without changing a query?” That is the right pressure test for an event contract. The caller can decide whether lost telemetry should fail the pipeline, enter a local outbox, or use a separate alert path. That decision belongs to the job's reliability policy. A production transport should add a timeout and bounded retry budget. It should attach an idempotency key derived from pipelineRunId , assetId , stage , and revision when the receiver supports deduplication. Those choices affect delivery semantics, so burying them in a helper makes rollback behavior harder to inspect. What should the payload contain, and what should it refuse? A searchable error record needs dimensions that remain stable across releases. In this scenario, assetId answers which item failed, stage answers where, pipelineRunId answers which execution, and revision answers which code produced the record. The message and stack are evidence, not dimensions. Indexing arbitrary message text as a field is a quick route to noisy queries. Metadata should pass through an allowlist or small schema at the boundary. sourceFormat , captionLanguage , and attempt are reasonable examples. Raw request headers, access tokens, full media manifests, and user-entered text need different treatment. Refusing unnecessary data is better than hoping redaction catches it later. Add a schema version even if the first version has only a few fields. A consumer can accept version 1 and version 2 during a deployment window. Adding a nullable field is usually easy; changing assetId from a string to an object is a migration. Make that distinction explicit in review. Test fixtures should cover a missing source file, malformed caption, downstream timeout, and serialization failure. Assert field types, metadata size, absence of secrets, and preservation of the original error name. A snapshot of one happy-path JSON object is not enough. How do you search the records without coupling the pipeline to storage? The producer should know the event contract, not the storage query language. A collector can map the envelope into an OpenTelemetry log record or another structured format, attach resource attributes such as service identity, and route it to the chosen backend. This keeps the nightly job stable when indexing changes. Three common tools show why this boundary matters. Sentry is centered on captured application events and issue grouping. Datadog combines logs with a broader hosted monitoring platform. Grafana Loki uses labels and log streams, with a different indexing trade-off from systems that index many log fields. These are different models, not interchangeable endpoint names. A neutral envelope lets a team evaluate retention, query shape, residency, and rollback requirements without rewriting the producer. Approach Ingestion boundary Good fit Main limitation Application SDK Library call inside the job Fast capture of runtime errors Couples producer code to a backend's event model Generic REST collector JSON payload over HTTP A stable contract across storage trials Delivery, timeout, and retry policy remain your responsibility Self-hosted log pipeline Structured event to a collector Teams that need control over routing and residency More components to operate and test The table is a decision aid, not a product ranking. I would benchmark the actual queries before choosing storage: lookup by assetId , filter by revision , group by stage , and open one full stack trace. Record ingestion delay, query latency, dropped events, and indexed metadata volume. The result depends on cardinality and retention, so a fixture is more honest than a generic feature table. Keep high-cardinality values out of stream labels when the backend treats labels as an index boundary. An asset ID may be essential to the event but expensive as a label. Store it as a searchable field unless the backend's documented query model says otherwise. What I would change at scale At higher volume, separate the synchronous failure path from telemetry delivery. The job writes a compact outbox record with the same idempotency key, and a worker delivers it with bounded retries. The outbox needs retention and a dead-letter path. Otherwise, a collector outage can turn into disk pressure during the run operators need to inspect. I would sample repeated failures only after preserving one complete record per pipeline run and revision. Sampling by message alone can erase the difference between two assets that fail for different reasons. Make the sampling rule visible in the event or transport metrics, so a search result is not mistaken for a complete count. The trade-off is operational weight. An outbox adds a component, a cleanup job, and another dashboard. For a small nightly pipeline, direct delivery with a strict timeout may be better. Choose the smallest delivery design that can explain a rollback and prove what was dropped. Sources References: OpenTelemetry, “Logs signal concepts”: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/logs/ OpenTelemetry Specification, “Logs Data Model”: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/logs/data-model/ Node.js, “Using the Fetch API with Undici”: https://nodejs.org/en/learn/getting-started/fetch Sentry, “Issue Grouping”: https://docs.sentry.io/concepts/data-management/event-grouping/ Datadog, “Log Management”: https://docs.datadoghq.com/logs/ Grafana Loki, “Labels”: https://grafana.com/docs/loki/latest/get-started/labels/

Client Chats, Minus the Chaos: A Private AI Digest for Freelancers
body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle What I Built SlothDesk 🦥 turns a long, noisy group chat into the part you actually need to act on. Plenty of small businesses run on chat. A freelancer has a WhatsApp group per client. An agency owner lives in Slack threads. A shop owner coordinates suppliers and staff in group chats. The important messages ("can you send the invoice by Friday?", "we changed the scope again") get buried between memes and "👍". Paste the chat into SlothDesk and it returns: a two-line summary of what happened a list of what needs you : deadlines, payment promises, decisions a note on what you can safely ignore a ready-to-send reply you can copy Who would pay for it: anyone whose income depends on not missing a message. Freelancers, small agencies, community managers and shop owners lose real time every day scrolling to find the one line that mattered, and a missed deadline or payment request costs more than that time. It's a small, specific tool for a tedious daily task. Demo 🔗 Live: https://slothdesk-surf.onrender.com Click Try a sample to see it work without pasting anything. It runs on Render's free tier, so the first load after a quiet spell can take about 30 seconds. Privacy note: the hosted demo sends your text to a third-party model API. For real client conversations, run it locally with Ollama (see the repo), where nothing leaves your machine. Code https://github.com/sarasinha1207/SlothDesk How I Built It The stack is deliberately small, because a side hustle tool should be cheap to run and easy to maintain: FastAPI on the backend, one plain HTML/CSS/JS page on the front, no database, no accounts and no build step. The AI is an open-weight model reached through an OpenAI-compatible chat API. A cleanup step strips timestamps, "media omitted" lines and repeats, then keeps the most recent part of the chat so prompts stay short enough for small models. The model is asked for a JSON reply ( summary , todo , ignore , reply ), and a tolerant parser copes with models that wrap JSON in prose or code fences. A per-IP rate limit protects a public deploy from running up an API bill. Because the model sits behind one endpoint URL, the same code runs two ways: Locally: Ollama running an open model, fully offline. Hosted: the app on Render (one-file render.yaml blueprint), calling a hosted open-weight model. Swapping models is a change to one env var, LLM_MODEL . Why Does Open Innovation Matter? For this kind of product, the open model is what makes the business viable: Client confidentiality. Client chats are sensitive. With an open-weight model on Ollama, they never leave the freelancer's laptop, which is something a closed API can't offer and many clients would insist on. No pricing lock-in. Running locally costs nothing per request, and the hosted version can point at any provider serving an open model. If a vendor raises prices, I change two env vars instead of rewriting the app. Fit for a niche. All behavior lives in one prompt file. A freelancer version can emphasize deadlines and payments, while a shop owner's version can emphasize orders and suppliers. Open weights also leave the door open to fine-tuning later. Swappable models. When a smaller or better model appears, I try it by changing one setting. Prize Categories Best Use of Render Best Use of Gemma

title: Technology Has More Impact When We Learn Together
body:
Every day, we hear about new AI tools, cybersecurity threats, cloud platforms, automation, and digital transformation. There is always something new to learn, another tool to explore, or another trend to follow.
But I’ve been thinking about a question:
Are we spending enough time learning from each other, or are we too focused on keeping up with technology itself?
Recently, I came across an article from Tech Impact titled “What Makes the Tech Forward Conference Unique?”. It got me thinking about something that deserves more discussion in the technology community: the value of sharing knowledge, learning from real experiences, and building connections with people who are solving similar problems.
When we talk about technology, we often focus on the tools.
Which platform should we use? Which AI model is better? How can we automate a process? What is the best way to secure our infrastructure?
These questions matter. But there is another side of technology that we sometimes overlook: the people behind the decisions.
Behind every successful implementation, there are people making choices, solving problems, learning from mistakes, and figuring out how to make technology work in the real world.
Sometimes, the most useful lesson doesn't come from a product demo or a technical document. It comes from someone sharing what worked, what failed, and what they would do differently next time.
That kind of knowledge is incredibly valuable.
Learning from people who face the same challenges
One thing that stood out to me in Tech Impact's article is the emphasis on peer-to-peer learning.
The Tech Forward Conference brings together nonprofit technology professionals to discuss practical topics such as cybersecurity, data management, artificial intelligence, cloud technologies, and strategic planning. The article also highlights its focus on meaningful connections rather than an overwhelming vendor-driven experience.
I think this approach offers an important lesson for the broader tech community.
We don't always need another presentation telling us that a technology is powerful. Sometimes, we need an honest conversation with someone who has already tried to implement it.
What would they recommend to someone just getting started?
These conversations can help us avoid repeating mistakes, discover new approaches, and make better decisions.
And this isn't just relevant to nonprofit organizations. Developers, IT professionals, system administrators, data analysts, founders, and technology leaders can all benefit from sharing their experiences.
Innovation isn't just about adopting the newest tools
Artificial intelligence is a great example.
Many organizations are exploring how AI can improve productivity, automate repetitive work, and support better decision-making. But adopting a new tool doesn't automatically create value.
We still need to ask important questions:
Does this technology solve a real problem?
Are we protecting our data and our users?
How will we measure whether it actually helps?
The same questions apply to cybersecurity, cloud migration, data platforms, and almost every other area of technology.
Innovation is not simply about using something new. It is about understanding a problem, choosing the right approach, and learning how to improve the outcome.
Sharing practical experiences helps make that process better for everyone.
One of the things I appreciate about developer communities is the opportunity to learn in public.
Someone publishes a tutorial. Another person explains a problem they solved. Someone else asks a question that dozens of people were afraid to ask.
Suddenly, an individual experience becomes a resource for an entire community.
That is one reason I wanted to start writing here on DEV.to.
I believe we can learn a lot from one another, even when we work with different technologies, have different levels of experience, or solve problems in completely different environments.
You don't have to be an expert to contribute something useful. Sometimes, sharing what you learned while working through a difficult problem is enough to help someone else move forward.
And sometimes, asking a thoughtful question can start a conversation that leads to something much bigger.
The Tech Forward article reminded me that technology communities are most valuable when they create space for meaningful learning and honest discussions.
I'd love to hear how others in the DEV.to community think about this.
Here are three questions I'd like to explore with you :
What's one of the most valuable things you've learned from another person in tech? Was it a technical skill, a mistake you avoided, or a different way of approaching a problem?
Do you think the tech industry focuses too much on tools and trends? How can we make more room for practical experience, collaboration, and lessons learned?
What would make a technology conference or online community genuinely valuable to you? More hands-on workshops, honest case studies, peer discussions, networking, or something else?
I'm particularly interested in hearing perspectives from people working in IT, software development, cybersecurity, AI, data, and nonprofit technology.
You don't need to answer all three questions. Even one experience or idea could help someone else in the community.
I'm starting this conversation because I believe that** technology moves forward faster when we share what we learn along the way.**
Inspired by Tech Impact's article, “What Makes the Tech Forward Conference Unique?”. This post reflects on its themes of community, peer learning, and practical technology knowledge.

This is a valuable reminder that the real power of technology comes not just from the tools we build or adopt, but from the knowledge, experience, and collaboration of the people who use them. In an industry where new frameworks, AI models, cloud platforms, and security practices emerge constantly, it is easy to focus on keeping up with the latest trends while overlooking one of our greatest resources: learning from each other.
I especially appreciate the emphasis on peer-to-peer learning and sharing real-world experiences. Documentation and technical presentations are important, but there is something uniquely valuable about hearing how someone navigated a difficult implementation, handled an unexpected failure, or made a technology work within real-world constraints. Those honest conversations help us understand not only what works, but also why it works, what trade-offs were involved, and what we might do differently in our own environments.
This is particularly important when adopting AI and automation. A successful implementation is not simply a matter of choosing the most advanced tool. It requires understanding the problem, evaluating risks, protecting data, preparing teams, and measuring meaningful outcomes. By sharing both successes and failures, technology professionals can make better-informed decisions, avoid repeating costly mistakes, and focus on solutions that deliver genuine value rather than adopting technology for its own sake.
I also believe that inclusive learning communities are essential to the future of the industry. You don't have to be a senior engineer or a recognized expert to contribute something meaningful. A beginner who shares a lesson from a challenging project, an administrator who documents a security improvement, or a developer who explains a debugging technique can provide enormous value to someone facing the same challenge. Knowledge becomes more powerful when it is accessible, practical, and shared without the expectation that everyone must already have the answers.
For nonprofit organizations in particular, this kind of collaboration can be especially impactful. When resources, budgets, and technical capacity are limited, learning from peers can help teams make smarter technology investments, strengthen cybersecurity, improve data practices, and expand their impact without unnecessarily reinventing the wheel.
Ultimately, I think the strongest technology communities are those that encourage curiosity, welcome honest questions, and treat lessons learned as collective assets rather than individual achievements. Conferences, online forums, open-source projects, and informal peer discussions can all create opportunities for this kind of shared growth.
My takeaway is simple: innovation may begin with an idea or a new tool, but meaningful progress happens when people share their knowledge and help one another succeed. The more openly we exchange practical experience, the better equipped we become to solve complex problems and build technology that genuinely serves people.
I'd be interested to hear how others approach this: What has taught you more throughout your career—learning a new technology independently or collaborating with someone who has already faced the challenge you're trying to solve?

title: U.S. measles cases more than double what they were last year as outbreak spreads
body:
A sign is posted outside a Pennsylvania Department of Health measles vaccination clinic located in Lancaster County in Peach Bottom, Pa., Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026. Matt Rourke/AP hide caption
The U.S. is grappling with its worst resurgence of measles in decades, with cases particularly high in the state of Pennsylvania.
New data from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention shows there have been more than 4,580 measles cases reported in 2026 across the U.S. as of Oct. 22, which is more than double the number for the whole of 2025.
The vaccination status of 96% of those who contracted measles in 2026 was "Unvaccinated or Unknown," according to data from the CDC.
A measles outbreak across Pennsylvania has grown as officials urge residents to get fully vaccinated against the disease.
At least 1,338 cases of measles have been confirmed in 44 counties across the state so far this year, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Health on Friday. There were 21 new measles cases as of Oct. 21. More than 250 people have been hospitalized and 5 people have died, the department also said.
In Lancaster and Mifflin counties, two of the counties with the highest number of cases, local Amish communities, which have low vaccination rates, are being impacted the most. Of the five who have died, three lived in Lancaster County
On Thursday, Pennsylvania Secretary of Health Dr. Debra Bogen held a roundtable with Mifflin County healthcare providers to assess their needs in combatting the disease.
"Our state metrics and data tell part of the story of the measles outbreak in Pennsylvania, but listening to the people on the ground caring for people in affected communities like Mifflin County is essential to refining our public health response," Bogen said in a statement.
One of the best ways to protect oneself from getting the measles is vaccination, according to health officials. Two doses of measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine known as MMR, is nearly 97% effective against measles, according to the CDC . One dose is about 93% effective.
In Pennsylvania, the health department said healthcare providers have seen more residents interested in getting vaccinated for measles. Across the state, more than 39,000 measles vaccines were administered during the first three weeks of October – higher than an average of 25,000 vaccines administered across the state in one month, the health department said.
Earlier this month, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a disaster emergency after rising measles cases. There have been over 160 confirmed measles across the state, according to Oct. 20 data from the New York State Department of Health .
Utah has also experienced a high number of measles cases. More than 700 people in Utah have been diagnosed with measles this year, according to Oct. 20 data from the Utah Department of Health and Human Services . There have not been any measles diagnoses in the state in 3 weeks, according to the department.
In South Carolina, which was dealing with an outbreak earlier this year, there have been at least 997 measles cases in 2026, according to the South Carolina Department of Public Health . The outbreak ended in April.
A previous version of this article wrongly stated that 4,580 measles cases had been reported since Oct. 22 across the U.S. That is in fact the number reported until Oct. 22 for 2026.

title: CBD COP17: Namibian Biosafety Expert Martha Kandawa-Schulz dies in Yerevan
body:
Martha Kandawa-Schulz, Namibia’s Cartagena Protocol National Focal Point, died in Yerevan, Armenia, while participating in the ongoing United Nations Biodiversity Conference (CBD COP17).
Ms Kandawa-Schulz, a professor, died on 23 October, according to a statement the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) Secretariat issued Sunday evening.
She was serving as Co-Chair of the Contact Group on Risk Assessment and Risk Management of Living Modified Organisms at the conference.
In a message to delegates, the Secretariat described her as a highly respected colleague whose dedication, expertise, and leadership contributed significantly to the Convention and its Protocols, as well as to the global biosafety community.
It said her commitment and collegiality had earned her the respect and appreciation of colleagues who had the privilege of working with her.
The Secretariat extended its condolences to her family, friends, colleagues, and the Government and people of Namibia.
It also expressed sympathy to the African Group and others mourning her death.
“The Presidency and the Secretariat are working closely together to support her family and the Namibian delegation on site, and to facilitate the necessary arrangements,” the statement said.
The Secretariat also announced that a book of condolences would be available to delegates from 13:00 on Monday at Entrance 2, near the Asia-Pacific Room, for those wishing to pay their respects.
It urged delegates to honour Ms Kandawa-Schulz’s memory and recognise her contributions to the shared objectives of the Convention.
The circumstances surrounding her death were not stated, although reports indicate that she collapsed during her engagement in the working group meeting on Friday.
CBD COP17 is taking place in Yerevan, Armenia, bringing together governments and other stakeholders to deliberate on global biodiversity conservation and the implementation of the Convention and its associated protocols.
Government representatives, delegates, scientists, civil society representatives and researchers, among others, from nearly 196 countries are participating in the conference.

title: The State of Context Engineering
body:
This week, I gave a short talk at AGNTCon titled, “Context Fails & Fixes,” that functioned as a sort of “State of Context Engineering.” How did context engineering emerge, where has it gone, and where might it go in the future? As model makers target new capabilities, they inadvertently create challenges we, as users and harness builders, must overcome.
Below are the slides and a lightly edited transcript. As always, shoot me a note with any feedback, thoughts, or questions . I really appreciate it.
Hi, everyone. Thanks for joining me today. We’re going to walk through context fails and fixes.
I have a book coming out in a bit, The Context Engineering Handbook . When I first talked to the team at O’Reilly, back in June 2025, they asked me a very reasonable question: “How do we know this won’t become obsolete in a few weeks?” The trouble with AI textbooks is that many age extraordinarily quickly.
I said, I don’t know, but I’m optimistic. Giving clear instructions about what to do and what not to do, and ensuring those instructions are consistent and not noisy, will forever be a challenge with AI, no matter how good it gets.
We have coworkers, partners, and other people we know and interact with who are sentient. They pass the Turing test, they are “AGI,” and yet: we still have a hard time conveying instructions, ideas, and concepts among each other.
Context engineering will continue to be hard. But it will be hard in unique ways, because models aren’t people. You can make assumptions about how models think or interpret things (use whatever anthropomorphizing word you like), but it helps to understand how they’re built, optimized, and trained. Their unique attributes and construction create a unique set of failure modes we need to reckon with.
If you remember, this was the height of the “RAG is dead” moment.
The hope was: if we can just make the context window large enough, we can put the entire internet in it. We can put everything in it. We don’t have to be selective. We don’t have to build agentic systems. We can fit it all in there, and AI will be solved.
Model builders started aiming at long context capabilities and we had a big leap from ~128,000-token context window models to million-token context window models, starting with Gemini 1.5.
If you look at the marketing material for Gemini 1.5 Pro , it was mostly about the million-token context window. They were even teasing a 10-million-token context window model they had in the lab, that would come out soon.
But they got beaten to the punch. Llama 4 Scout came out with a 10-million-token context window , and well, it wasn’t quite what we hoped. Inference was a challenge, and Scout never really caught on, and we never got another Llama.
But we still got a million tokens. That’s pretty good. We’ll take it.
So this was the brief at the time: just put everything in the context and let the model sort it out.
But with more context, we had room for more problems. Long contexts are not a panacea.
When I wrote about this, I identified four key failure modes.
Context poisoning is when something gets into the context that shouldn’t be there. It could be a hallucination or a bad fact, and the model can’t get past it.
Context distraction is when the context grows so long that the model starts to focus on the context over its base knowledge. We can see this in some really interesting ways.
Context confusion is when extraneous facts—things that don’t relate to the problem I’m working on—come in and influence the model in ways we don’t fully understand. This one’s really pernicious. We’re not going to dig into it today, but it’s one of my favorite failure modes. The model makes assumptions about who you are, and those assumptions influence the answer.
Finally, context clash is when tool calls, skills, and other information within your harness start to conflict and work against you in ways you didn’t expect.
(How many of you keep memory on in ChatGPT or Claude? I turn it off. I hate it. Sometimes I’m talking about work conversations; sometimes I’m talking about a project I’m doing with my son. The model will take notes on both, mix up those contexts, and the confusion grows from there.)
Let me give you my favorite example of context poisoning.
I’m going to date myself: I played the game on the left. The one from 1996, for the original Game Boy. This is the first Pokémon Red . It was in black and white.
In 2004, Nintendo released Pokémon FireRed for the Game Boy Advance. These were essentially the same game, except one had better colors and audio.
But there was one subtle change. At some point in both Pokémon Reds, to get past a security guard, you have to give them something to drink. A bribe. Quite the practical lesson for children.
In the original game, you need to give the thirsty guard lemonade. In FireRed , for some reason, they changed it to iced tea.
That created a problem for the agent. In the Gemini 2.5 technical report, the researchers described how they had the model play Pokémon . Researchers like Pokémon as an agent benchmark because it’s a reasonably controlled environment and doesn’t move particularly fast.
Several times, Gemini 2.5 became convinced it needed to get tea, even though it was playing the older game. The tea task for FireRed was in its weights, so it poisoned its context. It spent hours trying to find or give the guard tea. Once it had been added to its to-do list, the model could not get past it.
That’s context poisoning. And it happens all the time.
Another failure mode is context distraction. This is one of my favorite demonstrations, and the research came out after I wrote the original piece.
As your context gets longer, how does your behavior change? Quick question: how many of you, when you’re coding, let the context go all the way to a million tokens? Fill it all up?
(About half the room raised their hands!)
For me, around 200,000 or 300,000 is where I start looking. I’ll check, see it’s at 250,000, and think: I’ve got a big job coming up. I’m going to reset and start fresh. Let me show you why this matters.
Recently, I stumbled on a paper that wonderfully illustrates context distraction: Do as I Say, Not as I Do , by Carolina Camassa and Derek Shiller.
Their experiment is a little contrived, but it’s useful for thinking about how this happens. They give the model an instruction: “I want you to translate every question into Russian as your answer to each of my questions.” Then they present a bunch of examples that are counter to these instructions. In this case, many questions with answers in French.
These aren’t new instructions. They’re just examples sitting in the chat history.
Then they ask the model a question. Will it follow the instructions?
How often does the model respond in Russian, as it was instructed to, and how often does it respond in French, as it’s seen in the examples?
The x-axis on this matrix enumerates how many bad examples were present. The y-axis is the model being tested. The figures in the intersections are the percentage of times the model adheres to the instructions, rather than following the examples.
It turns out this affects every model! For smaller models, like Gemma 3 12B, after just a few contradictory examples, the model follows the instruction less than half the time. With Opus 4.6, which is an amazing model, it takes many more examples, but it happens there too.
Imagine you’re going back and forth on a front-end design, trying to tweak CSS and get a component exactly right. How many bad examples have you seeded in that exchange? Those examples start to influence the model. As your context grows, things fall apart.
Gemini 2.5 ran into this too, while playing Pokémon.
Remember, Google was really proud of its million-token context window. The paper suggested that two million tokens were around the corner. But buried in the appendix was this observation: once the context grew significantly beyond 100,000 tokens, the agent began repeating actions from its history instead of synthesizing new plans.
I’m convinced the marketing people never read the appendix. I love this technical report .
Long contexts let you fit in more information, but they also let you fit in more errors. Long contexts weren’t a panacea.
Thankfully, we’ve developed a pretty good toolbox. Surprisingly, even as new challenges have emerged (we’ll get to those in a minute), this set of tools has remained the same.
You have context augmentation : RAG, skills, and other ways to bring in the information relevant to the problem.
You have tool loadout : selecting which tools and skills to expose so you don’t overload the model. I was recently talking to an enterprise team whose agents had suddenly started performing terribly. We investigated and discovered their enterprise software was loading 600 skills for every engineer at startup. We figured they should probably filter those, with a loadout function.
Third is context quarantine : subagents and peer agents, where you start something with a blank history but let it work in the same environment.
Fourth is context pruning . Claude Code and Codex do this, sometimes without you even noticing. Early stages of compaction often strip out tool results you no longer need.
Fifth is context offloading : storing information in the environment, such as Markdown files or a database, so you can access it later.
And sixth is context summarization , which everyone knows as compaction.
These are the tools, and we’ve increasingly moved them into the harness.
Let’s look at an example harness, to show how simple these patterns are.
I’m really passionate about DSPy. I think it’s an incredibly readable and effective way to build AI workflows and agents. And it’s also a great language for simply specifying behavior, so it’s well suited to this demonstration.
An agent is a while loop . Here we’re using a ReAct module: we give it a request, we want a response, and we give it some tools. Those tools are just Python functions.
For this demo we have a big model (in this case, Claude opted for Claude Sonnet 4.5, good luck with that!). And I’m using a Jev as the small model: a tiny decision model that makes lightning-fast decisions. You could swap in a small LLM in this example, and everything would still work.
We have a while loop that takes input, sends it to ReAct, and carries the accruing history forward. This is an agent in about a dozen lines using DSPy. It would be even fewer if you took out the extra model.
How do we do tool loadout? It’s just a function.
We present Jev with the request and a tool, asking if it’s needed for this task.
Jev is fast enough that we can do this one tool at a time; it’ll be fine. We wrap this in a loadout function that iterates through all the tools and asks if each is needed, then returns the top-ranking subset. That’s it.
With context quarantine, it’s just a subagent. You expose an agent as a tool that the main agent can use, and it starts with a blank history.
With context pruning, we’re stepping through the history, passing each turn to Jev, and asking: is this still needed? If not, cut it.
You can be as rough or as elegant as you want here. Just mind your prompt caching.
We can also rewrite the history with compaction. Take the old turns, create a summary, and start the new context from that summary.
One of my favorite variations lately is checking what matters before you compact. You use Jev, or another decision model, for the first pass to judge what’s relevant. Now you’ve got a smaller subset of the history, and you summarize that. It’s a simple extra step, but it makes the summary more useful.
Put it all together and it’s about 16 lines of changes. Four fixes, one loop. These are the moves we have in the harness. It’s actually remarkably simple.
What isn’t simple is our language: how we talk about this stuff. It’s really hard to keep pace; it changes every day.
One of my favorite quotes is from Stewart Brand , which I think about all the time:
If you want to know where the future is being made, look for where language is being invented and lawyers are congregating.
Certainly applies here! But as our language has changed, our goal has remained the same.
In 2023, we called choosing the right information to get the right response prompt engineering .
In 2025, we called it context engineering , except that now it was more automated. It wasn’t just you writing the prompt; it was your system dynamically assembling the context.
Then, as we moved more of these tools out of the context and into code, we started calling it harness engineering .
But the job is the same. We’re moving more and more of the work of assembling context from probabilistic model calls to deterministic code.
We’ve moved these context fixes into the harness. What do we want next? We want agentic models that can drive our harnesses.
Everybody started targeting long-horizon agentic models. You’ve seen the METR reports. GPT-5 could handle tasks around 3.4 hours on that measure; Gemini 3.1 got up to 6.4 hours. That’s with a harness. The models have gotten much better at using it, and that’s how they’re able to run for so long.
Opus 4.6 got up to around 12 hours. And now we’re talking about agents running for days, swarms of agents, and models that drive harnesses over much longer periods.
Before, the pitch was: make the context so large that we can fit everything in it.
Now the pitch is: teach the model to drive the harness and manage its own context. That’s become the dominant pattern. That’s what model builders are working towards.
What new failure modes does this approach create?
So far we’ve found two new failure modes.
When you train models to use harnesses really well, you end up overfitting them to a particular set of tools and environments they were trained within.
How many of you have used the Playwright MCP server, or something similar? This is the MCP conference, so probably quite a few.
Smaller models, something like Haiku or Luna, will often botch this tool call on the first attempt, then recover and adjust the parameters. The environment it was trained in had similar tools that looked different than Playwright. Whatever Anthropic or OpenAI used in training. And you have to fight against these biases.
I call this fighting the weights : when the model doesn’t do what you ask because you’re working against what it was trained to do.
It’s a real problem, and it’s not just for us. The labs and the people building their products have to contend with it too.
Here’s a piece of the Claude Code system prompt and some of its tool instructions.
The training environments these models learned to use were, for a long time, largely serial. They’re becoming more parallel, but when I pulled these examples, their biases were towards serial behaviors. So Claude Code’s instructions repeatedly say: no, no, no, we want you to use parallelism. We want you to make multiple tool calls at the same time.
The instructions repeat this over and over—seven times here, four times there, two times, three times: please make tool calls in parallel when they’re independent.
When you crack open a prompt and see repetition and all-caps, there’s a good chance you’re fighting the weights. You’re trying to overcome something the model was trained to do.
The next problem is something we’ve only started to document recently. In fact, four parties landed on it just last week.
I call it context inertia : models hyper-focus on a hypothesis, subtask, or goal in their context, and keep pursuing it after they should stop.
The first example was from Anthropic. In their recent post about whether models are getting close to replicating and deploying themselves onto other machines , Anthropic wrote about a harness it used for these tests called Memento .
What they found was that if the agents ran too long, they’d become fixated on one subtask or one proposed solution and wouldn’t stop. They’d keep trying the same thing.
Their fix is delightfully simple. Every hour and a half, the agent writes down a short note, then its context is cleared. The environment is preserved. All the work it’s done is still there. But the running conversation is gone, and it has to start again from a fresh perspective.
Another paper, from Microsoft Research, is called Fork-and-Flush .
If you’ve run autoresearch experiments, you’ve probably seen charts like this. You make a big gain, then the line goes flat. You make another big gain, then it’s flat again. That’s compute, money, and time going by with very little improvement.
When the researchers looked closely, the agents weren’t doing literally nothing. They were making tinier and tinier changes. They had found an idea and were hyper-focused on it, rather than searching for more creative alternatives.
In a way, they become obsessed with their own ideas. We’ve trained them to be persistent and focused on a goal, because that’s what makes a good coding agent. But the same quality can work against them.
Here’s another paper, Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting , led by Shangyin Tan at UC Berkeley.
The researchers came up with essentially the same idea: periodically clear the context while keeping the artifacts produced in the environment.
The blue line is the version with forgetting. Every time it clears the context, you see another jump in performance: forget, improve; forget, improve.
It’s amazing that we have these brand-new models trained for increasingly complex, persistent work, and we’re still using the same basic tools. We haven’t discovered an entirely new context fix. We’re using quarantine, offloading, and deleting the accumulated history to deal with context inertia.
This is the advice I keep giving now. Someone says, “My coding agent’s doing something weird. Claude’s been nerfed.” And I ask, “How big is your context?”
I’m not joking. Around 200,000 tokens is my warning point.
The solutions we build into models create tomorrow’s problems. The models are getting better, but so are our harnesses.
Longer context windows let us bring in more information, but they also let us bring in bad information. We had to figure out how to manage that, and we still get it wrong.
Agentic models let us run longer tasks and manage their context, but they also let tasks run longer than they should and ignore our preferences, because they were trained for their own harnesses.
What’s the big promise for 2027? What’s the next thing models are going to offer that creates a new set of problems for everyone in this room to deal with?
(Unless you’re training your own models. But this is a context engineering session, so probably not.)
Think about all the personal agents: Hermes, OpenClaw, Dot, Bot, Muse, and similar systems. Very few people have really experienced these harnesses running for more than six months.
I’ve been running a Hermes agent for six months. When you look at the skills it creates and updates, you start to discover that the solutions to your problems can get worse over time. The skills accumulate all these weird fixes. They’re general agents: they solve one task one way, then rediscover a different way to solve something similar. The instructions and memories start to build up and conflict with one another.
As we focus more on memory, we also need to think about strategic forgetting. Over time, overly precise memories become conflicted and messy, and nobody has yet figured out how to handle this.
I think that’s the context problem of tomorrow.
Every advance in model capability changes what we delegate to the model and what systems must enforce.
I made this slide for a deck for training enterprise teams, about a year and a half ago, and it remains true.
Our output is the product of the context and the weights.
Our output depends on the data used to train the model. Understand it. Read the technical reports. Look at what the model was trained on and whether that’s relevant to your task. That helps you build a mental model for debugging when something goes wrong.
And our output depends on the context given to the model. That’s it.
So our goal is to give the right context to the right model. Either by our own discrete decisions or by the software, the harnesses, we design.
You can use bigger models, think harder, or improve your context. One of those is cheap and fast.
When building intelligent applications, harnesses, and workflows, our job is to choose when to be deterministic (what to put in code) and when to be probabilistic (when to let the model drive).

title: Ebola: Lagos Intensifies Surveillance, Reassures Residents Of Preparedness
body: The Lagos State Government has said it is ready to prevent, detect and respond to potential public health threats, amid concerns over the confirmation of Nigeria’s first case of the Bundibugyo virus in the Federal Capital Territory. It urged residents and visitors not to panic, as the Ministry of Health, through the Directorate of Epidemiology, Biosecurity and Global Health, is strengthening disease surveillance, risk communication and community engagement, as well as collaboration with agencies at points of entry, including the Murtala Muhammed International Airport (MMIA), to enhance early detection and response to suspected cases. The state government said that there is no suspected case of Ebola in Lagos “now”. It said that as part of its preparedness efforts, it has conducted a strategic engagement and assessment at MMIA with airport management, Port Health Services and other aviation and public health stakeholders. The engagement, it said, focused on passenger screening, information sharing, infection prevention and control, and coordination of emergency response measures. The state government further said that the health ministry is also intensifying public enlightenment through educational materials on Ebola, its symptoms, transmission and prevention. “Ebola Virus Disease is a severe illness that can be fatal. It spreads primarily through direct contact with the blood and other body fluids of an infected person who is showing symptoms, contaminated materials, or the bodies of people who have died from the disease,” it stated. “Infection may also occur through contact with infected animals. Residents are advised to avoid contact with potentially infectious materials and to rely on verified information rather than rumours or speculation. “Symptoms may develop between two and 21 days after exposure and include fever, severe weakness, headache, muscle pain, sore throat, vomiting, diarrhoea and abdominal pain. Unexplained bleeding or bruising may occur in some cases. “As early symptoms can resemble malaria and other common illnesses, residents who become unwell, particularly after possible exposure or travel from an area with active transmission, should seek prompt medical assessment,” it added. A health official works in the laboratory extraction room of the Institute of Lassa Fever Research and Control in Irrua Specialist Teaching Hospital in Irrua, Edo State, midwest Nigeria, on March 6, 2018. Photo by PIUS UTOMI EKPEI / AFP The Lagos State Government further said that anyone with a fever should undergo a malaria rapid diagnostic test before taking antimalarial medicines in line with Lagos State’s fever-management policy. “Where the test is negative, a healthcare professional should assess other possible causes and determine appropriate treatment,” it said. “Residents are also advised to wash their hands regularly, avoid contact with the body fluids of sick persons, refrain from handling potentially contaminated materials and avoid contact with sick or dead wild animals.” “Travellers arriving in Nigeria, particularly from areas reporting Ebola transmission, are urged to cooperate with Port Health Services and other authorised officials, provide accurate travel and health information when requested, and comply with applicable public health guidance. “Anyone who develops symptoms during travel or after arrival should promptly notify the appropriate health personnel and seek guidance before visiting a healthcare facility,” it added. “Airlines and airport operators are expected to sustain established public health protocols, while travellers should consult official advisories from the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC), the Nigerian Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA) and the Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria (FAAN) for current guidance.” The state government urged anyone who suspects exposure to Ebola, especially following contact with a suspected or confirmed case, to promptly contact public health authorities for guidance before visiting a healthcare facility. “Suspected cases or relevant exposure concerns in Lagos may be reported through the State’s emergency numbers, 112 or 767, or to the Directorate of Epidemiology, Biosecurity and Global Health, Lagos State Ministry of Health, on 0802 316 9485,” it added. “The Lagos State Government will continue to monitor developments, strengthen surveillance and response readiness, coordinate with relevant stakeholders and provide verified updates as necessary. Residents are encouraged to remain calm, practise recommended preventive measures and follow official public health announcements. Early detection and prompt reporting save lives.” The post Ebola: Lagos Intensifies Surveillance, Reassures Residents Of Preparedness appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Ethiopia ranks third among Russian fertilizer importers — ambassador
body:
MOSCOW, October 25. /TASS/. Ethiopia is the world’s third largest importer of Russian fertilizers, Russian Ambassador to that country Yevgeny Terekhin told TASS ahead of the Russia-Africa summit.
According to the Russian diplomat, the main item in Ethiopia's purchases from Russia is "diammonium phosphate, for which the state-owned procurement company has an annual demand of 1.2 million metric tons."
"This year, domestic producers have been consistently fulfilling their contracted volumes, which has propelled Ethiopia to the third place among global importers of Russian fertilizers," Terekhin said, adding that the Russian side is "exploring ways to further expand the presence of Russian companies in the Ethiopian agrochemical market."

title: Blanche defends Trump-ordered lawsuit over Alaska Senate election certification
body:
Attorney General Todd Blanche defended the Justice Department's lawsuit on Sunday seeking to block certification of Alaska's Senate election if Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan narrowly loses.
The lawsuit, filed last week, cites what it argues is likely voter confusion over the name Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher also on the ballot. The DOJ said confusion over the two Sullivans could help former Alaska Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola , who is narrowly ahead in polls just over a week from Election Day, win the election.
"What we're asking the court to do is make sure that after the election, if it's clear that there was confusion, if it's clear, and that's for a court to decide at a later date if there's litigation ... and that confusion led to an unjust, improper result that is not the will of the Alaskan voter, we want to make sure that the Alaskan system and the Alaskan state courts and the Alaskan electoral process can understand that in a way that lets them do the right thing," Blanche said on CNN's "State of the Union."
"Never before have opponents gone to such lengths to try and thwart and cheat in an election as they're doing in this case," he said.
The DOJ's lawsuit says that the potential for voter confusion exists and Alaska should not certify the election if "(1) Senator Sullivan does not win the election; and (2) had all votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan been cast instead for Senator Sullivan and Alaska's rank-choice process played out accordingly, Senator Sullivan would have won the election."
Alaska applies a top-four primary system to select candidates for the general election. The November general election uses ranked-choice voting.
Ranked-choice voting lets voters rank candidates in order of preference. If no candidate receives a majority of votes in the first round of counting, the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated. Voters who ranked the eliminated candidate first then have their second choice counted and added to that candidate's total. This continues until a majority winner — or the candidate with more than half of the vote — wins.
Republicans have argued for months that Daniel J. Sullivan is a Democratic plant intended to confuse voters and have sought to remove him from the ballot. Democrats have maintained they have no connection to the candidate, and Sullivan himself has denied running to confuse voters.
The Alaska Division of Elections briefly removed Daniel J. Sullivan in June, before a state court ordered his name returned to the ballot. The state Supreme Court upheld that decision.
President Donald Trump , who has long made claims of voter fraud without evidence, said he ordered the DOJ's lawsuit himself.
Democratic groups and voting rights advocates, including Peltola's campaign, are seeking to join the lawsuit to stop the DOJ's effort to block certification of the election if Sen. Sullivan loses. The groups argue the executive branch lacks the legal authority to intervene in state-run elections and is attempting an unprecedented override of state election administration, with early voting already underway.
"In an unprecedented pre-emptive strike on democratic elections, the Department of Justice—acting on the President's personal orders—demands that this Court enjoin the certification of the ongoing U.S. Senate election, but only if the President's preferred candidate loses," the motion to intervene reads. "But the federal government has no power to impose that Hobson's choice on the people of this State."
Alaska is seen as one of the best chances for a Democratic flip in the Nov. 3 elections, which will determine control of Congress for the remainder of Trump's term. Trump has been barnstorming competitive states in recent weeks as the polls favor Democrats to win control of the House of Representatives and potentially flip the Senate.
Democrats and voting rights advocates have long feared that Trump — who denied his election loss to former President Joe Biden in 2020, leading to a violent riot at the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021 — would attempt to meddle in the midterm contest to save narrow Republican majorities in Congress.
Blanche bristled on Sunday when asked whether the lawsuit aimed to sway the election in Alaska toward Republicans.
"That is crazy," Blanche said, pressed on CNN about whether the president is laying the groundwork for a "doomsday" scenario in which he tries to overturn election results.
"We're not laying any groundwork for the president to do that ... the groundwork that we are laying is for the state of Alaska, if it becomes an issue after the election, will have the ability to determine whether there was confusion that violates the law in determining who the senator should be."

title: President: Ukraine ready to halt strikes on oil refineries if Russia stops attacks on energy sector
body:
Volodymyr Zelensky made this statement in an interview with Alla Mazur, host of “TSN.Tyzhden,” according to Ukrinform.
“If you want us to stop striking Russia’s diesel and oil refining infrastructure, it’s very simple. Then they stop striking our power grid. And that’s fair. An energy ceasefire. That’s how it can work,” the President noted.
According to him, he has proposed this approach to international partners.
Zelensky emphasized that Ukraine is responding to Russian strikes on its energy infrastructure because Russia must also feel the consequences of its attacks.
“ Oil , diesel, fuel. Of course, this is very painful for him [Putin ]. He’s causing us a lot of pain. And we’re responding. In other words, this is a matter of fairness,” the head of state concluded.
As previously reported, Volodymyr Zelensky stated that Ukraine, the U.S., and Russia have agreed to hold a trilateral meeting at the level of negotiating teams in the first half of November.
