It is also important to distinguish between promoting government activities and ensuring public accountability. A responsible communication strategy must make information accessible, explain policies, provide verified updates, respond to emergencies and enable citizens to understand public expenditure and project implementation. It should communicate achievements while remaining open to scrutiny over delays, challenges and shortcomings. That is why Kebbi’s development story must be assessed through facts rather than assumptions about the number of times its Governor appears on national television. The administration’s education programmes, healthcare interventions, road projects, workers’ welfare initiatives, agricultural investments and other development activities should be examined on their merits, with claims verified against available records and measurable outcomes. Anwar’s own article acknowledges several of these initiatives, yet he uses the alleged lack of national visibility to condemn the professionals communicating them. This is the central contradiction in his argument. If the information is available to him, it is reasonable to ask whether his assessment has adequately considered the channels through which it has been disseminated. There is, of course, room for continuous improvement. Kebbi can strengthen its public information systems, expand access to project data, maintain a comprehensive digital archive, improve emergency communication and deepen engagement with national and international media organisations. Such measures would advance both visibility and accountability. But identifying opportunities for improvement is different from alleging wholesale professional failure. If Abba Anwar is seeking recognition, relevance or an appointment from any government, he should pursue such ambitions through professional merit, constructive engagement and evidence-based contributions, rather than resorting to what amounts to an attempt to blackmail a Governor’s media aides through sweeping allegations of incompetence. No individual’s desire for recognition should become a justification for misrepresenting the work of public officials or presenting unverified statistics as authoritative findings. This observation is not a substitute for examining his arguments on their merits; rather, it underscores the need for professional criticism to remain evidence-based, fair and free from insinuations designed to discredit others. The fact that Anwar writes from Kano does not invalidate his right to comment on Kebbi. However, it is reasonable to expect anyone undertaking such an assessment to familiarise himself with the realities on the ground, engage relevant stakeholders and examine the state’s media environment comprehensively before reaching sweeping conclusions. A serious assessment should be informed by direct engagement and verifiable information, not assumptions about what is happening in another state. Ultimately, Anwar’s article raises a legitimate question about how Kebbi can expand its national media presence, but it fails to establish that the Governor’s media aides are incompetent or that the state is invisible. Its statistics require verification, its causal arguments remain unproven, and its conclusions are far broader than the evidence presented. Kebbi’s development story belongs to its people, and communicating that story is a shared responsibility involving government media professionals, independent journalists, broadcasters, editors and digital publishers. The media team has made deliberate efforts to strengthen these relationships, including visits to major media organisations and initiatives to secure sustained coverage of the state’s development activities. These engagements reflect a continuing commitment to ensuring that the achievements of Governor Nasir Idris across all sectors are documented, communicated and brought to the attention of the wider Nigerian public. The team will continue to pursue this responsibility with professionalism, determination and a clear understanding that effective public communication is essential to keeping citizens informed about government policies and development programmes. There may always be more work to do, but it is unfair to transform the pursuit of greater visibility into an allegation of wholesale professional failure. Kebbi is not invisible. Its development story is being communicated, its media engagement is evolving, and its publicity efforts deserve to be evaluated through verifiable evidence rather than sweeping generalisations. The appropriate challenge to Abba Anwar is straightforward: publish the methodology behind the alleged media audit, substantiate the figures presented and undertake a comprehensive review of the state’s actual media coverage. Until then, his conclusions should be treated as opinions requiring verification, not as an authoritative verdict on the performance of Kebbi State’s media team. The ultimate test of Governor Nasir Idris’s administration remains the extent to which its policies and projects improve the lives of Kebbi’s people. Public communication has an important role in making those efforts understood, but neither governance nor professional competence should be judged through unverified media rankings. Kebbi deserves fair criticism, objective assessment and responsible public discourse—not a manufactured crisis of invisibility. Jombali is the Special Adviser on Public Enlightenment and Orientation to the Executive Governor of Kebbi State.

title: UK arrests pro-Palestinian activist for spitting on statue of British MP murdered in terror attack
body: A pro-Palestinian activist was arrested on Friday after posting a video on TikTok showing someone spitting on a statue of murdered British lawmaker David Amess, according to multiple news outlets.Essex Police said they arrested a man in his 30s in Westcliff-on-Sea, Essex, on Friday after receiving a report about the video on Wednesday and launching an investigation.The BBC reported that police questioned the man on suspicion of criminal damage and a public order offense, and he remained in custody.In the now-deleted TikTok video, a person was seen approaching the statue and saying, “These people were just bowing to this p----.He voted for the Iraq War. Shame.”A second clip showed a person pointing at the monument and saying “shame” before spitting in the statue's face.The TikTok user, who goes by the name "Angry Jesus," initially denied being the person in the footage.“It wasn't me who spat on Sir David. But if I catch the person who did it, I'll… #grrrrrr,” he wrote in the video's caption, The Telegraph reported.The Telegraph added that other videos posted to the account featured criticism of Israel and expressed pro-Palestinian views.British MP murdered in 2021 terrorist attackAmess, from former prime minister Boris Johnson's Conservative Party, was murdered in 2021 by Ali Harbi Ali, the son of a former media adviser to a Somali prime minister. Police classified the killing as a terrorist attack.A spokesperson for the Amess family condemned the video, saying, "To see his memorial treated in this way is deeply upsetting," according to the BBC.This is a sickening and disgusting act committed by a vile individual. Sir David was respectful, kind and a powerful advocate for free speech and expression. He always debated political differences with dignity. To disrespect his life and legacy in this way is dreadful.— Priti Patel MP (@pritipatel) October 21, 2026Dame Priti Patel, the MP for Witham and former UK home secretary, also condemned the footage in a post on X/Twitter, calling on Essex Police to investigate the “disgusting and offensive act” after the video was posted on social media on Tuesday.“Sir David was respectful, kind and a powerful advocate for free speech and expression. He always debated political differences with dignity.“To disrespect his life and legacy in this way is dreadful.”

title: Lula wins 4th term as Brazil's president, but Bolsonaro rejects results
body: Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a vocal critic of President Trump, was reelected Sunday in a result that provides relief to critics of Mr. Trump and keeps some distance between Latin America's biggest economy and Washington.With 100% of the vote counted, Brazil's electoral court announced that the soon to be 81-year-old Lula had a lead of nearly 4.4 million votes over opponent Flávio Bolsonaro, giving him 51.8% of the total vote. Bolsonaro quickly refused to concede defeat and asked for the election results to be annulled after an evening of chaos at some polling places that followed a last-minute decision to extend voting by two hours. That decision by a Supreme Court justice may trigger legal action by Bolsonaro.   Bolsonaro is the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, whom Lula defeated to take the presidency in 2022.Lula's triumph bucks a trend in Latin America, where increasing numbers of right-of-center presidential candidates allied with Mr. Trump have been winning, further extending the United States' influence in the region.Lula's victory leaves Mexico and Brazil, Latin America's two most populous nations, with left-of-center leaders.  It also means the nation with Latin America's largest economy, with a GDP of $2.6 trillion per year, will likely continue defying Mr. Trump's demands, despite the pressure of increased tariffs he imposed. The announcement kicked off a celebration of supporters in and out of the Sao Paulo hotel where Lula watched the count with first lady Rosângela da Silva, allies, and friends.Lula's victory, if confirmed by electoral authorities, will give him his non-consecutive fourth term as president. The next term begins on Jan. 5, 2027.It is the first time since Brazil's military dictatorship ended in 1985 that the second-highest vote-getter in the first-round elections won the presidency. Bolsonaro had 47% of the vote in the first round to Lula's 45%, a difference of 2.2 million votes. However, more than 33 million voters out of nearly 160 million did not turn out in the first round.A video published by Lula's campaign shows the veteran leader celebrating with first lady Rosângela da Silva and allies after his runoff victory was confirmed by Brazil's electoral court. Wearing star-shaped red glasses, he kissed his wife. Hundreds of his supporters began gathering on São Paulo's main artery to celebrate the victory.In addressing supporters, Lula expressed his gratitude to the Brazilian people, and pledged to respect all Brazilians, regardless of gender or religion. He also attacked Bolsonaro." "This was a defeat for denialism and lies. I must confess that every time I attended a debate, I felt embarrassed," he said. He also doubled down on his commitment to Brazil's sovereignty. "Either the homeland remains free, or we die for Brazil," he said. "This country will not accept being anyone's backyard." In Rio de Janiero, cars beeped their horns and a woman dressed in red — the color of Lula supporters — shouted "You lost! Cry harder!" to four men in yellow and green sipping beers, Bolsonaro's signature colors. A huge roar echoed in the street as the result was confirmed. Rodrigo Valentim, a 51-year-old businessman and supporter of Bolsonaro, said that another Lula government would harm the economy. He pointed to financial markets' positive reaction to the result of the first round, when Bolsonaro bested Lula."I don't understand how people can vote for Lula," he said. "The country is collapsing."Sunday's victory will likely be the last of the veteran leader's political career. Lula began his political career in the 1970s as a union leader. He then helped found the Workers' Party, which he represented as a presidential candidate three times until he finally won it in 2002. He was reelected four years later and was succeeded by one of his cabinet ministers, Dilma Rousseff, in 2010. She was reelected in 2014.Rousseff was impeached for accounting maneuvering in 2016 amid a sprawling corruption probe, which also ensnared Lula. He tried to run for president again in 2018 but was jailed in March after being convicted.  Lula was released from prison after 580 days and saw Brazil's Supreme Court annul his sentence after police found messages that showed the judge who convicted him was biased. He quickly became one of former President Jair Bolsonaro's biggest critics and narrowly beat him in 2022.  Lula admitted in 2024, two years into the job, that his administration had done little to earn the support of his voters.  Since he lost the first round, Lula reorganized his campaign, appealed to young voters, put millions of Brazilians on the streets to defend democratic values and his legacy, raised fears of another Bolsonaro administration and boosted several government initiatives.  Lula also defended Brazil's sovereignty and insisted that a Bolsonaro presidency would allow the U.S. to exert control over Brazil.  He joins Mr. Trump and Nicaragua's president, Daniel Ortega — all age 80 — as the oldest presidents in the Americas.Judge ruled to extend voting by 2 hoursThe electoral court's announcement ended an evening of confusion at polling places after Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin ruled three minutes before the scheduled end of voting to keep polls open for two more hours, following requests by both candidates. Lula's request came after issues with buses that provide transportation to polls in Sao Paulo and Salvador, two cities that tend to favor the incumbent. Bolsonaro's request was due to heavy rains in Brazil's south, where he was favored.In Brasilia, volunteers who oversaw the vote count at a school debated whether they needed to stay after the announcement to extend voting, but most left 15 to 20 minutes after polls closed and they had given count information to electoral authorities. At a polling station in Rio de Janeiro, the voting machines had already been switched off minutes after polls were set to close and couldn't be turned back on.  The decision delayed tallying the votes by two hours. It was unclear how many polling stations stayed open after the scheduled closing time.  Bolsonaro ally Nikolas Ferreira noted that Zanin, who made the decision, is Lula's former lawyer.Security and cost-of-living concernsLula, who first governed Brazil between 2003 and 2010, faced a tough reelection battle because of concerns about the cost of living and security. Bolsonaro made a tough-on-crime approach the cornerstone of his campaign and pledged to bring down food costs.Both had been hit by corruption suspicions involving family members and allies, with Bolsonaro implicated in a sprawling scandal rocking Brazil. Lula previously spent more than a year in prison on corruption convictions that were eventually annulled.Bolsonaro's admission that he accepted about $12 million from disgraced former banker Daniel Vorcaro to produce a film on his father's life has cast a shadow over his campaign. He is under investigation for corruption, money laundering and tax evasion in connection with the case.As Bolsonaro voted at a school in Rio de Janeiro, his supporters shouted "Lula, thief, your place is in prison" while Lula's supporters chanted in his support."The time of real change has arrived," Bolsonaro said. "Brazil can't go on for another four years on its current trajectory."In the lead-up to the vote, Lula frequently portrayed Bolsonaro, whose father is under house arrest for attempting a coup, as a threat to democracy. Bolsonaro has promised to seek an amnesty for his father if elected.Lula, trying to lure undecided voters, has invested in costly incentives. His government endorsed a debt relief program for small businesses and promised free public transportation on weekends. A major win then came when the Senate backed a popular proposal to end the six-day workweek.Lula thanked his voters for an outpouring of support while casting his ballot in the city of Sao Bernardo do Campo, where he began his political career as a union leader in the 1960s. "It is a lot of generosity, a lot of care, a lot of love. I will be forever grateful," Lula said.Lula voters respect his past; Bolsonaro voters want changeLula voters turned out Sunday driven by his history of supporting marginalized people and working to lift Brazilians out of poverty."Lula is a man of the people and he knows what it's like to be poor," Luzia da Souza, who runs a bar in Rio de Janeiro, said. "I find it impossible not to vote for him."Anderson Falcão, a 43-year-old journalist in Brasilia who sported a red shirt in support of Lula, said he worried about Bolsonaro's long-term political vision, which he called "exclusionary.""It's a project that harms the less fortunate, harms the worker, women, the forest, the Amazon," he said.Bolsonaro voters, many of whom wore yellow and green Brazil jerseys in support of the senator, said they wanted change."Things are really expensive and taxes are too high," Fabianne Borges Santoro, a 45-year-old physiotherapist in Rio de Janeiro, said. She added that she once voted for Lula's party but now associates it with corruption.Issues with public transportation affect the voteIn Bahia state, a stronghold for Lula, whose voters tend to live in areas that depend more heavily on buses, at least 75 public buses were prevented from leaving municipal garages during the presidential runoff vote, according to a state electoral judge. He ordered the arrest of the mobility secretary of the capital, Salvador, Pablo Souza, in relation to the case.Mayor Bruno Reis, a Bolsonaro ally, blamed trade unionists for illegally sticking Workers' Party materials onto transit vehicles for the measure.President of Brazil's Superior Electoral Court, Kassio Nunes Marques, confirmed that electoral authorities received a report on problems with buses in Bahia that is being analyzed. He did not confirm if voting would be extended, which Lula requested in Salvador and Sao Paulo, where issues with public transportation were also reported in the city with a mayor allied with Bolsonaro."We will not be robbed by mayors, governors or businessmen," Lula told the press. "These people need to respect democracy."Bolsonaro did not immediately comment on the issue.International observers earlier in the day said that voting was occurring peacefully and with transparency and did not immediately comment on the incident.The Trump administration looms largeLula criticized the U.S. president before Brazil's election, speaking about the risks of U.S. intervention in Brazilian elections after the Trump administration imposed high tariffs against Brazilian exports and classified drug-trafficking groups as foreign terrorist organizations. Experts say the moves may have been intended to make Lula look soft on crime.Bolsonaro has touted his proximity to the White House and insisted that Brazil needs to strike better deals with the Trump administration, including in the rare minerals economy. Brazil estimates that its deposits hold up to 21 million tons, second only to China. He denies he's being helped by the U.S. government.Mr. Trump said Sunday that he was watching the election but declined to endorse a candidate.

title: Netanyahu warns of sanctions, opponents warn of collapse: Who's scaring voters? - analysis
body: In the wake of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's comments on Friday about the possibility of using cryptocurrency to bypass economic sanctions, one thing is clear: someone is engaging in fearmongering just a few days before the election.The question is: Who is trying to frighten whom?Is it Netanyahu trying to frighten the public? At least that was the instant interpretation of some pundits after he discussed the matter on Friday in an interview with economic journalist Roy Katz on the Channel 10 economic program.But the full context matters.Katz asked whether Netanyahu was worried about the day after US President Donald Trump. Netanyahu answered, “Tell me, you're not worried?”After saying that the billions of dollars in US military aid would soon come to an end because the US had changed, Netanyahu added that Israel needed to understand that sanctions, including banking sanctions, were possible.“So you need to organize a bypass economy,” Netanyahu said. “You know, there are currencies that can bypass (sanctions). We are also working on that.”In looking at those comments, it is important to distinguish between what Netanyahu said and what was subsequently attributed to him.He did not present a crypto economy as his preferred option. He presented it as a contingency plan in the drawer for that rainy day.Preparing for such contingencies is part of a government's job. It does not mean that Jerusalem has thrown up its hands, resigned itself to widespread sanctions, and begun planning to disconnect Israel from the global economy.It means that if the country faces not a rainy day but a deluge of sanctions, the government wants something in the drawer to try to bypass them.Whether that something would work is a legitimate question. But it is a different question from whether Netanyahu wants to lead Israel into economic isolation.'Bibicoin' a threat to national security Because Netanyahu's campaigns have long warned of the diplomatic and military dangers awaiting the country if voters fail to support Likud, many in the media immediately saw this as the familiar pattern: he was scaring the public again.But it was not exactly clear how telling voters that Israel could face economic isolation after years under Netanyahu's leadership was supposed to draw them to his side. What was clear, however, was the frightening picture his opponents painted in response.Yashar party head Gadi Eisenkot called the “Bibicoin vision” a threat to national security – inflating a remark about a contingency plan into a full-blown vision.“After he finished dismantling Israeli society and weakening the IDF, Netanyahu has marked the next target: the dismantling of the Israeli economy for generations to come.”Marked the next target? Netanyahu spoke about preparing for possible sanctions. Eisenkot turned that into an intention to dismantle the economy.And then came the warning that if Netanyahu's “vision” were implemented, “Israelis will lose their pensions and all their investments, and many of them will leave the country.”Talk about trying to scare the voters.Naftali Bennett, too, got into the act, not to be outdone by his rival in the change bloc.“In [Netanyahu's] view, Israel will become a withdrawn and outcast country in the world, disconnected from the economy, academia, and the global technology, so that we will be forced to move to a crypto and isolated economy,” he said.The problem is that this is not what Netanyahu said. He did not say this was the future he wanted, or even that it would happen. He said Israel needed to prepare in case sanctions were imposed.Those statements are quite different. The opposition's responses simply erased what was originally said.Bank of Israel says cryptocurrencies cannot circumvent sanctionsThe Bank of Israel also weighed in, giving the controversy the added authority of the country's central bank. It said cryptocurrencies could not be used to circumvent sanctions.That is a substantive objection. If the proposed contingency plan cannot work, the public should know.But the bank did not stop there.“The right course for the Israeli economy is to maintain economic relations with our primary trading partners and to focus on preventing sanctions and their negative impact on the economy,” its statement said. “This is the responsibility of the political leadership, and it should act upon it.”Of course that is the right course. But who said otherwise?By setting out that course as a corrective to Netanyahu's remarks, the bank lent weight to the impression that he had proposed abandoning it: that instead of maintaining Israel's economic ties and preventing sanctions, the prime minister was preparing to retreat into a crypto economy.Yet saying that the government is working on a contingency plan does not mean it has raised the white flag on sanctions. Nor does it mean that Israel will stop working diplomatically to prevent them.Then came a group of 109 senior economists, the Economists' Forum for Democracy, which emerged from the 2023 protests against the judicial reforms, with a warning that banking sanctions would bring something approaching economic apocalypse.This, they said, would pertain to soaring unemployment, the disappearance of foreign investment, a collapse in Israel's global economic standing, unusable credit cards, no access to online retailers such as Amazon, and a mass departure of foreign workers unable to send money home.And Netanyahu was the one accused of frightening the public.The consequences of sweeping banking sanctions would plainly be serious. But discussing a fallback plan does not mean Netanyahu is announcing that sanctions are coming, much less choosing to bring them about, and presenting his remarks that way is itself peddling fear.None of this requires accepting that Netanyahu is above doing the same to win votes. Those looking for examples need not look far.On Sunday, he shared an AI-generated image on X/Twitter depicting a nuclear explosion over Tel Aviv, alongside a post by right-wing commentator Yuval Bloomberg warning that failing to elect a leader capable of confronting Iran could risk a “second Holocaust.”A nuclear explosion over Tel Aviv. A second Holocaust. Days before an election.That is fearmongering, and it deserves to be called out.But so does taking a contingency plan, calling it a vision, and warning voters that it will cost them their pensions, their investments, and their access to AliExpress.The opposition has enough real examples of Netanyahu's fearmongering without manufacturing another, and then engaging in its own version of spreading fear.

title: Opebi-Mende-Ojota Link Bridge To Be Opened Before Christmas, Says Sanwo-Olu
body: The Lagos State Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu has said that the Opebi-Mende Link Bridge is about 80 per cent complete, expressing confidence that the project will be opened to the public before Christmas. Governor Sanwo-Olu gave the assurance during an inspection of the project, acknowledging that the construction had exceeded the September completion timeline previously announced. He said his visit to the site was to establish the reasons for the delay and assess the progress of work, stressing that the project’s distinctive architectural design and engineering requirements must not be compromised by the pressure to meet the deadline. He explained that the bridge’s steel structure was designed to reflect the area’s historical association with cane weaving, thereby preserving its cultural identity. According to him, the project involves installing more than 300 tonnes of steel at heights of up to 25 metres, making it an unusually demanding engineering undertaking. The governor said three of the four major steel components, designed to resemble interwoven cane, had been completed, while work was ongoing on the remaining component. He added that light-emitting diode (LED) installations featuring the colours of Lagos State would enhance the structure and give it an iconic appearance. Governor Sanwo-Olu added that the state government would not sacrifice engineering quality and public safety for speed, despite the delay. He said additional activities, including site cleaning, repainting of kerbs, restoration of affected areas and landscaping, would be undertaken before the bridge is opened to the public. He envisaged the area becoming a destination for recreation, cultural heritage and tourism, adding that its redevelopment would enable residents to appreciate the history and identity of the community. The governor maintained that the bridge would become a significant infrastructure landmark in Lagos, combining innovation with cultural preservation. Sanwo-Olu commissioned the construction of the bridge in 2022 to ease congestion in Ikeja and environs. Governor Sanwo-Olu (centre) He said that the bridge, which is part of the ‘legacy project,’ was an innovative solution to the perennial gridlock around Opebi/Mobolaji Bank Anthony Way/Ojota/Mende corridor. The post Opebi-Mende-Ojota Link Bridge To Be Opened Before Christmas, Says Sanwo-Olu appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Board of Deputies passes motion declaring Green Party a 'racist party'
body: The Board of Deputies of British Jews (BoD) has passed a motion declaring the UK Green Party a racist party.This resolution, adopted at the board's October Plenary Meeting, condemns the Green Party's decision to adopt a policy branding Zionism as racism, deeming the policy racist and antisemitic. The board will now treat the Greens as it has treated other “racist parties.”“Today, representatives of Jewish communities across Britain have delivered a clear verdict,” BoD president Phil Rosenberg said.“By adopting an antisemitic platform, the Green Party of England and Wales has become a racist party. We will treat it accordingly.”“No political party has the right to tell Jews that a central part of our identity, rooted in thousands of years of history, faith and peoplehood, is racist,” he said.“The Green Party's policy brands much of our community, including our synagogues and communal organizations, with that slur. It gives prejudice against Jews a political license.”Rosenberg said the Green Party's leadership must now take responsibility for reversing this policy and “confronting the antisemitism it has legitimized.”He also noted that the BoD recognizes and commends those within the party who opposed the motion, including Jewish members whose warnings were disregarded. Rosenberg said these individuals deserved to be heard and supported.Motion proposer Ashley Hirst said he was proud that British Jews have “said clearly” that a party which declares that this is racist “is itself a racist party.”“The board will give effect to the resolution in its dealings with the Green Party of England and Wales and continue to challenge antisemitism wherever it appears in political and public life.”Green Party became first in Europe to declare itself anti-ZionistThe Green Party became the first mainstream party in Europe to declare itself openly anti-Zionist after voting in the controversial “Zionism is racism” motion at its party conference in Brighton, UK, at the start of the month.The motion recognizes Zionism as Israel's foundational ideology that has created and maintains an “apartheid regime” between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea.It further affirms the Palestinian people's right to self-determination and liberation. It supports the establishment of a “single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine, with Jerusalem as its capital.”

title: Why does Moody’s rate France above Israel? The economic gap deserves scrutiny – opinion
body: Moody's decision to keep France's credit rating well above Israel's raises a question: How much weight does the agency put on each country's economic performance?The US-based credit rating agency affirmed France's sovereign rating at Aa3 over the weekend. Israel remains at Baa1, four notches lower. Both ratings are investment grade, meaning they fall within the categories generally considered suitable for mainstream institutional investment. The difference nevertheless signals that Moody's considers lending to France substantially safer.Sovereign credit ratings assess a government's ability and willingness to repay its debt. They can influence borrowing costs and determine which investors are permitted to buy a country's bonds.Such assessments necessarily extend beyond a comparison of growth and debt figures. War, political stability, institutions, and access to financing all matter. Even so, the contrast between the French and Israeli economies deserves closer scrutiny.Moody's first downgraded Israel from A1 to A2 in February 2024, roughly four months after the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attack triggered the war in Gaza. In September 2024, it cut Israel's rating another two notches to Baa1, where it has remained.Israel's economy has nevertheless demonstrated considerable resilience, acknowledged in assessments by the International Monetary Fund, the international institution that monitors economies and provides financial assistance to member countries.France, meanwhile, has struggled with weak growth, substantial budget deficits, and political resistance to efforts to repair its public finances. Protests and unrest have added to the pressure on its government.The question is whether the size of the ratings gap adequately reflects those competing realities.A substantial gap in growth, debtConsider economic output per person, a widely used measure of a country's average prosperity.According to the IMF figures cited here, Israel's nominal GDP per capita is expected to reach approximately $72,400 in 2026, compared with about $51,400 in France. These figures measure output in current US dollars and are influenced by exchange rates; they do not directly measure household income or purchasing power.The growth forecasts also differ sharply. The IMF projects Israeli economic growth of approximately 4.5% this year, while the Bank of Israel, the country's central bank, forecasts 5.6%.France's economy is expected to expand by approximately 0.4%, according to both the IMF and the Banque de France, the French central bank.Rapid growth after a wartime slowdown requires context. Some of that expansion can reflect the recovery of activity lost during the conflict. Still, growth strengthens a government's tax base and can make its debt easier to manage. Prolonged stagnation makes those tasks harder.The debt comparison is particularly striking.France's public debt stands at approximately 118.5% of its annual economic output and is approaching 120%. Israel's debt-to-GDP ratio is approximately 68.6%.In practical terms, France owes more than the value of everything its economy produces in a year. Israel's debt amounts to roughly two-thirds of its annual output.Neither figure alone determines whether a country can repay its creditors. Financing costs, the maturity of outstanding debt, and investor confidence also matter. Nevertheless, the difference is substantial.France's budget deficit, the gap between government spending and revenue, exceeds 5% of GDP. Israel's reported deficit stood at approximately 3.2% as of September.These figures raise a reasonable question about how Moody's weighs France's fiscal vulnerabilities against Israel's security risks.How much confidence should promises command?In affirming France's rating, Moody's cited plans for €52 billion in spending cuts.Delivering those savings requires political support. French governments have faced sustained opposition to pension changes, spending restraint, and other measures intended to stabilize public finances.France enacted a pension reform in 2023 that provided for a gradual increase in the retirement age from 62 to 64. Subsequent legislation suspended the increases until 2028, illustrating the difficulty of sustaining politically contentious reforms.A credit assessment must therefore consider the likelihood that promised savings will materialize, as well as the government's stated intentions.Labor-market conditions offer another point of comparison. The figures cited here put French unemployment above 8.4%, compared with approximately 2.8% in Israel.Israel's low unemployment rate suggests a tight labor market, although wartime labor shortages and military reserve service complicate the picture. Its economy has shown an ability to adapt under extraordinary pressure. That capacity should carry meaningful weight in any assessment of its creditworthiness.France also benefits from its membership in the eurozone, the group of countries using the euro. Its access to a large common-currency financial market is relevant to its ability to finance debt and helps explain why a simple comparison of national economic indicators cannot tell the whole story.The issue is how these advantages and vulnerabilities are balanced.What bond markets can tell usGovernment bond yields provide another perspective. They show the return investors demand to lend money to a state.The figures cited here put the yield on French 10-year government bonds at 5.05%, compared with approximately 4.06%-4.18% for Israeli bonds of the same maturity.That comparison requires care. French government bonds are generally denominated in euros, while the Israeli domestic benchmark is denominated in shekels. Their yields reflect different interest-rate and inflation expectations, alongside credit risk and other factors.The yield gap alone therefore cannot establish that investors consider France more likely to default. A stronger comparison would examine borrowing costs on a comparable currency basis or other market measures of sovereign credit risk.Even with those qualifications, Israel's economic resilience and France's fiscal difficulties warrant a fuller explanation of the ratings gap.Moody's may reasonably place considerable weight on Israel's exposure to war and regional instability. It should also explain clearly how it weighs those risks against Israel's lower debt burden, stronger growth prospects, and demonstrated capacity to withstand disruption.Credit ratings carry practical consequences for governments, businesses, and taxpayers. A four-notch difference deserves an explanation grounded in evidence that investors and the public can examine.

title: Samson Awiah elected Ghana Cricket Association President, pledges nationwide representation
body: Former national team all-rounder Samson Kwasi Awe Awiah has been elected President of the Ghana Cricket Association (GCA), pledging to decentralise the sport and ensure nationwide representation in national team selection. Awiah polled 11 votes out of 25 valid ballots cast at the elective congress held last Saturday at the Cantonments Police Station Mosque in Accra. Incumbent Emmanuel Owusu-Ansah Asare garnered nine votes, while Prince Eugene King managed five. In his victory speech, the new GCA boss emphasised regional associations as a priority, promising active involvement of cricketers at the grassroots level. “The regional associations are one priority, making sure that we actively involve the cricketers each and every day, each and every week,” Awiah stated. “We want the national team players to be chosen from all the regions, so that we have equal representation when it comes to representing the nation.” He added: “We know where we’ve been, and we cannot wait to get out of where we’ve been.” Samuel Nana Ekow Biney Asamoah secured the vice presidency with 17 votes, defeating incumbent Oscar Nii-Adza Provencal, who polled eight. Devasia Shijo, Nihal Abbas Ali Safi and Vinod Punnackal were elected board members, while Angela Cassandra Allotey retained the treasurer’s position with 21 votes against Dharmendra Thadani’s four. The congress was graced by a speech from Ghana Olympic Committee (GOC) President Richard Akpokavie, read on his behalf by GOC General Secretary Mohammed Muniru Kassim. He urged the new board to prioritise “grassroots development, youth participation, good governance and the promotion of cricket at both national and international levels.” He also expressed appreciation to the outgoing board for its service and wished the new leadership “renewed energy, greater opportunities and remarkable achievements for Ghanaian cricket.”

title: Eunice is almost here (William Gibson, Agency)
body:
William Gibson's Agency (2020) is a mind-bending science fiction novel. Without getting lost in its intricate plot, one storyline takes place in an alternate San Francisco in 2017, where a young woman named Verity is hired to test an experimental AI assistant called Eunice.
At one point, we encounter this extraordinary exchange:
Verity: "Where'd you get this? It's wrong."
Eunice: "This no-name account, in Zurich. Part of me knew it was there, how to get it, how to get it here. Plenty more, but if I tried it again, they'd be on us."
Verity: "When did you have time to do any of that?"
Eunice: "Started when we were looking out the window. Before we left, up to the park, it was already points."
Eunice: "Frequent flyer. There's a global market, buy or sell. Hard to track..."
Verity: "You did this since I turned you on?"
Gibson published Agency nearly three years before ChatGPT's release, and six years before the emergence of today's increasingly autononomous AI agents.
We now have GPT-Live and emerging models like Block's Dessa , bringing us remarkably human-like full-duplex conversations. Meanwhile, OpenAI's Dots and Meta's Muse are introducing 24/7 agents capable of independently pursuing goals, taking action, and working in the background.
What makes Eunice remarkable isn't just that she can talk, it's that she's doing so much else while talking. The pieces are coming together.
As always, Gibson was right on the money. Eunice is almost here.

title: Venezuela opposition leader Maria Corina Machado returns to Venezuela
body: Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado has returned to the South American nation after nearly a year outside the country, she said on social media on Sunday."I'm here. With you all," the Nobel Peace Prize-winning Machado wrote on social media early on Sunday.Machado's press team shared images of her in central-western Lara state, in the Plaza del Pueblo de Santa Rosa, where Machado appeared at a church.Estoy aquí. Con ustedes— María Corina Machado (@MariaCorinaYA) October 25, 2026The issue of her return has strained her relationship with the US Trump administration, which she has sought to cultivate as an ally since before it removed President Nicolas Maduro from power in January.US President Donald Trump has repeatedly expressed support for interim President Delcy Rodriguez, Maduro's former deputy, and hailed deals on oil production and other business ventures by US companies in the South American country. Trump said in September it is too soon to consider democratic elections in Venezuela.Speaking at the White House on Sunday, Trump said he did not know anything about Machado's return to Venezuela and suggested that the US would continue to back Rodriguez."She's a very nice woman," he said, referring to Machado. "But we're doing really well in Venezuela.”During an interview on Fox News on Sunday, Trump also said that the US had "total control of Venezuela.""We're being very fair," he said. "But we're taking out millions of barrels of oil a week."Neither the White House nor the Venezuelan communications ministry, which handles all press queries for the government, immediately responded to requests for comment on Machado's return.Machado to meet with victims of devastating June earthquakeMachado plans to meet with victims of the deadly earthquakes that struck Venezuela in June, as well as the families of political prisoners, the international community and various leaders from the democratic movement in Venezuela, David Smolansky, her top foreign affairs adviser, told Reuters."She will work proactively for a date for free and fair elections," he added.International energy firms committed last month to expanding projects in the country in a signing ceremony overseen by Rodriguez and US Energy Secretary Chris Wright.Machado has said only a "serious, democratic government" can provide the stability needed by investors. In June, she said she would do whatever it took to come home and help the survivors of devastating twin earthquakes that month that killed at least 6,500 people and left thousands missing.Machado escaped Venezuela in 2025 after living in hidingMachado was barred by Maduro's government from exiting Venezuela, but she secretly left in late 2025 to receive the Nobel Peace Prize, after spending more than a year living mostly in hiding.Her desire to return had caused friction in Washington, with US officials asking her to delay her trip, Reuters reported in June.Machado did not disclose more details about her current location or how she returned.A faction of the opposition and the interim government held their latest session of talks this month, which aim to remake the top court and electoral council, among other goals, ahead of eventual elections. They do not include Machado's political movement.Edmundo Gonzalez, a former presidential candidate for Machado's movement who has been living in Spain, confirmed her return in his own post and said he would soon join her.

title: Lib Dems propose six more frigates for Royal Navy
body: The Liberal Democrats have proposed ordering six additional Royal Navy frigates and expanding British shipbuilding capacity as part of a defence package aimed at responding to the threat from Russia, according to plans published by the party. Under the proposal , three additional Type 26 anti-submarine warfare frigates and three additional Type 31 general-purpose frigates would be ordered for delivery by the mid-2030s. If added to existing government plans, the proposal would increase the planned Type 26 fleet from eight ships to 11 and the Type 31 fleet from five to eight. The government currently intends the two classes to form the core of the Royal Navy’s future frigate force alongside at least six Common Combat Vessels replacing the Type 45 destroyers. The Liberal Democrats estimate that three additional Type 31 frigates would cost around £1.2 billion, based on an assumed unit cost of approximately £400 million in 2025/26 prices. The party puts the cost of three additional Type 26 frigates at £2.85 billion, using an estimated cost of around £950 million per ship. A further £370 million would be allocated from the party’s proposed Defence Bonds scheme towards additional shipbuilding infrastructure. The party describes the policy as providing funding for four new shipyards, although the detailed costing accompanying the announcement says the £370 million figure is based on constructing two further facilities at approximately £185 million each, using BAE Systems’ Janet Harvey Hall on the Clyde as its benchmark. The frigate orders and shipbuilding allocation amount to approximately £4.42 billion of capital spending under the party’s published assumptions. The Liberal Democrats also propose increasing the Digital Services Tax from 2 per cent to 10 per cent and using part of the additional revenue to meet personnel and maintenance costs associated with the expanded fleet. The party says there are no current official estimates available for the through-life operating costs of the Type 26 and Type 31 fleets. Its own calculations assume annual running costs of £20 million for each additional ship by 2034/35, producing an estimated £120 million annual cost for the six vessels. Liberal Democrat Defence Spokesperson James MacCleary MP said: “We cannot afford to sit on our hands while Putin’s aggression intensifies and our national security weakens. We need a plan which gives confidence to British industry and allows our manufacturers to get on with delivering for Britain’s long-term security. “By investing now in six new warships and by expanding our ship-building capacity with four new British shipyards, we can regenerate our fleet, protect our vital underwater infrastructure, and ensure Britain has the defence capabilities we need to stand up to the Kremlin.” The announcement follows a Defence Committee report published on 22 October which warned of serious capability gaps affecting British operations in the High North. The committee said publicly available evidence of low availability among frigates, destroyers and attack submarines raised questions about the UK’s ability to meet its commitments in the region, while warning that Russian submarine and sabotage activity presents risks to undersea infrastructure and North Atlantic reinforcement routes. The Liberal Democrats also cited polling conducted by Savanta between 29 May and 1 June 2026 involving 2,234 UK adults. According to the results commissioned by the party, 60 per cent said the government was either probably or definitely not doing enough to protect critical infrastructure from Russian attacks, compared with 26 per cent who believed it was doing enough. Fourteen per cent answered that they did not know. The party argues that additional orders would also provide a longer and more predictable workload for British shipbuilding, allowing yards and suppliers to invest in workforce and infrastructure with greater confidence. The government’s existing shipbuilding programme includes eight Type 26 frigates and five Type 31 frigates, while the wider Hybrid Navy plan also envisages new crewed and uncrewed vessels operating together. The 2025 Strategic Defence Review placed particular emphasis on the Type 26 as part of Atlantic Bastion, the Royal Navy’s approach to countering the growing submarine threat in the North Atlantic. The Liberal Democrat proposal would go beyond those numbers by adding six crewed frigates to the planned force, with the party arguing that the additional hulls should be ordered during the next Parliament and delivered by the mid-2030s. The post Lib Dems propose six more frigates for Royal Navy first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: Zelensky: Energy truce could signal Russia’s readiness to end war
body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky made this statement in an interview with Alla Mazur, host of “TSN.Tyzhden,” according to Ukrinform.
“An energy ceasefire as a first step. I believe this is a signal,” Zelensky said.
He noted that Ukraine is ready for trilateral negotiations at the technical working group level, which should yield concrete results.
According to him, the parties could draft a document on ending the war, an agreement on an energy ceasefire, or the resumption of maritime transport.
As previously reported, President Volodymyr Zelensky stated that Ukraine, the U.S., and Russia have agreed to hold a trilateral meeting at the level of negotiating teams in the first half of November.

title: Voting at Serbia’s snap parliamentary elections over
body:
BELGRADE, October 25. /TASS/. Voting in Serbia’s snap parliamentary elections has finished as polling stations closed at 8:00 p.m. local time (7:00 p.m. GMT).
According to the Republic Electoral Commission (REC), voter turnout was 64.89% two hours before the end of voting.
A TASS correspondent reported earlier that people were queueing to polling stations in Belgrade.
The ballots featured 18 electoral lists. The main contenders are expected to be the United Serbia list of the ruling Serbian Progressive Party, led by Aleksandar Vucic, who stepped down as the country’s president on September 27, and the Student List coalition. The latter grew out of a protest movement that erupted in Serbia following the tragedy in Novi Sad in November 2024, when 16 people died when a concrete canopy at the train station collapsed.

title: America's Wagner Group: Starlink crisis in Ukraine shows dangerous reality for US allies - opinion
body: On October 14, 2026, Ukraine experienced speed throttling of its connections to Starshield, Starlink's military counterpart. The imposed strict speed ceilings restricted connections for any terminals or drones exceeding 100 miles per hour.That grounded or disconnected Ukraine's faster military strike and interceptor drones, which rely on communication with operators over long distances. Almost as soon as news of the newly imposed limits was disclosed by Ukrainian officials, the game of finger-pointing and shifting the blame between US President Donald Trump and Elon Musk, Starlink's CEO, began.Trump announced he had no knowledge of the decision, suggesting the initiative was wholly Musk's. In turn, Musk claimed to have received orders from the White House. The back-and-forth continued, with both Trump and Musk denying responsibility.It is not hard to deduce the sequence of events that led to the decision to reduce the coverage: the president and Musk had a conversation, with Trump complaining about Ukraine and how “ungrateful” it was. Musk suggested a way to teach the country a lesson by temporarily reducing Starshield's services.The president agreed that it would be a good idea, but suggested the White House should not be directly implicated, given the timing, a few weeks before the midterms, was very sensitive. Yet, no matter how Trump and Musk try to spin the story, the proverbial buck, as put by president Harry Truman, “stops here.”This avoidance of responsibility is not a new feature of American politics. But the other aspect of the affair has far-reaching consequences, going beyond national borders and carrying worldwide strategic implications.The US is a superpower possessing one of the most powerful militaries in the world. It is also the major supplier of weapons and military platforms to its allies and countries it deems friendly. Historically, the countries purchasing those weapons understood that their usage and proper maintenance depended on American political goodwill.The president and Congress could influence or even restrict American-made weapons' usage and deployment, and many countries have faced those limitations or the threats thereof. Yet it has always been a clear political decision. There was a clear channel of communication to discuss and agree on the matter. The White House was the responsible party on the American side. Its decisions were politically controlled by internal politics and bilateral relationships. The rules of the game were transparent and well known. That clarity provided the clients of American weaponry a sense of stability and well-placed dependence.But what if, in the decision to dial down Starshield's coverage in Ukraine, Musk played a role equal to Trump's? What if there is a new independent entity in America that can make decisions of a magnitude that, just a few months ago, only the president could?A slippery slope of who would control Starlink technologiesElon Musk is not bound by political considerations. His interests are completely independent of those of the president, another country, or bilateral relationships. He is an independent businessman with the power of a sovereign, deciding who wins, who loses, and who dies.And those decisions are driven not by the art of statecraft, but by his business interests, whims, and caprices. This is not merely the problem of one particular individual, even though, in Musk's case, that problem is huge.The wars in Ukraine, Karabakh, and Iran showed how technology has become a decisive force on the battlefield. Those conflicts proved beyond doubt that the huge military conglomerates of yesteryear are no longer capable of providing the technical support a modern military needs to win.The dinosaurs of old are too slow and cumbersome in a world where a fast pace of development, deployment, and refinement is a must. The American government and the US military have no choice but to rely extensively on start-ups founded by folks with very “interesting” ideas of how the world should be to supply themselves with needed platforms.Those companies, both private and public, may, as in the case of Starlink, possess dual-use technologies.Inevitably, the question arises: Who controls the switch? Who controls communication with those devices in the field? The question is of paramount importance because, as Musk has spectacularly displayed, someone in a land far away has the power and ability to stop a war, allow one side to win and another to lose, and effectively play god.Every American ally in a conflict zone, be it Israel and Ukraine in active wars, Europe awaiting another Russian invasion, Taiwan awaiting China's channel crossing, or South Korea awaiting another North Korean provocation, is shaken to the core by the Starlink fiasco.They have all purchased billions of dollars worth of American equipment under the assumption, perhaps no longer true, that its reliability is backed by American political power.But if that depends on the current state of mind of Musk or another brilliant founder with questionable interests and mental stability, then the US has stopped being an ally, and even a reliable source of weaponry. That means American credibility as a political and military power is lost.If the American military industry becomes an American version of the Wagner Group, then our power is on a slippery slope to the “dustbin” of history.The writer lives and works in Silicon Valley, California. He is a founding member of San Francisco Voice for Israel.

title: Russia may help Iran reduce dependence on southern ports — senior Iranian diplomat
body:
TEHRAN, October 25. /TASS/. Russia may help Iran reduce its dependence on its southern ports, Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Hamid Ghanbari said.
"Russia could become a supplier of essential goods, help reduce Iran’s dependence on southern ports, and facilitate trade with fewer banking restrictions," the Iranian state television quoted him as saying.
According to the senior Iranian diplomat, broad cooperation with Russia is possible, with the North-South transport corridor and the Resht-Astara railway, a project that is currently moving forward, serving as a basis for that. He also noted that the country’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, is scheduled to travel to Russia to participate in a gas forum.
He called China and Russia his country’s strategic partners in the economy and politics. He recalled that China has repeatedly voted in favor of Iran in the UN Security Council and objected to the United States’ idea the snapback mechanism, a process designed to restore UN sanctions on Iran.

title: Trump rules out Sunday strike on Iran as Netanyahu warns Israel faces imminent existential threat
body: US President Donald Trump said Sunday that the United States would not launch a military strike against Iran today.Asked by a reporter whether a US attack on Iran could take place as soon as today, Trump replied: “Would I tell you that? The answer is no. There will not be a strike today.”The president did not rule out military action at a later date.Earlier on Sunday, Trump told reporters that he has yet to make a decision on whether or not to renew strikes against Iran. “Should I finish the job - which would be very easy to do - or should I reach an agreement? That is the whole decision," he said.Trump says 'not much going on' at Iranian nuclear sites, Netanyahu claims Israel facing existential threatTrump added that the US is actively monitoring activity at Iran's Pickaxe Mountain nuclear site as well as three other sites that were allegedly destroyed in previous strikes. “There isn't much activity going on there,” he clarified.Trump's comments came after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu claimed in a post on X/Twitter that Israel is currently facing “real and tangible existential danger” coming from Iran.Netanyahu claimed that only a small window of time remains for Israel and the US to act and completely defeat Iran.Netanyahu also shared a video from one of the IDF's anti-missile batteries where he said: "The IDF is prepared on both defense and in offense. I warn our enemies – you will absorb strikes out of proportion, stronger than you can even imagine."Trump said on Friday that Washington is weighing another military operation against Iran, saying that the US “may do another little Epic Fury” during a pre-midterm election rally in Florida.US-Israeli strike on Iran: Not if, whenAdditionally, US officials believe that a joint US-Israeli strike on Iran is not a question of “if,” but “when.”“It appears that Trump has decided he wants to carry out a significant strike against Iran. The only question is when to do it,” one official told The Jerusalem Post.Another official said the president was “very close” to escalating US action against Iran.The prevailing assessment in Washington is that Trump will hold off on making a final decision on military action against Iran until after the November 3 midterm elections.On Sunday, Trump told Fox News in an interview: “I have a decision to make: Do I finish it off, which would be very easy to do, or do I make a deal? That's the decision.”

title: Opposition leader and Nobel Prize winner Maria Corina Machado returns to Venezuela
body: Opposition leader Maria Corina Machado has returned to Venezuela after nearly a ⁠year outside the country. "I'm here with you," the Nobel Peace Prize winner wrote on social media early on Sunday. Her media team shared images of her in central-western Lara state, in the Plaza del Pueblo de Santa Rosa, where ⁠she appeared at a church. The issue of her return has strained her relationship with US President Donald Trump 's administration, which she has ​sought to ⁠cultivate as an ally since before the toppling of long-time leader Nicolas Maduro in January. After her Nobel win, Ms Machado gave the prize to Mr Trump, who had said several times he thought he deserved it. He has repeatedly expressed support for interim President Delcy Rodriguez , Mr Maduro's former ​vice president, and hailed deals on oil production and other business ventures by US companies in the South American country. Mr Trump said in September that it was too soon to consider democratic elections in Venezuela . Estoy aquí. Con ustedes — María Corina Machado (@MariaCorinaYA) October 25, 2026 Speaking at the White House on Sunday, Mr Trump said he did not know anything about Ms Machado's return to Venezuela and suggested that the US would continue to back Ms Rodriguez. "She's a very nice woman," he said, referring to Ms Machado. "But we're doing really well in Venezuela.” This is not the first time she has tried to return to Venezuela after she escaped the country in December 2025 to receive her Nobel prize. She had gone into hiding after her detention during a protest against recent elections. Ms Rodriguez was named interim leader of Venezuela after Mr Maduro was captured by US forces in early January and taken to New York to face drug and weapons-related charges. She said there will be future elections but no date has been set. Ms Rodriguez's government has allowed politicians, activists and journalists who spent years in exile to return, including some of Ms Machado’s closest allies. Allowing Ms Machado to organise and campaign would be a most consequential move, while detaining her or restricting her activities could put pressure on Washington to respond. But the US has has given priority to political and economic stability over an immediate democratic transition. A major energy agreement in early September has given the US access to as much as 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s crude reserves. Ms Machado's desire to return had caused friction in Washington, with US officials asking her to delay her trip, Reuters reported in June. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said her return was the “direct result of the US-supported reconciliation talks". “The United States expects the freedoms of all sectors of Venezuelan politics to continue to be respected,” he said in a post on X. “Likewise, we expect all political actors to support these talks, which represent the best chance Venezuela has had in 30 years to peacefully achieve not just a free and fair election, but an enduring democracy.” Still, Ms Machado may have missed her chance at being part of the transition. US-backed talks between Ms Rodriguez’s government and a faction of the opposition ended their latest round this week with agreements to begin reviewing laws governing political disqualifications, parties and public demonstrations, among other measures.

title: Jewish Futures 2026 conference to explore how AI could reshape Jewish education
body: The Jewish Education Project will host its annual conference, Jewish Futures 2026: 'Becoming Tomorrow's Educators,' at Temple Emanu-El in New York City on Monday.The event will convene Jewish educators and thought leaders to examine how artificial intelligence and emerging technologies are changing how young people learn, connect, and process information, as well as how the role of educators must evolve alongside these shifts.Participants at the conference will take part in an interactive exercise called “Tzomet Games: Shaping the Jewish Future,” where teams will evaluate potential scenarios for Jewish life in 2050.The program is designed to help participants identify upcoming challenges, experiment with new methods of learning, and determine which foundational elements of Jewish education remain essential regardless of technological advancement.The Jewish Education Project stressed that educators must take an active role in responding to modern technological developments.Jewish education cannot react to changes in technology “We are living through extraordinary changes in how young people encounter information and make meaning,” said Samantha Vinokor-Meinrath, Senior Director of Knowledge, Ideas and Learning at The Jewish Education Project.“Jewish education cannot simply react to those changes after they happen. Our responsibility is to help educators understand what is coming, experiment with new possibilities, and also identify the deeply human elements of education that technology can never replace. Jewish Futures is about giving educators the opportunity to help shape that future rather than simply adjust to it.”The conference will feature a keynote address by technology entrepreneur Sam Glassenberg, called “The Jewish Neuron at Play: What Games and AI Can Teach Us about Learning, Identity, and Our Kids' Future.” Glassenberg, who leads Emerging Healthtech Initiatives at Sheba Medical Center in Israel and previously served as CEO of FTX Games and founder of Level Ex, will examine what educators can learn from systems built to capture attention.Drawing on game design, neuroscience, and AI, he will explore how games instruct through challenge, feedback, and reward, and how emerging AI tools offer new ways to examine Jewish history and identity, ranging from analyzing the Cairo Geniza to mapping the Jewish genome.The event will conclude with an interactive session titled “Educators Assemble!” led by Shoshana Bloom, an ICF PCC-certified coach and speaker who specializes in addressing burnout, overwhelm, imposter syndrome, and procrastination.Bloom will guide participants in identifying their individual strengths, examining how those traits complement fellow educators, and converting the conference's discussions about future challenges into actionable steps.

I know many of you are mourning the loss of the Arc browser, and I get it. It felt like the first app in a long time to really offer a new approach to browser design . Atlassian bought the company last year and shifted its focus to developing Dia , its even more AI-focused browser. And soon enough, Arc will officially be no more , leaving dedicated users in a lurch. But I abandoned Arc quite some time ago for the Zen Browser and haven’t really missed it. If you’re willing to deal with some minor inconveniences, I think you’ll find Zen is the Arc replacement you’re looking for.
Zen unabashedly rips off all the best bits of Arc. Visually, they’re almost indistinguishable. It has the launcher-like pinned sites, tab bar on the left, siloed spaces, and mods that let you customize the browser’s UI to your liking. It takes the bits that made Arc’s interface feel fresh, then strips out everything that made it bloated and drove me into the arms of another.
There’s no agent in a sidebar hounding me to let it handle tasks. I’m not worried about Zen training an LLM on my browsing activity. It’s just a web browser.
Zen prides itself on its privacy features: “Beautifully designed, privacy-focused, and packed with features. We care about your experience, not your data,” it proudly proclaims. Now, I’m no fool. I know that nothing I do on the internet is really private, but with Arc, it always felt like my data was an integral part of the business plan. That’s not the case with Zen. It’s a free and open-source project that relies on volunteers and donations.
In addition to Zen Mods that can do anything from tweak the look of an active tab to overhaul how PiP videos are handled, you can also install Firefox extensions. Yes, you can install Chrome extensions in Arc, but anecdotally, I’ve found that Zen handles extensions better. Both Zen and Arc are different enough from a UI perspective that not all extensions display properly, but Zen offers more workarounds.
Zen also just kind of lets me focus on the task at hand. Links open in “glance” view, which is a temporary pop-over tab, which is really great when you’re doing some window shopping or light research. If I want to open it in a proper tab, it’s just a click away. Zen also has a floating bar that pops up whenever you press Command+T or CTRL+T. From here you can launch a new tab, switch to an existing tab, perform a search from the search engine of your choice, and even trigger an extension.
Zen isn’t perfect. I love its clean UI and organizational features, but it can’t play DRM-protected video content right now. That means Netflix, Spotify, HBO, Disney+, and more do not work in Zen. The Zen Team is working to obtain a Widevine license from Google. In the meantime, I use Chrome when I want to watch a movie, which is fine. Zen is built on Firefox, and Firefox’s Web MIDI support is lacking. So I have to fire up Chrome semi-regularly anyway.
I also miss Arc’s Boosts in some cases, but I’ve learned to accept the web as it is. Zen implemented a similar Boost feature in May, but it’s not super obvious and, if there is an official, easily browsable repository of installable Boosts, I’ve yet to find it. Instead, you have to tweak individual sites’ appearance yourself.
If you tried Zen a long time ago and were turned off by its buggy early builds, rest assured it’s come a long way. Look, if you are all in on Arc’s AI features , Dia is probably more your speed. Personally, I always loved Arc’s interface, but never really dug the vibes. Zen just feels right.
Update October 25th: Added information about Zen’s implementation of Boosts.

title: CENTCOM chief flies over Strait of Hormuz during Middle East visit, affirms waterway clear of mines
body: US Central Command (CENTCOM) Adm. Brad Cooper visited the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday as part of the US effort to allow shipment movement and crude oil exports through the contentious waterway. Cooper observed the ongoing operations while flying in a US Army CH-47 Chinook helicopter over the strait."We continue to stand shoulder to shoulder with our Gulf partners and the shipping industry," said Cooper during the visit. "This visit underscores our strong commitment to continued freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz."Cooper affirmed that the Strait of Hormuz is "free and clear of Iranian sea mines," thanking the US service members who supported and took part in the mission."We remain intensely focused on keeping commercial traffic flowing as we work with our teammates in the US interagency, Gulf Cooperation Council, and shipping industry," he said. US clears mines from Hormuz, Trump accuses Iran of 'fabrications'In August, US President Donald Trump said the US Navy told him all mines had been cleared from the Strait of Hormuz.Trump added that "Iran has been notified that any ship or boat placing new mines will be immediately and systematically destroyed."A US official confirmed the matter to the The Jerusalem Post at the time, noting that both inbound and outbound shipping lanes in the strait have been cleared of mines by CENTCOM. On Thursday, however, Trump accused Iran of fabricating recent reports of attacks on oil tankers and naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz to drive up oil prices ahead of the November midterm elections.“Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of Oil prior to the US Midterm Election,” Trump wrote.“They are even making up fake hits, mines, and everything else, because more Oil is coming through the Hormuz Strait now than it did even prior to the beginning of the Conflict."James Genn, Amichai Stein, and Goldie Katz contributed to this report.

title: Bayern beat Freiburg to reclaim top spot as Kompany remains hospitalised
body: Bayern Munich reclaimed top spot in the Bundesliga with a 3-1 win at Freiburg on Sunday, days after coach Vincent Kompany was hospitalised when he collapsed at training. Bayern were missing several first-team players and Kompany, but cruised to a two-goal lead at half-time with Dayot Upamecano and Serge Gnabry scoring. Freiburg pulled one back and were pushing for a point in stoppage time when goalkeeper Mio Backhaus was caught out up the field, allowing Michael Olise to slide the ball into an empty net. Kompany remains in hospital and is being treated for a mystery virus, with Bayern saying Saturday the coach is likely to be out for “days, not weeks”. “I just opened my phone to a message from Vince saying ‘well done’ and he was happy,” assistant coach Aaron Danks told DAZN. “I just replied saying ‘brilliant — now go rest’. I sent him a kissing emoji, so hopefully he rests up.” Bayern sporting director Max Eberl gave an update on Kompany’s condition. “He’s stable. He no longer has a headache. He’s now undergoing a thorough examination. Everything is being handled,” he said. “There’s no diagnosis, nothing final yet.” With victory Bayern leapfrogged Borussia Dortmund to top the table ahead of the duo’s clash in Munich next week. Harry Kane had a close-range effort saved late in the second half but failed to find the net a day before the Ballon d’Or ceremony in London, with the England captain among the favourites. Bayern arrived in the Black Forest after a tumultuous few days which left them lacking leaders. With coach Kompany still in hospital after collapsing on Friday, Englishman Danks was in the dugout. The visitors were also without injured captain Manuel Neuer, Luis Diaz, Jamal Musiala, Aleksandar Pavlovic and Kim Min-jae, while midfielder and Germany captain Joshua Kimmich was on bereavement leave due to the sudden death of his father. Bayern were in the unusual position of sitting back and absorbing pressure as Freiburg pushed, but took the lead after 16 minutes when Upamecano started and finished a length-of-the-field counter. The France defender won possession near his own box, played a one-two with Olise before thundering goalwards and sending a cool shot past Backhaus. Bayern doubled up just before the break when Gnabry latched onto a Nathaniel Brown pass and nutmegged Backhaus to score. With 10 minutes remaining, Kane stung Backhaus’s palms from close range and the hosts went on an immediate counter, forcing Tom Bischof into conceding an own goal. The goal sparked Freiburg to life and Bayern ‘keeper Jonas Urbig needed to make crucial saves from Igor Matanovic in the dying moments. With Freiburg and Backhaus pushing high, Olise won possession and scored to wrap up the victory. – Hoffenheim hit 1,000 mark – Hoffenheim scored three goals in the final 11 minutes, including the 1,000th league goal in their history, as they snapped Bayer Leverkusen’s six-game winning streak with a 3-0 home victory. Hoffenheim, who beat Lyon by the same scoreline in the Europa League on Thursday, have now won three in a row. The best chance of the opening half fell to former Leverkusen forward Adam Hlozek when he rattled the post with 38 minutes gone. With the match looking headed for a scoreless draw, Leverkusen captain Edmond Tapsoba swept Fisnik Asllani’s ankle while defending a cross, with the referee pointing to the spot after a VAR review. Andrej Kramaric’s 79th-minute penalty was the milestone goal and put Hoffenheim on track for victory. With Leverkusen pushing for an equaliser, Hoffenheim broke on the counter and Alexander Prass scored, but he picked up a second yellow for removing his shirt in celebration, before leaving the pitch slapping himself on the forehead in dismay. Max Moerstedt added a third despite the one-man disadvantage in the sixth minute of stoppage time.
