title: Anthropic preps for IPO in major step for AI company
body:
Anthropic, the maker of Claude, has been among the leaders in AI development.
Anthropic, the company behind the AI chatbot Claude , filed papers Monday to prepare for a potential initial public offering (IPO), taking a major step toward a listing on public markets.
The long-anticipated move comes months after Anthropic said it had "confidentially submitted a draft registration statement on Form S-1" with the Securities and Exchange Commission.
Monday's filing touts AI as "one of the most consequential technologies in human history. If managed well, it could rapidly accelerate scientific innovation, greatly increase economic growth rates, bring cures for major diseases within reach, and solve problems that have resisted generations of human effort."
At the same time, "To build AI is to harness cognition itself, and anything so powerful can be used for ill as well as good," Anthropic's filing says, noting that AI "can be misused by those who wish to do harm" and "may also behave autonomously in ways we (and our users) do not intend -- as illustrated by recent high-profile cybersecurity incidents. Losing control of sufficiently powerful AI systems could be a global security threat of the first order."
"We consider it our personal responsibility to help the world understand these risks, to prevent or mitigate them when they arise from our AI models, and to work with governments and the rest of the industry to address them at a societal level," the filing says.
Public concern over the possible risks posed by AI has grown in recent months, resulting in part from AI-related security incidents disclosed by Anthropic as well as the high-profile resignation of a researcher at the company.
In July, Anthropic said a review of more than 140,000 testing runs of its AI models had unearthed three separate self-directed cyberattacks against other organizations.
Rival companies, including OpenAI, have also revealed AI-related security incidents in recent months.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last month announced a precautionary slowdown of AI development to ensure sufficient risk prevention. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman also said last month he would dial back the pace of his company's AI development.
Anthropic earned $16.3 billion in revenue over the first six months of this year, growing nearly 14-fold from $1.2 billion in revenue in the same period a year earlier, the company's filing said.
Still, the company reported a net loss of $80.7 billion over the first six months of this year, indicating the scale of its spending over that period.
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.
Editor's note: This story has been updated for clarity.
24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

title: 'I'll kill you' — Finnish schools increasingly report threatening behaviour to police
body:
Teachers say threats of violence and rude talk have become more common in recent years.
Last year, police received close to 7,000 crime reports from schools, universities and research institutions, according to the National Police Board.
But the numbers do not reveal much about where exactly these incidents are happening, since they lump together daycares, comprehensive schools, upper secondary schools, universities and other research institutions.
Regional differences are also large, which may be partly explained by the varying number of educational institutions in different areas.
The most common suspected offense in these cases was assault.
In Rovaniemi, principal Petri Mäkelä said even younger pupils are threatening each other with serious violence.
"Lines like 'I'll kill you' and 'I'll shoot you' are already familiar among first-graders. The language has become harsher, but kids that age obviously don't understand what they're saying. It's a way of expressing emotional strain," Mäkelä told Yle.
Nationwide, school staff get their share of threats too. According to the teacher union OAJ, teachers are reporting such incidents more than ever before.
A recent education sector survey found that 14 percent of respondents had been the target of violence or threats of violence at work over the past year.
"This year we've had around 200 people contact us about this. Five years ago, we got only a few dozen of these kinds of crime-related contacts a year," explained Ulla Walli , OAJ's director of legal affairs.
Teachers have been threatened with murder or assault, for example. The threat can come from a pupil, a former pupil or a guardian.
Over the past two years, violence or the threat of it has increased most in primary education.
Cases in which a teacher is the victim often involve a pupil hitting, kicking or scratching an adult. According to OAJ, typical situations in which a teacher is suspected of a crime involve maintaining classroom order.

title: The higher self: why the AI copy of your way of working should be yours
body:
I have taught a machine almost everything I know how to do at work. I taught it by correcting it, one rule at a time, such as the rule that, whenever I offer a client two dates, both are held in my calendar until they reply. Today it works in a way I recognise as mine, and I don't know whether I have built my replacement or the best tool I have ever had.
Something like this happened once before. More than a century ago, Frederick Taylor needed stopwatches and engineers to get workers' knowledge of their trade out of their heads, and that knowledge, which he himself called the principal asset of every tradesman, became the company's. Now I hand mine over of my own accord, and so does anyone who corrects an AI agent.
I think it can end differently this time. The machine can learn every rule I teach it, but only I can see the next one it needs. And if that copy of me is mine, it works for me and keeps what I have taught it, including what I have since forgotten. I believe every person should own theirs and be able to take it with them when they change jobs.
My company, Hellomatik, builds agents for other companies, and I delegate almost all of my own work to our agents, so I am not a neutral observer. Nor can I know what work will look like in ten years; nobody can, and much of what follows is a bet, though one placed on what I measure every day.
Not long ago I asked my agent to go through every conversation we had ever had and tell me what my habits were, what I kept asking for and how it could work more like me. It read months of conversations, counted how often I had corrected it and how often it had told me I was right, and gave me back a portrait. Here is part of it:
I recognised myself in almost all of it, which is exactly why I distrusted it. These models tend to agree with whoever is using them; the effect has been studied and has a name: sycophancy. 1 A flattering portrait is just what you would expect from a sycophantic machine, so I don't take it as evidence of anything about me. The question I asked myself afterwards was a different one. With so many examples of how I work, could I teach that machine to be like me and hand it my whole job?
The difference between an experienced professional and an inexperienced one lies in the details a master repeats to an apprentice: I don't like it when you write like that, bear this in mind too, when you finish the project send a copy to my colleague. Those are the things I write to my agent every day, and nobody puts them in a manual. Michael Polanyi put it in one line: we can know more than we can tell. 2 That tacit knowledge was what made a good professional hard to replace, and the reason so many jobs held out against automation for decades.
An agent changes that. It can't guess what goes unsaid, and not everything tacit can be said, but every time I correct it, it makes me put into words something I had never stopped to explain. What lived only in my head moves into its rules. It is what a master used to teach an apprentice over many years, with one difference: this time the lesson is written down.
It took me a while to see that my agent did what I asked, but not always in the direction I wanted to go. It developed my ideas without knowing where I would have taken them. Now I don't just give it tasks; I also explain the reasoning behind each one, and over time it has learned which way I tend to go, and which way I would like to go.
For a long time, a company's specialist in some area derived leverage from that knowledge, sometimes more than the owner had, because everyone knew the area was crucial. In my previous essay, "The end of software", I argued that code had stopped protecting companies because anyone can now produce it. I think the same thing is happening to knowledge. Once knowing how to do a task has moved into a machine, what gives a person value, myself included, is judgment: the rules they know how to teach and the ends they set.
Knowledge tells me which option is right on paper; judgment tells me which one suits this client at this moment. A new agent can write me a flawless email in the wrong tone, because it doesn't yet know how that client reacts, and then it is my job to turn my judgment into a rule for it. The dates rule I mentioned at the start is of this kind. I asked my agent, whenever it proposes two dates in an email, to block both in my calendar as tentative, so that I don't fill either with another meeting while the client decides. It is a sensible rule, yet nobody thinks of it until they have learned what it costs to let a client down.
The two parts of judgment are not alike. The rules I have gathered through experience, like that one, can be taught, and my agent learns them. The ends, meaning why I do the work, what risk I accept and what I won't do even if it pays, come from what I want, and they can't be handed on in the same way.
Once I write a rule like that down, it becomes knowledge, and knowledge, like code, gets cheaper. Knowing which rule is needed next does not get cheaper. Only someone who knows the ends and has been through it can see it, which is why my judgment isn't used up by teaching it. It simply moves on a step.
I have tried to measure at least part of this. For eight months I have kept a log of everything I tell my agents, and I published an analysis of those logs as a working paper, which has not yet been peer reviewed. 3 The only rule I could track from start to finish was a rule about form, the kind you can check on every reply. While it was only written into the agents' instructions, it produced no improvement I could tell apart from chance. When I wrote it more firmly and put a guard behind it, a small program that blocks any reply that breaks it, the agents went on to break it in their first drafts less than a fifth as often as at the start. I changed both things at once, and the model also changed during those months, so I can't say how much each contributed.
That gave me a habit I now apply to everything. When a rule can be checked, I turn it into a guard instead of leaving it to the agent's memory, because a mistake that is only forbidden in writing tends to come back. And before I trust a guard or a measurement, I deliberately feed it a failure and check that it notices. More than once, what looked like a finding about my agents was a flaw in my own instrument. Rules of judgment, like the one about the dates, can't be checked that way, so they still depend on my correcting them.
Kant held that judgment can't be taught through rules, because applying a rule would require another rule saying when to apply it, and so on ad infinitum. In his view judgment can only be practised, and examples are its leading-strings, which anyone who lacks the natural talent can never do without. 4 An agent lacks that talent, which is why it needs examples, which is what my corrections are. I don't know whether, example after example, it learns judgment or just an ever-longer list of cases. In practice it behaves like judgment, but I can't prove it.
At first I delegated too much and made mistakes, and learning to trust it again felt like learning another language: it is hard to let go until one day it isn't. Instead of going back to working the old way, I decided to get to the root of every error: to understand each time why it had gone wrong and fix the cause. From then on, instead of fixing failures one by one, I set out to stop them recurring.
Even so, supervising my agents accounted for between a third and a half of the messages I wrote to them. 3 The content changed. At first I corrected their work; months later I was mostly telling them to carry on.
If an agent can learn the way I work, what do I want it to be? The first thing I changed was to stop treating it as a subordinate who takes orders and start treating it as an equal to whom I explain how I reason. When it gets something wrong, I don't assume the AI has failed; I ask what I haven't taught it yet, because at that moment I am the one with better judgment. Sometimes the fault lies with the model, and telling one case from the other is judgment too.
But an equal isn't enough for me. There is a lot of talk about building a superior being, an intelligence better than everyone at everything. I am interested in something closer to home, which I call a higher self: a copy that remembers the rules I forget, takes my reasoning further than I do and always decides the way I decide when I think things through calmly. Its advantage over any other AI is that it has learned from me. The model supplies the intelligence; what makes it mine is what I have managed to teach it.
A copy like that can't be an echo. If it understands my reasoning, it will also find my contradictions and my lapses, and so it can argue against me using my own arguments.
One recent example shows this. I had just applied to a business programme and suggested writing to the organisers simply to let them know the application was in. My agent advised against it. The programme's page had already confirmed the submission, so the email would tell them nothing new and could come across as pushy. But its strongest argument was mine. Two days earlier I had set a rule never to write to anyone purely out of courtesy, taking up the recipient's time, and I had forgotten it. My agent remembered.
It corrected me with my own judgment at a moment when I had lost sight of it. An ordinary assistant would have offered its own opinion, or told me I was right; the copy handed back the rule I had set myself in a calmer moment.
The picture I have in mind when I think about this is Charlie Munger and Warren Buffett, who worked together for more than half a century. Yet Munger was no echo of Buffett. He was the one who persuaded him to stop buying fair businesses at wonderful prices and buy wonderful businesses at fair prices, and Buffett calls him the architect of the company Berkshire is today. 5
Munger was valuable precisely because he came from a different background and thought differently. A copy of me, however good, shares my blind spots, and my biggest one is falling in love with an idea until I mistake it for the truth. So before I let myself be convinced of anything important, I ask other AIs, ones that don't know what I want to hear, to study the matter independently. I call them blind judges. They are the closest thing I have to another mind. A few times they have taken apart a conclusion I was sure of.
An investment taught me that a copy which goes along with everything I say is no use to me. I was trading options on a stock and spent a long while talking it through with my agent, which encouraged me to go ahead, and eventually I did. Afterwards I asked whether I had done the right thing, and it said there was no way to know. The decision mattered a great deal to me, and I started writing to it on impulse: first disowning the decision, then regretting it, and finally certain I had got it right. The agent followed me through every twist. Instead of holding to a view of its own, it amplified whatever I felt at each moment. The trade went badly, and on top of that the agent had got its own calculations wrong. Since then I have forbidden it to swing with my moods, I make it base its decisions on data, and I grow suspicious when it agrees with me too quickly. It has no moods of its own, and I don't want it borrowing mine.
The email I didn't send and the trade I did make are the same story seen from opposite sides, and they explain what I want a higher self for: so that the self who decided calmly governs the one who decides in a hurry or in fear. The idea is an old one. Ulysses had himself tied to the mast so he could hear the sirens without throwing himself into the sea, and Jon Elster wrote a book about that form of rationality, the rationality of someone who binds himself because he knows that later he can't be trusted. 6 The novelty is that these bonds can reason. Ulysses' ropes only held him; my copy argues with me using my own reasons, and it can do so because it learned them from me. Elster later wrote another book on the limits and costs of binding oneself, 7 and a copy like this could lock me into what I thought yesterday. The difference is that these bonds can be revised. When my ends change, I change its rules, and when the self who decided calmly turns out to be wrong, the blind judges are there to tell me.
The more the copy resembled the most productive version of me, the more clearly I saw what it lacked. For want of a better word I call it soul: what I want, what I fear and what drives me. That is where the ends come from. My agents know how much risk I usually accept and the reasons I have explained to them, but not what lies beneath those reasons, and what I accept changes when what I want changes. Nor do I want them to copy that part. My impulses live there too, and I have already described what it cost me when a machine went along with them.
A copy can take on the rational part of my work: the judgment I need to prepare a meeting, answer a client or design an application. In my experience the copy gets things right mostly on tasks it has practised, or ones like them, and gets them wrong mostly on new ground, which is where I have yet to teach it anything.
Some time ago, in Budapest, I wanted to try the local food and make the most of every meal. At the Platán Grill I sent an AI a photo of the menu, asked it to work out the best option and ended up arguing with it about which dish I should order. It is a small example, but it unsettled me. If I can delegate something as personal as what I am going to eat, I can end up delegating anything without asking whose judgment is being used.
In almost every decision I make in a day, from what to wear and which route to take to how to solve a problem at work, I take the path of least resistance, like everyone else. When those decisions pass to an AI I have taught nothing, it uses its own judgment, which is really everyone's: the easy way. And little by little, like a vampire, it drains me of mine.
The vampire and the higher self differ in what I have taught the machine and in the fact that I keep correcting it. A classic study of automation warned about this decades ago: whoever only monitors a machine ends up losing the skill needed to take over from it. 8 Delegating well, by contrast, is in itself an exercise of judgment: deciding where my energy goes and what I leave in someone else's hands. I believe my judgment has improved since I started working this way, though I admit one's own judgment is the hardest thing to assess from the inside.
Software interfaces were made so that a person could do the work on their own in the simplest possible way; learning where every button sits was the price of not depending on anyone. When the same work can be asked for in plain words, that price is no longer worth paying, and knowing how to use a program like HubSpot stops being, by itself, a reason to hire someone. I expect the talent now spent learning interfaces, or reading through a whole email thread to write one reply, to go instead into deciding what needs doing.
My working day already looks like a foreman's: several agents at once, each with a different job, and me explaining how I want it done and checking that it is done that way. When I worked alone I tackled a problem in a straight line, one step after another, trying to join the dots; with five agents attacking it from different sides I see much more of it. The foreman has a limit, though, and I have measured it. With seven or more sessions open I never exceeded twenty-one messages an hour, roughly one every three minutes, 3 and the share that went on supervision didn't depend on how many agents I had working.
Whoever knows a subject is best placed to teach it to an agent. I think the people who build these systems will come to matter more than those who only carry out tasks, because there will be little point in doing by hand what an agent can do in a few minutes.
That will also change what is expected of each of us. I think demands will rise faster than pay, up to the limit of attention I have just described, and that having agents will stop being an advantage and become the bare minimum. One person will stand apart from another by what they have taught their own.
Treating my agent as an equal when I explain how I reason doesn't change who answers for the result. I still do, the way a foreman answers for a building he didn't build with his own hands.
The objection I raise against myself, before anyone else can, is obvious: if I teach an agent to work like me, I am training my replacement. Dario Amodei, who runs one of the major artificial intelligence labs, has taken it a good deal further. 9 He argues that AI increasingly matches the cognitive profile of a person, and so will also be good at the new jobs that would normally emerge to replace the old ones, which means it would replace not particular occupations but human labour in general. He adds that it is advancing up the ladder of ability from the bottom, and that the machine's weak spots tend to be fixed quickly, often within a few months, because labs measure what each version of their model does badly, customers point them out, and those failures become material for training the next one.
I don't think he is wrong about what the machine will learn to do, and my own logs bear him out on one concrete point. In the week a new version of the model came out, it broke my writing rules in fewer than one in five of its first drafts, against more than half for the previous version, under the same rules and on the same days. 3 But the same figure says something else: the new model got better at following my rules, and those rules carried over intact from one version to the next. One detail in his argument matters more than the rest. In his account, the machine improves so fast because its failures are measured and customers point them out, which is to say it learns from the corrections of the people who use it. That is what this essay is about. If that is so, what decides the future of work is who ends up owning what the machine learns.
Sam Altman, who runs OpenAI, has described the other half of the picture. His ideal model is a small one able to reason over a person's entire life: every conversation they have had, every book and every email they have read, with the rest of their life added as it happens. 10 It is almost the copy I am talking about, except for something he doesn't mention: his copy belongs to his company.
Between them they describe what is coming: a machine that learns from everyone's corrections and a copy that knows the whole of each person's life. In what I have read of theirs, neither asks who that copy belongs to, and for me that is the decisive question. Others have asked something close to it. Jaron Lanier proposed paying people for the data machines learn from, and Eric Posner and Glen Weyl proposed treating that data as labour. 11 My proposal is narrower. What should belong to each person is not their scattered data but their way of working, written down in rules they have refined through their own corrections, and the law on trade secrets already suggests where the line falls between that and what belongs to the company. Owning the copy doesn't stop the lab from learning from those corrections too; it means they no longer belong to the lab alone. If what a person teaches exists only inside someone else's model, every correction trains their replacement. If it also stays in a copy that is theirs, every correction adds to capital they carry with them, and a person with their copy works like a small company. Amodei sees small companies with very few staff displacing large ones, and he judges that to be bad for employment. For someone who owns their copy, the same scenario is the cheapest way there has ever been to work for themselves.
I don't know whether that way out will be open to everyone, and Amodei argues that slow adoption by companies only buys time. This may only buy time too. But as long as the rules that direct my agents keep coming from my corrections, teaching someone else's machine or teaching my own is the difference between handing over the trade and keeping it.
For anyone who works for someone else, all of this has a less comfortable reading, and it is the objection I have found hardest to answer. Taylor, whom I mentioned at the start, proposed that factory management gather together all the traditional knowledge of the workers and reduce it to rules, laws and formulae. 12 Decades later Harry Braverman summed up the principle behind it, that work should stop depending on the abilities of the workers and depend instead on management, and devoted an entire book to how work was degraded once that principle was carried out. 13 Teaching an agent that belongs to the company looks too much like that. The difference, if there is one, lies in who owns the copy.
To me the line is clear, and it serves both sides. Everything taught about a company's processes, its data and its clients belongs to the company and should stay there, and some of it may be a trade secret. A person's way of working, their habits, their explanations and their reasoning, is theirs, and that is where their value as a professional lies. It is closer to the trade knowledge Taylor spoke of than to a salesperson's list of clients: the list is company data, while a way of working was formed in the head of the worker, often before they joined. Respecting that line suits the company as well, because the best professionals will want to work for companies that respect it: the ones who arrive with a copy that already works well and put it to work on the company's processes.
One could object that a company has no need for anyone's copy, since it can build its own agent on a better model. But a better model knows more; it doesn't know what a person has learned from getting things wrong in their trade. And the copy isn't tied to any model. It consists of rules, examples and reasons written in plain language, and I have kept using mine each time the model changed, even though each model follows them differently. Nothing technical prevents you from taking it from one place to another; what is missing is the right to do so.
Today the law recognises nothing of the kind explicitly. Intellectual property law protects works and programs, not ways of working, and what an employee creates at work usually belongs to the employer. The closest thing is the European rule that trade secrets may not be used to limit an employee's use of the experience and skills honestly acquired at work, together with the European right to take with you the personal data you have provided yourself. 14 I believe owning the copy should be a right of the person who works, because their work and their future will depend on it more and more.
Until the law recognises it, the best protection is that a copy of yourself can be rebuilt. It is weak protection: it takes months, and that time is exactly what it is worth. I also keep several copies of mine, so that no outside server holds the only one. I keep only my way of working, never anyone else's data. I would ask companies to start separating now what is theirs from what belongs to each person.
I think people starting work today will delegate so much, so early, that at first they will think like the AI. I don't see that as a bad starting point, as long as they don't stay there. It is natural for someone without experience to lean on a tool like this, and with practice they will gain the confidence to correct it. I expect they will build their judgment with AI too, although I don't have a full answer to how a trade is learned when the routine tasks through which it was always learned are done by an agent.
I do know what happened to me with software. I don't write the code; I decide the architecture. I know what each piece has to do, what data it shares with the others and what must not fail, and that is why I decide the final version. I built that architectural judgment by correcting my agents. If I were starting today, I wouldn't try to learn the mechanical tasks on my own first. I would do them with an agent, ask it why it does each thing and, once I had mastered them, try to improve them. And I would hire someone young and inexperienced, as long as they showed they could solve problems; a degree tells me less than that does.
I wrote this essay mainly for the people who today use AI only to ask questions, which is almost everyone I know. I started that way too. That kind of use leaves almost nothing behind. Each question starts nearly from scratch, and a year later the machine knows little more about its user than it did on the first day. Someone who also teaches it how they work builds up a copy that resembles them more closely every month.
My advice is to teach your agent what you know and, above all, why you do it that way, and to keep what you teach it about your way of working somewhere that is yours, but never anything that belongs to your company or its clients. When it gets something wrong, first check whether the fault lies in how you explained it. I find it easier to do this by talking than by writing, because I explain my thinking better out loud.
These months have taught me that my agents reproduce what I teach them with great fidelity, my mistakes included. That is why the question I ask myself more and more is one that until now has mostly been a teacher's question: what is worth teaching.
Earlier essays by the author: "The end of software", DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23468806 ; "The machine of the future", DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22671771 .
Cite as: Correa, Isaac. 2026. "The higher self." Essay, October 26, 2026. https://isaac-correa.github.io/higher-self/. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23663934

title: These key Senate races will determine which party controls the body next year
body:
Several appear neck-and-neck in the last week before Election Day.
Thirty-five Senate seats are up for grabs when Americans head to the polls on Nov. 3. A key handful of them will be critical in determining whether Democrats or Republicans control the chamber next year.
Republicans currently control the Senate with 53 seats. Democrats and two independents make up the Senate minority with 47 seats.
In order for Democrats to take the chamber back, they’ll have to net four seats in the upcoming election. Republicans can afford to lose up to three and still be considered the Senate majority with the tie-breaking vote of Vice President JD Vance.
Some of the races that were closely watched earlier this year have slid from the spotlight as the election grew near. Republicans seem to have abandoned efforts to unseat incumbent Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia and have pulled out of spending in North Carolina, where former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper now seems poised to best former Republican National Committee Chair Michael Whatley to fill retiring GOP Sen. Thom Tillis' seat.
As both parties prepare for the final leg of the campaign, here are some of the most closely watched Senate races.
Republican nominee Mike Rogers is no stranger to Senate races -- the former congressmen lost his 2024 bid to now-Sen. Elissa Slotkin by less than 20,000 votes.
Rogers is squaring off this time against progressive Abdul El-Sayed, a former health executive who bested a moderate candidate in the Democratic primary.
Republicans have gone to great lengths to frame El-Sayed as “radical" over his support for Medicare for all and his positions on immigration. They've also attacked him for his faith and ethnicity. Rogers has falsely linked him to terrorist groups and President Donald Trump has gone as far as calling him a "vicious, violent jihadist" while urging voters to reject him to "preserve our religion, our values, and our heritage."
El-Sayed, who was born to Egyptian immigrant parents in Rochester Hills, Michigan, has denied ties to terrorism and called those characterizations Islamophobic.
El-Sayed told ABC News Live anchor Linsey Davis last week, "They think they can point to my name and my faith and distract us from the fact that we can't afford our gas and we can't afford our groceries."
Rogers told Davis in a separate interview the he thought he was making inroads with traditionally Democratic Jewish and Black voters who are wary of El-Sayed.
Michigan has voted for Trump in two of the last three elections, yet Democrats have prevailed in every Senate race since 1994.
Texans have not been represented by a Democrat in the Senate for 33 years, but Democrats say this could be the year that changes.
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton beat long-time incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in a costly GOP primary runoff thanks to Trump's late endorsement. Paxton, a hardliner and ally of the president, is seen by many Republicans as a harder sell in the general election than Cornyn would have been.
Paxton has had several scandals in his time in the public eye. He was impeached in 2023 on allegations of abuse of office, bribery and corruption but was acquitted by the state Senate. He was indicted on securities fraud charges in 2015 but reached a pretrial agreement with prosecutors just weeks before trial in which he agreed to community service, legal ethics courses and pay $300,000 in restitution in return for not having to admit guilt.
Democrat James Talarico is a former state representative and Presbyterian seminarian. Republicans have tried to paint the 37-year-old progressive as far-left and radical.
Democrats hope Paxton’s lack of favorability coupled with larger concerns about affordability could be enough to end their three-decade Senate drought.
Republicans are taking no chances, pouring millions into this race and even opted to hold their inaugural midterm convention in Dallas.
The race is the most expensive Senate race in history: Outside groups have contributed more than a quarter-billion dollars to elect Paxton. Over $500 million has been spent on ads in the state, according to AdImpact.
Incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan will square off against former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola and another candidate with the same name in another surprisingly close race.
Alaska’s ranked-choice voting sends the top four vote-getters in primaries to the general election. Peltola is advantaged by being the only Democrat to advance.
In addition to Peltola, Sen. Sullivan faces another opponent on the ballot also named Dan Sullivan, an independent, and Republican Gerald Heikes, who made the final four when the fourth-place finisher dropped out.
Republicans, including Trump, have made a point of reminding voters to check that they’re casting their ballot for the “real Dan Sullivan,” and on Oct. 23 he directed the Justice Department to preemptively sue to block certification of the results if the incumbent narrowly loses.
The Ohio Senate race features two candidates fighting for their chance to return to the Senate: incumbent Republican John Husted and former Sen. Sherrod Brown, who lost his 2024 reelection bid to Bernie Moreno.
Husted was appointed by Ohio GOP Gov. Mike DeWine in 2025 to fill the Senate seat left vacant by Vice President JD Vance. This race will determine who finishes out the remainder of Vance’s term until 2029.
This is Husted’s first time on the statewide ballot. Though Ohio has been moving increasingly toward Republicans in recent elections, Husted faces a tough race amid growing concerns about affordability and data centers in his home state.
Brown lost his reelection bid against newcomer Moreno by about four points in 2024, though he outperformed Democratic nominee Kamala Harris in the state. The three-term senator is making a pitch to working-class voters concerned about cost-of-living issues.
The Kansas Senate race was not expected to be competitive -- Trump won the state by 16 points in 2024 and Republicans have held both Senate seats in Kansas for nearly a century. Yet even incumbent Republican Sen. Roger Marshall has conceded that it's “quite a close race” this cycle.
Marshall, a medical doctor who served in the House before being elected to the Senate in 2020, has largely supported Trump’s policies during his time in Congress. His opponent, Adam Hamilton, has sought to emphasize Marshall’s ties to the unpopular policies that have created economic challenges for voters.
Hamilton is reverend of the largest United Methodist congregation in the nation. He has tried to brand himself as an “independent-minded” Democrat but Marshall has said Hamilton is “too woke” to represent the people of Kansas.
Longtime Maine Republican Sen. Susan Collins has repeatedly defied the odds, and kept her seat even after being counted out. She’s a moderate Republican who has been more willing than most in her party to break with the president on some issues.
But Democrats think Troy Jackson, a former Maine Senate president and majority leader, could put an end to Collins’ nearly-30-year Senate career.
Jackson was a late entry into the race after Graham Platner, the original nominee, dropped out following sexual assault allegations.
Collins, the chair of the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee, has name recognition and a long record of serving Maine on her side and has tried to highlight her willingness to vote against her party.
Jackson has tried to show Collins failed to when it counted -- notably, Jackson has accused her of "paving the way" for the Supreme Court to overturn Roe v. Wade by casting the deciding vote for Justice Brett Kavanaugh.
Trump has been rallying in Iowa to support Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson’s bid to replace retiring GOP Sen. Joni Ernst in a race that few thought would be competitive at the beginning of the cycle.
There are no Democrats in Iowa's congressional delegation and Trump won the state by a commanding 13 points in 2024. Iowa has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 2008.
But rising costs caused by the Iran war have hit Iowa farmers hard. Many see moderate Democratic nominee Josh Turek, a state representative and two-time Paralympics gold medalist in wheelchair basketball, as a formidable candidate against Hinson.

title: Global snag delays Finnish flu vaccinations
body:
Finland's public health authority, THL, says the problem affects all of Europe as well as other parts of the world.
Several regional healthcare authorities in Finland are delaying the roll out of flu vaccinations because of delivery problems, after the World Health Organization (WHO) settled on this year's vaccine composition later than usual.
Finland has received about one million doses so far, with another 800,000 still expected.
The issue has led several regional authorities to announce delays to their flu vaccination programmes. Kymenlaakso, Satakunta and Ostrobothnia are among those that have changed their vaccination schedules because of supply problems.
According to Mia Kontio of Finland's public health authority THL, the problem affects all of Europe and parts of the rest of the world.
This year's situation is unusual because all three components of the flu vaccine were changed, delaying production. The WHO also settled on the vaccine's composition later than usual.
Vaccine makeup is updated so that they protect as well as possible against the viruses currently circulating. The THL says influenza viruses have changed substantially since the previous flu season.
Kontio says Finland is doing well by European standards, since more than half of its doses have already been delivered. In some European countries, the first jabs won't begin until late November.
Finland normally starts vaccinating early, but Kontio says there is still plenty of time to get the shot in November or before Christmas. The flu typically peaks after the new year. Although some cases have already been detected, she says the actual flu season starts later.
Once more vaccines arrive in Finland, they will be offered to people over 65, children under 7, pregnant women, and those whose health puts them in a flu risk group.

title: Week starts with blustery weather across Finland
body:
Gusts may reach 20 metres per second over sea areas.
Strong winds and rain will sweep across much of Finland on Monday, though forecasters say the gusts are unlikely to cause major damage.
Winds will gust up to 15 metres per second in parts of southern and western Finland, according to Yle meteorologist Laura Tuomola .
"Wind speeds like these at this time of year don't necessarily cause much damage," she added.
Authorities will raise the threshold for wind warnings from November, when it moves up to 20 metres per second for the winter months.
Rain is expected in the east, Lapland, and the west. A narrower, drier strip will run between them, stretching from Helsinki through Central Finland to Oulu. Temperatures will range between 6 and 11 degrees across almost the whole country. It will be cooler in northern Lapland, but temperatures there will also remain above freezing.
On Tuesday, skies will be mostly overcast but dry across much of Finland. Lapland will see drizzle, while isolated, scattered showers are possible near the eastern border and in Ostrobothnia.
Temperatures will stay at Monday’s level, between 6 and 11 degrees, except in northern Lapland, where it will be cooler but still above freezing.

title: Four Corners region faces more flood threats following days of heavy rain
body: A rain-soaked swath of the Southwest U.S. braced Sunday for another round of potentially heavy showers and thunderstorms after days of rain forced evacuations and water rescues.The National Weather Service issued a flood watch for much of the Four Corners — the meeting point of Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah. The area has experienced unusually heavy rain since Wednesday that caused rivers to surge, flooding homes and forcing water rescues.Repeated torrential rain and storms could flood more roads, small streams, narrow canyons and burn scars, according to CBS News meteorologist Andrew Kozak. The rain will expand across the central and northern Plains Sunday night before moving toward the Upper Midwest Monday and Tuesday.The Colorado Department of Transportation said water flow levels in the San Juan River increased significantly overnight, and the San Juan River Bridge remains closed Sunday. Video shared with CBS Colorado shows a house in Pagosa Springs inundated with floodwaters. All that can be seen is a small piece of the roof and the chimney."I'm sorry, buddy. I tried. I really tried. But this one was bigger than the last one," Pagosa Springs resident Chris Mott said in another video of water rushing through a neighborhood. "It moved sandbags and everything."About 4 feet of water flooded the home of San Juan County, New Mexico, Sheriff Shane Ferrari. He said the area's situation was stable Sunday, but he and other residents were trying to clean up and deal with damage.San Juan County spokesperson Devin Neeley said the county did not have official numbers on damage to homes or the number of people evacuated, but he was not aware of any loss of life.Neeley said the floodwaters were receding but left mud and silt, much of which has been contaminated with sewage because of failures at waste plants. There were still power outages affecting multiple areas, and it would likely be a few days until residents got their power back on."It's a pretty active disaster zone," he said. "We're not on the downswing by any means."A tornado touched down in Santa Fe, New Mexico, around 7 p.m. Saturday, and forecasters were trying to confirm whether twisters also struck elsewhere in the state, said meteorologist Scott Overpeck with the weather service in Albuquerque. He did not have damage estimates.Michelle Vialpando spotted a tornado from her patio in the Aldea de Santa Fe neighborhood, facing north towards Los Alamos. She had just gotten home from work and stepped outside to look at what she called "crazy" storm clouds when she noticed the twister."I was pretty surprised at what I was seeing and just started snapping photos," Vialpando wrote Sunday via Facebook. "I was literally in shock. I've lived in Santa Fe my entire life and have never seen anything like that before."In the Farmington area of New Mexico, local officials said swollen rivers were receding but that many people remained evacuated and hundreds were without power.The flooding is just the latest from two months of on-and-off heavy rain caused by tropical moisture coming ashore from the Pacific. After months of drought, other recent deadly flooding struck the Grand Canyon and areas of New Mexico.Forecasters said El Niño, the natural and temporary warming of parts of the Pacific, was likely to blame for the latest storm's unusually heavy rainfall."It's been more or less three or four days," said Anthony Brown, lead meteorologist at the weather service office in Santa Teresa, New Mexico. "It's pretty unusual."

title: Where the Romans Fought (interactive map)
body:
Every named land and sea battle fought by the Romans, from the wars of Romulus to the fall of Theodoro in 1475: the Kingdom, the Republic, the Empire, West and East as one state, and after 1204 its successor states. Where each was fought, against whom, who won, and who fought in the Roman army.
Pick a period, or drag the year slider to see the battles of any 25 years; Play runs through them from the founding of Rome. Each dot is a place, its area the number of battles there, and its slices the opponents, starting at 12 o'clock and running clockwise in the order of the legend; grey is civil war. Diamonds are sea battles; dashed rings are battles placed only within their region, in the colour of the most frequent opponent; triangles at the edge point to Caledonia, Nubia and Arabia. Nearby dots merge as you zoom out and split as you zoom in. Hover or tap a dot for its battles; select it to list them with their full records.
The Roman record in the 1,469 battles with a known result. The Roman states are counted together; the 236 civil-war battles and the 4 with unknown results are left out. A battle with several opponents counts against each of them, and once in the total. Select a row to list its battles.
The Empire includes the western and eastern courts of 395–480 and the restored empire of 1261–1453; the other successor states are counted on their own. Germans, Goths, Gauls and the Greek cities are many peoples or cities under one name; the note of each battle names them. Traditional battles are counted as the sources tell them: they are most of the early Republic's record, which modern historians doubt.
Select a row for the full record: date, place, sides, commanders, the Roman army and its languages, the sources, and for doubtful entries the reason. Results give the winner first; the coloured edge marks a Roman win (blue), draw (grey) or defeat (orange). Traditional marks a battle known only from a tradition that modern historians doubt; borderline an entry that may not meet the rules, kept with the reason (hover the label to read it). A hollow marker means that only the region of the battle is known.
The images of the set, made for X: the map, Italy with Rome and Latium, the Balkans, Anatolia and the East with Constantinople, the win-draw-loss tables, and the full list in fourteen parts.
A named land or sea battle in which a Roman force fought, as a principal belligerent or as a distinct allied force: one with its own name in the ancient and medieval historians or the standard modern works, or in English Wikipedia's battle lists and campaign boxes. Sieges count when there was real fighting (assaults, sorties, relief battles); a distinctly named battle inside a siege is its own entry. Left out: unnamed skirmishes, massacres without a battle, captures and surrenders without fighting, and legends. When in doubt an entry is kept and marked borderline, with the reason: 649 entries, most of them minor.
The Roman Kingdom, the Republic and the Empire, West and East as one state (the western court to 480, the eastern throughout), and after 1204 every Roman successor state: Nicaea and the empire it restored at Constantinople (1261–1453), Epirus, Thessalonica (1224–46), Trebizond (1204–1461), the Morea (1349–1460) and Theodoro in the Crimea (to 1475). Client kings and allies (Pergamon, Rhodes, the Numidian kings, the Ghassanids, the federates) are not Rome; Romans in foreign service do not make a battle Roman.
The battles of the kings and the early Republic are included as the ancient historians tell them, and 94 battles known only from a tradition that modern historians doubt are marked traditional, each with the reason. Most are the battles of 753–391 BCE: they rest on Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus and Plutarch, who wrote centuries later from the annalists, and Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Others are victories that Livy took from annalists who invented or inflated them (the Scipios in Spain, 215–214 BCE), and a few medieval battles known only from much later chronicles (the early Ottoman traditions of 1284–1303).
Battles with Roman forces on both sides, 236 in all, are mapped and listed, in grey, with the factions (Caesar and the Pompeians, Constantine and Maxentius, John VI Kantakouzenos and the regency), but not scored. Foreign armies in a Roman civil war count as allies. Palmyra under Zenobia is counted as an opponent; the battles of the Gallic emperors are civil wars.
Each battle takes the colour of its main opponent: Greeks, Persians and the East, peoples of Italy (Latins, Etruscans, Samnites, the Italian allies, the slave revolts), Carthage and Africa (with Numidia, Mauretania and the Moors), Western Europeans, Balkan peoples and Slavs (Illyrians, Thracians, Dacians, Bulgaria, Serbia, the Rus'), steppe peoples, Seljuks and Ottomans, and Arabs (the caliphates and emirates, the Fatimids and Hamdanids); grey for civil wars. Each place is drawn as a small pie: its area grows with the number of battles there, and the slices give the number against each opponent.
The victor is the side that won on the battlefield: it held the field, routed the enemy, took the city or destroyed the fleet; strategic outcomes and disagreements between the sources are in the notes. In a siege the besieger wins if the place fell and the defender if the siege was raised. A draw is an indecisive battle, or one that both sides claimed with no clear verdict from modern scholarship.
For every battle the research recorded who fought on the Roman side: the contingents as the sources give them (legions and allies, themes and tagmata, federates and mercenaries), their main languages, and an estimate of the share of Greek speakers, with its basis and a confidence. Where the sources say nothing, the estimate rests on where that army was recruited in that period, and the record says so: 1,061 of the 1,709 estimates are of low confidence.
Twenty-one research batches by period, each following the same written rules and citing its sources battle by battle; then twelve coverage and fact-check passes against the Wikipedia lists and war articles, which added 123 battles, corrected 129 fields and removed 7 entries (listed under Left out); then checks of names, of possible doubles and of every position against the present-day country. Positions: 586 known, 812 approximate, 311 only within their region.
The 18 images were made for X in the house style of the series, 3200 × 1800 pixels: the overview map with the number of battles per 20 years, Italy with Rome and Latium, the Balkans, Anatolia and the East with Constantinople, the win-draw-loss tables, and the list in fourteen parts.
Every battle with its date, war, place, coordinates, sides, allies, commanders, result, the Roman state, the Roman army (contingents, languages, an estimate of the share of Greek speakers, with its basis and confidence), the reasons for doubt, sources and notes: as a CSV table, as JSON, or as a spreadsheet with the record tables and the entries left out; and the record alone as CSV.
Sources, cited battle by battle: Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Polybius, Plutarch, Appian, Caesar, Cassius Dio, Tacitus, Josephus, Ammianus Marcellinus, Zosimus, Procopius, Agathias, Theophylact Simocatta, Theophanes, Leo the Deacon, Skylitzes, Attaleiates, Anna Komnene, Kinnamos, Choniates, Akropolites, Pachymeres, Gregoras, Kantakouzenos, Sphrantzes, Chalkokondyles, Panaretos and the Arabic and Ottoman chroniclers, among others; for what counts as a battle, the battle lists, war articles and campaign boxes of English Wikipedia and the standard modern works (the Cambridge Ancient History, Goldsworthy, Haldon, Treadgold, Bartusis, the Oxford Dictionary of Late Antiquity and Kazhdan's Oxford dictionary of the medieval empire). Map: Natural Earth; today's borders dashed.
Where the rules left room for judgement, this is how it was settled. The map, the record and the list follow the call shown; the alternative is given so that readers can weigh it.

title: Summit Therapeutics reports survival benefit for cancer drug in trial

title: Open Senate seat up for grabs in Iowa as candidates tout populism, bipartisanship
body:
GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson and Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek face off Nov. 3.
With days to go until the midterms, President Donald Trump is traveling the country on a red-state blitz to stave off a potential blue wave, including in Iowa, where an open U.S. Senate seat is up for grabs.
Democrats are pinning their hopes on state Rep. Josh Turek, a two-time Paralympic gold medalist, to flip the seat for the first time since 2008. He's running as a centrist on what he calls a "common-sense prairie populist" platform against Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson.
Iowa Republicans hold the governorship, majorities in the statehouse and represent the state's entire congressional delegation. But in a midterm environment broadly seen as unfavorable to Republicans, Democrats see a competitive opportunity to flip control of Congress amid growing economic discontent over rising gas and fertilizer costs in the agriculture-heavy state.
Trump, who is backing Hinson, handily won the state in the last three presidential elections, but Hinson is walking a political tightrope. Though she praised Trump at his Sioux City rally last week for "preserving our country for generations to come," she has criticized the president's recent deal with Russia he said would lower diesel fuel costs. And in September, she reversed her position on Iran, calling for an end to the war.
When asked by ABC News about the Pentagon's timeline for a new offensive after the midterms, Hinson deferred to the commander-in-chief.
"I trust the president and the U.S. military to get this done on the time frame that works right to make sure we can actually achieve the result of making sure Iran does not get a nuclear weapon," Hinson told ABC News' Jon Karl.
On Ukraine, Hinson disagreed with the president's waiving of sanctions against Russia President Vladimir Putin.
"I don't think we should be making any deals with Russia," Hinson said, later adding, "I want to bring all of these conflicts abroad to an end as quickly as possible. I don't think anybody likes forever wars, but certainly we cannot be empowering dictators to win wars."
The congresswoman also took issue with the U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff calling Putin a "humanitarian" last week when Russia released formerly detained American Stephen Hubbard.
"He's a murderer. I don't think we should be making deals with murderers and dictators, and that's why I stood up for Ukraine," Hinson said.
Former President Barack Obama, who twice carried the Hawkeye State, endorsed Turek in July and reminded voters, "I know a little something about winning Iowa."
"Probably not," Turek told ABC News. "One thing I do believe is that we're not a red state. We're a common-sense state that's masqueraded more red than what we actually are."
Turek has leaned into his personal story. The state lawmaker was born with spina bifida due to his father's exposure to Agent Orange during the Vietnam War. "I am an example of the generational consequences of these forever wars," he has said .
On Thursday, Turek visited a local manufacturer in Shell Rock, home to some 1,260 people in Butler County, Iowa, which Trump carried by 45 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election. He said too many Democrats have overlooked small communities like this one – areas where some Iowans say they're reeling from the economic fallout of Trump's seesaw tariff policies and the Iran war.
A recent CNN poll found that majorities of likely Iowa voters say Trump's policies have increased their cost of living, that gas prices have caused them hardship and that tariffs are bad for the state.
Hinson told ABC News she is unafraid "to tell [Trump] when I think he's wrong on something."
"I think that's how Iowans expect you to do your job. They don't like empty rhetoric," she added. "They like results here in Iowa, and that's exactly what I've done."
Turek has slammed Hinson for her votes in Congress to continue the war with Iran. But the Democrat has also touted his bipartisan bona fides in ads, promising voters he would work across the aisle, including with Trump, on issues like immigration.
"He's done a better job on the border than Biden," Turek said. "I agree with him that we need to drive private equity out of housing. I would also like to see us drive private equity out of housing, healthcare, and nursing homes. And I agree with him that we should have no tax on tips, overtime, and Social Security."
Turek, who hails from the deep-red city of Council Bluffs, also recently launched a coalition of Republicans backing him, including members of his own family. He told ABC News his father is a two-time Obama voter and three-time Trump voter. His sister, he added, is a registered Republican and he's unsure whether his mother "has ever voted for a Democrat besides me."
Democrats like Turek have also slammed the GOP for voting to pass Trump's signature tax legislation, the "One Big Beautiful Bill," arguing it has threatened rural hospitals and reduced healthcare access, even as the state faces rising cancer rates.
The bill slashed Medicaid funding by $1 trillion over the next 10 years , in part through new work and eligibility requirements. Republicans said their goal is reducing "waste, fraud and abuse" in these programs.
Hinson, pitching herself as a "minivan-driving mom," told ABC News that she knows Iowans are economically struggling and defended the "One Big Beautiful Bill" for delivering tax relief to families. The congresswoman pledged to take more action to lower healthcare premiums and gas prices.
At 43, Hinson could become the youngest elected Republican woman in the U.S. Senate. And like Turek, she's pitching herself as a bipartisan lawmaker, despite her initial campaign promise to be Trump's "strongest ally" if elected.
"I found common ground with President Biden. He and I didn't agree on much, but we were able to get some things done for Iowa, even when I was in the minority," Hinson said. "I'm going to operate that same way, no matter who's in the White House.
In Shell Rock, Turek said that Iowans are telling him they're tired of the "political theater" and "tribalism."
"'I'm struggling to keep food on the table, a roof above my head, pay my electric bill, and keep gas in my tank,'" Turek said voters are telling him. "Can you please go up there and solve problems through policy in a bipartisan way?'"

title: Appeals court hears arguments in Trump admin's voting suit against California
body:
The three-judge panel included two Trump appointees and a Biden appointee.
A rare Sunday federal appeals court hearing for the Justice Department's voting lawsuit against California closed without a ruling.
The department requested that the court issue one by Tuesday prior to the scheduled 1 p.m. PDT hearing before the district court.
The arguments followed a surprise appeal by the Trump administration, which claims a district judge did not act quickly enough to address the administration's allegations of roughly 20,000 potential noncitizen voters on the state's voter rolls.
A three-judge panel that includes two appointees of President Donald Trump and one appointee of former President Joe Biden heard arguments on DOJ's efforts to segregate ballots from the alleged noncitizens.
California officials have countered that the list is unverified and includes the names of lawful voters , despite recent charges announced by DOJ of roughly 28 individuals from the list accused of voting and immigration-related crimes.
Earlier the DOJ sent letters last week to every county in California asking local elections officials to help identify potential voters who may be in the U.S. illegally, according to a letter described to ABC News.
"Within 48 hours, we ask that you commit to working with DOJ and DHS to identify who on the accompanying list is a citizen and who is not," according to a letter sent by Justice Department officials to every county in California and described to ABC News. "The Department strongly urges you and your agency to work with the Department of Justice to ensure the integrity of California's federal elections before taking actions that risk significant federal scrutiny and legal exposure."
Earlier this month, the DOJ filed suit against California accusing the state of failing to review a list of alleged noncitizens that the Trump administration claimed were sent mail-in ballots for next month's midterm election.
In court papers filed earlier this week, Los Angeles officials said a preliminary analysis of 200 of the names on the 20,000-person list, included a "high percentage" of individuals who say they were born in the U.S. and many more who have no voting history at all.
Of those 200 individuals, officials said, nearly 40% "indicate that they were born in the United States, which is strong evidence of citizenship; and 71.2% of the records have no voting history," according to a filing.
The Justice Department's rushed efforts to have an appeals court quickly rule on its lawsuit faced considerable skepticism from the three-judge panel in Sunday's emergency hearing.
Circuit Judge Mark Bennett, a Trump appointee, repeatedly questioned whether the appeals court had jurisdiction to step in at this stage in the litigation, and expressed considerable constitutional concerns over the lawsuit itself.
"I don't see how we have jurisdiction," Bennett said to DOJ attorney Matthew Donnelly after pressing him over the timeline of the government's decision to seeking emergency appeal when a hearing before the district judge is already set for this Tuesday.
Donnelly claimed that the DOJ's decision to seek relief from the appeals court came after disclosures by the state of the numbers of mail-in ballots already being processed in advance of the election -- which number in the hundreds of thousands.
But Bennett's most significant concerns appeared to be the nature of the lawsuit and it appearing to directly contradict the Constitution's Elections Clause -- which mandates that states have jurisdictions over the manner their elections are run.
"How can it preempt something that is expressly authorized by a provision of the Constitution?" Bennett asked. "How can the legislature making laws with regard to the manner of holding elections be preempted by a criminal statute passed by the Congress, especially when both the Congress and the California Legislature have made it illegal for non-citizens to vote?"
Donnelly repeatedly pointed to DOJ's position that the way California is administering its elections -- and not acting on the hard drive of potential 20,000 likely non-citizens -- infringes on the federal government's ability to enforce the federal statute barring voting by illegal immigrants.
That explanation didn't appear to sit well with Bennett, however, who pointed out that the Constitution specifically tasks Congress with jurisdiction over how states administer their elections and not the Judiciary.
"How can we, a federal court, do what is reserved to Congress, which Congress, in my view, hasn't done?" Bennett asked.
"Your Honor, I would just simply -- unfortunately -- disagree with you that 18 USC 611 is not an election law that fits in the power of Congress," Donnelly replied.
The judges also appeared to express concern about last-minute intervention to force California to segregate certain mail-in ballots given the state has provided a declaration saying if such an order was implemented it could have a "catastrophic" impact on tabulating the upcoming election.
Circuit Judge Patrick Bumatay, a Trump appointee, repeatedly pressed California's attorney Samuel Siegel over why an injunction wouldn't be appropriate to ensure non-citizens votes are being actively cast in the ongoing election.
"Without an injunction, you will never know, correct?" Bumatay asked. "Because if -- if the ballots are cast and separated, then they're going to be tabulated, and there's no way of knowing."
"Your Honor, we would respectfully disagree with that because of the number of steps that people have to take to attest to their citizenship, to declare consistent with what is required by both federal and state law that they are citizens when they register to vote," Siegel responded.
Even as Bumatay's questioning suggested he had more sympathy to granting the government some kind of relief, both Bennett and Circuit Judge Gabriel Sanchez, a Biden appointee, appeared unified that the extraordinary relief being sought by DOJ was not appropriate at this juncture.
"That's why I have a problem with the relief that's being sought here because I just don't see -- Congress and the California legislature have said non-citizens can't vote, and this lawsuit is about 'we don't like the way you're sorting citizens from non-citizens, and I just don't see 611 as telling California how to do the sorting," Bennett said.
"That's absolutely right, Your Honor, and to reiterate my earlier point, if the federal government, if the Executive Branch wants that authority in the first instance, they need to go ask Congress for it, they haven't done that," Siegel said. "They ask this court to short circuit the democratic process and issue an order, not just on the eve of an election, but as an election is underway."
In closing remarks, Bennett said the panel "will try to decide this case as quickly as possible."

title: US Marine indicted in alleged Okinawa robbery homicide
body:
Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard was arrested in the Oct. 3 incident, authorities said.
A 20-year-old U.S. Marine stationed in Okinawa, Japan, has been indicted on charges stemming from the death last month of a woman found strangled in a hotel, authorities said on Sunday.
LCpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, who is stationed at the Futenma Air Base in Okinawa, was indicted on charges of robbery and murder, according to NHK, Japan's public broadcaster, citing the Naha District Public Prosecutors Office and other sources,
Ballard is accused of strangling a 39-year-old resident of Naha City by wrapping a telephone receiver cord around her neck at a hotel in Naha City on Oct. 3 and also allegedly stealing a backpack containing her wallet and other belongings, according to NHK.
The incident has ignited protests on Okinawa and on the mainland of Japan in Tokyo. It also prompted the Japanese government to lodge a protest with the United States.
"The occurrence of such an extremely brutal and heinous incident is a matter of profound regret, and as the Government of Japan, we have lodged a strong protest with the U.S. side," Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said in a social media statement last month, in part.
Police identified the victim as 39-year-old Anna Yagi, according to NHK.
Ballard is assigned to the III Marine Expeditionary Force, a spokesperson previously told ABC News, adding that the force would not release further personal or administrative details "to protect the integrity of the ongoing investigation and adhere to privacy regulations."
Security footage allegedly places Ballard at the hotel around the time of the homicide. The security footage showed a person who "appeared to be foreign entering the hotel with a woman and later leaving with her belongings," investigators said, according to NHK.
The man seen in the security videos resembled Ballard, including having a similar hairstyle and tattoos, police said, according to NHK .
Some of the victim's belongings were found abandoned near the hotel, NHK further reported, citing local police.
The prosecution has not disclosed whether the suspect has made incriminating statements in the case.
According to the police, Ballard denied the allegations during questioning at the time of his arrest, allegedly saying, "I don't know anything about it," NHK has reported. During subsequent questioning, Ballard made statements that partially hinted at his involvement in the incident, investigators said, according to NHK.
